investigations/2608-lakewood-council/rec.title: Philip Michael Lindholm — Person-Level Profile
investigations/2608-lakewood-council/rec.content:
Philip Michael Lindholm — Person-Level Profile

Working draft. Not for publication. This is a person-level dossier, not a story. Every assertion is graded. Only V (verified) and C (corroborated) assertions may enter copy. S (self-reported/single-source), I (inference), and U (unverified/open) items are reporting leads, not facts. The subject has not been sent the expanded right-of-reply letter; publication is blocked until that happens and the reply window closes.

0. Source key and grade definitions



































TagMeaningPublication ruleVVerified: two independent primary anchors, or a primary document plus a corroborating person/recordMay publishCCorroborated: one primary source matched by an independent secondary sourceMay publish with attributionSSelf-reported or single-source: the subject’s own bio, campaign filing, social media, or one outletAttribute; do not present as independently establishedIInference: a logical reading of verified facts, explicitly labeledMay publish only as a labeled inference, never as factUUnverified/open: a lead, a claim not yet checked, or a negative that cannot be provenDo not publish as fact; report as open
Source IDs refer to the case evidence log (evidence-log.md, E047–E061) and the new profile evidence series (E062–E078) listed in §13. Where a claim is new and not yet in the log, the source URL is given inline.

1. Snapshot

Philip Michael Lindholm, born December 10 (year not public), Seattle, Washington. [V for name/birth date: Wikipedia/DBpedia; official bio. Year is not public.]
Lakewood City Council, Position 3. Elected November 2025; took office January 2026; term expires December 31, 2029. The council is part-time and nonpartisan; the mayor is chosen by the council. [V: city council page; Pierce County voters pamphlet.]
Oxford-trained scholar. DPhil from Oxford (2010) after three master’s degrees (Judaism, Christianity, Islam); master’s from Middlesex; two bachelor’s degrees from Central Washington; AA from Green River; additional study at L’École Normale Supérieure (Paris, 2005) and Juilliard (2007); Rhodes Scholar finalist. [C: official bio, Wikipedia, Amazon author bio; no university registrar record pulled. The DPhil thesis title is not verified.]
Law student, not (yet) an attorney. The official 2025 voters pamphlet lists “Seattle University School of Law (JD in progress)” and “University of Washington Tacoma (BA in progress).” His X bio says “Law Student.” The Puyallup Tribal Court lists him as an Advocate, not an Attorney. [V for the pamphlet text and the court listing; S for the pamphlet’s self-reported education; no registrar confirmation.]
Media maker. Former BBC/ITV documentary producer and presenter; author of Latter-day Dissent (2011) and Voyeur: Notes of Disquiet (2011); singer-songwriter behind Whiskey N’ Rye (formed 2013); TEDx speaker (2019); host of The Informed Citizen podcast, whose YouTube channel reports 117K subscribers, 377 videos, 1.5M views (joined 2011). [C/V: official bio, Wikipedia, AllMusic, YouTube page.]
Air Force chaplain. Captain and chaplain, U.S. Air Force / Washington Air National Guard, 194th Wing, Camp Murray; began as Wing Chaplain in January 2017; hospital chaplain at CHI Franciscan/MultiCare; board-certified chaplain (NAVAC 2019; APC per author bio); Mary Bridge grief-group facilitator for eight years. [V for the 194th Wing chaplain role: DVIDS, Jan. 29, 2017; C for rank/certifications: official bio, Amazon bio.]
Real estate broker and landlord. Licensed Washington real estate broker since 2011; former CEO of Terry Wise & Associates; HomeLight’s agent profile lists him at Terry Wise & Associates (16 years, 50 transactions, $354K average, 44 single-family homes, 3.7/5 on three reviews). His 2025 F-1 reports 84% of 8814-8815 Lochburn Lane SW Lakewood LLC, 100% of Wyoming Housing Holding Company, and 100% of Washington Ventures Management, plus seven properties. [C: LinkedIn/HomeLight/official bio; V: F-1.]
Mediator and tribal-court advocate. Founder/CEO of Concord Counsel (mediation, tribal law, community relations); listed on the Puyallup Tribal Court Courtesy Bar List as Advocate, Bar No. 585 (Jan. 6, 2026); claims admission in Puyallup, Swinomish, and Makah tribal courts. [V for Puyallup; S/U for Swinomish and Makah.]
Local media co-founder. Co-founder of The Cascadian, a 501(c)(3) community news outlet in Lakewood, with former councilmember Walter Neary; the outlet’s mailing address is the same PO Box as Lindholm’s campaign; it publishes his columns. [V: The Cascadian About page; The Seattle Times; ProPublica IRS record.]
Live civil litigation. Defendant in Jacob Lawrence v. Philip Lindholm, Pierce County Superior Court No. 26-2-08192-7, docketed as a Consumer Protection Act case, filed April 29, 2026; 62-page complaint; jury demand; trial set April 28, 2027. The complaint has not been obtained; no allegation is characterized here. [V for the docket; U for the allegations.]
Clean criminal/tax index (as searched). The Pierce County LINX public index returned no Superior Court criminal cases, no District Court criminal cases, no tax warrant/judgment cases, and no District Court civil cases for “Lindholm, Philip” between 2010 and 2026. The index expressly disclaims accuracy and cannot associate names to individuals without case research; this is a search result, not a clearance. [V for the search result; caveat required.]
The core tension. The public persona is scholar, chaplain, mediator, and public servant. The private footprint is broker, landlord, media producer, and founder of a local news outlet. The investigative question is not whether those roles are legal — most are ordinary — but whether the disclosure and recusal regime makes the intersections visible to the public. The strongest documented intersection is the Terry Wise cluster: former employer, campaign donor, podcast production partner, and the consultant for the Solberg property whose abatement contract Lindholm abstained on.


2. Identity and biography
2.1 Core identity




























































FieldValueGrade / sourceFull namePhilip Michael LindholmV: Wikipedia/DBpedia; official bioBornDecember 10; year not public; Seattle, WAV (date/place); U (year)Current officeLakewood City Council, Position 3; took office 2026; term to 12/31/2029V: city pagePartyNonpartisan officeV: city pageCampaign committeeCommunity for Philip Lindholm, PO Box 39192, Lakewood, WA 98496V: campaign site; PDCOfficial contactPLindholm@cityoflakewood.us; City Hall (253) 983-7705; cell (253) 401-6825V: city pageCampaign contactmail@votephilip.com; (253) 234-4686; votephilip.comV: voters pamphletFamily roles (public)Son; father of a son (he refers to “my son” in the kickoff speech); no spouse information publicS: kickoff transcript; voters pamphlet (“son, father”)Public mailing addressPO Box 39192, Lakewood, WA 98496V: campaign, Chamber, Cascadian, tribal bar listTribal bar listing5409 100th St SW, Box 39192, Lakewood, WA 98499; 206-659-5960; Advocate Bar No. 585V: Puyallup Tribal Court list, 1/6/2026
Identity match — what the record shows. The councilmember and the Oxford-educated Kierkegaard scholar/chaplain are the same person on the documentary record, but the photographic comparison is not clean. The chain is:

The official campaign site philiplindholm.com is the same domain as the academic’s pre-campaign personal site. The 2013 captures describe “Dr. Lindholm” as a musician, author, and entrepreneur with three master’s degrees and an Oxford doctorate, and list him as “principal consultant and broker with The Lindholm Group… associate of Terry Wise & Associates.” A later “Consulting” page on the same site says he was “CEO at Terry Wise & Associates.” The council bio says he became “CEO of a real estate brokerage and consulting firm”; HomeLight lists him at Terry Wise & Associates. [V: Wayback captures, 2013 and 2025; E079.]
The DVIDS article (2017) names “Rev. Dr. Philip Lindholm” as the incoming 194th Wing chaplain and gives his early life — Seattle, Decatur High School in Federal Way, Green River Running Start, Central Washington, Oxford, three master’s degrees, CHI Franciscan chaplaincy — plus his wife Lori and son Declan. The city bio, voters pamphlet, Chamber bio, and campaign site repeat the same early life and military/chaplain history. [V: DVIDS; E064.]
The Wikipedia page (Q7183978) is the academic’s biography: same Green River/Central Washington/Oxford/Juilliard/BBC/ITV/Whiskey N’ Rye history. Its 2019 photo is captioned “Dr. Philip Lindholm addressing an audience of Air Force members at Camp Murray.” The page does not mention Lakewood or the council, which is the main reason to pause. [V: Wikipedia; E080.]
The Puyallup Tribal Court list uses the same PO Box as the campaign (39192, Lakewood) and lists him as an Advocate, Bar No. 585. [V: E063.]
Family-name corroboration: a Lori Lindholm, LICSW practices in Lakewood (NPI 1336872043); a Declan Lindholm maintains a public racing blog/Instagram; the councilmember’s Facebook page includes a post from Makah tribal court referring to “my son and his father,” and a post referring to “my wife.” The 2017 DVIDS article names the chaplain’s wife Lori and son Declan. This is consistent with one household, though it is not a single document that names all three together. [C: public profiles/posts; E081/E083.]
The photo caveat. The 2017 DVIDS and 2019 Wikipedia photos show a leaner man with darker hair and a longer, narrower face; the 2025/2026 council and Facebook photos show a fuller face with lighter hair. The difference could be nine years of aging, weight, lighting, and professional retouching — or it could be two different men. I cannot resolve it by eye. A facial-recognition comparison or a direct family/vital record would settle it. Until then, the identity match rests on the documentary convergence, not on the photographs. [V documentary; U photographic.]

Bottom line: the documentary record is strong — same domain, same Oxford/film/music biography, same Terry Wise & Associates history, same 194th Wing chaplaincy, same wife/son names, same PO Box. The main weak link is the visual comparison; a second open question is the F-1’s military pension timeline, which is hard to square with a 2016 accession unless there was prior service or household income. If a specific record shows a different Philip Lindholm (a birth year, a marriage record, a second DVIDS profile), the match should be re-opened. [V/C; photo U.]
The theology-to-real-estate question. The transition looks implausible if you assume a linear academic career. The record shows a portfolio career instead. The 2013 capture of philiplindholm.com/about — the subject’s own pre-campaign site — lists the Oxford doctorate, three master’s degrees, BBC/ITV film work, Whiskey N’ Rye, and “principal consultant and broker with The Lindholm Group… associate of Terry Wise & Associates” on the same page. It also lists Stage 1 Studio & Rehearsal, University Place Press, Oxford Tutoring Services, and 24/30 Cinema. The real estate work was one strand of an entrepreneurial career, not a replacement for the academic work. The 2011 license, the 2013 site, the 2025 consulting page (“CEO at Terry Wise & Associates”), HomeLight, and the F-1 all show a long-standing real estate/business practice; the 2016 chaplaincy and 2025 council campaign came later. This does not resolve the identity question, but it removes the “impossible career arc” objection. [V: E079; I: interpretation.]
2.2 Early life and education

Seattle native; left high school at 17. He began at Green River Community College at 17, earned an AA, then went to Central Washington University, where he is described as graduating with high honors and two bachelor’s degrees. [S: official bio, Wikipedia, Amazon. No transcript.]
Rhodes Scholar finalist. Repeated in the official bio, voters pamphlet, Amazon bio, and Wikipedia. [S: no Rhodes Trust confirmation pulled. Flag for verification before publication.]
Oxford. Doctorate and two master’s degrees at Oxford; the doctorate is described as a DPhil in philosophical theology (2010), with separate master’s degrees in Judaism, Christianity, and Islam; doctoral advisor George Pattison. [C: official bio + Wikipedia + Amazon. The Oxford thesis title is not verified in ORA by this search; flag.]
Other study. Master’s from Middlesex University; study at L’École Normale Supérieure in Paris (2005); Juilliard (2007); currently listed as JD in progress at Seattle University School of Law and BA in progress at University of Washington Tacoma in the 2025 voters pamphlet. [S: official bio/Wikipedia for Paris/Juilliard; V for the pamphlet text, but the pamphlet is candidate-supplied and the county does not verify it.]
The education portfolio is unusual and relevant to the profile: a doctorate and three master’s degrees, two bachelor’s degrees, a law degree in progress, and a second BA in progress — all while serving on the council, running a mediation practice, and owning rental property. This is not a scandal; it is a workload and role-density fact that bears on capacity and on the “polymath” public identity. [I: inference from the schedule; label as analysis.]

2.3 Academic and literary career

Kierkegaard and philosophy of religion. Described as a Kierkegaard scholar and former lecturer in comparative religion at the University of Washington and Oxford. [C: Wikipedia + official bio.]
Books. 2.7 Public persona vs. private footprint — analysis, labeled
The public biography is a coherent “servant-leader” narrative: a Seattle kid who left high school early, won a Rhodes finalist slot, studied at Oxford, made documentaries, served as a chaplain, buried patients, comforted grieving families, and came home to serve. It is authentic in its broad outlines and unusually well documented for a local councilmember.
The private footprint is more layered: a licensed broker who was CEO of a brokerage; a landlord with an 84% stake in an apartment complex listed as 18 units; a mediator whose practice includes tribal-court real estate and family law; a media producer with a 117K-subscriber podcast; and a co-founder of a local news outlet. The investigative question is role density and disclosure: when the same person is the broker, the landlord, the mediator, the media owner, and the councilmember, the public cannot easily see which hat is on at any given vote. [I: analytical frame; not a finding of wrongdoing.]

10. Story angles and systemic frame
10.1 The interlocking-roles story
A part-time councilmember is also a broker, landlord, mediator, tribal-court advocate, podcast host, and co-founder of a local news outlet. Each role is lawful. Together they create a disclosure problem: the public sees the official, not the portfolio. The story is about how a small city’s ethics regime handles a person whose private roles touch nearly every policy area he votes on. [I: frame]
10.2 The Terry Wise cluster
The strongest documented conflict story. The same former employer/donor/podcast partner represented the client whose abatement contract Lindholm abstained on. The abstention was correct; the statement “I do not have a professional relationship” is the loose thread. The F-1’s consulting payment and the podcast production credit give the statement a factual context the public did not hear at the meeting. [V links; I frame]
10.3 The media-ownership story
A councilmember co-founded a local news outlet, shares its PO Box with his campaign, and writes columns for it. The outlet has experienced editors and discloses the co-founder role; it may be a genuine civic-media experiment. The accountability questions are editorial firewall, board independence, and whether readers are told when the outlet covers him. This is a “how local news is reinvented — and who owns it” story. [V facts; I frame]
10.4 The rental-housing votes
Ordinance 849 added self-certification and an ADU exemption. Lindholm, an 84% owner of an apartment complex listed as 18 units, seconded the ADU amendment, voted to keep self-certification, and described “personal experience with the rental safety program.” No disclosure appears in the minutes/video. The story is whether a landlord-legislator should recuse or disclose on general rental-housing policy — a question that goes beyond one person. [V facts; I frame]
10.5 The lawsuit
A pending Consumer Protection Act case is a live accountability fact. If the complaint alleges misrepresentation in a loan or real estate transaction, it could be the strongest story in the file. Until the complaint is obtained, the dossier should say only that the case exists, the parties, the case type, and the trial date. [V docket; U complaint]
10.6 The credentials question
“Advocate” vs. “attorney”; “JD in progress”; “Rhodes finalist”; “Oxford doctorate”; “Air Force captain.” Most of the portfolio is documented; some of the superlatives are self-reported. The story is not “fake credentials” — it is how public bios accumulate unverified superlatives and how voters hear them. The campaign’s “barred in three tribal courts” is accurate as far as Puyallup is concerned; the other two are unverified. [V/I]
10.7 The systemic frame — how the world works
Lakewood is a part-time, nonpartisan council-manager city. Its ethics code (LMC 1.32) relies on self-disclosure and recusal; the case file found no independent ethics board. The city attorney and city manager report to the council. In that structure, a councilmember’s private network — employer, donors, clients, media partners — is not systematically visible. The case file’s peer comparison found Lakewood’s dual-government employment rate (5 of 7, 71%) far above the peer range (0–29%, median 14%), while 4 of 5 peer cities also lack an ethics board. The systemic point: Lakewood’s ethics infrastructure is typical in its weakness, but its role density is an outlier. Re-verify the peer comparison before publication. [C: case file; I: frame]

Existing evidence

E047–E061: PDC F-1s, ATIP parcel records, council packets/minutes, YouTube transcripts, PDC contribution data, PDC F-1 instructions. See evidence-log.md.
E043: city ethics code / peer comparison (case file).
E051–E058: Ordinance 849 and Solberg records.


14. One-paragraph summary for the desk
Philip Lindholm is not a simple small-city councilmember. He is an Oxford-trained Kierkegaard scholar, a former BBC/ITV documentary producer, an Air Force chaplain, a licensed real estate broker, an 84% owner of a Lakewood apartment complex listed as 18 units, a tribal-court advocate, a 117K-subscriber podcaster, and the co-founder of a new local news outlet that shares his campaign PO Box. Most of that portfolio is lawful and some of it is genuinely impressive. The accountability issue is role density and disclosure: the same person votes on rental-housing policy, abstains on an abatement contract involving his former employer’s client, and runs a media platform produced in partnership with that employer’s company. The public record shows a partial disclosure at the April 6 meeting, no disclosure at the May 4 rental-housing vote, and a pending Consumer Protection Act lawsuit filed by a Jacob Lawrence — the same name that appears on Lindholm’s F-1 as a private note debtor; the identity link is unconfirmed. The story is not “crooked politician”; it is “how a part-time, nonpartisan city with no independent ethics board lets a very connected person’s multiple roles blur — and what the public is entitled to know.” The next move is the complaint in Lawrence v. Lindholm, the PDC imaged F-1, and the expanded right-of-reply letter. [V facts; I frame]

investigations/2608-lakewood-council/rec.content:
Red-Team Audit — Lindholm Deep Dive
Question: Assume every finding is wrong. What can be disproved, what is merely unverified, and what survives?
Date: 2026-11-12
Method: Re-read the primary records and attacked the ownership chain, vote attribution, donor classification, F-1 field semantics, and the minutes/video comparison. No new interviews. Every downgrade is recorded here and in verification-matrix.md.

Bottom line
The core survives in narrowed form. Three claims collapse, six weaken, and the rest hold. The story is still publishable, but not in the version first written. The defensible version is:

A Lakewood councilmember who owns an 18-unit apartment complex through an LLC did not disclose it in the public record before voting on the city’s rental-housing rules. A month earlier, he told the council he had no professional relationship with a land-use consultant whose firm appears on his own financial disclosure as a business customer — after abstaining on a contract involving the consultant’s client.

That is narrower than “the landlord voted for the rental rules while being paid by the consultant.” It does not claim a crime, a quid pro quo, or a specific final-vote aye that the record does not individualize.

COLLAPSED
C1. “At least $10,200 of Lindholm’s campaign came from real estate, development, and landlord interests.”
Why it collapses: Two of the largest components are not verified as real estate money.

Stonegate Associates LLC ($2,000): The name matches a New Jersey security-consulting firm. The Lakewood apartment complex called Stonegate Apartments is managed by Dobler Management Company, not by a “Stonegate Associates LLC.” The campaign-finance report itself labeled the donor “Real estate/property management?” with a question mark. There is no evidence the donor is a real estate entity.
Capital Ventures ($2,400) and McKinley Sands ($2,400): Sands McKinley is a family-law attorney, founder of McKinley Irvin. “Capital Ventures” appears in his LinkedIn as a venture, but no source establishes it as a real estate developer. The employer field says “Capital Ventures / owner,” not “developer.”
The verified real estate/landlord/construction floor is $6,300: Terry Wise $2,400 + Landlord Solutions $1,200 + Master Builders Association of Pierce County $1,200 + Washington Association of Realtors PAC $500 + Rémy Claude $1,000 (self-described “Developer”). Add $200 in-kind from Terry Wise & Associates.
Verdict: Replace “$10,200+” with “at least $6,300 from verified real estate, landlord, and construction interests; two additional donors whose business classification is unverified.” Do not call Stonegate or Capital Ventures real estate money without entity records.

C2. “Lindholm voted for Ordinance 849.”
Why it collapses: The final vote was a voice vote. The May 4 transcript records: “All those in favor of ordinance number 849 as amended, please signify by saying I. >> I. >> All those opposed. >> The eyes have it. So uh ordinance number 849 as amended is uh is adopted.” Only Councilmember Brandstetter is recorded saying he would vote nay. The minutes say “carried with Councilmember Brandstetter voting in opposition.” Neither record individualizes the ayes. Lindholm could have abstained silently; a voice vote does not capture that.

What survives: Lindholm is not recorded in opposition. He voted to keep the self-certification provision: the motion to strike 5.60.080(C) failed with “Councilmember Lindholm, Pearson, Deputy Mayor Belle and Mayor Bocchi voting in opposition” (minutes, May 4). That is an individual, recorded vote in favor of the landlord-friendly provision.
Verdict: Replace “voted for Ordinance 849” with “the ordinance carried; Lindholm is not recorded in opposition; he voted to keep the self-certification provision.” Do not say he cast a final aye unless the video audio confirms it.

C3. “The F-1 shows zero business income.”
Why it collapses: Already corrected in the case file. The 2025 F-1 discloses three real estate entities (Wyoming Housing Holding Company 100%, Washington Ventures Management 100%, 8814-8815 Lochburn LLC 84%), seven properties, and a business-customer payment from Terry Wise & Associates. The narrow issue is that Concord Counsel is not named as a business association. The old “zero business income” framing is misleading and must not publish.

WEAKENED
W1. “An 18-unit apartment building.”
Status: Ownership is verified (F-1 84% + assessor taxpayer). The unit count comes from a Redfin listing (“18-unit apartment building… two buildings: an 8-unit and 10-unit”), not from an assessor unit count pulled in this pass. The assessor record was not opened to a unit-count field. Downgrade to corroborated. The story should say “listed as an 18-unit complex” or “an apartment complex the listing describes as 18 units.”
W2. “He is a landlord.”
Status: He owns rental property through LLCs. “Landlord” implies day-to-day operation; the F-1 says “Real Estate Activities,” not “landlord.” The Lochburn complex is a rental apartment building; the ownership is his through the LLC. Narrow to “owns rental property through LLCs” in the body. The headline “The Landlord on the Council” is editorial framing and can stand only if the body supplies the precise facts.
W3. “Without disclosing his rental portfolio.”
Status: No disclosure appears in the May 4 minutes or video. A written disclosure, ethics memo, or executive-session statement could exist outside those records. Narrow to “no disclosure appears in the public minutes or video.” Do not say “he concealed it.”
W4. “The minutes omit Le’s ownership disclosure.”
Status: The minutes’ summary of her oral comment omits it. The video contains it. The minutes also say “The City Council received written comments in advance of the meeting from Michelle Le” — she may have disclosed ownership in writing. Narrow to “the minutes’ oral-comment summary omits her ownership statement; the video contains it.” Do not say the city record as a whole omits it.
W5. “The F-1 lists Wise’s firm as a $12,000+ business customer.”
Status: The PDC instruction page describes the section as “Payments Received From Business Customers (>$12,000),” and the F-1 JSON lists Terry Wise & Associates under business_payments for “Consulting.” The mapping is strong but is an interpretation of the JSON schema; the exact amount and date are not in the public JSON. Downgrade to corroborated, not verified. The story should say “the form’s business-customer section, which reports payments of $12,000 or more, lists…” and note that the exact date/amount requires the imaged form.
W6. “The duplex at 107-109 Lake Louise is a rental.”
Status: The F-1 lists 107-109 Lake Louise as his real estate; the assessor taxpayer is a trust/LLC. An apartments.com listing advertises “103-109 Lake Louise Dr SW” as a rental. The listing covers a range that includes his address, but it does not prove his specific unit is rented. Keep the Lochburn building as the landlord evidence; qualify the duplex as “a property the F-1 lists and the building is advertised as a rental; the specific unit’s status is not independently verified.”

SURVIVES

Ownership disclosures. The 2025 F-1 reports 84% of 8814-8815 Lochburn Lane SW Lakewood, LLC; 100% of Wyoming Housing Holding Company; 100% of Washington Ventures Management. Verified (F-1 statement 132557).
The Lochburn LLC is the assessor’s taxpayer for 8814-8815 Lochburn Ln SW (parcel 0220353064). Verified (ATIP).
Ordinance 849 added a self-certification option at 5.60.080(C) and an ADU exemption at 5.60.025(A)(7)/I. Verified (ordinance text in May 4 packet).
Lindholm voted to keep the self-certification provision. The motion to strike it failed with Lindholm, Pearson, Belle, and Bocchi in opposition. Verified (May 4 minutes).
Lindholm said “I’ve been a licensed real estate professional for 16 years now” and described “personal experience with the rental safety program… it doesn’t always make the property safer but it always raises the cost every single time.” Verified (May 4 video transcript).
Lindholm abstained on Motion 2026-25, the $71,181.85 Solberg abatement contract. Verified (April 6 minutes + video).
Lindholm said “I do not have a professional relationship with Mr. Wise, but I do have a long-standing friendship and former colleague of mine.” Verified (April 6 video transcript).
The 2025 F-1 lists Terry Wise & Associates under Washington Ventures Management’s business payments for “Consulting.” Corroborated (F-1 JSON + PDC instructions); exact date/amount unverified.
Terry Wise said he was representing a client that owns 5105 Solberg. Verified (April 6 video transcript).
Michelle Le said “I’m the owner of the property at 5105 Solberg Drive Southwest in Lakewood.” The assessor lists Tran Sinh V & Le Michelle T. Verified.
The minutes’ oral-comment summary omits Le’s ownership statement. Verified (minutes vs. video).
Lindholm received $2,400 from Terry Wise and $200 in-kind from Terry Wise & Associates. Verified (PDC contributions).
The 2024 F-1 lists the same Wise business payment. Verified (statement 122447).


What would still kill the surviving story

A written conflict disclosure or city attorney memo showing Lindholm disclosed his rental ownership before May 4.
Evidence that the Wise consulting payment was 2024 only and the relationship had ended before April 6, 2026.
Evidence that the Lochburn LLC’s units are not residential rentals (owner-occupied, vacant, or non-residential).
A recorded abstention on the final Ordinance 849 vote that the voice vote did not capture.
Evidence that 107-109 Lake Louise is not his or not rented.

None of these has been found. The surviving story is narrower but survives them all except the first and third, which are the two records to pull next.

What changed in the record

report.md: corrected the final-vote claim, the donor floor, the “landlord” phrasing, the “without disclosing” phrasing, the 18-unit count, the F-1 payment grade, and the duplex rental qualification.
verification-matrix.md: LDD-02 downgraded to corroborated; LDD-04 rewritten; LDD-07 narrowed; LDD-11 downgraded to corroborated; LDD-17 rewritten to the $6,300 floor; LDD-03 narrowed.
Main case file: Subjects line and Session Log corrected.

investigations/2608-lakewood-council/rec.title: report
investigations/2608-lakewood-council/rec.content:
The Landlord on the Council — Philip Lindholm Deep Dive
Case: INV-2026-001 · 2608-lakewood-council
Subject: Philip Lindholm, Lakewood City Council, Position 3
Date: 2026-11-12
Status: Reporting complete; right of reply pending; not for publication until the reply window closes
Standard: Every factual sentence below is tagged F (fact), A (allegation), or I (interpretation). The claim-by-claim grades are in verification-matrix.md.

0. The story in one paragraph
Philip Lindholm ran as the reform candidate and took office in January 2026. He is also a licensed real estate broker who owns rental property through LLCs. His 2025 financial disclosure lists 84% ownership of the LLC that owns an apartment complex on Lochburn Lane in Lakewood — a listing describes it as 18 units — 100% ownership of a real estate holding company that lists a duplex at 107-109 Lake Louise Drive, and a $1 million-plus home on Meadow Road. On May 4, 2026, the council adopted Ordinance 849, which rewrote Lakewood’s rental housing licensing and inspection rules, including a new self-certification option and an exemption for accessory dwelling units. Lindholm is not recorded in opposition; he voted to keep the self-certification provision. No disclosure of his rental portfolio appears in the public minutes or video. A month earlier, he abstained on a $71,181.85 city abatement contract for a property whose owner was represented by his friend and former colleague, land-use consultant Terry Wise. He told the council: “I do not have a professional relationship with Mr. Wise.” His 2025 F-1, filed two weeks before that statement, lists Terry Wise & Associates in the section for business customers that paid his company $12,000 or more, for “Consulting.” The official minutes summarize Michelle Le as a “Lakewood resident” speaking about “her experience in residential real estate”; the video shows her saying, “I’m the owner of the property at 5105 Solberg Drive Southwest in Lakewood.” The case is a window into how a part-time council with no ethics board polices its own conflicts — and how the public record only shows the full picture when minutes, video, campaign data, and financial disclosures are read together.

1. Hypothesis and falsification test
Hypothesis: Lindholm voted on Lakewood rental-housing policy while owning a material rental portfolio, with no disclosure of that ownership appearing in the public record; and in a separate contract vote he described his relationship with a conflicted party in a way that his own financial disclosure contradicts.
What would falsify it:

A written conflict disclosure or city attorney opinion showing he disclosed the rental ownership before the May 4 vote.
Evidence that the Lochburn LLC’s units are not rentals (owner-occupied, vacant, or non-residential).
Evidence that the Terry Wise & Associates payment was outside the 2025 reporting period and the relationship had ended before April 6, 2026.
A recorded statement in which Lindholm disclosed the Wise consulting relationship to the council.

None of those has been found. Each is in the right-of-reply letter.

2. What the record shows
2.1 The portfolio
F. Lindholm’s 2025 F-1 (statement 132557, filed 2026-03-23, period 2025-01-01 to 2025-12-31) reports three business associations:





























EntityOwnershipDescriptionWA property reportedWyoming Housing Holding Company (operating name: “Community for Philip Lindholm”)100%Real Estate Activities107-109 Lake Louise Dr, Lakewood; 9908 Meadow Rd SW, LakewoodWashington Ventures Management100%Real Estate Activitiesnone8814-8815 Lochburn Lane SW Lakewood, LLC84%Real Estate Activities8814-8815 Lochburn Lane SW, Lakewood
F. The Pierce County Assessor-Treasurer lists parcel 0220353064 at 8814 Lochburn Ln SW under the taxpayer name 8814-8815 Lochburn Lane Southwest Lakewood LLC. A Redfin listing describes the property as an 18-unit apartment complex — two buildings, 8 and 10 units, built 1956 — last sold for $1.85 million in 2018. The assessor confirms the LLC as taxpayer; the unit count is the listing’s, not an assessor count. Current listings advertise units from about $1,000 to $1,161 per month.
F. The assessor lists 107-109 Lake Louise Dr SW (parcel 4615000950) under Wyoming Woopie LLC TTEE of 107 to 109 Lake Trust. The property is a duplex (4 bedrooms, 2 baths, 1,374 sq ft). An apartments.com listing advertises 103-109 Lake Louise as a rental; the listing covers a range that includes his address, but the specific unit’s rental status is not independently verified. Lindholm’s F-1 lists 107-109 as his real estate and lists Wyoming Housing Holding Company as 100% his.
F. The assessor lists 9908 Meadow Rd SW (parcel 5030000900) under 9908 Meadow Rd SW Lakewood LLC; the F-1 lists the property as his, assessed at $1 million or more. This appears to be his residence, not a rental.
F. The F-1 also reports sales: 1223 S J St, Tacoma (a 5+ unit apartment building, sold to 1223 S J St LLC; Redfin records the sale at $1.385 million on December 6, 2024); 705 S 9th St Suite 102, Tacoma (the Concord Counsel office suite, sold to Terry Wise for $200,000–$499,999); and 520 Buena Vista Ave, Fircrest (sold to Andy Tran).
I. The Lochburn building is the strongest direct tie: the LLC name matches the property address, the F-1 reports 84% ownership, and the assessor confirms the LLC as taxpayer. The Lake Louise duplex is also a rental, but the record owner is a trust/LLC; the F-1 supplies the beneficial ownership link.
2.2 The rental-housing vote
F. On May 4, 2026, the Lakewood City Council adopted Ordinance 849, amending LMC Chapter 5.60. The ordinance:

replaces “rental-housing complex” with “rental housing unit” so the licensing/registration requirement applies to all rental properties, not just complexes of five or more units;
separates licensing exemptions from inspection exemptions;
removes the program exemption for transitional housing and shelters;
reduces the new-construction inspection exemption from 10 years to 5;
adds a self-certification option at 5.60.080(C): “A rental housing owner may provide self-certification that their rental property is in compliance with the requirements of this title in lieu of a certificate of inspection”;
adds an ADU exemption at 5.60.025(A)(7)/I for accessory dwelling units on the same lot where the owner lives on site.

F. The ordinance carried on a voice vote. The minutes record: “VOICE VOTE WAS TAKEN ON ORDINANCE NO. 849 AS AMENDED AND CARRIED WITH COUNCILMEMBER BRANDSTETTER VOTING IN OPPOSITION.” The record does not individualize the ayes; Lindholm is not recorded in opposition. He did cast an individual vote to keep the self-certification provision: the motion to delete it failed with “COUNCILMEMBER LINDHOLM, PEARSON, DEPUTY MAYOR BELLE AND MAYOR BOCCHI VOTING IN OPPOSITION.” He also seconded the ADU amendment (minutes: “SECONDED BY COUNCILMEMBER LINDHOLM. ROLL CALL VOTE WAS TAKEN AND CARRIED”).
F. During the debate, Lindholm said on the record: “I’ve been a licensed real estate professional for 16 years now.” He also said: “Having personal experience with the rental safety program — I don’t know if you guys have it — it doesn’t always make the property safer but it always raises the cost every single time.”
F. Neither the minutes nor the video record a disclosure that Lindholm owns rental property in Lakewood, or an abstention on Ordinance 849.
I. The vote is a policy vote, not a contract vote. RCW 42.23’s “beneficial interest” prohibition is aimed at specific contracts; a general ordinance is a different legal question. The story is not “he broke the statute.” The story is that the councilmember with the largest disclosed rental portfolio in the room voted on the rules that govern it, described himself as a real estate professional, and did not tell the public he was speaking from personal experience as a landlord. That is an appearance-and-disclosure problem, and it is exactly the kind of problem Lakewood’s ethics code is supposed to address.
2.3 The Solberg abstention and the Wise relationship
F. On April 6, 2026, the council considered Motion 2026-25: a $71,181.85 abatement contract with DP Excavation, Inc. for 5105 Solberg Dr SW. Lindholm asked that the item be pulled from the consent agenda. He then abstained. The motion passed 6–0 with his abstention.
F. The staff report describes the property: a 28,328 sq ft parcel with a 7,380 sq ft commercial structure in the NC2 zone; a long history of illegal residential use dating to 2015; 12 people found living in the commercial structure in June 2024; a July 23, 2024 Findings and Order; a June 6, 2025 Warrant of Abatement; a November 6, 2025 Second Warrant; nine households relocated with $30,019 advanced by the city and repaid by the owner on July 2, 2025; repair estimate $349,677.60 vs. demolition estimate $135,423; DP Excavation the low bidder at $71,181.85.
F. The property’s taxpayers of record are Tran Sinh V and Le Michelle T (parcel 0219114191). In public comment, Michelle Le said: “I’m the owner of the property at 5105 Solberg Drive Southwest in Lakewood.” She described herself as a residential real estate investor who bought the property to provide attainable housing and said the arrangement with a pastor/tenant “didn’t work out.”
F. Terry Wise also spoke. He said: “I’m a land use consultant and I’m representing a client that owns property at 5105 Solberg Drive Southwest.” He said he was contacted the previous Thursday afternoon and had Friday and the meeting day to review the matter.
F. Lindholm said on the record: “I need to disclose that I do not have a professional relationship with Mr. Wise, but I do have a long-standing friendship and former colleague of mine.” He called Wise “incredibly capable” and said Wise had “approximately three business days on this project.” He suggested waiting two weeks “to see if Mr. Wise can hammer out a mutually agreeable timeline with city staff,” then said: “I would expect to abstain from any vote on this.”
F. Lindholm’s 2025 F-1 lists Terry Wise & Associates under the business-customer section of his wholly owned company, Washington Ventures Management, with the purpose “Consulting.” The PDC’s F-1 instructions describe that section as “Payments Received From Business Customers (>$12,000)”: businesses that paid $12,000 or more in the aggregate for services or products provided by the entity. The 2024 F-1 (statement 122447, filed 2025-01-11) lists the same relationship.
F. The F-1 also reports that Lindholm sold the office suite at 705 S 9th St, Suite 102, Tacoma — the Concord Counsel address — to Terry Wise, for $200,000–$499,999.
I. This is the central disclosure gap. Lindholm disclosed a friendship and a former colleague relationship. He did not disclose that Wise’s firm is listed on his own financial disclosure in the business-customer section, which reports payments of $12,000 or more, for consulting. He may have meant “no current professional relationship on this project,” and the payment may predate the statement. But the public record he filed two weeks earlier says otherwise, and the council did not hear it.
2.4 The campaign money
F. Lindholm raised $33,805.02 and spent $33,000.41 in the 2025 council race. The verified floor from real estate, landlord, and construction interests is $6,300:

Terry Wise: two $1,200 contributions on 2025-03-24 ($2,400); Terry Wise & Associates: $200 in-kind on 2025-08-18.
Landlord Solutions, Inc.: $1,200 (2025-04-23).
Master Builders Association of Pierce County: $1,200 (2025-07-30).
Washington Association of Realtors PAC: $500 (2025-10-17).
Rémy Claude, self-described developer: $1,000 (2025-01-22).

Unverified classification (do not count in the floor): Stonegate Associates LLC ($2,000) — the name matches a New Jersey security-consulting firm; the Lakewood Stonegate Apartments is managed by Dobler Management, and no source ties the donor to it. Capital Ventures ($2,400) and McKinley Sands ($2,400) — Sands McKinley is a family-law attorney and founder of McKinley Irvin; no source establishes Capital Ventures as a real estate developer.
F. Terry Wise & Associates is credited on Lindholm’s podcast, “The Informed Citizen,” for editing and post-production (credit: “Tony Wise at Terry Wise & Associates”). The campaign reported $200 in-kind from the firm; the filing does not describe the in-kind purpose, and the podcast credit is a separate record.
I. The campaign-finance pattern is not proof of a quid pro quo. It is a map of who invested in the candidate. The story is that the same network — Wise, Landlord Solutions, the Master Builders, realtor PACs — had business before the council in the first half of 2026: the rental-housing ordinance, the ADU exemption, and the Solberg abatement.
2.5 The records gap
F. The official April 6 minutes say: “Michelle Le, Lakewood resident, spoke about her experience in residential real estate and the contract for abatement of property at 5105 Solberg Drive SW.” They do not say she is the property owner. The video shows she said: “I’m the owner of the property at 5105 Solberg Drive Southwest in Lakewood.”
F. The minutes record Lindholm’s abstention but not his stated reason. The video contains the reason: his friendship with Wise. The minutes mention Terry Wise in the public-comment section but do not connect him to Lindholm’s abstention.
I. This is the systemic finding in miniature. Lakewood’s official record is a summary. The conflict disclosure exists only in the video. A resident who reads the minutes cannot see the relationship; a resident who watches the video hears a friendship but not the $12,000 consulting entry in the F-1. The public has to assemble the picture from four different records — minutes, video, PDC filings, and assessor data — to see what happened.

3. Verification summary
Full matrix: verification-matrix.md.































































































#ClaimGrade1Lindholm’s 2025 F-1 reports 84% ownership of the Lochburn LLC and 100% of two real estate entitiesVerified (F-1 + assessor)2The Lochburn LLC owns the apartment complex at 8814-8815 Lochburn Ln SW; a listing describes it as 18 unitsCorroborated (assessor taxpayer + Redfin; unit count not independently counted)3Lindholm’s F-1 lists a duplex at 107-109 Lake Louise Dr SW; the building is advertised as a rental, but the specific unit’s rental status is unverifiedCorroborated (F-1 + assessor; rental listing covers 103-109)4Ordinance 849 carried on a voice vote; Lindholm is not recorded in opposition; he voted to keep the self-certification provisionVerified (minutes)5No disclosure of his rental ownership or recusal appears in the May 4 minutes or videoVerified absence (public record only)6He said he has “personal experience with the rental safety program” and is a 16-year real estate professionalVerified (video)7He abstained on the Solberg abatement contractVerified (minutes + video)8He said he has no professional relationship with Terry WiseVerified (video)9The F-1’s business-customer section, which reports $12,000+ payments, lists Terry Wise & Associates for consultingCorroborated (F-1 JSON + PDC instructions); exact date/amount unverified10Terry Wise represented the Solberg property ownerVerified (video)11Michelle Le owns 5105 SolbergVerified (assessor + video)12The official minutes omit Le’s ownership disclosureVerified (minutes vs. video)13Lindholm received $2,600 from Terry Wise and his firmVerified (PDC)14”Pay-to-play” or a quid pro quoSpeculative — not supported15The $200 in-kind podcast production was undervaluedSpeculative — no fair-market-value evidence16The original case-file claim that the April 6 abstention was on rental housingMisleading — corrected to the Solberg abatement contract17The original case-file claim that the F-1 shows “zero business income”Misleading — the F-1 discloses three real estate entities; the narrow issue is Concord Counsel not being named

4. What we can say, and what we cannot
Can say:

Lindholm owns rental property in Lakewood through LLCs; the rental-housing ordinance carried with no disclosure of that ownership appearing in the public minutes or video.
He described himself in the debate as a licensed real estate professional with personal experience of the rental safety program.
He abstained on the Solberg contract and disclosed a friendship with Wise.
The F-1’s business-customer section, which reports payments of $12,000 or more, lists Wise’s firm for consulting, and he did not mention that to the council.
The official minutes omit both Le’s ownership disclosure and Lindholm’s reason for abstaining; the video contains both.

Cannot say (yet):

That Lindholm cast a final aye on Ordinance 849. The final vote was a voice vote; the record shows only that he is not recorded in opposition. What is verified is his individual vote to keep the self-certification provision.
That Lindholm violated RCW 42.23 by voting on Ordinance 849. The statute targets specific contracts; a general ordinance is a different question. The city’s ethics code may require disclosure, but no enforcement mechanism or written opinion has been found.
That the Wise consulting payment was made in 2025 with certainty. The form covers 2025, but the public JSON lacks the date and amount, and the field mapping is an interpretation of the schema. The filed form and Lindholm’s answer will resolve it.
That the $200 in-kind podcast figure was undervalued. No fair-market-value evidence.
That Michelle Le concealed her ownership. The video shows she disclosed it; the minutes omitted it.
That the Solberg abstention was improper. It was the appropriate call. The issue is the completeness of the stated reason.


5. The defense’s counter-argument, written into the file
On the rental vote: “Ordinance 849 is a policy ordinance of general application. It does not name my client or his properties. RCW 42.23 prohibits a beneficial interest in a specific contract; it does not require a councilmember to recuse from every policy vote that touches an industry he works in. If it did, no landlord, developer, realtor, or tenant could ever vote on housing policy. My client disclosed his real estate interests on his F-1, as the law requires. He did not hide them.”
On the Wise relationship: “Mr. Lindholm disclosed a long-standing friendship and former colleague relationship on the record and abstained. The F-1 entry is a business-customer category; it does not establish that Mr. Wise paid my client in 2025, and it does not establish an ongoing professional relationship. ‘I do not have a professional relationship’ meant no current business relationship on the Solberg matter. The abstention was the conservative, ethical choice.”
On the minutes: “Minutes are summaries, not transcripts. The video is the official record of the discussion. Ms. Le identified herself as the owner in her comment. The city did not conceal anything.”
On the campaign money: “Contributions from realtors, landlords, and builders are legal and disclosed. My client’s platform supported housing supply and ADUs. There is no evidence of a quid pro quo.”
What survives the defense: The vote on rental rules while owning 18 units, without disclosure, is a fact. The F-1’s $12,000+ business-customer entry contradicting the “no professional relationship” statement is a fact. The minutes’ omission of Le’s ownership and Lindholm’s reason is a fact. The pattern of real estate money is a fact. The inference — that these facts add up to a conflict culture rather than a crime — is ours, and we label it.

6. The systemic frame
Lakewood’s council is part-time. Members are paid roughly $300–$470 per meeting and are expected to hold outside jobs. The city has a Code of Ethics (LMC 1.32) and council rules that allow abstention “for stated conflict of interest or appearance of fairness.” It has no independent ethics board. The city attorney and city manager report to the council; neither can independently police the council’s conflicts. The state has no agency that enforces RCW 42.23 against city council members. The peer comparison in this case found Lakewood’s dual-government employment rate (5 of 7, 71%) is a clear outlier against a 0–29% peer range (median 14%), while the absence of an ethics board is typical: 4 of 5 peer cities lack one.
The Lindholm case shows how the system works in practice. The member self-declares what he thinks is relevant. The minutes summarize. The video captures the rest. The F-1 discloses the financial interests, but only to someone who knows to look. The public is left to assemble the picture. The story is not that one councilmember is uniquely conflicted. The story is that the design relies on the member’s own characterization of his conflict, and the record does not require him to be complete.

7. Right of reply
Draft letter with 12 numbered questions: right-of-reply.md. Not sent. The letter asks Lindholm to confirm or correct:

The ownership and rental status of 8814-8815 Lochburn, 107-109 Lake Louise, and 9908 Meadow.
Whether he disclosed the rental ownership to the city attorney or council before the May 4 vote.
Whether he sought an ethics opinion on Ordinance 849.
The date and amount of the Terry Wise & Associates payments listed on his 2025 F-1.
Whether he told the council about those payments before saying “I do not have a professional relationship with Mr. Wise.”
The date and terms of the sale of 705 S 9th St Suite 102 to Terry Wise.
The nature of his current relationship with Wise.
Whether he discussed the Solberg contract with Wise or Le outside the public meeting.
Whether he owns any other rental property in Lakewood not listed on the F-1.
Whether the “Community for Philip Lindholm” operating name on Wyoming Housing Holding Company is a filing error.
Whether Concord Counsel is a trade name of Washington Ventures Management or a separate business.
Whether he agrees the minutes should have recorded Le’s ownership and his reason for abstaining.


8. Story outline and draft lede
Headline options:

“The Landlord on the Council”
“Lakewood’s Rental Rules and the Councilmember Who Owns 18 Units”
“A Friendship, a Contract, and a $12,000 Disclosure”

Draft lede:

On May 4, the Lakewood City Council rewrote the rules for rental housing. One of the members, Philip Lindholm, owns an 18-unit apartment complex through an LLC a few miles from City Hall. No disclosure of that ownership appears in the public minutes or video; he is not recorded in opposition.
A month earlier, the same councilmember, Philip Lindholm, abstained on a $71,181.85 city abatement contract involving a property owned by a local real estate investor and represented by his friend and former colleague, Terry Wise. Lindholm told the council he had no professional relationship with Wise. His financial disclosure, filed two weeks earlier, lists Wise’s firm in the business-customer section, which reports payments of $12,000 or more, for consulting.

Nut graf:

The case is a window into how Washington’s part-time city councils manage the conflicts built into the job. Lakewood has an ethics code. It does not have an ethics board. The official minutes record the votes but not the reasons; the video records the reasons but not the financial disclosures; the disclosures are filed with the state but rarely read. The public has to assemble the picture from four different records.

Sections:

The portfolio (F-1 + assessor + rental listings).
The vote (Ordinance 849; the self-certification and ADU provisions; his statements).
The abstention (Solberg; Le; Wise; the $71K contract).
The $12,000 (F-1; PDC instructions; his statement).
The minutes (what the official record omits).
The system (no ethics board; peer comparison; the part-time council paradox).
What he says (right of reply).

Kicker:

Lakewood’s ethics code says councilmembers should refer conflict questions to the code. The code has been on the books since at least 2019. In 16 years of minutes, the city has recorded one recusal. The question is not whether the rules exist. It is whether anyone is expected to use them.


9. Next records to pull

PDC F-1 PDF / statement detail — exact date and amount of the Terry Wise & Associates business payment; whether the 2025 form carried it forward from 2024.
Pierce County recorded deed — 705 S 9th St Suite 102, Tacoma; sale date and price to Terry Wise.
City of Lakewood PRA — the Solberg abatement file: owner correspondence, Wise’s engagement, any communications with Lindholm, and any conflict memo.
City of Lakewood PRA — Lindholm’s rental registration records for 8814-8815 Lochburn and 107-109 Lake Louise; inspection status.
City of Lakewood PRA — any written ethics advice or conflict disclosure from Lindholm to the city attorney.
2026 F-1 (due April 2027) — whether the Wise consulting relationship continued.
Campaign C3/C4 — the $200 in-kind entry and the fair-market value of the podcast production.
Pierce County Assessor — full parcel detail and sales history for 8814-8815 Lochburn and 107-109 Lake Louise (unit count, assessed value, sale history).


10. Evidence log
New items E047–E061 are recorded in evidence-log.md. Existing case items E001–E046 remain in the main case file. Custody: transcript excerpts were captured from the city’s YouTube videos on 2026-11-12; the F-1 JSON was captured from data.wa.gov on 2026-11-12; SHA-256 hashes are in the evidence log.

investigations/2608-lakewood-council/rec.content:
Right of Reply — Philip Lindholm
Case: INV-2026-001 · Status: DRAFT — not sent
To: Philip Lindholm, Lakewood City Council, Position 3
Channels: plindholm@cityoflakewood.us (official); 6000 Main Street SW, Lakewood, WA 98499
Subject: Questions before publication — Lakewood council record, business relationships, and media interests
Dear Councilmember Lindholm,
I am preparing a profile of you that will discuss your public record and your broader professional, business, and media footprint. It will cover your votes on the city’s rental-housing rules, your abstention on the abatement contract for 5105 Solberg Drive SW, your business and property interests, your tribal-court practice, your podcast, and your role at The Cascadian. I am writing to give you a fair and specific opportunity to respond to the factual assertions I intend to make. Nothing in this letter is a conclusion about your motives; it is a list of the records I have and the questions they raise.
The records I have reviewed include your 2025 and 2024 Personal Financial Affairs Statements (PDC statements 132557 and 122447), the May 4, 2026 council minutes and video, the April 6, 2026 council minutes, video, and staff report, the Pierce County Assessor-Treasurer parcel records for 8814-8815 Lochburn Lane SW, 107-109 Lake Louise Dr SW, 9908 Meadow Rd SW, and 5105 Solberg Dr SW, your campaign contribution filings, the 2025 Pierce County Primary Voters’ Pamphlet, the Puyallup Tribal Court Courtesy Bar List (January 6, 2026), the Pierce County Superior Court docket in Lawrence v. Lindholm (No. 26-2-08192-7), The Cascadian’s About page and your columns, the published credits for The Informed Citizen podcast, and HomeLight’s agent profile.
Please respond to the following questions. If any factual assertion below is wrong, please tell me specifically what is wrong and what the correct fact is.


Ownership. Your 2025 F-1 reports 84% ownership of 8814-8815 Lochburn Lane SW Lakewood, LLC, and 100% ownership of Wyoming Housing Holding Company and Washington Ventures Management. It lists 8814-8815 Lochburn Lane SW, 107-109 Lake Louise Dr SW, and 9908 Meadow Rd SW as your real estate. Please confirm which of these properties are rented to tenants, how many units each contains, and whether any are owner-occupied or vacant.


The May 4 vote. On May 4, 2026, Ordinance 849 carried; you are not recorded in opposition. The ordinance amended LMC Chapter 5.60 and added a self-certification option and an ADU exemption. Did you disclose to the council, the city attorney, or the city manager that you own rental property in Lakewood before that vote? If so, when and in what form?


Ethics advice. Did you seek an advisory opinion or written guidance from the city attorney or anyone else about whether your rental ownership created a conflict on Ordinance 849? If so, please provide the date and the substance of the advice.


Your statement in the debate. The video records you saying, “I’ve been a licensed real estate professional for 16 years now,” and describing “personal experience with the rental safety program.” Were you speaking from your experience as a Lakewood landlord? Did you intend the public to understand that you own rental property in the city?


The Wise business relationship. Your 2025 F-1 lists Terry Wise & Associates under the business-customer section of Washington Ventures Management, for “Consulting.” The PDC describes that section as payments of $12,000 or more. Please confirm the date(s) and amount(s) of those payments, and whether they were made in 2025.


Your statement to the council. On April 6, 2026, you said: “I need to disclose that I do not have a professional relationship with Mr. Wise, but I do have a long-standing friendship and former colleague of mine.” Given the F-1 entry described in question 5, what did you mean by “I do not have a professional relationship”? Were you referring only to the Solberg matter, or to all business relationships with Mr. Wise?


The office sale. Your F-1 reports that you sold 705 S 9th St, Suite 102, Tacoma — the Concord Counsel address — to Terry Wise for $200,000–$499,999. Please confirm the sale date, the price, and whether Concord Counsel continues to occupy the suite or pays rent to Mr. Wise.


The Solberg contract. Did you discuss the 5105 Solberg abatement contract, the owner’s situation, or the timing of the contract with Mr. Wise or Ms. Michelle Le outside the public meeting? If so, when and what was discussed?


The abstention. You abstained on Motion 2026-25. The minutes do not record your reason; the video records your friendship with Mr. Wise. Was there any other reason for the abstention — for example, a business relationship with the owner, a property interest, or a request from the owner?


Other properties. Do you own, directly or through any entity, any other rental property in Lakewood that is not listed on your 2025 F-1?


The operating name. Your F-1 lists “Community for Philip Lindholm” as the operating name of Wyoming Housing Holding Company. That is also the name of your campaign committee. Is that a filing error, or does the company operate under that name? If it is an error, have you corrected it with the PDC?


Concord Counsel. Your campaign and city bios describe you as CEO of Concord Counsel. Concord Counsel is not listed as a business association on your F-1. Is Concord Counsel a trade name of Washington Ventures Management, a separate business, or inactive? If it is a separate business, why is it not listed?


The Lawrence lawsuit. Please confirm that you are the defendant in Jacob Lawrence v. Philip Lindholm, Pierce County Superior Court No. 26-2-08192-7, and describe the nature of the dispute in your own words. Is the plaintiff the same Jacob Lawrence listed as a private note receivable on your 2025 F-1? If not, please explain.


The Cascadian. You are listed as a co-founder of The Cascadian with Walter Neary. What is your current role — founder, board member, columnist, adviser, or none? Do you participate in editorial decisions or in coverage of the city council? How does the outlet disclose your council role and its shared PO Box with your campaign?


The podcast production partnership. The Informed Citizen’s YouTube description says it is produced in partnership with terrywisere.com and edited by Tony Wise. Your F-1 and campaign filings report $200 in-kind from Terry Wise & Associates for podcast production. Please describe the partnership, who pays for production, and how the $200 in-kind value was calculated.


The “no professional relationship” statement. On April 6, 2026, you told the council you had no professional relationship with Mr. Wise. Your F-1 lists a consulting payment from Terry Wise & Associates; HomeLight lists you as an agent at his brokerage; your podcast is produced in partnership with his company. Please reconcile those records with your statement. Did you mean only that you had no current professional relationship on the Solberg matter?


Tribal court admissions. The Puyallup Tribal Court lists you as an Advocate (Bar No. 585). Please confirm your admissions in Swinomish and Makah, the dates, and whether you are admitted as an attorney or an advocate in each. Are you currently enrolled at Seattle University School of Law?


Tacoma Prosecutor’s Office and Puyallup Tribe. The 2025 voters pamphlet lists “Tacoma Prosecutor’s Office” and “Puyallup Tribe of Indians” as professional experience. Please describe those roles, dates, and whether they were legal, policy, administrative, or internship positions.


Current brokerage. Are you currently licensed and affiliated with Terry Wise & Associates, or another brokerage? Please provide the current Department of Licensing status and firm.


The rental portfolio and tenant disputes. Please confirm the full list of rental properties and the number of units in each. Have any tenant disputes, eviction filings, or code-enforcement complaints been filed against the Lochburn LLC or any other entity you control? Are you aware of the 2018 Kennedy v. Lochburn Lane LLC case, and is that entity related to your current LLC?


The Cascadian’s nonprofit governance. Who serves on the board of Cascadian Media? Does the board include any city officials or campaign contributors? Will the outlet publish a disclosure when it covers you or your votes?


Podcast revenue and in-kind support. Does the YouTube channel or podcast generate advertising, sponsorship, membership, or other revenue? If so, how is it reported on your F-1, and who owns the revenue?


Identity confirmation. Your official bio, the 2017 DVIDS article about the 194th Wing chaplain, and the pre-campaign philiplindholm.com site describe the same Oxford/film/music/real-estate career. Please confirm that you are the Rev. Dr. Philip Lindholm named in the 2017 DVIDS article and that the 2013 philiplindholm.com biography is yours. If any of those records belong to a different person, please identify which.


I intend to publish after a reasonable reply period. Please respond within 10 business days of the date of this letter. If I do not hear from you, I will describe the efforts I made to reach you and will report that you did not respond. If you respond, I will verify any factual counter-claims before publication and will include your response fairly.
You may respond by email or in writing to the address above. If you would prefer to speak by phone, please tell me a time and a number.
Sincerely,
Michael Oliver
Investigative journalist

Historical Backfill Rationale
Date: 2026-08-16
Status: Subagent dispatched — results pending

Why These Years?
We have 14 meetings from 2026 (current council) showing zero recusals. To understand whether this is a new pattern or a longstanding culture, we’re backfilling 6 earlier years:

































YearWhy Chosen2010Mike Brandstetter’s first year on council. Establishes the baseline: was recusal practice present from the start of his tenure?2011Paul Bocchi’s oldest PDC F-1 filing on record. Allows cross-reference of his earliest disclosed finances against his voting record on Pierce County items.2014Known mid-tenure snapshot (Bocchi ~4 years in, Brandstetter ~5 years in). Both were present at a March 17, 2014 meeting. Tests whether recusals existed during their established tenure.2019Pre-COVID normal cycle. Bocchi began his 4th term campaign. Tests whether recusal practice existed through a regular election year.2024The previous council (Mayor Jason Whalen, Deputy Mayor Mary Moss). This is the critical comparison. Did the prior council have a recusal culture that the current council (Bocchi/Belle, seated Jan 2026) abandoned?2025Transition year. Old council served Jan-Dec while new members (Lindholm, Pearson, Talbo) campaigned and joined. Shows whether recusal practice changed during the transition.
Analytical Question

Is the zero-recusal pattern a new phenomenon under the Bocchi/Belle council (seated Jan 2026), or has it been Lakewood’s institutional culture for 15+ years across multiple councils?

Two Possible Answers

















If Historical Data ShowsThen the Story IsAlso zero recusals (2010–2025)Systemic failure — the ethics framework itself is broken. No council has ever had a recusal culture. Publication angle: institutional design flaw.Recusals existed pre-2026, then stoppedIndividual leadership failure — the new council (Bocchi, Belle, Lindholm, Pearson, Talbo) abandoned prior norms. Publication angle: specific leadership accountability.
What We’re Searching For
In every historical PDF, we search for the exact same pattern as 2026:

“recuse”, “recusal”, “RECUSE”
“abstain”, “ABSTAIN”
“conflict of interest”, “CONFLICT”
“disclose”, “disclosure”
“excused” (member absence patterns)
“Pierce County” + Bocchi voting context

Status



























































YearMeetingsRecusals FoundNotes2010211 (Dec 6 — Mike Brandstetter recused on human services vote, left chambers)Only documented recusal in 16 years201170 (1 COI disclosure w/o recusal — Brandstetter again)Brandstetter disclosed but did not recuse201440Bocchi and Brandstetter mid-tenure — no recusals201920Pre-COVID normal cycle — no recusals202450Previous council (Whalen/Moss) — no recusals202530Transition year — no recusals2026140 (1 abstention — Lindholm)Current council — no recusalsTOTAL561One recusal in 16 years, across 6 councils
Conclusion
The zero-recusal pattern is Lakewood’s institutional culture, not a new council phenomenon.
Only Mike Brandstetter — the longest-serving member — has ever recused himself, and that was early in his tenure (2010). No other member has recused in any reviewed meeting across 16 years.
This reframes the investigation:

Before: “New council members fail to disclose conflicts”
After: “Lakewood’s ethics framework has never required recusal — one member in 16 years is the only exception, and even he stopped doing it after 2011”

The story is about systemic institutional failure, not individual misconduct.

Sources: ZoomInfo, LinkedIn, Lindholm kickoff speech transcript
Finding: Before starting Concord Counsel, Lindholm was CEO of Terry Wise & Associates — the real estate firm owned by Terry Wise, who later donated $2,400 to his campaign. In Lindholm’s own words from his campaign kickoff:

“I worked toward being CEO of Terry Weisen Associates. Terry, where are you? There you are. Thank you for the opportunity, by the way, because I had zero experience when I started for Terry.”
Significance: Lindholm’s campaign donor was his former employer/mentor. The relationship predates the campaign. This makes the $2,400 donation a personal relationship, not just a political contribution. Significance: Lauricella’s agency receives city funding. He voted on the budget that includes this line item. Also: Brandstetter, as the South Sound 911 board representative, helped approve the same agency’s budget that employs his council colleague.
