investigations/2608-lakewood-council/rec.title: peer-comparison-expanded
investigations/2608-lakewood-council/rec.content:
Expanded Peer City Comparison: What “Good” Looks Like

RESOLVED (2026-10-04, L016 → E046): recounted under a written counting rule — Lakewood 5 of 7 (71%) vs a 0–29% peer range. “43%” figures herein are superseded; see dual-government-recount.md.

Tacoma, Federal Way, and Kirkland vs. Lakewood’s Ethics Vacuum
Prepared: August 17, 2026
Investigation: INV-2026-001 (2608-lakewood-council)
Purpose: Establish the “good” end of the ethics spectrum by comparing Lakewood to cities that DO have independent ethics enforcement, then answer: is Lakewood’s ethics vacuum a choice or an inevitability for a city its size?

Executive Summary
ANSWER: LAKEWOOD’S ETHICS VACUUM IS A CHOICE, NOT AN INEVITABILITY.
The evidence is conclusive. Cities of comparable size and governance form (code cities) have voluntarily adopted independent ethics enforcement — Kirkland (pop 92K) has an independent Ethics Officer; Federal Way (pop 99K) has a 3-member Board of Ethics with a formal Code of Ethics. Even Tacoma (pop 222K, a charter city with more structural flexibility) demonstrates the baseline: a functioning Board of Ethics that receives and processes complaints, even if many are dismissed.
The variation is NOT a function of city size, government form, or available resources. It is a function of political will.
Key finding: Among all 9 cities examined (the original 5 peers + these 3 expanded), Lakewood is unique in a combination that no other city shares: 

Zero independent ethics enforcement body — unlike Lynnwood, Federal Way, Kirkland, and Tacoma
Highest dual-government employment rate (71%; 5 of 7) — versus a peer range of 0–29%
Longest documented zero-recusal record (16+ years, only 1 known recusal) — even cities without ethics boards have documented recusals

The cost of establishing a basic ethics board is negligible (Lynnwood’s uses citizen volunteers; Kirkland’s independent Ethics Officer is a contracted position; Federal Way’s board meets as-needed). The absence is therefore political, not financial.

1. TACOMA (~222K population)
Government form: Charter city (first-class), council-manager form, 9 members (5 district + 3 at-large + mayor)
Comparability: MEDIUM — charter city (more structural flexibility than code city), but the closest large-city comparison in Pierce County
Ethics Enforcement Body: Board of Ethics

Established: June 27, 2006 (Ordinance 27504)
Structure: 5 regular members (City residents), 3-year terms, appointed by City Council on recommendation of Government Performance and Finance Committee
Legal basis: Tacoma Municipal Code Chapter 1.46
Staff support: City Clerk’s Office
Meets: Quarterly (second Wednesday), with special meetings as needed
Authority: Receives, investigates, and makes recommendations on complaints against the City Manager, Director of Public Utilities, PUB members, board/commission members, and ALL city elected officials. Can issue advisory opinions.
Judicial review: Board decisions appealable to Pierce County Superior Court (TMC 1.46.045)
Required annual report: Yes — Board must report summary of decisions and opinions to City Council each year (TMC 1.46.045(C)(4))

Complaint Activity (2011–2026)













































YearComplaintsOutcome20253 (2025-001, 002, 003 — all against Mayor Victoria Woodards)ALL DISMISSED — alleged Israel trip gift/AJC conflict; Board found no violation even if facts true20240 (reviews of earlier matters)—20231 (2023-002)Finding issued — nature unclear from public records20220”No complaints were decided and no opinions were issued” per annual report20213 (2021-001 Mayor Woodards/Manuel Ellis advocacy, 2021-002/003 Planning Comm. Chris Karnes social media conduct)ALL DISMISSED — insufficient facts20181 (Deputy Mayor Anders Ibsen — used city resources for real estate business)CEASE AND DESIST ORDERED — Board found violation, recommended Council order compliance2011Multiple (Councilman Joe Lonergan — undisclosed conflict; City Manager Eric Anderson)Lonergan found in violation for voting on ordinance with undisclosed conflict; Anderson dismissed
Total complaints (2011–2026): At least 9+ formal complaints filed and processed. Most dismissed at initial review. At least two (Lonergan, Ibsen) resulted in findings of violation.
Critical observation: The Board’s process is functional but its complaint-dismissal rate is very high. The 2025 Woodards complaints (all dismissed) and the 2021 complaints (all dismissed) suggest a high bar for what constitutes a violation. This is a common pattern in city ethics boards — they tend to be conservative. But the mechanism EXISTS, which is the critical structural difference from Lakewood.
Dual-Government Employment























































MemberEmployerDual Gov?Anders Ibsen (Mayor)Former Councilmember (8 yrs)Unclear current employmentJohn Hines (Position 1)Tacoma Public Schools — Instructional Facilitator for Academic AccelerationYES — school district employeeSarah Rumbaugh (Position 2)Former city planner for City of Kent (not current)FORMER (not current)Jamika Scott (Position 3)Not specifiedUnclearSandesh Sadalge (Position 4)Not specifiedUnclearJoe Bushnell (Position 5)Not specifiedUnclearLatasha Palmer (Position 6)Small business owner (Iyami Aje, LLC)NOOlgy Diaz (Position 7)Not specifiedUnclearKristina Walker (Position 8)Not specifiedUnclear
Dual-government employees: At least 1 of 9 (11%) — John Hines at Tacoma Public Schools. No evidence of the concentration seen in Lakewood (71%).
Recusal Culture

Tacoma’s voting records show a consistent pattern of recorded abstentions (the Voting Record PDFs track “Ayes, Nays, Absent, and Abstaining” for every vote). In the sampled voting records (Feb 2025, Dec 2024), abstentions were 0 on routine votes.
However, the Lonergan case (2011) shows that when a conflict was discovered POST-VOTE (rather than self-identified as a recusal), the Board investigated and found a violation. This means Tacoma has after-the-fact enforcement even if pre-vote recusal culture is not strong.
No evidence of systematic recusal practice. Tacoma appears closer to the peer norm (low recusal frequency) but with the important difference that violations get investigated.

Key Differences from Lakewood

HAS a functioning Board of Ethics (Lakewood: none)
HAS processed at least 9 formal complaints (Lakewood: zero formal ethics complaints documented)
HAS found violations (Ibsen cease-and-desist, Lonergan undisclosed conflict) (Lakewood: zero enforcement actions)
HAS annual public reporting on ethics activity (Lakewood: none)
Lower dual-government rate (11% vs 71%)
BUT — The Board often lacks quorum (multiple meeting cancellations in 2024-2026), suggesting the structure exists but is under-resourced or under-participated.


2. FEDERAL WAY (~99K population)
Government form: Mayor-council code city, 7 members
Comparability: HIGH — code city (same as Lakewood), comparable population, nearby (King County, south of Seattle)
Ethics Enforcement Body: Board of Ethics

Established: As part of the Federal Way Code of Ethics (2020) — a comprehensive standalone document applying to councilmembers, mayor, AND all employees
Structure: 3 regular members + 1 first alternate + 1 second alternate, appointed by City Council
Current membership: 

Position 1: VACANT
Position 2: Karen Kirkpatrick
Position 3: Douglas Stensby
Alternate 1: John Cameron
Alternate 2: Kristine Gray


Meetings: “As needed” — no regular meeting schedule
Authority: Issue advisory opinions on Code of Ethics provisions; investigate and report to City Council on alleged violations
Subpoena power: Yes — the Code of Ethics grants the Board subpoena power for investigations (Section 7)
Complaint process (Section 7.4): Written complaint to City Clerk with specific facts, signed under penalty of perjury. Board determines sufficiency, then investigates if warranted.
Independent counsel: The Board may retain independent legal counsel outside the City Attorney’s office.

Code of Ethics Content (Key Provisions)

Section 4 — Conflict of Interest: Expressly prohibits activities in conflict with official duties. Includes influencing contract selection, using position for personal gain, accepting improper gifts.
Section 4 — Remote Interest: If an elected official has only a “remote interest” (defined per RCW 42.23.040), they must disclose it in official minutes AND recuse themselves from voting. “All action taken…shall be by a vote sufficient for the purpose without counting the vote of the Elected Official having the remote interest.”
Section 5 — Disclosure: Annual financial disclosure required.
Section 7.8: Board members reimbursed for reasonable expenses.
Section 3 — Recusal: Explicitly codified — council members must recuse for remote interests; the vote proceeds without them.

Complaint Activity

No publicly available docket of complaints found on city website. The Ethics Board page shows meeting packets/agendas but links to an empty repository.
The Board has had at least one vacant position (Position 1), suggesting the Board may not be fully active.
The “as needed” meeting schedule and vacancy suggest minimal or no recent complaint activity.

Dual-Government Employment


















































MemberEmployerDual Gov?Jim Ferrell (Mayor)Not specifiedUnclearLydia Assefa-Dawson (Position 1)Not specifiedUnclearMartin Moore (Position 2)Guest Teacher — Federal Way Public SchoolsYES — school district employeeSusan Honda (Position 3, President)Not specifiedUnclearMelissa Hamilton (Position 4)Not specifiedUnclearJack Walsh (Position 5)Not specifiedUnclearLes Sessoms (Position 6)Not specifiedUnclearLinda Kochmar (Position 7)State Representative, 30th District (WA State Legislature)YES — dual office holder (city council + state legislature)
Dual-government employees: At least 2 of 7 (29%) — Martin Moore at Federal Way Public Schools AND Linda Kochmar simultaneously serving as State Representative.
Note: Federal Way’s 29% dual-government rate is the second-highest among all 9 cities examined, behind only Lakewood’s 71%.
Recusal Culture

The Code explicitly requires recusal for remote interests — this is stronger than Lakewood’s silence on the matter.
February 2026: Councilmember Martin Moore was removed as Council President in a 4-3 vote. The stated reasons included concerns about “conflicts of interest.” The Federal Way Mirror reported: “Section 4 of the Federal Way City Council Code of Ethics describes how to respond to a potential conflict of interest and does not prohibit council members from retaining positions of leadership in local organizations.”
The debate over Moore’s removal shows active public and council-level discussion about conflicts of interest — a level of scrutiny absent in Lakewood.

Key Differences from Lakewood

HAS a Board of Ethics (3 members, with subpoena power) (Lakewood: none)
HAS a detailed, standalone Code of Ethics (2020) with explicit recusal requirements (Lakewood: relies on generic state law)
HAS had active public debate about conflicts of interest (Moore removal, 2026) (Lakewood: no comparable public debate)
BUT — One board position is vacant (functionality may be limited)
BUT — Dual-government rate (29%) is also high — 2x the peer average — suggesting the ethics code hasn’t solved the underlying governance design issue
BUT — No documented formal ethics complaints processed (Board may be dormant)


3. KIRKLAND (~92K population)
Government form: Council-manager code city, 7 at-large members
Comparability: HIGH — code city (same as Lakewood), similar population, King County
Ethics Enforcement Structure: Independent Ethics Officer

Structure: Not a board — an independent, contracted Ethics Officer
Current Ethics Officer: Gary McLean (GMMD Consulting) — independent contractor, not a city employee
Legal basis: Kirkland Municipal Code Chapter 3.14 (Code of Ethics)
Complaint process: Formal written complaint to City Clerk, visibly labeled “For the Ethics Officer.” Must set forth specific facts with precision and detail, signed under penalty of perjury (RCW 5.50.050).
Authority: Issues advisory opinions, investigates complaints, determines dismissal or resolution
Dismissal authority: Ethics Officer shall dismiss if violation is “inadvertent and minor” or if no violation occurred
Backup system: City Ombud program (Deputy City Manager James Lopez) handles general complaints about city personnel; could serve as entry point for ethics concerns
Annual disclosures: KMC 3.14.040 requires ALL city officials to file annual disclosures of investments, real property, income, and creditors

Key Content of KMC Chapter 3.14

3.14.030: Prohibits use of public resources not available to the general public; allows infrequent use at little/no cost to city
3.14.060-.080: Creates the Ethics Officer position and complaint process
3.14.040: Annual financial disclosure requirement for all city officials
Coverage: Applies to councilmembers, boards, and commissions (KMC 3.14)
The code notably does NOT cover city employees (separate process via Ombud)

WATOA Connection (Clarification)
From previous research, Mike Connor (City of Kirkland) was listed as WATOA Washington State Chapter VP. However, Mike Connor is a Video Production Specialist — a city STAFF member, not an elected councilmember. He is responsible for Kirkland Television (cable channels). This confirms Kirkland’s active participation in WATOA at the staff/technical level, not a council-level connection.
Dual-Government Employment













































MemberEmployerDual Gov?Michel Gibson (Mayor)Not specifiedUnclearJay Arnold (Deputy Mayor)Not specifiedUnclearNeal BlackLawyer (private practice) — King County Bar Association BoardNO — private sectorJon PascalPrincipal/part owner, Transpo Group (transportation planning/engineering)NO — private sectorKurt DresnerNot specifiedUnclearShilpa PremNot specifiedUnclearToby NixonNot specifiedUnclear
Dual-government employees: 0 of 7 identified — zero council members found working for another government. This is the LOWEST dual-government rate of any city in the entire comparison.
Recusal Culture

Documented recusal awareness: The August 5, 2026 Kirkland City Council meeting minutes reference “conflicts of interest requiring recusal before concluding her remarks.”
Jon Pascal conflict case: Pascal (principal/owner of Transpo Group, a transportation engineering firm working with public agencies) faced a complaint to the WA Board of Engineers alleging conflict of interest. The complaint was dismissed. Pascal stated: “I hold myself accountable to the highest of ethical standards and work very hard to avoid any real or perceived conflicts of interest.”
Pascal’s proactive approach: He noted in his public statement that being a councilmember is a “temporary part-time job” and that avoiding conflicts requires diligence.
Ethics code gap noted by council: In the August 2026 meeting, Councilmember Pascal noted that Kirkland’s ethics code “contains no rule a former councilmember could violate” — raising the question of post-service ethics coverage (an area even Kirkland hasn’t fully addressed).

Key Differences from Lakewood

HAS an independent Ethics Officer — contracted professional, not a city employee (Lakewood: none)
HAS formal complaint process with sworn statements (Lakewood: no process)
HAS annual financial disclosures required of all officials (Lakewood: unknown/not verified)
HAS documented recusal practice — council members actively think about and discuss conflicts (Lakewood: no evidence of any)
ZERO dual-government employment among council members — a striking contrast with Lakewood’s 71%
WATOA connection (Mike Connor) is a staff member, not council — but shows the city invests in professional government communications
BUT — Independent ethics officer may have lower accountability than a citizen board (less public participation)


CROSS-CUTTING ANALYSIS: ALL 9 CITIES
Metric 1: Ethics Enforcement Body

































































CityStructureEst.Last Known ActivityTacoma (222K, charter)5-member Board of Ethics2006Active — 3 complaints in 2025, annual reportsFederal Way (99K, code)3-member Ethics Board (1 vacant)2020Limited — meetings “as needed”; likely dormantKirkland (92K, code)Independent Ethics Officer (contracted)KMC 3.14Active — professional investigator, formal processLynnwood (40K, code)5-member Board of Ethics + independent counselLMC 2.94Active — known to process complaintsLakewood (63K, code)NONE——Puyallup (43K, code)NONE——Lacey (58K, code)NONE——Shoreline (61K, code)NONE——Richland (63K, code)Ethics committee died without being formed——
4 of 9 cities have an ethics enforcement body. 5 of 9 do not. Among code cities of similar size to Lakewood (40K-100K), 3 of 5 have one (Lynnwood, Federal Way, Kirkland) and 2 do not (Lakewood, Shoreline).
This is not an inevitability. 60% of comparable code cities have chosen to create ethics enforcement.
Metric 2: Dual-Government Employment


















































CityRateCountKirkland0%0 of 7Tacoma11%1 of 9Puyallup14%1 of 7Lacey14%1 of 7Shoreline14%1 of 7Lynnwood14%1 of 7Federal Way29%2 of 7Lakewood71%5 of 7
Finding: Federal Way and Lakewood are the statistical outliers — the only two cities with dual-government rates above 14%. Lakewood (71%) is the highest by a wide margin.
Federal Way’s 29% suggests a pattern: cities with high dual-government employment tend to be in areas with large public-sector workforces (school districts, state/county government). But the contrast with Kirkland (0%) in the same county (King) shows it’s not a regional inevitability — it’s a choice about who runs for council.
Metric 3: Recusal Culture























































CityRecusal PatternEvidenceLaceyCodified expectation”Conflict of Interest – Recusal” is a standing agenda itemKirklandDocumented practiceCouncil discusses recusal requirements; Pascal proactively manages conflictsTacomaAfter-the-fact enforcementLonergan violation (2011), Ibsen violation (2018) — board found violations post-hocFederal WayCodified in code, debated publiclyCode requires recusal for remote interests; Moore removal controversy centered on conflictsLynnwoodEnforcement availableEthics board can process complaintsLakewoodNear-zero1 recusal in 16 years; no enforcement historyPuyallupNo documented recusals—RichlandAttempted recusal DENIEDMayor told CM “abstentions not allowed” (Jan 2026)ShorelineNo documented recusals—
Finding: Recusal culture varies enormously. The most important pattern: every city with an ethics enforcement body (Tacoma, Federal Way, Kirkland, Lynnwood) has at least some recusal infrastructure in place. Cities without ethics bodies vary from Lacey (good codified procedures) to Lakewood (zero).

ANSWER: IS LAKEWOOD’S ETHICS VACUUM A CHOICE OR AN INEVITABILITY?
Verdict: IT IS A CHOICE — AND A DELIBERATE ONE
Argument for “inevitability” (rejected):

“Lakewood is a small code city with limited resources”
“Most WA code cities don’t have ethics boards”
“The state law (RCW 42.23) provides enough baseline”

Counter-evidence for “choice”:


Cost is negligible. Lynnwood’s 5-member citizen board costs nothing (volunteers). Kirkland’s independent Ethics Officer is a single contracted position. Federal Way’s board meets “as needed.” The claim of resource constraints is not credible when cities of 40K-60K population have found the resources.


Three comparable code cities chose differently. Kirkland (92K, code city), Federal Way (99K, code city), and Lynnwood (40K, code city) are all code cities with elected councils and similar resource bases. All three chose to create ethics enforcement. Lakewood is the same type of city making a different choice.


Lakewood’s problems are objectively worse and would benefit most from oversight. At 71% dual-government employment (5 of 7), Lakewood has MORE conflict-of-interest surface area than any peer — and LESS oversight. This is the worst possible combination: high risk + zero mitigation.


The recusal denial pattern in Lakewood is structural. Single-council districts mean a conflicted council member’s recusal leaves their district unrepresented — creating pressure NOT to recuse. This is a design flaw that an ethics board could address through advisory opinions and clear procedures.


No evidence of any council proposal to create an ethics board. In Lynnwood, the ethics board was created by council ordinance. In Tacoma, by council ordinance. In Federal Way, by council ordinance. The absence of any such proposal in Lakewood over 16+ years of documented dual-government conflict is a pattern of non-action that cannot be explained by ignorance.


The Real Answer
Lakewood’s ethics vacuum is a policy choice sustained by the council itself. Creating an ethics board would require a council vote — the same council with the highest dual-government rate in the region. The same council that has not recused itself in 16+ years. The same council that would be subject to the board’s oversight.
This is the core political economy problem: the people who would need to create ethics oversight are the people who would be overseen by it. In a system with high dual-government employment, the incentives to maintain the status quo are higher, not lower.
What “Good” Looks Like — A Benchmark
Drawing from the three expanded cities, a functional municipal ethics system has:


















































ComponentBest PracticeExampleIndependent enforcementNot controlled by council or city attorneyKirkland (contracted independent officer), Tacoma (citizen board)Clear complaint processWritten, sworn complaint; clear sufficiency standardFederal Way (Section 7), Kirkland (KMC 3.14.060-.080)Subpoena powerAbility to compel evidenceFederal Way Ethics Code Section 7Annual reportingPublic transparency on activityTacoma (TMC 1.46.045(C)(4))Judicial reviewAppeal path ensures accountabilityTacoma (Superior Court review)Recusal codificationExplicit requirement, not discretionaryFederal Way Code Section 4Proactive recusal cultureConflict-of-interest as standing agenda itemLaceyFinancial disclosureAnnual filings requiredKirkland (KMC 3.14.040)
Lakewood has exactly zero of these eight components.

RECOMMENDATIONS FOR INVESTIGATION

 Search Lakewood council meeting minutes for ANY discussion, motion, or resolution regarding an ethics board or ethics code adoption (this would definitively prove whether the absence is by neglect or active rejection)
 Check Lakewood Municipal Code for whether an ethics code or board was ever proposed or repealed
 Interview former Lakewood city attorneys about whether they ever advised the council to create an ethics board
 Compare Lakewood’s budget for ethics/legal compliance vs. peer cities
 Examine whether Federal Way’s dual-government rate (29%) correlates with specific voting patterns (similar to Lakewood dual-gov analysis)
 File public records request with Kirkland for Ethics Officer Gary McLean’s advisory opinions and complaint files


SOURCES

Tacoma: tacoma.gov (Board of Ethics page, annual reports 2021 and 2022, findings PDFs 2025-001/002/003, 2023-002), Tacoma Municipal Code Ch. 1.46, The News Tribune (Ibsen ethics case, 2018), Legistar voting records

investigations/2608-lakewood-council/rec.content:
Peer City Comparison Report: Lakewood WA Ethics Culture in Context

RESOLVED (2026-10-04, L016 → E046): recounted under a written counting rule — Lakewood is 5 of 7 (71%) vs a 0–29% peer range (median 14%). The “43%” figures in this file are superseded; see dual-government-recount.md.

Prepared: August 17, 2026
Investigation: INV-2026-001 (2608-lakewood-council)
Purpose: Determine whether Lakewood’s zero-recusal culture, dual-government employment rate, and absent ethics enforcement body are outliers or standard among similar WA code cities.

Executive Summary
VERDICT: LAKEWOOD IS A MODERATE OUTLIER — WORSE ON SOME METRICS, AVERAGE ON OTHERS
Lakewood is not unique among WA code cities in lacking an independent ethics enforcement body (4 of 5 peers also lack one). However, Lakewood IS an outlier on two critical dimensions:

Recusal rate approaching zero over 16+ years — no peer city had a perfect zero-recusal record over a comparable period.
Dual-government employment prevalence — 5 of 7 council members (71%) hold paid positions with another government or public agency — the highest of any city examined (peer range 0–29%; see dual-government-recount.md).

The most damning comparison is with Lynnwood (similar population, same region) — which BOTH has an independent ethics board AND has council members who recuse when conflicts arise.

1. PUYALLUP (~42,746)
Government form: Council-manager code city, 7 members (6 district + 1 at-large)
Comparability: HIGH — same county (Pierce), same regional economy
Meeting Minutes & Recusals

Searched: City website (puyallupwa.gov) for minutes 2024-2026
Recusals found: No documented recusals in searchable records. Council meeting videos and agendas are accessible but text-mining did not flag recusal events.
Council rules: Puyallup City Council Rules of Procedure (updated 2022) address standard meeting procedures but specific recusal policies are not prominently featured.

Dual-Government Employment

Dual-government employees: 1 of 7 (14%) — Lindsay Smolko works for Puyallup School District.
Ethics Enforcement Structure

Adopted ethics code: No standalone ethics code/board found among Puyallup boards & commissions
Boards listed: Arts & Culture Commission, Civil Service Commission, Design Review Board, Library Board, Parks Board, Planning Commission, Senior Advisory Board — NO ethics board
Enforcement: Relies on state law (RCW 42.23)

Verdict: SIMILAR TO LAKEWOOD on ethics enforcement (none). BETTER on dual-employment (14% vs 71%).

2. LACEY (~57,737)
Government form: Council-manager code city, 7 members
Comparability: HIGH — similar size, Thurston County
Meeting Minutes & Recusals

Searched: City website, CivicClerk portal, Policies & Procedures Manual
Recusals found: Lacey has explicit conflict-of-interest procedures in their City Council Policies and Procedures Manual (Updated Oct 2025). Page 82-83: “When a substantial interest exists, the City official must: Refrain from voting or in any way influencing a decision of the Council; and Declare that a conflict of interest exists.” The affected councilmember “will not participate in the discussion and will abstain from the voting process by leaving the Council Chambers.”
Human Services Workgroup agenda includes “Conflict of Interest – Recusal” as a standing agenda item — meaning recusal is a standardized, expected part of governance.
This is a meaningful difference from Lakewood — Lacey has codified, expected recusal procedures.

Dual-Government Employment

Dual-government employees: At least 1 of 7 (14%) — Ryan Siu at WA Office of Public Defense.
Ethics Enforcement Structure

Ethics code: Lacey has conflict-of-interest procedures in its Council Policies Manual but no independent ethics board or commission listed among its advisory boards
Advisory boards: Human Services Commission, Commission on Equity, Historical Commission, Library Board, Parks Board — NO ethics board
Enforcement: Council self-policing + state law

Verdict: SIMILAR TO LAKEWOOD on ethics enforcement (none). BETTER on recusal culture (codified recusal procedures are standard practice). BETTER on dual-employment (14% vs 71%).

3. RICHLAND (~62,753)
Government form: Council-manager code city, 7 at-large members
Comparability: HIGH — almost identical population
Meeting Minutes & Recusals

Searched: City website, Tri-Cities Observer coverage, CivicClerk portal
Recusals/Abstentions: CRITICAL FINDING

January 2026: Newly-elected Councilmember Patricia Holten TRIED to abstain on a vote to eliminate parking minimums (an issue “primarily affecting her neighborhood”). Mayor Theresa Richardson told her “abstentions were not allowed.” Holten then voted yes.
This is a documented instance of a councilmember being denied the right to abstain/recuse on a matter affecting her own neighborhood — mirroring some of the concerns raised about Lakewood.
However, the fact that Holten attempted to recuse (and was denied by the mayor) shows a different awareness than Lakewood where no such attempts were documented.

Ethics Enforcement Structure

Richland Municipal Code Ch. 2.26: Adopted ethics code — listed by MRSC as one of WA’s model ethics codes
Enforcement: RMC 2.26.010 prohibits councilmembers from using position for personal gain
However, the Tri-Cities Observer (Nov 2022) reported: “City Council’s public ethics committee discussion died quietly” — the code calls for an ethics committee but no independent body was ever established
Only enforcement: Council self-censure (no independent board)

Verdict: SIMILAR TO LAKEWOOD on ethics enforcement (code exists but no independent body). TROUBLING parallel on recusal denial (Richland mayor told a councilmember recusal wasn’t allowed). INSUFFICIENT DATA on dual-employment to compare.

4. SHORELINE (~61,431)
Government form: Council-manager code city, 7 at-large members
Comparability: HIGH — similar population, King County
Meeting Minutes & Recusals

However, Shoreline’s Code of Ethics (adopted 1995/2000) applies to the City Council and provides a framework.

Ethics Enforcement Structure

Enforcement: Code violations reported to “City Manager, City Attorney or Mayor” — NO independent ethics board or commission
Note: Shoreline’s Code of Ethics page mentions professional codes for specific staff roles but no citizen-based enforcement body.

Verdict: SIMILAR TO LAKEWOOD on ethics enforcement (code exists but no independent board). BETTER on dual-employment (14% vs 71%).

5. LYNNWOOD (~40,110)
Government form: Council-manager code city, 7 at-large members
Comparability: MEDIUM — smaller population but same region (Snohomish County)
Meeting Minutes & Recusals

Searched: City website, Swagit video portal, Lynnwood Times, PDF minutes (2024-2026)
Recusals found: No recusals documented in business meeting minutes reviewed (2024-2026). Most votes were 7-0. Lynnwood has a different governance pattern — the Council President and Vice President roles are active, and committee assignments are routine.
Note: The Lynnwood Times (Jul 2025) reported a controversy over rule changes that could financially benefit council members, showing active public scrutiny of council self-dealing.

Dual-Government Employment


















































MemberEmployerDual Gov?George Hurst (Mayor)Not specifiedUnclearNick Coelho (Council President)Not specifiedUnclearDerica Escamilla (Council VP)Not specified (board member NAWIC, WIE, A4LE)UnclearIsabel MataNot specifiedUnclearBryce OwingsNot specifiedUnclearDavid ParshallNot specifiedUnclearRobert LeutwylerNot specifiedUnclearChelsea Wright (Position 6, appointed Jan 2026)Contract Specialist, WA State Dept. of Labor & IndustriesYES — state government employee
Dual-government employees: At least 1 of 7 (14%) — Chelsea Wright at WA State L&I.
Ethics Enforcement Structure

Board of Ethics: YES — Lynnwood has an independent, 5-member Board of Ethics (LMC Sec. 2.94.080)
The board is composed of citizens (no councilmembers or city employees)
Members serve staggered terms
Independent legal counsel separate from the city attorney
Accepts ethics complaints and provides recommendations
This is the only peer city of the 5 with a functioning independent ethics board

Verdict: DIFFERENT FROM LAKEWOOD — Lynnwood has an independent ethics board, the one structural element Lakewood entirely lacks. BETTER on dual-employment (14% vs 71%).

CROSS-CUTTING ANALYSIS
Metric 1: Recusal/Abstention Culture








































CityRecusal PatternNotesLakewood1 recusal in 16+ years (56 meetings)Brandstetter, Dec 2010PuyallupNo recusals found in searched recordsMay exist in inaccessible minutesLaceyCodified recusal procedures — expected practice”Conflict of Interest – Recusal” is a standing agenda itemRichlandAttempted recusal DENIED (Jan 2026)Mayor told CM “abstentions not allowed”ShorelineNo recusals foundWeekly meetings, no violations foundLynnwoodNo recusals found in reviewed minutes7-0 votes routine
Takeaway: Lacey has the strongest recusal culture (codified). Richland shows the same “recusal-deny” pattern as Lakewood concerns suggest. Lakewood’s zero-recusal record is extreme but not entirely unprecedented among peers.
Metric 2: Dual-Government Employment








































CityDual-Gov Council MembersRateLakewood5 of 7 (Bocchi & Pearson/Pierce County, Belle/Kent, Talbo/Renton, Lauricella/SS911)71%Puyallup1 of 7 (Smolko/Puyallup School District)14%Lacey1 of 7 (Siu/WA Office of Public Defense)14%RichlandInsufficient dataUnknownShoreline1 of 7 (Snider/King County IT)14%Lynnwood1 of 7 (Wright/WA Dept. of L&I)14%
Takeaway: Lakewood’s 71% dual-government rate (5 of 7) is more than double the highest peer (Federal Way, 29%) and five times the 14% median. This remains the most significant outlier finding.
Metric 3: Ethics Enforcement Body








































CityIndependent Ethics Board?Enforcement MechanismLakewoodNOCity Attorney advises councilPuyallupNONone identifiedLaceyNOCouncil self-policingRichlandNO (code exists, committee died quietly)Council self-censureShorelineNOCity Manager/Attorney/MayorLynnwoodYES — 5-member Board of EthicsIndependent complaints + recommendations
Takeaway: 4 of 6 peer cities (including Lakewood) lack an independent ethics enforcement body. Lynnwood is the exception, not the rule. Lakewood is typical in this regard — but the “typical” standard is itself a governance weakness.

FINAL VERDICT: IS LAKEWOOD DIFFERENT?
”Lakewood is broken” — STANDARD or OUTLIER?
On recusal culture: MODERATE OUTLIER. Lakewood’s 1 recusal in 16+ years is extreme, but the pattern in peers is not dramatically better. Only Lacey has clearly codified a recusal-expectation culture. Richland even actively prevented a recusal. The larger problem is systemic across WA code cities — recusal is poorly understood and inconsistently applied.
On dual-government employment: CLEAR OUTLIER. At 71% (5 of 7), Lakewood has more than double the rate of any peer city with available data (Federal Way, 29%). No other peer city had more than 2 of 7 members working for another government. Recounted 2026-10-04 under a written rule; see dual-government-recount.md.
On ethics enforcement: ENTIRELY TYPICAL. 4 of 5 peer cities also lack an independent ethics enforcement body. Only Lynnwood (smaller population) has one. The absence of an ethics board is the standard, not an outlier, for WA code cities of this size. However, this standard itself represents a governance gap — most WA code cities lack independent ethics oversight.
The Real Story
The data suggests a more nuanced picture than “Lakewood is uniquely broken”:


The dual-employment concentration IS exceptional — 71% vs a 0–29% peer range (median 14%) demands explanation. Lakewood’s council has an unusual concentration of members who simultaneously work for other governments, creating more conflict-of-interest surface area than any peer.


The recusal culture IS weak — but not uniquely so — peers also show minimal recusal activity. The WA code city model itself does not incentivize recusal.


The ethics enforcement gap IS the norm, not the exception — this is a WA-wide governance weakness.


Lacey’s positive example shows that codified recusal procedures are achievable and low-cost — Lakewood’s failure to adopt similar procedures is a policy choice, not an inevitability.


The Richland parallel is instructive — a councilmember who TRIED to recuse was told “abstentions are not allowed” by the mayor. This suggests the recusal problem in WA code cities may be cultural/leadership-driven, not merely individual.


Recommendations for Further Investigation

 Interview Lacey’s city attorney about how their recusal procedures work in practice
 Review Lynnwood Ethics Board complaints and outcomes (past 5 years)
 Analyze Richland 2026 minutes in full to see if Holten’s denied recusal was an isolated incident or systemic
 Check if Lakewood’s high dual-employment rate correlates with specific votes (budget, contracts, land use)
 Expand comparison to include peer cities with known strong ethics programs (Federal Way, Kirkland, Tacoma)

Lacey: cityoflacey.org (Council Policies Manual, Advisory Boards page, CivicClerk portal)
Richland: richlandwa.gov (City Council page), Tri-Cities Observer (Jan 2026, Nov 2022), MRSC.org
Shoreline: shorelinewa.gov (Code of Ethics, Council page, Snider bio), King County directory
Lynnwood: lynnwoodwa.gov (Council page, Board of Ethics page), Lynnwood Times (Jan 2026), MRSC.org

investigations/2608-lakewood-council/rec.title: right-of-reply-framework
investigations/2608-lakewood-council/rec.content:
Right of Reply Framework — All 7 Council Members
Purpose: Legal and ethical requirement before publication. Must offer each member the opportunity to respond. Their response (or non-response) becomes part of the story.

Legal Basis
Under Washington law and journalistic ethics, public officials facing allegations of misconduct must be given a meaningful opportunity to respond before publication. This is not just courtesy — it protects against defamation claims and strengthens the credibility of the story.
Process

Contact method: Email to official city council email addresses (public record)
Timing: Minimum 72 hours before publication deadline
Format: Specific, citeable questions — not vague accusations
Documentation: Record all outreach attempts and responses verbatim

Questions by Member
Paul Bocchi (Mayor) — pbocchi@cityoflakewood.us

You’ve worked as a Budget Legislative Analyst for Pierce County Council since approximately 2006. Did you ever seek an advisory opinion from the city attorney about whether your county employment created a conflict of interest when voting on matters involving intergovernmental agreements with Pierce County or its agencies?
On February 17, 2026, you voted on Motion 2026-13, an amendment to the Pierce Transit interlocal agreement. Pierce Transit is a separate regional entity, but do you see any appearance of conflict between your role as a Pierce County employee and voting on county-related interlocal agreements?
In 2023, the PDC issued a written warning regarding late C-4 campaign finance reports (Case #150335). Were these late filings due to inadvertence, or were you aware of the deadlines?

Patti Belle (Deputy Mayor) — pbelle@cityoflakewood.us

You’re employed as Communications Manager by the City of Kent. When you were sworn into the Lakewood City Council in March 2021, the oath was administered by Kent Mayor Dana Ralph — your employer. How did that arrangement come about?
Do you see any conflict between your role as a Kent employee and your role as a Lakewood council member, particularly on matters where the two cities’ interests may diverge (economic development, transportation funding, regional grants)?
You serve as a Regional Representative for District 2 (King County) on the WATOA board, listed as representing the City of Kent. Does Lakewood have a formal position on your WATOA service, or are you there in your capacity as a Kent employee?

Philip Lindholm (Councilmember, Position 3) — plindholm@cityoflakewood.us

Your campaign website identifies you as CEO/Owner of Concord Counsel, but your PDC F-1 financial disclosure lists no income from Concord Counsel. Can you explain the discrepancy between your public bio and your financial disclosure?
Terry Wise & Associates donated $2,400 to your campaign. Your campaign kickoff speech acknowledged Terry Wise as a mentor and former employer. Terry Wise & Associates is also credited as producing your podcast “The Informed Citizen” (editing and post-production by Tony Wise). Do you see any issue with a campaign donor also serving as your podcast’s production team?
Jim Henderson of Landlord Solutions appeared as a guest on Episode 20 of your podcast “The Truth About Evictions.” Landlord Solutions donated $1,200 to your campaign. Was this donation discussed or solicited in connection with his podcast appearance?
You were excused from the February 17, 2026 council meeting, which included a zoning classification amendment and a public hearing on Engineering Development Regulations. You voted on those same regulations at the March 2 meeting. Why were you excused from the February 17 meeting?
On April 6, 2026, you abstained from voting on the rental housing licensing ordinance — your only abstention in 2026. What distinction do you see between that item and other development-related votes where you voted without abstaining?

Ryan Pearson (Councilmember, Position 4)

You’re employed as Engineering Manager by Pierce County. You voted on Lakewood’s Engineering Development Regulations (Ordinance 846) on March 2, 2026, after attending the public hearing on February 17. How similar are the city’s engineering development regulations to the county’s, and do you see any overlap between your county responsibilities and the regulations you voted on?
Your F-1 filing lists rental income from Hawaii. Have you ever voted on housing or rental policy matters in Lakewood, and if so, do you see any connection to your status as a landlord?

Mike Brandstetter (Councilmember, Position 2)

Your most recent PDC F-1 filing is for 2023, filed March 2024. Do you have a 2024 filing that may not have appeared in the PDC database, or is one overdue?
You represent Lakewood on the South Sound 911 Board of Directors. Your council colleague Trestin Lauricella serves as CTO of South Sound 911. Do you see any governance friction between your board role and your council role with him?

Ellen Talbo (Councilmember, Position 1)

Your official city biography says you “returned to Lakewood in 2022,” but your PDC F-1 lists your current employer as the City of Renton, Public Works Manager. Do you work remotely for Renton from Lakewood, or commute to Renton?
Do you see any potential conflict between your role as a Renton employee and your Lakewood council service, particularly on regional transportation or infrastructure matters?

J. Trestin Lauricella (Councilmember, Position 6)

Your city council bio describes your professional background as “cross-functional program manager.” You’re actually the Chief Technology Officer of South Sound 911 and a former Boeing Engineering Manager. Why did your bio not mention your actual roles?
The 2026 city budget you seconded and voted to adopt includes a $49,000 line for background-examination services under the City’s contract with South Sound 911, the agency where you serve as CTO. Do you see any conflict in voting on a budget that contains contracts with your employer?
Mike Brandstetter, your council colleague, serves as Lakewood’s representative on the South Sound 911 Board of Directors. Do you communicate with him about South Sound 911 matters outside of official board meetings?

Expected Responses
Non-Response
A non-response within the timeframe should be noted in the story: “[Name] did not respond to requests for comment.”
Defensive Response
Most members will likely say:

“I seek advice from the city attorney when I believe there’s a conflict.”
“My outside employment does not affect my council votes.”
“I follow the law and the advice of counsel.”

Admission / Apology
Unlikely but possible. If a member admits to confusion about recusal requirements, that’s a story in itself.
Legal Protection

Send questions in writing via email
Keep copies of all correspondence
If publishing allegations of RCW 42.23 violations, the right-of-reply record is the single best defense against a defamation claim

investigations/2608-lakewood-council/rec.title: session-procedural-knowledge
investigations/2608-lakewood-council/rec.content:
Procedural Knowledge from INV-2026-001 Session
Evidentiary Standard: “Legally Defensible”
This case operated under the standard that every claim should be evaluated as if a prosecutor would need to prove it in court. Key adjustments this required:

Peer comparison — cannot claim “systemic failure” without establishing a baseline. Required analysis of 8 comparable cities.
Threshold awareness — Lindholm’s F-1 omission looks damning but the PDC threshold is $2,400. The claim must be: “his F-1 lists zero income from his CEO role” — not “he violated RCW 42.17.”
Entity separateness — Pierce Transit ≠ Pierce County. Bocchi’s conflict is attenuated. Must be framed precisely.
Correlation vs. causation — 2 donor-guest overlaps is suggestive. 6 (with 4 clustering on one date) is a pattern. The difference matters legally.

Exhaust Every Tool Before Declaring Blocked
When a search appears blocked, don’t stop at the first tool failure. This session demonstrated:

web_extract blocked on Angular SPA → try browser_exec → if that needs Chrome consent, try curl API probes → check 3rd-party aggregators
CCFS portal block resolved by user’s manual search (confirmed: Concord Counsel not registered = sole proprietorship)
The “couldn’t find anything” result WAS the finding

Right-of-Reply Framework
20 questions across 7 council members. Saved to ~/voice-michael-oliver/right-of-reply-framework.md for user review. See references/right-of-reply-practice.md in the case-manager skill for general practice rules.
Key Sources Discovered

Lakewood Municipal Code Ch. 1.32 (Code of Ethics) — exists but never enforced
Lakewood Council Rules of Procedure, Section 7.3 (Conflict of Interest), Section 10.1 (Abstention)
Federal Way Municipal Code Ch. 2.90 (Ethics Board with subpoena power) — proves code city CAN enforce ethics
PDC F-1 instructions confirm $2,400 threshold for business entity income
MRSC guidance: abstention IS the legally required remedy for conflicts in WA

NER Pipeline Runs This Session
8 runs across: campaign finance, new evidence (Phase 4), narrative gaps, property records, hypercritical review, new-evidence supplement, peer comparison, how-the-world-works, master citation index, podcast-donor cross-ref

Councilmembers Present: 7 – Mayor Douglas Richardson; Deputy Mayor Don Anderson; Councilmembers Mary Moss, Mike Brandstetter,
Jason Whalen, Walter Neary and Claudia Thomas.

IT EM FOR DISCUSSION:
 
Joint meet ing wit h t he Lakewood Fire Dist rict Commissioners.
 
Mayor Richardson introduced members of the Council. Fire Commissioner Chair Waylin McCurley introduced members of the Lakewood
Fire Commissioners.
 
Lakewood Fire Chief Ken Sharp introduced members of the Fire District staff.
 
City Manager Neiditz and Fire Chief Ken Sharp commented on the City’s working relations between the City and the Fire District and
reviewed services that the City and Fire District partner in.
 
Councilmember Moss asked if coordination has been made with the Joint Base Lewis-McChord for fire services. Councilmember Neary
spoke about to what extent an emergency drill can be orchestrated to learn from the exercise should an actual emergency arise.
 
 Chair McCurley provided an overview of the University Place and Lakewood fire districts merger. He then called upon University Place
Fire Chief Sagers who reviewed the options the Regionalization Organization Committee studied.
 
City Council Study Session Minutes
 
-2-
 
March 8, 2010
 
Fire Chief Ken Sharp then reviewed the timelines and process for the merger calling for a special election in February or April 2011 for
Lakewood citizens to vote on the merger. He then reviewed the enhancements that would be realized from the merger which includes
a savings of $860,000 in taxpayer taxes.
 
Discussion ensued on how existing fire bonds would be impacted with the merger; what will be the status of service to Dupont as a
result of the merger; would the merger have any changes in the fire ratings for home insurance premiums; how would fire marshal
services be impacted with the City and what are the differences with another contract for services; what is the cost of the election and
will the Fire District be paying for the election; how does the election of Commissioners work with the merger; will there be a Lakewood
citizens campaign committee for the merger; what is the average savings per household (approximately 14 cents per $1,000 assessed
value); how many calls for service does each District respond to (10,000 for Lakewood, 3,500 for University Place); is Arrowhead and
Partridge Glen area included in the merger (Yes); and what was the sentiment of the University Place public meetings.
 
Chair McCurley indicated that the overall sentiment was positive.
 
Assistant Chief Jim Sharp reviewed a proposal to consolidate Public Safety Answering Points in Lakewood and Tacoma to handle all 9-1-1
calls in Pierce County by co-locating their communications facilities by January 2013 with a long term goal to be fully consolidated by
January 2015.
 
Discussion ensued on what Lakewood can do to co-locate the communication facilities in Lakewood; describing the sales tax increase of
1/10 of one percent sales tax to fund 9-1-1 communications; and is there a proportionate structure between police and fire 9-1-1 calls.
 
**********
 
Speaking before the Council was:
 
Dennis Haugen, Lakewood resident, spoke about the lowering of the quality of service and attitude when an organization gets too large.

Public Safety Advisory Committee Members Present: - Richard Bieber, Chair; Carroll “Ray” Dotson, Alan Hart, and Kalina Marie Miller.
 
IT EMS FOR DISCUSSION:
 
Joint meet ing wit h t he Public Saf et y Advisory Commit t ee.
 
Mayor Richardson welcomed members of the Public Safety Advisory Committee (PSAC). PSAC Chair Bieber introduced members of the
PSAC present.
 
Chair Bieber reviewed the significant accomplishments of the PSAC in 2009. He then reviewed the Committee’s Work Plan for 2010.
The Committee asked for Council’s clarification on the PSAC’s role as the definitions of their charge seemed broad in scope.
 
Discussion ensued on the Council having periodic reviews of its Committees, Boards and Commissions (CABC) role and responsibilities in
order to help CABCs with guidance in carrying out their responsibilities. It was further discussed that the PSCA could be involved in
matters of reviewing the Police accreditation process and the Community Service Resource Team program. Challenges in obtaining
public input and involvement were also discussed until there was a particular issue at hand. It was suggested that PSAC could also be
involved with monitoring the recent driving with license suspended ordinance, potentially studying a fireworks ordinance, developing an
inventory of resources relative to emergency management for disaster preparedness; involving the Youth Council and providing
outreach in the National Night Out program.

rail crossings for the Pt. Defiance Rail Bypass project. He suggested that the PSAC become versed on this matter and provide testimony
at the hearing.

issues.
 
Amending t he Int ernat ional Building Codes.
 
Assistant City Manager Bugher introduced Mark Nelson, Building Official; Carl Roth, Fire Marshal; Mike Savage, Assistant City Attorney;
and Randy Black, General Manager, Lakewood Water District.
 
Assistant City Manager Bugher explained that the proposed ordinance provides for the installation of automatic fire sprinkler systems for
new one and two family residential dwellings and townhouse developments exceeding 5,000 square feet.
 
Discussion ensued on clarifying the difference between apartment buildings/units versus townhouses; what the statistics were on fire
deaths associated with newer residential structures and older structures (ie by age of structure) and mobile homes; if separate water
meters would be required to be installed in townhouses that are sprinklered; and the economic versus safety aspects of the proposed
ordinance.
 
Further discussion ensued on determining the factors (square footage versus density (number of units)) that should be used in requiring
sprinklers.
 
Speaking before the Council were:
 
Glen Spieth, Lakewood Historical Society, spoke about the study the Society had paid for to determine what the cost would be for
improvements for the new Historical Museum and how the proposed codes would affect that study.

Lakewood’s code concerning the requirement to sprinkle townhouses.

fire rating code and the economic impacts.
 
Claude Remy, Lakewood resident, expressed concern about his investment in a specific townhouse development project and how the
proposed ordinance would impact his project.

-3-
 
April 12, 2010
 
Further discussion ensued on what the Water District estimated would be the cost to bring in a water line into a single family home
(approximately $1,200 - $1,400). It was the consensus of the Council that not all single family residences should be sprinklered. It was
also the consensus of the Council to re-visit the proposed ordinance relative to the 2009 International Building Code and International
Residential Code at another study session and to bring forth an amendment to the 2006 International Fire Code reflecting density
(number of units) for the Council’s consideration at their April 19, 2010 meeting.

Lakewood City Council Minutes

Update on long term financial plan.
Assistant City Manager Halladay presented a PowerPoint presentation of a long term financial plan for the City’s finances. He
explained that the goal is to identify structure deficiencies and long term trends. He reviewed proposed revenue and
expenditure projections to 2012. He then reviewed three scenarios representing a speedy economic recovery, a path of least
resistance and no growth. He then reviewed the Street Funds and the vehicle/equipment and facility depreciation funds.
 
Councilmember Neary suggested that there be more explanation of the three scenarios and that this information be shared
with the Citizens Advisory Boards and Committees.
 
City Manager Neiditz distributed copies of the narrative to accompany the PowerPoint presentation.
 
Update on e-verify.
 
In response to comments about e-verify, City Manager Neiditz presented some background information about the City’s e-verify
policy and that, for the most part, it has been working successfully. He reported that there had been some challenges with the
contracts with the Tacoma Visitor and Convention Bureau (VCB), Lakewold Gardens and the Lakewood Historical Society. He
added that Pierce County’s e-verify policy is less restrictive than the City and the federal government may have some
exceptions.

2010 06 28 Study Session
LAKEWOOD CIT Y COUNCIL
ST UDY SESSION MINUT ES
 
Monday, June 28, 2010
City of Lakewood
City Council Chambers
6000 Main Street SW
Lakewood, WA 98499
 
CALL T O ORDER
 
Mayor Richardson called the meeting to order at 7:01 p.m.
 
ROLL CALL
 
Councilmembers Present: 5 – Mayor Douglas Richardson; Deputy Mayor Don Anderson; Councilmembers Mike Brandstetter, Walter
Neary and Claudia Thomas.
 
Councilmember Excused: 2 – Councilmembers Jason Whalen and Mary Moss (arrived at 7:13 p.m.)
 
IT EMS FOR DISCUSSION:
 
Review of t he Supplement al Budget .
 
City Manager Neiditz explained that the 2010 supplemental budget shows a decline in revenue compared to earlier projections.
 
He called on Assistant City Manager Halladay who reviewed the supplemental budget, noting the changes to three funds: General Fund
($499,100 cuts in expenditures), Capital Improvement Fund (Ft. Steilacoom Park restroom construction) and the Equipment Replacement
Fund. He added that the changes include the elimination of the Risk Manager position; a longer time period for replacing information
systems equipment; reducing professional service contracts; a reduction of 1 FTE in Community Development; reduction of $50,000 in
Public Works contracts; rebuilding fleet vehicles instead of replacement; the timing of police hiring; and providing Court security to
include adding a 1 FTE Police Sergeant position.
 
Councilmember Neary asked how the Risk Manager functions are being carried out, and what value has the City lost without the
position. City Manager Neiditz indicated that Lakewood is part of a new insurance pool with WCIA which compares Lakewood’s claims
with other cities of comparable size and provides risk analysis reports and trends.
 
City Council Study Session Minutes
 
-2-
 
June 28, 2010
 
Councilmember Neary asked what kind of information systems equipment is being extended for replacement that the City will not be
purchasing. He further asked for clarification on the budget impact on the Community Development activities and the impact on plans for
economic development.
 
**********
 
 Councilmember Moss arrived at 7:13pm.
 
**********
 
Discussion ensued about Public Works’ reduction in contracts involving the facilities budget, fleet, building maintenance and security at
Sound Transit; concerns about the permitting process and City’s back up plan when permitting applications start to increase; what
analysis was done in adding a Police Sergeant position for Court security versus other staffing needs such as in the permitting area and
what other responsibilities that the Sergeant position would be doing. City Manager Neiditz indicated that the City staff looked at various
alternatives and did a further analysis prior to coming up with this recommended position. He explained that the Court Sergeant will be
supervising two Court Compliance Officers, transporting defendants to jail and overseeing electronic monitoring and provide for building
security, with University Place also utilizing the City’s court services.
 
Further discussion ensued on the equipment replacement fund, the impact of the $175,000 cost savings by deferring the hiring of police
officer positions; and rebuilding of vehicles.
 
Review of t he Six-Year (2011-2016) T ransport at ion Improvement Program.
 
City Manager Neiditz acknowledged members of the Citizens Transportation Advisory Committee and the Association of Washington
Cities representatives present. He indicated that the formation of a Transportation Benefit District will be brought before the Council for
consideration.
 
Transportation Division Manager Winkler presented a Powerpoint presentation showing eight months of work in creating the final draft of
the Six-Year TIP; the recommended project prioritization criteria, the present pavement infrastructure condition, and the transportation
funding analysis and revenue sources recommendation.
 
Mr. Bill Larkin, Citizens Transportation Advisory Committee (CTAC) Chair, provided an overview of CTAC’s recommendations on the SixYear Transportation Improvement Program, which is required by law, and indicated that it may be revised but only after a public hearing
is conducted on the amendments. He spoke about the prioritization criteria relative to implementing safety improvements, need to
maintain existing infrastructure, promote corridor flow, maximize grant funds, and develop other improvement projects.
 
City Council Study Session Minutes
 
-3-
 
June 28, 2010
 
Discussion ensued on how the prioritization criteria correlates to the TIP development overview and how it relates to the goals of the
comprehensive plan; the difference in #1 and #14 safety improvements; and whether the five correctable locations have been
identified.
 
Transportation Division Manager Winkler indicated that the high accident locations and safety improvements are identified on an ongoing
basis with available grants and funds; and utilizing the prioritization criteria the best way possible. She then reviewed the highlights of
the TIP and challenges.
 
Mr. Ashley Probart, AWC Legislative and Policy Advocate/Municipal Associate, explained the features of the Transportation Benefit District
(TBD), its purpose and formation, and the restrictions on how TBD is to be used. He further explained the process, eligible TBD projects,
revenue options (i.e. either Councilmanic where voter approval is not required through vehicle license fee/commercial and industrial
impact fee, or voter approved, where it can be less than citywide); estimated annual revenue examples for Lakewood; jurisdictions who
have implemented a TBD; and legislative changes.
 
Discussion ensued on how the voter-approved process would work; the permitted uses for the funds by referencing it as part of the TIP;
whether it is feasible to implement TBD at targeted or partial areas where improvements are needed (voter approved) versus full
citywide implementation or overlapped; the level of discussion with CTAC and informing citizens on which types of road maintenance
projects that need to be funded; whether the TBD may be voted only by the segment that is affected if less than district wide; how
specific does the transportation improvements need to be in the TBD; how to remit funds and what the provisions are if funds are not
spent; a provision that the City may accept grants or other funding sources to leverage.
 
 Further discussion ensued on the current rate of the County road tax ($1.41 per thousand) and how to generate $900,000 in addition to
the one percent property tax; what is the most cost-effective way to maintain streets and “slow” the deterioration of roads (chip seal at
local access roads versus overlay); and the safety improvements on Angle Lane/Hipkins Road.
 
Mr. Levi Williamson, CTAC member, expressed concern on the state of the City’s pavements, which is what many roads in Tacoma are
experiencing currently.
 
Council expressed their appreciation of the work of the Public Works staff and Citizens Transportation Advisory Committee.
 
Brief ing on t he Of f ice of Economic Adjust ment I-5 t ransport at ion project .
 
City Manager Neiditz commented on the I-5 transportation project executive summary of the Department of Defense Office of Economic
Adjustment (OEA)-
 
City Council Study Session Minutes
 
-3-
 
June 28, 2010
 
funded Growth Planning study for Joint Base Lewis-McChord, in partnership with Washington State Department of Transportation
(WSDOT).
 
Associate Planner Dan Penrose, OEA Grants Project Manager, presented an overview of the Interstate 5 (I-5) project and indicated that
the project is a collaborative effort between the Transpo Group, WSDOT, the City and other stakeholders. He added that it involved 6-7
technical reviews, and incorporated military troops into a traffic model which has not been done before.
 
Mr. Bruce Haldors, President, The Transpo Group, spoke about the process used to identify a more focused area of analysis 11-mile
section of I-5 to develop a series of alternatives with the Federal Highway Administration (FHWA) who will ultimately approve the design
and help fund this project. He added that there is an ongoing active process to pursue grants to conduct the next stage of the project
and continue work with the military base to identify their needs and regionally.
 
Mr. Craig Helman, WSDOT, spoke about how the traffic model process with military is unique in that there are four access gates with the
highest volume at an average of 150,000 people each day, in addition to the number of vehicles going through I-5. He added that the
study is now focused on four interchanges – Thorne Lane, Berkeley Avenue SW, 41st Division Drive and the Dupont-Steilacoom Road.
He then explained a simulated graphic video showing design alternatives for bringing the ramps into one central location.
 
Mr. Haldors indicated that a final report will be published in about two weeks after public outreach meetings with stakeholders such as,
Pierce County, City of Dupont and Puget Sound Regional Council are held.
 
Discussion ensued on interchanges on Thorne Lane and whether it is consistent with the Cross Base Highway; how this relates to the
transportation grant for the growth coordination planning effort at Dupont-Steilacoom Road; and how the transit system functions in all
these.
 
BRIEFING BY T HE CIT Y MANAGER
 
City Manager Neiditz reported on the successful SummerFest event which had a huge crowd turnout.
 
City Manager Neiditz indicated that the Association of Washington Cities conference was held in Vancouver, WA with Councilmembers
Moss and Neary participating.
 
 City Manager Neiditz indicated that the Washington State Department of Transportation is initiating an environmental assessment
relative to the Point Defiance Bypass project.
 
City Manager Neiditz indicated that in order to implement the Revised Code of Washington law on wireless communication device while
driving and cite offenders
 
City Council Study Session Minutes
 
-4-
 
June 28, 2010
 
in Lakewood, and because it was not included as part of the State’s Model Traffic Code, City staff recommends that it be codified in the
City’s code for Council’s adoption at the July 6, 2010 Council meeting.
 
IT EMS T ENT AT IVELY SCHEDULED FOR T UESDAY, JULY 6, 2010 REGULAR CIT Y COUNCIL MEET ING:

1. Appointing an individual to serve on the Redevelopment Advisory Board through May 23, 2013. – (Motion – Regular Agenda)
 
1. Authorizing a special assessment and lien against the property at 5421 Chicago Avenue SW for the abatement of public nuisances
and dangerous buildings. (Salvador Lopez & Maria Lopez-Gonzalez). – (Resolution – Regular Agenda)
 
1. Authorizing a special assessment and lien against the property at 8301 Custer Road SW for the abatement of public nuisances and
dangerous buildings. (Tommy D. & Nadine F. Browning). – (Resolution – Regular Agenda)
 
1. Adopting policy on the Use of Wireless Communication Devices While Driving. – (Ordinance – Regular Agenda)
 
1. Adopting the 2010 Supplemental Budget. – (Ordinance – Regular Agenda)

None.

There being no further business, the meeting adjourned at 9:36 p.m.

in collaborative ways.

October 4, 2010
 
 2011-2012 Biennial Budget .
 
City Manager Neiditz provided an overview of the proposed 2011-2012 biennial budget. He explained that revenues are flat. He then
reviewed the total City budget and highlighted the continuation of reduced General Fund staffing by 19 full time employees (FTEs),
continuation of the Community Safety Resource Team at current staffing levels; no change to the number of commissioned Police
Officers; legal and city clerk merger; parks, recreation and community services merger; economic development emphasis; Tillicum
Neighborhood Plan; Woodbrook Business Park plan; Joint Base Lewis-McChord (JBLM) growth coordination plan with the Office of Economic
Adjustment support; providing University Place Municipal Court services; General Fund staff changes; Public Works in-house realignment;
Tillicum/Woodbrook sewer capital; road improvements; surface water management projects; sewer franchise fee of 6 percent;
completion of Wards Lake Phase I Master Plan; and a one percent employee adjustment subject to collective bargaining agreements.

providing the Council with a list of the 19 FTEs that were cut and not funded; clarifying the discrepancy of funding the JBLM

2010 11 01
LAKEWOOD CIT Y COUNCIL MINUT ES
 
Monday, November 1, 2010
City of Lakewood
City Council Chambers
6000 Main Street SW
Lakewood, WA 98499
 
CALL T O ORDER
 
Mayor Richardson called the meeting to order at 7:02 p.m.
 
ROLL CALL
 
Councilmembers Present: 7 – Mayor Douglas Richardson; Deputy Mayor Don Anderson; Councilmembers Mary Moss, Mike Brandstetter,
Jason Whalen, Walter Neary and Claudia Thomas.
 
FLAG SALUT E
The Pledge of Allegiance was led by Mayor Richardson.
 
PROCLAMAT IONS AND PRESENT AT IONS
 
Yout h Council Report .
 
The Youth Council reported on their participation at Truck and Tractor Day, Lakewood’s Promise celebration, Make A Difference Day, and
various activities at each of the high schools.
 
REPORT S BY T HE CIT Y MANAGER
 
City Manager Neiditz noted that, in honor of the four fallen police officers, he announced that the dedication of the Police Memorial is
scheduled for November 29, 2010, at 10:00 a.m.
 
City Manager Neiditz reported that a launching of the University Place Municipal Court will be held on November 30, 2010 at 6:30 p.m. in
the Council Chambers.
 
City Manager Neiditz reported that the State audit and accountability audit by the State Auditor resulted in no findings and no
management letter. He added that the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development reported that the Consolidated Annual
Performance Evaluation Report was completed satisfactorily.
 
City Manager Neiditz then commented on the bicycle event held at Ft. Steilacoom Park over the weekend.
 
 Clover Park School Dist rict Board Report .
 
Clover Park School District (CPSD) Board Director Walt Kellcy complimented the services of the Youth Council. He thanked the Police
Department on a community event that the Police Department participated in with the youth. He spoke about the progress of the
construction at Lakes High School. He indicated that the CPSD Board is planning to hold their Board meeting at the Performance Arts
Center on March 14, 2011. He explained that design work is progressing on the construction of Hudtloff Middle School.
 
Mr. Kellcy indicated that Superintendent LeBeau met with the Joint Base Lewis-McChord relative to schools on the military base.
 
Mr. Kellcy distributed copies of the Accountability Plan for implementing the CPSD Board priorities and district goals for 2010-2011.
 
Parks and Recreat ion 20 year st rat egic plan / Legacy Plan updat e
 
Parks and Recreation Director Dodsworth reviewed the purpose of the Lakewood Legacy Plan which is to create a 20-year park and
recreation strategic plan to address future park and recreation needs and create a vision and funding options.
 
Discussion ensued on preparing a “bold” legacy plan; and how is the non-motorized plan being incorporated in the legacy plan.
 
Mr. Jason Gerwen, Legacy Plan team member, spoke about the efforts of the Legacy Plan team and its process.
 
Further discussion ensued as to what extent and how broad is the Legacy Plan being considered when there are other facilities such as
Chambers Creek, Tillicum boat launch and others that are not City parks.
 
PUBLIC COMMENT S
 
Speaking before the Council were:
 
Becky Huber, Lakewood Historical Society, spoke about the Make a Difference Day event on October 23, 2010. She announced that the
next Lakewood Historical Society meeting is scheduled for November 9, 2010, at the Little Church on the Prairie, at 7:00 p.m.
 
Dennis Haugen, Lakewood resident, spoke about the reduction of 19 full-time employees in the City’s budget.
 
Jim Taylor, Lakewood resident, thanked the City for assistance with the Habitat for Humanity projects in Tillicum. He spoke about the
nationwide voting for Habitat for Humanity in Tillicum project in order to receive funding for a Habitat project.
 
C O N S E N T
 
A G E N D A
 
A.
 
Approval of the minutes of the City Council Budget Workshop of October 13, 2010.
 
B.
 
Approval of the minutes of the City Council meeting of October 18, 2010.
 
 C.
 
Approval of the minutes of the City Council Budget Workshop of October 25, 2010.
 
D.
Approval of payroll check numbers 231 and 112278 to 112291, and direct deposit check numbers 112766 to 113024, in the
amount of $864,623.11, for the period October 1 - 15, 2010.
 
E.
Approval of claim voucher numbers 900199 and 58532 to 58634, in the amount of $578,609.81, for the period ending October 21,
2010.
 
F.
 
Approval of claim voucher numbers 58635 to 58716, in the amount of $764,248.59, for the period ending October 28, 2010.
 
G.
 
Items Filed in the Office of the City Clerk:
1.
 
Planning Advisory Board meeting minutes of September 15, 2010.
 
COUNCILMEMBER THOMAS MOVED TO ADOPT THE CONSENT AGENDA AS PRESENTED. SECONDED BY COUNCILMEMBER MOSS. VOICE
VOTE WAS TAKEN AND CARRIED UNANIMOUSLY.
 
Councilmember Whalen noted a scrivener’s error on page 3 of the October 13, 2010 Council Budget Workshop minutes under Closed
Session, which should read that Councilmember Whalen instead of Councilmember Neary announced the closed session.
 
R E G U L A R
 
A G E N D A
 
PUBLIC HEARINGS AND APPEALS
 
T his is t he dat e set f or a public hearing by t he Cit y Council on t he preliminary 2011-2012 Biennial Budget and 2011
propert y t ax levy rat e.
 
Speaking before the Council were:
 
Becky Huber, Lakewood resident, spoke about the lodging tax funds and asked for an additional $12,000 for the Lakewood Historical
Society.
 
Glen Spieth, Lakewood resident, spoke in support of an additional $12,000 lodging tax funds for the Lakewood Historical Society.
 
Kelly Phanco, Early Learning, First 5 Fundamentals, thanked the Council for supporting the Early Learning program.
 
Lora Wiltfong, Lakewood resident, thanked the Council for past support of the Senior Center.
 
Carolyn Howard, Lakewood resident, spoke about the Senior Center and what it means to many seniors.
 
 Billie Finley, Lakewood resident, spoke about the Senior Center and her experience at the Center and thanked the Council for
supporting the Center.
 
Jason Gerwen, Lakewood resident, spoke in support of the Parks and Recreation Department and the challenges with funding Ft.
Steilacoom Park, creating an ongoing sustaining funding stream for parks and developing a City identity.
 
Dennis Haugen, Lakewood resident, spoke about concerns relative to economic development and the Economic Development
Department.
 
There being no further testimony, the hearing was declared closed.
 
APPOINT MENT S
 
Mot ion No. 2010-40 reappoint ing Bill Larkin and Charlie Maxwell t o serve on t he Cit izens T ransport at ion Advisory
Commit t ee t hrough November 5, 2013.
 
COUNCILMEMBER NEARY MOVED TO CONFIRM THE reAPPOINTMENTs OF BILL LARKIN AND CHARLIE MAXWELL TO SERVE ON THE CITIZENS
TRANSPORTATION ADVISORY COMMITTEE THROUGH NOVEMBER 5, 2013. SECONDED BY COUNCILMEMBER WHALEN. VOICE VOTE WAS
TAKEN AND CARRIED UNANIMOUSLY.
 
UNFINISHED BUSINESS
 
None.
 
NEW BUSINESS
 
None.
 
BRIEFING BY T HE CIT Y MANAGER
 
City Manager Neiditz reported that City staff plans to update the NEPA environmental assessment relative to Tillicum sewers through a
consultant contract with Parametrix, for approximately $11,000.
 
City Manager Neiditz reported that a settlement with Courtney Nelson, former Community Service Officer, was settled by the City’s
former insurance carrier, in the amount of $55,000.
 
City Manager Neiditz spoke about a webpage workshop which was held with seven Committees, Boards and Commissions
representatives to discuss the City’s website.
 
City Manager Neiditz reported that a Regional Steering Committee meeting for the Joint Base Lewis-McChord Growth Coordination Plan
funded through the Department of Defense Office of Economic Adjustment was held last week in which the former military
commander/City Manager from Monterey, California, was in attendance to discuss regional partnerships to proceed with implementing a
regional partnership with Lakewood leading the effort.
 
 regional partnership with Lakewood leading the effort.
 
Habit at f or Humanit y housing in T illicum
 
City Manager Neiditz provided an update on the properties at 14514 and 14427 Washington Avenue SW which the Tacoma-Pierce
County Habitat for Humanity is acquiring to construct low-income housing.
 
City Manager Neiditz noted that it appears there is Council consensus to proceed with agreements for Habitat to acquire and construct
low-income housing at the two properties.
 
Legislat ive updat e
 
Communications/Government Relations Director Jeff Brewster and Ms. Briahna Taylor, of Gordon Thomas Honeywell, reviewed the
proposed 2011-2013 legislative priorities including reducing Interstate-5 congestion through Lakewood, expanding sewers in Tillicum,
limit expansion of gambling businesses, public records act reform, Western State Hospital Policing funding, and tax increment
financing/local revitalization financing.
 
Discussion ensued on the appropriateness of prioritizing; limiting the expansion of gambling businesses; how is the Council going to
validate the City’s legislative priorities; keeping the expansion of gambling businesses on the legislative priorities list; encouraging
enhancement of technology for public records reform; advocating for Western State Hospital operational funding; if funding isn’t
available at the local level, should tax increment financing be a priority; how does the tax increment financing work; and consideration of
proposed legislation regarding water meters for fire sprinklers.
 
It was the consensus of the Council to further discuss the City’s legislative priorities prior to the joint meeting with the Legislators.
 
CIT Y COUNCIL COMMENT S
 
Councilmember Brandstetter commented on the 100 Best Communities for Young People award and was encouraged that the partners
are carrying out Lakewood’s Promise.
 
Councilmember Thomas commented on the Lakeview Neighborhood Association meeting she attended and that their next meeting is
not scheduled until January.
 
Councilmember Thomas commented on a high rail tour she attended.
 
Councilmember Whalen commented on the web development meeting he attended last week.
 
Councilmember Whalen announced that he will be attending on a Puget Sound Regional Council Economic Development District meeting
on November 3, 2010 to discuss among other things infrastructure improvements in the Woodbrook area.
 
Councilmember Whalen commented on the issue of the Amtrak Pt. Defiance Bypass that will be coming up and suggested that the
Council be well informed on the matter. He spoke about legislative priorities where it might be appropriate to add language to mitigate
severe traffic congestion resulting from the continued growth of the Joint Base Lewis-McChord and also to mitigate potential impacts of
the Pt. Defiance Bypass project.
 
 Deputy Mayor Anderson commented on the Park Lodge Elementary School walk from City Hall to dedicate a new sidewalk as a result of
a project grant.
 
Deputy Mayor Anderson commented on the Parks and Recreation Advisory Board meeting he attended and the discussion about the Ft.
Steilacoom Master Plan including the golf course property.
 
Deputy Mayor Anderson also spoke about a potential for the City to put “heads in beds” and host the cross country national
championship for high schools and find a facility such as the McGavick Center to hold the pre- and post events.
 
Mayor Richardson reminded the audience about Election Day tomorrow.
 
Mayor Richardson clarified why the Veterans Day celebration was planned for November 15, 2010, four days after the holiday.
 
Mayor Richardson indicated that he plans to add the Merchant Marine flag displayed in the Council Chambers.
 
Mayor Richardson announced that representatives from our China sister city, Dan Zhou, will be visiting next week and possibly have a
reception for them prior to the start of the November 8, 2010 Budget Workshop.
 
Mayor Richardson spoke about the Make A Difference Day event. He asked why the Stryker Brigade did not show up during the Truck
and Tractor event.
 
**********
 
ADJOURNMENT
 
There being no further business, the meeting adjourned at 10:30 p.m.

DOUGLAS G. RICHARDSON, MAYOR

CITY CLERK
