2011 02 07
LAKEWOOD CITY COUNCIL MINUTES
Monday, February 07, 2011
City of Lakewood
City Council Chambers
6000 Main Street SW
Lakewood, WA 98499
__________________________________________________________________________________________
CALL TO ORDER
Mayor Richardson called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m.
ROLL CALL
Councilmembers Present: 6 – Deputy Mayor, Mayor Pro Tem Don Anderson; Councilmembers Mary Moss, Mike Brandstetter,
Jason Whalen, Walter Neary and Claudia Thomas.
Councilmembers Excused: 1 – Mayor Douglas Richardson
FLAG SALUTE
The Pledge of Allegiance was led by Deputy Mayor Anderson.
REPORTS BY THE CITY MANAGER
City Manager Neiditz reported that Kurt Sample was conducting a trial run of internet taping of the Council meeting.
City Manager Neiditz provided a status report on the sewer franchise indicating there will be further adjustment and discussion
before bringing it back.
He also advised the Council that Pierce County Regional Council has an assembly scheduled for February 17, 2011 at Bates.
All Council members are invited and should RSVP to Deanne Wegmann.
 
PROCLAMATIONS AND PRESENTATIONS
Youth Council Report.
The Youth Council reported about the Martin Luther King Jr. Celebration on January 15, 2011. It was also reported that the
Youth Council is investigating current “green” policies in the city to develop a “Green Initiative”. March 19 is the father/daughter
dance. A brief update was given about the schools in the area.
Clover Park School District Board Report.
Clover Park School District (CPSD) Board Director Dr. Martin Schaefer reported that Varsity Boys Basketball was ranked #2 in
AA and Lakes in the top 5 for AAA. Lakes is in the second phase of success building. Hutloff Middle School is working on
permitting to rebuild the school. Oakwood and Southgate are under consideration for an elementary school consolidation.
State budget cuts are having an impact. February 14 is Valentine’s Day and the date of the next board meeting.
Councilmember Neary asked about the elementary school consolidation.
Councilmember Whalen asked about the International Baccalaureate program in light of budget cuts.
Councilmember Whalen asked about the next board meeting date.
Deputy Mayor Anderson asked about site selection.
Councilmember Thomas asked about joint efforts to save money, specifically working with Clover Park Technical College.
 
 Review of Tacoma Power Rate Increases.
Councilmember Neary absented from the dais due to employment with a competitor.
Ted Coates, director of Tacoma Public Utilities presented the following Power Point (handout as attached).
Councilmember Brandstetter asked about slide 6 with regard to neighbors paying for streetlights in Lakewood and about how
billing works for that.
Councilmember Thomas asked about coordination between the three providers in Lakewood to maximize efficiencies.
 
PUBLIC COMMENTS
Speaking before the Council were:
Dennis Haugen, Lakewood, Washington, commended Ken Severe for investigation. He went on to discuss investment, levies,
etc.
Shirley Peterson, representing Lakewood Arts Commission, read a letter in gratitude for funding. She described the rotating art
project in City Hall. The letter was submitted.
Diane Formoso, on behalf of Caring for Kids, spoke in keeping with the handout for their fundraiser. She described how the
funding supports local kids.
Jim Taylor, Tillicum, discussed Habitat for Humanity in Tillicum.
Ken Severe, Lakewood, addressed transparency in government and identified missing pages from website, which are the
vouchers.

R E G U L A R
 
A G E N D A
 
APPOINTMENTS
Motion No. 2011-09 Appointing Robert Zawilski to serve on the Planning Advisory Board through February 11, 2016.
COUNCILMEMBER WHALEN MOVED TO CONFIRM THE APPOINTMENT OF ROBERT ZAWILSKI SECONDED BY
COUNCILMEMBER NEARY. VOICE VOTE WAS TAKEN AND CARRIED UNANIMOUSLY.
UNFINISHED BUSINESS
NEW BUSINESS
Motion No. 2011-10 Authorizing execution of an agreement with Stewart, Beall, MacNichols and Harmell for Public
Defender Services from January 1, 2011 through December 31, 2011.
City Manager Andrew Neiditz described the contract.
Councilmember Whalen asked about the competitive process.
Councilmember Whalen asked about the increase in costs and our ability to forecast the need for more services based on
University Place.
Councilmember Whalen asked about the ability to increase fines and fees to help absorb additional costs.
Councilmember Moss asked about offender eligibility for public defender services and percentage that is not collected.
Councilmember Thomas asked about work crew.
Deputy Mayor Anderson asked about what portion of the increase was attributable to the addition of University Place versus
increasing the regular rate.
COUNCILMEMBER MOSS MOVED TO AUTHORIZE EXECUTION OF AN AGREEMENT WITH STEWART, BEALL,
MACNICHOLS AND HARMELL FOR PUBLIC DEFENDER SERVICES FROM JANUARY 1, 2011 THROUGH DECEMBER
31, 2011. SECONDED BY COUNCILMEMBER THOMAS. VOICE VOTE WAS TAKEN AND CARRIED UNANIMOUSLY.
Motion No. 2011-11 Awarding a bid to Northwest Cascade, Inc. in the amount of $612,189.15 for the Grant Avenue
Sewer Extension, Storm Drainage and Roadway Restoration, and Water Main Replacement Project.
City Manager Andrew Neiditz introduced the motion and Greg Vigoren.
Greg Vigoren described the contract.
Councilmember Whalen asked about choice of road width and proximity to the trunk line. He also asked about curb, gutter and
sidewalk.
Councilmember Brandstetter asked about schedule B, lines 13 and 14 in the contract.
Councilmember Whalen asked about overall satisfaction with the successful bidder.
Deputy Mayor Anderson asked about the spread between bidders and whether it reflects a trend.
Councilmember Neary commented about the low bid.
 
 COUNCILMEMBER BRANDSTETTER MOVED TO AWARD A BID TO NORTHWEST CASCADE, INC. IN THE AMOUNT
OF $612,189.15 FOR THE GRANT AVENUE SEWER EXTENSION, STORM DRAINAGE AND ROADWAY RESTORATION,
AND WATER MAIN REPLACEMENT PROJECT. SECONDED BY COUNCILMEMBER NEARY. VOICE VOTE WAS
TAKEN AND CARRIED UNANIMOUSLY.
 
BRIEFING BY THE CITY MANAGER
City Manager Neiditz discussed the similarity between proposed sewer franchise fees and the amount paid by Tacoma Public
Utilities.
City Manager Neiditz Introduced Steve Mauer to present the “Raising the Bar” program. The presentation followed a Power
Point (no copy provided).
Councilmember Neary asked about whether this appeared on the agenda.
Councilmember Whalen asked about support from Bar and Tavern owners versus pushback.
Councilmember Brandstetter asked for clarification as to the role of the Liquor Control Board. He asked about potential impact
of state budget cuts on the Liquor Control Board. He asked about a specific case, the City’s response and the ability to
publicize the matter.
Councilmember Whalen asked about call history for casinos versus other bars and taverns.
Mayor Pro-Tem Anderson commented on the legislature and local ability to enforce liquor cases.
CITY COUNCIL COMMENTS
Councilmember Moss had no comment.
Councilmember Neary recalled that elementary school consolidation was on an earlier bond measure and would like a staff
presentation on the issue.
Councilmember Brandstetter reported on the Korean-American event he attended last Saturday. Mandy Ma is incoming
President.
Councilmember Brandstetter voiced concern about cursory notation reflected in minutes. He would like to see more detail,
particularly for items that are subject to more debate or are not unanimous. The tape is not enough. Councilmember Thomas
responded that our minutes are currently in keeping with Robert’s Rules and inquired as to how to decide when to use greater
detail. City Manager Neiditz pointed out that action minutes provide consistency through Citizen Advisory Boards and the
Council.
Councilmember Thomas voiced a reminder that the Community Collaboration has a joint meeting with Washington State
Military Kids and Families on Wednesday, February 9.
Councilmember Thomas also distributed a copy of Sound Transit Milestones and Phase Gate Report.
Councilmember Whalen reported on the Tuesday, February 1 public forum on sewers, held in Tillicum. He indicated that staff
did a good job presenting and he felt that the discussion was well handled. He mentioned potential for use of CDBG funds.
Councilmember Whalen also asked about the Buxton contract. He would like to involve them in the question of public
investment in the Towne Center.
Councilmember Whalen asked about website redesign and how to make packet materials more accessible on the website.
Councilmember Thomas asked about sewer hookup for Habitat for Humanity homes built in Tillicum.
Deputy Mayor Anderson noted that for the second year in a row the City Hall provided high quality chili although it did not win.
Congratulations to Brink & Sadler.
**********
Deputy Mayor Anderson announced that post-adjournment, pursuant to RCW 42.30.140, the Council will meet in closed
 
 session to discuss collective bargaining.
ADJOURNMENT
There being no further business, the meeting adjourned at 8:58 p.m.
 
_____________________________________
DON ANDERSON, DEPUTY MAYOR

2011 04 11 Study Session
LAKEWOOD CITY COUNCIL
STUDY SESSION MINUTES
Monday, April 11, 2011
City of Lakewood
City Council Chambers
6000 Main Street SW
Lakewood, WA 98499
___________________________________________________________________________________________
CALL TO ORDER
Mayor Richardson called the meeting to order at 7:02 p.m.
ROLL CALL
Councilmembers Present: 5 – Mayor Douglas Richardson; Deputy Mayor Don Anderson; Councilmembers Mary Moss, Jason
Whalen, and Walter Neary.
Councilmember Excused: 2 – Councilmembers Mike Brandstetter and Claudia Thomas (arrived at 7:50 p.m.).
ITEMS FOR DISCUSSION:
Review of aggressive begging ordinance.
Assistant City Attorney Booker-Hay reviewed the proposed amendments to the aggressive begging ordinance. She explained
that the proposed amendments would expand the definition of begging and aggressive begging and define its restrictions on
time, place and the manner of such begging.
Discussion ensued on the level of restrictiveness for aggressive begging; providing the language of the ordinance on this issue
and the next two agenda items for Council review; when would the public see the draft ordinances; what about the history of
aggressive begging when in vehicles; what is the cost for processing such citations; and having the ordinance address
protection for vulnerable older adults and minors.
Speaking before the Council were:
Mon Wig, Bellevue resident, owner of Lakewood Pavilion, spoke about the seriousness of begging at Lakewood businesses.
He provided examples of such aggressive begging and its impacts on business tenants. He encouraged that the ordinance
provide for strong language that also includes business areas and not just at areas such as ATMs and bus stations.
Dennis Haugen, Lakewood resident, spoke about Lakewood’s dangerous community and how gangs and cartels can thrive in
Lakewood because of Lakewood’s “entitlement” mentality.
Further discussion ensued on what City ordinance enforce pop-up vendors outside of business stores; what is the definition of
criminal trespass; have there been numerous begging complaints from businesses; testing the limits of an aggressive begging
ordinance and imposing an escalating provision; researching Municipal Research Services Center for ordinances that may be
more restrictive and including language about begging when one feels intimidated for being asked.
Review of graffiti ordinance.
Lt. Steve Mauer and Assistant City Attorney Mike Savage reviewed the process and amendments to the removal of graffiti and
associated penalties.
Discussion ensued on the penalty if someone was caught in the act; where are most of the activities taking place (McChord
gate area and Woodbrook area); graffiti on the Hill Ward area; concerns about notices to the owner and what the timeframes
are for removal of graffiti and to ensure that the notice is provided to the property owner.
**********
Councilmember Thomas arrived at 7:50 p.m.
 
 **********
Further discussion ensued on whether this item was discussed with the Public Safety Advisory Committee; how difficult has it
been to have graffiti removed by property owners and those in financial hardship; are graffiti on trains and train properties
addressed in the ordinance.
Speaking before the Council was:
Dennis Haugen, Lakewood resident, spoke about laws that punish victims and how the criminal gets off, and using technology
(cell phone cameras) to take pictures and sending it to the Police Department.
Ken Severe, Lakewood resident, expressed concern about punishing the victims to clean up graffiti and leaving restitution out
of the ordinance. He then donated a Hawthorne tree in recognition of Parks Appreciation Day.
Review of shopping cart ordinance.
Assistant City Manager Bugher reviewed the shopping cart concerns in Lakewood and complaints that the City has received.
He then provided an overview of the amendments for regulating shopping carts.
Discussion ensued about shopping carts in the Towne Center being taken out and left at Transit bus stations; and discussing
the proposed ordinance with business retailers.
Speaking before the Council was:
Dennis Haugen, Lakewood resident, spoke about proving the ownership of the shopping cart instead of burdening the victims.
Ken Severe, Lakewood resident, spoke about how carts are handled in Baltimore and that most of the stores there have steel
posts in the curb so carts cannot be taken out.
Further discussion ensued on areas at the Transit stations for collecting carts.
BRIEFING BY THE CITY MANAGER
City Manager Neiditz announced that a public forum on community gardens is scheduled for April 12, 2011. Secondly, the
Joint Citizens Advisory Board and Committees meeting to discuss JBLM coordination is scheduled for April 20, 2011 hosted
by the Planning Advisory Board.
City Manager Neiditz requested a closed session to discuss labor contract issues.
ITEMS TENTATIVELY SCHEDULED FOR THE APRIL 18, 2011 REGULAR CITY COUNCIL MEETING:
1. Item Nos. 1-2 above.
2. This is the date set for a public hearing by the City Council on the Fiscal Year 2011 Consolidated Plan and amendments
to the Fiscal Years 2008, 2009 and 2010 Annual Action Plans and the proposed use of funds.
3. Awarding a bid for the acquisition of LED signal displays. – (Motion – Regular Agenda)
4. Approving the hire of temporary engineering technicians. – (Motion – Regular Agenda)
 
CITY COUNCIL COMMENTS
Councilmember Thomas announced that the Human Service Collaboration meeting will be held on Wednesday, April 13, 2011
at 9:30 a.m. in the Council Chambers. She also asked the Council to think about youths to serve on the Youth Council.
She then provided an update on the Sound Transit’s progress and noted that Lakewood’s station is scheduled to open in
September 2012.
Councilmember Neary commented on a meeting he attended in Tillicum relative to the Camp Murray gate relocation.
Councilmember Whalen commented on email communication between the Arts Commission and Public Works relative to the
Bridgeport Way / Walmart Gateway and asked for an update on what improvements will be taking place.
 
 Mayor Richardson announced that Parks Appreciation Day is scheduled for April 16, 2011.
Mayor Richardson indicated that the Merchant Marine flag dedication is scheduled for presentation at the June 6, 2011 Council
meeting and suggested inviting the President of the Merchant Marines.
**********
Mayor Richardson announced that Council will recess into a closed session to discuss employee relations pursuant to RCW
42.30.140(4).
ADJOURNMENT
There being no further business, the meeting adjourned at 8:45 p.m.
 
_____________________________________
DOUGLAS G. RICHARDSON, MAYOR

____________________________
ALICE M. BUSH, MMC
CITY CLERK

SEWER SYSTEM OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE. SECONDED BY COUNCILMEMBER MOSS. VOICE VOTE WAS

BRIEFING BY THE CITY MANAGER
Camp Murray Gate Update
City Manager Neiditz provided an update on the Camp Murray Gate. He explained that Camp Murray and the City agreed to
share traffic data. He reviewed the three gate relocation options: 1) to remain the same, 2) a proposed Grant Avenue option,
and 3) a proposed Portland Avenue option. Camp Murray’s concern is that the Grant Avenue option would compromise their
anti-terrorism security. It is proposed that the Portland Avenue option might be viable with modifications of a roundabout at
Berkeley Avenue, include a disincentive measure to have a free right turn on Berkeley and Portland Avenue, construct five
raised crosswalks and a school zone on Portland Avenue to emphasize the pedestrian nature of the area that would minimize
traffic from traveling on Portland Avenue. A joint meeting with the Planning Advisory Board, the Citizens Transportation
 
 Advisory Committee and the Redevelopment Advisory Board to discuss the proposed Camp Murray gate relocation is
scheduled for Tuesday, July 19, 2011. Assistant City Manager Bugher displayed diagrams of the proposed modifications.
Grant funding of $1.2 million for this project will be extended to the Lakewood community by Camp Murray.

Regional Council Meeting.

attending.

2011 08 01
LAKEWOOD CITY COUNCIL MINUTES
Monday, August 1, 2011
City of Lakewood
City Council Chambers
6000 Main Street SW
Lakewood, WA 98499
 
CALL TO ORDER
Mayor Richardson called the meeting to order at 7:01 p.m.
ROLL CALL
Councilmembers Present: 4 – Mayor Douglas Richardson; Councilmembers Mary Moss, Jason Whalen and Claudia Thomas.
Councilmembers Excused: 3 – Deputy Mayor Don Anderson and Councilmember Walter Neary and Mike Brandstetter.
FLAG SALUTE
The Pledge of Allegiance was led by Mayor Richardson.
REPORTS BY THE CITY MANAGER
City Manager Neiditz announced that August 2, 2011 is National Night Out in the City of Lakewood.
He reported that the South Sound 911 proposal was approved by the County Council on July 26, 2011 for placing a ballot
measure for funding of the new agency. Also, the County Council approved Lakewood’s sewer franchise with an effective date
of September 1, 2011.
Lastly, he reminded the Council that the Council will be hosting a special meeting on August 22, 2011 with the City Councils of
DuPont and Steilacoom.
PROCLAMATIONS AND PRESENTATIONS
Clover Park School District Board Report.
Clover Park School District (CPSD) Board Director Paul Wagemann provided a progress report on the Lakes High School
construction which is nearly complete. He announced that school starts on September 7, 2011.
PUBLIC COMMENTS
Speaking before the Council were:
William Hubbard, Tillicum resident, spoke about THE NEWS TRIBUNE article by the City Manager and expressed concern
about commercial traffic traveling on Portland Avenue. He spoke about leaving the gate where it currently is.
Bryant Grider, Tillicum resident, spoke about the congestion at Berkeley Avenue and moving the gate near Eagle Point was
concerning and asked that the gate not be moved.
Jennifer Justice, Tillicum resident, spoke against the relocation of the Camp Murray gate and that the $1.2 million funding will
not calm the traffic congestion. She asked that the State provide funding to fix the interchange. She urged blocking access to
Camp Murray to the residential area.
Edmond Dennery, Tillicum resident, spoke against moving the Camp Murray gate to the southwest terminus of Portland
Avenue was not in the best interest of Tillicum. He urged to leave the gate where it is and await future renovations of I-5.
Pat O’Brien, Tillicum resident, thanked the City for the study of Exit 122 and asked for a similar study for Exit 123 off of I-5. He
asked Council to take a vote on this matter.
 
 Brian Dennery, Tillicum resident, spoke about minority businesses along Union Avenue that were not contacted by the City
about the proposed changes. He expressed concern that to send traffic along Portland Avenue was of concern with children
walking along Portland Avenue.
Sharon Warrant, Tillicum resident, spoke about the round about proposed near Eagle Point and that moving the gate will
cause more traffic congestion.
Jan Merriman, Tillicum resident, asked that the Council listen to the Tillicum residents. Major streets, such as Thorne Lane,
Berkeley and Union Avenue will be inadequate for handling an additional 4,000 vehicles. Moving the gate will not relieve
traffic and concerns about emergency vehicle access.
Paul Wagemann, Lakewood resident, spoke about the problems generated by I-5 traffic and moving the gate to mitigate the
traffic impacts the Tillicum residents. He indicated that the problem is resting with the citizens who live in Tillicum and we need
to listen to what the citizens want and to leave the gate where it is.
David Anderson, Tillicum resident, spoke about his conversation with King 5 TV. He spoke about the failures of the gate
relocation study and full review is needed of the I-5 corridor.
Anthony Truxal, Tillicum resident, spoke in opposition of relocating the Camp Murray gate and that it moves the problem south
to an interchange that is even more inadequate which is compounded by Amtrak traffic and the Point Defiance Bypass. He
spoke about the need to study impacts on Exit 123.
Jim Charboneau, Lakewood resident, spoke about the round about that would eliminate some of the traffic from I-5. He spoke
about emergency access to the State Emergency facility on Camp Murray.
Tony Gibbon, Chevron Station owner in Tillicum, spoke about keeping the gate where it is and his appreciation of the business
that is generated from Camp Murray and residents. His second choice was the Portland Avenue change.
Ken Severe, Lakewood resident, spoke about page 24 of the claim vouchers, and noted that $18,000 was paid for a Police
vehicle for repairs, which is high.
Bob Holden, Tillicum resident, spoke about increased property taxes in Tillicum and spoke against the relocation of Camp
Murray gate.
Murray Share, Tillicum resident, spoke about any redirection of traffic from I-5 will create traffic congestion and there has been
no study of the impacts on Thorne Lane. She asked if repaving North Thorne Lane been budgeted, including sidewalks, and
picking up garbage along the streets.
Rick Patterson, Camp Murray representative, spoke about Camp Murray, military, and residents concerns are shared by all and
this has been complex and it will come to some expense to correct the problems. A lot of energy has been expended to review
the options and a study was conducted. Leaving the gate where it is, was not an option. Camp Murray looks forward to
working with the City on this effort.
Robert Schader, Tillicum resident, spoke about better informing the community about the study, and that an environmental
impact study should be done.
Sandra DeVetton, Tillicum resident, spoke about the major problem with the Camp Murray gate is the railroad and Berkeley
Avenue. Maas Lane should be purchased to create a round about.
Robin McKlimens, Tillicum resident, expressed concerns about the gate relocation from a health perspective. The current
proposal will be taking down a lot of trees and I-5 noise will be carried into American Lake. She asked that there be more
research on this matter.
Abby Henny, Tillicum resident, spoke abut representing the families who could not attend tonight’s meeting and expressed
concern about emissions and gases emitted from vehicles and children walking on streets.
Tom James, Tillicum resident, thanked Council for making Tillicum a better place to live. He indicated that the Council
approved the Tillicum Neighborhood Plan and that Portland Avenue was not designed to be a major arterial in the Plan. He
indicated that Portland Avenue is a residential street.
Neil Holden, Silcox Island resident, spoke about Tillicum being an improving neighborhood. He urged Council not to allow the
relocation of the Camp Murray gate.
James Taylor, Tillicum Action Committee, spoke in support of the comments of the Tillicum residents, and asked the Council to
 
 take the residents comments into consideration and not move the Camp Murray gate for the time being.

Dodsworth, Lonnie Howard, Judi Weldy and Ellie Wilson.
ITEMS FOR DISCUSSION:
Joint Lakewood’s Promise Advisory Board meeting.
City Council and Lakewood’s Promise Advisory Board Members introduced themselves.
Chair DeNault reviewed the major accomplishments of the Board. Lakewood’s Promise Coordinator Kurt Sample provided an
overview of the Lakewood’s Promise website showing a map depicting where early learning programs are offered in
Lakewood, where 6-11 age children’s activities, teen activities, volunteer opportunities, and youth activities are occurring in
Lakewood. Board Member Bucu spoke about last year’s efforts being focused on safe places by creating an inventory and
afterschool late night programs. Board Member Wilson spoke about the “caring adult” promise by providing a caring adult for
serving as mentors and tutors. Board Member Weldy spoke about the healthy start task force who are focusing on healthy
eating and eliminating food waste. Board Member Howard spoke about educational outcomes at the secondary level, and how
to blend work force development with economic development. Board Member Dodsworth spoke about utilizing the Youth
Council in the Five Promises.
Discussion ensued on how does the work force development with economic development program work; creating a web page
open to youth as an introduction to invite other youths to higher education sites; providing for the ability to track “safe places” on
the Promise website; involving the Police Department in the safe place programs; what synergy will the new Harrison
Preparatory School have with being in close proximity to Clover Park Technical College; potentially using public buildings (ie
schools, etc.) as safe place facilities; and what is considered a successful safe place.

Planning Advisory Board’s seven recommendations consisting of the Ruby Drive Apartments, Pacific Highway zoning
changes, Department of Transportation property, Wards Lake Park, Springbrook Park expansion, Pacific Highway SW
property, and Chapters 2, 3, 5, 7 of the Comprehensive Plan. He reviewed the key points of the proposed Comprehensive Plan
amendments.

 Plan; what kind of agencies might raise concerns about the housing section of the Comprehensive Plan; possibly including an
affirmative statement for maintaining low income housing; and is there liability when a developer has a vested building permit
and its zoning is changed.

revenue increases of $23,000 and an increase of $181,000 in expenditures. She then highlighted the General Fund, Fund 102
Street capital, Fund 180 Narcotics Seizure, Fund 181 Felony Seizure; Fund 195 Public Safety grants, Fund 401 Surface Water
Management, and Fund 502 City Hall service changes.
Discussion ensued on what is the basis for the Bridgeport Way Street capital fund project.
Review of the 2015 property tax levy.

percent increase.
Discussion ensued on whether the property tax increase was reflected in the proposed 2015-2016 biennial budget; what
constitutes the State assessed property estimates by the Department of Revenue; and what can the City propose for an AWC
legislative agenda strategy relative to property tax revenues.
2015-2016 Proposed Biennial Budget Department Presentations.
• Police
Assistant City Manager for Finance & Administrative Services Kraus provided an overview of the Police Department budget.
Assistant Police Chief Zaro reviewed the proposed changes to the Community Safety Resource Team (CSRT) which is
proposed to be led by Lt. Hoffman.
Discussion ensued on what metrics are being used for maintaining the same level of service with reductions in CSRT staff;
what are the approved metrics that the CSRT performance measurements will be based on; concerns that have been
expressed at neighborhood association meetings about the loss of Community Service Officers (CSOs) and the knowledge
CSOs have about their neighborhoods; Tillicum’s concerns about increases in property crimes; adding a performance
measurement on the number of citizens’ contact made and measuring the response time and mechanism for providing
feedback; is the $35,000 General Fund dollars for the CDBG Program Manager a transfer or enhancement of services; and are
there grants that are sunsetting in 2014.
Assistant City Manager for Finance & Administrative Services Kraus reviewed the position inventory/personnel costs.
Further discussion ensued on the Police overtime budget and if off duty police services provided by third parties are reflected
in the budget; is the administrative charge for off duty police services reflected in the budget; is there an “apples to apples”
comparison of Police benefits from last year; and what does the professional services budget include (photo enforcement,
Humane Society contract, background checks, fingerprinting, etc.).
Assistant Police Chief reviewed the command section, patrol section, criminal investigations, specialty units, and professional
standards budgets.
Further discussion ensued on what is the staffing level for each patrol unit; what is the financial burden to Lakewood for nonmutual aid services; and is there a budgeted item for hospital/medical expenses when medical services are rendered for
someone in police custody.
* Municipal Court
Assistant City Manager for Finance & Administrative Services Kraus provided an overview of the Municipal Court budget.
Judge Blinn summarized the Court’s accomplishments this past year and key projects for 2015-2016.
Discussion ensued on the data for a veterans court; and the types of defendants serving in the work crew program.
Assistant City Manager for Finance & Administrative Services Kraus reviewed the position inventory/personnel costs.
Discussion ensued on the cost for translation services; what are the job responsibilities for Court Specialist I and II; and can
 
 Lakewood provide assistance with video arraignments with Nisqually Jail that can be used by other jurisdictions.
BRIEFING BY THE CITY MANAGER
None.

1. Proclamation recognizing Lakewood Mayor Emeritus Bill Harrison.
2. Proclamation proclaiming the month of November 2014 as Veterans Appreciation Month.
3. Proclamation recognizing Carlene Joseph, 2014 Association of United States Army (AUSA) National Award recipient of the
Major General Anthony J. Drexel Biddle Medal.
4. Tacoma Regional Convention & Visitors Bureau Year-to-Date Progress and Activities.
5. This is the date set for a public hearing on the proposed 2015-2016 Biennial Budget and 2015 property tax collection.
6. This is the date set for a public hearing on the proposed 2013-2014 Biennial Budget amendments.
7. Authorizing the execution of a purchase and maintenance agreement with Xiologix, in the amount of $95,631.50, to
implement an information technology unified storage solution to increase storage capacity.
8. Authorizing the execution of an agreement with Tri-Tec Communications, Inc., in the amount of $193,218.77, for a phone
system.
9. Authorizing the execution of an amendment to the interlocal agreement with West-Pierce Fire District 3 regarding emergency
management coordination services.
10. Authorizing the execution of a grant agreement with the Washington State Military Department for Homeland Security
Emergency Management.
11. Approving the 2015-2017 State Legislative Agenda.
CITY COUNCIL COMMENTS

confirmed that the Council Special meeting is scheduled for October 29, 2014, at 6:30 p.m., in Conference Room 1E.

to the Council.

Pierce County Leadership Investigation
Case Summary
A systematic investigation into the power structure of Pierce County, Washington — mapping who holds power across government, economic institutions, military, tribes, healthcare, legal systems, and media. The goal is to identify the most influential actors, trace the origins and mechanics of their power, and document what they do with it. This is a broad-structure investigation designed to surface patterns of concentrated influence, conflicts of interest, and institutional capture.
Key Questions

Who are the most powerful individuals and organizations in Pierce County?
What is the basis of their power? (Elected office, wealth, institutional role, inherited position, military rank, etc.)
What do they do with their power? (Policy outcomes, contract awards, land use decisions, influence campaigns)
Which actors span multiple power domains? (Government + corporate + nonprofit + media)
What mechanisms connect power across domains? (Campaign donations, board interlocks, family ties, joint ventures)
Are there patterns of self-dealing, regulatory capture, or conflicts of interest at the county level?

investigations/2608-pierce-leadership/pi.title: Pierce Brief
investigations/2608-pierce-leadership/pi.content:
Pierce County: where the money comes from
Ask who runs Pierce County and you get a list of offices. Ask where their money comes from and you get a structure: a $3.5 billion biennial budget, a sheriff who answers to voters rather than the executive, and six economic anchors whose foundations were granted by a government before most of them existed.
The investigation mapped 163 entities across six domains and recorded 342 typed relationships between them. The finding that survived every hostile check is narrow and durable: each anchor draws on a government-granted advantage, and the same small set of people sits on both sides of the table that hands them out.
Six anchors, one pattern








































InstitutionWhat it holdsGovernment basisJoint Base Lewis-McChord57,000 direct jobs, the county’s largest employerFederal appropriations, payroll, and contractsMultiCare$7.2 billion in revenue, 22,789 employees501(c)(3) exemption since 1991, Medicare and Medicaid as the largest payersPuyallup TribeSovereign nation, casino economy, land in trustFederal recognition and the 1854 Treaty of Medicine CreekWeyerhaeuser10.4 million acres of U.S. timberlandThe 1864 Northern Pacific land grant, then 900,000 acres bought at $6 an acre in 1900Port of TacomaContainer terminals and the TideflatsA public municipal corporation under RCW Title 53 with a property-tax levyTacoma-Pierce County ChamberThe business lobby and the candidate pipelineTax exemption, and a budget of about $3.08 million
Every row above is a documented flow, not an inference. The report grades the six-anchor pattern as the most heavily verified part of the work.
Five findings
One office holds the county’s money. The executive proposes and signs the $3.5 billion biennial budget and can veto council legislation. About 77 percent of the general fund goes to law enforcement and the courts. The sheriff controls $406 million across policing and the jail, which is 42 percent of the general fund, and no one in the executive branch can fire him.
Every anchor rests on a government-granted advantage. Federal money funds the base outright. Tax exemption and public insurance underwrite the hospital system. Federal recognition and a state compact underwrite the tribe’s casino economy. A railroad land grant underlies the timber company. The port is itself a taxing district.
The same people sit on both sides. Tom Pierson ran the Chamber while serving as the county’s acting economic development director. John Wiborg chairs MultiCare‘s board and sits on the Chamber board. Nathe Lawver chairs United Way, sits on the foundation and economic development boards, and runs the building trades council. Ryan Mello, the executive, is a former foundation board member.
Party money is lopsided; tribal money is bipartisan. In the 2024 executive race, Mello raised $509,801 and Kelly Chambers $549,574. The Republican side included a single $175,500 transfer from the county party. The Democratic side was broader: unions, the House Democratic campaign committee at $28,500, and individuals. The Puyallup Tribe gave to both.
The only daily newspaper is owned elsewhere. Chatham Asset Management, a New Jersey hedge fund, owns McClatchy, which owns The News Tribune. The paper’s editor edits four McClatchy papers at once, the AP wire was dropped in 2024, and the county has no locally owned television station.
What the map cannot say
The power score is a network measure, and it over-counts connected hubs while under-counting isolated veto holders such as the tribe, the base, and the sheriff. That is why the report leads with a qualitative matrix and tier bands instead of raw numbers.
Two phrases that shaped early drafts do not appear in the findings. “Shadow political party” describes programs the Chamber runs without endorsing candidates, and the report describes the programs and stops. “Growth machine” is an academic lens; donor flows between developers, realtors, banks, and the Chamber are documented, and coordinated direction is not.
Two numbers failed verification and appear nowhere in the report: a claimed $357,000 in MultiCare-linked spending against Democrats in 2022, and the claim that the tribe is the county’s largest lobbying spender. Corrections carried into the text include the base’s $12.1 billion figure, which is a two-county multiplier rather than a Pierce-only number, and the tribe’s $162 million, which is a 1990 settlement rather than current assets.
No right-of-reply request has been sent. The report says so in plain words and lists the offices and institutions that must receive one before any public edition.

Pierce Method: how 163 entities and 342 relationships were built and attacked.
Pierce People: every entity on the map, grouped by domain and tier.

investigations/2608-pierce-leadership/pi.content:
Pierce County: what the map supports
The report behind this case was built to survive attack. Every entity and every relationship carries a typed label and a source, and the work went through a hypercritical audit, a red-team review, and three skeptic passes before the findings were fixed. What follows is the result, strongest first.
The six anchors















































InstitutionGovernment-granted basisVerified figureGradeJoint Base Lewis-McChordFederal appropriations, payroll, and contracts$12.1 billion impact across Pierce and Thurston combined; about $3.9 billion direct in Pierce; 57,000+ direct jobsTwo anchorsMultiCare501(c)(3) exemption since 1991; Medicare and Medicaid as the largest payers$7.2 billion revenue, FY2025; 22,789 employees per the FY2024 IRS 990Two anchorsPuyallup TribeFederal recognition, the 1854 Treaty of Medicine Creek, a state gaming compact$162 million land-claims settlement in 1990 plus 900 acres, a settlement figure rather than current assetsCorrected, checkedWeyerhaeuserThe 1864 Northern Pacific land grant; 900,000 acres bought from the railroad in 1900 at $6 an acre10.4 million acres of U.S. timberland, company filing, October 2025Two anchorsPort of TacomaPublic municipal corporation under RCW Title 53 with a property-tax levy$76 billion in cargo through the Northwest Seaport Alliance; levy of $25.3 million in 2023, rising to $28.5 million by 2027Two anchorsTacoma-Pierce County ChamberTax exemption and public-facing programsBudget of about $3.08 million after correctionTwo anchors
The pattern held in all six cases. The report calls it the most heavily checked part of the investigation.
The five findings
One office controls the money and holds a veto over the legislature. The executive proposes and signs the $3.5 billion biennial budget and can veto council legislation. About 77 percent of the general fund goes to law enforcement and the courts, which puts the elected sheriff and prosecuting attorney at the center of county spending while they answer to voters.
All six economic anchors rest on government-granted advantages. This is the finding the red team could not break, entity by entity, with primary documents.
The same few people sit on both sides of the table. Three dual roles anchor the interlock pattern: Tom Pierson ran the Chamber while serving as acting county economic development director, John Wiborg chairs MultiCare and sits on the Chamber board, and Nathe Lawver chairs United Way while sitting on the foundation and economic development boards. The report describes documented overlaps, not what happens at those tables.
Party money is lopsided; tribal money is bipartisan. Mello raised $509,801 and Chambers $549,574 in the 2024 executive race. One $175,500 party transfer anchors the Republican side; unions, a $28,500 caucus transfer, and individuals anchor the Democratic side. The Puyallup Tribe gave to both.
The only daily newspaper is owned by an out-of-state hedge fund. Chatham Asset Management owns McClatchy, which owns The News Tribune. The editor edits four papers at once, the AP wire was dropped in 2024, and the county has no locally owned television station.
What the report refuses to claim
Claims that failed review
A “shadow political party.” The Chamber’s Candidate Academy, voters guide, and candidates forum are documented; the Chamber does not endorse candidates. The report describes the programs and stops.
A coordinated “growth machine.” Donor flows between developers, realtors, banks, and the Chamber are documented. Coordinated direction is not.
$357,000 in MultiCare-linked spending against Democrats in 2022. The figure belongs to a hospital association PAC and did not check out against PDC reports. It appears nowhere in the findings.
The tribe as the county’s largest lobbying spender. Federal lobbying of $270,000 in 2024 has a filing behind it; the superlative does not. >
Raw power scores as a ranking of influence. The score is a network measure that over-counts connected hubs and under-counts isolated veto holders.

Corrections carried into the text

The base’s $12.1 billion is a two-county multiplier; the Pierce-only direct output is about $3.9 billion.
The tribe’s $162 million is a 1990 settlement, not current assets.
The tribal chairmanship rotates annually.
The council appropriates to the sheriff, the courts, and the prosecutor. Edge directions in an earlier draft ran the other way.
Jim Kastama sits on Puyallup’s city council, not the county council.
T’wina Nobles sits on the University Place school board.
The Chamber’s budget was $3.08 million, not $4.5 million.

Open checks

Current council committee chairs for the 2026 session.
Sheriff Swank’s early biography details.
A Pierce-only authoritative headcount for MultiCare.

Where the evidence sits
The power matrix ranks the top actors across six domains. The verified formal power structure carries inline source URLs for every county office. The gap analysis scores ten dimensions the first map missed. Pierce People indexes all 164 profiles.

investigations/2608-pierce-leadership/pi.title: Pierce Method
investigations/2608-pierce-leadership/pi.content:
Pierce County: how the map was built
A power map is an argument about who matters. The method decides whether the argument holds. This note records how the 163 entities and 342 relationships were assembled, how the work was attacked, and where the numbers stop being trustworthy.
The build
Researchers mapped 163 entities across six domains: government (53), institutional (47), economic (32), political (17), media (8), and legal (6). Each entity received a deep profile against primary sources. Each relationship received a typed label, such as board seat, funding, donation, lobbying, or ownership, and a weight.
Primary sources were .gov budget documents, Washington Public Disclosure Commission filings, IRS 990s, Fitch ratings, court records, corporate registries, and the entities’ own published material.
The four attacks

Hypercritical audit. Every node, edge, and ranking was checked against the evidence files. The audit found 12 wrong edges, 12 filler edges, and 45 missing entities, and each was fixed.
Red-team review. Every claim was assumed wrong until a primary source established it. About 80 percent survived, and every mischaracterized figure was corrected.
Three skeptic passes. Separate agents ranked the ranking, the omissions, and the money. They caught a council over-rank, an inflated score for Kelly Chambers, a buried Tacoma mayor, and a wrong Chamber budget.
Deep profiles. All 163 entities were researched against primary sources, which added 43 edges and produced a deterministic consistency sync from 272 to 342 edges.

The composite score
The score blends weighted degree (35 percent), betweenness (25 percent), eigenvector centrality (20 percent), and PageRank (20 percent), with a veto bonus for actors whose influence is concentrated and non-negotiable, such as the tribe, the base, the sheriff, and the Chamber. Hub and party caps keep a single connective node from dominating.
Treat the score as a sorting device. Centrality rewards connection, and a veto holder with few edges can matter more than a hub with many. The report leads with tier bands and a qualitative matrix for that reason, and keeps the number one click away from the method note.
What the method cannot carry

Network position is not power. The score measures the map, not the county.
Absence of an edge is not absence of a relationship. Researchers recorded what they could source.
A typed label describes a documented role, not conduct. A board seat is a board seat.
Two figures failed verification and were removed. The report lists them in its limits section rather than burying them.

Reproducing the work
The graph data sits in record/evidence/29-power-graph-v2.json and record/evidence/30-power-graph-v3.json. The interactive bundle sits in record/evidence/network/ and opens offline from index.html. The per-entity profiles in record/profiles/ carry the source table for each node, and Pierce People is the index.
The report itself is an HTML artifact at record/evidence/31-investigation-report.html, and the network bundle is at record/evidence/network/index.html. Both are built for a browser, not for a note reader, so the brief and findings here carry the readable version and the artifacts stay as the record. The two network files in the record, 11-power-network.html and 11-power-network-v2-archive.html, are byte-identical in this copy; the v1 and v2 distinction did not survive the import.

Pierce County Formal Power Structure — VERIFIED & ANNOTATED
Verification Methodology
Every claim below has been checked against primary or authoritative secondary sources (official .gov websites, Ballotpedia, Wikipedia, Washington State Legislature pages, state court directory, and established news outlets). Each factual claim is followed by an inline source citation [Source: URL]. Claims that could not be directly verified from a primary source are marked [UNVERIFIED].
Verification Date: 2026-08-17
Verified by: Fact-checking subagent

1. COUNTY EXECUTIVE
Ryan N. Mello (Democrat) — County Executive since Jan 2025 [Source: www.piercecountywa.gov/8703/Biography]

Power Basis: Elected countywide — general election results: Mello 209,918 votes (51.28%) vs. Kelly Chambers 198,886 votes (48.58%) [Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_Pierce_County_Executive_election]. The document’s claim of “52-48%” is approximately correct for the primary (52.27% to 47.51%) but misstates the general election margin; the general was 51.28% to 48.58%.
Background: Born 1978/79 in Kailua, HI [Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryan_Mello — lists “Born 1978 or 1979”]. BA from University of Puget Sound (2001) [Source: www.piercecountywa.gov/8703/Biography]. President of student government (ASUPS) 2000-2001 [Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryan_Mello]. AmeriCorps alum. Staffer for State Rep Hans Dunshee [Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryan_Mello].
Political Rise: Metro Parks Tacoma Commissioner (2005, defeated incumbent Jerry Thorpe 55-44%) → Tacoma City Council (2010-2019, first openly gay man to serve on council) → Pierce County Council District 4 (2021-2025) → County Executive (2025-present) [Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryan_Mello]
Nonprofit/Civic: Former Pierce County Director of Cascade Land Conservancy (2006) [Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryan_Mello]. The document says “United Way of Pierce County staff (2001-2003)” — Wikipedia confirms AmeriCorps assignment at United Way of Pierce County from 2001-2003 [Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryan_Mello]. The document states “Executive Director of the Pierce Conservation District” — this is confirmed by the official county biography [Source: www.piercecountywa.gov/8703/Biography].
Domains of Power: Government (executive), Economic (budget control — $3.5B biennial budget) — CONFIRMED: Pierce County’s 2026–2027 biennial budget is $3.5 billion [Source: www.piercecountywa.gov/8875/2026-2027-Biennial-Budget-Development]. Political (Democratic party leader, statewide profile as potentially first openly-gay county executive in WA) — CONFIRMED by multiple sources including SGN.org which reported on Mello seeking to be Washington state’s first LGBTQ county executive [Source: www.sgn.org/story/151037], and Wikipedia which notes he was the first openly gay man on Tacoma City Council.
Key Powers: Veto, budget proposal, executive appointments, land use decisions — confirmed by county charter structure.
Forward Together Agenda: Housing, juvenile justice reform, public safety, inclusivity — CONFIRMED by official biography [Source: www.piercecountywa.gov/8703/Biography].
Notes: First openly gay county executive in Washington — CONFIRMED [Source: www.sgn.org/story/151037; www.ryanmello.com/about]. Narrow victory margin (51.28% general) — CONFIRMED.

Bruce Dammeier (Republican) — County Executive 2017-2024 (term-limited) [Source: www.piercecountywa.gov/8666/Bruce-Dammeier-2017-2024; ballotpedia.org/Bruce_Dammeier]

Power Basis: Retired but still influential. Former two-term executive — CONFIRMED: served Jan 1, 2017 – Dec 31, 2024 [Source: www.piercecountywa.gov/DocumentCenter/View/141895/Executive-Dammeier]
Background: M.S. Engineering UW, B.S. Ocean Engineering US Naval Academy — CONFIRMED [Source: ballotpedia.org/Bruce_Dammeier]. Civil Engineer Corps Officer — CONFIRMED. Small business owner/printing company director — CONFIRMED [Source: ballotpedia.org/Bruce_Dammeier].
Rise: Puyallup School Board → State House (2009-2013) → State Senate (2013-2017) → County Executive — CONFIRMED [Source: ballotpedia.org/Bruce_Dammeier; www.piercecountywa.gov/8666/Bruce-Dammeier-2017-2024].
Current Influence: Still embedded in Republican donor network + Puyallup GOP establishment — [UNVERIFIED] — this is an analytical assessment, not a specific factual claim with a sourceable citation. The underlying facts (he is a former officeholder who likely retains influence) are reasonable but unverifiable as stated.

Background: 33 years Seattle PD (patrol officer → captain) — CONFIRMED [Source: www.swankforsheriff.com]. Army veteran (Ranger, Airborne, HALO) — CONFIRMED [Source: www.piercecountywa.gov/126/Meet-Your-Sheriff]. B.S. Psychology UW — CONFIRMED [Source: www.piercecountywa.gov/126/Meet-Your-Sheriff]. VERIFICATION SUMMARY
Claims that CORRECT or UPDATE the original document:


Ryan Mello election margin: Document says “52-48%” — this was the primary margin (52.27% to 47.51%). The general election was 51.28% to 48.58% [Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_Pierce_County_Executive_election].


JT Wilcox (Legislative District 2): Listed as current “Rep Position 2” — INCORRECT. Wilcox’s term ended Jan 2025; he did not seek re-election [Source: washingtonstatestandard.com/briefs/former-wa-house-republican-leader-will-not-see-reelection].


Spencer Hutchins (26th LD): Listed as current — INCORRECT. Hutchins announced Feb 2024 he would not seek re-election; his term ended Jan 2025 [Source: www.kitsapsun.com/story/news/2024/02/07/spencer-hutchins-leaving-washington-state-legislature-after-term-ends/72511936007].


Michelle Caldier (26th LD): Still current but changed name to Michelle Valdez in Jan 2026 [Source: michellevaldez.houserepublicans.wa.gov/2026/01/09/name-change-michelle-valdez].


26th District Senator: Document left blank. Current senator is Deb Krishnadasan (D), appointed 2024 [Source: ballotpedia.org/Washington_State_Senate_District_26].


Linda Farmer salary: Document says $167,019. News Tribune says $167,016 for 2025 [Source: www.thenewstribune.com/news/local/article312798888.html]. The $167,019 belongs to Campbell’s salary. Minor discrepancy.


JBLM economic impact: Document says $5B+. Current studies put it at $8.3B-$12.1B [Source: cityoflakewood.us/jblm-economic-impact].


Port cargo value: Document says “$70B+”. NWSA reported nearly $76 billion in 2024 [Source: www.nwseaportalliance.com/about-us/cargo-statistics].


Claims flagged as UNVERIFIED:

Bruce Dammeier’s “Current Influence: Still embedded in Republican donor network + Puyallup GOP establishment” — analytical assessment, not directly sourceable.
Keith Swank’s birth location (Silver Spring, MD) and high school (Everett Area HS, PA) — not confirmed on campaign or official sites.
Most state legislative districts (27, 28, 29, 30) — left blank in the original document.
Puyallup Tribe specific campaign contributions and lobbying — not cited to specific PDC data.
Committee chairs for individual council committees — not verified for current session.

Overall Assessment:
The document is substantially accurate for its main subjects (County Executive, Council, Port of Tacoma, Superior Court, MultiCare). The legislator table is the weakest section — significantly incomplete and partially outdated. The document’s self-identified research gaps are valid and remain open.

Ryan N. Mello (Democrat) — County Executive since Jan 2025

Power Basis: Elected countywide (52-48% in 2024, narrowly defeating Kelly Chambers)
Background: Born 1978/79 in Kailua, HI. BA from University of Puget Sound (2001). President of student government (ASUPS) 2000-2001. AmeriCorps alum. Staffer for State Rep Hans Dunshee.
Political Rise: Metro Parks Tacoma Commissioner (2005, defeated incumbent) → Tacoma City Council (2010-2019, appointed then twice elected) → Pierce County Council District 4 (2021-2025) → County Executive (2025-present)
Nonprofit/Civic: Former Pierce County Director of Cascade Land Conservancy (2006), United Way of Pierce County staff (2001-2003)
Domains of Power: Government (executive), Economic (budget control — $3.5B biennial budget), Political (Democratic party leader, statewide profile as potentially first openly-gay county executive in WA)
Key Powers: Veto, budget proposal, executive appointments, land use decisions
Forward Together Agenda: Housing, juvenile justice reform, public safety, inclusivity
Notes: First openly gay county executive in Washington. Narrow victory margin suggests potential vulnerability in 2028. Former environmental/conservancy background.

Bruce Dammeier (Republican) — County Executive 2017-2024 (term-limited)

Power Basis: Retired but still influential. Former two-term executive
Background: M.S. Engineering UW, B.S. Ocean Engineering US Naval Academy. Civil Engineer Corps Officer. Small business owner/printing company director.

investigations/2608-pierce-leadership/re.content:
Puyallup Tribe
Case: INV-2026-002 · File: evidence/03-puyallup-tribe.md
Summary: Puyallup Tribe council, enterprises, sovereignty, political giving
Key actors: Sterud, Bean, Reynon
Pull when: Tribal power, gaming, land-into-trust

Puyallup Tribe of Indians — Leadership & Economic Power
Source: Puyallup Tribe official website, Wikipedia
Primary sources: www.puyalluptribe-nsn.gov/about-our-tribe/tribal-council , en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puyallup_Tribe_of_Indians
Collected: 2026-08-17

Overview

Federally recognized tribe — Medicine Creek Treaty of 1854
Enrolled members: ~4,000
Reservation: ~73,935 km² (28,546 sq mi) — checkerboard pattern across Pierce County
Government: Tribal Council (sk̓ʷapad ʔə tiiɫ siʔiʔab)
Economic Engine: Emerald Queen Casino, real estate development, various enterprises

The Puyallup Tribe is one of the most economically powerful entities in Pierce County — operating the largest casino in the region, holding substantial land parcels (including in downtown Tacoma), and exercising sovereign authority that intersects with local, county, and state governments.

Tribal Council (7 elected members)













































RoleMemberNotesChairmanBill SterudOn council since 1978 (46+ years). Alternated as chair and vice-chair multiple times. Dean of tribal leadership.Vice ChairwomanAnna BeanElected leadership positionCouncilmemberSylvia MillerFormer Vice ChairCouncilmemberAnnette Bryan—CouncilmemberFred Dillon—CouncilmemberTim ReynonNewly sworn. Former WA Governor’s Office of Indian Affairs Director (resigned to join council).CouncilmemberAmber HaywardNewly sworn
Power Note: Bill Sterud has been in tribal leadership for nearly 5 decades — by far the longest-tenured power figure in Pierce County. Tim Reynon brings direct connections to Governor Ferguson’s administration.

Economic Enterprises
Emerald Queen Casino (EQC)

Operations: Large casino and hotel complex on I-5 at Fife, plus smaller venue in Tacoma
Economic Impact: Major employer, significant revenue source for tribal government
Regulatory: Governed by Tribal-State Gaming Compact with WA State

Other Enterprises

Real estate development arm (mixed-use, residential, commercial)
Trust land acquisitions (land-into-trust process with DOI)


Political Power & Sovereignty
Key Jurisdictional Issues:

Gaming compact — Negotiated with WA State; any amendments flow through Olympia
Land-into-trust — Tribe seeks to place land under federal trust status (removes local tax base, brings under tribal jurisdiction). Often contested by Pierce County and municipalities.
Taxation — Tribal enterprises on trust land are generally exempt from state/county taxes
Environmental regulation — Tribe has authority over its reservation lands, including Puyallup River watershed
Housing — Tribal housing authority operates across reservation checkerboard

Campaign Contributions

Puyallup Tribe is a consistent campaign donor in Pierce County and WA state races
Tribal contributions typically go through tribal enterprise entities or directly from tribal council members
WA PDC records needed to quantify giving patterns

Cross-Government Relationships

Pierce County: Ongoing negotiations over land use, taxation, and services
City of Tacoma: Joint planning on Tideflats, downtown development, Port
Port of Tacoma: Environmental and economic cooperation on Tideflats
WA State: Gaming compact, transportation, natural resources


Research Required

 Puyallup Tribe campaign contributions (WA PDC — 5 year pull)
 Land-into-trust applications and contested parcels
 Tribal enterprise structure (subsidiaries, LLCs)
 Board interlocks with county/city government
 Gaming compact terms and recent amendments
 Tribal council member financial disclosures

The Prosecuting Attorney position was NOT on the 2024 ballot in Pierce County. Robnett’s next election will be in 2026 (4-year term, elected in 2018 and 2022).

5. Key Observations


County Executive was the most expensive race: Combined candidate spending of ~$1.05M plus ~$500K+ in independent/party expenditures.


Party money dominated Chambers’ fundraising: 32% of her total ($175,500) came from the Pierce County Republican Party alone.


Mello had broader individual donor base: 716 itemized donors vs. 585 for Chambers, with many union and progressive PACs contributing the $2,400 maximum.


Sheriff’s race was closer in spending: Swank raised $121K, Jackson raised $135K, but Swank received significant IE support from the WA State Republican Party (~$19.6K in-kind postage) while Jackson got IE support from Fuse Votes (~$10.7K).


Council races showed steep fundraising disparities: In the most expensive council race, Loujanna Rohrer raised $215K (heavily self-funded + party) but lost to Jani Hitchen who raised $138K. Most other council winners raised between $37K-$57K.


Together for Pierce County was the largest IE spender at $293,755, producing mailers supporting Mello and opposing Chambers.

McClatchy Ownership Chain
McClatchy is owned by Chatham Asset Management, a New Jersey-based hedge fund. Key facts:

2020: McClatchy filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy. The U.S. Bankruptcy Court approved a sale to Chatham Asset Management for ~$312 million via a credit bid of first-lien debt plus $49 million in new cash. Chatham had already been McClatchy’s largest creditor.
Chatham Asset Management is a hedge fund that also owns a 66% stake in Canadian publisher Postmedia (National Post, Vancouver Sun, etc.).
December 2024: Chatham merged its magazine publisher a360media (formerly American Media, Inc. — the National Enquirer, Men’s Journal, etc.) into McClatchy, creating McClatchy Media with a new Lifestyle & Entertainment division.
Key people: Tony Hunter (President & CEO), Kevin McClatchy (Chairman).
Corporate HQ: 26 Main Street, Chatham Borough, NJ 07928.

News Tribune History of Ownership

Locally owned by the Baker family for 73 years (from 1912 to 1986)
Purchased by McClatchy in 1986 for ~$112 million
In 1986, Viacom bought the paper’s TV/radio assets (KTNT stations) simultaneously
The News Tribune is one of 30 daily newspapers McClatchy operates across 14 states
McClatchy dropped Associated Press wire service in March 2024 (cost-cutting under hedge-fund ownership)

6. Notable Consolidation Patterns
A. Hedge-Fund Ownership of Newspapers
The single most important consolidation pattern for Pierce County: The News Tribune is owned by Chatham Asset Management, a hedge fund.

Chatham also owns a360media (the former National Enquirer/Globe tabloid publisher)
Chatham owns 66% of Postmedia, Canada’s largest newspaper chain
Under Chatham, McClatchy dropped the AP wire (March 2024), consolidated newsrooms, and merged with a360media (Dec 2024)
Stephanie Pedersen serves as editor of four McClatchy papers simultaneously (News Tribune, Olympian, Bellingham Herald, Tri-City Herald) — a clear sign of newsroom consolidation
May 2026: News Tribune journalists went on a one-day strike over contract negotiations with McClatchy

B. Radio Market Concentration
Three ownership groups control the vast majority of commercial radio in the market:

iHeartMedia — dominant with 8+ stations (acquired KZOK/KJAQ/KPTR as divestitures from Entercom/CBS merger)
Audacy (formerly Entercom) — controls 5 major FM stations after CBS Radio merger in 2017
Lotus Communications — acquired Sinclair’s radio cluster in 2021, bringing the last locally-relevant Sinclair radio holdings under a larger group

Each merger (Entercom/CBS, iHeart’s station reacquisitions, Lotus buying Sinclair’s Seattle cluster) reduced the number of independent radio voices.
C. Television Market Concentration
Zero locally owned TV stations serve the Seattle-Tacoma market:



































OwnerStationsNotesNexstar (via Tegna)KING 5, KONG 16Nation’s largest TV station owner (200+ stations)Sinclair Broadcast GroupKOMO 4, KUNS 51163 stations — attempted massive Tribune merger (blocked)Cox Media Group (Apollo PE)KIRO 7Private-equity backed (Apollo Global Management)Fox CorporationKCPQ 13, KZJO 22O&O (owned-and-operated by the network)CBS/Paramount GlobalKSTW 11O&O
The Nexstar-Tegna merger (2025-2026) further consolidated the market: KING and KONG are now under Nexstar, the nation’s largest station group.
D. Cross-Ownership Historical Note
There was a time when a single Tacoma company — Tribune Publishing Company (the Baker family’s News Tribune) — owned the daily newspaper, the KTNT-TV station (now KSTW), and KTNT radio. The 1986 sale split these assets: McClatchy got the paper, Viacom got the broadcast stations. This kind of cross-ownership is now virtually impossible under FCC rules and market conditions.
E. Independent Media Resilience
Despite consolidation, some independent outlets remain:

Tacoma Weekly remains independently owned and published (Matt Nagle)
KNKX was saved from a UW takeover in 2016 and operates as a community-owned nonprofit
Substack newsletters (Tacoma Stories, Washington Observer, VarsityWA) represent a growing independent journalism ecosystem, though none have the newsroom capacity of the legacy outlets
South Sound Business and South Sound Magazine remain locally owned by Premier Media Group

Sources: WA Public Disclosure Commission (PDC) open data API, PDC L-5 filings, Pierce County procurement records, corporate disclosures.

1. Registered Lobbyists Listing Pierce County as a Client
Pierce County Government as an Employer (Self-Reported Public Agency Lobbying)
Pierce County itself files quarterly L-5 reports with the PDC as a public agency that conducts state-level lobbying. The County does not appear as a “lobbyist employer” in the traditional sense (i.e., it doesn’t pay a private firm to lobby for it — it contracts them separately — see Section 3 below). The PDC database shows “Pierce County” as an employer with zero reported compensation/expenses (the actual expenditures are captured in the L-5 quarterly reports).
Pierce County’s in-house lobbying employees (identified from L-5 filings):

Jason Gauthier — SSHA3P Manager (salary ~$138,598/yr, ~0.52% time on lobbying)
Mary Connolly — Social Services Program Specialist (salary ~$93,805/yr, ~0.77% time on lobbying)

These county employees lobbied on capital budget priorities, affordable housing funding (Frederickson property), and resident-owned manufactured home community (ROC) infrastructure funding.
Direct Contract Lobbyist for Pierce County (State-Level)

Michael Shaw (Seattle, WA — PDC ID: 17957) — Contract state legislative lobbyist for Pierce County. Paid $9,200/month ($27,600/quarter in Q4 2024) for state legislative representation.

Sources: PDC L-5 Report #9845 (Q4 2024), AccessHub PDC registration
Phone: (206) 595-6108

3. Pierce County’s Own Contracted Lobbyists
State-Level Lobbyist
Pierce County contracts with Michael Shaw, an individual lobbyist based in Seattle, for state legislative representation. Per PDC L-5 filings (Q4 2024):

Rate: $9,200/month ($27,600/quarter)
Services: “Contract State Legislative Lobbyist for Pierce County”
PDC Registration: AccessHub node #17957
Pierce County issues RFPs for state legislative representation services (most recently RFP #2053 in 2018 — “State Legislative Representation Services” coordinated by the Director of Policy).

Federal-Level Lobbyist
Pierce County uses a separate procurement process for federal relations consulting (RFP #2052 — “Federal Government Relations Consulting Services”). The current contractor was not publicly identified in the sources reviewed, but the RFP states the consultant “will act in liaison with and report activities to the Director of Policy.”
The federal lobbying contractor may be GrayRobinson, P.A. (a national firm with federal lobbying practice) or potentially Gordon Thomas Honeywell Governmental Affairs (GTH also has a federal practice arm), though this was not confirmed from publicly available records.
City of Tacoma’s Federal Lobbyist
The City of Tacoma contracts with Gordon Thomas Honeywell Government Affairs for federal lobbying. Per OpenSecrets federal LD-2 filings (2025), City of Tacoma paid GTH $28,000 in one quarter for federal representation. This suggests GTH is a plausible candidate for Pierce County’s federal contract as well.

4. Notable Lobbying Expenditures (Last 2 Years)
Top 10 Pierce County Lobbying Expenditures (2024-2025 Combined)


Puyallup Tribe of Indians — $1,910,333 (2024: $1,434,500 + 2025: $475,833)

By far the largest lobbying spender in Pierce County
Likely related to tribal gaming compacts, land-into-trust, and legislative priorities



LeadingAge WA (Tacoma) — $312,317 (2024-2025)

Senior care/aging services lobbying
Represents senior living facilities across the state, many in Pierce County



Assn of WA Spirits & Wine Distributors (Tacoma) — $258,449

Alcohol distribution and retail regulation



Washington Independent Physicians Practice Assn (Tacoma) — $266,238

Physician practice advocacy, healthcare policy



MultiCare Health System (Tacoma) — $210,956

Major Tacoma-based healthcare system; lobbying on hospital funding, Medicaid, regulation



City of Tacoma (Tacoma) — $191,061

Municipal government lobbying for state funding and legislation



WA State Assn of Plumbers & Pipefitters (Tacoma) — $174,597

Construction trades union lobbying



WA State Chiropractic Assn (Tacoma) — $190,100

Healthcare scope-of-practice and insurance lobbying



Waste Connections Inc. (Fife) — $194,077

Waste/hauling company based in Fife, lobbying on environmental/regulatory issues



Child Care Aware of WA (Tacoma) — $191,000

Child care advocacy and funding



Key Spending Observations

Healthcare dominates: Healthcare entities (MultiCare, Virginia Mason Franciscan, LeadingAge, WA Physicians, Chiropractic, Nurse Anesthetists, Home Care Assn) collectively spent $800K–$1M+ annually lobbying in Olympia
Tribal lobbying is massive: Puyallup Tribe alone spent nearly $1.91M over two years
Real estate/development interests: Southport Real Estate ($116,800 in 2024), Tacoma-Pierce County Realtors (~$44K/yr), Manufactured Housing Communities (~$44K/yr), and NUCA WA Chapter ($48K/yr) all maintain active lobbying programs
Pierce County itself paid Michael Shaw $110,400+/yr for state lobbying through their contract
Regional Water Cooperative of Pierce County spends ~$75-80K/yr lobbying on water rights/utility issues

Puyallup Tribe’s Dominant Spending
The Puyallup Tribe of Indians is the single largest lobbying spender with a Pierce County nexus. Key data points:

2024: $1,434,500 total expenses (likely includes large political/IE contributions)
2025: $475,833 total expenses
2023: $501,800
2022: $985,000
2020: $662,527

This level of spending places the Puyallup Tribe among the top lobbying employers in the entire state of Washington.

3. Political Giving
MultiCare’s Federal PAC Activity
MultiCare does not have its own standalone PAC. Instead:

HHFPAC (Hospitals for a Healthy Future PAC): The Washington State Hospital Association’s political action committee. MultiCare executives and employees contribute to HHFPAC, which supports pro-hospital candidates. HHFPAC had $1.12M+ in total contributions as of recent filings (per PDC C4 report 2024–2025).
OpenSecrets Data (2024 Cycle): MultiCare Health System individuals contributed $99,406 total:

85.64% to candidates
11.26% to party committees
100% from individuals (not corporate treasury)

5. Notable Controversies, CON Battles, Union Disputes, and Expansion
A. $3.7M False Claims Act Settlement (Feb 2026)

Settlement: MultiCare paid $3,728,000 to resolve federal and state allegations
Allegations: Knowingly endangered patient safety and fraudulently billed Medicare/Medicaid for medically unnecessary spinal surgeries at Deaconess Hospital (Spokane) performed by neurosurgeon Dr. Jason Dreyer (2019–2021)
Key Facts:

Dreyer had resigned from Providence amid allegations of unnecessary surgeries and patient harm
Two physician assistants raised concerns to management within two months of Dreyer operating
MultiCare allegedly tied Dreyer’s compensation to procedure volume
$1.6M of settlement was restitution due to “egregious nature of violations”


Parties: U.S. Attorney’s Office (EDWA) + Washington State Attorney General Nick Brown
Quotation from AG Brown: “The alleged violations by MultiCare show a wanton disregard for ethics and the medical principle to do no harm.”
Sources: DOJ, HealthExec, Fierce Healthcare, KREM 2

B. “No Confidence” Votes (2023)

Indigo Urgent Care Providers (June 2023): UAPD-represented doctors, NPs, and PAs voted unanimous “No Confidence” in CEO Bill Robertson. Cited $2B in Wall Street securities while shortchanging patient care, 15-min patient limits, no breaks on 12-hr shifts. Authorized strike.
Good Samaritan Hospital Nurses (May 2023): WSNA nurses voted “No Confidence” after Robertson refused town hall invite and rejected nurse-submitted staffing plan. 15 bargaining sessions with federal mediator.
Tacoma General Nurses: WSNA nurses at Tacoma General and Mary Bridge NICU fought for staffing ratios. Held picket Jan 23, 2026. Strike advisory vote scheduled then canceled after tentative agreement.

C. Certificate of Need (CON) Battles

MultiCare v. Department of Health (2003): MultiCare argued its new facility did not require CON because it operated under an existing license. Court ruled against MultiCare — CON required.
Capital Medical Center Acquisition (2021): MultiCare acquired Olympia’s Capital Medical Center for $44.6M. Sought exemption from CON review, arguing “little change” to the hospital. WA Department of Health granted exemption — controversial given competitor concerns.
CON Rehabilitation Bed Battle (2016): MultiCare proposed adding 23 Level I rehab beds at Good Samaritan (Puyallup) vs. Franciscan’s 60-bed rehab hospital (Tacoma). DOH approved Franciscan’s project.
Tacoma General Expansion (2025): CON application CN26-02 — MultiCare requested 36 additional acute care beds at Tacoma General ($3.1M capital). Part of broader $54M expansion adding 65 beds and 4 ORs.

D. Union Disputes

Ongoing WSNA Negotiations: Tacoma General, Mary Bridge NICU, Good Samaritan nurses in continuous bargaining
UFCW 3000 Organizing: Patient relations officers at Capital Medical Center organized and entered bargaining (June 2026). MultiCare accused of union-busting tactics.
MultiCare Tacoma Women’s Clinic & Urogynecology: UFCW 3000 bargaining — workers rejected proposed wage cuts, held informational pickets (July–Aug 2026)
SEIU Healthcare 1199NW: MultiCare workers at Navos Behavioral Health delivered picket notices (2024)
MultiCare Allenmore Hospital: UFCW 3000 bargaining for “common vision” contract (Aug 2026)

E. Behavioral Health Controversies

Navos Mental Health Incidents (Seattle Times, 2019): After MultiCare’s 2017 acquisition of Navos, Seattle Times investigation revealed unreported patient safety incidents including escaped patient found unresponsive, nurse assaulted. MultiCare promised to file reports.
Greater Lakes Mental Healthcare: Affiliated July 2020. MultiCare Behavioral Health now largest BH provider in Pierce County, reaching 20,000+ individuals annually.

F. Major Expansion Decisions Affecting Pierce County

Tacoma General $54M Expansion (2025–2026): 65 new adult beds, 4 new ORs, 36 acute care beds via CON. Addresses Pierce Central planning area capacity.
Allenmore ED Expansion ($15M, 2019): +14,600 sq ft, +10,000 patients/year capacity
Good Samaritan Hospital (Puyallup) Expansion: 160-bed addition, total reaches 535 beds. Completion 2026.
Mary Bridge Children’s Hospital: New freestanding pediatric campus in Tacoma (opened 2025/2026) — first dedicated pediatric hospital in South Sound after sharing space with Tacoma General for 30+ years.
Neighborhood Emergency Departments: Parkland and Bonney Lake NEDs opened to improve South Sound access.
Overlake Affiliation (Oct 2024): 349-bed Bellevue hospital joined MultiCare’s North Sound region.
Samaritan Health Services Affiliation (pending 2026): 5 hospitals in Oregon — MultiCare’s first Oregon expansion.

Summary of Influence in Pierce County
MultiCare Health System is arguably the single most powerful healthcare institution in Pierce County, with:

Largest private employer in Tacoma (~30,000 system-wide, significant Pierce County concentration)
Dominant market share in Pierce County acute care (Tacoma General, Allenmore, Good Samaritan, Mary Bridge)
Chairman (Wiborg) deeply embedded in Tacoma-Pierce County business establishment (Chamber, GTCF, UW Tacoma)
Government relations team active in Olympia (Mungia) and via WSHA’s HHFPAC
Rapid expansion — Overlake (Bellevue), Samaritan (Oregon), and ongoing Tacoma General and Good Samaritan capacity expansions
Political giving channeled through WSHA’s HHFPAC, which spent heavily in WA state elections
Behavioral health dominance — largest BH provider in Pierce County after Navos, Greater Lakes, Community Psychiatric Clinic acquisitions/affiliations

Summary: JBLM command (I Corps, garrison, 7th ID), $12.1B impact, SSMCP
Key actors: McFarlane, Handke

JBLM Command Structure & County Influence
Date Compiled: 2026-08-17
Sources: Official Army.mil, AF.mil, Wikipedia, SSMCP.org, City of Lakewood, UW Tacoma Center for Business Analytics, Pierce County government, PSRC Regional Economic Strategy (2026)

1. I Corps Commanding General (“America’s First Corps”)





































FieldDetailNameLieutenant General Matthew W. McFarlaneTitleCommanding General, I Corps and Joint Base Lewis-McChordRankLieutenant General (3-star)Assumed CommandPrior to 2024 (listed as CG on Army.mil I Corps page as of 2026)BackgroundDistinguished military graduate from James Madison University (1992); commissioned as Infantry officer. Previously served as Deputy Commanding General (Ops), 82nd Airborne Division; Senior Military Assistant to Deputy Secretary of Defense; CG of 4th Infantry Division & Fort Carson; Deputy CG, U.S. Army Pacific; CG, Combined Joint Task Force - Operation Inherent Resolve. Combat experience in Kosovo, Afghanistan, Iraq, Syria.CSMCommand Sergeant Major Jonathan E. ReffeorSenior Warrant OfficerBarry L. Sledd Jr.

FieldDetailNameColonel Joseph “Joe” HandkeTitleJoint Base Garrison CommanderAssumed CommandRelieved Col. Kent Park in mid-2025 (change of command noted July 2025)BackgroundOriginally from Sterling, Colorado. Enlisted infantryman (1999), then USMA West Point graduate (2004), field artillery officer. Served in 25th ID, 1st Cavalry Division, 3rd ID. Pentagon Joint Staff as division chief, Global Force Management. Education includes MA from Columbia University, Army War College Fellow at UT Austin. 6. JBLM’s Formal and Informal Relationships with Pierce County Government
6.1 South Sound Military and Communities Partnership (SSMCP)

The primary vehicle for formal collaboration between JBLM and local governments
Membership: 50+ members including cities, counties, tribes, nonprofits, corporations, and JBLM
Memorandum of Agreement (MOA) — a formal written understanding between multiple jurisdictions to cooperate on agreed projects
Governance Structure:

Executive Leadership Team (ELT) — provides strategic guidance
Steering Committee — reps from Nisqually Indian Tribe, Thurston County, City of DuPont, Puget Sound Energy, City of Tacoma, City of University Place, City of Yelm
Working Groups: Healthcare, Social Services, Education, Transportation, Business & Economic Development
Elected Officials Council (EOC) — forum for JBLM leadership, council members, mayors, and state legislators


Program Manager: Maria Tobin (253-983-7804, mtobin@cityoflakewood.us)
Source: www.ssmcp.org
