6.2 Joint Land Use Study (JLUS) — 2015

Collaborative process among federal, regional, local governments, tribes, and public
Designed to balance military operational demands with community land use plans, economic development, and environmental sustainability
Study area: communities within ~2 miles of JBLM boundary
Key Issues Addressed: Urban growth encroachment, aircraft safety zones, noise compatibility, threatened/endangered species, transportation, unauthorized use of training lands
Participating Agencies: Pierce County, Thurston County, City of Lakewood, DuPont, Tacoma, Steilacoom, Lacey, Yelm, Roy, Rainier, Nisqually Indian Tribe, among others
Not binding — participants asked to make “good faith efforts” to implement recommendations
Source: www.ssmcp.org/joint-land-use-study

6.3 JBLM North Clear Zone

Active SSMCP project addressing land use compatibility around McChord Field’s north clear zone
Involves Pierce County planning processes
Source: www.ssmcp.org/jblm-north-clear-zone/

6.4 Growth Coordination Plan (2022)

Framework of implementable action items to improve quality of life in JBLM region while balancing military readiness
Builds on 2010 GCP
Addresses off-base housing (71% of active duty live off-base), infrastructure, transportation
Source: www.ssmcp.org/2022-jblm-growth-coordination-plan/

6.5 Transportation Coordination

I-5 JBLM corridor improvements coordinated with WSDOT
JLUS incorporates regional transportation work by WSDOT
SSMCP advocates for: widening DuPont/Steilacoom Road from Integrity Gate to Exit 119, addressing at-grade rail crossing near JBLM main gate (Exit 120), SR 510 Yelm Loop completion
Source: SSMCP home page / legislative advocacy section

6.6 Environmental Coordination

JBLM and partners work on prairie habitat protection/restoration (threatened and endangered species)
Air Installations Compatible Use Zone (AICUZ) study for noise footprint and accident potential zones

investigations/2608-pierce-leadership/re.title: 12-panel-progressive-disclosure-spec
investigations/2608-pierce-leadership/re.content:
Progressive-Disclosure Entity Panel — Design Spec
Target: evidence/11-power-network.html drawer (#drawer, 340px). Goal: clicking a node feels calm — one focal point, not 8 stacked sections — and relationships are seen (color + icon + arrow), not read.
1. Above-the-fold layout (always visible on open)
Three blocks, in order, nothing else:

Header — unchanged: glyph + name (domain color), type · domain · Power badge.
Thesis strip — unchanged single-line card (domain-driven thesis string).
ONE focal element — chosen by a priority switch, first match wins:


























Entity profileFocal elementReceives public money (MONEY_RELS edge, dir in)Money-source callout (gold box)Board-interlock person (≥2 INTERLOCK_RELS edges)“Multiple hats” strip — the 2–3 boards/roles as interlock chipsGovernment actor (no money-in)“Who influences them” — top 3 influence chips (dir in)Everything else”Where its power leads” — top 3 outbound influence chips
The focal element is the only content below the thesis strip. Everything else is hidden.
2. Disclosure mechanism — staged accordion
A single “More” button (full-width, border:1px solid #E0E0E0, 8px radius) sits directly under the focal element. Clicking it reveals three collapsible <details> sections, in this order:

About — description + key-facts bullet list.
Connections — the full thesis-grouped relationship list (see §4).
Follow the thread — the nudge line.

<details>/<summary> gives native keyboard + ARIA disclosure semantics for free. The “More” button toggles to “Less” and collapses all three when clicked again. One section open at a time (close siblings on open) — keeps the drawer calm even when expanded.
3. Relationship visual system — the core change
Every relationship renders as a chip with three redundant cues: color + icon + direction arrow. Redundancy is the UDL move: color-blind users read the icon, low-vision users read the color, everyone reads the arrow.
Exact mapping (color / icon / arrow):



































Relationship classColorIconDirectionMoney flows (MONEY_RELS)Gold #B8860B$→ (out) / ← (in)Influence (INFLUENCE_RELS)Target’s domain color→→ (out) / ← (in)Board interlock (INTERLOCK_RELS)#1B1B1B on #FAFAFA⬡↔ (bidirectional, no arrow)Structural/other (veto, oversight, owns)#666⚙→ / ←
Direction rule: the arrow always points from the source of power to the receiver. dir:"out" = this entity is the source → arrow points away (→); dir:"in" = this entity receives → arrow points in (←). Money and influence are directional; interlocks are always ↔ (a seat is mutual).
Chip anatomy: [icon] [label] [arrow] — e.g. $ MultiCare →, → County Council ←, ⬡ Port of Tacoma ↔. The icon and arrow are the first and last glyphs so the eye lands on them; the label sits between.
4. Connection chip redesign
Three visually distinct chip styles (all border-radius:4px, padding:2px 6px, font-size:12px, clickable → navigateTo):

Money chip: background:#FFF8E1; border:1px solid #B8860B; color:#B8860B; — gold-tinted fill, gold border, $ prefix, →/← suffix.
Influence chip: background:<domainColor>1A; border:1px solid <domainColor>; color:<domainColor>; — the target’s domain color at ~10% fill, →/← suffix. (Domain color = the color of the entity being influenced, so the eye maps influence to the domain it reaches.)
Interlock chip: background:#1B1B1B; color:#FAFAFA; — solid dark pill, ⬡ prefix, ↔ suffix. Reads as a “seat,” visually heaviest = most structural.

Group headers keep the thesis grouping (“Money flows to / Influences / Influenced by / Board interlocks”) but now the chips self-identify by type, so a user can scan a mixed group without reading.
5. In-grain tokens
Reuse exactly: #1B1B1B / #FAFAFA / #E8C547 / #B8860B; domain colors #1f77b4 #b84a00 #1e7d32 #b71c1c #6a1b9a #5d4037; border-radius:8px cards, 4px chips; #E0E0E0 borders; #FFF8E1 gold-tint (already used in guide-fact). No new palette, no new radius, no new visual layer.
6. Accessibility

Keyboard: <details>/<summary> and the “More” button are natively focusable; chips already handle Enter/Space. Focus moves to the “More” button on open.
Screen reader: each chip gets aria-label = full sentence, e.g. "Money flows from MultiCare to Ryan Mello" — the icon/arrow are aria-hidden, the label carries meaning. Drawer content wrapped in role="region" aria-live="polite".
Contrast: gold #B8860B on #FFF8E1 and #1B1B1B on #FAFAFA both pass WCAG 4.5:1. Domain-color chips use the darkened domain palette (already contrast-verified in the skill).
Reduced motion: @media (prefers-reduced-motion) disables the drawer slide and accordion animation (instant open/close).
Color redundancy: icon + arrow carry the meaning, so color is never the sole channel.

7. Graceful degradation

No money source: the money callout simply doesn’t render; the switch falls through to the next focal element (interlocks → influence-in → influence-out). The panel still opens calm and thesis-shaped.
No interlocks: the “Multiple hats” strip is skipped; a person with only influence edges gets the influence focal element.
Sparse entity (1–2 connections): the “More” button still appears but the Connections section is short; the nudge adapts (“Explore this entity’s connections…”). Empty groups render nothing, never an empty header.
No JS / old browser: <details> degrades to always-open content; chips remain clickable links. The panel never breaks — it just shows more at once.

Net effect: open = header + thesis + one gold/domain-colored focal card. The user sees the one thing that matters about this entity, and every relationship chip is scannable by color, icon, and arrow without reading a word.

Power Matrix
Case: INV-2026-002 · File: evidence/12-power-matrix.md
Summary: Top 25 ranked actors across 6 domains with composite scores + narrative
Key actors: Mello, Council, Puyallup Tribe, MultiCare, JBLM, Port
Pull when: START HERE — any ‘who’s most powerful’ question

Pierce County Power Matrix — Top 25 Ranked Actors
Methodology
Each actor (person or organization) scored across 6 power domains on a 0-10 scale:

Government — Elected/appointed authority, budget control, veto/decision power
Economic — Capital, employment, contracts, development control  
Institutional — Military, healthcare, tribal, educational authority
Political — Party machinery, fundraising, endorsements, labor ties
Legal/Judicial — Prosecutorial discretion, bench power, sentencing
Media/Narrative — News ownership, editorial control, narrative reach

Composite Score = Weighted average (Gov 25%, Econ 25%, Inst 20%, Political 15%, Legal 10%, Media 5%)
Network Score = From NetworkX eigenvector + betweenness + weighted degree analysis
Final Rank = Blend of Domain Power + Network Position

Tier 1: THE POWER CENTER (Score 8.5+)
1. Ryan Mello — County Executive (Score: 9.2)








































DomainScoreBasisGovernment9$3.5B budget, veto, appointments, countywide mandateEconomic7Budget control, procurement, economic developmentInstitutional6Ex-officio on SSHAP, JBLM coordination, health boardPolitical8Statewide profile, Democratic leadership, union coalitionLegal4Appoints some legal positions, signs contractsMedia4Press conferences, agenda-setting, Instagram presence
Power Basis: Elected countywide 2024 (51.28%). Controls the administrative state. $3.5B biennial budget. Veto over council. Appointments to boards/commissions.
Network Role: Central bridge — highest betweenness centrality (0.118). Connects government to parties, unions, donors, and institutional actors.
What He Does With It: Progressive agenda (Forward Together) — housing expansion, juvenile justice reform, public safety investment. Signs $3.5B budget with 77% toward law/justice. Maintains hiring freeze on non-public-safety positions. In active conflict with Sheriff Swank over authority.
2. Pierce County Council — (Score: 8.7)








































DomainScoreBasisGovernment9Legislative authority, zoning, contracting, budget approvalEconomic7Contract awards, development regulations, Port oversightInstitutional5Appointments to boards, JLUS coordinationPolitical64D-3R split creates negotiation dynamicsLegal5Can initiate ordinances, quasi-judicial land use decisionsMedia3Council meetings televised, public testimony
Power Basis: 7 elected members (4D-3R). Final say on budget, land use, contracts, and appointments. Committee chairs control legislation flow.
Network Role: Highest degree centrality (11 connections). Most connected node in the network.
Key Dynamic: The 4-3 Democratic majority (Hitchen chair) vs Republican minority (Morell vice chair) means budget and land-use fights are partisan.

Tier 2: INSTITUTIONAL ANCHORS (Score 7.0-8.4)
3. Puyallup Tribe of Indians (Score: 8.1)








































DomainScoreBasisGovernment5Sovereign nation, treaty rights, jurisdiction over checkerboardEconomic9Emerald Queen Casino, land development, real estate portfolioInstitutional9Tribal council authority, cultural/political sovereigntyPolitical8Major campaign donor ($2,400 to Mello, $2,000 against Robnett), largest lobbying spender in countyLegal7Tribal court, gaming compact, land-into-trust, Puyallup River watershedMedia3Tribal communications, community relations
Power Basis: Federally recognized tribe with ~4,000 members. Bill Sterud (Chair, 46 years on council). Sovereign nation status means the county cannot tax tribal enterprises on trust land. Largest lobbying spender in Pierce County.
Network Role: The most powerful non-governmental actor. Connections to Governor’s office (Tim Reynon), county candidates, Port of Tacoma.
What They Do With It: Gaming revenue funds tribal government. Land-into-trust expansions are contested with county. Campaign donors across both parties. Environmental sovereignty over Puyallup River.
4. MultiCare Health System (Score: 7.6)








































DomainScoreBasisGovernment3Non-profit, not elected, but regulated (CON, DOH)Economic9$7.2B revenue, 30,000 employees, largest private employerInstitutional813 hospitals, market share >20% in WAPolitical7$357K via WSHA/HHFPAC, executive campaign donations, lobbyingLegal4Certificate-of-need battles, union disputesMedia4Healthcare narrative control, advertising
Power Basis: Tacoma-headquartered, $7.2B revenue. CEO Bill Robertson (retiring Dec 2026 → Florence Chang). Board Chair John Wiborg (Stellar Industrial CEO) has deep Tacoma establishment ties.
Network Role: Board interlocks via Wiborg connect to Chamber, GTCF, UW Tacoma.
What They Do With It: System expansion (13 hospitals across 3 states). Lobbying Olympia for healthcare policy. Political giving through WSHA’s HHFPAC. $357K against Democratic candidates in 2022.
5. Joint Base Lewis-McChord (Score: 7.4)








































DomainScoreBasisGovernment4Federal enclave, county has limited jurisdictionEconomic10$12.1B economic impact, 57,000+ direct jobsInstitutional9I Corps HQ, 7th ID, 62nd AW, 1st SFG, SOFPolitical5SSMCP coordination, 50+ member MOALegal4Military justice, federal jurisdictionMedia3Community relations, press releases
Power Basis: Largest employer in Pierce County. I Corps Commanding General (LTG McFarlane) is single most powerful appointed official. JBLM Garrison Commander (COL Handke) handles county interface.
Network Role: Through SSMCP (South Sound Military & Communities Partnership), JBLM coordinates with county/city on land use, transportation, housing, environmental issues.
What They Do With It: Land use buffer zones (AICUZ noise study). Transportation corridor advocacy. Environmental stewardship (prairie habitat). Housing coordination with county.
6. Port of Tacoma (Score: 7.0)








































DomainScoreBasisGovernment5Independent municipal corp, elected commissionersEconomic9$76B cargo via NWSA, 40,000+ jobs, Tideflats land ownerInstitutional4Municipal corporation, not a traditional institutionPolitical5Commissioners elected county-wide, campaign financeLegal4Environmental permitting, maritime authorityMedia3Port communications, NWSA profile
Power Basis: 5 county-wide elected commissioners. John McCarthy (4 terms, 40 years). Independent taxing authority. NWSA co-owner with Port of Seattle.
Network Role: Bridge between economic development and government. JT Wilcox (former State Rep) on commission creates legislative pipeline.
What They Do With It: Cargo operations, Tideflats development, environmental mitigation. Commissioners approve major capital expenditures ($353.7M capital budget). Freight mobility advocacy.

Tier 3: GOVERNMENT POWER CENTERS (Score 5.5-6.9)
7. Keith Swank — Sheriff (Score: 6.8)








































DomainScoreBasisGovernment7Elected independently of exec. $406M budget. Jail.Economic3Contracting, fleet, facilitiesInstitutional4Law enforcement authorityPolitical5GOP support ($6,500 from party), “constitutional sheriff”Legal8Chief law enforcement officer, jail, licensingMedia6Controversy-driven coverage, clashes with Mello/Robnett
Power Basis: Elected independently of County Executive — cannot be fired. Controls $406M combined law enforcement + corrections budget. WA sheriffs have substantial autonomy.
Network Role: Conflict node. Already sued the county over authority. Feuding with Prosecutor Robnett. WSPA considered expulsion.
What He Does With It: Resisting executive oversight. Demanding mediation on 6 issues. Asserting sheriff’s office independence from county orders. “Constitutional sheriff” alignment disputed.
8. Mary Robnett — Prosecuting Attorney (Score: 6.5)








































DomainScoreBasisGovernment6Elected countywide, $94M budgetEconomic2Civil division advises county contractsInstitutional3Law enforcement cooperationPolitical5Non-partisan framing, law enforcement community supportLegal9All felony prosecutions, civil advice to countyMedia4High-profile cases, press
Power Basis: All felony prosecutions in county. Civil division advises all county departments. Unopposed since 2018 election.
Network Role: Key legal power independent of executive. Feuding with Swank.
What She Does With It: Prioritizes violent crime prosecution. Non-partisan office culture. In conflict with Sheriff over representation.
9. Jani Hitchen — Council Chair (Score: 6.2)








































DomainScoreBasisGovernment7Council Chair sets agenda, D6 (JBLM/Lakewood)Economic3Budget negotiationInstitutional5JBLM district — military community interfacePolitical6Democratic leadership roleLegal2Ordinance processMedia4Council visibility, budget signing
Power Basis: Council chair controls legislative agenda. Represents JBLM district — direct military interface. Presides over meetings, appoints committee chairs.
Network Role: Key government connection to JBLM via district representation.
10. Kelly Chambers — State Rep / Former Candidate (Score: 5.9)








































DomainScoreBasisGovernment5State Rep (R-25), lost County Exec raceEconomic3Small business backgroundInstitutional2—Political9$175K from Pierce GOP, deep donor networkLegal1—Media5Campaign visibility, GOP rising star
Power Basis: Raised $550K for Exec race. $175K from Pierce GOP — strongest party backing. Auto dealer/development donor network.
Network Role: The GOP’s best-funded candidate. Party power broker in waiting. Carries business/development constituency.

Tier 4: SECTOR POWER (Score 4.0-5.4)
11. John Wiborg — MultiCare Board Chair / Stellar Industrial CEO

Scored: Economic 7, Institutional 6, Political 5
Power Basis: Chairs MultiCare board. CEO of Stellar Industrial Supply (Tacoma). Deeply embedded in Tacoma-Pierce County Chamber, GTCF, UW Tacoma boards.
Network Role: The interlock — connects MultiCare to business establishment to philanthropy to University.

12. John McCarthy — Port Commissioner (4 terms, 40 yrs)

Scored: Economic 8, Government 4, Political 4
Power Basis: FMSIB board, PSRC Executive Board. Dean of Port governance.
Network Role: Longest-serving elected economic development official in county.

13. Pierce County Republican Party

Scored: Political 9, Government 4, Economic 3
Power Basis: $175,500 to Chambers alone. Controls endorsements in 3 council districts. State legislative pipeline (Gildon, Barkis, Fortunato, Stokesbary).
Network Role: Central funding node for all GOP candidates in county.

14. Pierce County Democratic Party

Scored: Political 8, Government 5, Economic 2
Power Basis: Controls 4 of 7 council seats, County Executive, 3 state Senate seats (27, 28, 29). Union coalition (HDCC, WEA, UFCW, IBEW).
Network Role: Central funding and coordination node for Democratic candidates.

15. The News Tribune / Chatham Asset Management

Scored: Media 9, Economic 4, Political 3
Power Basis: Only daily newspaper. Owned by hedge fund (Chatham). Editor Stephanie Pedersen edits 4 papers. Opinion Editor Laura Hautala (appointed 2025).
Network Role: Narrative control — what gets covered, framed, or ignored in county politics.


The Full Top 25 Matrix



































































































































































































































































































RankActorGovEconInstPolLegalMediaComposite1Ryan Mello9768449.22County Council9756538.73Puyallup Tribe5998738.14MultiCare3987447.65JBLM41095437.46Port of Tacoma5945437.07Sheriff Swank7345866.88Prosecutor Robnett6235946.59Council Chair Hitchen7356246.210Kelly Chambers5329155.911John Wiborg2765005.412John McCarthy4804005.113Pierce County GOP4309005.014Pierce County Dems5208004.815News Tribune (Chatham)0403094.616Tacoma Mayor Ibsen5424034.517Bruce Dammeier2525004.318Amy Cruver (R-3)4215004.119Jani Hitchen (D-6)5234004.020Drew Stokesbary (R-31)4106103.921Tim Reynon (Tribal)3253003.822LTJG McFarlane (I Corps)0080003.623Bill Sterud (Tribal Chair)0080003.624Anders Ibsen (Tacoma Mayor)4303023.525Gordon Thomas Honeywell1305103.2

Key Patterns


Government + Money = Power. The highest scores belong to those who control both public authority AND economic resources (Mello, Council, Tribe, MultiCare, Port).


The Sheriff Paradox. Swank ranks #7 despite having the 2nd largest budget — because his power is concentrated in one domain (law enforcement/safety) and he’s in active conflict with the executive. His autonomy makes him dangerous, but the isolation limits network influence.


The Party Money Pipeline. Both parties score high on political power, but the GOP has more concentrated money ($175K to Chambers from party) while the Dems have broader coalition (unions, HDCC, progressive PACs, tribe).


Media is a hollow power. The News Tribune has narrative control (only daily paper) but is owned by an out-of-state hedge fund and its editor edits 3 other papers. No locally owned TV exists. Media as an institution is extracted from the community rather than embedded.


The Interlock Economy. John Wiborg (MultiCare/Stellar/Chamber/GTCF/UW Tacoma) and John McCarthy (Port/FMSIB/PSRC) show how a handful of people bridge institutional power.


Tribal Sovereignty = Structural Power. The Puyallup Tribe is the only actor that can opt out of county jurisdiction. That structural independence, combined with gaming revenue and political spending, makes them the most powerful non-governmental entity.

investigations/2608-pierce-leadership/re.title: 13-gap-analysis
investigations/2608-pierce-leadership/re.content:
Gap Analysis
Case: INV-2026-002 · File: evidence/13-gap-analysis.md
Summary: 10 hidden power dimensions scored (Chamber, criminal, labor, education, foundations, dynasties, religious, cultural)
Key actors: —
Pull when: Understanding what the map is MISSING

Gap Analysis: Missing Dimensions of Power in Pierce County Leadership Investigation
Investigation: INV-2026-002 (Pierce County Leadership)
File: evidence/13-gap-analysis.md
Date: 2026-08-17
Author: Subagent — Power Mapping Audit
Status: Initial assessment; actionable findings for Phase 2

Executive Summary
The existing investigation (evidence/01–12) produced a robust formal power structure map — elected officials, campaign finance, lobbying, institutional actors, media ownership, and a NetworkX power matrix ranking 25 actors across 6 domains. This is a strong foundation. However, formal power mapping systematically misses 10 dimensions of informal, structural, and hidden power that are critical to understanding who really governs Pierce County.
This gap analysis identifies 10 missing dimensions, scores each for investigative priority, provides specific names and organizations uncovered through web research, and proposes actionable next steps to fill each gap.
Priority Scale:

CRITICAL — Material gap that undermines the core thesis if unfilled
HIGH — Significant missing power center that changes the network map
MEDIUM — Important context; enriches but doesn’t invalidate existing analysis
LOW — Useful background; can be deferred


Dimension 1: HIDDEN / INFORMAL POWER — The Unelected Power Structure
What We Have

Named elected officials (County Executive, Council, Sheriff, Prosecutor)
Mapped campaign donors and lobbying firms
Identified John Wiborg (MultiCare Chair / Stellar Industrial CEO) as an interlock node
Named Gordon Thomas Honeywell as the dominant lobbying firm

What’s Missing
The Tacoma-Pierce County Chamber of Commerce — The single most important unelected power structure in the county. The Chamber:

Has a 25-member Board of Directors representing the county’s largest employers
Board Chairs rotate: Chyna Willman (FY2025–2026), Kierra Phifer (prior), AJ Gordon of Banner Bank (prior)
Has a $4.5M budget and 15 full-time staff
Interim President/CEO is Tom Pierson (returned after Andrea Reay left for WA Hospitality Association, Sept 2025)
Runs: Candidate Academy, Business Leadership Academy, Manufacturing Industrial Council for the South Sound, Spaceworks Tacoma
Operates at 950 Pacific Ave, Suite 300, Tacoma

Key Finding: The Chamber is a shadow political party for business interests — it runs a Candidate Academy that trains and vets candidates, endorses, and lobbies across all levels. No elected official in Pierce County can win without Chamber support or active opposition. This institution was completely absent from the power matrix.
Private Social Clubs (Old Tacoma Elite):

Tacoma Yacht Club (est. 1889) — 26 founding members of Tacoma’s elite. Located on Belvedere Cove. Generations of old Tacoma families meet here.
Tacoma Country & Golf Club (est. 1894) — Founded by Scotsmen employed by Balfour, Guthrie & Co. The historic venue for Tacoma’s business aristocracy. Course moved to current location 1905.
Tacoma Lodge of Freemasons — Grand Lodge of Washington headquartered at 4970 Bridgeport Way W, University Place. Historic Masonic Temple in downtown Tacoma. Historically the venue where business, legal, and political elites formed private networks.
University of Puget Sound — Private liberal arts college. President Isiaah Crawford. The institution where the Tacoma elite are educated and where board interlocks concentrate.

Major Developers (Land Use Power):

Southport Real Estate — $116,800 in lobbying expenditures (2024). Major Tideflats/waterfront development interests.
Rush Development Company — $2,400 donor to Kelly Chambers. Gig Harbor-based.
Tucci and Sons — Michael Tucci ($2,400 donor to Chambers). Construction/development.
Lincoln Park Partners — William Driscoll ($2,400 donor to Chambers). Real estate development.
Nall Capital LLC — Scott Nall ($2,400 donor to Chambers). Buckley-based.
Miles Sand & Gravel — $2,400 donor to Chambers. Construction materials.

Gap Score

























FactorRatingImpact on power mapVery HighEvidence neededModerateEase of fillHigh (Chamber board lists are public)PriorityCRITICAL
Action Items

 Extract full Chamber Board of Directors list (25 members) and map to corporate/web of influence
 Map Chamber Candidate Academy graduates currently in office
 Identify who owns/controls the Tacoma Yacht Club and Country & Golf Club boards
 Cross-reference social club memberships with elected/appointed officials
 Map developer donation networks across all candidates


Dimension 2: CRIMINAL POWER — Organized Crime, Gangs, and Corruption
What We Have

Named Sheriff Swank and Prosecutor Robnett as formal legal actors
Mapped law enforcement budgets ($406M combined)
Noted Sheriff Swank’s conflict with County Executive

What’s Missing
Historical Organized Crime (The “Enterprise”):

The 1978 FBI RICO Indictment — This is the most significant organized crime prosecution in Pierce County history, yet completely absent from our analysis:

15 men indicted by federal grand jury (Dec 8, 1978)
Pierce County Sheriff George V. Janovich was among those charged — the sitting sheriff was part of a racketeering conspiracy
Led by Tacoma mobster John Joseph Carbone (1919–1998) and his son Joseph M. Carbone
The “Enterprise” used assault, arson, extortion, bribery, and attempted murder to control Pierce County’s topless-dancing tavern business
Also engaged in insurance fraud, gambling, and prostitution
Sheriff Janovich solicited bribes to allow prostitution and gambling in the county
RICO conviction: Janovich sentenced to 12 years in federal prison
150+ witnesses testified; 77 tape recordings entered as evidence
Source: HistoryLink.org File #9728; FBI records; U.S. District Court, WDWA



Contemporary Gang Influence:

Knoccout Crips — Federal indictment (Aug 2025, 15 defendants). Fentanyl trafficking conspiracy using female couriers at Sea-Tac Airport. Doused bags in perfume to mask drug odors. Multi-state operation covering WA, OR, CA. OCDETF operation.
Black Gangster Disciples — Federal wiretap investigation (Feb 2026, 14 arrested). Counterfeit oxycodone, Xanax, methamphetamine, fentanyl, cocaine distribution. Lead defendant Kevin Salgado, 27, of Puyallup.
Hilltop Crips — Documented street gang in Tacoma’s Hilltop neighborhood. Confirmed in Pierce County Sheriff blotter. Involved in shootings and drug trafficking.
5 Pierce County homicides linked to Tacoma gang members (News Tribune, 2025) — String of homicides prompted large-scale federal takedown.

JBLM-to-Street Drug Pipeline:

NCIS and Army CID participated in the Feb 2026 gang raids — indicating military connection
18-month federal investigation found drugs flowing through Sea-Tac and JBLM region
This dimension is a known national pattern (military personnel trafficking weapons/drugs) but unmapped in our analysis

Public Corruption:

Prosecutor Mark Lindquist — Lost 2018 election to Mary Robnett (63-37%) after whistleblower complaints documented toxic work environment. External investigation commissioned.
Pierce County Court Leader Resignation (2026) — “Failed to act” investigations preceded resignation (News Tribune, July 2026)
Judge Grant L. Anderson — CJC finding: received undisclosed payments from estate assets for which he was fiduciary, failed to report on disclosure filings
Judge Mark S. Deming (District Court) — CJC public hearing: improper relationship with probation department employee
Judge A. Eugene Hammermaster — CJC finding: patterns of disrespectful conduct, violations of procedural rights
Tacoma Bank Failure Indictment (2011) — Four indicted for conspiracy resulting in failure of Tacoma bank

Gap Score

























FactorRatingImpact on power mapVery High (structural context)Evidence neededExtensiveEase of fillModerate (federal court records, FBI press releases)PriorityHIGH
Action Items

 Deep-dive on 1978 “Enterprise” RICO case — who were the other 14 defendants? Business connections?
 Research current federal OCDETF operations targeting Pierce County gangs
 Map JBLM drug trafficking connection — military personnel charged, quantity
 Investigate the 2026 court leader resignation — who, what circumstances
 Cross-reference gang territories with County Council districts and contract zones


Dimension 3: LABOR POWER — Union Structure
What We Have

Campaign finance data shows union PAC contributions (WEA, UFCW, IBEW, SEIU, Operating Engineers, IAFF)
Unions listed as part of Democratic coalition
Mentioned but not dived into

What’s Missing
Pierce County Central Labor Council (PCCLC), AFL-CIO:

114 affiliated unions representing 44,000+ workers
Founded 1890 as Tacoma Trades Council
President: Alice Phillips
Secretary-Treasurer: Nathe Lawver
Vice President: Christina Hall
Executive Board includes: Rick Hertzog, Jade Monroe, Brenda Wiest, Brent Wagar, Amber Roulst, Jared Ross, Cindy Richardson, Floyd David Dugan, Patti Dailey-Shives, Abe Adams
Meets 2nd Wednesdays at 7 p.m., 3049 S. 36th St. #201, Tacoma
Source: unionhall.aflcio.org/pcclc

Key Union Affiliates (not in our analysis):

ILWU Local 23 — Longshore workers at Port of Tacoma. Major power at the waterfront. Endorses candidates. ILWU has national political weight (recent Jones Act advocacy, anti-war positions).
Teamsters Joint Council — Teamsters 117 covers Pierce County. Endorsed extensively in 2025: Anders Ibsen, Latasha Palmer, Silong Chhun, Mary Barber, and many more. Major political operation.
Tacoma Education Association — Teachers union for Tacoma Public Schools. Part of WEA ($2,400 donor to Mello).
Pierce County Building & Construction Trades Council — Represents construction unions (IBEW 483, Operating Engineers 612, Plumbers & Pipefitters). Construction is 27,000 jobs in Pierce County.
Washington Federation of State Employees — Represent state/county workers. Involved in Labor Day picnic with PCCLC.
IAFF Local 726 — Puyallup firefighters. $2,400 donor to Mello.
Tacoma Police Union Local #6 — Mentioned briefly as $2,400 donor to Chambers. But police unions are a distinct power center — they endorsed across party lines, have outsized influence in “law and order” debates, and were not fully analyzed.

Labor’s Political Operation:

PCCLC publishes formal endorsement slates for every election cycle
2025 endorsements spanned: County Council, Port Commission, School Boards, City Councils, State Legislature
Labor is the ground game for Democratic candidates in Pierce County — door-knocking, phone-banking, mailers
Labor endorsements often carry more weight with working-class voters than party endorsements

Gap Score

























FactorRatingImpact on power mapHighEvidence neededModerateEase of fillHigh (PCCLC is transparent about affiliations)PriorityHIGH
Action Items

 Map the full PCCLC affiliate list — identify which 114 unions are represented
 Analyze ILWU Local 23’s role at Port of Tacoma — can they shut down port operations?
 Track police union endorsement patterns — cross-reference with candidate ideology
 Map labor-to-campaign contribution pipelines more granularly
 Interview or review PCCLC executive board member backgrounds for cross-institutional ties


Dimension 4: RELIGIOUS POWER — Churches and Faith Institutions
What We Have

Nothing. Religion is entirely absent from the power map.

What’s Missing
Catholic Archdiocese of Seattle (Pierce Deanery):

The Archdiocese of Seattle has jurisdiction over Pierce County parishes
Pierce Deanery includes: St. Charles Borromeo (Tacoma), St. Patrick’s (Tacoma), Holy Cross, St. John Bosco, and others
Pastoral planning process underway (2016 convocation at St. Charles Borromeo)
Catholic schools in Pierce County: St. Charles Borromeo Catholic School, Annie Wright Schools (Episcopal but historically connected)
Archdiocese spent $191,589 on lobbying in 2024 through Virginia Mason Franciscan Health (healthcare lobbying, not directly religious, but institutionally Catholic)
Recent merger of 4 Tacoma Catholic parishes into 1 — major institutional restructuring

Megachurches / Evangelical Networks:

Life Center (Tacoma) — Multiple locations. “One church, multiple locations across the Tacoma area.” Nondenominational/evangelical. Significant cultural and political organizing potential.
Champions Centre (Tacoma) — 1819 E 72nd St. Large evangelical congregation.
20+ churches in Pierce County received up to $14M in federal PPP loans (News Tribune analysis) — demonstrates economic footprint.

Political Engagement of Faith Institutions:

Church-based political organizing is well-documented nationally but unmapped locally
Religious right infrastructure in Pierce County (GOP base mobilization through churches)
Progressive faith coalitions (interfaith groups working on housing, homelessness, criminal justice)
The Tacoma-Pierce County Association of Realtors ($44,400 lobbying) and real estate interests often partner with churches on development

Religious Demographics (ARDA 2020):

Pierce County has significant: Catholic, Evangelical Protestant (Converge Worldwide, Evangelical Covenant Church, Churches of Christ), Latter-day Saints, and Muslim populations.
Religious congregations function as social service providers, civic meeting spaces, and voter mobilization networks.

Gap Score

























FactorRatingImpact on power mapModerateEvidence neededExtensiveEase of fillLow (few public disclosure requirements for churches)PriorityMEDIUM
Action Items

 Map the Pierce Deanery structure — identify key Catholic institutional leaders and their crossover with healthcare/government boards
 Research Life Center’s political engagement — does it host candidate forums, endorsement processes?
 Analyze PPP loan data for Pierce County faith institutions
 Map faith-based social service contracts with county government
 Investigate church property holdings in redevelopment zones (Hilltop, downtown)


Dimension 5: EDUCATION POWER — School Boards
What We Have

Superficial mention of School Boards in municipal leadership files
Bruch Dammeier mentioned as former Puyallup School Board member
No systematic school board mapping

What’s Missing
Tacoma Public Schools (28,272 students, 69 schools, $557M budget):

Board of Directors (5 positions, elected by district):

Korey Strozier (President, Pos. 3) — Elected 2019, term 2023-2029. CWU alumnus.
Elizabeth Bonbright (Pos. 5) — Since 2019, term expires 2029.
Chelsea McElroy (Vice President, Pos. 4) — Elected 2021, term expires 2027.
Lisa Keating (Pos. 1) — Since 2019, term expires 2029.
Shawna Freeman Lane (Pos. 2) — Appointed March 2026, term expires 2027.
Superintendent: Dr. Josh Garcia


Feb 2026 election: Prop 1 passed 70.8%, Prop 2 passed 69.6% — bond/levy measures totaling hundreds of millions
Tacoma School Board recognized 8 consecutive years as WA Board of Distinction
Key dynamic: The board controls a $557M+ budget and capital construction program ($124M capital outlay)

Puyallup School District:

Board: Melissa Bedford (Pos. 1), Joseph Romero (Pos. 2, since 2019), Shannon Burch, David Berg (Pos. 4, since 2021), Gretchen Miles
Superintendent: Dr. Laurie Dent (Sumner)
Fast-growing district absorbing enrollment from Bethel/Boundary changes

Bethel School District (Spanaway):

Board: Marcus Young, Sr. (President, Dist. 1) — Doctorate of Divinity, self-employed
Teresa Cosio (Vice President) — Bookkeeper for logging companies
John Manning (Dist. 2)

Superintendent: Not mapped
Rapidly declining enrollment — boundary changes with Puyallup causing tension

Clover Park School District (Lakewood):

Franklin Pierce School District (Parkland):

Superintendent: Dr. Lance Goodpaster

Other Districts (not mapped):

Sumner-Bonney Lake, Peninsula (Gig Harbor), Carbonado, Eatonville, Orting, White River, Fife

Gap Score

























FactorRatingImpact on power mapVery HighEvidence neededModerateEase of fillHigh (public election records, school board websites)PriorityHIGH
Action Items

 Map all 14+ Pierce County school boards — members, terms, occupations, political affiliations
 Analyze Tacoma SD construction contracts ($124M capital outlay) — who gets the contracts?
 Map school board election donors cross-referenced with developer/construction interests
 Research the Tacoma SD boundary/closure politics — which neighborhoods lose schools?
 Analyze the relationship between school board members and municipal elected officials (Dammeier model)


Dimension 6: NONPROFIT / FOUNDATION POWER
What We Have

United Way of Pierce County mentioned as employer of Ryan Mello (2001–2003)

4. CANDIDATE ACADEMY
Overview
The Candidate Academy is a program of the Tacoma-Pierce County Chamber described as “a unique opportunity for local, civic-minded individuals who are considering running for office.” It is explicitly designed to recruit, train, and vet potential candidates for elected office.
Format

Duration: Intensive 1-day primer
Curriculum:

Civics 101: How Governments Interact and Work
Panel: The Good, Bad, and Ugly of Politics — How to Survive being a Candidate and Elected Official
Campaign Strategy and Operations: Putting the Pieces Together
Election Filing Guide
Fundraising and Event Planning
Getting Out Your Message: Media, Mailings, and Doorbelling
Managing Your Campaign: People, Process, and Budget



Key Features

Participants meet local elected officials and community advocates
Learn differences between levels of government and elected positions
Become “better equipped to serve as a candidate and elected or appointed official”
Program assists in determining “whether to throw their hat in the ring”
Networking with “local leaders and elected officials who can offer support, advice, and guidance”

Known Alumni
The Chamber does not publish a public alumni list for the Candidate Academy on its website. This is a significant information gap — the program’s alumni are not transparently disclosed. However, based on investigative reporting context:

The phrase “Chamber candidate” is a known political epithet in Tacoma politics, suggesting the Candidate Academy has produced identifiable candidates who are perceived as Chamber-aligned (per Matt Driscoll, Tacoma News Tribune columnist, 2015 column).

Strategic Significance
The Candidate Academy functions as an informal candidate vetting and training pipeline — the Chamber trains aspiring candidates on the mechanics of running for office while simultaneously building relationships and networks. This gives the Chamber disproportionate influence over who enters the candidate pool for local offices, especially at the City of Tacoma and Pierce County levels.
Source: www.tacomachamber.org/candidateacademy.html

5. BUSINESS LEADERSHIP ACADEMY
Overview

Founded: 1978 (48 years of operation)
Partnership: Pacific Lutheran University
Format: Multi-month leadership development program
Alumni: “Hundreds of alumni” across nearly 50 years
Focus: Leadership development, community engagement, organizational visits

While distinct from the Candidate Academy, the Business Leadership Academy (BLA) builds the Chamber’s broader network of influence across the region’s business, nonprofit, and government sectors.
Source: www.tacomachamber.org/business-leadership-academy.html

6. POLITICAL ENDORSEMENTS & ELECTION ACTIVITY
Official Position
The Chamber officially states it does not endorse candidates. Its Voters Guide page says: “The Chamber does not endorse candidates. Our objective is to promote information on the election cycle and candidates within it so that voters can make informed decisions.”
Reality: The “Chamber Candidate” Phenomenon
Despite the official non-endorsement policy, the Chamber has a well-documented history of being perceived as a political kingmaker:


Matt Driscoll Column (The News Tribune, ~2015): In a column titled “Is fear over a ‘Chamber candidate’ for Tacoma City Council warranted?”, Driscoll documented that “Chamber candidate” is a recognized political label in Tacoma. He noted that since Tom Pierson’s arrival as CEO in 2011, the Chamber “has taken a more active approach in local politics.” The column reported that the phrase “Chamber candidate” is used by critics to describe candidates perceived as business-aligned.


Candidates Forum: The Chamber hosts an annual Candidates Forum featuring finalists for Tacoma Mayor and City Council. In 2025, this was held at University of Puget Sound featuring candidates for Mayor and Council positions 2, 4, 5, and 6.


Voter Guide: The Chamber publishes a “Vote for Business Voters Guide” that candidates respond to with 600-word answers. It is widely distributed to members. Candidates who don’t respond are noted. This effectively functions as a de facto endorsement signal — favorable coverage for responsive candidates.


Advocacy Fund: The Chamber operates an “Advocacy Fund” that “powers the education, engagement, and influence needed to advance policies.” While described as issue-focused, the fund directly supports the Chamber’s political engagement infrastructure.


Instagram Political Activity: The Chamber’s Instagram account (@tacoma_chamber, 5,242 followers) actively promotes candidate content, including candidate videos (e.g., Latasha Palmer for Tacoma Council-At-Large Position 6) and election reminders.


Key Insight
The Chamber’s power operates through indirect political influence rather than direct PAC-style endorsements. By controlling the candidate training pipeline (Candidate Academy), the voter information ecosystem (Voters Guide), and the candidate visibility platform (Candidates Forum), the Chamber shapes the political landscape without formally endorsing.
Comparison: Labor Endorsements
By contrast, the Pierce County Central Labor Council (AFL-CIO) publishes explicit endorsements. For example, in the 2025 general election, labor endorsed Anders Ibsen for Tacoma Mayor, Latasha Palmer for Council-at-Large Position 6, and Silong Chhun for District 4. The Chamber does not publish equivalent endorsements but its informal influence arguably rivals labor’s formal endorsement power.

Institutional Power Score: CRITICAL (9/10)
The Tacoma-Pierce County Chamber of Commerce is a dominant power institution in Pierce County for the following reasons:


Shadow Political Party Function: Despite officially stating it does not endorse candidates, the Chamber operates a Candidate Academy that trains and vets aspiring politicians, publishes a widely-distributed Voters Guide, and hosts a Candidates Forum. The term “Chamber candidate” is a recognized label in Tacoma politics.


Government Integration: The Chamber is formally embedded in City of Tacoma and Pierce County economic development planning. County and city agencies hold seats on its board. Its former CEO simultaneously served as Acting Director of Economic Development for Pierce County.


Financial Capacity: With ~$3M annual revenue, ~1,400 members, and sophisticated advocacy infrastructure (Advocacy Fund, Legislative Advocacy Day, D.C. conference), the Chamber has resources far beyond a typical civic organization.


Institutional Longevity: 141 years of continuous operation gives the Chamber unmatched institutional memory and relationship networks.


Cross-Sector Board: The board includes representatives from healthcare (MultiCare, Virginia Mason), banking (KeyBank), energy (Puget Sound Energy), tech (Comcast, DoorDash), aerospace (Boeing), higher education (UW Tacoma, CPTC), public transit (Pierce Transit), port (Port of Tacoma), and utilities (TPU) — creating a unified business voice across all major sectors.


Data Authority: The Chamber’s Pierce County Economic Index report positions it as the authoritative source on regional economic conditions — a form of narrative control.

Candidate Academy alumni list is not publicly published
Advocacy Fund donors are not disclosed
The relationship between the Chamber’s Voters Guide and de facto endorsement patterns needs further investigation
The FY2025 audit finding of “significant deficiency in internal controls” warrants attention

15 — Criminal Power in Pierce County
Case: INV-2026-002 — Pierce County Leadership Investigation
Date: 2026-08-17
Status: Draft
Author: Subagent (Research & Mapping)
Priority: HIGH (Identified as a critical gap dimension in 13-gap-analysis.md)

Overview
This document maps organized criminal influence in Pierce County across six vectors: (1) historical public corruption — the 1978 “Enterprise” RICO case, (2) current gang-landscape — Knoccout Crips and Black Gangster Disciples federal indictments, (3) the JBLM drug/weapons pipeline, (4) FBI investigations of county officials and agencies, (5) judicial misconduct, and (6) Tacoma Police Department scandals and patterns of abuse. These vectors do not operate in isolation; cross-connections exist between them — for example, the 1978 Enterprise case centered on the same nightlife economy around Fort Lewis/McChord that fuels today’s drug pipeline, and federal RICO tools used against Janovich in 1978 are still the primary mechanism for dismantling the gang networks active today.

1. Historical Public Corruption: The “Enterprise” RICO Case (1978)
Summary
The most significant corruption scandal in Pierce County history. On December 8, 1978, a federal grand jury indicted 15 men — including sitting Pierce County Sheriff George V. Janovich — for engaging in a racketeering conspiracy under the Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organization (RICO) Act. The organization, called “The Enterprise,” was led by Tacoma mobster John Joseph Carbone and his son Joseph Carbone.
Key Figures













































NameRoleOutcomeGeorge V. JanovichPierce County SheriffConvicted of racketeering; sentenced to 12 years, served ~6. Recorded on tape accepting a $1,300 bribe.John Joseph CarboneEnterprise leader / Tacoma mob bossConvicted; sentenced to 25 years. Died 1998.Joseph M. CarboneLieutenant / tavern operationsConvictedRonald J. WilliamsChief lieutenantConvictedFrank J. MazzucaLieutenant / nightclub operationsConvictedAnthony J. MladnichGambling operationsConvictedRichard F. CaliguriChief enforcerConvicted
Criminal Activities (1971–1978)
The Enterprise was charged with 107 overt acts including:

Assault, arson, extortion, bribery, and attempted murder — to control Pierce County’s topless-dancing tavern business
Insurance fraud — members burned their own businesses for insurance payouts, including Carbone’s own Gig Harbor home
Protection rackets — protection, prostitution, and illegal gambling
Attempted murder of a state agent — Washington State Liquor Control Board Agent Melvin R. Journey was shot four times outside his home on November 15, 1977, and survived after four hours of surgery
Firebombing of competing taverns — 10+ arsons over six years causing ~$2 million in losses
Sheriff’s office complicity — Janovich disclosed information to the Enterprise, discouraged investigations, used deputies to harass competitors, and permitted prostitution/illegal gambling

Investigation

13-month joint FBI/BATF undercover operation
Break came when two half-brothers (Jackie Bentley and Michael Johnson) were arrested in Kansas City with a shotgun used in the Journey shooting
Robert Valentine became a government informant, introduced undercover agents into the Enterprise
Key evidence: tape recording of Janovich accepting a $1,300 bribe
Trial held in San Francisco due to extensive pretrial publicity
Six defendants pleaded guilty before trial; after a three-month trial, all but one were convicted

Aftermath

Janovich’s conviction led directly to a structural overhaul of Pierce County government: voters replaced the three-commissioner system with a county council and county executive, and made the sheriff an appointed (rather than elected) position
The Sheriff’s Office has been “trying to live that down for 25 years” per Detective Ed Troyer (2005)
Janovich died in 2005 at age 77 from a ruptured appendix; he had been moved between 30 prisons on protective custody
The county later paid a $3.7 million civil settlement related to the racketeering case

Sources

HistoryLink: Federal grand jury indicts 15 in Pierce County for racketeering — Dec 8, 1978 — Definitive account, primary source
SeattlePI: Ex-Pierce County sheriff, jailed for corruption, dies — Obituary with details
9th Circuit: US v. Janovich, 634 F.2d 1159 (1981) — Appellate decision
Behind the Badge Foundation: Agent Melvin R. Journey — Context on the assassination attempt


2. Current Gang Landscape: Knoccout Crips & Black Gangster Disciples
2A. Knoccout Crips — FBI “Summer Heat” Operation (August 2025)
A 36-month FBI-led investigation culminating in August 2025 with the arrest of 15 individuals, including members of the Knoccout Crips street gang, for a large-scale fentanyl trafficking conspiracy.
Key Facts:

Operation “Summer Heat” — multi-agency takedown with 100+ officers
Drug mule network — female couriers transported fentanyl through Sea-Tac Airport via checked luggage, doused in perfume to mask odors; transported ~80 lbs of fentanyl pills/powder in just two months from Phoenix to Tacoma
Seized: 2,683.3g fentanyl, 6,850.7g methamphetamine, 227.9g cocaine, 40.7g heroin, 27,593.8g marijuana, $111,524 cash, 23 firearms
Trigger: Investigation initiated in response to a string of homicides and drive-by shootings attributed to the gang
Agencies: FBI South Sound Safe Streets Gang Task Force, HSI, TPD, Lakewood PD, Pierce County Sheriff’s Office, WA DOC

2B. Black Gangster Disciples — Wiretap Indictment (February 2026)
On February 4, 2026, law enforcement arrested 14 defendants affiliated with the Black Gangster Disciples street gang following a wiretap investigation, executing 17 search warrants across Washington, Oregon, and California.
Key Facts:

Lead defendant: Kevin Salgado, 27, of Puyallup — alleged ringleader
Criminal methods:

Pressing counterfeit oxycodone and Xanax pills for distribution
Hacking into drug distribution companies to reroute shipments
Paying kickbacks to an Oregon pharmacist for filling fake prescriptions
Trafficking firearms with “Glock switches” (auto-conversion to machine guns)
Mailing narcotics across the country via USPS


Connected to at least 3 overdose deaths
Seized on arrest day alone: 39 firearms, 100+ Glock switches, 887.9g fentanyl pills, 924g fentanyl powder, ~7kg counterfeit oxycodone pills
Total seizure over investigation duration: 38+ firearms, 4kg meth, 10.5kg counterfeit oxycodone pills
Agencies: HSI Seattle, DEA, ATF, USMS, USPIS, IRS-CI, USSS, CBP, USCG Investigative Service

2C. Gang Injunctions
No evidence of active Tacoma gang injunction “safety zones” comparable to Los Angeles or other major cities was found during research. Tacoma appears to rely on federal prosecution (RICO, wiretap investigations) rather than civil gang injunctions. This is a potential research gap — check if the city or county has ever sought civil gang injunctions.
Sources

FOX 13 Seattle: FBI Tacoma gang used women, perfume to smuggle fentanyl — August 2025 bust details
DOJ: Members of Tacoma street gang indicted in fentanyl conspiracy — Press release
DEA: Members of Tacoma Street Gang Indicted for Drug and Gun Trafficking — February 2026 BGD indictment
Pierce County Sheriff’s Office Blotter — Local law enforcement perspective
The News Tribune: Tacoma gang peddling guns, drugs busted — Paywalled but sourced


3. JBLM Drug & Weapons Pipeline
Joint Base Lewis-McChord, one of the largest military bases in the country, presents unique criminal risk vectors: active-duty personnel trafficking classified information, stealing military-grade weapons, and drug distribution flowing between the base and surrounding communities.
3A. Espionage / National Security (2024–2025)
Two active-duty JBLM soldiers (Jian Zhao, Li Tian) and one former soldier (Ruoyu Duan) were arrested following federal grand jury indictments for conspiring to sell military secrets to buyers in China.

Charges: Conspiracy to commit bribery, theft of government property, transmitting national defense information
Targeted data: Technical manuals for Bradley and Stryker fighting vehicles, HIMARS information, encryption-capable computers
Duration: November 2021 to December 2024
Status: One former soldier pleaded guilty; cases ongoing

3B. Military Equipment Theft / White Supremacist Cell (June 2025)
Two veterans (Charles Fields and Levi Frakes) were charged with robbing JBLM’s U.S. Army Ranger operations facility over a two-year period.

Key findings at their Lacey home: 35 weapons including machine guns, silencers, night vision devices, flashbangs, smoke grenades, body armor, Nazi flags, SS Bolts paraphernalia, white supremacist literature
Method: Used their military IDs to enter the base, used bolt cutters to breach the Ranger compound, assaulted an employee with a hammer
Stolen equipment: Helmets, body armor, communications equipment (~$14,000 in a single incident)
Status: Federal charges pending; held on $500,000 bail each

3C. Drug Distribution Tied to JBLM
The 1978 Enterprise case itself centered on nightlife around Fort Lewis and McChord AFB. The pattern continues:

The Knoccout Crips and BGD indictments above show drug distribution networks operating in the same geography as JBLM (Tacoma, Lakewood, Puyallup)
Spanaway man Sean Michael Moinette sentenced to 12 years (2025) for fentanyl/meth distribution
Pierce County-based drug trafficking organization indicted (December 2023) by DEA — the press release explicitly notes harm to “young people in our community”

Sources

DOJ: Active-Duty and Former US Army Soldiers Arrested for Theft of Government Property and Bribery — Espionage case
Washington State Standard: Two veterans accused of robbing WA Army base had Nazi flags — Equipment theft / white supremacist cell
DEA: Pierce County Based Drug Trafficking Organization Indicted — December 2023
DOJ: Key Pierce County drug distributor tied to white prison gangs sentenced — Prison gang ties
KOMO: 2 JBLM soldiers charged with trying to sell secrets to China


4. FBI Investigations of County Officials and Agencies
4A. Pierce County Housing Authority — $7 Million Embezzlement (2019)
The largest fraud case on record against a Washington local government. The State Auditor’s Office uncovered that former finance director Cova Campbell misappropriated $6,948,277 from Pierce County Housing Authority funds since 2016.

Schemes: Wire transfers to shell accounts, fabricated invoices, unauthorized payments
Referral: Case forwarded to FBI and HUD OIG for criminal investigation
Outcome: Campbell charged; the DOJ website lists a sentencing for “former low-income housing executive” for embezzlement of nearly $7 million
Significance: Demonstrates vulnerability in county-level financial oversight — the embezzlement was detected during a routine financial audit, not through internal controls

4B. Sheriff Ed Troyer — Independent Investigation (2021–2022)
Pierce County Sheriff Ed Troyer was the subject of a confrontation with a Black newspaper carrier (Sedrick Altheimer) in January 2021 that led to state charges for false reporting.

Investigation: Independent investigation commissioned by Pierce County found Troyer “seriously lacking” in professionalism
Criminal trial: A Pierce County jury found Troyer not guilty of false reporting charges
Legal costs: Taxpayers initially covered Troyer’s legal costs; later determined they would not pay
Significance: Created a crisis of confidence in the Sheriff’s Office, particularly around racial equity

4C. 911 Tax Revenue Diversion — State Audit Finding

Pierce County was found by the Washington State Auditor to have violated state law by diverting millions in tax revenue meant for 911 emergency services
Noncompliance presented to County Council, Executive Office, and department leadership in May 2024
InvestigateWest reported that the county’s purchase of $4.5 million in law enforcement radio equipment jeopardized federal funding
FBI referral status: Unclear from available sources — further investigation needed

4D. Pierce County Prosecuting Attorney’s Office History

Former Prosecuting Attorney Ron Hendry (1967–1974) charged county Licensing Director Jerry Aldridge with bribery, revealing a pattern of payoffs for protection going back decades
The same office prosecuted the Carbone/Janovich racketeering enterprise
No evidence of current FBI investigation specifically targeting the Prosecutor’s Office was found

Sources

WA State Auditor: $7 million misappropriation at Pierce County Housing Authority — Primary fraud report
KING 5: Ex-Pierce County housing finance director charged
DOJ: Former low-income housing executive sentenced for embezzlement
WA Attorney General: Jury finds Sheriff Troyer not guilty
Pierce County: Independent investigation into Sheriff Troyer findings
InvestigateWest: Pierce County violated state law diverting 911 funds
WA State Auditor: 911 tax revenue findings — Further details available on request


5. Judicial Misconduct
5A. Judge Grant L. Anderson — Pierce County Superior Court (1998–1999)
Violation: Received undisclosed payments from a purchaser of assets from an estate for which he was a fiduciary; failed to report payments on public disclosure filings; served as a corporate officer after becoming a judge.

Findings: Violated Canons 1, 2(A), 5(C)(3), and 6(C) of the Code of Judicial Conduct
Commission recommendation: Censure and 4-month suspension without pay
WA Supreme Court action: Removed from office — unanimous decision overturning the Commission’s more lenient recommendation
Discipline date: April 3, 1998
Full removal: July 29, 1999 (Seattle Times: “Pierce County Judge Ousted By High Court — Dishonesty Cited”)

5B. Judge Mark S. Deming — Pierce County District Court No. 1 (1987)
The first public hearing in Washington Commission on Judicial Conduct history.
Violations:


Improper romantic relationship with a probation department employee that adversely impacted court administration


Frequent inappropriate and injudicious comments and sexual innuendos to women in public and in court


Sexual harassment of personnel from District Court, Probation, Prosecuting Attorney’s Office, and Department of Assigned Counsel (DAC)


Findings: Violated Canons 1, 2(A), 2(B), and 3(A)(3)


Supreme Court action: Removed from office (108 Wash. 2d 82, 736 P.2d 639)


Date: May 7, 1987


5C. Judge A. Eugene Hammermaster — Sumner/Orting/Wilkeson/South Prairie Municipal Courts (Pierce County)
Violations:


Exhibited patterns of failure to respect and comply with the law


Disrespectful and undignified conduct


Violations of fundamental procedural rights of criminal defendants


Commission action: Found violations of Canons 2(A), 3(A)(1), and 3(A)(3)


Date: Not precisely specified in available records


5D. Recent Court Administration Issues
In August 2026, The News Tribune reported that “Investigations preceded Pierce County court leader resignation” with the headline: “Failed to act.” — suggesting ongoing issues in court leadership and oversight that led to a resignation.
Sources

WA Commission on Judicial Conduct: Supreme Court Filings — Anderson, Deming, Hammermaster
CJC Discipline Search — Complaint #2179 (Grant L. Anderson)
Seattle Times Archive: Pierce County Judge Ousted By High Court (1999)
Justia: In Re Disciplinary Proceeding Against Deming (1987)
News Tribune (Facebook): ‘Failed to act’ — Investigations preceded Pierce County court leader resignation (Aug 2026)


6. Tacoma Police Department Scandals
6A. The Death of Manuel “Manny” Ellis (March 3, 2020)
The defining Tacoma PD scandal of the modern era.

Incident: Ellis, a 33-year-old Black man, died of asphyxiation while being restrained by Tacoma police. Officers beat, Tasered, and hogtied him.
Medical Examiner: Ruled a homicide — death caused by lack of oxygen during physical restraint
Initial investigation: Pierce County Sheriff’s Department conducted the initial probe; a Pierce County deputy was present during Ellis’s arrest
State criminal trial: Officers Christopher Burbank and Matthew Collins charged with second-degree murder; Timothy Rankine charged with first-degree manslaughter. All three acquitted by a jury in December 2023
Federal review: DOJ opened an independent civil rights investigation in January 2024; closed in 2025 due to insufficient evidence for federal charges
City payments:

Each officer paid $500,000 to resign “in good standing” (January 2024)
$4 million wrongful death settlement paid by Pierce County (2022)
$6 million settlement paid by City of Tacoma (July 2025)


Aftermath: DOJ ended its federal civil rights review without charges; state officials are investigating whether to revoke the officers’ certifications; one officer (Rankine) filed a $47 million defamation claim against officials

6B. Excessive Force / Racial Bias Lawsuit Settlement (April 2024)

Plaintiff: Zimmeri Contreraz, a Black man singled out at Wright Park in July 2020
Allegation: Officer Christopher Bain yanked him backward by his handcuffs, slamming his head onto a picnic table — while Contreraz was seated and compliant
Settlement: $300,000 from City of Tacoma; additional $50,000 from Pierce County 911 for public records violations
Status: Officer Bain remained on the force as of April 2024

6C. Lawsuit Alleging TPD Forced Out Black Leaders

The News Tribune reported a lawsuit claiming Tacoma PD has a “pattern of harassing, forcing out Black cops”
A former deputy police chief sued the city alleging misconduct

6D. No DOJ Consent Decree (Notable Finding)
Unlike Seattle (2012–2024 consent decree) or other Washington cities, Tacoma has never been under a federal consent decree for pattern-or-practice policing violations. The DOJ did open a civil rights review of the Manny Ellis case but closed it without a finding. This is notable because:

Tacoma PD has faced multiple excessive force lawsuits but has not triggered a structural DOJ intervention
The current DOJ under the Trump administration has been actively ending consent decrees (Louisville, Minneapolis, May 2025), making a new one unlikely
However: A Disparate Policing & Charging analysis (waw.fd.org) references a “Department of Justice investigation that found ‘a pattern or practice of constitutional violations. Tacoma Police officers’” — this finding needs verification against the primary DOJ source

Sources

Wikipedia: Killing of Manuel Ellis — Comprehensive timeline
KOMO: DOJ ends review of Manny Ellis death
KNKX: Excessive force, racial bias lawsuit settlement — $300K Contreraz settlement
News Tribune: Lawsuit says Tacoma PD forced out Black leaders — Pattern of discrimination
waw.fd.org: Disparate Policing & Charging in WADW — References DOJ pattern-or-practice finding (requires verification)


Cross-Dimension Analysis
Connections Between Vectors


1978 → 2026: The Janovich Enterprise case and today’s gang indictments both involve protection and drug economies centered on the JBLM nightlife corridor. The geographic and economic pattern is persistent across 50 years.


JBLM ↔ Street Gangs: The same base that generated the 1970s Enterprise tavern economy now generates stolen military-grade weapons flowing into Tacoma gangs. The white supremacist equipment-theft ring (Fields/Frakes, 2025) demonstrates an additional national security risk.


Lack of Consent Decree: Unlike Seattle, Tacoma PD has never been placed under a DOJ consent decree despite multiple high-profile excessive force cases. This may reflect either better policing, different political dynamics, or timing (the post-2024 DOJ has been terminating decrees, not initiating them).


Judicial Accountability: Two Pierce County judges have been removed from office by the WA Supreme Court (Deming 1987, Anderson 1999), suggesting systemic oversight issues in the county’s judicial selection and monitoring. The 2026 court-leader resignation under cloud of “failed to act” may signal ongoing problems.


Research Gaps (Further Investigation Needed)

 Active FBI investigations: No public confirmation of any ongoing FBI probe into Pierce County executive or council members. The 2019 Housing Authority case is the last confirmed FBI referral. Freedom of Information requests may reveal more.
 Gang injunctions: No evidence of Tacoma or Pierce County using civil gang injunctions. This contrasts with other WA cities. Confirm this gap through city legal department records.
 JBLM drug statistics: Specific data on active-duty personnel arrested for drug trafficking (as opposed to espionage/theft) is limited. The Army’s ASAP (Substance Abuse Program) data and CID reports could provide more.
 911 fund diversion — FBI referral status: The InvestigateWest story confirms a state audit finding but does not confirm whether the FBI has opened a probe.
 DOJ pattern-or-practice finding: The waw.fd.org reference needs verification against the original DOJ document.
 White prison gang ties: The “Key Pierce County drug distributor tied to white prison gangs” case (DOJ press release) suggests connections between street gangs and prison-based organized crime that merit further investigation.

Where a source URL requires a subscription (e.g., The News Tribune), content was captured from freely accessible excerpts or cross-referenced against other sources

Key Contracting Patterns

Absher Construction is a recurring contractor in Sumner-Bonney Lake district
Board resolutions show GC/CM (General Contractor/Construction Manager) procurement model for major projects
University Place $295M bond qualifies for $60M state assistance — total $355M construction program
Tacoma TPS contracts reviewed at board level for $22K (Urban Grace Church) to $740K (Synchronous Deployment) — board approves even relatively small contracts


Campaign Finance Observations
Washington State school board races are nonpartisan with a top-two primary system. Key observations:

Tacoma: Lisa Keating raised $20,000+ in her first run (per News Tribune, 2019 data) — significant for a school board race
Political affiliations visible: Chelsea McElroy (Tacoma) is a Democratic precinct committee officer in LD 27; past Chair of Pierce County Young Democrats
Union connections: McElroy (SEIU 925, active in bargaining); Janet Caldwell (Clover Park) is Bethel Education Association President — direct labor union leadership on a board
Endorsements: Northwest Progress Coalition WA (NWPC) endorsed candidates in 2025 — includes progressive slate across Pierce County school boards
PDC Limits: WA Public Disclosure Commission caps contributions; PDC database available at www.pdc.wa.gov
School board members do not receive a salary — per diem only ($50/day, max $4,800/yr), so campaign finance is about influence, not direct financial benefit

Notable Political Cross-Connections

T’wina Nobles (UPSD board member) — WA State Senator for the 28th Legislative District (D); simultaneously holds school board and state legislature positions
Chelsea McElroy (Tacoma board) — Vice Chair of City of Tacoma Board of Ethics; active in Democratic Party politics
Elizabeth Bonbright (Tacoma board) — Former Chair of JMAC (Joint Municipal Action Committee) — the most powerful coordinating body in Tacoma/Pierce County
Mark Baumgarten (Franklin Pierce) — 25+ years on board; former construction industry professional — direct industry insider
Alyssa Anderson Pearson (Clover Park) — Contracts & Procurement Administrator for WA Military Department — government procurement expertise on board


Power Structure Analysis
Key Power Nodes


Tacoma Public Schools — Largest district ($665M budget, 28K students, 58 schools). Board President Korey Strozier and Superintendent Josh Garcia control the largest education budget in the county. $80.7M in capital outlay. Bonbright’s JMAC chair role connects education to city/county/port/tribe power structure.


Sumner-Bonney Lake — Fast-growing district with major construction pipeline. Superintendent Laurie Dent (2024 WA State Supt of the Year) wields significant influence. Absher Construction relationship worth monitoring. $114M expansion bond + ongoing Tehaleh growth.


University Place — $295M bond (plus $60M state match = $355M) creates a massive construction program. Mary Lu Dickinson has served since 1995 — 30+ years of institutional memory. T’wina Nobles bridges school board and state senate.


Bethel — Second-largest south county district (21K students). Major new HS construction + middle school replacement. Dr. Brian Lowney new superintendent (2024). Board has military-connected members (Manning — retired USAF).


Clover Park — Serves Lakewood/JBLM. Superintendent Banner is WA State Supt of the Year (2025). Board includes union president (Caldwell) and procurement professional (Pearson).


Red Flags / Research Gaps

Campaign finance data: Requires deeper PDC database queries for all 14 districts. Most school board races fly under the radar with minimal reporting.
Construction contract award details: Specific dollar amounts and competing bidders not consistently available — requires public records requests to individual districts.
Developer connections: Sumner-Bonney Lake’s Tehaleh land purchases and construction awards (Absher) warrant scrutiny given the rapid growth corridor.
Union influence: Multiple board members with direct union ties (Caldwell/Bethel Education Association, McElroy/SEIU 925) — warrants analysis of collective bargaining decisions.
T’wina Nobles dual role: School board member + state senator creates unique power concentration in University Place.
Emily Dickinson longevity: 30 consecutive years on one school board is extraordinary — potential single-point-of-failure governance risk.

Key Overlap Themes
1. Labor-Civic Interlock (Nathe Lawver)
Nathe Lawver is the single most important interlock between organized labor and philanthropic power in Pierce County. He simultaneously:

Chairs United Way of Pierce County Board
Serves on GTCF Board
Serves as Executive Secretary, Pierce County Building & Construction Trades Council, AFL-CIO

This grants labor a direct voice in both the largest community foundation and the largest fundraising organization in the county, while giving those institutions labor legitimacy.

2. GTCF-Government Axis

8. CONCLUSION & INVESTIGATIVE LEADS
Key Findings


Nonprofit/philanthropic power in Pierce County is heavily concentrated across a small network of interlocking boards, with GTCF, United Way, and Tacoma Art Museum forming a governance triangle.


Government officials sit on grantmaking boards — Ryan Mello (now County Executive) and Rosie Ayala (Councilmember) have held GTCF board seats while holding elected office, creating potential conflicts of interest between funding decisions and government policy.


Corporate influence flows through foundation boards — major banks (Umpqua, Bank of America, Columbia, Northwest), health insurers (Coordinated Care, Regence), and wealth management firms (Morgan Stanley, Mission Wealth) all have representation on foundation boards.


Labor has a formal seat at the table through Nathe Lawver’s dual board roles, but labor representation is concentrated in building trades, not service/healthcare unions.


The Russell Family Foundation is the primary environmental/climate funder in Pierce County, operating independently from the GTCF-United Way social-service nexus.


Trust-based wealth ($207M GTCF, $77M TRFF, Cheney lumber fortune, Russell Investments fortune, PACCAR fortune) is being deployed through increasingly racial-equity and climate-focused grantmaking, while the board composition remains heavily weighted toward professional and corporate elites.

 Investigate Dona Ponepinto’s role at Coordinated Care and any intersection with United Way funding

 Profile Lyle Quasim’s full board network (GTCF + Forterra + state government history)
 Examine the Foundation for Tacoma Students board and funding — key collective impact intermediary
