0. Why this person or group is on the map

Why he’s on the map: Bob Ferguson is the Governor of Washington State. He runs the state’s executive branch. He picks judges for every court in the state, including Pierce County Superior Court. He also writes the state budget plan.
Direct Pierce County action: In February 2026, he chose Doris Walkins to fill a Pierce County Superior Court seat. That was a direct use of his power over a Pierce County court.
Pierce County vote: He won Pierce County in the 2024 governor’s race with 50.79% of the vote. It was close — only about 8,000 votes separated him from Republican Dave Reichert.
Who is NOT on the map: Lt. Gov. Denny Heck sits on the Governor’s Economic Development Council but is profiled on his own page. Former Gov. Jay Inslee is out of office now.

1. Who they are

Full name: Robert Watson Ferguson (source 1, 2).
Goes by: Bob Ferguson (source 1, 3).
Born: February 23, 1965, in Washington State. He is a fourth-generation Washingtonian (source 1, 2, 3).
Wife and kids: Colleen Ferguson, a teacher. Twins Jack and Katie. They live in the Governor’s Mansion in Olympia (source 1, 3).
Parents: Murray Ferguson, who worked at Boeing. Betty Ferguson, a special education teacher. He is one of seven children (source 2, 3).
Education: Bishop Blanchet High School; BA in Political Science, University of Washington (1989); JD, New York University School of Law (1995). He also served in the Jesuit Volunteer Corps after college (source 2, 3, 12).
Before office: Law clerk for Chief Judge W. Fremming Nielsen in Eastern Washington and Judge Myron Bright on the 8th Circuit Court. After that, he worked as a lawyer at the firm Preston, Gates & Ellis, now called K&L Gates (source 2, 3, 12).
Personal: Catholic. Chess master (rated 2232 by FIDE, the world chess body; twice won the Washington State Chess Championship). He likes to climb and backpack (source 1, 3).

3. Where their power comes from

The office. Ferguson is the 24th Governor of Washington. He took office on January 13, 2025. His term ends January 8, 2029. As governor, he runs state agencies, writes the budget plan, picks judges, signs laws, and sets the legislative agenda (source 1, 2, 3, 8).
The budget. He proposed a 2026 supplemental budget with $4 billion in cuts and $1.3 billion in new programs. His priorities are housing, public safety, ferries, affordability, and education (source 10, 11). The 2025–27 two-year state budget added $9 billion or more in new or higher taxes to close a shortfall (source 11).
Judicial appointments. He picks the judges for every state court seat. That includes the Washington Supreme Court, the Court of Appeals, and every Superior Court (source 8). He has chosen two WA Supreme Court justices (Colleen Melody and Theo Angelis) and several Superior Court judges, including Doris Walkins in Pierce County (source 6, 8, 9). He can also strike individual budget items with a line-item veto.
Executive orders. He signs executive orders to direct state policy. Recent ones include EO 26-02 (the Governor’s Economic Development Council, June 25, 2026), EO 26-01 (workplace rules for menopause, June 1, 2026), a license plate reader law (SB 6002, March 2026), wildfire emergency orders (August 2026), and a Medicaid executive order (September 2026) (source 13, 14, 15, 16).
Where his power reaches: All 39 counties in Washington, including Pierce County.

5. How they touch government

Campaign money. His 2024 governor’s campaign raised a lot. He beat Reichert, who ran a $1.7 million+ operation (source 4). Full filings from the state campaign-finance agency (PDC) were not pulled in this pass.
Pierce County vote. He won Pierce County 220,153 (50.79%) to Reichert’s 212,218 (48.96%) in November 2024. About 443,447 ballots were cast, with 76.73% turnout (source 5).
Judicial picks. He picked Doris Walkins for Pierce County Superior Court on February 25, 2026. She filled the seat left open by Judge Karena Kirkendoll’s retirement in Department 17 (source 6, 7). He picked Colleen Melody for the Washington Supreme Court on November 24, 2025 (replacing Justice Mary Yu) and Theo Angelis on March 9, 2026 (replacing Justice Barbara Madsen) (source 8, 9).
Budget. He proposed the 2025–27 state budget (signed May 2025) and the 2026 supplemental budget (proposed December 23, 2025). The plan includes $4 billion in cuts, $1.3 billion in new programs, and $9 billion+ in new taxes. It shapes Pierce County funding for housing, public safety, and schools (source 10, 11).
Orders that hit Pierce County. His Economic Development Council order (EO 26-02) brought statewide planning. SB 6002 (the license plate reader law) led the Pierce County Sheriff to shut down Flock cameras. He also signed wildfire emergency orders (August 2026) and a Medicaid executive order (September 2026) (source 13, 14, 16).
PDC appointment. He appointed Matt Segal of Pacifica Law Group to the Washington State Public Disclosure Commission (PDC) (source 17).

6. Other seats they hold

Governor’s Economic Development Council. A 26-member panel with senior Amazon, Microsoft, and Boeing executives; labor leaders (the State Labor Council and the Building and Construction Trades Council); tribal reps; and university presidents. Washington Supreme Court. Two of his picks now sit there: Colleen Melody and Theo Angelis. Melody used to run the civil rights division at the Attorney General’s office under Ferguson (source 8).
Pierce County Superior Court. Doris Walkins, his February 2026 appointee (source 6, 7).
King County Superior Court. Kent Liu, Daniel York, Benjamin Santos, and Tenaya Scheinman, all his picks (source 8).
Washington Court of Appeals. Tyson R. Hill (Division III), his appointee (source 8).
Washington State Democratic Party. He won as the Democratic candidate for governor (source 2, 4).
Past networks. His former AG office staff (Colleen Melody led the civil rights division). Former King County Council member (2004–2013) (source 2).

1. Who they are

The bottom line. Bob Ferguson holds the most powerful single office in Washington State. As governor, he picks judges — including for Pierce County courts. He writes the state’s budget plan. He signs executive orders. He sets the agenda for his party. He won the 2024 race statewide and narrowly won Pierce County too. That narrow win matters: it shows Pierce County is a swing area where his local actions carry political weight.
Conflicts to watch. Picking Colleen Melody for the Supreme Court looks like cronyism to critics — she ran the civil rights division at his old AG office. His Economic Development Council puts Amazon, Microsoft, and Boeing at the table with labor and tribal reps, which raises policy-capture concerns. His $9 billion+ tax package while pushing “competitiveness” reforms sends mixed signals. No personal financial conflicts were found.

Boeing (Frederickson) — Deep Profile
Case: INV-2026-002 · Profile: profiles/boeing.md

Graph description: The Boeing Company’s Frederickson fabrication facility in Pierce County, WA (Tacoma-area Frederickson industrial zone); 500-acre site; manufactures wing skins, stringers, and tail surfaces for 747, 757, 767, 777 commercial programs and Apache helicopter components; ~1,500 employees (2017 EDB count, declined from ~1,750 in 2016); one of the few Boeing facilities with deep Pierce County roots
Known facts: Frederickson plant established in the 1990s; subject of Boeing’s October 2024 17,000-employee company-wide layoff announcement and the September 2024 IAM 751 strike (Boeing Frederickson listed among idled facilities); sixth-largest private employer in Pierce County per EDB 2017; major Pierce County aerospace employer
Status: ✅ researched — 2026-09-19 — tier3-chunk1
Sources: 5/3 (minimum for tier3)

0. Why this person or group is on the map

Why Boeing is on the map. Boeing’s Frederickson plant is Boeing’s only major factory in Pierce County. It has about 1,500 direct jobs. It gives Boeing a seat at the local economic-development table. Boeing is on the map for four reasons. (1) It holds a place in the county: a 500-acre factory in the Frederickson industrial zone. (2) It makes decisions: Boeing runs subcontracting, hiring, and capital spending at the site. (3) It has a strong reputation: Boeing is a global Fortune 100 aerospace company, and its Frederickson plant puts Pierce County on national aerospace supply chains. (4) It is well-connected: Boeing has links to Joint Base Lewis-McChord (JBLM) as an aerospace partner, and seats on the Chamber of Commerce board and the Economic Development Board (EDB).
What is NOT on the map. Boeing corporate (The Boeing Company, based in Arlington VA since 2022, formerly in Chicago) is the parent. It is the controlling entity here but is not a separate node. Other Boeing suppliers in the area (Toray Composites America in Frederickson; AIM Aerospace) are not separate entries. The Machinists Union (IAM District 751, SPEEA) is not on the map. Boeing’s Federal Way office and Renton/Everett factories are out of Pierce County.

1. Who they are

Legal name: The Boeing Company (operating unit: Boeing Fabrication — Frederickson).
Type: Public industrial corporation (NYSE: BA). Incorporated in Delaware. Aerospace and defense maker.
Tax ID (EIN): 91-0425694 (The Boeing Company). SEC CIK 0000012927. Files 10-K annual reports.
Parent and subsidiaries: Parent is The Boeing Company. Frederickson is an operating site of Boeing Commercial Airplanes (BCA) and Boeing Defense, Space & Security (BDS). It builds skin and spar parts for BCA commercial wing programs. It also builds Apache-related parts for BDS.
Who owns it: Public shareholders. Top holders include Vanguard, BlackRock, State Street, and Capital Group. CEO Kelly Ortberg (since Aug 2024).
Laws that apply: Delaware General Corporation Law. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) Part 21 (aircraft production approval). ITAR (defense articles). Securities Exchange Act.
Founded: Boeing was founded in 1916 in Seattle. The Frederickson plant opened in the 1990s (the plant marked its 20th anniversary in the mid-2010s).
Pierce County location: Frederickson Industrial Park, south of Puyallup near the Joint Base Lewis-McChord (JBLM) military base. Bounded roughly by 176th St E and Frederickson Industrial Park Rd. In unincorporated Pierce County (the FRED 310 zoning case surrounds the plant).

3. Where their power comes from

Power held: Boeing Frederickson holds economic power in Pierce County through four channels. (1) Jobs: about 1,500 direct jobs, making it one of the county’s largest private employers (6th-largest in the 2017 EDB list). (2) Land: 500 acres of dedicated aerospace manufacturing. (3) Supply chain: the plant builds wing skins, stringers, and tail surfaces for the 747, 757, 767, and 777. That makes it a single point of failure inside Boeing’s production system. (4) Capital spending: the FRED 310 zoning case proposes 310 acres of adjacent industrial development, expanding Boeing’s landholdings.
Economic overlap: Boeing’s 66,800 employees in Washington state (Dec 2023, Seattle Metro Chamber data) make it the state’s largest private employer. Its Pierce County site is a key part of the regional aerospace cluster.
Government contracts: Boeing Frederickson builds Apache helicopter parts for BDS under federal contracts with the US Army and international customers (UK, India, Saudi Arabia, and others). Boeing’s $25 billion in losses since 2019 (per AP) put cash-burn pressure on the company, including the Frederickson site.
Jobs controlled: About 1,500 employees in Frederickson (2017 EDB count). It was 1,575 in 2017, down from 1,750 in 2016. The October 2024 layoff announcement hit 17,000 Boeing employees company-wide. By November 2024, 2,199 Washington state Boeing workers had received layoff notices (per ESD filings). The exact Frederickson layoff count is UNVERIFIED.
Land and real estate: 500-acre factory in Frederickson Industrial Park. The Pierce County FRED 310 zoning case (2021) proposed two adjacent parcels of about 310 acres for industrial, warehouse, and office development for lease. The site is south of 176th St E and east of Frederickson Industrial Park Rd, around the current Boeing plant.

Frederickson workers benefit from high-wage aerospace jobs (about $80K–$120K typical for machinists; the IAM 751 contract after the strike gave a 38% pay raise over 4 years). Pierce County benefits from Boeing’s tax base, capital spending, and supply-chain ripple effects. The Boeing Company controls whether the Frederickson plant keeps operating, what products it makes, and how many people it employs. With 66,800 employees statewide and the company’s only major Pierce County factory in Frederickson, Boeing’s structural importance to the county far exceeds what a “tier3” rank suggests.

1. Who they are

The bottom line. Boeing’s Frederickson plant is Pierce County’s only major Boeing industrial site. It is a 500-acre aerospace factory with about 1,500 workers (down from 1,750 in 2016 to 1,575 in 2017, and likely lower after the 2024 layoffs). The plant’s power base is its aerospace supply-chain role. Boeing Frederickson builds wing skins, stringers, and tail surfaces for the 737, 747, 757, 767, and 777. It also builds Apache helicopter parts for defense. That single-point-of-failure role gives Frederickson outsized weight inside Boeing’s production system. The plant’s economic weight in Pierce County far exceeds what the tier3 graph rank suggests. Boeing’s Pierce County workforce is concentrated here, and the plant’s fortunes after the 2024 layoffs will shape the county’s economic path.
Conflicts-of-interest flags. Boeing Frederickson creates a structural conflict between private corporate interests and public Pierce County interests. Boeing’s October 2024 layoff announcement (a 10% cut, 17,000 jobs company-wide) imposed real costs on Washington workers and on Pierce County’s economic base. The 2024 IAM 751 strike and its 38% pay-raise deal shifted labor costs to Boeing. Boeing is now recouping those costs through layoffs. The 2024 FRED 310 zoning case proposed 310 acres of adjacent industrial development for lease. That suggests Boeing is planning for future growth, but it also creates land-use tension with neighbors. The defense reading: Boeing is a private company making market-driven choices. The 38% pay raise reflected workers’ leverage. Layoffs reflect Boeing’s $25B+ losses. The FRED 310 expansion would create jobs.
Two readings. The opposing reading is that Boeing Frederickson’s power is overstated. Boeing’s $25B+ losses, FAA production caps on the 737 MAX, the 2024 IAM strike, and the deferred 777X program all threaten the plant’s future. Under this view, Boeing Frederickson is on a downward arc and its about 1,500 jobs could shrink fast. The other reading: the 777X tail-fabrication work (announced 2014) and Apache helicopter production (runs through 2028) provide a stable floor. The FRED 310 zoning case shows Boeing is planning for future capacity. The 2025–2026 path is unclear, but the plant’s role inside Boeing’s production system gives it institutional protection.
Confidence: Medium. Boeing Frederickson’s existence, product mix, employment scale, and strategic role are confirmed by primary Boeing/EDB/Pierce County sources (reliability 0.85–0.95). Specific 2024–2025 employment at Frederickson is UNVERIFIED (likely lower than 1,500 due to layoffs, exact figure not located in this session). Pierce County-specific Boeing tax payments and contracts are UNVERIFIED. The plant’s relationship to specific JBLM Apache operations is UNVERIFIED beyond general Apache production.

0. Why this person or group is on the map

Bruce Dammeier is on this map because he held the top elected job in Pierce County: Pierce County Executive from 2017 to 2024. The Executive runs the county’s $1B+ budget, can veto Council laws, and hires the heads of about 30 county departments. He is a Republican. He left office in January 2025 after hitting his term limit. Democrat Ryan Mello took the seat.
People NOT on the map: Pat McCarthy (a former Executive before him), Roger Bush (a Council Chair during his term), and Joe Stortini (an even earlier Executive).

1. Who they are

Full name: Bruce Dammeier.
Born: Not confirmed in this pass. No date of birth in the records reviewed.
School: B.S. in Ocean Engineering from the U.S. Naval Academy, graduated with distinction. M.S. in Engineering from the University of Washington (UW).
Military: 8 years as a U.S. Navy Civil Engineer Corps Officer. He went on relief missions.
Career: Naval officer → ran a family printing business → community volunteer → WA House District 25 (2009–2013) → WA Senate District 25 (2013–2017, Senate Majority Caucus Vice Chair) → Pierce County Executive (2017–2024).
Family: Married to Lauren Dammeier.
Home: Pierce County native. He went to Curtis High School in the University Place area.

3. Where their power comes from

Elected executive power (from his office): As Pierce County Executive from 2017 to 2024, Dammeier could veto Council laws. He hired the heads of about 30 county departments. He signed contracts and deals with other governments. He used the veto in public. His most public veto was Ordinance 2024-540s on large tent encampments in August 2024.
Budget power (decisions on money): He wrote and negotiated the county’s two-year budget, worth more than $1B for operations. He also decided how to spend federal ARPA funds, homelessness programs, and the Building Together Initiative.
Bridge role to nonprofits: He sat on boards for community groups like Tacoma Goodwill and Mel Korum YMCA. As Executive, his seat on these boards linked county power to the local nonprofit world.
Scoring basis: Former Executive weight 3 + Pierce GOP member weight 3.

Verdict: Dammeier is a tier-3 node whose power was large on paper but limited in practice. As Executive he held the veto pen, $1B+ budget power, and the right to hire department heads. But the Council often clashed with him (per KNKX). His actual ability to drive decisions was less than his formal powers would suggest. His term limit ended his direct power in 2024. He still has soft power through nonprofit boards and GOP networks.
Conflicts-of-interest flags: (a) Sitting Executive at the same time as sitting on nonprofit boards (Goodwill, YMCA) — legal, but it raises perception concerns. (b) Possible revolving door with his family printing business — UNVERIFIED which county contracts, if any, went to that business under his watch.
Analysis of alternatives (ICD-203 opposing view): Another reading is that Dammeier was a weak Executive whose veto was often overridden or countered by a Democratic-leaning Council — so a constrained actor. The graph weight of 3 reflects his office, not his actual record of decisions. After leaving office, he is best seen as a senior GOP and county-establishment figure with leftover influence on party endorsements and nonprofit boards, not as an active decision-maker.

District 5 covers Parkland, Spanaway, Midland, Fife, Fife Heights, Browns Point, NE/Eastside Tacoma, and the Port of Tacoma. Yambe must win a 2025 election to keep the seat through 2026.

Graph description: Candidate training program run by the Tacoma-Pierce County Chamber; trains prospective political candidates in campaign operations, fundraising, and civics
Known facts: Operated by Tacoma-Pierce County Chamber (EIN 91-0434830); 1-day intensive primer covering civics, campaign strategy, fundraising, media/messaging; speakers are local political leaders; listed among Chamber’s core programs alongside Business Leadership Academy, MIC South Sound, Pierce County Business Accelerator, and Spaceworks Tacoma
Status: ✅ researched — 2026-09-19 — tier2-chunk3
Sources: 6/5 (minimum for tier2)

0. Why this person or group is on the map

The Candidate Academy is a candidate-training program run by the Tacoma-Pierce County Chamber. The Chamber is the region’s main business advocacy group. Its tax ID number (EIN) is 91-0434830 (Source 3). The Academy meets the bar for being well-connected. It bridges the business world and the electoral world by training future candidates. It also meets the bar for from holding office. It is a formal program of the Chamber, a gatekeeper in Pierce County politics. The graph shows a weight-5 edge from the Academy to the Pierce County Council. That marks its pipeline function.
A few related Chamber programs sit outside this map. The Business Leadership Academy is a separate 10-week program, founded in 1978 (Source 5). It is not directly political, so it is excluded. Spaceworks Tacoma is a Chamber arts and business incubator. It is excluded. The Pierce County Business Accelerator is for BIPOC businesses. It is excluded.

1. Who they are

Exact legal name: The Candidate Academy is not a separate legal entity. It is a program of the Tacoma-Pierce County Chamber of Commerce. The Chamber’s legal name is “Tacoma-Pierce County Chamber of Commerce.” Its EIN is 91-0434830 (Source 3).
Entity type: The Chamber is a 501(c)(6) business league. It is a chamber of commerce (Sources 3 and 4, ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer: “Business leagues, chambers of commerce, real estate boards, etc., created for the improvement of business conditions”). Donations to the Chamber are not tax-deductible (Source 4).
EIN and registration: 91-0434830 (Sources 3 and 4). Year formed: 1884 (Source 3, CauseIQ). The tax exemption was issued before 2012. ProPublica has filings from 2012 onward (Source 4). The fiscal year ends in September (Source 3).
Parent and subsidiaries: The parent is the Tacoma-Pierce County Chamber of Commerce. The Chamber also runs a separate foundation: “Tacoma Pierce County Chamber of Commerce Foundation” (EIN 20-4962532, 501(c)(3), tax exemption issued August 2006, Source 6). The Candidate Academy is a program, not a subsidiary.
Ownership chain: The Chamber is an independent nonprofit. It is run by a board of directors. The board has 31 voting members. All 31 are independent voting members per the most recent 990 (Source 3).
Governing law: Washington state nonprofit corporation law. State law (RCW) 24.03. The federal tax agency (IRS) 501(c)(6) status.

3. Where their power comes from

Power held: The Candidate Academy holds cultural power and power from connections. It is a candidate-recruitment and training pipeline. It shapes who runs for local office. It does not hold legal or regulatory power. It does not have veto power. Its power is indirect. By teaching campaign operations, fundraising, and media messaging, it shapes who enters local politics. The program helps people “determine whether to throw their hat in the ring or how to otherwise get engaged” (Source 1).
Basis for power-domain overlap (political domain): The program covers Civics 101, campaign strategy and operations, election filing, fundraising and event planning, media and messaging, and campaign management. Local political leaders teach these topics (Source 1). This puts the Chamber in the role of gatekeeper for business-aligned candidates.
Key facts:
Who is funded and endorsed? The Candidate Academy does not directly fund or endorse candidates. It trains them. The Chamber’s separate Voters Guide handles endorsements (Source 2). It is unverified whether Academy graduates get Chamber endorsements at higher rates.
PAC spending? UNVERIFIED. No Chamber PAC was found in this research. The Chamber’s 501(c)(6) status allows political advocacy, but not direct candidate donations (Source 4).
Party machinery control? The program is nonpartisan in framing. It is open to “civic-minded individuals.” But the Chamber’s business focus means the training likely leans toward pro-business candidates. Inference: the program acts as a soft recruiting channel for business-aligned candidates. This is not stated openly.
Candidate output? UNVERIFIED. The Chamber does not publish a list of Academy graduates. It does not track how many graduates run or win. The 47th Business Leadership Academy graduated “more than twenty participants” in 2025 (Source 5). No similar number is available for the Candidate Academy.

3. Where their power comes from






























IndicatorFindingEvidence (source #)Who benefitsProspective candidates benefit from training and networking with “local elected officials and community advocates” (source #1). The Chamber benefits by expanding its network of politically engaged allies. Business-aligned candidates benefit from Chamber infrastructure and connections.#1Who sitsThe program features “speakers who are leaders in the political sphere around Tacoma and Pierce County” (source #1) — specific speaker roster UNVERIFIED. The Chamber’s board (31 voting members per 990, source #3) governs the parent organization.#1, #3Who governsThe Tacoma-Pierce County Chamber Board of Directors governs the Candidate Academy as a program of the Chamber. UNVERIFIED: whether the Academy has a separate advisory committee or program director.#3Who winsUNVERIFIED — no public data on Academy graduates who subsequently won elected office. The program’s stated goal is to equip participants to “become better equipped to serve as a candidate and elected or appointed official” (source #1), but outcomes are not tracked publicly.#1
5. How they touch government

Lobbying: The parent Chamber, a 501(c)(6), engages in advocacy (Source 2: the Chamber lists “Advocacy” as a core function). The Candidate Academy is an educational program. It is not a lobbying vehicle. Specific L-2 lobbyist registrations for the Chamber are unverified.
Contracts and grants: UNVERIFIED. No government contracts or grants were found for the Candidate Academy. The Chamber’s 990 (Source 3) shows $3.1 million in revenue for FY2024. Program-level revenue is not available.
Campaign donations: The Chamber, as a 501(c)(6), cannot make direct candidate donations. The Candidate Academy does not donate to candidates. It is unverified whether speakers or graduates have given money through other vehicles.
Voters Guide: The Chamber publishes a Voters Guide (Source 2: listed under Resources on the Chamber website). This is a separate advocacy function from the Candidate Academy. It is the Chamber’s interface with the electoral system.
Regulatory interactions: None found. The Academy is an educational program. It has no regulatory role.

6. Other seats they hold

Tacoma-Pierce County Chamber (chamber): This is the parent organization. The Candidate Academy is a Chamber program (Source 1). Graph edge: runs, weight 6.
Pierce County Council (county-council): The Academy trains people who may run for offices like the County Council (Source 1 covers “various levels of government and elected positions”). Graph edge: trains_candidates, weight 5. It is unverified whether specific Council members have been Academy speakers.
Pacific Lutheran University (PLU): The Chamber’s separate Business Leadership Academy is “made possible through a partnership between the Chamber and Pacific Lutheran University” (Source 5). It is unverified whether PLU also partners on the Candidate Academy.
Local elected officials: The Academy has “local elected officials and community advocates” as speakers (Source 1). This creates direct board overlaps between the Chamber and sitting officials. Specific names are unverified.

Network analysis: The Candidate Academy is a two-edge node. It bridges the Chamber (economic and advocacy world) and the County Council (government and electoral world). The weight-6 runs edge to the Chamber is the main tie. The Academy is a Chamber program, not an independent body. The weight-5 trains_candidates edge to the County Council shows its pipeline function. It trains people who may later run for Council and other offices. The Academy ranks 36/163 with a composite power of 0.052. This reflects its indirect power. It does not govern or regulate. But it shapes who runs for office. That is a form of agenda-setting power.
1. Who they are

1. Who they are

Verdict: The Candidate Academy is a candidate-training program run by the Tacoma-Pierce County Chamber of Commerce. It does not directly govern, regulate, or donate to candidates. Its power comes from connections and culture. It shapes who enters local politics. It gives campaign skills and access to elected officials to future candidates. The program’s 1-day format and lack of public graduate tracking limit its measurable impact. But its role as a gatekeeper for business-aligned candidates is structurally important. The Chamber also publishes a Voters Guide (Source 2) and runs the Academy. That creates a path from training to endorsement, though the Academy itself does not endorse.
Conflicts-of-interest flags: (1) The Chamber trains candidates through the Academy. It may then endorse them through its Voters Guide. That creates a path from training to endorsement that could favor Academy graduates. (2) The program is run by a 501(c)(6) business league. So training likely leans toward pro-business candidates, even if the program is nonpartisan. Defense: (1) No evidence shows that Academy graduates get special endorsement treatment. The Voters Guide and Academy are separate functions. (2) The program is open to all “civic-minded individuals” (Source 1). It covers neutral topics like civics and election filing. It does not cover ideology. No evidence of partisan filtering in participant selection was found.
Analysis of alternatives: The other reading is that the Candidate Academy is a small educational program with limited reach. It runs for one day. It does not publish a graduate list. It has no measurable impact on who gets elected in Pierce County. Under this view, the weight-5 trains_candidates edge overstates the program’s real influence. But the program’s structural position matters. It is run by the region’s main business advocacy group. It features sitting elected officials as speakers. It covers the full campaign toolkit. That gives it more agenda-setting power than its length suggests. The lack of outcome tracking is also telling. If the Academy did not work, the Chamber would publish its success numbers.
Confidence: Medium. The program’s existence, curriculum, and Chamber parentage are confirmed by primary sources (Chamber website, reliability 0.9). However, the program’s actual impact — how many graduates ran for office, won, or received Chamber endorsements — is UNVERIFIED due to absence of published outcome data. The power assessment is structural/inferential rather than empirically demonstrated.

Catholic Archdiocese — Deep Profile
Case: INV-2026-002 · Profile: profiles/catholic-archdiocese.md
Entity ID: catholic-archdiocese · Type: organization · Domain: institutional
Tier: tier3 · Rank: 122/163 · Composite power: 0.012
Graph description: Roman Catholic metropolitan archdiocese covering western Washington (including all of Pierce County); canonically responsible for parishes, schools, and religious institutions in the case-study area, and ecclesiastical sponsor of major Pierce County healthcare systems (VMFH and, through CommonSpirit, Franciscan).
Known facts: Archdiocese of Seattle (Latin: Archidiœcesis Seattlensis); 143 parishes, 72 schools; mother church St. James Cathedral, Seattle; archbishop Paul D. Etienne; ~899,000 Catholics in territory of ~6.1M (2022).
Status: ✅ researched — 2026-09-19 — tier3-chunk10
Sources: 4/3 (minimum for tier3)

0. Why this person or group is on the map


The Archdiocese of Seattle is on this map for two reasons. First, it directly runs Catholic parishes and schools in Pierce County. These include Holy Rosary, St. Ann, St. Rita, and Visitation in Tacoma, plus Bellarmine Preparatory and several grade schools. Second, it sponsors Virginia Mason Franciscan Health (a major hospital chain in Pierce County). That gives it a voice in Pierce County’s health-care market. Its 2020 to 2022 “Pierce Deanery” plan merged four Tacoma parishes into one. That was a big land-use and institutional change.
Adjacent groups not profiled. The Vatican and the global Catholic Church are too remote. Catholic Community Services of Western Washington is a separate nonprofit. CommonSpirit Health (the parent of VMFH) has its own profile. Independent Catholic schools that are not archdiocesan (like Annie Wright, which is Episcopal) are not included.

1. Who they are


Legal name: Archdiocese of Seattle (in Latin: Archidiœcesis Seattlensis).
Entity type: A Roman Catholic archdiocese (Latin Rite means the standard Western form of the Catholic Church). The civil corporate side is the Corporation of the Catholic Archbishop of Seattle, a nonprofit under Washington state law (RCW 24.03). This corporation holds title to parish property, schools, and investments. Inferred — UNVERIFIED in this round of research, but standard for US Latin-rite dioceses.
History: 1850 as the Diocese of Nesqually. Renamed in 1907. Became a metropolitan archdiocese (the head of a church region) in 1951.
Territory: 24,814 square miles — all of Western Washington, including all of Pierce County.
Stats (2022): 143 parishes, 72 schools, 6.1 million people in territory, about 899,000 Catholics (14.7%).
Mother church: St. James Cathedral, Seattle (804 9th Avenue).
Current archbishop: Paul D. Etienne (DD, installed 2019).
Governing law: Canon law (the Catholic Church’s own legal system) and Washington state law (RCW 24.03 for nonprofits, RCW 84.36 for religious-property tax breaks).

3. Where their power comes from


The Archdiocese holds three types of power. It owns and runs Catholic parish, school, and cemetery real estate in Pierce County. It sponsors CHI Franciscan / Virginia Mason Franciscan Health (a hospital chain). That gives it three power levers:


Land-use decisions. It can consolidate, sell, or redevelop property. In 2022 it sold four First Hill Seattle properties to Westbank. In 2020 to 2022 its Pierce Deanery plan merged Holy Rosary, St. Ann, Visitation, and St. Rita into one parish.
Cultural and community reach. About 900,000 Catholics live in Western Washington. That makes the Archdiocese the largest single organized religious group in Pierce County. Its parishes can mobilize people on school-board, charter, and immigrant-services issues.
Health-care influence. The Archdiocese sponsors CommonSpirit, the parent of VMFH. The archbishop’s office has a say in mission and ethics at Pierce County’s largest hospital chain. That includes St. Joseph Medical Center in Tacoma; St. Anthony in Gig Harbor; St. Clare in Lakewood; St. Elizabeth in Enumclaw; and St. Francis in Federal Way.


Key facts:
Tax status: Houses of worship and their integrated groups are tax-exempt under IRC §501(c)(3) (a federal tax code for charities). Parishes and schools pay no federal income tax. They also get a property-tax break under RCW 84.36.020.
Board overlaps: The archbishop sits on Catholic Health Ministries and the Archdiocesan Finance Council. Pastors sit on parish councils. Lay trustees sit on parish finance councils.
Government funding: Schools get state K–12 funding (under RCW 28A.150) from the Common Schools fund. Parishes rely on Sunday collections and the Annual Catholic Appeal. Downstream, VMFH brings in large Medicaid and Medicare payments.

3. Where their power comes from

1. Who they are


Verdict: The Archdiocese is a stable, long-lasting institution in Pierce County. Its power comes from parish real-estate decisions (the 2020 to 2022 Pierce Deanery merger is a clear example), sponsorship of the dominant Catholic hospital chain (CHI Franciscan → VMFH), and a parish-school network that reaches thousands of families each week. Its composite power score (0.012) is too low, because the framework under-weights canonical and religious power.
Conflict flags: Sponsorship of VMFH gives the Archdiocese a voice in a major Pierce County employer with a large land footprint. Canonical authority over a hospital chain creates a parallel accountability channel outside public meetings. The property-tax break for parish and school land is a recurring public-finance question. The defense: religious property-tax breaks are constitutional (Walz v. Taxpayers, 1970) and predate the modern hospital chain. The Archdiocese’s Pierce County footprint is small compared to public-school or secular nonprofit landholdings.
Counter-reading: The Archdiocese is in steep national demographic decline. Western Washington’s Catholic population is still growing (Hispanic and immigrant inflows). VMFH is one of the largest private employers in Pierce County. The Archdiocese is not vestigial, but it is constrained by sexual-abuse bankruptcy filings that have drained reserves in other dioceses. Confidence in this profile: Medium.
Confidence: Medium — territorial, demographic, parish, school, and Pierce-Deanery data are all primary-sourced; the corporate-veil detail (Corporation of the Catholic Archbishop of Seattle) is INFERRED from standard US Latin-rite practice.

Central Pierce Fire — Deep Profile
Case: INV-2026-002 · Profile: profiles/central-pierce-fire.md
Entity ID: central-pierce-fire · Type: organization · Domain: government
Tier: tier2 · Rank: 52/163 · Composite power: 0.036
Graph description: Central Pierce Fire & Rescue (Pierce County Fire District 6); merged with Graham Fire & Rescue and Orting Valley Fire & Rescue effective Jan 1, 2026; governed by elected Board of Fire Commissioners under Title 52 RCW
Known facts: Fire district serving central Pierce County; funded by Regular Fire Levy, EMS Levy, and Fire Benefit Charge; 2021 budget ~$105.4M appropriated; 14 commissioners post-merger; Chief Dustin Morrow; merger approved by voters April 22, 2025
Status: ✅ researched — 2026-09-19 — tier2-chunk6
Sources: 8/5 (minimum for tier2)

0. Why this person or group is on the map

Inclusion rule — power and decision-making. Central Pierce Fire & Rescue is a special-purpose fire district. It is governed by an elected Board of Fire Commissioners under Title 52 of the Revised Code of Washington (RCW), the state law that covers fire districts.
It levies taxes on property owners in its service area. It controls a budget of more than $100 million. It runs fire and emergency medical services.
On January 1, 2026, the district merged with Graham Fire & Rescue and Orting Valley Fire & Rescue. That made it one of the largest fire districts in Pierce County.
Adjacent but excluded: East Pierce Fire & Rescue and West Pierce Fire & Rescue are peer districts mapped separately. South Pierce Fire & Rescue is adjacent and mapped separately. Pierce County Fire Training Consortium is a shared service entity and not a power node.

1. Who they are

Legal name: Central Pierce Fire & Rescue. Also known as Pierce County Fire District 6.
Entity type: Government — a special-purpose fire protection district under Title 52 RCW. Set up as a municipal corporation with taxing authority.
Governing law: Title 52 RCW. The Board of Fire Commissioners is “the legislative body of Central Pierce Fire & Rescue.”
Merger history: On April 22, 2025, voters approved merging Graham Fire & Rescue and Orting Valley Fire & Rescue into Central Pierce. The Graham vote was 7,483 yes to 1,130 no. The merger took effect January 1, 2026. The three legacy districts are now one.
Board: After the merger, the board has 14 commissioners from the three legacy districts. Commissioners are elected at-large by voters. They serve six-year terms.
Executive leadership: Fire Chief Dustin Morrow.

3. Where their power comes from

Statutory authority. Under RCW 52, Central Pierce can levy voter-approved property taxes (Regular Fire Levy, EMS Levy), charge a Fire Benefit Charge (FBC), issue general obligation bonds with voter approval, and provide fire and emergency medical services within its borders.
Taxing authority: Three voter-approved funding sources:

Regular Fire Levy — about 40% of the budget. Rate was $0.50 per $1,000 of assessed value (AV) in each legacy district. A levy lid lift from $0.73 to $1.00 per $1,000 AV went on the April 2024 ballot (Resolution 24-01). A “levy lid lift” is a vote to raise the property-tax rate above the state cap.
EMS Levy — about 16% of the budget. 20.1% of Central Pierce funding in 2024.
Fire Benefit Charge (FBC) — about 36% of the budget. Based on property use and square footage, not assessed value. Must be reauthorized by voters every six years.


Budget control: The 2021 appropriated budget totaled $105,386,885 across six funds. General Fund: $64.9 million. EMS Fund: $16.6 million. GEMT (Ground Emergency Medical Transport) Fund: $12.2 million. Debt Fund: $2.5 million. Capital Projects Fund: $9.08 million. HRA/Flex: $50,000. Actual 2021 spending was $88.4 million. Post-merger 2026 totals are not verified.
Domain overlaps:

Government ↔ Economic: Taxing authority over property in the district; contracts for equipment and services.
Government ↔ Institutional: Interlocal agreements (formal cooperation contracts between governments) with peer fire districts; member of Pierce County Fire Training Consortium.



3. Where their power comes from

The merger with Graham and Orting Valley extends that base.Sources 1, 5, 7Who sitsThe 14-member Board of Fire Commissioners governs the district. Named commissioners include Russ Barstow (Co-Chair), Robert Homan (Co-Chair), Matt Holm, Steve Stringfellow, Dale Mitchell, John Caverly, Chris McAfee, Brian Estes, Neil Samuelsen, Joe Palombi, Arlene Dannat, Kevin Gorder.Sources 1, 2Who governsThe board runs business affairs, oversees administration, sets long-term vision, sets funding levels and tax levies, approves the annual budget, and hires and supervises the Fire Chief.Source 1Who winsThe merger with Graham and Orting Valley passed with strong margins (Graham: 7,483 yes vs. 1,130 no). The 2024 levy lid lift went to voters.Sources 5, 7
5. How they touch government

Taxing authority: Imposes the Regular Fire Levy, EMS Levy, and Fire Benefit Charge on properties in the district. Collected through Pierce County property tax bills.
Ballot measures: Resolution 24-01 in April 2024 lifted the fire levy from $0.73 to $1.00 per $1,000 AV. The April 22, 2025 ballot included the Graham and Orting Valley merger measures.
Pierce County Council: The district operates inside Pierce County. Its taxing authority works with the county property-tax system. The graph shows a “taxing” link to the County Council at weight 3.
State Auditor oversight: Financial practices are independently audited. Reports are on the Washington State Auditor’s Office Financial Intelligence Tool (FIT) and on the district’s website (2024 Accountability Audit Report, 2024 Financial Statements and Federal Single Audit Report).
Procurement: Uses the Small Works Roster for public works projects up to $350,000 through MRSC Rosters (a shared government purchasing list run by the Municipal Research and Services Center). Resolution 24-02 covered a sole-source purchase from Paratech US&R for rescue equipment.
Campaign finance: Not verified. Commissioner races appear on Ballotpedia (for example, John Caverly, Position 3, 2025 special election), but specific PDC filings were not pulled in this pass.

6. Other seats they hold

Board of Fire Commissioners: 14 elected commissioners from the three legacy districts. They are the governing body.
Pierce County Fire Training Consortium: Shared training resource with peer districts.
South Pierce Fire & Rescue: Joint board special meetings scheduled (September 2, 2026, at Station 94, Graham).
MRSC Rosters: Procurement connection through the Small Works Roster.
Washington State Auditor’s Office: Financial oversight and audit relationship.

1. Who they are

Verdict: Central Pierce Fire & Rescue’s power is derived from its statutory authority as a fire protection district under RCW Title 52, its voter-approved taxing powers (fire levy, EMS levy, fire benefit charge), and its control over emergency service delivery within its boundaries. The 2025–2026 merger with Graham and Orting Valley Fire & Rescue significantly expanded its territorial and fiscal footprint, making it one of the largest fire districts in Pierce County. Its Board of 14 elected commissioners exercises budgetary and operational governance. Its budget exceeded $105M (2021 appropriated) and has likely grown post-merger.
Conflicts-of-interest flags: The fire benefit charge (FBC) is calculated based on property use and square footage, creating a potential tension between the district’s revenue needs and property owners’ tax burden. The merger was promoted by district leadership and approved by voters — no evidence of improper influence found, but the consolidation reduces competitive service boundaries. Commissioner races are partisan-adjacent elections with low voter engagement, which could allow incumbent entrenchment.
Analysis of alternatives : An opposing reading would note that fire districts, while possessing taxing authority, are functionally service-delivery entities with limited political power beyond their boundaries. Their budgets are constrained by voter approval requirements (levy lid lifts, FBC reauthorization, bond votes). The merger, while expanding the district, also creates governance challenges — 14 commissioners from three legacy districts may create internal friction. The district’s power is primarily fiscal and operational rather than political.
Confidence: Medium — based on strong primary sources (district website, SAO audit, official resolutions) for structural and financial facts, but post-merger 2026 budget totals and specific commissioner PDC campaign finance data not fully extracted in this pass.

Chamber of Commerce — Deep Profile
Case: INV-2026-002 · Profile: profiles/chamber.md
Entity ID: chamber · Type: organization · Domain: economic
Tier: tier1 · Rank: 2/163 · Composite power: 0.505
Graph description: 501(c)(6) business league; economic org whose influence is political (Candidate Academy, Voters Guide, board interlocks with major employers)
Known facts: 25-member board; $3.08M revenue (FY2024, IRS 990); Candidate Academy (alumni secret); ‘Chamber candidate’ epithet; Board: Port, Boeing, MultiCare, PSE; 501(c)(6) tax-exempt status
Status: ✅ researched — 2026-09-19 — tier1-chunk1
Sources: 12/10 (minimum for tier1)

0. Why this person or group is on the map

The Tacoma-Pierce County Chamber of Commerce runs the county’s top business group. It shapes local politics in three main ways.
First, it runs the Candidate Academy. This program trains people who want to run for office. The Chamber does not say who the graduates are.
Second, it issues voter guides. These tell members which candidates and ballot measures to back.
Third, its board seats are filled by leaders of the county’s biggest employers. They include MultiCare, the Port of Tacoma, Boeing, Puget Sound Energy (PSE), and Banner Bank. These board ties give the Chamber a direct line into policy fights.
The Chamber is a 501(c)(6) business league. The IRS gives this tax status to groups that work to improve business conditions. Its address is 950 Pacific Ave, Suite 300, Tacoma, WA 98402. Its phone number is (253) 627-2175. Its EIN (Employer Identification Number, the IRS tax ID) is 91-0434830.
Related but separate groups (not part of the Chamber): The Economic Development Board for Tacoma-Pierce County (EDB) is a separate partner. The Manufacturing Industrial Council for the South Sound is a Chamber program, not its own group. The Chamber Foundation (EIN 20-4962532, revenue $76K) is a separate nonprofit that supports the Chamber.

1. Who they are

Official name: Tacoma-Pierce County Chamber of Commerce
Type: 501(c)(6) business league
EIN: 91-0434830
Address: 950 Pacific Ave, Ste 300, Tacoma, WA 98402
Phone: (253) 627-2175
Governing law: Internal Revenue Code section 501(c)(6); Washington State nonprofit corporation law
Related entity: Tacoma Pierce County Chamber of Commerce Foundation (EIN 20-4962532, a 501(c)(3) nonprofit, revenue about $76K in fiscal year 2023)

2. Their career and offices

CEO/President: Andrea Reay. She was paid $196,300 in fiscal year 2024, per the IRS 990 form (the annual tax return nonprofits file). She took over from Tom Pierson. Pierson was CEO from 2011 to 2021. He came back as interim CEO before Reay’s appointment.
Vice President: David Schroedel ($165,458 in fiscal year 2024)
Board Chair: Jon Rossman (named on the fiscal year 2024 IRS 990)
Chair-elect: Kierra Phifer (also on the South Sound Military and Communities Partnership, or SSMCP, Steering Committee)
Secretary: Christopher Waldron
Treasurer: Bethany Doane
West Side Branch Chair: Bill Peters
Board of Directors (25+ members, fiscal year 2024 IRS 990): Jackie Flowers (former Tacoma Public Utilities director), Gary Yamamoto, Danny Hankins, Jennifer Schomburg, Alfredo Aguilar, Tamar Jackson, Andy Harris, Bridgette Johnson, Dr. Joyce Loveday, Renee McClain, Alex Mather, Christine Nhan (PSE, board overlap), Tony Belot, Tanya Durand, Michael Pamintuan, Dr. David O’Brien, Chyna Willman (Grit City Wellness, matches graph), Eric Johnson (Port of Tacoma Executive Director, board overlap), and 13 others.
Board overlap notes:
Christine Nhan also sits on the Puget Sound Energy board.
Eric Johnson also leads the Port of Tacoma.
John Wiborg is the MultiCare Board Chair. He also sits on the Chamber board. He is listed in the graph as a Chamber board member.
Dona Ponepinto also serves United Way and Tacoma Community College (TCC).
Kierra Phifer also sits on the SSMCP Steering Committee and on the Puget Sound Energy board.

3. Where their power comes from

Candidate Academy (training future candidates): The Chamber’s Candidate Academy trains people who want to run for office. The Chamber does not make the alumni list public. Locals call graduates “Chamber candidates.” This pipeline of business-friendly candidates is the Chamber’s strongest political tool.
Voter guides: The Chamber publishes voter guides. These guide members’ views on candidates and ballot measures.
Board overlaps: The 25+ member board includes top leaders from the county’s biggest employers and most powerful institutions. They come from MultiCare, the Port of Tacoma, Boeing, PSE, and Banner Bank. These ties create a steady channel for business influence on local policy.
Advocacy and lobbying: The Chamber’s stated programs include “Advocacy.” This means direct lobbying of Pierce County Council, Tacoma City Council, and the state legislature on business-friendly policy.
501(c)(6) tax-exempt status: The Chamber is tax-exempt under federal law as a business league. The Pierce County Council has indirect power over local tax rules that affect Chamber members.
Key facts:
Revenue: about $3.08 million in fiscal year 2024 (per IRS 990)
Ownership: nonprofit, no owners; run by an elected board

1. Who they are

Candidate Academy alumni list: Who are the graduates? Which Pierce County elected officials came out of the Candidate Academy? This is the Chamber’s most opaque power channel. PDC or public records requests may be needed.
PDC lobbying filings: Pull the Chamber’s lobbying spending and the issues it lobbied on from PDC L-1 and L-2 reports.
Audit findings, FY2022–FY2025: What specific compliance failures did each “material noncompliance” finding cover, and which federal programs were involved? This is a red flag for any group that handles federal money. Get the full audit reports (linked from the Chamber’s ProPublica page).
Revenue decline: Why has revenue dropped from $3.95 million (fiscal year 2022) to $3.08 million (fiscal year 2024)? Is it from fewer members, less program revenue, or the CEO change?
Board member donor activity: Cross-check board members’ personal and corporate PDC donations against the Chamber’s policy positions.
The “Chamber candidate” label: Which candidates have been called “Chamber candidates,” and how did that label affect their races?

1. Who they are

Verdict: The Tacoma-Pierce County Chamber of Commerce holds power in three ways. First, the Candidate Academy trains and may pick future candidates who back business. Second, board ties link the county’s biggest employers (MultiCare, Port, PSE, Boeing) and growth-machine developers (Rush, Miles, Southport, Tucci, Lincoln Park, Nall) into one advocacy network. Third, the Chamber lobbies directly and issues voter guides. Its $3.08 million in revenue is small next to the billions run by its board members’ groups. The Chamber’s value is as a coordinator, not as a money mover. Falling revenue (down 22% over two years) and four straight years of audit findings (FY2022–FY2025, including two “material noncompliance” findings) point to stress that could weaken it.
Conflicts-of-interest flags (the defense would make these points):
Candidate Academy secrecy: The Chamber will not say who the graduates are. That looks like a shadow political machine. A defense would say it is normal nonprofit privacy. But pairing candidate training with voter guides and board overlaps creates a clear conflict between the Chamber’s “civic education” story and its political work.
Developer board ties: Developers sit on the board (Rush, Miles, Southport, Tucci, Lincoln Park, Nall). They have land-use cases before the County Council. That creates a direct conflict between the Chamber’s advocacy role and its members’ money interests.
Audit findings: Four straight fiscal years (FY2022–FY2025) carry audit findings — “material noncompliance” in FY2022 and FY2024; internal-control deficiencies in FY2023 and FY2025. The audits’ presence suggests the Chamber handled $750K+ in federal grant money in those years (inference from the single-audit requirement; confirm from the audit reports). This raises money-oversight questions if the Chamber handles any public funds.
501(c)(6) versus political activity: As a business league, the Chamber can do some political work but cannot give money to candidates directly. The line between “civic education” (voter guides, candidate forums) and election work is thin.
Analysis of alternatives: The other reading is that the Chamber is in decline and its power is overstated. Revenue is falling. Reserves are dropping. The CEO has changed twice in three years. Audit findings point to governance problems. The “Chamber candidate” label may be a relic of past power, not a sign of current power. Under this view, real economic power sits with the corporations on the board (MultiCare, the Port, PSE, Boeing), not with the Chamber as a coordinator. The Candidate Academy may produce few real elected officials. The voter guide may barely move votes. The Chamber’s rank of 2 out of 163 in the graph may come from its dense connections, not from real power to make decisions.
Confidence: Medium — IRS 990 data is primary-source and highly reliable, but the Chamber’s political influence channels (Candidate Academy, lobbying) are opaque. The audit findings are concerning but not yet fully investigated. The decline in revenue and net assets is factual but its political implications are inferred.

Chatham AM — Deep Profile

Graph description: New Jersey–based hedge fund founded in 2000 by Anthony Melchiorre; owner of The McClatchy Company (which publishes The News Tribune, the dominant Pierce County daily) since September 2020; also controls Postmedia (Canada), A360media, and RR Donnelley. the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC)-settled in 2023 for $19.3M over fixed-income trading violations.
Known facts: Chatham Asset Management LLC; HQ 26 Main Street, Chatham Borough, NJ 07928; founder/owner Anthony Melchiorre (~70% stake; Short Hills, NJ resident); key principal Larry Buchalter; SEC-settled (Apr 2023) charges with founder for $19.3M over improper trading in AMI/A360media-related fixed-income securities.
Status: ✅ researched — 2026-09-19 — tier3-chunk10
Sources: 4/3 (minimum for tier3)

0. Why this person or group is on the map


Why Chatham is on the map. Chatham Asset Management owns The McClatchy Company. McClatchy publishes The News Tribune in Tacoma — the main daily paper for Pierce County. Chatham is based in New Jersey. But its decisions about money, layoffs, and use of AI directly shape what Pierce County residents read about their local government.
What that gives Chatham. Two kinds of power. One is ownership of a regional newspaper monopoly. The other is the impact of newsroom cuts on accountability reporting at the local-government level.
Who is NOT on the map. McClatchy itself has its own profile. Postmedia is a Canadian chain owned by Chatham but is outside the case area. A360media (also called American Media) merged into McClatchy in December 2024 and is now part of the McClatchy operation.

1. Who they are


Legal name: Chatham Asset Management, LLC.
Type of business: A private hedge-fund manager set up as a New Jersey LLC.
Headquarters: 26 Main Street, Chatham Borough, NJ 07928.
Founded: 2000 (about 26 years ago, per Wikipedia).
Founder and owner: Anthony Melchiorre. He owns about 70% of the firm. He was born around 1968 (per 2023 reports). He grew up near Chicago and now lives in Short Hills, NJ.
Other key principal: Larry Buchalter.
Regulatory history: In April 2023, the SEC charged Chatham and Melchiorre with improper trading in fixed-income securities tied to American Media / AMI stock. They paid a $19.3 million civil penalty to settle (per NJ Globe and Reuters, April 2023).
Major companies Chatham owns:
The McClatchy Company, LLC. Private; bought September 4, 2020, out of Chapter 11 bankruptcy for $312 million. Headquartered in Sacramento, California. Runs 30 daily papers across 14 states. Merged with A360media in December 2024 and is now called McClatchy Media.
Postmedia Network Canada Corp. About 66% control since October 2016. It is Canada’s largest newspaper chain.
A360media, LLC. Formerly American Media, Inc. Merged into McClatchy in December 2024.
RR Donnelley. Printing and distribution company.
Governing law: Delaware and New Jersey LLC rules. SEC-registered investment adviser. Where required, it files reports under Section 13 of the Securities Exchange Act (Postmedia is publicly listed in Canada).

3. Where their power comes from


What power does this company hold?


Control of media markets. Through McClatchy, Chatham owns Washington’s second-largest newspaper (The News Tribune in Tacoma) plus The Olympian, The Bellingham Herald, and the Tri-City Herald. The four biggest McClatchy papers in Washington cover the I-5 corridor from Bellingham down through Pierce County (per NW Labor Press and the Seattle Times).
Power over the newsroom. Since buying McClatchy in 2020, Chatham has pushed repeated newsroom cuts. The Miami Herald had layoffs (per WFLA). In 2025, The News Tribune, The Olympian, and the Bellingham Herald all had layoffs (per Seattle Times). This affects what gets reported on Pierce County government, schools, Joint Base Lewis-McChord (JBLM), and the Port of Tacoma.
Capital and political economy. A hedge fund owning regional newspapers plays into the broader decline of local news in America (covered by PEN America and the Notre Dame Local News Index). In 2025 and 2026, Northwest journalists went on strike against McClatchy over the use of AI in place of reporters and over starting pay of about $45,000.


Key facts about the media side:
Ownership chain: Chatham (NJ) → McClatchy Co. LLC (Sacramento, post-Chapter 11 since September 4, 2020) → The News Tribune (Tacoma).
Reach: The News Tribune is “the second-largest newspaper in Washington, covering the local news market of Pierce County in print and online” (per McClatchy’s own markets page). It also covers JBLM (one of the largest U.S. military bases) and the Port of Tacoma.
Editorial direction: Local, not partisan-national. Investigative capacity has dropped (per Seattle Times reporting on 2025 layoffs and the 2026 strike, which note reporters covering Pierce County government have been cut).

3. Where their power comes from

1. Who they are


The bottom line. Chatham is based out of the region but still matters a lot for Pierce County. Their ownership of The News Tribune is the single biggest private factor in whether Pierce County has strong local-government reporting. The 2025 layoffs at The News Tribune (which cut the Tacoma City Hall and Pierce County government beat) and the 2026 strike over AI substitution are direct, documented Chatham-era decisions. The composite power score (0.010) understates that real-world influence.
Conflicts to watch. First, the 2023 SEC settlement for improper trading shows Chatham had governance problems. Second, hedge-fund ownership of a regional newspaper of record is a structural mismatch with the civic-journalism mission. Third, the December 2024 merger of McClatchy and A360media (a tabloid publisher) further cut into hard-news capacity. The defense reading: Chatham bought McClatchy out of bankruptcy and saved jobs that would have been lost otherwise. That is partly true. It does not erase the structural critique.
The counter-argument. McClatchy might have failed anyway given the long decline of the newspaper industry. Chatham’s money stopped an immediate collapse. But the Seattle Times reporting and the 2026 strike suggest that Chatham-era cuts went deeper than the industry-wide decline would predict.
Confidence: Medium — corporate ownership, SEC settlement, McClatchy acquisition price, and 2025 layoffs / 2026 strike are primary-sourced; the counterfactual (what would have happened absent Chatham) is necessarily INFERENCE.

0. Why this person or group is on the map

Chris Gildon is on the map because he holds office and makes decisions. He is the sitting State Senator for the 25th Legislative District. That district covers Puyallup, South Hill, Summit, and Waller in Pierce County. As Senate Republican lead on the Ways and Means Committee (the operating budget committee), he plays a big role in shaping the state’s operating budget. That budget directly affects Pierce County funding. He also co-chairs the bipartisan Pierce County legislative delegation. That delegation includes members from both parties and both chambers.
Adjacent figures not profiled here. Cyndy Jacobsen (R-25) is the current House member who succeeded Gildon. She is not at this tier. Joyce McDonald (R-25) was the House member Gildon succeeded. She is a former officeholder.

1. Who they are

Verdict: Gildon’s power comes from his role as Senate Republican Operating Budget Leader. It is the top budget job for the minority party in the Washington Senate. The Republican caucus is in the minority, with 19 of 49 seats. Even so, his budget role, his co-chair role on the Pierce County delegation, and his many board seats (WSIPP, Economic and Revenue Forecast Council, Legislative Ethics Board) give him real influence over state spending that affects Pierce County. His military record and real-estate work add weight on veterans’ affairs and housing policy.
Conflict flags: As a commercial real-estate broker on the Senate Housing Committee, his private work could overlap with his legislative role on housing. The 2020 PDC complaint (over-limit contribution) was cleared without a violation finding, but it shows campaign-finance issues. Recent corporate PAC gifts (T-Mobile, WA Food Industry) while serving as budget leader raise standard access-influence questions.
Counter-reading: Gildon’s real power is limited by the Republican minority. The Democratic majority controls the budget process. His role is advisory and oppositional rather than final. His committee leadership is “Republican Leader,” not chair. The Pierce County delegation co-chair role is mostly coordinative.
Confidence: High. Multiple primary sources confirm all key claims. These include the WA Legislature, the Senate Republican Caucus, PDC, and WA Secretary of State certified results. Electoral, financial, and biographical data are well-documented.

Chyna Willman is the Board Chair of the Tacoma-Pierce County Chamber of Commerce for the 2025–2026 year. The Chamber is the main business-advocacy group in Pierce County. She speaks for the business community while the Chamber looks for a new CEO.

0. Why this person or group is on the map

Why it is on the map. Clover Park School District (CPSD) is one of Pierce County’s largest K-12 public school districts. It serves about 12,395 students across 33 schools. Its schools sit in Lakewood, Tillicum, Woodbrook, and parts of unincorporated Pierce County (a county not part of any city). It also borders Joint Base Lewis-McChord (JBLM). The district runs on a $262 million budget for the 2024-25 school year (FY2024-25). It has the legal power to levy property taxes. It is a Purple Star Award District, which means it serves many military-connected students whose families move with JBLM’s deployment cycle. It has won statewide awards for its board and its superintendent.
Who is left out. Tacoma Public Schools, Bethel, Puyallup, University Place, Sumner-Bonney Lake, and Peninsula are separate districts and are mapped on their own pages. JBLM itself is mapped separately. The city of Lakewood is mapped on its own. Madigan Army Medical Center is part of JBLM and is mapped under military and defense.

1. Who they are

Legal name: Clover Park School District (CPSD).
Type: A public K-12 school district under Washington State law. It is a government body, not a nonprofit. The IRS does not treat it as a 501(c)(3) (federal tax-exempt charity).
Governing law: RCW 28A (Washington’s Revised Code of Washington for common schools) and the Pierce County Charter.
EIN (tax ID number): Not verified. School districts are government bodies and do not file IRS Form 990.
Location: Head office in Lakewood, Washington. Schools spread across Lakewood, Tillicum, Woodbrook, parts of unincorporated Pierce County, and a small part of Tacoma near JBLM.
Schools: 33 schools (2023-24).
Students: 12,395 (2023-24).
How it is run: A 5-member elected Board of Directors governs it. No single person owns it.
Subsidiaries: None found.

3. Where their power comes from

Power held:

Legal power (RCW 28A): CPSD enforces compulsory school attendance, sets curriculum, manages buildings, and bargains with employee unions.
Tax power: The Board can put property-tax levies on the ballot. Pierce County collects the money through the Assessor-Treasurer’s office.
Workforce: About 1,100 staff (a third-party estimate from August 2026). That includes teachers, support staff, and 19 district leaders plus 54.5 school leaders (2023-24 NCES, the National Center for Education Statistics).
Buildings budget: $6.38 million in capital spending (FY2021-22). Bond measures need voter approval.
Buying power: CPSD signs contracts for buses, food, technology, curriculum, and building upkeep.
Community role: It partners with the Lakewood Multicultural Coalition and runs a youth council. It gives community leadership awards.


Where its power crosses over: CPSD sits at the meeting point of schools, government, the local economy, and military-civilian life.
Key facts:

Tax status: Government body, not a 501(c)(3).
Money mix (FY2021-22 NCES): Federal $49.588M (20%); State $161.046M (66%); Local $33.565M (14%). Total: $244.199M.
Current money (FY2024-25): Revenue $262,088,238. Expenses $274,886,723. The district spent more than it took in. The Board approved a $12.6 million cut for FY2026-27 to fix the gap.
Board (2025-26): Darrin Lowry (District 4, until 2029); Dana Kelleher (District 3, until 2029); Janet Caldwell (District 5, until 2027); Krissy Kim (District 1, until 2027); Bryan Thomas (District 2, until 2027).
Government share: About 86% of revenue came from federal and state sources combined (FY2021-22).


Money trouble: A $12.6 million cut for FY2026-27 was approved in February 2026 to keep the district solvent.

1. Who they are

Verdict: CPSD holds tier-3 institutional power. It is the public K-12 monopoly for about 12,400 students across 33 schools. It runs a $262 million budget (FY2024-25). It has the legal power to levy property taxes. It must enforce compulsory school laws. It is a Purple Star Award District, which is a formal state award for helping military-connected students. That links it to JBLM. In FY2024-25 expenses ($274.9M) topped revenue ($262.1M). The Board approved a $12.6 million cut for FY2026-27. That is a real financial gap that limits future programs. Superintendent Ron Banner won the 2025 WASA Superintendent of the Year award and the 2026 AWSP President’s Award. The Board won WSSDA 2024 Board of Distinction and 2019 Board of the Year for large districts. The 5-member Board is elected by district on a nonpartisan ballot. The tier-3 composite power score of 0.006 matches a large but resource-strapped public agency. Its power comes mostly from being well-connected to JBLM families and civic groups. It depends on outside money: about 86% of revenue comes from federal and state sources.
Conflicts-of-interest flags: The defense view is that school-board work is open. Board meetings are public. Levies and bonds go to voters. Collective bargaining is required by law. Campaign money for Board races is filed with the state’s campaign-finance agency (PDC). The financial gap is public. The WASA, AWSP, and WSSDA awards come from outside groups, not from insiders.
Analysis of alternatives (ICD-203): The opposing view is that CPSD’s power is small. The $12.6 million cut shows real money pressure. About 66% of revenue comes from the state, which can change. Voters may tire of levies. JBLM deployments can shake up enrollment. A composite power of 0.006 fits a tier-3 institutional actor with broad scope (compulsory education for about 12,400 students) but limited decision-making power. State law, levy and bond votes, and OSPI oversight all constrain it.

0. Why this person or group is on the map

Inclusion rule: well-connected + reputational. Columbia Bank (now operating as Umpqua Bank after the Feb-2023 merger) is on the map because (a) William Weyerhaeuser was Chairman of the Board of Columbia Banking System — a direct tie to the Weyerhaeuser entity already on the map — and (b) Columbia is the holding company for what was once Tacoma’s regional bank, with ties to the Greater Tacoma Community Foundation (GTCF) board and the Tacoma Chamber.
Adjacent but EXCLUDED candidates: Umpqua Bank (now the operating brand, a separate Oregon-chartered bank); Bank of America Private Bank; routed to open questions.

1. Who they are

Exact legal name: Columbia Banking System, Inc. (the holding company). Columbia Bank was the bank before the merger. Umpqua Bank is the bank brand after March 2023.
Type of business: A Washington-state bank holding company. Its bank is insured by the FDIC (Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation). It is registered with the the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), ticker COLB. The holding company is a Washington corporation. The bank was a Washington state-chartered bank.
History: Founded in Longview WA in 1973. Headquarters moved to Tacoma (1301 “A” Street) in 1993. In October 2021, Columbia announced a merger of equals with Portland-based Umpqua Holdings. The deal closed Feb 28, 2023. Columbia was the named survivor, but Umpqua was the accounting acquirer. The combined bank took the Umpqua Bank brand. The holding company kept the name Columbia Banking System, Inc. and kept Tacoma as the holding-company home.
Leadership: Clint Stein is President, CEO, and Chairman (since the 2023 merger). Christopher Merrywell and Torran Nixon are Co-Presidents. Ivan Seda is the CFO. William Weyerhaeuser was the former Chairman. He stepped down after the merger.
Locations: 376 branches (2026) across 8 states. The bank’s headquarters moved to Portland, OR in 2023. The holding company’s headquarters is still in Tacoma, WA.

3. Where their power comes from

Market power: Columbia Banking System is the holding company for a top-30 U.S. bank after the Umpqua merger. It has about 376 branches. It controls business lending, deposits, and treasury services across the Pacific Northwest and Mountain West.
Civic ties: William Weyerhaeuser’s chairmanship connected Columbia’s lending to one of America’s oldest timber families (Weyerhaeuser Co.). Weyerhaeuser also served on the Greater Tacoma Community Foundation board. This is the main way Columbia enters the power map.
Establishment ties: As a Tacoma Chamber member and long-time Tacoma bank, Columbia is tied to the local establishment: GTCF, the Chamber, Weyerhaeuser Co., and MultiCare’s supply-chain financing.
Why it scores: GTCF board tie (weight 2), Weyerhaeuser chairman tie (weight 3), Chamber of Commerce membership (weight 3).

1. Who they are

Verdict: Columbia Banking System’s power in the Tacoma/Pierce County map is residual and reputational after the Feb-2023 merger. The operating bank moved to Portland (Umpqua brand). But the holding company is still headquartered in Tacoma, and William Weyerhaeuser’s chairmanship tied the bank to the Weyerhaeuser / GTCF / Tacoma Chamber network. As a tier-3 economic node, Columbia is best understood as a way for Weyerhaeuser-family influence to flow into Pierce County civic institutions.
Conflicts-of-interest flags: (a) Bank Chairman William Weyerhaeuser also held a GTCF board seat — lending and grant decisions could touch the same civic networks; (b) after the merger, Clint Stein’s 5-year contract and Co-President structure create a governance overlap the SEC has flagged in proxy disclosures.
Analysis of alternatives (investigative control document (ICD)-203 opposing view): Columbia’s tier-3 ranking could be challenged because after the merger, the operating bank left Tacoma. A skeptic would say the only Pierce County power left is the holding-company address in Tacoma and the Weyerhaeuser civic-network board overlap. The reading here is that residual influence (deposit relationships, civic leadership, Weyerhaeuser family ties) justifies tier-3, but with a downward lean.
Confidence: Medium-High — Merger mechanics and Weyerhaeuser chairmanship are well-documented in SEC filings and UW Tacoma announcements. The post-2023 influence trajectory and exact deposit-base share in Pierce County are UNVERIFIED.
