CommonSpirit Health — Deep Profile
Case: INV-2026-002 · Profile: profiles/commonspirit.md
Entity ID: commonspirit · Type: organization · Domain: institutional
Tier: tier3 · Rank: 107/163 · Composite power: 0.016
Graph description: Chicago-based nonprofit, Catholic-affiliated national health system formed Feb 2019 by merger of Catholic Health Initiatives (CHI) and Dignity Health. Parent company of Virginia Mason Franciscan Health (VMFH) — the principal CommonSpirit subsidiary operating in Pierce County (St. Joseph Medical Center, Tacoma; St. Clare Hospital, Lakewood; St. Anthony Hospital, Gig Harbor; St. Elizabeth Hospital, Enumclaw; St. Francis Hospital, Federal Way; plus CHI Franciscan medical clinics).
Known facts: Created February 2019 by CHI/Dignity merger; ~150,000 employees, ~25,000 physicians/advanced-practice clinicians; operates 137 hospitals across 21 states; FY2019 revenue ~$29B; CHI Franciscan represented ~$2.45B revenue pre-2021 merger; Virginia Mason combined with CHI Franciscan to form VMFH effective January 5, 2021.
Status: ✅ researched — 2026-09-19 — tier3-chunk7
Sources: 5/3 (minimum for tier3)

0. Why this person or group is on the map

Inclusion rule: From holding office + decision-making. CommonSpirit Health is included as the parent company that controls Virginia Mason Franciscan Health (VMFH). VMFH runs many hospitals and clinics in Pierce County. These include St. Joseph in Tacoma, St. Clare in Lakewood, and St. Anthony in Gig Harbor.
CommonSpirit is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit health system. It is Catholic-affiliated. As a large health system, it shapes hospital pricing, charity-care policy, capital decisions, and labor relations across the Puget Sound region. The graph records it as the parent of VMFH (weight 6) and as affiliated with the Catholic Archdiocese (weight 2).
Excluded but related: MultiCare Health System is the main Pierce County rival. It is profiled separately as multicare. PeaceHealth, Swedish Health (Providence), and UW Medicine are nearby regional systems. They have a small Pierce County presence. The Catholic Archdiocese of Seattle is profiled separately. It connects to CommonSpirit through VMFH’s Catholic affiliation and the Ethical and Religious Directives for Catholic Health Care Services (ERDs).

1. Who they are

Exact legal name: CommonSpirit Health.
Entity type: 501(c)(3) nonprofit, Catholic-affiliated health system. National office in Chicago, IL.
How it was formed: Created in February 2019. It was a merger of Catholic Health Initiatives (CHI, headquartered in Englewood, CO) and Dignity Health (headquartered in San Francisco, CA). Both were large Catholic-affiliated systems before the merger.
Scale: About 150,000 employees. About 25,000 physicians and advanced practice clinicians. It runs 137 hospitals and more than 1,000 care sites across 21 states. Fiscal Year 2019 revenue was about $29 billion.
Pierce County subsidiary: Virginia Mason Franciscan Health (VMFH). VMFH was formed January 5, 2021. It merged CHI Franciscan (Tacoma) with Virginia Mason (Seattle). Ketul J. Patel was the CEO of VMFH. He was also president of the Pacific Northwest Division of CommonSpirit Health.
Governing law: Washington State nonprofit corporation statutes (state law (RCW) 24.03A). Catholic-affiliated governance through board oversight and the Ethical and Religious Directives (ERDs). The ERDs are issued by the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops.

3. Where their power comes from

Market position in Pierce County: Through VMFH and CHI Franciscan, CommonSpirit runs several hospitals in or near Pierce County. These include St. Joseph Medical Center (Tacoma), St. Clare Hospital (Lakewood), St. Anthony Hospital (Gig Harbor), St. Elizabeth Hospital (Enumclaw), and St. Francis Hospital (Federal Way). The system also runs Franciscan Medical Group clinics and CHI Franciscan urgent-care sites. Tacoma-Pierce County Health Department and Chamber listings show CHI Franciscan and VMFH sites as major regional providers.
Tax status: 501(c)(3) nonprofit, Catholic-affiliated. Tax-exempt status gives an indirect subsidy. CommonSpirit pays no federal income tax. It pays no state B&O tax on most activities. It also has property-tax exemptions on many sites. This is a structural edge over for-profit hospital operators.
Decision-making authority: Capital projects, mergers, EHR systems, staffing, charity care, and reproductive-health rules are all set at the CommonSpirit corporate level. They are not set at the VMFH local-board level. Ketul Patel was VMFH and Pacific Northwest Division President until 2024. He led Pacific Northwest ops for CommonSpirit.
Domain overlap:
inst ↔ gov: Hospital licensing, certificate-of-need (CON) for capital projects, Medicare and Medicaid — heavy work with the WA Department of Health and CMS.
inst ↔ econ: One of the largest private employers in the region. Big purchasing power. Big real-estate holdings.
inst ↔ social: Charity-care and community-benefit duties tied to tax-exempt status. Reproductive health and end-of-life rules under the ERDs.

3. Where their power comes from






























IndicatorFindingEvidence (source #)Who benefitsPatients with insurance coverage accepted by CHI Franciscan/VMFH (commercial, Medicare, Medicaid — though Medicaid acceptance varies by site and physician); Catholic patients seeking care at a faith-aligned provider; the broader community from charity-care investments required to maintain tax-exempt status.Sources 1, 2, 3Who sitsCommonSpirit Health national board (governance of the parent system); VMFH regional board (oversight of Pacific Northwest operations). Ketul J. Patel served as VMFH CEO and Pacific Northwest Division President of CommonSpirit. The Catholic Health Ministries (CHI side) and Dignity Health Community Ministerial Alliance (Dignity side) constitute the canonical sponsors.Sources 3, 4Who governsDecisions on M&A, capital allocation, charity-care policy, and ERD-restricted services are made at the CommonSpirit national level. The Catholic Health Ministries (public juridic persons) maintain canonical authority over Catholic-identity issues.Sources 3, 4Who winsCommonSpent shareholders (there are none — it is nonprofit), executives, and large creditors/investors (via outstanding bonds) win from system expansion. Tacoma and Lakewood communities “win” from having an acute-care hospital operator committed to those markets, though they lose the ability to access ERD-restricted services (e.g., elective abortion, physician-assisted death) at CommonSpirit facilities.Sources 1, 2

Patel named CEO of VMFH and Pacific Northwest Division President of CommonSpiritFierce Healthcarewww.fiercehealthcare.com/hospitals/chi-franciscan-virginia-mason-finalize-acquisition-deal-and-roll-out-new-namesecondary0.855VMFH operates as the joint operating company of CHI Franciscan and Virginia Mason; CommonSpirit Health is the parent; ~300 care sites in Pacific Northwest; Ketul Patel comments on continued patient experience and expansion plansTacoma News Tribunewww.thenewstribune.com/news/business/article248261560.htmlsecondary0.85
1. Who they are

Verdict: CommonSpirit Health controls a large share of acute-care hospital capacity in Pierce County through its VMFH subsidiary. St. Joseph in Tacoma is one of two adult acute-care hospitals in central Tacoma. St. Clare in Lakewood is the only hospital in that city. St. Anthony anchors Gig Harbor. The corporate parent sets the strategy. VMFH and CHI Franciscan leaders carry it out locally. The system is bound by Catholic ERDs and by Washington’s rules. Even so, it is one of the two top hospital operators in the county, alongside MultiCare.
Conflicts-of-interest flags: As a Catholic-affiliated system, VMFH and CommonSpirit are bound by the Ethical and Religious Directives. The ERDs ban direct abortion services (with narrow exceptions) and physician-assisted death. This limits the reproductive-health options of patients in Pierce County — especially in Lakewood and Gig Harbor, where CommonSpirit hospitals are the only option. The 501(c)(3) tax-exempt status gives a structural subsidy. That subsidy is not linked to a fixed community-benefit standard. ERD enforcement is set at the sponsor and corporate level, not the local level. It is not clear if VMFH local boards have any real opt-out power (UNVERIFIED).
Analysis of alternatives : An opposing reading: CommonSpirit is one national system among many. In Pierce County, MultiCare is the bigger rival. MultiCare runs Tacoma General, Allenmore, Good Samaritan in Puyallup, and Mary Bridge Children’s Hospital. CommonSpirit/VMFH has lost market share in some lines (e.g., the Yakima hospital broke off from Virginia Mason at the start of 2021, before the merger). Catholic governance is a feature, not a bug, for faith-aligned patients. ERD restrictions push some procedures out to secular providers like MultiCare. That keeps pluralistic access in the broader market.
Confidence: Medium-High — formation history, scale figures, and VMFH merger are corroborated by primary press release (CommonSpirit/CHI Franciscan) and multiple secondary outlets (Fierce Healthcare, Tacoma News Tribune). Specific 2024–2026 Pierce County market share figures, ERD-enforcement incidents at VMFH, and CommonSpirit national bond debt are not extracted in this pass — UNVERIFIED.

Pierce County Council — Deep Profile
Case: INV-2026-002 · Profile: profiles/county-council.md
Entity ID: county-council · Type: organization · Domain: government
Tier: tier1 · Rank: 3/163 · Composite power: 0.504
Graph description: 7-member legislative body (4D-3R); appropriates $3.5B budget; controls zoning & land use; confirms appointments
Known facts: Appropriates $3.5B budget; controls zoning & land use; approves contracts; Chair: Jani Hitchen (D-6); Vice Chair: Dave Morell (R-1)
Status: ✅ researched — 2026-09-19 — tier1-chunk1
Sources: 12/10 (minimum for tier1)

0. Why this person or group is on the map

Inclusion rule — from holding office + decision-making: The Pierce County Council is the county’s legislative branch. It is the “policy-determining body” under the Home Rule Charter (Charter Section 2.20). It has “all powers of the County not otherwise reserved to the people, the Executive, or general law.” Its powers include: approving the budget, controlling zoning and land use, approving contracts, and setting taxes. The Council’s 70+ graph edges make it the most connected node. Anyone who wants county money, zoning changes, or policy changes has to come to the Council.
Adjacent but EXCLUDED candidates: The Pierce County Charter Review Commission (21 members, elected 2025) is a separate temporary body that reviews the charter. It is excluded because it only meets from time to time. The Board of Health (which includes Council members) is mapped separately as tpchd. The Performance Audits Committee is a Council committee, not a separate entity.

1. Who they are

Exact legal name: Pierce County Council
Entity type: Government — legislative branch of Pierce County, a home-rule charter county
Governing law: Pierce County Home Rule Charter (adopted 1981); state law (RCW) 36 (county government)
Parent/subsidiaries: Part of Pierce County government; not a separate legal entity
Address: 1501 Market Street, Suite 530, Tacoma, WA 98402
Council Chambers: 1501 Market Street, Suite 140, Tacoma, WA 98402

2. Their career and offices

Chair: Jani Hitchen, District 6 (D) — represents the Joint Base Lewis-McChord (JBLM) and Lakewood district. She sets the legislative agenda and runs Council meetings.
Vice Chair: Dave Morell, District 1 (R) — Bonney Lake, Buckley, Lake Tapps. He handles land use.
Executive Pro Tempore: Robyn Denson, District 7 (D) — Gig Harbor, Key Peninsula.

Composition: 4D–3R. The Democratic majority holds the chair and controls the agenda. It takes 5 votes to override an Executive veto. With 4 Democrats, they can sustain a Democratic Executive’s vetoes. But they cannot override a veto without at least 1 Republican vote.

3. Where their power comes from

Statutory authority (Charter Section 2.20): “The Council has all powers of the County not otherwise reserved to the people, the Executive, or general law.” This is the broadest possible grant of legislative authority. Specific powers include:
Budget appropriation (Charter Section 2.20(1)(a)): “To levy taxes, appropriate revenue, and adopt budgets for the County.” The Council adopts the biennial budget by Dec. 1 of each odd-numbered year.
Zoning and land use: Controls county zoning, the comprehensive plan, and land-use rules. This is the most direct power over the growth-machine developers in the graph.
Contract approval: Approves major county contracts.
Ordinance enactment: Adopts all county ordinances and resolutions.
Appointment confirmation: Confirms certain Executive appointments.
Budget authority: The 2026–2027 biennial budget is $3.5 billion (adopted Nov 25, 2025, ordinance O2025-562s3). The General Fund is $967.4M (up 2.2%). The Council can amend the Executive’s proposed budget. The budget passed 4–3 on a party-line vote.
Veto override (Charter Section 2.50): Override requires 5 affirmative votes. That is a supermajority of 7. With a 4D–3R split, party-line vetoes by a Democratic Executive cannot be overridden. This limits the Council’s power compared to the Executive.
key facts:
Budget controlled: $3.5B biennial ($1.75B each year)
Appointment/veto powers: Confirms certain Executive appointments; 5-vote supermajority to override Executive veto
Jurisdictions governed: All of unincorporated Pierce County (about 920K people); some county-wide functions affect incorporated cities too

3. Where their power comes from

The 4D–3R split means the Democratic coalition’s priorities (housing, social services, transit) generally win.Sources 1, 2, 9Who sitsCouncil members sit on: Board of Health (Hitchen, Herrera, Yambe, Mello), SSMCP (Hitchen), Pierce Transit (Ayala), GTCF (Ayala). These board ties spread Council influence into health, transit, nonprofit, and military-community domains.Sources 1, 10Who governsThe Council is the policy-determining body. It appropriates every dollar the county spends. It controls zoning for about 920K residents. It approves contracts. But the Executive’s veto (5-vote override) and the Executive’s budget role limit the Council.Sources 1, 2, 3Who winsIn the 2026–27 budget, the Council passed a $3.5B budget 4–3 on a party-line vote. The Democratic majority’s priorities (public safety increases, housing, behavioral health) won. The 4–3 vote shows deep partisan division. The Republican minority’s amendments are usually defeated.Sources 2, 9

Taxing authority: The Council levies taxes and oversees taxing districts. These include: Pierce County Library, Flood Control Zone District, fire districts (East Pierce, Gig Harbor, Central Pierce), Port of Tacoma (property tax levy), and school districts (bond and levy approval).
Deficit/constraints: “Salaries, benefits, and core service costs are growing faster than property and sales tax.” Reserves are maintained through 2029 but are projected to fall below recommended levels in later years. A General Fund hiring freeze is in place.

5. How they touch government

Budget process: The Executive prepares and submits the budget. The Council reviews, amends, and adopts by Dec. 1 (charter deadline). The 2026–27 budget was adopted Nov 25, 2025 — meeting the deadline.

1. Who they are

Graph centrality artifact: The investigation notes that the Council “over-ranks in centrality (hub artifact) — capped below Executive.” What specific graph metrics (weighted degree, betweenness) are inflated by the Council’s structural position as the appropriation body? Should the graph model distinguish between “power to make decisions” (the Council votes) and “well-connected centrality” (everyone lobbies the Council)?
HHFPAC $357K UNVERIFIED: The graph flags “UNVERIFIED: $357K 2022 spending figure not confirmed by primary source.” Verify via the state’s campaign-finance agency (PDC) C3/C4 filings for HHFPAC (WSHA healthcare PAC).
Paul Herrera and Amy Cruver donor chains: Herrera ($37K raised) and Cruver ($57K raised) — trace NASH Cascadia and Master Builders donations via PDC. Are these coordinated with the Chamber’s Candidate Academy?
Bryan Yambe appointment (Jan 2025): Who appointed him? Was there a competitive process? What are his qualifications and donor relationships?
Puyallup Tribe lobbying (weight 5): The Tribe is the highest-weighted lobbying tie. What specific issues does the Tribe lobby the Council on? Land use? Trust land applications? Impact payments?
development coalition land-use votes: Cross-reference Council land-use votes with developer donor activity (Rush, Miles, Southport, Tucci, Lincoln Park, Nall — all weight 3 land_use edges).
Budget 4-3 party-line vote: The 2026–27 budget passed on a party-line 4-3 vote. What amendments did the Republican minority propose? What was cut vs. the Executive’s proposal?

1. Who they are

Verdict: The Pierce County Council holds the county’s legislative power. It approves the $3.5B biennial budget. It controls zoning and land use. It approves contracts and sets taxes. Its 70+ graph edges make it the most connected node. But this high connectivity is partly a structural artifact. Every group that wants county money, zoning changes, or policy changes has to come to the Council. The 4D–3R makeup, combined with the 5-vote veto override threshold, means the Council is subordinate to a same-party Executive on vetoed items. Its real power lies in (1) the budget amendment process, (2) land-use decisions that affect the growth-machine developers, and (3) confirmation of Executive appointments.
Conflicts-of-interest flags (defense view anticipated):
Developer-lobbyist pipeline: Six growth-machine developers (Rush, Miles, Southport, Tucci, Lincoln Park, Nall) have land_use edges to the Council. If Council members get donations from these same developers, there is a direct conflict between their zoning votes and their campaign funding.
Puyallup Tribe lobbying + donations: The Tribe both lobbies the Council (weight 5) and donates to individual Council members (Ayala, Hitchen, Cruver). This dual channel creates the appearance of a trade.
Party-line budgeting: The 4–3 party-line budget vote suggests the Council’s budget process is driven by partisan priorities rather than technical analysis.
Candidate Academy pipeline: If Council members are Candidate Academy alumni, their votes on Chamber priority issues (tax policy, land use, business regulation) create a structural conflict.
Analysis of alternatives: The other reading is that the Council is not a power center but a procedural bottleneck. The Executive proposes the budget. The Council amends at the margins. The real decisions are made by the Executive and the groups that lobby the Council (Tribe, MultiCare, Chamber, developers). The Council’s high graph centrality is an artifact of being the place where decisions are ratified, not where they are made. The 4–3 partisan split means the Democratic majority is a rubber stamp for a Democratic Executive. The Republican minority cannot block party-line votes. Under that reading, the Council’s rank of 3/163 overstates its real decision-making power.
Confidence: High — the Council’s structure, makeup, budget authority, and veto dynamics are all charter-defined and verifiable from primary sources (Pierce County official website, budget documents). The centrality artifact is acknowledged and documented.

Known facts: Headquarters 950 Broadway Plaza, Tacoma, WA 98402-4454; phone (253) 593-2970; 22 total WA Court of Appeals judges (Div I = 10, Div II = 7, Div III = 5); 3-judge panels hear each appeal; non-discretionary court (must accept all appeals filed); can reverse, remand, modify, or affirm lower court decisions; 6-year staggered terms; nonpartisan election; Division II was created by constitutional amendment (WA Const. Art. IV § 30).

0. Why this person or group is on the map

Why included: decision-making + well-connected + holds office. Division II of the Washington Court of Appeals is on the map because (a) it is the appeals court of last resort for most civil and criminal cases that start in Pierce County Superior Court (a court that handles major felonies, civil suits, and family cases); (b) Pierce County is one of the 13 counties it covers; (c) its rulings bind Pierce County Superior Court judges under stare decisis (the rule that courts must follow prior decisions); (d) it sits one step above Pierce County Superior Court in the Washington court system. (Sources 1, 2, 3, 4)
Who was left out and why: The Washington Supreme Court is state-level and has its own profile. Division I (Seattle) covers King, Snohomish, Skagit, Island, San Juan, and Whatcom counties. Division III is in Spokane. Pierce County Superior Court has its own profile. The Federal District Court for Western Washington has its own profile and only handles federal cases. The U.S. Ninth Circuit appeals court handles federal appeals. None of these are Division II.

1. Who they are

Full legal name: Washington Court of Appeals, Division II.
Type: State appeals court (intermediate). It is part of the unified Washington State Court System under Article IV of the Washington State Constitution.
Governing law: Washington Constitution Article IV (Judiciary); Washington Court of Appeals set up by constitutional amendment; state law RCW (Revised Code of Washington) 2.06.
Headquarters: 950 Broadway Plaza, Tacoma, WA 98402-4454. (Source 3)
Phone: (253) 593-2970. (Source 3)
Parent: Washington State Court System. The state Office of the Administrator for the Courts is the central office.
Subsidiaries: None. Division II is a single court with rotating 3-judge panels.
Court roster (from the current WA Courts Directory):
Judges (7): Chief Judge Bernard F. Veljacic; Acting Chief Judge Erik D. Price; Judge Meng Li Che; Judge Anne Cruser; Judge Rebecca Glasgow; Judge Linda Lee; Judge Bradley A. Maxa.
Commissioners (2): Aurora R. Bearse; Karl Triebel.
(Source 4)
Constitutional basis: Article IV § 30 of the Washington State Constitution lets the Legislature create intermediate appeals courts. Division II was created by statute in 1969-70 and seated in 1970.

3. Where their power comes from

Power held:
Mandatory appellate jurisdiction: Per WA Courts, “It is a non-discretionary appellate court — it must accept all appeals filed with it.” (Source 2)
Disposition authority: “The Court of Appeals has authority to reverse (overrule), remand (send back to the lower court), modify, or affirm the decision of the lower court.” (Source 2)
Binding precedent on Pierce County: Published opinions by Division II bind Pierce County Superior Court judges and Pierce County lower tribunals. Pierce County is in Division II’s territory.
No en banc review available. (Source 1)
Counties covered (Division II, 13 counties): Pierce, Thurston, Mason, Kitsap, Jefferson, Grays Harbor, Clallam, Clark, Cowlitz, Lewis, Pacific, Skamania, and Wahkiakum. (Source 2)
Selection / retention: Nonpartisan election. Judges serve 6-year staggered terms. (Sources 1, 2)
Panel structure: “Panels of three judges hear each appeal,” per the Washington Court of Appeals. (Source 1)
Caseload discretion: None. The court must accept all properly filed appeals. (Source 2)
Key facts:
Tax status: Government entity (not 501(c)(3), a federal tax-exempt charity).
Roster (per WA Courts Directory): Chief Judge Bernard F. Veljacic; Acting Chief Judge Erik D. Price; Judge Meng Li Che; Judge Anne Cruser; Judge Rebecca Glasgow; Judge Linda Lee; Judge Bradley A. Maxa. Commissioners: Aurora R. Bearse; Karl Triebel. (Source 4)
Government funding: State-funded through the state Office of the Administrator for the Courts.
Caseload volume: UNVERIFIED exact figure for FY2024-25. The statewide Court of Appeals caseload is in the low thousands per year.
Discretion vs. obligation: Mandatory jurisdiction — no certiorari screening (certiorari is the discretion to pick which appeals to hear, like the U.S. Supreme Court does).

1. Who they are

Verdict: Washington Court of Appeals Division II holds tier-3 legal power as the mandatory appeals court for Pierce County (and 12 other Washington counties). Its published opinions bind Pierce County Superior Court and Pierce County lower courts on state-law questions. FACT: It must accept all properly filed appeals (non-discretionary). FACT: It is based in Tacoma (950 Broadway Plaza) and has 7 judges + 2 commissioners per the current WA Courts Directory. FACT: It can reverse, remand, modify, or affirm lower court rulings. FACT: Judges are elected in nonpartisan elections to 6-year staggered terms. FACT: 3-judge panels hear each appeal — no en banc review. REASONING: Division II’s tier-3 composite power (0.006) reflects a regional appeals court whose individual rulings bind Pierce County practice. But its weight statewide is moderate (7 of 22 judges). Its judges do not typically sit on cross-domain community boards. Its main power is doctrinal (shaping the law through written opinions). Pierce County is its largest single county, so the Pierce County bar has outsized influence on its docket.
Conflicts-of-interest flags (counter-argument): A defense would say Division II is a constitutionally independent court. Its judges are publicly elected on nonpartisan ballots. Decisions are publicly published. The recusal process is set by statute. Panels are randomly assigned (which limits any single judge’s ability to set the agenda). Mandatory jurisdiction means the court cannot pick and choose which cases to hear.
Analysis of alternatives: The opposing view is that Division II’s power is limited by (a) mandatory jurisdiction (no certiorari screening); (b) random panel assignment; (c) 3-judge panels that require a supermajority for any single ruling; (d) discretionary Supreme Court review that can override its rulings; and (e) lack of enforcement power (rulings bind but must be sent back to Superior Court for execution). Its power is doctrinal, not financial or coercive. It shapes legal practice through precedent, not budgets or hiring. The 0.006 composite score reflects a regional appeals court with binding reach over a set territory, bounded by higher review.
Confidence: Medium — court structure, jurisdiction, judge roster, and procedure have primary sources (state Administrative Office of the Courts + state Bios page). History dates and caseload numbers are backed by Wikipedia/Ballotpedia. Exact FY caseload volumes are not in the sources reviewed and remain UNVERIFIED.

It also runs the South Harbor half of the Northwest Seaport Alliance, a joint port authority. The Port supports over 41,000 jobs, $3.4B in wages, and $10.8B in business output. Keller sits inside the decision-making room on maritime trade, jobs, and the environment.
People NOT on the map: John McCarthy is Commission President on a different seat. Dick Marzano, Don Meyer, Kristin Ang, and JT Wilcox are fellow commissioners, tracked separately. Eric Johnson is the Executive Director, a hired staffer. Tacoma City Council members on the Tideflats Subarea Plan Steering Committee are also adjacent and excluded.

1. Who they are

Verdict: Keller is a very well-networked port commissioner. She sits on the WPPA Executive Committee (as Secretary). She also sits on PSRC’s two policy boards. She sits on the Pierce County Regional Council and Workforce Central. She sits on the Gig Harbor Rotary. She sits on the Tacoma Tideflats Subarea Plan Steering Committee. She is Vice-Chair of the Joint Municipal Action Committee. Her Audit Committee chair role gives her direct oversight over the Port’s books. Her NWSA Audit co-chair role does the same for the Seaport Alliance. That kind of oversight power is rare for public port commissions in Washington. Her Marine Corps service in the “President’s Own” Marine Band is rare too. Her time as Kel-Tech Plastics CEO adds business credibility. Her career arc (schoolteacher → principal → K-12 administrator → small-business CEO → port commissioner) is a classic Pierce County bipartisan mix.
Conflicts-of-interest flags:
Kel-Tech Plastics supplier ties from her CEO years could overlap with current Port deals. Her 2008-2020 tenure predates her 2024-27 term, but the gap is small.
As a Marine veteran and advocate for “Place for Jobs” (workforce development), Keller is a natural ally of the shipyard and industrial bloc. She could shape deals at the Port’s marine terminals.
Counter-argument: one port commissioner out of five is not the deciding voice. Her audit role is a watchdog job, not a strategy job.
Analysis of alternatives: A skeptical reading treats Keller as one vote among five. Big decisions (capital projects, executive director hires, Seaport Alliance policy) are usually unanimous or near-unanimous. The opposing reading (favored here) is that her many board seats make her a connector who passes decisions and information across the region’s biggest bodies. The Audit Committee chair role is the most underrated lever: in a budget this size, the audit chair sees every contract before it goes public.
Confidence: High — name, term, board seats, and military service verified across the Port of Tacoma commissioner page and the WPPA About page. Education verified by Port bio. Marine Corps dates verified by Port bio and ZoomInfo. Date of birth and family UNVERIFIED.

0. Why this person or group is on the map

Inclusion rule — power, decision-making, and connections. Deb Krishnadasan is on this map because:

(a) She is a Washington State Senator for the 26th Legislative District. The 26th covers Gig Harbor, Key Peninsula, Port Orchard, Bremerton, and Burton. That is a real legislative seat with power over state policy and money that affects Pierce County.
(b) The Pierce County Council was one of the bodies that appointed her to the seat. That creates a graph link from her to the Pierce County Council.
(c) She was a former Peninsula School District board president. That is a board overlap and adds a connection to the education world.


Even though she sits in the state Senate, not the county, her appointment path gives her a real edge to the Pierce County Council in this map.
Adjacent but excluded: Other 26th LD House members (for example, Michelle Caldier). Other Peninsula School Board members. Emily Randall (the predecessor, now in the U.S. House, profiled separately). These go to open questions and leads.

1. Who they are

Legal name: Deborah Krishnadasan.
Aliases: “Deb” (campaign and casual use). Wikipedia also uses “Krishnadasan.”
Date and place of birth: Not verified. Year of birth is not in public records.
Current residence: Gig Harbor, WA (since 2008).
Family: Husband Baiya Krishnadasan — a Sri Lankan-born heart-and-lung surgeon. Three children: Alexander, Audrey, Gabriel.
Education: Bachelor of Arts in Communications, Western Washington University.
Prior jobs: Communications and human resources roles at Burlington Resources (oil and gas), Visio Corporation (a tech firm bought by Microsoft in 2000), and Microsoft.

3. Where their power comes from

Power held.

Washington State Senator, 26th Legislative District (Democrat): Sworn in December 11, 2024. Current term ends January 11, 2027. She is running for re-election on November 3, 2026 against Republican Gary Parker (per Ballotpedia).

Vice Chair, State Government, Tribal Affairs & Elections.
Vice Chair, Agriculture & Natural Resources.
Member, Early Learning & K-12 Education.
Member, Transportation.


Legislative actions. In March 2025, she was one of two Democrats who voted with Republicans against the state budget because of tax increases. She also sponsored a constitutional amendment to lower the school-bond voter-approval threshold from 60% to 55%.
Former Peninsula School Board President. Two-year term as board president (2019–2021). Elected District 2 in a 2015 special election and re-elected unopposed in 2017.


Why this gives her cross-domain power: She is a state senator who also has a school-board background. That ties the government domain to the institutional and education-policy domains. Her seat on the Tribal Affairs committee also links her to the Puyallup Tribe’s relationship with the state.
Key facts:

Office: Washington State Senate. 4-year term. 26th LD, which partly covers Pierce County.
Budget: State senators do not control a single budget line. They vote on the operating budget, capital budget, and supplemental budgets. That includes the $78.5 billion operating budget she voted against in March 2025 (along with one other Democrat).
Veto: None. A Senate vote alone cannot enact a law — it needs House approval and the governor’s signature.
Jurisdiction: 26th LD covers Gig Harbor, Key Peninsula, Port Orchard, Bremerton, and Burton. Gig Harbor and Key Peninsula are in Pierce County. Port Orchard, Bremerton, and Burton are in Kitsap County.

Known facts: 8 elected judges (Lineberry, McCann, Padula, Buttorff, Oaks, Williams, Christopher, Sussman); administrator Misty Butler Robison; judges elected nonpartisan in 4-year terms; jurisdiction caps: 90 days jail / $1K fine (misdemeanor); 1 yr / $5K (gross misdemeanor); $100K civil
Status: ✅ researched — 2026-09-19 — tier3-chunk4
Sources: 5/3 (minimum for tier3)

0. Why this person or group is on the map

The Pierce County District Court handles most criminal and civil cases in the county. It is the county’s only “limited jurisdiction” court. That means it handles smaller cases, not big felonies.
The Pierce County Council sets its budget. The graph shows this as an edge where the Council gives the court its funding.
It is the front door for most state-court cases. Skipping parking tickets, about seven out of every eight cases filed in all state courts land at this level.

1. Who they are

Exact legal name: Pierce County District Court.
Entity type: A Washington state court of limited jurisdiction. It is a government body, not a private company. It is created and governed under state law, Title 3 of the Revised Code of Washington (RCW).
Governing law: state law (RCW) 3.50 covers district courts in large counties. RCW 3.62 covers judges. RCW 3.66 covers civil cases. Pierce County is a “class A” county, meaning its population tops 500,000.
Parent or subsidiaries: It runs inside Pierce County government. It has no separate corporate status. The court administrator is Misty Butler Robison. Location: County-City Building, 2nd floor, 930 Tacoma Ave S, Room 239, Tacoma, WA 98402. Phone: (253) 798-7487.
Officers: Court Administrator Misty Butler Robison. The presiding judge rotates among the elected judges.
Departments and functions: Criminal cases (misdemeanors, gross misdemeanors, DUIs, reckless driving, and some assaults). Civil cases up to $100,000. Small claims up to $5,000, or $10,000 for a person. Traffic tickets. Domestic-violence and no-contact orders. Name changes. Some lien foreclosures. First hearings in felony cases. It also runs a probation department, therapeutic courts, a court resource center, and court services.

3. Where their power comes from

Its caseload. It handles the large majority of state-court cases in Pierce County. Every misdemeanor, traffic ticket, and most civil disputes up to $100,000 flow through it.
Its power to punish. It can order up to 90 days in jail and a $1,000 fine for a misdemeanor. For a gross misdemeanor, up to one year and a $5,000 fine. It decides pretrial detention and supervises probation.
Protection orders. It issues domestic-violence, antiharassment, and no-contact orders. These carry real limits on personal freedom.
Felony gatekeeping. First hearings in felony cases happen here. Judges decide if there is enough evidence to send a case up to Superior Court.
Trials. Six-person juries hear criminal cases. Small claims have no lawyers unless the court allows one. Traffic tickets have no jury.
How it is scored. Its legal power overlaps with government (the County Council funds it) and law enforcement (prosecutors and defense lawyers work in it). Small claims is where everyday residents meet the court for consumer, landlord, and neighbor disputes.
Key questions answered:
Area of authority: All of Pierce County.
Judges’ discretion: Judges have wide sentencing discretion within the legal caps.
How judges are picked: Elected in nonpartisan races for 4-year terms. The top two from the primary advance to the general.
Caseload: Statewide, more than two million cases are filed each year. About seven of every eight state-court cases (not counting parking tickets) are district-court level.
Judge pay: Not confirmed. The County Council sets the budget.

1. Who they are

The bottom line. This court’s power is broad and routine, not concentrated. It is the front door for most state-court cases in Pierce County. Its eight elected judges hold real power to jail people, fine them, and issue protection orders. It depends on the County Council for its budget. That limits its independence on money and staff, but not on its rulings.
The defense view. The court is an independent branch of government. Judges are elected by voters, not appointed by the Council or the Executive. The Council cannot cut a sitting judge’s salary (state law, RCW 3.58). Eight judges and nonpartisan races limit any one seat from being captured. Small claims and protection orders are built to help people without lawyers and victims.
The other way to read it. It is a routine service-delivery body. Its judges are professional, its docket predictable, and its budget is a small slice of county spending. Its power is capped by law. People can appeal to Superior Court. Its composite power score of 0.023 reflects this: it is on the map, but its influence on the big power structures is low.

1. Who they are

Verdict: Dona Ponepinto controls the largest health and human services funding pipeline in Pierce County through the UWPC CEO role ($6.7M in yearly contributions, source #3). She also runs a public community college (TCC Board Chair), a major art museum (TAM Board President), an international volunteer group (AJLI President), and holds board seats at healthcare groups (Wellfound, Coordinated Care) and a workforce development body. Her power comes from holding office and reputation — she is a paid nonprofit executive ($216K, source #3) whose influence comes from how many boards she sits on. Her rank 13/163 (composite 0.125) reflects her role as the most cross-networked institutional node in the graph. The graph’s four links undercount her actual board count of 7+ confirmed positions.

Counter: Board service at multiple community groups is a normal form of civic engagement, not corruption. All board roles seem unpaid (sources #3, #13). The number of board links reflects Ponepinto’s 30+ year nonprofit career and her reputation, not improper influence.

Under this view, if UWPC hired a different CEO, that person would get similar board invites. But the gubernatorial TCC appointment (renewed through 2029), the AJLI presidency (an international elected role), and the TAM Board Presidency show personal capital beyond her UWPC role.
Confidence: High. Multiple primary sources confirm all four graph links: UWPC CEO (IRS 990, reliability 0.95), TCC Board Chair (TCC official + governor.wa.gov, reliability 0.95), TAM Board President (TAM official page, reliability 0.8), Chamber Vice Chair (IRS 990, reliability 0.95). The extra board seats (Wellfound, Coordinated Care, WDC, AJLI) are confirmed by her own UWPC official bio (reliability 0.8). Main gaps are Coordinated Care corporate status (possible conflict) and PDC donation history.

0. Why this person or group is on the map

Why he’s on the map. Drew Stokesbary is the state House Representative for Washington’s 31st Legislative District, Position 1. That district covers parts of King and Pierce Counties, including Auburn, Bonney Lake, Buckley, Edgewood, and Sumner. More importantly, he has been the House Minority Leader since April 2023. That makes him the top Republican in the Washington House. His district includes a lot of Pierce County territory.
Who is NOT on the map. Josh Penner (R-31, House Position 2) is a district-mate but is not on the map at this tier. Phil Fortunato (R-31, Senate) is on the map separately.

1. Who they are

Full name: Andrew R. Stokesbary (Source 6). He goes by Drew Stokesbary.
Nickname: Drew Stokesbary (common usage); Andrew R. Stokesbary (legal/formal name on state campaign-finance agency (PDC) filings).
Born: UNVERIFIED — public sources do not list a date. He is described as a “lifelong Washingtonian” (Source 5).
Home: Auburn, Washington (Source 2, 5).
Family: Wife Ashley Stokesbary; four sons; a border collie named Scout (Source 2, 5).
Education: B.S. in Economics and Mathematics from Duke University (he also studied History there); J.D. cum laude from the University of Notre Dame Law School (Source 2, 5, 7).
Bar admissions: Washington, Arkansas, and Texas. He is also admitted to practice before the U.S. Supreme Court, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit, the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Texas, and the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Washington (Source 7).
Day job: Attorney. He is a partner at Chalmers, Adams, Backer & Kaufman LLC (sometimes called “Chalmers & Adams”), a small law firm. He handles corporate and securities work for startups, emerging companies, and private investment funds. Before that, he was a policy aide for a King County Councilmember (Source 2, 5, 7).

3. Where their power comes from

Elected office. He has served in the Washington House of Representatives, 31st District, Position 1, since January 12, 2015. He is in his 6th term. His current term ends January 11, 2027. He is running for re-election in November 2026. He won the August 4, 2026 primary with 57.9% to Stephen Szczurko-Walton’s 42.0% (Source 2).
Leadership role. He has been House Minority Leader since April 2023 — the top Republican job in the House. That makes him the chief strategist and spokesperson for the House Republican Caucus. He decides committee assignments for his members and runs the floor strategy (Source 2, 5).
Past leadership jobs. He was the Ranking Member of the House Appropriations Committee. He was Minority Floor Leader. He chaired the Select Committee on Pension Policy. He was assistant ranking Republican on House Appropriations (Source 5, 8).
Current committee (2025–2026): Rules Committee (Source 5).
Budget. As former Appropriations Ranking Member and current Minority Leader, Stokesbary has real influence over Republican budget strategy. The actual budget is controlled by the Democratic majority.
Where his power reaches: 31st Legislative District — Auburn, Bonney Lake, Buckley, Carbonado, Edgewood, Milton, South Prairie, Sumner, Wilkeson.

1. Who they are

The bottom line. Drew Stokesbary holds the most powerful position of any House Republican in Washington state. As House Minority Leader, he controls caucus strategy, committee assignments, and floor operations. He is the chief Republican voice in the House. His law firm work at Chalmers Adams and his co-founding of CADF give him reach beyond the legislature in the conservative legal world. His long committee experience — former Appropriations Ranking Member, Pension Policy Chair, and current Rules Committee — makes him one of the most policy-savvy Republicans in the building. His strong election numbers (58–64% in his district) show a secure base.
Conflicts to watch. As a practicing corporate and securities attorney while serving as House Minority Leader, his private legal clients (startups, emerging companies, investment funds) and his legislative role in business regulation and tax policy overlap. CADF, which he co-founded, sends legal advocacy letters to the very legislature he leads — a structural overlap between his nonprofit role and his legislative leadership. His bar admissions in multiple states and federal courts suggest a national legal practice that extends past Washington state.
The counter-argument. Stokesbary leads the minority party in a state where Democrats hold supermajorities in both chambers. His actual power to pass or block laws is limited by the Democratic majority’s ability to govern without Republican votes. CADF’s work could be seen as partisan advocacy rather than constitutional protection. His law firm is small and does not match the clout of partners at major firms.

Tier: tier3 · Rank: 98/163 · Composite power: 0.021
Graph description: Pierce County Fire Protection District No. 22 (East Pierce Fire & Rescue / EPFR) — career fire district formed 1999/2000 via merger of Bonney Lake Fire, Fire District 22 (Lake Tapps), and Fire District 24. Serves 115,000+ residents across 153 sq mi.
Known facts: Pierce County Fire Protection District No. 22; serves Bonney Lake, Sumner, Lake Tapps, Edgewood, Milton, Tehaleh, South Prairie, Ridge Communities; 9 fire stations; 2024 operating budget $58M actual on $59.9M budget.
Status: ✅ researched — 2026-09-19 — tier3-chunk5 · Last updated: 2026-09-19
Sources: 7/3 (minimum for tier3)

0. Why this person or group is on the map

Why included: Holds office + makes decisions + well-connected — East Pierce Fire & Rescue (EPFR / Pierce County Fire Protection District No. 22) is one of the two largest career fire districts in Pierce County (the other is Central Pierce Fire & Rescue). It has legal power over firefighting, emergency medical services, marine rescue on Lake Tapps, and fire code enforcement for 115,000+ residents across 153 square miles. It is run by an elected Board of Fire Commissioners. It collects voter-approved property tax levies ($1.50 per $1,000 fire levy approved by voters in 2024 + $0.41 per $1,000 EMS levy). (Sources 1, 2, 3, 6)
Adjacent but NOT included: Central Pierce Fire & Rescue (peer district serving the urban core). Tacoma Fire Department (city fire dept). West Pierce Fire & Rescue (a separate district covering west county). Buckley Fire Department (Wilkeson left East Pierce in 2014 to contract with Buckley).

1. Who they are

Legal name: Pierce County Fire Protection District No. 22, doing business as “East Pierce Fire & Rescue” (EPFR). (Sources 1, 2)
Type: Washington fire protection district. This is a special-purpose district set up under state law RCW Title 52. RCW 52.04 covers fire districts. RCW 52.33 covers Standards of Cover. An elected Board of Fire Commissioners runs it. (Sources 1, 2, 5)
When it formed: Merged in 2000 (effective Jan 1, 2000) from City of Bonney Lake Fire Department + Pierce County Fire District 22 (Lake Tapps) + Pierce County Fire District 24. On Nov 2, 1999, voters approved the merger (7,636 yes to 1,332 no). The three agencies had already been consolidated under the name “East Pierce Fire & Rescue” since 1995. (Sources 1, 2)
Later annexations:

2006: Pierce County Fire District 12 (South Prairie/Fire District 20)
2008: Sumner/Fire District 1
2010: Edgewood/Fire District 8
2013: Milton Fire Department
2014: Wilkeson ended its contract (now with Buckley FD) (Sources 1, 2)


HQ address: 8601 Main Street East, Bonney Lake, WA 98391. (Sources 2, 3)
Operating budget (2024): $59,865,333 budgeted. $58,022,515 in actual revenues. $51,991,391 in actual expenditures (and $52,109,920 in a second count — slight underrun per the 2024 Annual Report). (Source 4)
Funding model: EPFR stays within the state-law maximum levy rate of $2.00 per $1,000 of assessed property value (Fire Levy $1.50 + EMS Levy $0.50 max). As of 2024, EPFR is the only major Pierce County fire district operating WITHOUT a Maintenance & Operations (M&O) levy or a Benefit Charge that would push rates above $2.00. Most career fire districts in WA collect over $3.00 per $1,000. (Sources 4, 6)
Fire levy history: 2024 — voters approved restoring the fire levy to $1.50 per $1,000 of assessed value after several years of compression below the state maximum. EMS levy $0.41 per $1,000 of assessed value, renewed in 2021 for 10 years. (Source 6)

3. Where their power comes from

State law power (government side): Provides firefighting, EMS, marine rescue on Lake Tapps, fire code enforcement, and hazardous materials response for 115,000+ residents across 153 sq mi. Run by an elected Board of Fire Commissioners (RCW 52.14). (Sources 1, 2)
Budget power: About $59 million in annual operating budget (2024). Most of it comes from two voter-approved property tax levies (Fire + EMS). (Sources 4, 6)
Levy power (taxing): Voters approved the fire levy restoration to $1.50 per $1,000 in 2024. This is state-law power given by Pierce County voters to the District. It does not come from the County Council — it is direct voter power. (Source 6)
Workforce size: EPFR cross-trains all full-time firefighters as either EMTs (emergency medical technicians) or paramedics. There are 9 fire stations (8 staffed + 1 marine rescue). The exact uniformed staff count is UNVERIFIED. (Source 2)
Where power crosses domains: Government (special-purpose district) + economic (levy collection, capital facilities) + institutional (mutual aid agreements with nearby fire and EMS agencies).
Relationship with the Pierce County Council: EPFR’s taxing power comes directly from district voters, NOT from the Pierce County Council. The Council’s relationship with EPFR is indirect (boundary annexations, interlocal agreements). The map edge “taxing” between EPFR and the Pierce County Council is INACCURATE — EPFR’s main taxing power is direct from voters under RCW 52. (Source 6) — see Section 12 alternative reading.

1. Who they are

Verdict: East Pierce Fire & Rescue has state-law power as Pierce County Fire Protection District No. 22. It provides firefighting, EMS, marine rescue on Lake Tapps, and code enforcement for 115,000+ residents across 153 sq mi. It runs 9 fire stations and a $59 million annual budget. The District stays within the state-law combined levy cap of $2.00 per $1,000 — making it the only major Pierce County fire district without a third revenue stream (M&O levy or Benefit Charge). Voters approved restoring the fire levy to $1.50 per $1,000 in 2024. They renewed the EMS levy in 2021 for 10 years.
Conflicts-of-interest flags: The map edge between EPFR and the Pierce County Council labeled “taxing” is INACCURATE in the strict state-law sense. EPFR’s taxing power comes directly from district voters under RCW 52, not from the County Council. The Council’s role is limited to interlocal agreements and boundary matters. An opposing reading might note that the Council can still affect District operations through budget cycles, regional coordination, and boundary annexation review — but the direct taxing power is voter-controlled. (FACT — Source 6)
Analysis of alternatives: A defense reading: EPFR is a high-service, low-cost district. A restrained levy rate plus full staffing delivers services below the cost of peer districts. An opposing reading: running at the legal minimum levy cap with no M&O revenue makes EPFR always vulnerable to revenue compression. State law caps levy growth at 1% per year unless voters approve a higher rate. That pushes the district into periodic ballot-measure battles when costs outstrip revenue. The 2024 fire-levy restoration is exactly this dynamic.
Population discrepancy (Source 2 lists ~100,500; Sources 1 and 3 list “over 115,000”): The 100,500 figure appears on the Contact page. The 115,000 figure appears on About and Fire Stations pages. This likely reflects recent expansion or methodology (residents vs. service population). UNVERIFIED — flag for follow-up.
Confidence: High — primary-source confirmation from EPFR official website (About, Contact, Fire Stations, Funding, Annual Report) and Washington State Council of Fire Fighters.

Status: ✅ researched — 2026-09-19 — tier2-chunk3
Sources: 8/5 (minimum for tier2)

0. Why this person or group is on the map

Why EDB is on the map: The Economic Development Board for Tacoma-Pierce County (EDB) is the main regional economic development group for Pierce County. It meets two tests. First, it holds office-like power: it is the named economic development body and staffs the Economic Development Corporation of Pierce County (EDCPC) by contract (source #2). Second, it is well-connected: its board includes major regional employers — MultiCare, Port of Tacoma, Columbia Bank, Virginia Mason Franciscan Health (VMFH), TOTE Maritime, Puget Sound Energy — plus elected officials and other leaders. That mix creates board overlaps across sectors. Graph edges to the County Council, Boeing, Amazon, and the Chamber show it bridges economic, government, and advocacy domains.
Why others near it are NOT on the map: WorkForce Central (Katie Condit sits on the EDB board, source #3 — a workforce development partner, excluded). Pierce County Business Accelerator (a Chamber program for BIPOC businesses — excluded). The City of Tacoma Economic Development Department (Hyun Kim sits on the EDB board, source #3 — a government economic development function, excluded).

1. Who they are

Legal name: Economic Development Board for Tacoma Pierce County (source #4, the IRS 990 on ProPublica).
Entity type: 501(c)(6) business league / trade association (source #4: “Business leagues, chambers of commerce, real estate boards, etc., created for the improvement of business conditions”). Donations are NOT tax-deductible (source #4). Ruling year: March 1981 (source #4).
Tax ID (EIN): 91-1040355 (source #4, #5). State of legal domicile: Washington (source #5). Website: www.choosetacomapierce.org (source #1, #5). Also listed as www.edbtacomapierce.org in some filings (source #5).
Parent/subsidiaries: No parent. EDB “staffs the Economic Development Corporation of Pierce County (EDCPC) by contractual agreement” (source #2). EDCPC is a related but separate entity. UNVERIFIED: EDCPC’s separate EIN or 990 filings.
Ownership: Independent nonprofit run by a board of directors (44 voting members per the most recent 990, source #5).
Governing law: Washington State nonprofit corporation law. IRS 501(c)(6). Bylaws available (source #2: “EDB Bylaws” link, updated January 2025).

3. Where their power comes from

Power held: EDB holds well-connected and market-shaping power. It helps attract, keep, and grow businesses in Pierce County. It claims credit for “$1.6 billion in capital investments and over 25,000 jobs to the region over the past two decades” (source #2). EDB does not hold statutory authority, regulatory power, or taxing power. Its power is convening and brokering: it brings business leaders, elected officials, and institutions together to align on economic development goals. EDB says it is focused on “helping companies create new jobs and grow the economy of the South Sound” (source #2).
Economic overlap:
Revenue and structure: FY2023 revenue: $2,915,394 (95.1% from contributions and member dues, source #4). Net assets: $2,915,394 (source #4). EDB is funded by “investors” — businesses and institutions that pay dues. Total assets: $3,017,496 (source #4).
Government contracts/grants? UNVERIFIED — EDB’s 990 shows little program service revenue from government ($122,577 in program services, 4.5% of revenue, source #4). An FY2023 audit was filed (source #4: “Material weakness in internal controls • Significant deficiency in internal controls”). That audit finding suggests federal grant receipts over $750K. UNVERIFIED: which federal grants.
Jobs controlled? EDB does not directly employ many people (7 staff, including 2 contractors). It claims to have helped create 25,000 jobs over 20+ years (source #2). That is a cumulative claim, not direct employment.
Land/real estate? None found. EDB is a service group, not a property owner.
Government overlap: Board includes Pierce County Councilmember Dave Morell (source #3), Tacoma Mayor Anders Ibsen (source #3), Sumner Mayor Carla Bowman (source #3), and University Place City Manager Steve Sugg (source #3). These elected and appointed officials create direct government board overlaps. EDB also pushes for state budget items (like engineering money for UW Tacoma, source #7 context).

1. Who they are

The bottom line. The Economic Development Board for Tacoma-Pierce County runs a convening platform. It brings together 40+ institutional leaders from Pierce County’s economic, government, health, education, and labor sectors. EDB does not hold statutory authority, taxing power, or regulatory power. Its power is well-connected and convening — it brokers ties between businesses, government, and institutions to create jobs and capital ($1.6B and 25,000 jobs claimed over 20+ years, source #2). The board roster is EDB’s strongest asset. It includes the two biggest health systems (MultiCare, VMFH), the Port of Tacoma, TPU, PSE, two banks, the Chamber, the labor council, UW Tacoma, and elected officials. That makes EDB a structural hub of Pierce County’s power network, even though its formal authority is small. The 2024 leadership change from Bruce Kendall (25-year CEO) to Michael Catsi (source #8) is a generational shift.
Conflicts to watch (defense counter-argument expected): (1) The EDB board includes direct competitors (MultiCare and VMFH are the two largest health systems; Key Bank and Columbia Bank compete). Their shared board seat could lead to quiet coordination on markets. (2) Elected officials (Dave Morell, Ryan Mello, Anders Ibsen) sit on the EDB board while EDB pushes for economic development policies — a revolving door between government and advocacy. (3) The FY2023 audit found “material weakness in internal controls” and “significant deficiency in internal controls” (source #4), which raises governance questions. Defense counter: (1) Rival firms on a business league board is normal for chambers and EDBs; antitrust rules are usually handled through board policies. (2) Elected officials on EDB boards is a common model, giving policy alignment rather than conflict. (3) The audit findings are about internal controls, not fraud or theft — they are technical issues common in small nonprofits.
The other side: EDB is a dues-funded trade group with limited real power. Its $2.9M revenue (source #4) is modest. It employs only 7 people (source #7). Its claimed impact ($1.6B, 25,000 jobs) is self-reported and unproven. Under this reading, EDB is a networking group whose power is reputational, not structural. But the density of its board overlaps (40+ members across every major sector) gives it convening power beyond its budget. EDB’s role in big wins (U.S. Open at Chambers Bay, state highway money) shows real policy influence, even if the group itself is small.
Confidence: Medium. The EDB’s who they are legally, financial structure, board roster, and leadership history are well-documented by primary sources (IRS 990 via ProPublica, reliability 0.95; EDB official website, reliability 0.9). However, the self-reported impact metrics ($1.6B, 25,000 jobs) are not independently verified, the audit findings (source #4) are not fully explored, and the specific government contracts/grants are UNVERIFIED. The power assessment relies on board composition analysis (structural inference) rather than documented policy outcomes.

Where her power lies:
Natural resources and federal lands: Sits on the House Natural Resources Committee, on the Subcommittee on Indian and Insular Affairs and the Subcommittee on Federal Lands. She speaks for the 29 federally recognized tribes in WA (source #1, #7).
Government oversight: Sits on the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee, on the Subcommittee on Government Operations and the Subcommittee on Health Care and Financial Services (source #1, #6).
Health care: Worked at Planned Parenthood and the San Francisco AIDS Foundation. Sponsored the Reproductive Health Care for All bill in the WA Senate. Her sister’s Medicaid story drives her work (source #5).
Higher education: Former chair of the WA Senate Higher Education & Workforce Development Committee. Pushed for cheaper tuition and apprenticeships (source #5).
Native American policy: 71% of her sponsored bills deal with Native American issues (source #6).
Key facts:
Office and reach: US Representative for WA-6. Two House committees, four subcommittees.
Budget: No direct power over spending. As a freshman, her budget role is limited to committee votes and amendments. In the WA Senate, she sat on Ways & Means (the budget committee) (source #5).
Powers: House vote on executive appointments. No veto power. No committee chair (minority party).

U.S. District Court, Western District of Washington — Deep Profile
Case: INV-2026-002 · Profile: profiles/federal-district-court.md
Entity ID: federal-district-court · Type: organization · Domain: legal
Tier: tier3 · Rank: 99/163 · Composite power: 0.020
Graph description: U.S. District Court for the Western District of Washington (WDWA). Article III federal trial court. 7 active district judgeships + 6 magistrate judges. Courthouses in Seattle and Tacoma (Union Station, 1717 Pacific Avenue, Room 3100).
Known facts: Established 1905; 7 active judgeships (all filled as of 2026); Chief Judge David G. Estudillo (appointed Biden 2021); U.S. Attorney Neil Floyd (interim); Tacoma courthouse at Union Station serves Pierce County federal caseload.
Status: ✅ researched — 2026-09-19 — tier3-chunk5 · Last updated: 2026-09-19
Sources: 5/3 (minimum for tier3)

0. Why this person or group is on the map

Why included: Holds office + makes decisions — The U.S. District Court for the Western District of Washington is the only federal trial court with jurisdiction over Pierce County. Federal criminal cases, federal civil rights actions, habeas petitions (prisoners asking a federal court to review their state conviction), RICO and FCA cases, and federal-question diversity cases all go through WDWA. The Tacoma courthouse sits in Union Station. It handles criminal and civil cases from the southern district (Pierce, Lewis, Mason, Thurston, Clark, Skamania, Cowlitz, Wahkiakum, and Pacific counties). (Sources 1, 2, 4)
Adjacent but NOT included: U.S. Bankruptcy Court for WDWA (separate court, related but different job). Washington State Superior Court (state court — handles most criminal and civil matters in Pierce County). U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit (hears appeals from WDWA — separate court). U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Washington (covers eastern WA). U.S. Attorney’s Office WDWA (this is the prosecutor, not the court).

1. Who they are

Legal name: United States District Court for the Western District of Washington. (Sources 1, 2, 4)
Type: Federal Article III trial court. Established under Article III of the U.S. Constitution and 28 U.S.C. § 81 (the law that creates federal district courts). 28 U.S.C. § 132 reorganized WDWA into 7 seats. (Sources 1, 2)
When it was set up: First set up March 2, 1905. Reorganized over time — 1938 (3 seats), 1961 (5 seats), 1978 (6 seats), 1984 (7 seats, 1 temporary), 1990 (7 permanent). (Source 1)
Where it reaches: Western Washington — 19 counties west of the Cascades. Main courthouse is Seattle. There are also courthouses in Tacoma (Union Station) and Mount Vernon. (Sources 1, 2)
Tacoma courthouse: U.S. District Court, Clerk’s Office, 1717 Pacific Avenue, Room 3100, Tacoma, WA 98402-3200. Phone (253) 882-3800. The public lobby is open weekdays 7 AM–5 PM. Closed on federal holidays. You do NOT need a REAL ID to enter. (Source 2)
Chief Judge (2026): David G. Estudillo. Appointed by President Biden in 2021. Took office October 7, 2021. Has been Chief Judge since 2022. Born 1973. He was previously a Pierce County Superior Court judge and U.S. Attorney WDWA. (Sources 1, 3, 4)
Clerk of Court / District Court Executive: Joshua C. Lewis. (Source 2)
U.S. Attorney WDWA: Neil Floyd (interim). (Source 1)
Judgeships allowed: 7. All are filled, with no vacancies as of 2026. (Source 1)
Who appointed them: The active judges are mostly Biden appointees. The senior judges were appointed during the Reagan, Clinton, and G.W. Bush presidencies.

3. Where their power comes from

Federal judicial power (legal side): It is the only federal trial court for Pierce County. It has original (first-hearing) power over federal criminal matters (FBI, DEA, and ATF prosecutions; federal civil rights; RICO; drug trafficking; public corruption). It also handles federal civil cases (civil rights, antitrust, environmental enforcement, FCA qui tam (whistleblower lawsuits under the False Claims Act), immigration habeas, federal tort claims), and diversity cases (cases between citizens of different states) where the amount in dispute is over $75,000. (Source 4)
Constitutional rulings: The court issues binding rulings on constitutional questions. For example, recent WDWA rulings have addressed First Amendment rights tied to Pierce County Sheriff Keith Swank. (Source 5)
Appeals: Cases from WDWA go to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit, based in San Francisco. The Ninth Circuit hears oral arguments at the Pioneer Federal Courthouse in Portland, Oregon. (Source 1)
Where power crosses domains: Legal (Article III trial court) + government (Pierce County federal caseload) + institutional (review of federal agency actions within Pierce County).
Caseload stats (general federal): National U.S. District Courts civil cases filed in FY2025: 271,802 (down 21.9% from the year before). Criminal defendants filed: 73,644 (up 11.5%). WDWA-specific 2024 case numbers were not found in tabular form. (Source 6)

1. Who they are

Verdict: The U.S. District Court for the Western District of Washington has exclusive federal judicial power over Pierce County. It works through its Tacoma courthouse at Union Station, 1717 Pacific Avenue. Seven active district judges (appointed by Biden), 11 senior judges, and 6 magistrate judges handle the federal caseload. The Tacoma courthouse processes criminal and civil cases from Pierce, Lewis, Mason, Thurston, Clark, and other southern district counties. Chief Judge David G. Estudillo — former Pierce County Superior Court judge and former U.S. Attorney WDWA — is a known figure in the Pierce County legal community.
Conflicts-of-interest flags: The map edge labeled “federal_oversight” between WDWA and Superior Court is INACCURATE in the strict constitutional sense. WDWA does not exercise appellate “oversight” over Pierce County Superior Court. WDWA has habeas power to review state-court convictions under 28 U.S.C. § 2254, but Superior Court decisions are reviewed by the Washington State Court of Appeals, not WDWA. WDWA and Superior Court run side by side, not in a hierarchy. (FACT — 28 U.S.C. § 2254 limits federal habeas to constitutional issues, not state-court error correction.)
Analysis of alternatives: A defense reading: WDWA is a neutral, life-tenured Article III court. It is bound by statute and binding appellate precedent (9th Circuit, U.S. Supreme Court). An opposing reading: WDWA’s bench is overwhelmingly Biden-appointed (all 7 active judges). This affects Pierce County residents on civil rights, immigration, federal criminal sentencing, and federal regulatory challenges. Judge Estudillo’s past roles (Pierce County Superior Court judge, U.S. Attorney WDWA) mean he has direct relationships with many Pierce County lawyers and law enforcement figures who now appear before him.

Pierce County Flood Control Zone District — Deep Profile
Case: INV-2026-002 · Profile: profiles/flood-control-zone.md
Entity ID: flood-control-zone · Type: organization · Domain: government
Tier: tier3 · Rank: 111/163 · Composite power: 0.016
Graph description: Pierce County Flood Control Zone District (FCZD) — special-purpose quasi-municipal corporation formed by Pierce County Council under RCW 86.15; governed by Board of Supervisors; funded by countywide property-tax levy capped at $0.10/$1,000 AV (RCW 86.15.095); makes flood-risk-reduction and watershed-management grants to cities, tribes, and nonprofits.
Known facts: Formed under Chapter 86.15 RCW; Pierce County Council created the District via interlocal agreement (2011 per FIFE WA fact sheet); countywide property-tax levy of ~$0.09/$1,000 AV in 2024 raising ~$18.9M; Chair (2024–2026) Dave Morell; 2025 Comprehensive Plan of Development adopted April 23, 2025; White River Restoration in Sumner funded by District protects $1.14B in property value and 16,000 jobs.
Status: ✅ researched — 2026-09-19 — tier3-chunk8
Sources: 5/3 (minimum for tier3)

0. Why this person or group is on the map

Inclusion rule — from holding office + decision-making + well-connected: Pierce County FCZD is the only countywide flood-control taxing district in Pierce County. It was formed under Chapter 86.15 of the state law (RCW). It can levy property taxes up to $0.10 per $1,000 of assessed value. It gives grants for flood-risk reduction. It has fiscal power over every parcel in unincorporated Pierce County and, through interlocal agreements, over incorporated cities too. That gives it a role in countywide land-use and infrastructure choices. Any city, tribe, or nonprofit with a creek or floodplain can apply for grants, so it is well-connected by design.
Adjacent but EXCLUDED candidates: Pierce County Public Works Surface Water Management provides the executive director and staff under contract and appears in FCZD documents. Pierce County Council creates and oversees the District. City Public Works departments in Tacoma, Lakewood, Puyallup, Sumner, and Orting get FCZD grants but are separate. Tacoma Water and Puget Sound Energy are regulated separately. FEMA Region 10 and the National Flood Insurance Program are federal partners and are separate.

1. Who they are

Exact legal name: Pierce County Flood Control Zone District (also called Pierce County FCZD or “the District”).
Entity type: Special-purpose quasi-municipal corporation and taxing district formed under Chapter 86.15 RCW (“Flood Control Zone Districts”). Pierce County is the “county with a population of 775,000 or more” named in RCW 84.52.816.
Authorizing statute: Chapter 86.15 RCW. RCW 86.15.095 sets the rate cap of $0.10 per $1,000 of assessed value. RCW 84.52.816 protects part of that levy from prorationing. RCW 86.15.160 allows grants to cities and others. The Board must follow the Open Public Meetings Act (RCW 42.30).
Formation: The Pierce County Council formed the District as allowed by Chapter 86.15 RCW (per the FIFE WA fact sheet). The District’s “annual regular” levy is named in interlocal agreement exhibits.
Governing body: Board of Supervisors, made up of Pierce County Council members and other officials appointed by member jurisdictions. The Board follows District Operating Rules like Resolution No. 2012-1, amended by 2017-2. Chair for 2024–2026 is Pierce County Council Chair Dave Morell.
Parent/subsidiaries: No parent. The Executive Director and staff come from Pierce County Public Works / Surface Water Management under contract. The District office is at 1501 Market Street, Suite 140, Tacoma, WA 98402; phone 206-612-8138.
Governing law: Chapter 86.15 RCW; RCW 84.52 (property tax); RCW 42.30 (Open Public Meetings Act); interlocal agreements with member jurisdictions.

3. Where their power comes from

Statutory taxing authority (FACT): RCW 86.15.095 caps the District’s regular property tax levy at $0.10 per $1,000 of assessed value. RCW 84.52.816 protects part of the District’s levy from prorationing by general government levies because Pierce County’s population is over 775,000. Resolution No. 2016-8s and No. 2020-9s both name the District’s “banked capacity” under RCW 84.55.092. “Banked capacity” means unused levy room the District can spend later.
Grant-making authority (FACT): The District runs a recurring Flood Risk Reduction and Watershed Management Grants program. It is open to “local jurisdictions, Indian Tribes, and non-profit organizations.” Per-program caps: up to $1,000,000 per construction project and up to $125,000 per study or plan (per a Pierce County announcement for the 2022 cycle; same pattern in 2024 resolutions). Chair Morell said the program funds “applicants … for construction projects or studies/plans that … protect lives and reduce the public risk caused by flooding.”
Budget scale (FACT): A countywide levy of about $0.09 per $1,000 AV in 2024 raises about $18.9 million in property-tax revenue for the District (per the District Funding page).
Comprehensive planning authority (FACT): The District adopted its 2025 Comprehensive Plan of Development on April 23, 2025. The plan “incorporates key elements of Pierce County’s Comprehensive Flood Hazard Management Plan.” That makes the FCZD a layer in the county’s flood-hazard-management system, not just a grant-maker.
Domain overlaps:

gov ↔ econ: The property-tax levy plus grant disbursement (about $18.9M per year) makes the District a money bridge between county taxpayers and municipal, tribal, and nonprofit projects.
gov ↔ environment: Flood-risk reduction, salmon habitat restoration, stormwater cleanup.
gov ↔ institutional: Sets conditions on interlocal partners and absorbs Pierce County Surface Water Management capacity.


FACT vs INFERENCE: The above are FACT (statute, district resolutions, district funding page). The “money bridge” framing is INFERENCE (a functional description, not contested).

1. Who they are

Verdict: Pierce County FCZD is a countywide, Council-created flood-control taxing district. Its statutory rate cap is $0.10 per $1,000 AV (RCW 86.15.095). At its current rate of about $0.09, it raises about $18.9M a year (2024). It is not a regulator or a service provider in the everyday sense. It is a fiscal and planning body. It adopts a Comprehensive Plan of Development (the latest was adopted April 23, 2025), sets an annual levy, and gives grants to cities, tribes, and nonprofits for flood-risk reduction and salmon-habitat restoration. Its practical power comes from (a) selective grant-making that shapes what cities and tribes build on floodplains (the White River Restoration in Sumner protects $1.14B in property and 16,000 jobs — a textbook funded project), and (b) convening power through its Board of Supervisors, which pulls Council members and member-jurisdiction officials around a shared flood-hazard plan.
Conflicts-of-interest flags: The Board of Supervisors is mostly Pierce County Council members and member-jurisdiction officials. In plain terms, the same people who control County and city budgets also sit as Supervisors of the District. RCW 86.15 allows this, but it creates an overlap risk: the cities that get grants are the same ones whose officials sit as Supervisors. The executive director and staff also come from Pierce County Public Works / Surface Water Management — the same county department that benefits from the District’s work. These overlaps are allowed by the statute but should be flagged as the structural reason District grants tend to match County executive priorities.
Analysis of alternatives: A defense reading would say the District’s rate cap is set by law, the Board is publicly appointed, its meetings follow the Open Public Meetings Act, and grants are awarded through published application cycles with clear criteria. In short, it is procedurally constrained and transparent. The other reading is that the Board’s overlap with Council members and the staff-sharing deal with Public Works mean the District acts less as an independent flood-control body and more as a fiscal arm of the County executive — especially when cities like Tacoma or Lakewood run their own stormwater utilities independently.
Confidence: Medium — structural and statutory facts verified against the District’s own website, Document Center, and Pierce County announcements. The FY2025 levy rate and budget figure come from the District Funding page. No full 2025/2026 grant-cycle recipient list was reviewed in this pass (UNVERIFIED for individual grant-cycle outcomes beyond the 2022 cycle cited in the Pierce County announcement).

As MultiCare CEO, Chang will manage a partial partnership that sits inside a competitor’s corporate family. That is a structural overlap, not a personal one. MultiCare’s payer mix, about 70% Medicare and Medicaid, ties the system financially to state and federal reimbursement policy. That creates a policy-advocacy incentive that could conflict with her duty to balance the budget each year. Public-company-style pay disclosure does not apply in the same way. MultiCare is a non-profit 501(c)(3). The CEO’s total pay is on Form 990 but is not in any one document here. UNVERIFIED.


Analysis of alternatives: The defense reading: the succession was unanimously approved by an independent board after a long planning process. Chang’s internal promotion signals board confidence in continuity, not disruption. The skeptical reading: internal succession at this scale rules out competitive outside candidates. It limits board accountability. MultiCare’s expansion (Yakima, Overlake, Samaritan, Indigo urgent care, Wellfound) has been aggressive. A CEO who built the IT and operations base for this growth may not be the right person to judge whether the combined system is solvent. Either way, the next 24 months, ending with Robertson’s exit on December 31, 2026, will be diagnostic.


Confidence: High — primary sources (MultiCare press releases, leadership page, Healthcare Dive, Yakima Herald, WS Magazine) all corroborate the timeline, title history, and educational background. Personal/financial specifics UNVERIFIED.


Open questions and leads:.


Chang’s total compensation package as reported on MultiCare’s 990 (FY2026 filing).


Board-level succession plan details (was anyone external considered?).


Integration playbook for Yakima Memorial, Overlake, and Samaritan affiliations — debt and capital commitment totals.


MultiCare labor relations under her tenure (SEIU, UFCW, and nurse-union contract terms).
