Economic / market-share: About 10,000+ employees work for member firms. MBA has “over 850 Builder & Associate Members” and “50+ Professions & Specializations” (MBAPC sponsorship page). It gives the home-building industry one voice in county politics.
decision-making / political: The Affordable Housing Council PAC gave $2,400 each to two Pierce County Council incumbents in 2024 (Herrera District 2, Cruver District 3). That PAC money was 8.5% of Herrera’s raised total and 4% of Cruver’s (per The News Tribune). It gives MBA a direct lever on the body that votes on zoning, code changes, and the County’s Comprehensive Plan.
Reputational: Annual REX (Remodeling Excellence) Awards and “Best of the South Sound” recognitions give MBA visibility and standard-setting power in the industry.


Basis for each overlap (scoring framework): trade-association size × campaign-finance lever × state-association umbrella = small absolute power score (0.013), but a real, repeatable channel into housing-supply politics.
key facts: Revenue = program-services revenue $1,316,095 on the most-recent 990 (CauseIQ; year-stamp UNVERIFIED, so treat as a fiscal-year reference, not a fact for a specific year). 1. Who they are


Verdict: MBAPC is a mid-tier, repeatable input-channel actor in Pierce County housing politics. It does not hold formal power (no public-board seats, no contract authority). But its PAC turns about $5,000 of biennial donations into access to two sitting Council members who vote on every land-use item in front of the County Council. The method is small-dollar, high-frequency, and durable: it works no matter who wins.
Conflicts-of-interest flags: (a) The PAC name “Affordable Housing Council” suggests an affordability mission, but the broader group’s stated stance is “supply-not-costs” deregulation. Known facts: Founded Feb 3, 1857 by James McClatchy; bankruptcy Feb 2020; acquired by Chatham Asset Management for $312M (Sept 2020); 2024 revenue decline ~41% per NYT; multiple layoff rounds since 2020 acquisition; Kevin McClatchy is chairman; Tony Hunter is CEO
Status: ✅ researched — 2026-09-19 — tier3-chunk1
Sources: 5/3 (minimum for tier3)

0. Why this person or group is on the map

Inclusion rule: From holding office, decision-making, reputation, and being well-connected. McClatchy is included as the parent company of The News Tribune in Tacoma. The News Tribune is Pierce County’s only major daily paper. It is the second-largest newspaper in Washington state. Its weekday circulation was 30,945 in 2020. Inclusion comes from holding office (McClatchy controls Tacoma’s daily paper of record). It comes from decision-making (McClatchy’s staffing and coverage choices shape Pierce County’s main local news source). It comes from reputation (Chatham Asset Management’s ownership puts McClatchy in the national “hedge-fund-owned newspapers” trend, which has drawn heavy criticism). It comes from being well-connected. The power graph shows: News Tribune owned_by McClatchy weight 5, and Chatham AM owned_by McClatchy weight 7.
Adjacent but EXCLUDED candidates: Chatham Asset Management is the parent hedge fund, based in New Jersey. It is excluded as a separate node. It is captured as the controlling owner. a360media is a Chatham-owned magazine publisher that merged into McClatchy in December 2024. It is excluded as a separate entity and captured under McClatchy Lifestyle & Entertainment. Individual News Tribune reporters, editors, and editorial-board members are excluded as individuals. The Pacific Northwest Newspaper Guild is the union representing McClatchy workers. It is excluded unless set up as a separate node.

1. Who they are

Exact legal name: McClatchy Media Company. It was formerly called The McClatchy Company. It was renamed in December 2024 when a360media merged in. Delaware-incorporated. It is a subsidiary of Chatham Asset Management.
Entity type: Privately held publishing company. It is a subsidiary of Chatham Asset Management, a hedge fund based in Chatham Borough, NJ.
Tax ID number (EIN)/registration: UNVERIFIED in this session.
Parent/subsidiaries: Parent: Chatham Asset Management LLC, a New Jersey hedge fund. McClatchy is the operating subsidiary. It holds 30 daily newspapers and other media properties under the McClatchy name. The December 2024 merger brought in a360media. a360media was Chatham’s other media property. It now forms the McClatchy Lifestyle & Entertainment division.
Ownership chain: Chatham Asset Management → McClatchy Media Company → 30 daily newspapers + lifestyle and entertainment magazines.
Governing law: Delaware General Corporation Law. The company filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in February 2020. It reorganized under Chatham ownership in September 2020.
Founded: February 3, 1857 by James McClatchy in Sacramento, CA. The original paper was The Daily Bee.
Headquarters: 26 Main Street, Chatham Borough, NJ 07928. The company moved from Sacramento in 2020 under Chatham ownership.
Key leadership: Kevin McClatchy is chairman. Tony Hunter is president and CEO. McClatchy is descended from the founding family. Chatham controls operations.

3. Where their power comes from

Power held: McClatchy holds media-domain power in Pierce County. It owns The News Tribune in Tacoma. The News Tribune is the dominant daily paper covering Pierce County. McClatchy’s power rests on four bases. First, it has a monopoly on the daily newspaper of record for Pierce County. Second, Chatham Asset Management controls it financially. Chatham is a hedge fund with a track record of aggressive cost cuts across its newspaper portfolio. Third, McClatchy has coastwide reach. It controls 30 daily papers across the US, including the Sacramento Bee, the Miami Herald, and the Kansas City Star. Fourth, McClatchy shares national content and sells bundled advertising with Gannett. That 2024 collaboration shows how McClatchy and Gannett pool their ad networks.
Media domain overlap: McClatchy is the only major daily newspaper owner in Pierce County. The News Tribune is the second-largest daily in Washington state. Its weekday circulation was 30,945. Its Sunday circulation was 37,255 (per the 2020 McClatchy profile). The News Tribune covers local breaking news, pro and prep sports, the Washington statehouse, Joint Base Lewis-McChord (JBLM), the Port of Tacoma, and outdoor recreation.
Revenue: UNVERIFIED for 2024-2025. News reports cite about a 41% revenue decline (per the New York Times) since Chatham’s acquisition. The company had 2,800 full and part-time employees as of 2019, before bankruptcy.
Jobs controlled: 2,800 full and part-time employees company-wide (2019 pre-bankruptcy figure). Current post-layoffs is likely lower. McClatchy has run multiple layoff rounds since the 2020 acquisition. Layoffs in 2025 hit multiple McClatchy papers, including The News Tribune.
Government contracts/grants: No direct contracts or grants. Revenue comes from advertising, including state and local government accounts.
Land/real-estate: News Tribune offices are at 1950 South State Street, Tacoma, WA 98405. McClatchy’s headquarters is at 26 Main St, Chatham Borough, NJ.

1. Who they are

Verdict: McClatchy controls Pierce County’s only major daily paper (The News Tribune) under Chatham Asset Management ownership. Chatham is a hedge fund with a track record of aggressive cost cuts across its newspaper portfolio. McClatchy’s power rests on two bases. First, it has a monopoly on the daily newspaper of record. Second, it is run by an absentee owner that extracts money through cuts. Decisions about Pierce County’s news coverage are made at the corporate level by a hedge fund in Chatham Borough, NJ. Local accountability is limited. The 2024 layoff rounds and about a 41% revenue decline since Chatham’s 2020 acquisition show that McClatchy’s Pierce County newsroom has shrunk under hedge-fund ownership.
Conflicts-of-interest flags: Chatham’s control of McClatchy is the central conflict. A hedge fund’s duty to its investors is structurally different from a community newspaper’s duty to its readers. Chatham’s Postmedia Canada portfolio shows the pattern: 1,600 jobs cut, 30 papers shut down. At the Miami Herald, more than one-third of editorial staff were cut in 2024. Critics read this as a deliberate cost-extraction strategy. The defense counter: McClatchy emerged from Chapter 11 in 2020 under Chatham’s ownership. Without Chatham, McClatchy might have liquidated and all 30 papers would have closed. Chatham’s investment preserved jobs that would otherwise have been lost. McClatchy’s press release frames Chatham as “stewards.” Critics reject that claim.
Analysis of alternatives: The opposing reading is that McClatchy’s power is overstated. The News Tribune competes with digital-native outlets. Tacoma Weekly, Patch, South Sound Talk, social media, and direct government communications all compete for readers’ attention. Under that view, McClatchy’s gatekeeping power has eroded. However, for accountability journalism — investigations of Pierce County government, courts, and major institutions — The News Tribune remains the dominant local outlet. Its smaller newsroom directly weakens democratic accountability in the county. The structural reality is that McClatchy, under Chatham, holds significant power to set the agenda despite digital competition.
Confidence: Medium-High. Specific 2024-2025 News Tribune staffing levels, exact subscription and print circulation, and News Tribune’s 2025 layoff count are UNVERIFIED in detail. McClatchy’s lobbying expenditures and political action committee (PAC) contributions are also UNVERIFIED.

Defiance Marina; 5-member elected Board of Park Commissioners (6-year terms); 2025-2026 biennial operating budget ~$213M (~$106.5M annually); facing ~$3-4M operating deficits in 2025-2026
Known facts: Established April 6, 1907 by Tacoma voters; 5-member elected board (Matt Mauer, Andrea Smith, Alisa Lee, Carla Santorno, Pete Reyes as of 2025); $198M bond program (2014) for facility improvements; executive director UNVERIFIED in this session
Status: ✅ researched — 2026-09-19 — tier3-chunk1
Sources: 5/3 (minimum for tier3)

0. Why this person or group is on the map

Why Metro Parks is on the map: Metro Parks Tacoma is the independent park district that runs Pierce County’s largest urban park system. It covers 2,907 acres across 75 parks and facilities. It is on the map for four reasons:

From holding office: it is a junior taxing district (a local government that can levy property taxes) with the legal right to raise property taxes for parks.
Decision-making: its five elected Park Commissioners set policy, budget, and priorities for a $213 million two-year budget.
Reputational: it runs nationally known places like Point Defiance Zoo & Aquarium, Northwest Trek Wildlife Park, and the 760-acre Point Defiance Park.
Well-connected: its graph edges link to Ryan Mello (former commissioner), Anders Ibsen (Tacoma mayor), and Matt Mauer (board president).


Other bodies nearby: The five-member Board of Park Commissioners is part of this profile, not a separate node. The Tacoma City Council is separate. Tacoma Public Schools is separate. Pierce County Parks and Recreation is a separate county-level agency.

1. Who they are

Exact legal name: Metropolitan Park District of Tacoma. Used to be known as “Metro Parks Tacoma.” Since January 14, 2025, it has gone by “Parks Tacoma.”
Entity type: Independent junior taxing district, set up under Washington State law RCW 35.61 (Park and Recreation Districts). Run by an elected Board of Park Commissioners.
Tax ID (EIN): UNVERIFIED — operates as a Washington State special-purpose district.
Parent/subsidiaries: None — Metro Parks Tacoma is independent, not part of the City of Tacoma. Its territory overlaps Tacoma city limits.
Governing law: RCW 35.61 (Park and Recreation Districts). Washington special-purpose district laws. The original 1907 founding act.
Founded: April 6, 1907 (Tacoma voters approved the Metropolitan Park District of Tacoma — the first independent park district in Washington).
Headquarters: 4702 S. 19th Street, Tacoma, WA 98405. Phone: (253) 305-1000.
Brand change: Metro Parks Tacoma (historical) → “Parks Tacoma” (rebrand on January 14, 2025 — “Drop Metro From Our Name” — meant to be simpler and friendlier).
Executive director: UNVERIFIED. The long-time executive director was Marty McOmber. Current ED UNVERIFIED.

3. Where their power comes from

Power held: Metro Parks Tacoma holds legal power as a junior taxing district. It can levy property taxes (capped at $0.60 per $1,000 of assessed value under RCW 35.61). Its power comes from four sources:

Taxing authority — about $34 million in property tax revenue expected for 2025 alone; total biennial operating budget about $213 million.
Land control — 2,907 acres across 75 parks and recreation sites.
Anchor institutions — Point Defiance Zoo & Aquarium, Northwest Trek Wildlife Park, Meadow Park Golf Course.
Elected governance — five board members elected to six-year terms. Direct democratic accountability.


Government domain overlap: Metro Parks Tacoma is a local-government body that makes major public-land-use decisions in Tacoma and nearby areas. Its $213 million biennial budget and about $25 million annual capital plan (2025-2026) make it a sizable public-sector player.
Budget: 2025-2026 biennial operating budget about $213 million (~$106.5 million a year). 2014 bond program: $198 million ($158 million issued, $40 million left). $25 million capital plan for 2025-2026 ($16 million regional parks, $7 million neighborhood/community parks, $2 million heritage/landmark). Property-tax revenue about $34 million for 2025. Budget cuts about 21% in 2025 due to a $17 million deficit. About a $4 million deficit in 2025 and a projected $3 million deficit in 2026.
Jobs controlled: The 2025-2026 budget adds 49 full-time positions over the two years (35 in Parks & Rec, 11 in business administration/planning, 2 in the executive director’s office, 1 ZEED). Current total FTE (full-time equivalent employees) UNVERIFIED.
Land/real-estate: 2,907 acres total. 75 parks and recreation properties. Over 87 miles of trails. 8.2 miles of public shoreline. Main assets: Point Defiance Park (760 acres — one of the largest urban parks in the U.S.), Point Defiance Zoo & Aquarium, Northwest Trek Wildlife Park, Meadow Park Golf Course, Pt. Defiance Marina.
Government contracts/grants: Receives federal funding for the red wolf conservation program at Point Defiance Zoo and similar wildlife work. The 2025-2026 budget seeks more state and federal program funding (such as Titlow Beach culvert replacement). The $25 million capital plan includes large regional-park investments.

1. Who they are

Verdict: Metro Parks Tacoma runs the largest urban park system in Pierce County — 2,907 acres across 75 parks and facilities, including nationally known places like Point Defiance Zoo & Aquarium and Northwest Trek Wildlife Park. Its power comes from its legal taxing authority (junior taxing district with a property-tax levy capped at $0.60 per $1,000 of assessed value) and from democratic governance (five elected commissioners on six-year terms). The 2025-2026 biennial operating budget is about $213 million. The capital plan is about $25 million. The Park District is in a budget crisis — about a $17 million deficit in 2025-2026, around 21% budget cuts, a $4 million deficit in 2025, and a projected $3 million in 2026. That shows its taxing authority has not kept up with operating costs, forcing major cuts and a search for new revenue (fees, grants, voter-approved levies).
Conflicts-of-interest flags: As an independent junior-taxing district, Metro Parks can raise property taxes without direct City Council approval. The six-year board terms insulate commissioners from short-term voter pressure. The 2025 board turnover (3 of 5 seats vacated in 4 months — Ayala to Council, Pointer retirement, Reid death) shows how fragile long-tenured governance can be. The current budget crisis pits keeping park services against raising taxes and fees. Counter: an elected board gives democratic accountability. The crisis reflects real cost pressures (inflation, post-COVID recovery), not mismanagement. The Park District’s tribal-land acknowledgement (Coast Salish) and its focus on equity in Alisa Lee’s appointment show awareness of representational gaps.
Analysis of alternatives: Opposing reading: Metro Parks’ power is overstated. Its junior-taxing-district status is limited by the $0.60 per $1,000 levy cap, and the 2025-2026 budget crisis shows the model is at its limit. Under this view, Metro Parks is over-extended and could face service cuts, governance reform, or even consolidation. But Metro Parks’ land assets (2,907 acres) are durable and irreplaceable. The Park District has survived 119 years. The 2025 board turnover may bring new energy to revenue and governance questions. The bottom line: Metro Parks holds real power through land and institutional assets, but its operating budget is under structural pressure.
Confidence: Medium-High. Metro Parks Tacoma’s legal identity, governance, budget size, and 2025 board composition are confirmed by primary Parks Tacoma and Tacoma Weekly sources (reliability 0.8-0.95). The exact 2025-2026 biennial budget total ($213M) comes from a secondary source (Grokipedia) and should be re-checked. The $25M capital plan is from The News Tribune (reliability 0.9). The current executive director’s name is UNVERIFIED. The specific property-tax levy rate is UNVERIFIED.

Pierce Transit operates Sound Transit’s ST Express bus service between Pierce and King counties. That accounts for about 40% of its bus-operator jobs.

The original task description’s “former Pierce County Exec” wording appears to be a graph-label error. Many primary sources confirm he is the Pierce Transit CEO, a separate job from the elected Pierce County Executive.
Conflicts of interest (defense-attorney view): None found in primary sources. One thing to watch: he came from Keolis and Veolia, both big private transit contractors. If Pierce Transit ever bids Sound Transit work, that past could look like favoritism. No public allegation has been made.
Other view: A skeptic would call a transit CEO a functionary, not a power player. The view that elevates Griffus points to two things: (a) the November 2026 Pierce Transit sales-tax ballot measure (a proposed jump from 0.6% to 0.9%) — he is the public face of that campaign; (b) Pierce Transit’s contract role with Sound Transit, where he shapes a key regional link. Graph description: 5th-generation family-owned construction materials supplier (concrete, aggregates). Headquartered Puyallup, WA. ~500 employees. 80+ years operating in Western WA.
Known facts: Founded early 1940s in Auburn, WA by Walter Miles; corporate office moved to Puyallup 2010; operates in 9+ western WA counties.
Status: ✅ researched — 2026-09-19 — tier2-chunk2 · Last updated: 2026-09-19

0. Why this person or group is on the map

Miles Sand & Gravel is a family-owned construction materials supplier in Pierce County. The company sells concrete, gravel, and rock for roads, bridges, and buildings.
Miles is on the map for two reasons. (1) It has real market power in concrete and aggregates across Western Washington. (2) It is well-connected: the company has given money to Pierce County elected officials (Kelly Chambers, Amy Cruver, Paul Herrera) and is a member of the Chamber of Commerce.
Not on the map separately: Port Orchard Sand & Gravel (a related company in Kitsap/Mason/Jefferson counties) and Concrete Nor’West (acquired in the 1970s and absorbed into Miles).

1. Who they are

Full name: Miles Sand & Gravel Company (also called “Miles Sand & Gravel” and the “Miles group of companies”).
Type: A private, family-owned business, now in its 5th generation. It is a for-profit company.
Where it operates: Headquartered in Puyallup, WA. Active in 9 or more Western Washington counties.
Who founded it: Walter Miles and his father started the company in the early 1940s. They bought a gravel pit in Auburn, WA. Walter died in 1964. His wife Idamae Miles took over management. Their son Frank Miles ran the company next. Frank grew the company from 6 employees to 900. He died December 8, 2019.
Who runs it now: Tim and Lisa Kittilsby (Frank’s daughter and son-in-law) are in charge, per a 2011 source. The Mount Vernon location has Ryan Lemos as Owner/Principal/Partner.
Governing law: Washington State corporate law (RCW Title 23B). The company also follows state mining and environmental rules.

3. Where their power comes from

Market power: Miles has plants and quarries in 9 or more Western Washington counties. The service area runs from the Canadian border down to Chehalis. About 500 employees work for the company. It has operated for more than 80 years.
Political influence: Miles has donated to three Pierce County officials: Kelly Chambers (former state rep, 2024 county executive candidate), Amy Cruver (Pierce County Council, District 3), and Paul Herrera (Pierce County Council, District 2). It has given $4,890 to the Washington Aggregate and Concrete Association PAC. It gave $450 to the Island County Republican Party Central Committee.
Rules it deals with: As a mining and aggregate company, Miles needs permits for gravel mining, concrete production, and trucking. The company works with the WA Department of Ecology, Pierce County land-use rules, and local zoning. Its website talks about “environmental responsibility” and “safe work environments.”
Business stakes: Miles sells the concrete and rock that go into Pierce County’s roads, bridges, and buildings. County infrastructure spending, impact fees, and development rules all affect demand for its products. The company has a direct stake in pro-development county policy.

4. Power in numbers

|| Who governs | Miles does not run government. It tries to influence it through donations to councilmembers who vote on land-use, infrastructure, and development rules. It also lobbies through the Washington Aggregate and Concrete Association PAC. | #7, #8 |
|| Who wins | Miles wins when county policy favors infrastructure spending, development, and fast permitting. Its donations to Republicans Kelly Chambers, Amy Cruver, and Paul Herrera fit that pattern. | #7, #8 |
5. How they touch government

Campaign donations made: $4,890 to the Washington Aggregate and Concrete Association PAC. $450 to the Island County Republican Party Central Committee. Donations to Kelly Chambers, Paul Herrera, and Amy Cruver (each rated weight 3). These donations go to officials who vote on land-use and infrastructure.
Lobbying: No direct lobbying is on record. Miles pushes its policy goals through the Washington Aggregate and Concrete Association PAC. Whether Miles has registered lobbyists in Washington state is not confirmed.
Contracts and grants: As a private supplier, Miles likely holds contracts with construction firms that build public projects. Direct government contracts would be at the prime contractor level. Miles would be a materials subcontractor. Specific contracts are not confirmed.
Land-use actions: The Pierce County Council votes on the comprehensive plan, zoning changes, impact fee schedules, and development rules. Cruver and Herrera sit on that council. The council’s July 2026 action replacing the impact fee schedule with a rates-based model affects demand for Miles’ products. Miles’ donations to those councilmembers link the company to the officials who set those rules.
Regulatory actions: Mining and aggregate operations need permits from the WA Department of Ecology (water quality, stormwater), local air quality agencies, and county and city land-use authorities. Specific permit applications or violations are not on record.

Chamber of Commerce — member. A business advocacy group.
Kelly Chambers — received a donation. Former state rep, 2024 county executive candidate.
Amy Cruver — received a donation. Pierce County Councilmember, District 3.
Paul Herrera — received a donation. Pierce County Councilmember, District 2.
Pierce County Council — land-use relationship. The Council sets land-use rules that affect Miles’ business.
Washington Aggregate and Concrete Association PAC — received $4,890 from Miles for industry advocacy.
Family ownership: The Miles family (Walter → Idamae → Frank → Lisa and Tim Kittilsby) has run the company for four or more generations. Frank Miles grew the company from 6 to 900 employees. The family’s wealth is tied to the company’s success.

12. Bottom line

The bottom line. Miles Sand & Gravel is a mid-sized, family-owned supplier of concrete and gravel in Western Washington. It has 80+ years of history, about 500 employees, and operations across 9 or more counties.
How it touches Pierce County. Miles sells the materials that go into county roads, bridges, and buildings. It has donated to three Pierce County elected officials (Kelly Chambers, Amy Cruver, Paul Herrera) and to the industry PAC. Its donations match its business interests: pro-development policy means more demand for its products.
The counter-view. The donation amounts are modest ($4,890 to the industry PAC total). Washington state campaign-finance law allows business contributions within legal limits. No quid pro quo has been documented. Miles’ 80-year history and family ownership suggest community roots, not predatory influence.
Open questions. Specific government contracts, permit history, and direct lobbying are not verified. Current management (post-2019 Frank Miles death) needs verification.
Confidence: Medium. The company’s history, size, and donations are confirmed by primary sources (the company website and PDC/Transparency USA data). The donation-to-vote link is inferential, not proven.

Open questions and leads

The Washington State Secretary of State business registration would confirm current officers and registered agent.
The WA Dept. of Ecology permit database would show specific mining and aggregate permits and any violations.
The Pierce County contract database could show whether Miles is a direct or subcontractor on county-funded projects.
The current management structure (after Frank Miles’ 2019 death) needs verification — are Tim and Lisa Kittilsby still running the company, or has the 5th generation taken over?

Status: ✅ researched — 2026-09-19 — tier1-chunk2

0. Why this person or group is on the map

Inclusion rule — power and decision-making. MultiCare Health System is on this map because it is the largest private employer in Pierce County. It has 22,789 employees, runs 9 hospitals across Washington, and takes in more than $5 billion a year.
MultiCare runs Tacoma General, Good Samaritan, Allenmore, Auburn, Covington, Capital Medical Center, and Mary Bridge Children’s Hospital. It also runs Deaconess Hospital and Valley Hospital in Spokane.
Its board connects to Tacoma Community College (TCC), the Tacoma-Pierce County Chamber of Commerce, the Washington State Hospital Association (WSHA), and Pacific Lutheran University (PLU). All four are on this map.
MultiCare’s choices about what services to offer, where to expand, and whom to hire shape Pierce County’s healthcare and its job market.
Adjacent but excluded: MultiCare Foundations (EIN 91-1514257) is the giving arm. Mary Bridge Children’s Foundation (EIN 94-303-0039) raises money for one hospital. Rockwood Clinic in Spokane and Indigo Urgent Care are also MultiCare, but outside Pierce County or not power nodes.

1. Who they are

Legal name: MultiCare Health System. Also known as Tacoma General Hospital, Good Samaritan Hospital, Capital Medical Center, Mary Bridge Children’s Hospital, Allenmore Hospital, Covington Hospital, and Auburn Medical Center.
Entity type: 501(c)(3) public charity. Files IRS Form 990 (the federal tax-return form for nonprofits).
EIN: 91-1352172 (a tax ID number from the IRS).
Year formed: 1987.
NTEE code: E22 (Hospital, General). NAICS code: 622 (Hospitals). These are federal category codes.
Parent/child status: Central organization. Parent of MultiCare Foundations, Mary Bridge Children’s Foundation, and the hospital subsidiaries.
Governing law: Washington State nonprofit law. Federal tax-exempt status under IRS code 501(c)(3) since May 1991.
Headquarters: PO Box 5299, Tacoma, WA 98415; 315 Martin Luther King Jr Way, Tacoma, WA 98405.
Hospitals (9): MultiCare Tacoma General; MultiCare Good Samaritan (Puyallup); MultiCare Allenmore (Tacoma); MultiCare Auburn Medical Center; MultiCare Covington; MultiCare Capital Medical Center (Olympia); MultiCare Deaconess (Spokane); MultiCare Valley (Spokane); Mary Bridge Children’s Hospital (Tacoma).
Licensed beds: 1,743 adult + 152 pediatric = 1,895 total.

2. Their career and offices

CEO and President: William G. “Bill” Robertson. CEO since 2014. Retiring end of 2026. Pay in 2024: $7,786,801. Before MultiCare, he ran Adventist HealthCare in Maryland and Shawnee Mission Medical Center in Kansas. He has a BS in Accounting and an MBA.
Incoming CEO (Jan 1, 2027): Florence Chang. Current President since 2022. Joined MultiCare in 2006 as SVP/CIO. Became COO in 2012. Pay in 2024: $4,290,542.
Board Chair: John Wiborg. Unpaid board member.
Vice Chair: Deedra Walkey. Unpaid board member.
Board (10 people, all unpaid): John Wiborg (Chair), Deedra Walkey (Vice Chair), John Hall (Treasurer), Sally B. Leighton (Secretary), L. Dale Sowell, Janine Terrano, John Folsom, Rob R. Roth MD, Luke Xitco, Robert A. Yost.
Board members who are also map nodes: Dale Sowell, John Wiborg, Bill Robertson, Florence Chang, and Jason Thompson all appear elsewhere on this map.
Other top officers (2024 pay from IRS Form 990): James Lee (CFO/EVP Population Health, $1,234,642); Timothy W. Lynch (SVP/CAO Clinical Services, $915,039); Alex Jackson (SVP/CEO Inland NW & Yakima); Bradd Busick (SVP/CIO).

3. Where their power comes from

Market power: MultiCare is the largest community-based, locally governed health system in Washington. In 2024 it had $5.01 billion in revenue and 22,789 employees. It operates 9 hospitals with 1,895 beds. In 2024 it logged 84,327 admissions, 431,429 patient days, 75,990 surgeries, 9,704 births, 480,752 outpatient visits, and 612,092 ER visits. That gives it the dominant share of the hospital market in Pierce County.
Employment power: With 22,789 employees, MultiCare is the largest private employer in Pierce County. That comes from the IRS Form 990 and from MultiCare’s own claims.
Tax-exempt power: As a 501(c)(3), MultiCare does not pay property tax or sales tax. Donors can write off gifts. That is a big public subsidy.
Philanthropy and influence: MultiCare’s community fund gave 66 grants in 2024, totaling $10.8 million. This builds goodwill and softens public scrutiny.
Lobbying and policy: MultiCare belongs to WSHA (Washington State Hospital Association). CEO Bill Robertson was WSHA Board Chair from 2020 to 2021. MultiCare also lobbies the Pierce County Council on health policy.
Key facts:

Tax status: 501(c)(3) public charity, tax-exempt since May 1991.
Board size: 10 unpaid directors. Board seats overlap with TCC, the Chamber, WSHA, and PLU.
Government funding share: About 95.7% of revenue comes from Medicare and Medicaid (the federal health programs for seniors and low-income people). That is $4.795 billion of $5.01 billion.

1. Who they are

What is the exact dollar value of MultiCare’s property tax exemption in Pierce County? Requires Pierce County Assessor data on tax-exempt parcels owned by MultiCare.
What are MultiCare’s specific lobbying expenditures at the state and county level? Requires WA PDC L2 lobbyist filing search.

1. Who they are

Verdict: MultiCare Health System controls the dominant share of hospital healthcare delivery in Pierce County through market position (9 hospitals, 1,895 beds, $5B revenue, 22,789 employees) and institutional influence (WSHA board chair, Chamber/TCC/PLU board overlaps, $10.8M/yr in community grants). Its power derives from three reinforcing sources: (1) statutory tax exemption (501c3) providing fiscal subsidy; (2) near-total dependency on government healthcare reimbursement (~95.7% of revenue from Medicare/Medicaid), making it effectively a government-funded enterprise operating with private governance; (3) board overlaps with educational, business, and political institutions that create a web of mutual obligation. MultiCare got to this position through decades of acquisition (Auburn, Covington, Capital Medical Center, Deaconess, Valley) and organic growth, expanding from a Tacoma-centric hospital system to a statewide empire under Robertson’s leadership (2014-2026).
Conflicts-of-interest flags (defense counter-argument): The defense would argue MultiCare’s power is benign — it is a nonprofit providing essential healthcare services, its tax exemption is legally granted by IRS, and its community grants demonstrate genuine philanthropic intent. The ~95.7% government revenue share is a function of the U.S. healthcare financing system, not a power grab. board overlaps are standard nonprofit governance practice, not evidence of coordination. The CEO’s WSHA chair role is industry advocacy, not regulatory capture.
Analysis of alternatives : The opposing reading is that MultiCare’s market dominance and tax-exempt status represent a form of privatized governance — public money (~$4.8B/yr in government healthcare payments) flows through private governance structures with no direct public accountability. The 10-member board is self-perpetuating (no public elections, no government appointees), yet the organization’s financial viability depends on public funds. The community grants program could be interpreted as institutional capture — buying goodwill from organizations that might otherwise scrutinize MultiCare’s pricing, billing practices, or expansion plans.
Confidence: High — financial data sourced from IRS Form 990 (primary, reliability 0.9+); leadership and board data from MultiCare’s own newsroom and ProPublica 990 extractions (primary, reliability 0.8-0.95); market position claims cross-referenced between 990 program descriptions and audited financial statements.

Known facts: EIN 91-1669422; tax-exempt since January 1996; located at 1801 Dock St, Tacoma WA 98402; 2026 capital campaign underway; receives Tacoma Creates funding.

§0 why this entity is on the map
Museum of Glass is on this map because it is the lasting project of the Russell family. George F. Russell Jr. (1932–2025) co-founded and bankrolled the museum. He built it as an anchor for the Thea Foss Waterway redevelopment. The museum is now a flagship of Tacoma’s “Museum Row” cultural cluster.
Its 501(c)(3) tax status, its annual revenue of about $5 million, its capital expansion project, and its broad board ties make it a network node. It links Tacoma arts donors to waterfront redevelopment.
§1 who they are legally
FACT Museum of Glass is a registered 501(c)(3) charitable organization. Its federal tax ID number (EIN) is 91-1669422. Its tax exemption began in January 1996.
Source: www.museumofglass.org/press-release-archive (primary; reliability 0.95); projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/911669422 (primary; reliability 0.95); www.charitynavigator.org/ein/911669422 (primary; reliability 0.9)
FACT The museum sits at 1801 Dock Street, Tacoma, WA 98402. It opened in 2002 on a former Superfund site. Building the museum kicked off the Thea Foss Waterway cleanup and the surrounding museum district. Six museums now sit within walking distance.
Source: www.linkedin.com/company/museum-of-glass (secondary; reliability 0.85); www.museumofglass.org/george-russell (primary; reliability 0.95).
FACT The most recent IRS Form 990 (per ProPublica and Charity Navigator) shows the following. Contributions ranged from about $1.6 million to about $3.1 million in recent years. Program services brought in $1.3 million to $1.6 million. Investment income ranged from $17,000 to $296,000. Total annual revenue sits in the $3 million to $6 million range.
Source: projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/911669422 (primary; reliability 0.9).
FACT The Board of Trustees is chaired by Kenneth Farmer, Jr., M.D. He is the Principal of Ken Farmer Advisors, LLC and a retired U.S. Army Major General. The Vice Chair is Walt Riehl. The Secretary is Todd Gilman. He is SVP, Deputy General Counsel, and Secretary of TrueBlue, Inc. Other trustees include Barry Anton, Rex Bates, Jonah Bergman, Joanna Carey Cleveland (UPS), Mary Carstensen, Clemencia Castro-Woolery, Curtis Cox, Calvin Gasaway, Brent Heilesen, Ian MacNeil, Marc Mangel, Megan Mead, Altaf Merchant (Milgard Endowed Dean, UW Tacoma), Katelyn Smith, and others.
Source: museumofglass.org/board (primary; reliability 0.9).
§2 Power basis
FACT The museum runs a working Hot Shop. It is one of the largest and most active museum glass studios on the West Coast. That gives it cultural power. The museum curates national traveling shows, runs artist residencies, and shapes Tacoma’s identity as a glass-arts city. Tacoma is the birthplace of Dale Chihuly.
Source: www.linkedin.com/company/museum-of-glass (secondary; reliability 0.85); museumofglass.org/board (primary; reliability 0.9)
FACT The museum receives Tacoma Creates funding. Tacoma Creates is a voter-approved city fund for arts, culture, and science. The museum also runs a 2026 capital campaign for expansion. Its mix of donations and program-service revenue shows blended public and private support.
Source: www.museumofglass.org (primary; reliability 0.9); projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/911669422 (primary; reliability 0.9).
FACT George F. Russell Jr. (1933–2025) co-founded the museum with Phil Phibbs. He co-chaired the founding Board of Trustees with Jane Russell. The museum’s Hot Shop is named the “Jane Russell Hot Shop” in her memory after her early death.
Source: www.museumofglass.org/george-russell (primary; reliability 0.95).

The board cuts across many sectors.Who governsThe Board of Trustees governs the museum. The executive leadership runs daily operations. Derek Klein is listed as staff on LinkedIn.Who winsThe Russell family legacy is permanently anchored in Tacoma’s waterfront. Tacoma’s cultural tourism brand wins.
§7 who they are connected to
Museum of Glass is a cultural-anchor node. It bridges three things. First, the Russell family’s giving legacy (graph edge: russell-family → museum-of-glass, weight=4). Second, higher education. Altaf Merchant, the Milgard Dean at UW Tacoma, sits on the board. Joanna Carey Cleveland of the University of Puget Sound also sits on the board. Third, downtown Tacoma’s museum cluster, with six museums within walking distance. The museum sits on a cleaned-up Superfund site, making it a waterfront-redevelopment success story.

Case: INV-2026-002 · Profile: profiles/nash-cascadia.md
Entity ID: nash-cascadia · Type: organization · Domain: economic
Tier: tier3 · Rank: 101/163 · Composite power: 0.019
Graph description: Developer of Tehaleh (Bonney Lake / Pierce County). NASH Cascadia Verde, LLC is the project’s master developer; bi-directional PDC giving to both Tacoma-municipal and state-legislative races (R and D alike).
Known facts: 4,756-acre Tehaleh site (Pierce County UGA); 2011 acquisition from bankruptcy; vest-right Development Agreement (Ord. 2015-31s, 2018-90s); $85,050 in state-level contributions (2017–2022, transparencyusa.org); ~6,400 entitled homes.
Status: ✅ researched — 2026-09-19 — tier3-chunk6 · Last updated: 2026-09-19
Sources: 4/3 (minimum for tier3)

0. Why this person or group is on the map

NASH Cascadia Verde, LLC (NCV) is on the map for three reasons. First, it owns and entitles the 4,756-acre Tehaleh planned community in the Pierce County Urban Growth Area. That is the largest single private landholding on the county’s eastern plateau. Second, NCV gives money to both Democrats and Republicans in Pierce County Council, Tacoma city, and state legislature races. Its donor list includes Fey, Dammeier, Gildon, Stokesbary, Mello, Jinkins, O’Ban, and Chambers. That gives NCV standing across the political map.
Excluded but related:
Newland Communities — NASH’s co-developer / joint venture (JV) partner at Tehaleh (per Panattoni and NASH releases). NCV is the legal fee-simple owner and the named party to the Pierce County Development Agreement. So NCV is the profile, not Newland.
Brookfield Properties (Brookfield Residential Washington) — listed as the JV partner on NASH’s own marketing site. But Brookfield does not sign the County DA.
Panattoni Development — only entered via a separate Frederickson industrial parcel, not Tehaleh.
All three are routed to open questions and leads.

1. Who they are

Legal name: NASH CASCADIA VERDE, LLC (a Washington profit LLC; UBI 603-091-079 on Washington Secretary of State records).
Type: Washington Limited Liability Company. Status is “Active” per Washington Company Directory. Registered agent is Corporation Service Company, 300 Deschutes Way SW STE 208 MC-CSC1, Tumwater WA.
Date/place of formation: February 25, 2011 in Washington.
Tehaleh acquisition date: March 23, 2011, by direct purchase from the bankruptcy estate of Cascadia Development Corporation.
Registered office: 19001 Cascadia Blvd E, Bonney Lake WA 98391-9613 (MapQuest listing).
JV partner of record: Brookfield Properties (Brookfield Residential).
Trademark “TEHALEH” (Registration No. 4318141, Serial 85490794) registered December 2011 to NASH CASCADIA VERDE, LLC. It covers homeowner-association and online information services.
Brand: Tehaleh is a master-planned community. The name is Salish-derived. It means “the land above” or “highlands.” Grand opening was in 2012. NASH bills it as the best-selling single-family community in the Puget Sound region since opening.

3. Where their power comes from

Land-use veto power (decision-making): NCV owns 4,756 acres in fee-simple title. The land is zoned Employment-Based Planned Community (EBPC). The 2018 Phase 2 Development Agreement (Ordinance 2018-90s) vests development rights under state law (RCW) 36.70B.170–.210. The Pierce County Council must approve NCV’s Project Master Plan (under PCC 18A.75.080) to allow more than 6,400 entitled residential units plus a 419-acre employment center. NCV sets the pace, mix, and order of growth on the Bonney Lake plateau.
Market concentration (economic): NCV is the sole developer of record for Tehaleh. Its 2024 amendment (per the News Tribune) raised the Phase 2 dwelling-unit cap to 2,490 units (60% above the 2018 cap) before the new arterial road is finished. That means NCV can pull forward permit revenue and home-builder commitments on its own schedule.
Political influence (well-connected): NCV gave $85,050 in Washington state political contributions from 2017 to 2022 (Transparency USA). The donor roster is unusual. NCV gave to both parties. Pierce County Council members (Dammeier, Mello). Tacoma-area Democrats (Jinkins, Fey). Suburban Republicans (Gildon, Stokesbary, Chambers, O’Ban, Barkis). NCV also gave $25,000 in one donation to the Sumner-Bonney Lake Citizens for Schools committee (a school bond vehicle).
Brand/IP control: NCV owns the trademarked TEHALEH mark. That gives it exclusive rights to the community identity, signage, and HOA-services language tied to the brand.
Scoring overlap basis: graph edges (donated to Ryan Mello weight 4; donated to Amy Cruver weight 4 — Cruver is the graph’s state-legislative recipient; this matches transparencyusa.org data). Plus decision-making weight from the Development Agreement.

1. Who they are

Verdict: NASH Cascadia Verde, LLC is a tier-3 economic-and-decision-making node. Its power is concentrated in land-use vesting, not raw cash. The 2018 Phase 2 Development Agreement and the 2024 amendment give NCV de facto co-governance over the timing of thousands of dwelling units on Pierce County’s largest single private landholding. Politically, NCV hedges both parties. It gave to Dammeier and Mello alike. It bankrolled the Sumner-Bonney Lake schools political action committee (PAC). That shows NCV’s lobbying posture is issue-driven (school capacity, transportation vesting) rather than party-driven.
Conflicts-of-interest flags: (a) The 2024 amendment lets Phase 2 dwelling permits speed up before the planned new arterial is built. That pushes the cost of road capacity onto Pierce County taxpayers via concurrency requirements. NCV produced the very traffic study used to justify the cap raise. That is the classic self-dealing pattern. (b) NCV’s $25,000 to the school-bond vehicle in Sumner-Bonney Lake — the same district serving Tehaleh residents — creates a clear quid-pro-quo risk on school capacity and impact-fee decisions. (c) Brookfield Residential is named JV partner on NASH’s marketing site but does NOT sign the Pierce County DA. So it is worth asking if Brookfield holds economic interest without regulatory disclosure (UNVERIFIED).
Analysis of alternatives (investigative control document (ICD)-203 opposing view): NASH could be read as a national master-planned-community developer that competes on placemaking and sustainability branding. Its political donations could be read as normal development-industry engagement rather than capture. That reading is defensible only if donation patterns track industry peers (e.g., master-planned community competitors) and if the 2024 traffic-study amendment survives an independent peer review.
Confidence: Medium — four independent sources confirm who they are legally, donation patterns, and the Development Agreement; Brookfield JV interest is asserted by NASH’s own site but not corroborated by an independent Pierce County filing. The exact NASH ownership chain (parent LLC, members/managers) is not publicly disclosed in the records reviewed.

0. Why this person or group is on the map

The News Tribune is on the map because it is the main daily newspaper in Pierce County. It covers the county government, city politics, and the Port of Tacoma.
The paper can shape what people read and talk about. It can also endorse candidates in local elections. Those endorsements carry weight.
Not included: Tacoma Weekly (a smaller weekly paper), KNKX (public radio, listed separately), and The Olympian (covers Thurston County). They have fewer readers or a different focus.

1. Who they are

Name: The News Tribune. It is published by The McClatchy Company.
Type of business: A privately held newspaper. McClatchy is a Delaware corporation.
Who owns it: The News Tribune → McClatchy Media Company → Chatham Asset Management (a hedge fund in New Jersey). McClatchy went bankrupt on Feb 13, 2020. Chatham bought the company in a court-approved sale that closed Sep 4, 2020, for $312 million.
Old owners: McClatchy bought the News Tribune from the Baker family in 1986 for about $112 million. The Bakers had owned it since 1912.
Tax status: A private company. It pays taxes. It is not a nonprofit.
Where it is: 1950 South State Street, Tacoma, WA 98405.
When it started: 1880 (as The Tacoma Ledger). The current name came from a 1918 merger.

2. Their career and offices

Editor: Stephanie Pedersen.
CEO of McClatchy: Tony W. Hunter became CEO when Chatham bought the company in 2020. The current CEO is not confirmed.
Publisher: Not publicly listed.
Board: As a private company, McClatchy’s full board is not public. Two independent members were named at the 2020 sale.
Who shows up in our map: Stephanie Pedersen is the only News Tribune figure in our power map.

3. Where their power comes from

Power: The News Tribune holds cultural power. It is the main local news source.
What it controls: The paper picks which stories get top billing. It covers county government, city politics, and the Port of Tacoma. Its endorsements carry weight in local races.
Reach: Second-largest daily newspaper in Washington state (as of 2020).
Declining: Daily print copies fell from 130,000 in 2001 to about 30,945 in 2020. In March 2024, the paper cut back to three print days a week. Even with cuts, it is still the main paper of record.
Who owns it now: McClatchy → Chatham Asset Management (a hedge fund) since 2020.
Editorial line: Mainstream and centrist. It makes endorsements in local races.

The bottom line. The News Tribune shapes the local news story in Pierce County. But its power is fading. Daily print circulation dropped from 130,000 in 2001 to about 31,000 in 2020. Print dropped to 3 days a week. McClatchy has cut staff again and again (most recently a third of unionized workers in 2024). The paper can still set the agenda. It is still the only daily paper covering Pierce County government. But its ability to do deep investigative work has been gutted by hedge-fund ownership. FACT: The News Tribune is the newspaper of record for Pierce County. INFERENCE: With fewer reporters, the paper leans more on press releases and less on original reporting. That gap can help incumbents stay in power with less public scrutiny.
Conflicts-of-interest flags (defense counter-argument): A defense attorney could argue that the News Tribune’s endorsements are biased and shaped by corporate (Chatham) priorities. The 2024 layoffs mean less independent coverage. Hedge-fund ownership creates tension between profit and journalism.
Analysis of alternatives: The opposing reading: the News Tribune is still a credible, professional news outlet with dedicated journalists. Editorial endorsements go through a transparent process. Layoffs are an industry-wide response to digital change, not a plan to weaken watchdog reporting. The paper still does significant local reporting on Tacoma City Hall, Pierce County government, and the Port of Tacoma.
Confidence: Medium — Key facts (ownership, circulation, layoffs, editorial endorsements) are well-documented from multiple sources, but current financial data and full leadership roster are unverifiable due to private company status.

Northwest Seaport Alliance — Deep Profile
Case: INV-2026-002 · Profile: profiles/nwsa.md
Entity ID: nwsa · Type: organization · Domain: economic
Tier: tier3 · Rank: 131/163 · Composite power: 0.010
Graph description: Marine cargo operating partnership of the Ports of Seattle and Tacoma; manages container, breakbulk, auto and some bulk terminals.
Known facts: Formed Aug 4, 2015 under RCW 53.57; FMC-approved port development authority; CEO John Wolfe (also Port of Tacoma CEO); HQ Tacoma; co-chaired by home port commission presidents.
Status: ✅ researched — 2026-09-19 — tier3-chunk12-rescue
Sources: 4/3 (minimum for tier3)

0. Why this person or group is on the map

Inclusion rule: decision-making + economic. The Northwest Seaport Alliance (NWSA) is the only bi-county port-operating joint authority in the U.S. It runs the marine cargo terminals that drive Pierce County’s biggest private-sector employer cluster (logistics, longshore, drayage). It is also a Federal Maritime Commission–regulated body. Its actions affect every trade-dependent employer in the South Sound.
Adjacent but EXCLUDED candidates: Port of Seattle (parent). Port of Tacoma (parent, kept as a separate node port-tacoma). SSA Marine and Northwest Container Services, which lease terminals from NWSA. Individual shipping lines (Maersk, MSC, ONE, etc.).

1. Who they are

Exact legal name: The Northwest Seaport Alliance (NWSA).
Entity type: Port development authority under state law (RCW) 53.57 (Wash. Rev. Code, “Joint Port Authorities”). Federal Maritime Commission–approved operating agreement (FMC Agreement No. 201228).
Formation date: August 4, 2015, via an Interlocal Agreement between the Port of Seattle and the Port of Tacoma.
Governing law: Washington RCW 53.57; FMC oversight. Interlocal agreement effective 8/4/2015. Current Alliance Agreement effective 9/18/2023.
HQ: P.O. Box 2985, Tacoma, WA 98401-2985. Office space is also in Tacoma.
Parents: Jointly owned by Port of Seattle and Port of Tacoma as equal members. Each port keeps ownership of its own real estate and assets.
CEO: John Wolfe. He is also Port of Tacoma CEO. He was the first CEO when NWSA formed.
Charter/Bylaws: Third Amended PDA Charter (effective 9/18/2023). Sixth Amended Bylaws (signed 1/7/2025).
Governance body: “Managing Members” = the two 5-member port commissions acting together. The president of each home-port commission serves as co-chair of the NWSA Managing Members. They meet monthly, in public, on the first Tuesday. Meetings are streamed live.

3. Where their power comes from

Statutory authority: RCW 53.57 lets two ports form a port development authority. NWSA has joint operating power over marine cargo terminals. It can bind both ports on terminal leases, capital projects, and labor rules.
Market position: The combined gateway is the 6th-busiest U.S. container port by volume. It handles about $68 billion of waterborne trade with 175 trading partners (NWSA 2025 stats). 2024 international container volume: 3,340,733 TEUs (up 12.3% YoY). 2025: down 5.5% to 3.2M TEUs.
Economic leverage: NWSA operations support about 52,000 jobs statewide and about $14 billion in business output (2025 Community Attributes study).
Federal nexus: Subject to Federal Maritime Commission oversight (FMC Agreement No. 201228). It competes for federal INFRA and MEGA grants (e.g., Puget Sound Gateway Program Executive Committee — Marzano sits there).
Veto power: Each port commission (5 elected members) can block alliance actions through the Managing Members structure. It acts like a two-house check.

3. Where their power comes from

Every claim above is grounded in primary documents (NWSA official site, FMC filings, Port of Tacoma news releases, Wikipedia for general reference, News Tribune for revenue context).

1. Who they are

Verdict: The NWSA is a new kind of legal tool. It is the first North American inter-port operating authority. It pulls cargo-terminal decisions for two big U.S. ports into one 10-member Board. For Pierce County the effect is clear. 5 of 10 votes on every lease, capital project, and labor rule sit with Pierce County voters through their port commissioners. That makes the Port of Tacoma commission — especially its president, who co-chairs the NWSA — a structural lever on regional trade policy.
Conflicts-of-interest flags: Commissioner Dick Marzano (Port of Tacoma, Position #2) served six years as ILWU Local 23 president before his 1995 election. He sits on the Tacoma-Pierce County Economic Development Board and the WSDOT Puget Sound Gateway Program Executive Committee. Those overlap with NWSA interests.
Analysis of alternatives: The defense reading: NWSA is a transparent public body with audited financials and a two-house check. The critical reading: Pierce County holds 50% of votes on a body that drives billions in trade-dependent activity. The environmental and labor costs land in Tacoma Tideflats neighborhoods.
Confidence: High. Primary-source governance docs, NWSA newsroom, Port of Tacoma newsroom, and FMC filings all agree on formation, structure, and 2025 leadership.

Prosecuting Attorney’s Office — Deep Profile

Graph description: Elected county prosecutor’s office with criminal, civil, and family support divisions; ~263 FTE positions, $88.6M proposed budget.
Known facts: Led by elected Prosecuting Attorney Mary Robnett (since 2019). Three divisions: Criminal, Civil, Family Support. 263 total positions (197 in Criminal Division, 65%). RCW 36.27 governs.
Status: ✅ researched — 2026-09-19 — tier2-chunk1
Sources: 7/5 (minimum for tier2)

0. Why this person or group is on the map

Why included: The Pierce County Prosecuting Attorney’s Office is on this map because it holds a key legal office and makes major charging decisions. It is the only office that can bring felony charges anywhere in Pierce County. It also prosecutes misdemeanors outside city limits. And it represents every county office in civil lawsuits. State law (RCW 36.27.020) gives it this power. The office has about 263 full-time positions and an $88.6 million proposed budget for two years. The elected prosecutor has independent power under state law. She is not under the County Executive or Council. (sources #1, #2)
Adjacent but NOT included: Pierce County Public Defender’s Office (separate office, not on the map). Washington State Attorney General’s Office (state-level, helps on some cases under RCW 43.10). Tacoma City Attorney’s Office (handles city-only misdemeanors). These are nearby but not in the map at this level.

1. Who they are

Legal name: Pierce County Prosecuting Attorney’s Office
What kind of office: County government office led by an elected prosecutor. Created under state law RCW Chapter 36.27.
Governing law: RCW Chapter 36.27 covers the prosecutor. It sets who can serve (RCW 36.27.010: must be a lawyer in Washington and a U.S. citizen). It lists the duties (RCW 36.27.020). It lets the prosecutor hire deputies (RCW 36.27.040). It says the office must be at the county seat (RCW 36.27.070).
Location: 930 Tacoma Ave S, Rm 946, Tacoma, WA 98402 (source #3)
Federal tax ID (EIN): Not applicable — it is part of Pierce County, not a separate legal body.
Parent: Pierce County government
Current head: Mary Robnett, elected Prosecuting Attorney. Took office January 2019 (source #1).

3. Where their power comes from

State law power: RCW 36.27.020 sets the duties. The office must prosecute every criminal case in the county. It must represent the county in civil lawsuits. It must advise county officials. This gives the office a monopoly on felony prosecution in Pierce County.
Charging power: The office chooses which cases to charge. This lets it control what enters the criminal justice system. In 2024, it received 7,155 case referrals. About 54% of those were violent crimes (source #5).
Three divisions:

Criminal Division — handles all felony cases in Pierce County and all misdemeanors outside city limits. It has 197 full-time positions (65% of the total 263). It also runs therapeutic court programs (sources #4, #5).
Civil Division — represents county officials and departments in lawsuits. It supports civil commitment-forcing involuntary treatment under state law (source #4).
Family Support Division — protects children, establishes who the parents are, and enforces child support (source #4).


Budget: The proposed budget for 2024–2025 was $88.6 million (source #4). The office also faces $3.35 million in cuts. Twelve positions paid with federal COVID aid will end by 2026 (source #5).
Where the office reaches: All of Pierce County (about 920,000 people). Felonies county-wide. Misdemeanors only outside city limits (cities have their own prosecutors).
How the head is chosen: Prosecuting Attorney is an elected office. Terms are four years. Elections are non-partisan (no party listed on the ballot). Mary Robnett won in 2018 and took office in January 2019 (sources #1, #6).

3. Where their power comes from

5. How they touch government

County Council funding: The Pierce County Council approves the prosecutor’s budget. The Council approved the $88.6 million proposed budget for 2024–2025 (source #4).
Federal COVID aid: Twelve positions paid with American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA) money will end by 2026–2027. That saves about $3.35 million but cuts the Criminal Division by 6.5% (source #5).
Federal cases: The office works with federal prosecutors at WDWA (the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Washington) when cases cross federal and state lines.
Superior Court: The office prosecutes cases in Pierce County Superior Court.
Campaign finance filings: Mary Robnett filed to run for Pierce County Prosecutor in 2018. Her campaign raised $325,656.40 and ended with $10,928.80 in debt, per the state Public Disclosure Commission (PDC) (source #6).

County canvassing board: Under RCW 29A.60.160, the prosecuting attorney sits on the county canvassing board. This board checks election results.

Mary Robnett — elected Prosecuting Attorney. Before that, she was Chief Criminal Deputy in the same office (1994–2012). Then she worked in the Sexually Violent Predators unit at the Washington Attorney General’s Office. She spent 10 years in the Special Assault Unit. She is linked to the Sexual Assault Center of Pierce County (source #1).
Pierce County Council — approves the prosecutor’s budget.
Pierce County Superior Court — the prosecutor brings felony cases here.
Federal District Court (WDWA/Tacoma) — the prosecutor coordinates federal cases here.

1. Who they are

Verdict: The Pierce County Prosecuting Attorney’s Office has a monopoly on felony prosecution in the county. It also represents county government in all civil lawsuits. With 263 positions and an $88.6 million two-year budget, it is a major power center. Its charging choices shape criminal justice outcomes for about 920,000 residents. The office is independent of the County Executive and Council because the prosecutor is elected separately. But the Council still controls the budget. The end of ARPA funding (12 positions cut by 2026, 6.5% Criminal Division cut) is a current strain on the office.
Conflicts-of-interest flags: The prosecutor’s seat on the county canvassing board (RCW 29A.60.160) could mix election oversight with partisan interests, even though the office is non-partisan. The conflict with Keith Swank (map weight 3) needs more checking — UNVERIFIED from primary sources. Mary Robnett’s past work at the AG’s Office is a coordination tie, not a conflict.
Analysis of alternatives: The opposing reading is that the office is more limited than it looks. Charging decisions are bound by state law, evidence rules, and judges. The felony backlog (~1,800 cases) and flat staffing from 2000 to 2018 show the office is resource-limited, not powerful. Still, its monopoly on felony charging makes it structurally important.
Confidence: High — official county website, RCW statutes, PDC filings, and county budget documents provide strong primary-source grounding.

Former President Pro Tempore of the Senate (2023-2025) — first woman to hold the position. Elected 1992, 1998, 2004, 2010, 2016, 2022. Secured ~$500M in CDS and $5B+ in direct WA funding for FY2026.
Status: ✅ researched — 2026-09-19 — tier2-chunk8

0. Why this person or group is on the map

Inclusion rule: decision-making and from holding office. Murray is the senior U.S. Senator from Washington State. She serves as Vice Chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee. That committee is the most powerful funding committee in Congress. She controls Congressionally Directed Spending (CDS) for Washington State. That includes Pierce County projects.

She secured more than $121 million in CDS for WA projects in FY2026 alone. She also brought in more than $5 billion in direct state funding (source #1, #2).
Her former role as President Pro Tempore (2023–2025) placed her third in line for the U.S. presidency. That was the highest federal position held by anyone in this investigation’s scope.

Adjacent but EXCLUDED candidates: Sen. Maria Cantwell is Washington’s junior senator. She is on the map separately. Gov. Bob Ferguson handles state-level executive power. Rep. Emily Randall (D-6) handles district-level Pierce County representation.

1. Who they are

Legal name: Patricia Lynn Murray (née Johns) (source #2).
Born: October 11, 1950, in Bothell, Washington (source #2, #4).
Lives in: Washington State (specific city UNVERIFIED — public records do not list a home address, given her former President Pro Tempore status and security concerns).
Family: Husband Rob Murray (married 1972). Two children (source #2). Her father was a WWII veteran and Purple Heart recipient. He later developed MS. Her mother worked to support the family (source #1).
Education: B.A. in Physical Education from Washington State University, 1972 (source #2, #3).
Career before Senate: Preschool teacher at Shoreline Community College. Citizen lobbyist for environmental and education issues. Shoreline School Board (1985–1989). Washington State Senate, 1st District (1989–1993). She served as whip from 1990 to 1992 (source #2, #4).

3. Where their power comes from

Elected office: U.S. Senator from Washington (senior senator). She took office on January 3, 1993. This is her sixth term, won in 2022. Her next election is 2028 (source #2, #5).

Vice Chair, Senate Appropriations Committee (since January 3, 2025) (source #1, #2).
Former Chair, Senate Appropriations Committee (2023–2025) (source #1).

Senate Democratic leadership member since 2007 (source #1).

Former Chair, Senate Budget Committee (113th Congress). First female chair (source #1).
Former Chair, Senate HELP Committee (source #1).

Federal appropriations: She is Vice Chair (formerly Chair) of Appropriations. She co-controls all federal discretionary spending, about $1.7 trillion a year. She is Ranking Member of the Energy and Water Development Subcommittee (source #1, #6, #7).
Health, education, and labor: She sits on the HELP Committee. She shapes health care, education, and labor policy. As former Chair, she helped negotiate the No Child Left Behind rewrite, the 21st Century Cures Act, and COVID relief (source #1).
Budget: Senate Budget Committee member (source #6, #7).
Veterans’ affairs: Senate Veterans’ Affairs Committee member. As former Chair, she expanded women’s veterans’ benefits and caregiver support (source #1).
Child care and paid leave: A leading Senate advocate for child care and paid leave (source #1).


key facts:

Appointment and veto: She has Senate confirmation authority over executive appointments. She has no veto power. Her Appropriations role gives her an effective veto over funding for federal programs.

0. Why this person or group is on the map

The PCCLC is the Pierce County Central Labor Council, AFL-CIO. It is the main political body for organized labor in Pierce County. It represents 114 affiliated unions and more than 44,000 workers.
PCCLC is on the map for three reasons. (1) It exercises political power through endorsements and PAC (political action committee) spending. (2) Its officers sit on other boards: Nathe Lawver on the Greater Tacoma Community Foundation (GTCF) board, Alice Phillips on the Clover Park Board of Trustees. (3) Its endorsement process is driven by delegates, so it can pull labor votes behind a single candidate.
Not on the map separately: the Washington State Labor Council (state parent body), Pierce County Labor Community Services Agency (the nonprofit arm), and each individual member union.

1. Who they are

Full name: Pierce County Central Labor Council, AFL-CIO (PCCLC).
Type: A 501(c)(5) labor organization. It is a chartered local labor council of the AFL-CIO.
Parent: The AFL-CIO (national federation) and the Washington State Labor Council (state body).
Founded: 1890 as the Tacoma Trades Council. The AFL chartered it as the Tacoma Central Labor Council. It later became the Pierce County Central Labor Council.
Address: 3049 South 36th St., Suite 201, Tacoma, WA 98409.
Governing law: The National Labor Relations Act (NLRA) and the AFL-CIO constitution.

3. Where their power comes from

Endorsement power: PCCLC endorsements come from “union delegates representing more than 44,000 working people across Pierce County after a democratic process.” Endorsements bring volunteer capacity, get-out-the-vote (GOTV) work, and PAC support. In 2025, PCCLC endorsed candidates for State Senate District 26 (Deborah Krishnadasan), Tacoma Mayor (Anders Ibsen), Tacoma City Council (Latasha Palmer, Silong Chhun, Joe Bushnell), Puyallup City Council, and multiple school board races.
PAC spending: PCCLC has a political action committee that files with the state PDC (Public Disclosure Commission). Older records show $24,650 in 2014, $45,550 in 2016, and $32,150 in 2018. Current cycle spending is not confirmed.
Candidate training: PCCLC recruits and trains labor-aligned candidates for local office. Its endorsement pipeline feeds into the Pierce County Democratic Party.
Solidarity work: PCCLC calls itself “a democratic hub where unions come together to organize, advocate, educate, and build solidarity across industries and communities.”

4. Power in numbers

|| Who benefits | Endorsed candidates get volunteers, GOTV, and PAC support. The 44,000+ union members get labor movement coordination. Member unions get political leverage through collective action. | #1, #3, #5 |

|| Who governs | Delegate-driven governance. Monthly delegate meetings at 7 to 9 PM. Endorsements and resolutions are voted on by delegates. The executive board runs things between meetings. | #1, #5 |
|| Who wins | Endorsed candidates gain labor vote share. PCCLC backed the Pierce Transit ballot measure to expand transit. It named May 2026 Hispanic Heritage Month by resolution. | #3, #5 |
5. How they touch government

Campaign finance and PAC: PCCLC files political expenditure reports with the state PDC. Older totals were $24,650 (2014), $45,550 (2016), and $32,150 (2018). Current cycle totals are not yet confirmed.
Endorsements: PCCLC endorses candidates for local, county, and state races. 2025 endorsements include State Senate District 26, Tacoma Mayor, Tacoma City Council, Puyallup City Council, Gig Harbor City Council, Steilacoom Mayor, and several school board races.
Ballot measures: PCCLC endorsed the Pierce Transit ballot measure to expand transit service.
Lobbying: As a 501(c)(5), PCCLC can do political activity and lobbying beyond what a 501(c)(3) can do. Specific lobbying registrations are not confirmed.
Government contracts: None identified. Not confirmed.

6. Other seats they hold

Alice Phillips — President. IBEW Local 483 member (retired Business Manager, longest-serving, 30 years). Sits on the Clover Park Board of Trustees. 40 years of labor movement experience. First woman in several IBEW Local 483 leadership roles.
Nathe Lawver — Secretary-Treasurer. Also Executive Secretary of the Pierce County Building and Construction Trades Council AFL-CIO. Sits on the GTCF board At-Large. Connects PCCLC to philanthropy and the building trades.
Christina Hall — Vice President.
Executive Board: Rick Hertzog, Jade Monroe, Brenda Wiest, Brent Wagar, Amber Roulst, Jared Ross, Cindy Richardson, Floyd David Dugan, Patti Dailey-Shives.
Patti Dailey-Shives — Executive Board member. Also sits on the Pierce County Labor Community Services Agency board.
Member unions: ILWU Local 23, Teamsters, plus 112 other affiliated unions.
Pierce County Democrats: Aligned. PCCLC endorsements usually match Democratic Party candidates.
Ryan Mello: Endorsed. Now the Pierce County Executive.

12. Bottom line

The bottom line. PCCLC is the central voice of organized labor in Pierce County. It has 114 affiliated unions and more than 44,000 members. It can move labor votes through endorsements and PAC spending.
Why it matters. Endorsements bring volunteers and money. The PCCLC pipeline feeds into the Pierce County Democratic Party. It endorsed Ryan Mello, who is now County Executive. Its leaders also sit on the GTCF board and the Clover Park school board.
The counter-view. Union density has dropped nationally. The PAC totals of $24,000 to $46,000 (2014 to 2018) are small compared to independent-expenditure campaigns. The 44,000-member number may overstate how many members are politically active.
Why PCCLC still matters. The delegate-driven endorsement process and the dense board overlaps give PCCLC real structural influence. Its leaders connect labor, philanthropy (GTCF), and education (Clover Park).
Confidence: Medium. The AFL-CIO website provides strong primary sourcing for the council’s structure and leaders. PAC totals come from a secondary source (the Freedom Foundation). Current-cycle PDC data was not pulled.

0. Why this person or group is on the map

Why we added Phil Fortunato: He holds office. He is the sitting State Senator for Washington’s 31st Legislative District. The district covers southeast King County and northeast Pierce County. It includes Auburn, Bonney Lake, Buckley, Carbonado, Edgewood, Milton, South Prairie, Sumner, and Wilkeson. The district covers a large slice of Pierce County. He sits on four Senate committees: Law and Justice, Transportation, State Government/Tribal Affairs/Elections, and Business/Trade/Economic Development. His district overlaps with many Pierce County cities and towns.
Other people we did not add: Drew Stokesbary (R-31, House Position 1) and Josh Penner (R-31, House Position 2) are his district-mates. They are added in this investigation separately. Pam Roach, a former D31 Senator who came before Fortunato, is excluded because she no longer holds office.

1. Who they are

Legal name: Philip D. Fortunato (Source 1).
Common name: Phil Fortunato.
Birth: Born 1953 or 1954 (Source 1). Birthplace not verified.
Home: Auburn, Washington (Source 1, 2, 5).
Family: Wife Suzanne Fortunato (married 42 or more years per Source 5). Five children. Three of the children served in the U.S. Marine Corps (Source 1, 5).
Education: Rutgers University, New Brunswick (Source 1).
Job: Owner and founder of Eco-3. Eco-3 is an erosion and stormwater management company based in Kent, WA. He has been a contractor for 30 or more years. He started his first business at age 18 (Source 2, 4, 5). He is a recognized expert on the federal Clean Water Act, which controls water pollution. He was the first person in Washington certified as a CESCL instructor. CESCL stands for Certified Erosion and Sediment Control Lead. The Washington State Department of Ecology certifies them (Source 4).
Group memberships: Knights of Columbus, Buckley Eagles, Sons of Italy, Washington Arms Collectors, the National Rifle Association (NRA), Renton Fish and Game Club, and Black Diamond Gun Club (Source 5). He is a past president and founding director of the Pacific Northwest chapter of the International Erosion Control Association, or IECA (Source 4).

3. Where their power comes from

Elected office: Washington State Senator, 31st Legislative District, since January 7, 2017. Current term ends January 11, 2027. He is running for re-election in the November 2026 general election. He advanced from the August 4, 2026 primary with 53.9% of the vote against Tamara Stramel (D), who got 46.0% (Source 2). Before that, he served in the Washington House of Representatives, 47th District, from January 11, 1999 to January 8, 2001 (Source 1).
Committees (2025–2026 session): Law and Justice; Transportation; State Government, Tribal Affairs and Elections; Business, Trade and Economic Development. He also serves on joint committees: Joint Committee on Veterans’ and Military Affairs; Horse Racing Commission; Capitol Campus Design Advisory Committee; Election Administration and Certification Board; Puget Sound Partnership Ecosystem Coordination Board; Financial Education Public-Private Partnership; and School Safety Summit (Source 3).
Past statewide campaigns: He ran for Governor of Washington in 2020. He finished 6th in the primary with 4.0% (99,265 votes) (Source 1, 2). He ran for Insurance Commissioner in 2024. He lost the general election to Patricia Kuderer (D), 43.3% to 56.6% (Source 2).
Budget power: Fortunato is in the minority party. He does not control a budget on his own. He takes part in budget talks through his committee seats.
Jurisdiction: 31st Legislative District — Auburn, Bonney Lake, Buckley, Carbonado, Edgewood, Milton, South Prairie, Sumner, Wilkeson (Source 5).

1. Who they are

Verdict: Fortunato’s power comes from his long tenure as State Senator for the 31st District and his wide committee portfolio (Law and Justice, Transportation, State Government/Elections, Business/Economic Development). He does well at the district level (consistently 55 to 60% in his district) but does not win statewide races. He lost the Insurance Commissioner race by 13 points and placed 6th in the gubernatorial primary. His business, Eco-3, sits at the meeting point of his private commercial work and his legislative role overseeing construction, environmental rules, and economic development.
Conflicts of interest: Eco-3, Fortunato’s erosion control company, works in a field directly regulated by the state he helps govern. His seats on the Business, Trade and Economic Development committee and the Transportation committee overlap with his business in construction-related environmental compliance. His CESCL training certification from the Washington State Department of Ecology is a state-recognized business relationship. His NRA and gun club memberships signal an ideological match that may shape his work on the Law and Justice committee.
The other view: Fortunato is a back-bench minority party senator with limited real power. The Republican caucus holds only 19 of 49 Senate seats. His repeated statewide runs (Governor, Insurance Commissioner) have failed. His influence is confined to his conservative district. His wide committee list may reflect a lack of seniority-based specialization rather than strong influence. His company is a small enterprise, not a major contractor.
Confidence: High — many primary sources (the WA Legislature, the PDC, the WA Department of Ecology, the Senate Republican Caucus, and certified WA Secretary of State results) confirm the key claims. The SRCC bio note that he was “elected to the House but appointed to the Senate before sworn in” is a small biographical wrinkle, but it stays consistent across sources.
