Graph description: Pierce County (WA) Economic Development Department — a division of Pierce County government under the County Executive. Housed at 950 Pacific Ave., Suite 720, Tacoma. Oversees business development, loan programs, tourism, Lodging Tax Advisory Committee, Tourism Promotion Area Commission, Arts Commission, and the 1 Percent for the Arts program.
Known facts: Long-serving Director Betty Nokes Capestany (now Betty Baublits) led 2018–2026; she moved to EDB Director of Investor Relations April 2026. Tom Pierson (Tacoma-Pierce County Chamber President & CEO) was appointed Acting Director while a permanent replacement is recruited.
Status: ✅ researched — 2026-09-19 — tier3-chunk13-rescue · Last updated: 2026-09-19
Sources: 4/3 (minimum for tier3)

0. Why this person or group is on the map

Inclusion rule (decision-making + well-connected): This department sits inside Pierce County government’s executive branch. The County Executive oversees it (per the 2026 job posting). It runs loan funds, tourism money, and the 1% for-Art program. It staffs three advisory bodies: the Lodging Tax Advisory Committee, the Tourism Promotion Area Commission, and the Arts Commission. It is a boundary-spanning unit. It is governmental in budget and reporting line. But it works like a quasi-quango with the EDB and the Tacoma-Pierce County Chamber.
Excluded but related:
EDB (Economic Development Board for Tacoma-Pierce County) is a separate nonprofit. Now led by Bruce Kendall (transitioning to Meredith Neal). It is adjacent.
Tacoma-Pierce County Chamber is a separate 501(c)(6). Its President and CEO Tom Pierson is also Acting Director of this department in 2026. That is a network overlap, not a duplicate.
City of Tacoma Community & Economic Development is a separate municipal department.
Port of Tacoma is a separate special-purpose district. It is not part of this department.

1. Who they are

Exact legal name: Pierce County Economic Development Department (also “Economic Development Department, Pierce County” in board rosters).
Entity type: Government department / executive-branch agency (Pierce County, Washington).
Governing law: Pierce County Charter and state law (RCW) 36 (counties). The 1% for-Art program follows RCW 36.32.235 et seq. as applied county-wide.
Tax ID number (EIN) / registration: N/A. It operates under the Pierce County government EIN.
Parent / subsidiaries: Sub-unit of the Pierce County Executive’s office. It works with the Economic Development Corporation of Pierce County. Its board has reps from Tacoma, Port of Tacoma, MBDA, Pierce County Central Labor, Lakewood, Puyallup, and private industry.
Address: 950 Pacific Ave., Suite 720, Tacoma, WA 98402. Phone (253) 798-6150.
Director classification (per official spec): “Director of Economic Development.” Salary band is $140,105 to $189,216 a year (GovernmentJobs posting 26-00251, opened 3/13/2026, closing 4/17/2026).

3. Where their power comes from

Statutory authority: County-government department. It has no independent taxing power. It spends money from the County General Fund and pass-through lodging-tax receipts.
Decision-making authority: Oversees business-development programs. Runs loan funds. Manages tourism funding and the Lodging Tax Advisory Committee. Manages the Tourism Promotion Area Commission and the Arts Commission (including 1% for-Art grants).
Power-domain overlap basis (scoring framework):
Government — 0.5 weight: executive-branch department.
Economic (Workforce + Capital) — 0.4 weight: loan programs and tourism money.
Cultural/Arts — 0.2 weight: Arts Commission and 1% for-Art grants.
Tourism/Lodging — 0.2 weight: Tourism Promotion Area Commission staff.

1. Who they are

Verdict: The Pierce County Economic Development Department is a small executive-branch unit. It does not set tax rates. It does not hold electoral power. But it runs staff work behind county tourism, Arts Commission grants, 1% for-Art money, and business loans. The 2026 leadership change (Capestany → Pierson-as-acting) made it a bridge between the county executive, the Chamber, and the EDB.
Conflicts-of-interest flags:
Tom Pierson’s dual role is a clear COI. He is Chamber CEO and Acting Director of a county department that contracts with the Chamber. The County Executive’s office flagged it when the dual role was set up.
Lodging-tax committee seats can be captured by the hotel industry. The 1% for-Art money can be steered toward development-friendly public art.
Analysis of alternatives : A skeptical reading says the department is mostly a “marketing and ribbons-cutting” operation. Its loan fund is small compared with private capital. The opposing reading (favored) is that the coordination function is the real product. The department exists to staff and fund the convenings between the EDB, the Chamber, the City of Tacoma, and the Port.
Confidence: Medium — director salary band, mission, address, programs, and staff roster confirmed by Pierce County primary sources; the Pierson acting-director appointment confirmed via LinkedIn and the 2026 GovernmentJobs posting; 2026 acting status is the current state.

Pierce County Library System — Deep Profile
Case: INV-2026-002 · Profile: profiles/pierce-county-library.md
Entity ID: pierce-county-library · Type: organization · Domain: government
Tier: tier3 · Rank: 110/163 · Composite power: 0.016
Graph description: Pierce County Library System (PCLS) — Pierce County Rural Library District, a junior taxing library district operating under RCW 27.12. Formed by ballot measure November 7, 1944; began operating January 2, 1946. 20 library locations serving ~680,000 residents in unincorporated Pierce County and 15 cities/towns that have annexed for library service. Property-tax funded. Governed by five-member Board of Trustees appointed by the Pierce County Executive.
Known facts: 20 library branches; serves 580,835 (per 2016 stats) / ~680,000 (per 2026 trustee application); circulation 6.9–7.4M items/year; budget $31.9M (2016 reference); 5-member Board of Trustees (5-year terms, appointed by County Executive); current Executive Director Gretchen Caserotti; Chair Neesha Patel, Vice-Chair Ryan Wheaton, trustees Pam Duncan, Pat Jenkins, Tono Sablan. 2018 levy (Levy Sustainability Fund) passed.
Status: ✅ researched — 2026-09-19 — tier3-chunk7
Sources: 7/3 (minimum for tier3)

0. Why this person or group is on the map

Why it’s on the map: Pierce County Library System is included as a junior taxing library district under state law (RCW) 27.12. It raises property taxes over a defined service area. That area covers unincorporated Pierce County plus 15 annexed cities and towns. It runs a multi-million-dollar annual budget. It serves about 680,000 residents through 20 branches. The graph edge pierce-county-library → county-council, taxing, weight=3 shows its tie to the County Council.
Neighbors NOT added to the map: Tacoma Public Library is a separate system inside the City of Tacoma. Puyallup Public Library serves the City of Puyallup. Both are separate and excluded. The Washington State Library coordinates statewide but is outside this profile’s scope.

1. Who they are

Exact legal name: Pierce County Library System (PCLS). Formally the Pierce County Rural Library District.
Entity type: Washington junior taxing library district. A government entity under RCW 27.12 (Library Districts). It is separate from municipal libraries (Tacoma Public Library, Puyallup Public Library) and from the Pierce County government’s general-purpose departments.
Formed: Established by ballot measure passed by voters in unincorporated Pierce County on November 7, 1944. Began operating January 2, 1946. Opened seven station branches in its first year.
Service area: Unincorporated Pierce County plus 15 cities and towns that have annexed for library service. Excludes the City of Tacoma (which has its own library system) and the City of Puyallup (which has its own library system).
Branches: 20 library locations. They include:
Administrative Center and Library, 3005 112th St. E., Tacoma / Summit-Waller area.
Anderson Island.
Bonney Lake.
Buckley.
DuPont.
Eatonville.
Fife.
Gig Harbor / Peninsula.
Graham.
Key Center.
Lakewood.
Milton / Edgewood.
Orting.
Parkland / Spanaway.
South Hill.
Steilacoom.
Summit (Tacoma).
Sumner.
Tillicum (Lakewood).
University Place.
Busiest: Gig Harbor, South Hill, Lakewood, University Place, Parkland / Spanaway.
Board of Trustees: Five members. They are appointed by the Pierce County Executive (current executive: Ryan Mello). Five-year terms, with the option of up to two consecutive terms. Meetings are the second Wednesday of each month at 3:30 pm at the Administrative Center.
Executive leadership: Executive Director Gretchen Caserotti (one of five directors in PCLS history; predecessors: Marion Cromwell, Carolyn Else, Neel Parikh, Georgia Lomax).
Collection: About 1.2 million items. Circulation about 6.9 to 7.4 million items a year. 334,362 members (2016). About 2.2 million in-person visits a year (2016). Website had about 3.5 million visitors (2016).

3. Where their power comes from

Power from the law: As a library district under RCW 27.12, PCLS can levy property taxes (subject to Washington’s 1% cap, also called the levy lid). It can issue bonds with voter approval. It can sign contracts, hire staff, buy property, and provide library services inside its boundaries.
Taxing power: Property taxes are the main funding source per PCLS’s own statement: “Property taxes are the primary source of funding for the Library System.” The 2018 levy (Levy Sustainability Fund) was approved by voters. It builds savings for long-term stability. Per the 2026 Budget Book, Washington’s 1% property tax cap limits annual revenue growth. In 2025, General Fund expenses exceeded revenues. The budget had to be balanced carefully.
Budget control (2026 figures): Total budget about $31.9M (2016 reference figure from Wikipedia, citing Washington Public Library Statistical Report 2016). The 2026 budget summaries show several separate funds:
General Fund operating budget.
Capital Improvement Fund.
Election Fund.
Debt Service Fund.
Levy Sustainability Fund.
Property and Facility Fund.
The specific 2026 total is UNVERIFIED — budget summary PDFs show fund-level detail but the total was not added up in this pass.
How it touches government:
Board picks: The Pierce County Executive (Ryan Mello since Jan 2025) appoints all five trustees. They are subject to County Council confirmation (UNVERIFIED — confirmation rules vary by RCW).
Annual budget approval: The Board adopts the annual budget. It is subject to public hearings and final public-hearing rules per RCW 27.12.
State Auditor oversight: Subject to SAO accountability audits (UNVERIFIED — specific 2024 / 2025 SAO report not pulled).

1. Who they are

Verdict: PCLS runs a multi-million-dollar public library district. It delivers lending, programming, and community-space services to about 680,000 Pierce County residents across 20 branches. Its power is mostly fiscal and service-delivery. It levies property taxes (subject to the 1% cap). It adopts annual budgets. It runs a regional library system. The five-member Board of Trustees — appointed by the Pierce County Executive — sets policy direction. PCLS is limited by Washington’s property-tax cap (RCW 84.55). It is also limited by voter approval rules for levy lid lifts and bonds. In 2025, General Fund expenses exceeded revenues, creating fiscal pressure. The 2018 Levy Sustainability Fund was set up to manage that constraint.
Conflicts of interest: Several Board members have direct professional ties to Pierce County or its affiliated groups. Ryan Wheaton is the Chief Planning Officer at Pierce Transit (a separate Pierce County agency). Pam Duncan chairs the Tacoma-Pierce County Affordable Housing Consortium. She chairs the Washington State Community Action Partnership. She also sits on the Washington Low-Income Housing Alliance. Tono Sablan sits on the Greater Tacoma Community Foundation Board. These cross-board memberships create alignment of interests in funding and policy choices. No specific conflict has been alleged. Trustee picks by the County Executive (Ryan Mello since Jan 2025) create political accountability but no formal confirmation gate is documented — UNVERIFIED.
The other reading: An opposing reading: PCLS is a service-delivery group with limited political power. Its choices affect library patrons but not the broader political economy of Pierce County. It is one of several library systems in the county (Tacoma Public Library, Puyallup Public Library). It competes for patron attention. The 2025 General Fund shortfall suggests fiscal pressure. That pressure may force service cuts or a levy lid lift (which would need voter approval). The trustee-appointment setup by the County Executive makes PCLS open to political capture. It also brings democratic accountability through executive elections. The board’s makeup (multiple members with nonprofit and social-service backgrounds rather than business or government) tilts its policy stance toward equity, literacy, and community services.
Confidence: High. The official PCLS website, primary board packets, and Wikipedia confirm formation history, governance setup, financial scale, and current board makeup. The 2016 budget figure ($31.9M) is from the 2016 Washington Public Library Statistical Report referenced in Wikipedia. The current 2026 budget total is UNVERIFIED at the aggregate level. Fund-level detail is available in the 2026 Budget Summaries PDF.

Pierce Dems — Deep Profile
Case: INV-2026-002 · Profile: profiles/pierce-dem.md

Graph description: Pierce County Democratic Party (PCDCC) — county-wide umbrella organization; endorses candidates, trains campaigns, controls PCO network
Known facts: Controls 4 council seats + Exec; 3 state Senate seats; Union coalition (HDCC, WEA, UFCW, IBEW); 17 graph edges; campaign finance violation settlement $38,520 (2017)
Status: ✅ researched — 2026-09-19 — tier1-chunk3
Sources: 11/10 (minimum for tier1)

0. Why this person or group is on the map

Inclusion rule — power and decision-making. The Pierce County Democratic Central Committee (PCDCC) is on this map as the county Democratic Party. It backs candidates with endorsements, trains campaigns, fills empty elected offices, and runs the Precinct Committee Officer (PCO) network.
The PCDCC is a statutory party organization under Washington law. It has formal powers to endorse candidates and to fill vacancies in partisan offices.
Important caveat: Party nodes are an artifact of how the graph works. They collect all the “member” edges from legislators who share that party label. That makes them look more connected than they really are. The PCDCC’s 17 graph edges mostly come from Democratic officials — that is party affiliation, not a chain of command. The composite score is capped at 0.12 to correct for this.
Adjacent but excluded: The Washington State Democratic Central Committee (WSDCC) is the parent. King County Democrats is a peer. Pierce County Republicans is the counterpart. LD-level Democratic groups (2nd, 25th, 26th, 27th, 28th, 29th, 31st) are sub-units, not separate map nodes.

1. Who they are

Legal name: Pierce County Democratic Central Committee (PCDCC).
Common name: Pierce County Democrats / Pierce Dems.
Entity type: Political committee registered with the Washington State Public Disclosure Commission (PDC). Not a 501(c)(3) or 501(c)(6). Governed by state law (RCW 42.17A) and the WSDCC charter.
EIN or PDC registration: Not verified. Political committees usually file with the PDC, not the IRS.
Parent and sub-units: Under the Washington State Democratic Central Committee. Legislative District (LD) Democratic groups (2nd, 25th, 26th, 27th, 28th, 29th, 31st) work under the PCDCC.
Ownership chain: Democratic National Committee → Washington State Democratic Central Committee → Pierce County Democratic Central Committee → LD Democratic organizations.
Governing law: RCW 42.17A (Public Disclosure Commission); WSDCC charter; PCDCC bylaws.
Address: PO Box (per the official site). Office: 3049 S 36th St, Tacoma, WA 98409 — same building as PCCLC.

2. Their career and offices

2025–2026 Officers (from the official website):

Previous Chair: Kathy Orlando. The move from Orlando to Hyke is not verified in detail.
Board overlaps: Jenn Marie Strickling-Severns serves as both PCDCC Vice Chair of Communications and Chair of the 25th LD Democrats. That is a confirmed overlap inside the party. No other officer shows up as a separate map entity.
Full central committee: Includes all elected and appointed PCOs plus dues-paying members. PCO lists live in Google Sheets on the website. The exact PCO count is not verified.

3. Where their power comes from

Power held. The PCDCC has statutory party power under Washington law. It endorses candidates, fills vacancies in partisan Democratic offices, organizes the PCO network, and coordinates campaigns across Pierce County.
Its real power is mediated and limited. The PCDCC does not tell elected Democrats how to vote. It can endorse, train, and organize volunteers. The graph’s cap of 0.12 composite reflects this: 17 edges inflate the count, but actual decision-making power is weaker than that suggests.
Political domain: The main power levers are candidate endorsements and PCO organizing. Endorsements matter in primary elections — they signal support and direct volunteer and donor energy.
Government domain overlap. The PCDCC’s endorsed Democrats hold many offices: Ryan Mello (Pierce County Executive), Laurie Jinkins (Speaker of the WA House, 27th LD), Melanie Morgan (29th LD), Yasmin Trudeau (27th LD Senate), T’wina Nobles (28th LD Senate), Steve Conway (29th LD Senate), Emily Randall (6th LD Senate, now in Congress), Marilyn Strickland (10th CD), Maria Cantwell (US Senate), Patty Murray (US Senate). The graph’s 10 “member” edges are party affiliation, not a command structure.
Labor domain overlap. The Pierce County Central Labor Council (PCCLC) is “aligned” with the PCDCC, weight 4. PCCLC’s 2026 endorsements overlap with PCDCC picks. The Washington Education Association (WEA) PAC is also “aligned,” weight 3. The union coalition — House Democratic Campaign Committee (HDCC), WEA, United Food and Commercial Workers (UFCW), and International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers (IBEW) — provides volunteers and money.
Economic domain overlap. MultiCare Health donated to the PCDCC, weight 3. The Puyallup Tribe donated, weight 3. Those are institutional donors in the economic space.
Key facts:

Who is endorsed? The PCDCC backed Amanda Cuthbert and Davida Haygood for Puyallup School Board in 2023. The 2026 endorsement process is on the website.
PAC spending? Not verified. The PCDCC files C3 (contributions) and C4 (expenditures) reports with the PDC. A 2017 complaint showed $63,643 in unreported contributions and $90,357 in unreported spending over three years.
Party machinery. The PCDCC controls the PCO network, runs the PCO handbook, and coordinates with LD organizations.
Candidate training? The website links to candidate resources. The Chamber’s Candidate Academy trains candidates across party lines — adjacent to PCDCC, but not PCDCC-run.

4. Their money

Budget: Not verified for the current year. The 2017 complaint showed about $30K to $45K per year in contributions and spending for 2015–2017. Current numbers require pulling PDC C3/C4 reports.
Funding sources: Membership dues ($27 regular, $15 hardship); ActBlue donations; institutional donations (MultiCare, Puyallup Tribe); possible labor coalition contributions.
Government funding: None. Political parties do not get government money.
Tax status: Political committee. Not tax-exempt under 501(c)(3) or (c)(6). Donations are not tax-deductible.

Levy or bond history: Not applicable.

5. How they touch government

Campaign donations. The PCDCC gives to endorsed candidates. The graph shows donations to Ryan Mello (weight 5), Rosie Ayala (weight 4), and Jani Hitchen (weight 4). These are PDC C3 filings. Exact amounts need PDC lookup.
Campaign finance violations. In August 2017, the Washington State Attorney General filed a complaint against the PCDCC. The PCDCC settled for $38,520 ($31,780 fine with $15,890 suspended for four years). Violations included $63,643 in late-reported contributions (92 reports, up to 179 days late), $90,357 in late-reported spending (16 reports, up to 171 days late), and $34,791 in unreported debts. The PCDCC did not file any 2017 reports until after the AGO opened its investigation. This is a confirmed, legally documented controversy.
Lobbying. Political parties do not register as lobbyists. The PCDCC’s advocacy is electoral, not legislative lobbying.
Contracts or grants. None. Political parties do not receive government contracts.
Regulation. The PCDCC is regulated by the Washington Public Disclosure Commission (PDC) and RCW 42.17A. The 2017 AGO action is the main documented regulatory interaction.
Vacancy fills. Under Washington law, the PCDCC can fill vacancies in partisan Democratic offices. When a Democratic officeholder resigns, the PCDCC’s PCOs pick a replacement. That is a real governmental power. Specific recent fills are not verified.

1. Who they are

PDC C3/C4 reports: Retrieve the PCDCC’s current campaign finance reports from the WA PDC database. What is the current annual budget? How much does it donate to candidates? What are the exact contribution amounts from MultiCare, Puyallup Tribe, and other institutional donors?
2017 AGO settlement compliance: Has the PCDCC committed any additional violations since the 2017 settlement? The $15,890 suspended fine was contingent on no additional violations for four years (through ~2021). Check PDC enforcement actions post-2017.
Endorsement process: How does the PCDCC endorsement process work? Who votes? What threshold is required? Are there contested endorsements? Retrieve PCDCC bylaws from the website.
Vacancy fills: Has the PCDCC filled any elected office vacancies in recent years? When a Democratic officeholder resigns, the PCDCC PCOs nominate a replacement. This is a significant governmental power — trace specific instances.
PCO count: How many PCOs does the PCDCC currently have? Count from the Google Sheets linked on the website (source #2). This quantifies the PCDCC’s grassroots organizing capacity.
PCDCC–PCCLC relationship: The PCDCC and PCCLC share an office address (3049 S 36th St, source #8, #11). Is this a formal partnership? Does the PCDCC rent from the PCCLC? This physical co-location suggests a deep organizational tie.
Centrality artifact analysis: The graph caps party nodes at 0.12 composite. Verify this cap by comparing the PCDCC’s actual decision-making power (endorsement + vacancy fill + PCO organization) against its 16-edge who they are connected to. Should the cap be lower?

1. Who they are

Verdict: The PCDCC controls the Democratic Party endorsement machinery in Pierce County — it endorses candidates, organizes PCOs, fills vacancies in partisan offices, and coordinates with aligned labor organizations (PCCLC, WEA PAC). However, its actual power is weaker than its who they are connected to suggests: the 10 ‘member’ edges from Democratic elected officials represent party affiliation, not directed control. The PCDCC cannot tell Laurie Jinkins (Speaker of the House) or Maria Cantwell (US Senator) how to vote. The graph’s cap at 0.12 composite correctly accounts for this centrality artifact. The PCDCC’s real power levers are: (1) endorsement signals in primary elections, (2) PCO organization and volunteer capacity, (3) vacancy-fill authority, and (4) coordination with the labor coalition.
Conflicts-of-interest flags (defense counter-argument anticipated): (1) The 2017 campaign finance violations ($63K unreported contributions, $90K unreported expenditures, source #5) demonstrate a history of financial opacity. (2) Institutional donations from MultiCare (a health system) and Puyallup Tribe (a sovereign economic entity) to a political party that endorses candidates who oversee health policy and tribal relations create potential conflict-of-interest concerns. (3) Sharing an office address with PCCLC (source #8, #11) suggests an organizational melding that may compromise the PCDCC’s independence from labor. Defense counter: (1) The 2017 violations were settled and the PCDCC paid $38,520 in penalties; the suspended fine created a compliance incentive. (2) Institutional donations to political parties are legal and common; they are publicly reported through PDC filings. (3) Co-location with PCCLC is an efficiency measure, not evidence of improper control — many political organizations share office space with aligned groups.
Analysis of alternatives : The opposing reading is that the PCDCC is a volunteer-run political organization with limited actual power — its endorsements are often rubber-stamps for incumbents, its PCO network is incomplete, and its financial resources are modest (~$30K–$45K annually based on 2015–2017 data, source #5). Under this reading, the PCDCC’s rank 15/163 is entirely a centrality artifact and should be much lower. The counter to this: the PCDCC’s vacancy-fill authority is a genuine governmental power (when a Democratic officeholder resigns, the PCDCC chooses the replacement), and its endorsement signal materially affects primary outcomes in a Democratic-leaning county.
Confidence: Medium. Primary sources confirm the PCDCC’s existence, officer roster, and endorsement activity (official website, reliability 0.8). The 2017 AGO complaint is confirmed by the Attorney General’s own press release (reliability 0.95). However, current financial data (budget, donation amounts, expenditure totals) is UNVERIFIED — requires PDC C3/C4 retrieval. The 10 ‘member’ edges are confirmed by public party affiliation records but overstate the PCDCC’s actual power over those officials. The centrality-artifact caveat is well-supported by the graph structure.

Known facts: Chair: Dave McMullan (re-elected); VP: Connie Coleman-Lacadie; Treasurer: David Patrick; total contributions (non-exempt committee): $437,656; exempt committee: $195,634 (2024 cycle)

0. Why this person or group is on the map

The Pierce County Republican Party (PCRP) is on this map as a key hub in the power graph. The investigation framework caps its composite power at 0.12. It earned its place because it is well-connected and has strong name recognition. The party endorses candidates, channels donor money, trains campaigns, and links elected Republicans to each other and to the state party.
Its endorsement process and donor network make it a hub, even though the party itself does not hold direct government power.
The Washington State Republican Party (WAGOP) is the parent. It is not a separate graph node. The Pierce County Democrats are a parallel node. Individual Republican officials are separate person nodes.

1. Who they are

Full legal name: Pierce County Republican Party (PCRP). Also known as “Pierce County Republican Central Committee.”
Type: Political party organization. It is registered with the state campaign-finance agency (PDC) as two committees:

Pierce County Republican Party Exempt (PDC committee ID: 15410) — federal/exempt funds.
Pierce County Republican Party Non-Exempt (PDC committee ID: 15541) — state/non-exempt funds.


Governing law: State law (RCW) 29A.80 for political parties. WA PDC rules. WAGOP bylaws. PCRP bylaws.
Federal tax ID (EIN): Not publicly listed. Address: 10209 Bridgeport Way SW, c-1, Lakewood, WA 98499.
Parent group: Part of the Washington State Republican Party (WAGOP). WAGOP Chair: Jim Walsh (State Rep, 19th LD). PCRP is in WAGOP Region 7 with Thurston County.
Website: piercegop.org

Verdict: The Pierce County Republican Party is a hub in the power graph. It links Republican officials, donors, and candidates in Pierce County. The party itself holds no office, so its direct government power is zero. But its endorsement, donor channeling, and training roles give it real indirect political power. Its ~$633K combined 2024 budget is small compared to some candidate war chests, but it acts as a coordinating body. The graph caps its composite power at 0.12, which fits its role as a conduit rather than a top power-holder.
Conflicts-of-interest flags (defense counter-argument anticipated): A defense lawyer would say PCRP is a normal political party doing standard democratic work: endorsing, fundraising, organizing. The Puyallup Tribe donation is unusual in a Democratic-leaning county, but tribal donations to both parties are common and legal. The counter: money flowing through the party can hide the real source of influence.
Analysis of alternatives : The opposing view: PCRP is a weak party in a county that has trended Democratic (Pierce County voted for Biden in 2020 and Murray/Cantwell consistently). Graph description: Pierce County Public Transportation Benefit Area Corporation (Pierce Transit) — primary public transit operator in Pierce County; bus, vanpool, paratransit; governed by 10-member elected Board of Commissioners; sales-tax funded
Known facts: Founded 1979; commenced operations Jan 1, 1980; 2025 budget $367M; 29 routes, 174 buses; 7.83M annual ridership (2025); sales tax 0.6% (proposed increase to 0.9% on Nov 2026 ballot)
Status: ✅ researched — 2026-09-19 — tier1-chunk4
Sources: 12/10 (minimum for tier1)

0. Why this person or group is on the map

Inclusion rule: Pierce Transit is on this map on the grounds of “from holding office,” “decision-making,” and “well-connected.” It is the main public transit operator in Pierce County. It controls a $367 million annual budget. It runs the county’s bus and paratransit service.

Its Board of Commissioners is made up of elected officials from Tacoma, Pierce County, Lakewood, Puyallup, and other cities. That creates direct board overlaps with municipal governments. Pierce Transit has its own sales tax. The current rate is 0.6 percent. A proposal would raise it to 0.9 percent. That is direct taxing power over all purchases in the Public Transportation Benefit Area (PTBA).

Adjacent but EXCLUDED candidates: Sound Transit is a separate regional transit agency (mapped as sound-transit). Community Transit is in Snohomish County, outside the boundary. King County Metro is also outside the boundary. The Pierce Transit Workers’ Union, ATU Local 758, has a non-voting seat on the board. It is not on the map as a separate node.

1. Who they are

Exact legal name: Pierce County Public Transportation Benefit Area Corporation (also called “Pierce Transit”)
Entity type: Government — municipal corporation (Public Transportation Benefit Area, PTBA)
Governing law: state law RCW 36.57A (Public Transportation Benefit Areas). Pierce Transit was formed under Chapter 36.57A of the Revised Code of Washington.
tax ID number (EIN) and registration: UNVERIFIED. Pierce Transit is a government municipal corporation. Its EIN is not publicly listed in easily accessible sources.
Parent and subsidiaries: None. It is an independent municipal corporation.
Founded: November 6, 1979. Voters approved a 0.3 percent sales tax to fund the PTBA. Service began January 1, 1980. The agency adopted the name “Pierce Transit” in June 1980.
Headquarters: 3701 96th Street Southwest, Lakewood, WA 98498.

2. Their career and offices

3. Where their power comes from

Statutory authority: RCW 36.57A lets PTBAs levy sales tax (with voter approval), run transit service, contract with other agencies, and own and operate property. Pierce Transit runs fixed-route bus, dial-a-ride (SHUTTLE paratransit), vanpool, and rideshare services.
Taxing authority: Pierce Transit currently levies a 0.6 percent local sales tax within the PTBA. The last increase, from 0.3 to 0.6 percent, was approved by voters in 2002. A November 3, 2026 ballot measure (Resolution 2026-006) would raise the rate to 0.9 percent. That is a 0.3 percentage-point increase (3 cents on a $10 purchase). If approved, it would fund a 47 percent boost in service and bring in about $64 million a year.
Market share: Pierce Transit is the main (near-monopoly) public transit provider in Pierce County. It runs 29 routes and 174 buses. Weekday ridership averages about 29,700 (Q2 2026). Annual ridership was 7,833,600 in 2025.
Regulatory capture: Limited. Pierce Transit must follow FTA rules and WSDOT oversight. It needs voter approval for tax increases.
Domain overlaps: Government (transit authority and taxing power), economic (transportation infrastructure that supports commerce), and political (board members are elected officials who campaign on transit positions).

Sales tax rate: 0.6 percent. This is the lowest rate among similar-sized transit agencies. The last voter-approved increase was in 2002.
Financial health: Pierce Transit has healthy reserves. It carries no debt. The budget is balanced. Expenses are expected to outpace revenue as early as 2027 due to inflation.
Tax status: Pierce Transit is a government municipal corporation. It is not a tax-exempt nonprofit. It is a taxing authority.
Property holdings: The headquarters is at 3701 96th St SW, Lakewood. Pierce Transit also owns transit centers, park-and-ride lots, and bus bases. Specific assessed values are UNVERIFIED.
Levy and bond history: Pierce Transit has no property-tax levy authority. Revenue comes from a sales tax approved by voters. Voters approved a 0.3 percent rate in 1979. They raised it to 0.6 percent in 2002. A 2026 ballot measure would raise it to 0.9 percent.

5. How they touch government

Tacoma City Council (tacoma-city-council): Three board members (Walker, Diaz, Hines) are Tacoma council members. The City of Tacoma holds 3 of the 9 voting board seats. That is the largest single-city share.
Sound Transit (sound-transit): Pierce Transit contracts with Sound Transit to operate regional bus service. That contract is worth $60.9 million a year. Pierce Transit also operates the Hilltop light rail extension for Sound Transit under FTA requirements.
Jake Fey (jake-fey): Washington State Representative. He appears in the graph as transit_funding (weight 5). State legislative appropriations for transit move through WSDOT grants.
FTA (Federal Transit Administration): The FTA funds capital projects like bus purchases and facility upgrades. Pierce Transit must follow FTA requirements for the Hilltop extension.
Campaign donations: Pierce Transit does not make campaign donations. It is a government entity. Board members may donate in their personal capacity. See their individual profiles.

1. Who they are

PDC lobbying expenditures: Pierce Transit’s state lobbying spending was not verified in this pass. PDC L2 filings are needed.
Property holdings valuation: Headquarters, transit centers, and park-and-ride lots have not had their assessed values pulled from the county assessor.
Contract recipients: The largest vendor contracts are unknown. The $367 million budget includes major procurement. Pierce Transit board meeting minutes need to be checked for contract awards.
2026 ballot measure outcome: The November 3, 2026 sales tax increase (0.6% to 0.9%) awaits the voters’ decision. The result will shape Pierce Transit’s power going forward.
ATU Local 758 influence: The non-voting labor seat is a formal channel for union influence. The question is how ATU 758’s political activity intersects with board members’ campaigns.

1. Who they are

Verdict: Pierce Transit controls the county’s main public transportation system. It has a $367 million annual budget and sales tax authority. Its power flows through a board of elected officials. That creates direct board overlaps with Tacoma, Pierce County, Lakewood, Puyallup, and other cities. The CEO runs day-to-day operations. The proposed 2026 ballot measure (0.6% to 0.9% sales tax) is a major expansion of its taxing power. If passed, it would generate about $64 million a year and fund a 47 percent service increase. The agency’s finances are stable (no debt, balanced budget, healthy reserves). But inflation could push it into a structural deficit by 2027 without the tax increase.
Conflicts-of-interest flags (defense counter-argument anticipated): A defense attorney would note that three of nine voting board members are from Tacoma (Walker, Diaz, Hines). That could skew service and investment toward Tacoma at the expense of other Pierce County communities. The ATU 758 non-voting seat creates a formal labor-management board overlap. That could shape labor contract talks. The counter: board makeup reflects population (Taco is the largest city). The labor seat is non-voting.
Analysis of alternatives : The opposing reading is that Pierce Transit’s power is limited by its dependence on voters. It cannot raise taxes without voter approval. The 2026 measure may fail, as transit ballot measures are not guaranteed passage. Its $367 million budget is large but small compared to the County’s $3.5 billion biennial budget or the City of Tacoma’s $4.7 billion biennial budget. Under that reading, Pierce Transit is a service-delivery organization with limited independent political power. That would place it below its graph rank of 18/163.

0. Why this person or group is on the map

Why PLU is on the map: Pacific Lutheran University (PLU) is on the map for three reasons. First, its president, Allan Belton, is a board-overlap node in the graph. Second, PLU co-signed the February 2024 Partnership for Health Innovation with MultiCare and WSU. Third, PLU controls land use and workforce training in central Pierce County (Parkland). It now hosts a WSU medical-school satellite on campus.
Who is NOT on the map: The WSU Elson S. Floyd College of Medicine is excluded as the parent of record. PLU is the host partner. Pacific Lutheran Theological Seminary in Berkeley, California is excluded. It is a separate campus. Concordia University Wisconsin is excluded. It is a different ELCA school. Open questions and leads are listed below.

1. Who they are

Legal name: Pacific Lutheran University, Inc. (a Washington nonprofit corporation).
Entity type: 501(c)(3) private university. A 501(c)(3) is a tax-exempt nonprofit under U.S. tax law. It is affiliated with the Evangelical Lutheran Church in America (ELCA). It is a tax-exempt nonprofit. It is governed under state law RCW 24.03 (Washington Nonprofit Corporation Act) and Title 28B RCW (Higher Education).
Parent and subsidiaries: No parent company. PLU Foundation, Inc. is a separate fundraising arm. PLU Tacoma is the main campus. It is in Parkland, an unincorporated part of Pierce County. The mailing address is Tacoma, WA 98447.
Founding: Started in 1890 by Rev. Bjug Harstad. The 14th president, L. Allan Belton, was picked by the Board of Regents. He started April 3, 2019. He had been acting president since 2017.
Provost: Joanna Gregson. Faculty: 340. Students: 2,754 (2,366 undergraduate and 388 postgraduate). Campus: 156 acres in suburban Parkland, WA.
Endowment: $123.1 million (Wikipedia infobox, FY24 figure).

3. Where their power comes from

Decision-making power (institutional): PLU’s Board of Regents sets tuition. It approves the academic-medical partnership. It governs the on-campus MultiCare Medical Center that opens in 2025–26. That gives the Board veto and approval power over any clinical site on its 156-acre campus.
Cultural influence (symbolic): PLU is the largest ELCA university on the West Coast. It is the only private four-year school in central Pierce County. That makes it a key name for Lutheran employers, regional hospital systems, and Tacoma-area civic boards.
Workforce-pipeline power: Through the Partnership for Health Innovation, PLU channels MultiCare hiring, WSU medical-school rotations, and NIH and HRSA grant applications. HRSA is the Health Resources and Services Administration, a federal agency. NIH is the National Institutes of Health. In short, PLU sits at a key point for the Pierce County healthcare workforce.
How the score covers different domains: board overlap (Belton graph weight 5), partnership (MultiCare graph weight 5), and reputational role as the only private university in unincorporated Pierce County.

The bottom line: PLU is a tier-3 institutional node whose power is indirect but structural. PLU does not control budgets the size of MultiCare’s. But it controls who trains where in central Pierce County. And it controls whose medical school sits on its campus. The February 2024 Partnership for Health Innovation turned PLU from a passive reputational asset into an active decision-making node in the regional healthcare economy.
Conflicts-of-interest flags: (a) The MultiCare Medical Center at PLU is funded and run by MultiCare. But it sits on land controlled by an ELCA board. Questions of mission drift and the scope of reproductive and health services are foreseeable. (b) Allan Belton’s role straddles academic governance and a quasi-development partnership. The PLU Board of Regents’ conflict-of-interest policy should be reviewed.
Analysis of alternatives: PLU could also be seen as a small liberal-arts school whose national rankings have slipped. US News has moved PLU out of top-tier regional categories in recent years. Its inclusion in this map rests almost entirely on the Belton board overlap and the MultiCare partnership. It is not based on raw institutional scale. If the MultiCare partnership is renegotiated or unwound, PLU’s graph weight drops sharply.

Verdict: Pierce Military & Business Alliance has tier-3 institutional power as a coalition of 28+ companies. It pools private donations for JBLM-support programs. George “W. George” Cargill has been president for 20+ years. He also leads multiple defense nonprofits (AUSA, AFA, MOAA, Navy League, Madigan Foundation). FACT: PMBA has been a 501(c)(3) tax-exempt public charity since September 2003. EIN: 38-3675245. It files IRS Form 990-EZ. FACT: Revenue jumps around — $92K (2019) → $15K (2020) → $88K (2023) → $29K (2024). This matches a pass-through donation model rather than a stable operating budget. FACT: Cargill’s 2024 JBLM Civilian Hall of Fame induction is a formal federal recognition of PMBA’s standing. INFERENCE: PMBA’s power comes mainly from its network, not its budget. Conflicts-of-interest flags (defense counter-argument): A defense would say PMBA is a transparent 501(c)(3) with public IRS filings, an unpaid volunteer board, and formal Army recognition. The coalition model spreads decisions across 28+ companies. The gap between the self-reported “$145,000 annually” Facebook figure and IRS-booked revenue is best explained by donations passing through in the same year (so they do not show up as “revenue”). No executive is paid.
Analysis of alternatives (investigative control document (ICD)-203): Another reading is that PMBA’s tier-3 score (0.006) reflects a small-budget institution whose weight is amplified by Cargill’s many nonprofit roles (AUSA, AFA, MOAA, Navy League, Madigan Foundation) and the symbolic value of the JBLM Hall of Fame. PMBA is a soft-power broker, not a hard-power actor. Its ability to move resources depends on member companies giving each year. Its annual donation cycle shows how engaged local companies are with JBLM.
Confidence: Medium — IRS Form 990-EZ filings (ProPublica) give primary-source financials and personnel with high reliability. Facebook and LinkedIn are self-reported and less reliable. JBLM Civilian Hall of Fame news is a primary military source. The $145K annual donation figure was NOT confirmed against IRS filings (likely a pass-through total, not booked revenue).

Graph description: Public port district under RCW 53; major container terminal; governed by 5 elected commissioners; operates via NWSA with Port of Seattle

Status: ✅ researched — 2026-09-19 — tier1-chunk2

0. Why this person or group is on the map

Port of Tacoma is on the map because it holds power through office, makes big decisions, and drives the local economy. It is a public port district under state law (RCW) Title 53. It works as an independent city-like government with elected commissioners. It runs container terminals, industrial property, and rail-truck interchanges. Through the Northwest Seaport Alliance (NWSA), it shares control of one of the largest container ports in North America. Its commissioners are elected county-wide, which gives it direct democratic legitimacy. Its board members also sit on the Chamber of Commerce and the Economic Development Board (EDB). It hires ILWU Local 23 longshore workers.
Groups not profiled here. Port of Seattle — separate port in King County, but connected through NWSA. NWSA is profiled as its own node (nwsa) — it is a Port Development Authority (PDA), not a port district. The Washington Public Ports Association is a trade group, not a power node. Foss Waterway Development Authority is a subsidiary.

1. Who they are

Exact legal name: Port of Tacoma [Source #1, #2]
Entity type: Independent city-like government and special purpose district [Source #1]
Governing law: Title 53 of the Revised Code of Washington (RCW 53) — including:
RCW 53.08: Powers of port districts
RCW 53.12: Commissioner elections
RCW 53.35: Budgets (legal budget rules)
RCW 53.36: Finances (general-obligation debt)
RCW 53.40: Revenue bonds and warrants
RCW 53.57: Port development authority (the basis for NWSA)
[Source #1, #3]
Tax ID (EIN) or registration: UNVERIFIED — port districts are government bodies, not IRS 501(c)(3) filers.
Parent and subsidiaries: No parent company. Port of Tacoma is one of two equal members of the Northwest Seaport Alliance (NWSA), a Port Development Authority formed under an RCW 53 change in 2015. [Source #4, #5]
Ownership chain: Public body — owned by Pierce County citizens through elected commissioners.
Designation: Special purpose district under Washington law [Source #1]

2. Their career and offices

Executive Director: Eric Johnson — joined Port of Tacoma as executive director in 2019. He runs the port. Before that, he was Executive Director of Washington Public Ports Association. He is from Pierce County. He earned a BA in Biology and Political Science from Pacific Lutheran University. He also earned an MPA (Master of Public Administration) from the University of Washington. It focused on environmental policy and natural resources. He sits on the boards of the Tacoma-Pierce County Chamber of Commerce. He also sits on the Economic Development Board for Tacoma-Pierce County (EDB). That includes the EDB Executive Committee. [Source #6]
Chief Financial and Administrative Officer: Erin Galeno — runs finance, accounting, contracts, purchasing, and security. She joined the Port in 2009. Before that, she spent 23 years at Weyerhaeuser. Her last role was Director of Internal Audit. She is a licensed CPA. She has a BA from the University of Puget Sound. She also has an Executive Leadership certificate from Seattle University. She sits on the Advisory Board at UW Tacoma. [Source #6]
Chief External Strategy Officer: Alisa Praskovich — runs Real Estate and Economic Development, Government Affairs, and Communications. Before this, she was Vice President of Sustainability at Crowley. She was also a White House Ocean Policy Advisor. She is a retired Coast Guard Commander. She has a BA in Biology from Eckerd College. She also has an MS in Marine Affairs from UW. [Source #6]
Chief Human Resources Officer: Vanessa Audett — joined in 2025. She came from the City of Federal Way, where she was HR Director. Before that, she worked for the City of SeaTac and UtilX Corporation. She holds SHRM-SCP and SPHR certifications. These are human-resources credentials. [Source #6]
Chief Information Officer: Martyn Adamson — named the first CIO in 2025. He has been at the Port since 2003. He has a BS in Computing from Edinburgh Napier University. [Source #6]

Dick Marzano — Position #2, current term Jan 2026-Dec 2029; first elected 1995; Commission President; former ILWU Local 23 longshore worker (52 years) and 6-year Local 23 president; past president of the Washington Public Ports Association; sits on the Tacoma-Pierce County EDB and the Puget Sound Gateway Program Executive Committee [Source #8]

3. Where their power comes from

Legal authority: RCW 53.08 gives port districts broad powers. They can buy and run terminals, build industrial sites, levy taxes, issue bonds, set rates, and manage real estate. The Port of Tacoma uses these powers on the Tacoma Tideflats — one of the largest industrial waterfronts on the West Coast. [Source #3]
Economic engine: Through NWSA, the Port co-runs cargo operations that handled nearly $68 billion in waterborne trade with 175 trading partners in 2025. NWSA facilities support over 52,000 jobs and $14 billion in business output for Washington state. [Source #11]
Taxing authority: Port districts can levy property taxes under RCW 53.36 and 53.40. The graph shows a property-tax-levy edge with the County Council (weight 5). The Port’s 2025 budget includes the legal budget and tax levy adopted Nov 19, 2024. [Source #1, #4]
Land-use power: The Port controls industrial land use on the Tideflats — zoning, leasing, and environmental permits. The graph edge to Communities for a Healthy Bay (oversees, weight 4) points to environmental review work. [graph]
Key facts:
Offices and authority: 5 elected commissioners plus an appointed executive director; independent city-like government [Source #1]
Budget: 2025 budget adopted Nov 19, 2024; includes a 2024 staffing budget of $45.8 million ($12M salaried + $17.8M hourly + benefits) [Source #4]
Average salary: $129,469 (excluding the Executive Director) [Source #4]
Powers: The Commission hires the executive director, sets policy, and approves major spending [Source #1]
Jurisdictions: Port district covers Pierce County; commissioners are elected at-large countywide [Source #1]

1. Who they are

Open questions:
What is the exact Port of Tacoma property-tax rate, and how much does it raise each year? Needs Port budget detail and Pierce County Assessor data.
What are the PDC campaign-finance filings for each commissioner? Who are their donors?
What is the Port’s total acreage and assessed value of Tideflats property? Needs Port real estate records.
How is NWSA revenue split between Port of Tacoma and Port of Seattle? What is the exact formula?
What is the GTH Gov Affairs lobbying relationship? What issues are lobbied?
What environmental enforcement actions or violations has the Port faced? Needs EPA records.
What is the link between Commissioner Marzano’s ILWU history and labor talks at the Port? Possible conflict of interest?
How does JT Wilcox’s background as former state legislator (House Minority Leader) shape the Port’s legislative strategy?
What is the Port’s total outstanding bond debt and debt-service load?

1. Who they are

Verdict: Port of Tacoma controls one of the largest container-port complexes on the U.S. West Coast. Its power comes from five elected commissioners, elected at-large countywide. It also comes from an appointed executive director. All work under RCW Title 53 as an independent city-like government. Its power rests on four sources. (1) Legal power over port operations, real estate, and taxation. This is under RCW 53.08, 53.36, and 53.40. (2) Economic scale. Through NWSA, the Port moves $68B in waterborne trade, supports 52,000+ jobs, and generates $14B in state business output. (3) Property-tax levy authority. The Port is one of the few Pierce County bodies that can tax property directly. (4) Board overlaps. The ED sits on Chamber and EDB boards. The CFO came from Weyerhaeuser, where she worked 23 years. Commissioner Marzano is a former ILWU Local 23 president. Commissioner Wilcox is a former state House Minority Leader. The NWSA structure splits governance with Port of Seattle. It creates both shared power and potential conflict over resources.
Conflicts of interest (defense view): The defense would say port operations are open. Commissioners are elected. Meetings are public under the Open Public Meetings Act. Budgets are published. NWSA is a rational regional model, not a power grab. Marzano’s ILWU background gives labor a voice in port governance. That is democratic representation, not conflict. Property-tax levies are set by law and reviewed through commissioner elections. The Port’s economic contribution ($14B output, 52K jobs) supports its tax authority.
Counter-reading: Port of Tacoma could be seen as unaccountable economic governance — an independent city-like body with taxing power that is not under Pierce County government. At-large elections mean commissioners answer to all ~900K county residents, most of whom have no direct stake in Tideflats operations. The ILWU-Marzano link creates a structural labor bias. The NWSA structure means Tacoma’s port revenue is shared with Seattle. The mix of former legislators (Wilcox), labor leaders (Marzano), and corporate alumni (Galeno/Weyerhaeuser) on Port governance creates an insider network that may resist outside scrutiny.
Confidence: High. Governance structure, commissioner identities, and legal framework all come from Port of Tacoma’s official website and RCW. They are primary sources rated 0.9 to 0.95. NWSA financial data comes from the NWSA annual report. It is a primary source rated 0.9. Budget data comes from official Port budget documents. It is a primary source rated 0.95. Salary, exact levy rates, and PDC filings remain UNVERIFIED.

PMG controls a large share of the regional magazine-ad channel. Pierce County businesses use it to reach top decision-makers. 0. Why this person or group is on the map

Puget Sound Energy (PSE) is the largest power and gas company in Washington. It is on this map because it serves Pierce County and most of the Puget Sound region. It holds power through three things: a state-granted monopoly, the rates it charges, and the lawmakers it talks to.
It has over 1.24 million electric customers and 881,000 gas customers across 8 or more counties. About 425,000 of those live in Pierce County.
PSE’s profits go to five big foreign pension funds. The state Utilities and Transportation Commission (UTC) sets its rates.

1. Who they are

Full legal name: Puget Sound Energy, Inc.
Type of company: A private power and gas company. It is the main operating arm of Puget Energy, a Washington holding company.
the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) filing: CIK 81100; File No. 1-4393. PSE files 10-K reports with the SEC even though it is privately held.
Parent company: Puget Energy owns PSE. All operations run through PSE.
Who owns Puget Energy: Five foreign pension funds. They are: AIMCo (Alberta Investment Management Corporation, 13.6%), BCI (British Columbia Investment Management Corporation, 20.9%), OMERS (Ontario municipal employees pension, 23.9%), PGGM (Dutch pension fund, 10%), and CPPIB (Canada Pension Plan Investment Board, with a continuing stake). Macquarie Infrastructure Partners sold its 44% stake in 2018.
Who regulates them: The Washington Utilities and Transportation Commission (UTC) under state law RCW 80. PSE is a state-licensed monopoly.
Founded: 1997. A merger of Puget Sound Power & Light Company and Washington Energy Company.
Headquarters: Bellevue, Washington.

3. Where their power comes from

Statutory monopoly: The state lets PSE be the only gas and electric utility in most of its 6,000 square mile area. About 1.2 million electric customers and 900,000 gas customers must buy from PSE if they want gas or electric service in its territory.
Big revenue and assets: PSE made $4.86 billion in revenue in 2024. It had $754 million in operating income in 2025 and $602 million in 2024. Electric utility revenue was $3.89 billion in 2025 and $3.33 billion in 2024.
Workforce: PSE has 3,257 employees. It is a Fortune 1000 company, ranked #710.
Power plants and lines: PSE owns or controls 6,524 megawatts of power capacity. About 3,339 megawatts of that is PSE-owned. It has a 25% stake in the Colstrip Generating Station in Montana, which is about 700 megawatts.
No government grants: PSE does not get government grants. Its rates are set by the UTC. PSE must follow state laws like the Clean Energy Transformation Act (CETA).

3. Where their power comes from

5. How they touch government

Rate cases: PSE files rate cases with the UTC. On Feb 15, 2024, PSE filed a case asking for 6.7% electric and 19.0% gas hikes for 2025, and 9.3% electric and 2.1% gas hikes for 2026. A 2026 case (UTC Docket 260005) asks for 29% electric and 20% gas hikes over three years. The state Attorney General says the hikes are too high.
Lobbyists: PSE has five registered lobbyists in 2025. They lobby at the state capitol on energy bills.
Campaign donations: No data found in this research. Would need a search of state PDC records.
No government contracts: PSE does not get grants. It earns money by charging customers. The UTC approves the rates.
Land-use cases: PSE needs local permits for big projects. The Energize Eastside power line (started 2020) was controversial and needed local approval.

6. Other seats they hold

PSE’s full board of directors is private. CEO Mary Kipp’s other board roles are not confirmed.

Puyallup School District — Deep Profile
Case: INV-2026-002 · Profile: profiles/puyallup-schools.md
Entity ID: puyallup-schools · Type: organization · Domain: institutional
Tier: tier3 · Rank: 117/163 · Composite power: 0.014
Graph description: Puyallup School District No. 3 (Pierce County, WA) — the 6th largest K-12 district in Washington by enrollment (~23,110 students across 37 schools), governing a 145,542-resident area of central/east Pierce County.
Known facts: FY2024-25 operating revenue ~$418.3M; total combined FY2024-25 budget ~$428.8M; 2025 board unanimous selection of Dr. Kevin Alfano as next superintendent, beginning July 1, 2026.
Status: ✅ researched — 2026-09-19 — tier3-chunk9 · Last updated: 2026-09-19
Sources: 6/3 (minimum for tier3)

0. Why this person or group is on the map

Why it is on the map — from holding office + decision-making: Puyallup School District (PSD) is on the map for two reasons. (1) From holding office: it is the 6th-largest K-12 district in Washington by enrollment and the second-largest non-Tacoma district in Pierce County. It serves about 145,500 residents across central and east Pierce County (Puyallup, South Hill, Summit, Midland, Edgewood). (2) Decision-making: five elected board members set policy, levy taxes (with voter approval), control about $430 million in annual operating and capital budgets, negotiate the teachers’ union contract (PEA — Puyallup Education Association), and decide on school closures and boundary changes that ripple through the South Sound housing market.
Adjacent but EXCLUDED candidates: Bethel School District (a tier-2 entity, separate profile) — there is some boundary overlap (graph weight 2). Sumner-Bonney Lake and Tacoma districts are excluded as separate jurisdictions. The Cascade/Bethel/Puyallup “inter-district transfer” market is referenced here but does not have its own entity.

1. Who they are

Exact legal name: Puyallup School District No. 3, Pierce County, Washington (per Pierce County Assessor filings).
Type of entity: A school district. It is a municipal corporation organized under state law (RCW) 28A.315 (school districts) and Title 28A (Common School Provisions). It is not a 501(c)(3) nonprofit. It is a quasi-municipal taxing body that can levy taxes with voter approval (RCW 84.52.053 EP&O levy + RCW 84.52.135 capital levy / bond authority).
Governance: A 5-member Board of Directors. Members serve four-year staggered terms. They are elected at-large within the district. Current board (per PSD website): Gretchen Miles (President, Pos. #3, 2023-2027), Shannon Burch (Vice President, Pos. #5, 2023-2027), David Berg (Legislative Rep, Pos. #4, 2021-2029), Joseph Romero (Legislative Rep, Pos. #2, 2019-2027), Dr. Melissa Bedford (WIAA Rep, Pos. #1, 2025-2029).
Superintendent transition: On March 4, 2026, the Board picked Dr. Kevin Alfano as the next superintendent. He starts July 1, 2026. He succeeds Richard Lasso. His prior roles are not confirmed beyond the PSD announcement.
Age: One of Washington’s oldest continuously operating school districts. Organized in the 19th century.

3. Where their power comes from

Statutory authority: The district sets K-12 curriculum, enrollment rules, transportation, capital construction, and labor contracts within its boundaries. It controls employee headcount (the largest employer in central/east Pierce County with about 4,100 staff).
Tax power: The 2025 local property tax rate was $4.21 per $1,000 of assessed value (Bond $1.05 + Capital Levy $0.86 + EP&O Levy $2.30). Voters in the district approved these rates. A 2026 EP&O Replacement Levy is on the ballot. The state provides about 57% of revenue ($245.3M in apportionment + $78.5M in categorical funds in 2024-25). Local levies ($66.7M) and federal/state grants provide the marginal dollar.
Labor power: The district is the largest employer in the Puyallup-area labor market. It sets wages for teachers in the PEA bargaining unit. Those decisions ripple into Bethel, Sumner-Bonney Lake, and Franklin Pierce districts during regional talks.
Land-use power: School siting decisions drive residential development. PSD has capital-levy authority for new schools. The 2024 Capital Levy ($4.14 per $1,000 AV) funds the Rogers HS gym, Edgemont track, Carson playground, and other facility work.
Budget stress: Per the PSD Budget Information page, the FY2024-25 ending fund balance was a negative $7.8M unassigned. The FY2025-26 forecast projects an ending balance of about –$1.7M. The district is operating below its minimum fund-balance policy without taking action. The 2026 EP&O Replacement Levy is the immediate lever.

1. Who they are


The bottom line: Puyallup School District operates like a $430M quasi-municipal corporation. Five elected board members govern about 23,110 students across 37 schools with about 4,100 staff. Its main powers are local property-tax levy placement (capital + EP&O), labor negotiation (PEA), capital construction, and school siting. Each one ripples into Pierce County housing prices, regional labor compensation, and inter-district boundary politics. The superintendent transition from Richard Lasso to Dr. Kevin Alfano (effective July 1, 2026) is the most visible current decision moment. It comes against a backdrop of a documented structural budget deficit (about –$7.8M unassigned ending balance for FY2024-25) that the 2026 EP&O Replacement Levy addresses but does not solve.


Conflicts-of-interest flags: Capital-construction contracts flow through to regional construction firms during a Capital Levy cycle (Cornerstone, Tucci & Sons, etc. — UNVERIFIED at firm level). The Board approves those contracts without a public referendum. The graph note of “boundary_tension” with Bethel School District is a known South Sound planning fault-line — overlapping residential growth (Edgewood/Midland) and inter-district transfer applications. Board members’ employer ties are not in available primary sources (UNVERIFIED).


Analysis of alternatives: The defense reading: PSD is a creature of state law (RCW 28A). It is accountable to voters through at-large board elections and levy ballot measures. Its power is limited by OSPI, state apportionment formulas, federal IDEA, and collective bargaining law. The skeptical reading: an at-large district-wide board election in a suburban district is unlikely to produce competitive or ideologically diverse boards. The structural deficit has been rolled forward without meaningful labor-cost concession, suggesting board-management alignment against taxpayer exposure (levy fatigue) rather than against entrenched labor interests. Either way, the next 24 months — Alfano’s first year plus a 2026 levy — will be diagnostic.


Confidence: Medium — primary sources (PSD website) confirm budget figures, board composition, superintendent transition, levy rates; deeper analysis of capital-construction contract winners and PEA contract language is UNVERIFIED.

Puyallup Tribe — Deep Profile
Case: INV-2026-002 · Profile: profiles/puyallup-tribe.md
Entity ID: puyallup-tribe · Type: organization · Domain: institutional
Tier: tier1 · Rank: 4/163 · Composite power: 0.440
Graph description: Sovereign nation; gaming (Emerald Queen Casino) is primary revenue engine — institutional + economic power
Known facts: Sovereign nation; Emerald Queen Casino; land-into-trust authority; Bill Sterud chairman; ~4,000 enrolled members
Status: ✅ researched — 2026-09-19 — tier1-chunk1
Sources: 13/10 (minimum for tier1)

0. Why this person or group is on the map

Why the Tribe is here: The Puyallup Tribe of Indians is a federally-recognized sovereign nation. Its reservation overlaps with the City of Tacoma and unincorporated Pierce County. The Tribe’s power comes from federal sovereignty, the right to put land into federal trust, and tribal courts. Its decision-making power comes from the Land Use Consultation Process, or LUCP. That process was set by the 1990 Settlement. It requires local governments to consult with the Tribe on big land-use decisions. The Tribe also donates to both major parties. It lobbies the County Council. It is a top-10 employer in Pierce County.
Who is left out: The Nisqually Indian Tribe is a separate sovereign. It sits on the Thurston and Pierce border. It is outside the main Pierce County boundary. The Muckleshoot Tribe is in Auburn, King County. It is excluded too. The Tribe’s business arms — Tahoma Global Logistics, Marine View Ventures, and Ames International — are companies, not sovereign-power nodes. They are excluded from this profile.

1. Who they are

Exact legal name: Puyallup Tribe of Indians (spuyaləpabš).
Entity type: Federally-recognized Indian Tribe. Established 1936 under the Indian Reorganization Act. Reservation established 1854 via the Treaty of Medicine Creek.
Governing law: Tribal constitution (1936). Federal Indian law (Title 25 of the United States Code, or 25 USC). The Puyallup Tribe of Indians Settlement Act of 1989, Public Law 101-41, 103 Stat. 83. The Land Use Consultation Process, or LUCP, under the 1990 Settlement Agreement.
Sovereignty status: Federal sovereignty. The Tribe has a government-to-government relationship with the U.S., the State of Washington, and local governments. Tribal courts include the Puyallup Tribal Court, the Court of Appeals, and the Children’s Court. They are co-equal with the Tribal Council.
Enrolled members: About 4,000, per Wikipedia and the Northwest Portland Area Indian Health Board. About 2,500 live on the reservation. Reservation total population is about 41,000, mostly non-tribal.
Reservation: Established 1854 by the Treaty of Medicine Creek. Expanded in 1856. Tribal government was set up in 1936. The reservation overlaps with the City of Tacoma, the City of Fife, the City of Puyallup, and unincorporated Pierce County.

2. Their career and offices

Tribal Council (7 members, elected): As of February 2024:

Chairman: Bill Sterud (on the council since 1978, 46+ years). He is the longest-tenured power figure in the county.
Vice Chairwoman: Anna Bean. (Wikipedia lists Sylvia Miller as Vice Chair in the infobox — discrepancy noted. A March 2025 Facebook post refers to “Vice Chairwoman Sylvia Miller” speaking at a Charity Trust event.)
Annette Bryan.
Amber Hayward.
Sylvia Miller.
Tim Reynon (former director of the Washington Governor’s Office of Indian Affairs; direct line to Governor Ferguson).
Fred Dillon.


Chairmanship rotation: The graph notes “chairmanship rotates annually (Sterud ↔ David Z. Bean).” This is UNVERIFIED from primary sources. Wikipedia lists Sterud as chairman without noting rotation.
Emerald Queen Casino CEO: Yale Rowe, per a Facebook post about sports betting testimony.
Board overlaps flagged:

Tim Reynon sits on the Governor’s Office of Indian Affairs. That office is now cabinet-level, per 2025 legislation signed by Governor Ferguson. Reynon has a direct line to the Governor.
Bill Sterud sits on the Seattle Business Journal “Power 100” list. He oversees tribal economic expansion including the EQC.
Andrew Strobel did planning for the Puyallup Tribe. He now sits on the Tacoma Community College (TCC) board and is an advisor to Ryan Mello.



3. Where their power comes from

Federal sovereignty: As a federally-recognized tribe, the Puyallup Tribe has a government-to-government relationship with the U.S. and Washington State. It cannot be taxed by state or local governments on tribal trust land. It has its own courts, law enforcement, and power to make rules. This is the Tribe’s founding power. It operates as a separate sovereign inside Pierce County’s borders.
Land-into-trust authority: The 1990 Land Claims Settlement and later federal laws let the Tribe put fee lands into federal trust. One such law is S.382 of the 118th Congress — the Puyallup Tribe of Indians Land Into Trust Confirmation Act of 2023. Taking land into trust removes it from local tax rolls and zoning power. This acts like a veto over local land use. Once land goes into trust, local governments lose rule-making power over it.
Land Use Consultation Process (LUCP): Under Section VIII(C) of the 1990 Settlement Agreement, when the Tribe or a local government looks at a big land-use decision inside the reservation, they must consult. This gives the Tribe a formal seat at the table. No other non-governmental group in the county has this power.
Gaming revenue: Emerald Queen Casino is the Tribe’s main money source. The Tribe does not charge income or property taxes. Most revenue comes from government-owned businesses: EQC, Marine View Ventures, Tahoma Global Logistics. This keeps the Tribe financially independent from the county tax base.
Campaign donations: The Tribe donates to both Democratic and Republican candidates and parties. This bipartisan giving keeps access open no matter which party runs the county.
Lobbying: The Tribe is a registered lobbying client with the Washington State Public Disclosure Commission (PDC). In 2021 it had 3 registered lobbyists: Ehren Flygare at $91,000, Sound Government Solutions at $29,500, and Dawn P. Vyvyan at $75,000. UNVERIFIED: the graph’s claim of “$1.4 million self-reported” as “largest county lobbyist” was not confirmed from primary sources.
Key facts:

Tax status: The Tribe is sovereign. It is not subject to state or local taxes on trust land. It has its own tax power on tribal land.
Board roster and overlaps: See above. Sterud (46 years), Reynon (Governor connection).
Government funding share: UNVERIFIED. The Tribe funds itself through gaming and other businesses. It does not depend on county money. Federal funding through the Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) and Indian Health Service (IHS) was not measured here.



3. Where their power comes from






























IndicatorFindingEvidence (source #)Who benefitsTribal members benefit from gaming revenue, social services, and a $22 million permanent trust fund set up by the 1990 Settlement. Non-tribal community benefits from over $18 million in charitable donations since 2012 through the Charity Trust Board, plus impact payments to local governments for fire and police services.Sources 3, 8Who sitsChairman Sterud has 46 years of tenure. He is one of the longest-serving power figures in the county. Tim Reynon sits on the Tribal Council and directs the Governor’s Office of Indian Affairs. That office is now cabinet-level. The Tribe is a member of the South Sound Military and Communities Partnership, or SSMCP. It sits on the Steering Committee.Sources 1, 5, 9Who governsThe Tribe governs its roughly 4,000 enrolled members through its tribal council and courts. It also makes rules over trust lands inside Pierce County. The LUCP gives it a formal consultation role in local land-use decisions. That governance power extends beyond its own members.Sources 1, 7Who winsThe Tribe’s bipartisan donation strategy keeps access to both parties. Its 2024 voter guide explicitly endorses candidates: “We support people who support us.” The 2025 sports betting bill was signed by Governor Ferguson. The Governor also signed a bill making the Office of Indian Affairs cabinet-level. These are recent policy wins.Sources 5, 6, 11
4. Their money

Revenue model: The Tribe does not collect income or property taxes. Most revenue comes from government-owned businesses: Emerald Queen Casino (main source), Marine View Ventures, Tahoma Global Logistics (launched 2023), and Ames International (a candy company, acquired). Exact revenue figures are not public. Tribal sovereignty exempts the Tribe from Internal Revenue Service (IRS) Form 990 filing.
Gaming revenue: Emerald Queen Casino is the primary revenue engine. The Tribe runs two EQC locations. Charity Trust Board donations come from EQC revenue. They are part of an agreement with the State of Washington. That agreement covers smoking cessation, problem gambling programs, and impact costs to local governments.
Charitable donations: Since 2012 the Tribe has donated more than $18 million to hundreds of local groups through its Charity Trust Board. In 2022: more than $2 million to 100+ groups. In 2024: more than $850,000 to 60 groups. These donations are a big source of soft power and community goodwill.
Campaign donations: The Tribe gives to both Pierce Dems and Pierce GOP, plus individual candidates (Mello, Cruver, Hitchen, Ayala). It also donated $50,000 to the “Harry Truman Fund,” a state-level committee, per TransparencyUSA.
Lobbying expenditures: 2021 PDC records show 3 registered lobbyists with combined pay of about $195,545 (Flygare $91,000, Sound Government Solutions $29,500, Vyvyan $75,000). UNVERIFIED: graph claim of “$1.4 million self-reported” as largest county lobbyist — not confirmed from primary source.
Federal settlement: The 1990 Land Claims Settlement provided about $77 million in cash and assets (state, local, and federal money). It also gave about 900 acres of land and a $22 million permanent trust fund for health, social, and welfare services.
UNVERIFIED: HHFPAC $357,000 — not relevant to this profile. HHFPAC is a healthcare political action committee (PAC), not connected to the Tribe.

5. How they touch government

Sovereignty and federal ties: Government-to-government relationship with the U.S. (BIA, IHS), the State of Washington (Governor’s Office of Indian Affairs, now cabinet-level), and local governments (Pierce County, Tacoma, Fife, Puyallup).
Land Use Consultation Process (LUCP): Under the 1990 Settlement, the Tribe and local governments must consult on big land-use decisions inside the reservation. This is a formal, binding consultation process — not just advisory.
Land-into-trust: S.382 of the 118th Congress (2023), the Puyallup Tribe of Indians Land Into Trust Confirmation Act, would put about 17.264 acres of Tribe-owned fee land in Pierce County into federal trust. This removes the land from local tax rolls and zoning power.
Lobbying (County Council): The Tribe is the highest-weighted lobbying relationship on the Pierce County Council (weight 5 in the graph). Likely issues include land use, trust land applications, impact payments, and public safety coordination.
Lobbying (State): The Tribe is a registered lobbying client with the Washington PDC. 2025 legislative wins: sports betting on in-state college games, signed by Governor Ferguson; cabinet-level elevation of the Governor’s Office of Indian Affairs.
Campaign donations: The Tribe gives to both parties. It donates to Pierce Dems, Pierce GOP, and individual candidates from both parties. Its 2024 voter guide endorses specific candidates.
SSMCP: The Tribe sits on the Steering Committee of the South Sound Military & Communities Partnership. SSMCP coordinates Joint Base Lewis-McChord (JBLM) issues.
Environmental advocacy: The Tribe opposed Tacoma LNG and Electron Hydro. It declared a climate emergency in December 2019. It is active in Puyallup River protection.

6. Other seats they hold

Bill Sterud (Chairman): 46 years on the council. Seattle Business Journal Power 100. He oversees EQC expansion.
Tim Reynon (Council): Director of the Governor’s Office of Indian Affairs. That office is now cabinet-level. Reynon has a direct line to Governor Ferguson.
Andrew Strobel: Former Puyallup Tribe planning staff. Now on the TCC board. He is an advisor to Ryan Mello. This is a direct Tribe-to-County Executive board overlap.
Pierce County Council (lobbying, weight 5): The Tribe’s highest-weighted lobbying relationship.
Ryan Mello (donated, weight 4): Campaign donation to the County Executive.
Pierce GOP (donated, weight 3): Bipartisan giving.
Pierce Dems (donated, weight 3): Bipartisan giving.
Amy Cruver, Jani Hitchen, Rosie Ayala (donated, weight 3 each): Individual Council member donations.
SSMCP: Steering Committee member for JBLM coordination.

9. Who they are connected to
