1. Who they are

UNVERIFIED: “Tribe = largest county lobbyist” ($1.4M self-reported): The graph flags this as unverified. The 2021 PDC records show about $195,000 in lobbyist pay. The $1.4 million figure may include in-house lobbying, campaign donations, and other costs not captured in lobbyist registration. Verify via PDC L-2 annual lobbying reports.
Sterud chairmanship rotation: The graph says “chairmanship rotates annually (Sterud ↔ David Z. Bean).” Wikipedia lists Sterud without noting rotation. Is this a formal rule of the constitution or just an informal practice?
Andrew Strobel as Tribe-to-Executive board overlap: Strobel is former Puyallup Tribe planning staff. He is now an advisor to Mello and on the TCC board. This is a direct pipeline from the Tribe to the County Executive. What is the nature of his advisory role?
LUCP use frequency: How often has the Tribe used the Land Use Consultation Process? Which specific land-use decisions have triggered it? This would measure the Tribe’s actual veto-like power.
EQC revenue: The Tribe is exempt from IRS Form 990 filing. Is there any public disclosure of EQC revenue (for example, state gaming compact reports)?
2024 voter guide endorsements: Which specific candidates did the Tribe endorse in 2024? Cross-reference with donation records.
Tahoma Global Logistics and Ames International: What is the revenue and employment of these non-gaming businesses? Do they create new how they touch government (for example, port, trade)?

1. Who they are

Verdict: The Puyallup Tribe of Indians holds power through four channels. (1) Federal sovereignty gives the Tribe a government-to-government relationship. It cannot be taxed or regulated by state or local governments on trust land. It has its own courts and law enforcement. (2) Land-into-trust authority lets the Tribe take land off local tax rolls and zoning. It acts like a veto over local land-use control. (3) Gaming revenue from EQC gives the Tribe financial independence from the county tax base. It funds an $18 million-plus charitable donation program. (4) Bipartisan political donations and lobbying — the Tribe donates to both parties. It is the highest-weighted lobbying relationship on the County Council. Chairman Sterud’s 46 years on the council make him the longest-serving power figure in the county. Tim Reynon’s role as director of the Governor’s Office of Indian Affairs gives a direct line to the state’s chief executive.
Conflicts-of-interest flags (defense-attorney counter-argument):

Donation-to-lobbying pipeline: The Tribe donates to individual Council members (Ayala, Hitchen, Cruver). At the same time, it lobbies the Council (weight 5). A defense attorney would argue this creates an appearance of buying access on land-use and trust-land decisions.
Sovereignty shield: The Tribe’s exemption from local taxes and zoning on trust land creates an imbalance. The Tribe can influence local government through donations and lobbying. But local government cannot regulate the Tribe’s trust land. This is a structural imbalance.
LUCP as veto: The Land Use Consultation Process gives the Tribe a formal role in local land-use decisions. No other private group has this. A defense attorney might call this an undue veto over local democratic processes.
Strobel board overlap: Andrew Strobel’s move from Tribe planning to Mello advisor creates a possible channel for tribal influence into the Executive’s office.


Other reading: The opposing reading is that the Tribe’s power is overstated. Its roughly 4,000 enrolled members are a small share of Pierce County’s roughly 920,000 people. EQC revenue, while big, is a fraction of the county’s $3.5 billion budget. The LUCP is a consultation process, not a veto. Local governments can move forward with land-use decisions after consultation. The bipartisan donation strategy ($3,000-weight edges to each party) is modest compared to the Chamber’s structural influence. The Tribe’s sovereignty is real but limited to trust land, which is a small share of the county’s land area. Under this reading, the Tribe’s rank of 4 out of 163 reflects the novelty of tribal sovereignty in a power map, not the actual size of its influence on county-wide decisions.
Confidence: Medium — the Tribe’s sovereignty, settlement history, and charitable donations are well-documented from primary sources. However, key financial figures (EQC revenue, total lobbying expenditures) are not publicly disclosed due to tribal sovereignty. The “$1.4M largest county lobbyist” claim remains UNVERIFIED. The chairmanship rotation claim is unconfirmed.

Why she is on the map: Robyn Denson is on the map because she holds office and makes decisions. She is a sitting member of the Pierce County Council. She holds the Executive Pro Tempore role. She chairs two of the Council’s most powerful committees: Rules & Operations and Community Development & Environment. Those committees shape land use, the environment, and Council rules. She represents District 7, which covers Gig Harbor, the Key Peninsula, and parts of North and West Tacoma. She also sits on the Puget Sound Regional Council and the Tacoma-Pierce County Health Board.
What that means: Her power is procedural and tied to her committees. Under the Laumann/Marsden/Prensky 1983 framework, she is well-connected (PSRC, joint boards, South Sound 911) and a decision-maker (committee chairs).
Who is NOT on the map: Derek Young, her predecessor. Other 2022 primary candidates (Mitch Anderson, Josh Harris, Paula Lonergan, Chuck West). Gig Harbor City Council members. Pierce County Conservation Futures Advisory Board members.

It controls zoning and land use. It confirms appointments.
Executive Pro Tempore: The Council’s third-ranking officer (after Chair and Vice Chair). She runs Council sessions when the Chair and Vice Chair are absent.
Two committee chairs:
Rules & Operations Committee (Chair) — sets the agenda, the Council rules, and ethics enforcement.
Community Development & Environment Committee (Chair) — oversees land use, growth rules, environmental rules, and the Comprehensive Plan (a key decision tool for unincorporated Pierce County).
Member committees: Economic & Infrastructure Development; Public Safety.
Outside boards (from official roster): Alliance for a Healthy Sound, Executive Board of Crystal Judson Family Center, Joint Determining Board, Flood Control Zone District Board of Supervisors, Pierce County Regional Council, Pierce County Reserve Officers Board of Trustees, Puget Sound Regional Council (PSRC, member — PSRC controls federal transportation money for the region), South Sound Military & Communities Partnership (alternate), South Sound 911 Governing Board, Tacoma Narrows Airport Advisory Commission (ex officio, by virtue of her office), Tacoma-Pierce County Health Board (alternate), Transportation Benefit District, West Sound Partners for Ecosystem Recovery.
Cross-domain ties: Her decision-making power (Council vote plus two committee chairs plus Executive Pro Tempore) crosses into regional policy (PSRC, Transportation Benefit District) and the environment (Alliance for a Healthy Sound, Flood Control Zone District). These are key levers for the rural and suburban west-of-Tacoma corridor.

Authority: Pierce County Council vote; committee chair agenda-setting; PSRC vote on regional transportation funds.
Budget: She does not control a budget line directly. But her committee chairs oversee the proposals that go through Rules & Operations and Community Development & Environment.
Veto: Councilmembers do not have veto power. The Executive Pro Tempore presides in absence of the Chair and Vice Chair.
Where she governs: Pierce County (about 1.1 million residents) with regional ties through PSRC and joint boards.

1. Who they are

Verdict: Robyn Denson is a tier-3 decision-maker. Her power is procedural and modest in scope. Fact: She is one of seven Pierce County Councilmembers (graph weight 4 edge). Fact: She is Executive Pro Tempore. She chairs the Rules & Operations and Community Development & Environment committees. Those committees shape Council procedure and the most important land-use decisions for unincorporated areas. Fact: She sits on 13 outside boards, most importantly PSRC (federal transportation money), the Flood Control Zone District Board of Supervisors, and the Transportation Benefit District. Fact: She succeeded a Democrat, won about 58% in D7 in 2022, and is not running again in 2026. Inference: Her agenda-setting authority over Rules & Operations makes her a gatekeeper for which Council proposals get a vote. Her Community Development & Environment chair gives her leverage over zoning and the Comprehensive Plan in her rural-suburban district. Her housing-policy background (5 WA House sessions) fits with her PSRC, transportation, and conservation work.
Conflicts-of-interest flags (defense counter-argument): A defense would argue Denson’s power is institutional, not personal. She is one vote of seven. The Chair and Vice Chair outrank her. Her committee chairs are assigned by the Council Chair. Her term ends in 2026 (she declined to run again). Her many environmental and conservation board seats are typical for a West Sound Councilmember and reflect constituent priorities, not self-dealing.
Analysis of alternatives (investigative control document (ICD)-203): The other reading is that Denson is a relatively low-power junior Councilmember. Her two committee chairs are routine. Her outside-board seats are mostly honorific. Her 2022 win was a single-cycle event in one district. She is leaving in 2026. Her pre-Council career (housing policy analyst, small business, non-profits) is documented but not very prominent. The fairest view: a competent, district-focused incumbent whose influence is procedural, not structural.

0. Why this person or group is on the map

Why she is on the map: Rosie Ayala is included for three reasons. First, she holds office as an elected Pierce County Councilmember for District 4. She votes on the county budget, county laws, and land-use decisions. Second, she makes decisions on several boards, like Pierce Transit, the Greater Tacoma Community Foundation (GTCF), the Puget Sound Regional Council (PSRC), and the Flood Control Zone District. Third, she is well-connected. She is the first Black, Indigenous, or Person of Color (BIPOC) woman to serve on the Pierce County Council. Her district covers downtown Tacoma, Hilltop, South Tacoma, and nearby areas.
Who is NOT on the map: Other Pierce County Councilmembers are profiled separately. Ryan Mello, who held District 4 before her, is now the County Executive and has his own profile. Her 2024 opponent, Rodney Robinson, is not profiled.

Other names: CM Ayala (Councilmember); CMRosieAyala (social media)

Lives in: District 4, Pierce County (downtown Tacoma / Hilltop / South Tacoma)

Before Council: Worked in non-profits and government. Her focus was on homeless services, healthcare access, education, and youth job programs. Exact employers and dates are not in public records.

Parks Tacoma Board: Elected to the board. She left in December 2024 when she won the County Council seat. Three new commissioners were named in 2025, including Pete Reyes who took her seat.
Pierce County Council, District 4: Won the November 5, 2024 general election. She defeated Rodney Robinson, also a Democrat. The primary was August 6, 2024. She took office in late December 2024 or early January 2025. She is the first BIPOC woman on the Council. She succeeded Ryan Mello, who is now the County Executive.
She raised $43,501 in the primary: $26,819 from individuals, $9,768 from other sources, and $6,050 from political committees.

3. Where their power comes from

Power held:
Elected office: Councilmember for District 4. She votes on the county budget, county laws, and land use. The Council is the law-making body for Pierce County, a county of about 920,000 people.
Committee leadership: Chair of the Economic & Infrastructure Development Committee. Vice Chair of Health & Human Services. Member of Community Development & Environment. Alternate on Rules & Operations.
Board seats (17+): She sits on more than 17 boards. Historic role: First BIPOC woman on the Council — this gives her symbolic and moral weight.
Cross-domain ties: Her Council seat touches economic, transportation, institutional, and environmental groups. It crosses into economic boards (Economic Development Board, EDCPC). It reaches transportation (Pierce Transit, PSRC). It links to institutions (GTCF, Tacoma Arts Live). And it covers the environment (Flood Control Zone District, Community Development & Environment).

Authority: Council vote on the county budget (about $2 billion), laws, and board appointments.
Budget power: As Chair of Economic & Infrastructure Development, she shapes spending on economic development and infrastructure.
Veto power: The Council confirms some Executive appointments. The Council does not have veto power.
District: Pierce County (unincorporated areas plus cities for some functions). District 4 covers downtown Tacoma, Hilltop, Central, Lincoln District, South Tacoma, Fircrest, and University Place.

It has done over 100 projects. Rush shapes the housing market and commercial building in the region. These are sister companies under the same owners, Gordon Rush and Matt Smith.

1. Who they are

Exact legal name: Rush Development Company Inc (per Better Business Bureau and Washington State Department of Labor and Industries (L&I) records).
Entity type: For-profit corporation. It is a general contractor and a real estate developer.
Parent/subsidiaries: A division of The Rush Companies, a partnership of six companies with shared ownership. Sister companies are Rush Capital, Rush Commercial, Rush Properties, Edison47, and Rush Residential.

Headquarters: Gig Harbor, WA. The office is at the Park Plaza building. Rush built it in 2003 as a speculative project. Rush has used it as its HQ since then, with about 55 employees at that location.
Founded: 1987. The first project was a speculative home in Tacoma’s North End.

3. Where their power comes from

Market power: Rush Development is one of the most active developers in the Puget Sound region. It has done over 100 projects. It holds $1.2 billion or more in assets. It has built over 3,600 apartment units. It has built over 645,000 square feet of medical and office space. The company works in Pierce, Kitsap, King, Thurston, Snohomish, and Skagit counties. In Pierce County, key projects include Proctor Flats and Madison25 in Tacoma. It also built the Mary Bridge Children’s Therapy Center with MultiCare (a hospital system).
Entitlement expertise: Rush markets its ability to “navigate complex entitlement processes across Puget Sound jurisdictions.” That is a real edge. It means Rush knows how to win land-use approvals from local governments like the Pierce County Council and the Tacoma City Council.
Land/real-estate holdings: $1.2 billion or more in assets. That includes Rush-owned apartments, medical and office space, and single-family communities. Rush usually keeps most ownership in joint ventures, so partners’ interests stay aligned. Specific Pierce County parcel holdings were UNVERIFIED in public sources (would need a Pierce County Assessor search).
Government contracts/grants: No direct government contracts or grants found. Rush works in the private market. It benefits from public land-use decisions like rezones, permits, and subdivisions.
Jobs controlled: Over 130 team members across The Rush Companies (as of about 2022). Rush Development itself hires development managers like Steve Yester and Alex Willing, plus project teams.

1. Who they are

Verdict: Rush Development controls a big share of apartment and mixed-use building in Pierce County and the broader Puget Sound. Its integrated platform gives it that share. Its power comes from its market position: $1.2B+ in assets, 100+ projects. It also comes from knowing how to win land-use approvals in many places. It comes from Chamber and NAIOP membership, which give it access to leaders. The donation to Kelly Chambers and the land-use tie to Pierce County Council show Rush engages with political and regulatory decision-makers.
Conflicts-of-interest flags: A defense attorney would say Rush is a successful private developer working within legal rules. Land-use approvals are public processes. Campaign donations are normal political activity. The counter: Rush’s mix of market dominance, land-use know-how, and political donations creates a structural edge. That edge may not equally serve all community interests, especially on contested projects like the Gig Harbor wetlands development.

That reading would place Rush’s composite power lower than rank 41/163.

Known facts: The Russell Family Foundation (TRFF) established 1999; HQ Gig Harbor, WA; 90% impact-aligned investments; co-founders George + Jane Russell.
Status: ✅ researched — 2026-09-19 — tier3-chunk5 · Last updated: 2026-09-19
Sources: 6/3 (minimum for tier3)

0. Why this person or group is on the map

The Russell Family Foundation (TRFF) is one of the biggest family foundations in Pierce County. It is based in Gig Harbor. It was set up in 1999 with money from the sale of the Frank Russell Company to Northwestern Mutual Life. George F. Russell Jr. and Jane Russell started it.
It has $77.3 million in assets. In 2023, it gave out 124 grants worth $1.24 million. It has given about $41 million over its life. Most of its money (90%) goes to “impact-aligned” investments: climate, forests, renewable power, and affordable housing.
TRFF runs Jane’s Fellowship Program. It trains Pierce County residents to be civic leaders. Since 2004, 159 people have gone through the program.

1. Who they are

Full legal name: The Russell Family Foundation (TRFF).
Type: Private family foundation. It is a 501(c)(3) tax-exempt nonprofit. Founded 1999.
Federal tax ID (EIN): 91-1663336.
Office address: 3025 Harborview Drive, Gig Harbor, WA 98335.
Founders: George F. Russell Jr. and Jane T. Russell.
Parent or subsidiaries: None. Russell Investments is a separate company. It is not part of TRFF.
Who governs it: Washington State nonprofit law (state law (RCW) 24.03). It also has a 501(c)(3) tax exemption from the federal tax agency (IRS).
CEO: Kathleen Simpson.
Board: Sarah Cavanaugh (President), Tim Cavanaugh (Treasurer), Mimi Chau (Vice President), Dion Rurik (Secretary), Josh Cavanaugh (Investment & Audit Committee Chair), plus Evlyn Andrade, Sarah Cleveland, and Rashad Morris. Many board members are part of the Russell family.

3. Where their power comes from

Philanthropic power: TRFF uses 90% of its investments to back causes it cares about: climate, sustainable forestry, clean energy, and affordable housing. It runs four programs: Catalytic Climate Finance, Environmental Education, Food for Climate Solutions, and Jane’s Fellowship Program.
Grantmaking scale: $1.24 million across 124 grants in 2023. About $41 million over its life across 800 plus grants. In April 2024, it gave $819,000 to 27 groups for youth outdoor education. In April 2026, it announced $2.3 million in environmental education and food-for-climate grants. In Feb 2025, it announced $19.5 million in catalytic climate finance grants and investments.
Leadership pipeline: Jane’s Fellowship Program (JFP) started in 2004 to honor Jane Russell. Each year, up to 15 grassroots leaders join. Fellows must be 24 or older and live in Pierce County. Each fellow gets $8,500 plus up to $2,500 for coaching and training. 159 leaders have graduated since 2004 across 13 classes.
No government funding: TRFF gets no government money. It is fully funded by the Russell family endowment.
Leadership training: JFP picks Pierce County grassroots leaders and trains them for civic leadership roles.

1. Who they are

Verdict: The Russell Family Foundation sets the agenda in Pierce County on climate, environmental education, food systems, and grassroots leadership. It is funded by a $77.3 million endowment from the 1999 sale of Frank Russell Company. Its 159-strong Jane’s Fellowship alumni network is a major leadership pipeline. With 90% impact-aligned investments and $19.5 million in catalytic climate finance, TRFF shapes how climate money gets spent in the region.
Conflicts-of-interest flags: TRFF’s board is mostly Russell family members and their relatives (Cavanaugh and Rurik surnames). Many generations sit on the board. That means one family controls decisions with little outside input. The foundation does not have to report political spending like a political group. Some JFP alumni have moved into political and advocacy roles.
Analysis of alternatives : A defense view: TRFF is small compared to giant foundations like the Gates Foundation. Its grants are modest. JFP is not coercive. An opposing view: A 25-year-old family-controlled foundation with a 159-strong alumni network shapes who gets heard in Pierce County civic life. It is a textbook case of soft power through nonprofit channels.

1. Who they are

Exact legal name: Russell Investments Group, LLC (current parent holding).
Entity type: Private investment-management firm — Delaware LLC operating worldwide. Subsidiaries include Russell Investment Management Company (RIMCo, 909 A Street Tacoma WA — old HQ address), Russell Fund Services Company, Russell Financial Services Inc., and Russell Insurance Agency Inc.
Founded: 1936 in Tacoma WA by Frank Russell. Reorganized under Northwestern Mutual Life, which bought Frank Russell Co. in 1999 in a $1.2B-scale deal. The firm rebranded as Russell Investment Group. It is now mostly owned by TA Associates Management, L.P., with minority stakes held by Reverence Capital Partners, L.P. and certain employees plus Hamilton Lane Advisors LLC minority stakes.
Leadership (current): Zach Buchwald — Chairman and CEO (joined February 2023 from BlackRock, where he ran the $2T Institutional Business). Kate El-Hillow — President and CIO (since 2022).
HQ: Russell Investments Center, Seattle WA (current HQ; old Tacoma 909 A Street address kept by some subsidiaries).
Assets: ~$418 billion (August 2026) under management. $2.6 trillion under advisement across 32 countries. Russell is the 4th-largest adviser in the world. Employees: about 1,350 (2019).

3. Where their power comes from

Market and financial power: Russell is a top-5 global investment-outsourcing firm. It created the Russell 2000 and Russell 3000 indexes (now under FTSE Russell / LSEG — UNVERIFIED transition date here). Russell controls how trillions of dollars are benchmarked and how hundreds of billions are actively managed. Major clients have included AT&T, Boeing, and Union Pacific Railroad.
Civic bridge power: The Russell family (Jane and George Russell Jr.) founded The Russell Family Foundation in Gig Harbor WA in 1999 with part of the Northwestern Mutual sale proceeds. The foundation funded the Museum of Glass (opened 2002 in downtown Tacoma), environmental sustainability, and Pacific NW impact-aligned investments. George Russell was honored after his death by Tacoma Mayor Victoria Woodards.
Institutional bridge power: Jason Thompson joined Russell in 1994. He serves as director of the firm’s Americas Institutional business. He joined the MultiCare Board of Directors in January 2025 — creating a direct Russell to MultiCare pipeline. MultiCare CEO Bill Robertson’s firm could have a $418B-AUM advisory relationship with Russell.
Basis for scoring overlap: Russell Family Foundation (founded_by graph weight 5). Jason Thompson director link (graph weight 4) — the latter is the most concrete Pierce County tie.

Verdict: Russell Investments is a tier-3 economic node. Its current direct Pierce County power is modest (operations are now Seattle-based), but its family-mediated reach is real. The Russell Family Foundation’s Pacific NW grant-making (Gig Harbor-based, environmental focus, Museum of Glass legacy), plus Jason Thompson’s January-2025 MultiCare board seat, make Russell a meaningful pipeline into the region’s healthcare-power network. George Russell’s 2023 death marked the end of the founder era. Ownership now rests with private-equity sponsors TA Associates and Reverence Capital, who are return-on-capital actors rather than civic figures.
Conflicts-of-interest flags: (a) Jason Thompson’s two roles — Russell’s Americas Institutional director and MultiCare board director — open a channel for investment-management business between the two firms. MultiCare’s investment policy and Russell’s institutional business could touch. (b) The 1999 sale to Northwestern Mutual raises ongoing questions about the family’s retained influence despite the Russell Family Foundation’s formal independence.
Analysis of alternatives (investigative control document (ICD)-203 opposing view): A skeptic would call Russell Investments a Seattle-based PE-owned investment firm with a Tacoma-origin story but no current Pierce County operations. The civic reach runs through the Russell Family Foundation (a separate 501(c)(3)) rather than Russell Investments itself. The graph weight here likely overstates Russell Investments’ direct Pierce County reach and understates the foundation’s separate role.

0. Why this person or group is on the map

Ryan Mello is the most powerful elected official in Pierce County, Washington. He is the County Executive, the top job in county government. He runs the county’s departments, writes the budget, and can veto almost anything the County Council passes.
He controls a $3.5 billion two-year budget. That money touches every part of the county: roads, police, courts, parks, and public health.
The county’s other top elected officials (the Sheriff, the Prosecuting Attorney, the Auditor) are mapped separately. The former Executive, Bruce Dammeier, is also mapped but no longer in office.

1. Who they are

Name: Ryan N. Mello
Born: about 1978 or 1979, in Kailua, Hawaii
Lives in: Tacoma, Washington
Family: His partner is named Sean. Mello is openly gay and was the first openly gay County Executive in Washington.
Education: Bachelor’s degree in politics and government from the University of Puget Sound (2001). He was student-body president there in 2000–2001.

2. Their career and offices

He has climbed a steady ladder of local offices over twenty years: parks board, city council, county council, and now the top job.
3. Where their power comes from

The office itself. The County Executive is the chief executive of the county under its home-rule charter. He prepares the budget and runs all the departments.
The veto. He can veto any law the County Council passes. To override him, the Council needs 5 of its 7 votes. With a 4-to-3 Council, a party-line veto is nearly impossible to overturn. This is his strongest power.
The budget. He controls a $3.5 billion two-year budget. About 76% of it goes to law enforcement, courts, and the justice system.
Regional transit boards. He is Vice Chair of Sound Transit (a regional transit agency) and sits on the Pierce Transit board. That gives him a say over billions in transportation spending.

1. Who they are

The bottom line. Ryan Mello holds the most concentrated power in Pierce County government. He writes the budget, runs the departments, and can veto the Council with a nearly unbreakable veto. He earned that power through a twenty-year climb up the county’s elected ladder, and he won it narrowly (51–49%) in 2024.
The counter-argument. A defender would say his narrow win means he has no strong mandate, that his veto power is checked by the Council’s control of the purse, and that his transit-board seats are advisory. 0. Why this person or group is on the map

Saltchuk Resources is the parent company of the Foss family of companies. It connects to Pierce County through TOTE Maritime Alaska, which runs ships between Tacoma and Anchorage. Foss Maritime also operates tug and barge boats along the Pacific Northwest coast.
Saltchuk is on the map because it is well-connected and makes major decisions. The Foss family controls the company, so Saltchuk links Pierce County’s port economy to a private family business empire based in Seattle.
Not on the map separately: Crowley Maritime, Matson Navigation, and the Foss family as individuals (they are covered under foss-family).

1. Who they are

Full name: Saltchuk Resources, Inc. The public brand is “Saltchuk.”
Type of company: A private family holding company. Founded in 1982 in Seattle, WA.
Headquarters: 450 Alaskan Way S, Seattle, WA 98104.
Ownership: The Foss/Tabbutt family owns Saltchuk. Mark Tabbutt is the Chairman. Denise Tabbutt is the Principal Shareholder. Timothy Engle is on the board. Michele Seaver was part of the family ownership group until she passed away.
Structure: Saltchuk is the parent. It owns seven lines of business. These include Saltchuk Marine, Saltchuk Logistics, Saltchuk Aviation, NorthStar Energy, TOTE Group, Tropical, and OSG. Those lines run brands like Foss Maritime, TOTE Maritime Alaska and Puerto Rico, Carlile Transportation, Northern Air Cargo, and Tropical Shipping.
Governing law: Washington state corporate law. Saltchuk is private, so it does not file with the SEC (the Securities and Exchange Commission).
Size: In 2023, the company had about $4.85 billion in revenue and around 7,600 employees (about 761 in Washington state, the rest elsewhere). More recent reports put revenue near $5.5 to $6 billion and total employees near 10,000.

3. Where their power comes from

Market power: Saltchuk holds a strong position in shipping to Alaska, Hawaii, Puerto Rico, the Caribbean, and Florida. It runs Jones Act ships (a U.S. law that requires goods moved between U.S. ports to be carried on U.S.-built, U.S.-flagged, and U.S.-crewed ships). TOTE Maritime Alaska carries about one-third of the cargo on the Alaska Railbelt route.
Tacoma link: TOTE Maritime Alaska has its office at 909 A Street, Suite 1100, Tacoma, WA 98402. The Port of Tacoma is home to a major Saltchuk presence. Saltchuk is a key counterparty on port leases and labor deals with the longshore union (ILWU) and the Inlandboatmen’s Union.
Pierce County jobs: About 761 Saltchuk employees work in Washington state.
Capture risk: Because Saltchuk is private, it does not file public reports on investments, lobbying, or political donations. Its political influence runs through industry groups like the American Association of Port Authorities (AAPA) and the Chamber of Maritime Commerce.

12. Bottom line

The bottom line. Saltchuk is a private Seattle family company. It dominates shipping to Alaska, Hawaii, and the Caribbean. It runs Tacoma’s TOTE Maritime Alaska operation. Its 2023 revenue was $4.85 billion. Its Tacoma office is a major port-side counterparty.
Why it matters for Pierce County. The Tacoma to Anchorage trade lane moves through the Port of Tacoma. Foss Maritime operates along the whole Pacific Northwest coast. Any port or labor deal at the Port of Tacoma runs through Saltchuk’s tenants.
The counter-view. A defender would say Saltchuk has no Pierce County political role. It does not file public lobbying or campaign-finance reports. Its tier-3 score (0.006) reflects that. The acquisition of Great Lakes Dredge & Dock brings dredging in-house, but that is normal for a family holding company.
The open question. The 44,000-member figure may overstate active political engagement. Specific contracts and lobbying activity remain unverified.

Sheila Edwards Lange is the top leader (Chancellor) of the University of Washington Tacoma (UW Tacoma). UW Tacoma is one of three UW campuses. It is the only one in Pierce County. Lange has been Chancellor since September 16, 2021.
Lange holds power because she runs the campus. She makes decisions on which academic programs open or close. She hires senior faculty. She leads the campus master plan (the long-range plan for buildings and land). She runs fundraising and major programs, like the Dressel Scholars program.
UW Tacoma is a key player in the South Sound economy. It trains local workers. Lange sits on the board of the Tacoma-Pierce County Economic Development Board (EDB). That puts her inside the county’s economic decision-making.

Sound Transit — Deep Profile

Graph description: Central Puget Sound Regional Transit Authority (Sound Transit); 18-member Board of Directors; 2026 budget $3.3B revenue / $3.5B expenditures; $34.5B ST3 budget shortfall; CEO Dow Constantine (since April 2025); formed under RCW 81.104 & 81.112
Known facts: Regional transit authority for King, Pierce, Snohomish Counties; 2026 budget $3.3B revenues, $3.5B expenses; $34.5B ST3 budget shortfall; CEO Dow Constantine (former King County Executive); Board Chair Dave Somers (Snohomish County Executive); Vice Chair Ryan Mello (Pierce County Executive); voter-approved ST1 (1996), ST2 (2008), ST3 (2016)
Status: ✅ researched — 2026-09-19 — tier2-chunk6
Sources: 9/5 (minimum for tier2)

0. Why this person or group is on the map

Why we added Sound Transit: Sound Transit is a regional government agency. Its full name is the Central Puget Sound Regional Transit Authority. It plans, builds, and runs high-capacity transit across King, Pierce, and Snohomish Counties. It has a multi-billion-dollar budget. Voters have approved its taxing power. Its 18-member Board includes Pierce County Executive Ryan Mello as Vice Chair. All this makes it a key power node for roads and money in Pierce County. The agency faces a $34.5 billion ST3 budget shortfall. That pressure shapes regional transportation decisions for decades to come.
Other agencies we did not add: Pierce Transit is mapped separately as pierce-transit. It is a separate local agency. King County Metro is outside Pierce County. WSDOT, the Washington State Department of Transportation, is a state agency mapped separately if applicable. PSRC, the Puget Sound Regional Council, is a planning body, not a transit operator.

1. Who they are

Legal name: Central Puget Sound Regional Transit Authority (doing business as Sound Transit).
Entity type: A government regional transit authority. It is a municipal corporation formed under state law. The laws are RCW 81.104 (Public Transportation Systems) and RCW 81.112 (Regional Transit Authorities).
Governing law: RCW 81.104 and RCW 81.112. The King, Pierce, and Snohomish County councils created the agency under RCW 81.112.030.
Voter approvals: ST1 (November 5, 1996), ST2 (November 4, 2008), and ST3 (November 8, 2016). Voters in the Sound Transit district approved each one to fund regional high-capacity transit.
Board structure: 18-member Board of Directors. Members include elected officials from the three member counties and the WSDOT Secretary. As of February 2026: Dave Somers (Chair, Snohomish County Executive), Claudia Balducci (Vice Chair, King County Council member), and Ryan Mello (Vice Chair, Pierce County Executive).
Executive leadership: CEO Dow Constantine (former King County Executive). The Board appointed him on March 27, 2025. He officially joined in April 2025. Interim CEO Goran Sparrman came before him.

3. Where their power comes from

Statutory authority: Authorized under RCW 81.104 and RCW 81.112. It can plan, build, and permanently run high-capacity transit for the central Puget Sound region. It can levy voter-approved sales taxes, property taxes, and motor vehicle excise taxes, or MVET. It can also issue bonds.
Budget scale: The 2026 adopted budget has $3.3 billion in revenues and other financing sources. It has $3.5 billion in expenses and outlays. Total revenues dropped 26.1% ($1.2 billion) from 2025. That drop comes mainly from lower bond and TIFIA loan proceeds. TIFIA stands for Transportation Infrastructure Finance and Innovation Act. It is a federal loan program. Tax revenues make up 75% of total revenue. The 2026 property tax revenue is $183 million (up 3.8% from $176.2 million in 2025). The Board approved a 1% property tax increase to get there. Passenger fare revenue is $85 million (28.4% higher than the 2025 forecast).
ST3 expansion program: Sound Transit 3 (approved November 2016) is a $54 billion or more capital program. It faces a $34.5 billion budget shortfall because construction costs have soared. The Board adopted Motion M2025-36. That motion tells staff to build a new Regional Transit Long-Range Plan. It is the first major update since 2014. The Board aims to adopt it in the third quarter of 2026. That plan will set the framework for ST4.
Domain overlap:
Government meets economy: The multi-billion-dollar capital program creates construction jobs, contracts, and transit-oriented development. The Equitable Transit-Oriented Development (TOD) program includes 234 affordable homes at the Spring District in Bellevue.
Government meets institutions: The Board is made up of elected officials from member counties and cities. The WSDOT Secretary is an ex officio member. Ex officio means the seat is automatic because of the office held.
Government meets politics: Board members are elected officials. Their work on Sound Transit touches their own electoral politics.

3. Where their power comes from

CEO: Dow Constantine.Sources 1, 4Who governsThe Board of Directors governs agency strategy. It approves budgets, sets tax rates, and oversees the CEO. There are four standing committees: Executive, Rider Experience and Operations, System Expansion, and Finance and Audit. Each committee can approve deals under $50 million.Sources 4, 5Who winsDow Constantine won the CEO appointment (Board vote March 27, 2025). The Board approved a 1% property tax increase for 2026. Voters approved ST3 (2016), which authorized the expansion program. Pierce County Executive Ryan Mello holds a Vice Chair position, giving Pierce County strong board-level influence.Sources 1, 3, 6, 8
5. How they touch government

Taxing power: Sound Transit levies voter-approved sales taxes, property taxes, and MVET inside the Sound Transit district. 2026 property tax revenue is $183 million. The Board approved a 1% property tax increase for 2026.
Budget adoption: The 2026 Adopted Budget and Financial Plan ($3.3 billion revenue / $3.5 billion expenses). The system expansion budget is $1.9 billion (mostly Stride bus rapid transit, or BRT, at $710 million). Debt service is $230 million. Operations and maintenance outlays are $38 million annualized. The estimated cash position at the end of 2025 is about $7.2 billion.
Bond issuance: Sound Transit holds AA and AAA credit ratings. It issues bonds and uses TIFIA loans for capital financing. Lower bond and TIFIA proceeds drove the 26.1% revenue drop from 2025.
Pierce County representation: Ryan Mello (Pierce County Executive) serves as Vice Chair. He also sits on the System Expansion Committee. Kristina Walker (Tacoma City Council member) sits on the Board. She chairs the Rider Experience and Operations Committee. Hunter George (Fircrest Council member) also sits on the Board.
Federal grants: Sound Transit receives Federal Transit Administration (FTA) formula grants (sections 5307, 5337, and 5339). It also receives Federal Highway Administration (FHWA) Surface Transportation Block Grant (STBG) and Congestion Mitigation and Air Quality (CMAQ) funds through PSRC project selection.
State funding: Move Ahead Washington is a state transportation package. It was led by Rep. Jake Fey (D-27). It includes state transportation funds that flow to Sound Transit projects.
Legislative ties: The Washington State Legislature appropriates transportation funding. Sound Transit works with WSDOT. WSDOT Secretary Julie Meredith sits on the Board.

6. Other seats they hold

Ryan Mello (Pierce County Executive) — Vice Chair of the Sound Transit Board. He also sits on the System Expansion Committee. He is the main Pierce County link to the board.
Kristina Walker (Tacoma City Council member) — Board member. She chairs the Rider Experience and Operations Committee. She is the link between the board and the Tacoma City Council.
Hunter George (Fircrest Council member) — Board member. He sits on the Rider Experience and Operations Committee and the Finance and Audit Committee.
Dave Somers (Snohomish County Executive) — Board Chair. He sits on the Executive Committee and the System Expansion Committee.
Dow Constantine (CEO) — Former King County Executive. He was a longtime Sound Transit Board member before being named CEO. He is a key executive-level board tie.
WSDOT — Secretary Julie Meredith is an ex officio Board member. This is a state transportation funding tie.
PSRC — Sound Transit projects are programmed through the PSRC Transportation Improvement Program (TIP). Move Ahead Washington funds flow through PSRC.
Pierce Transit — Sound Transit coordinates with Pierce Transit on local transit links. Ryan Mello serves on both boards.

1. Who they are

Verdict: Sound Transit’s power comes from three things. First, its legal standing as a regional transit authority under RCW 81.104 and 81.112. Second, its voter-approved taxes on sales, property, and vehicles. Third, its huge capital program (ST3 is over $54 billion, though it now faces a $34.5 billion shortfall). The 2026 budget of $3.3 billion in revenue and $3.5 billion in spending makes it one of the largest public agencies in the Pacific Northwest. Its 18-member Board is filled with elected officials from King, Pierce, and Snohomish Counties. That creates direct board ties to county and city governments. Pierce County Executive Ryan Mello’s Vice Chair seat gives Pierce County strong influence over regional transit decisions worth billions. The CEO appointment of Dow Constantine, former King County Executive and longtime Board member, centralizes executive power in a leader with deep political ties.
Conflicts of interest: The $34.5 billion ST3 shortfall creates pressure. The Board must scale back voter-approved projects, find new money (a possible ST4 ballot measure), or raise taxes. Each choice creates political winners and losers. Board members are elected officials who may face voters over tax increases or service cuts. The 1% property tax increase for 2026 was approved by the Board. That Board includes officials who set county-level property tax policy. CEO Constantine’s move from King County Executive (a Board seat) to agency CEO creates a revolving-door concern. The Equitable TOD program (234 affordable homes at the Spring District) channels public funds to private developers.
The other view: Sound Transit’s power is limited by voter approval rules. It cannot raise taxes without a ballot measure. ST1, ST2, and ST3 were all voter-approved. The $34.5 billion shortfall actually weakens the agency. It cannot deliver the promised projects without more money. The Board’s structure (18 elected officials with different priorities) creates internal friction. The agency’s reliance on sales tax (which falls in a recession) and property tax (which is politically sensitive) limits its fiscal flexibility. The CEO pick of a politician (Constantine) rather than a transit professional could be seen as valuing political management over operational skill.
Confidence: High — based on many primary sources (the Sound Transit 2026 Adopted Budget PDF, the official Board committees page, the Q2 2026 financial report, and agency resolutions) and several secondary sources (Lynnwood Times, The Center Square, The Daily UW). The budget figures, board make-up, governance structure, and the ST3 shortfall are all confirmed.

0. Why this person or group is on the map

Inclusion rule: Reputational and media reach. South Sound Business is the only monthly magazine in the South Sound that covers only business topics. It serves Pierce, South King, Kitsap, and Thurston counties, plus Bainbridge Island. It is the main chronicler of the Pierce County business community. It covers the port, MultiCare (a hospital system), and Joint Base Lewis-McChord (JBLM) contractors. It also covers regional banks and the local Chamber. The magazine calls itself the “#1 business communication media in the South Sound since 1985.” Its editorial choices shape which businesses get steady regional attention.
Adjacent but EXCLUDED candidates: The News Tribune, the main daily paper, is owned separately. Seattle Business Magazine and 425 Business are run by Premier Media Group. KNKX is public radio. Tacoma Weekly is another local outlet. KING5 runs a South Sound bureau.

1. Who they are

Publication title: South Sound Business (current brand). Earlier called South Sound Biz from 1985 to 2021 under Business Examiner Media.
Publisher: Premier Media Group (PMG), based in Tacoma, WA. Mailing address: P.O. Box 1362, Tacoma, WA 98401-1362. Phone: (253) 588-5340. Web: www.southsoundbiz.com/.
Acquisition history: Launched in 1985 by Business Examiner Media, founded by Jeff and Jill Rounce. Acquired by Premier Media Group, founded by Josh and Michelle Dunn, around August 19, 2021. Rebranded from “South Sound Biz” to “South Sound Business” after the sale.
Editorial staff (current, per About page): Jeff Burlingame is Editor in Chief. He worked at Seattle University and the Gates Foundation. He won a Sigma Delta Chi award from the Society of Professional Journalists (SPJ). Joanna Kresge is Managing Editor.
Recognition: 2023 Silver Best of Show Excellence Award for Best Website. The award came from the Alliance of Area Business Publishers at its summer conference in Detroit.

3. Where their power comes from

Niche dominance: The magazine calls itself the “only local media dedicated exclusively to business topics in the South Sound.” No other outlet fills that niche since PMG bought Business Examiner Media.
Geographic reach: It covers 24 cities across Pierce, South King, Kitsap, and Thurston counties. It also covers Bainbridge Island. It is produced in Tacoma. It reaches leaders at CHI Franciscan, JBLM, MultiCare, Dillanos, Heritage Bank, and Umpqua.
Award-winning: 2023 Alliance of Area Business Publishers (AABP) Silver Best of Show for Best Website.
Format: Monthly print and digital, plus “Hallmark Events” like Women to Watch. These events are both marketing tools and access points for the region’s business elite.

1. Who they are

Verdict: South Sound Business holds a structural monopoly on regional business-magazine coverage in the South Sound. No daily paper, TV station, or public radio outlet fills that niche. Its parent, Premier Media Group, also publishes the Eastside’s 425 Business. That makes the Dunn family the dominant regional business-magazine consolidator. The publication’s editorial choices shape the reputation of Pierce County’s business elite. Spotlight on Business Awards, Women to Watch, and “Lessons from a Leader” features act as informal reputation currency.
Conflicts-of-interest flags: Editor-in-chief profiles, “Lessons from a Leader” features, and Spotlight on Business Awards are advertising-adjacent formats. The line between editorial and advertorial blurs when advertisers are also subjects. The defense: the publication discloses paid partnerships and runs a separate “advertising” section.
Analysis of alternatives: A defense-friendly reading is that the magazine is a normal regional business-to-business (B2B) publication. It serves the information needs of South Sound executives. A critical reading is that — combined with sibling titles 425, 425 Business, South Sound, and West Sound — the Dunn family controls an outsized share of regional business journalism. Josh Dunn sits on the UW Milgard School of Business board. He also sits on the Association of Washington Business board. That gives the company direct policy and education access.

0. Why this person or group is on the map

Southport Financial Services is on the map because it makes decisions and has strong ties. It is a national affordable housing developer with a Tacoma office. It works with Pierce County government on big subsidized housing projects. One example is Cedar Flats (276 units, with $7 million from the county).
The company focuses on Low Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC) properties. LIHTC is a federal program that gives tax credits to developers who build affordable housing. That focus gives it special know-how in federal, state, and local affordable housing finance. It sits on the board of the Affordable Housing Consortium of Pierce County. That gives it a direct line into the local affordable housing policy network.
The graph records ties to Kelly Chambers (donated), Pierce County Council (land use), and the Chamber of Commerce (member).
Who is left out: Macdonald Ladd Development, LLC is named by The Urbanist as the Cedar Flats lead developer. Pierce County’s own social media names Southport as a partner. This needs to be checked. Macdonald Ladd is not on the map unless it turns out to be a partner or subsidiary. The Maureen Howard Affordable Housing Fund (a county program) is not an entity. Southport’s Tampa HQ is outside Pierce County, so it is not in this map.

1. Who they are

Legal name: Southport Financial Services, Inc.
Type: For-profit corporation. It does real estate development, construction, and property management.
Tax ID (EIN)/registration: Founded 1995. The full EIN is unverified. NAICS code 237210 (per VisualVisitor) or 522292 (per Prospeo). SIC 615. NAICS and SIC are government codes for business type.
Parent/subsidiaries: No parent found. Southport appears to be independently owned. The company website (sphome.com) says it keeps “everything in the family.”
Ownership: J. David Page is named as Southport’s leader or founder in Housing Finance magazine. Specific ownership is unverified. VP of Finance: Stephane Varenne (per VisualVisitor).
Governing law: Florida corporate law (HQ in Tampa). Registered in Washington State for the Tacoma office.
Headquarters: 5403 West Gray Street, Tampa, FL 33609.

3. Where their power comes from

Market power: Southport has developed over 120 LIHTC properties. It holds about 12,000 units in 18 states. It has “built or acquired a substantial number of market rental housing projects.” It has “a demonstrated ability to secure LIHTC allocations, as well as volume cap tax-exempt bond allocations in multiple states.” That multi-state LIHTC know-how gives it special power in affordable housing finance.
Pierce County presence: Southport has a Tacoma office at 1911 65th Ave W. That makes it one of the few national affordable housing developers with a physical office in Pierce County. Its VP, Zac Baker, sits on the board of the Affordable Housing Consortium of Pierce County. That gives the company a direct line into the local affordable housing policy network.
Government partnerships: Pierce County named Southport as a partner in the Cedar Flats groundbreaking. Cedar Flats is a 276-unit affordable housing complex in the Puyallup / South Hill / Frederickson area. The county put $7 million from the Maureen Howard Affordable Housing Fund into the project. NOTE: The Urbanist names “Macdonald Ladd Development, LLC” as the Cedar Flats lead. The relationship between Southport and Macdonald Ladd is unverified. They may be co-developers. Or Southport may be the LIHTC partner while Macdonald Ladd leads development.
Revenue: Unverified from public sources (private company). The scale (12,000 units, 120+ LIHTC properties, 18 states) suggests large revenue from development fees, property management, and LIHTC syndication (selling tax credits to investors).
Jobs: 11-50 employees across three offices. More jobs come from construction projects and property management.
Land and buildings: About 12,000 units in 18 states. Specific Pierce County holdings beyond Cedar Flats are unverified. The company also runs regular apartment complexes in central Florida and the southeastern U.S.

It includes larger units for families and reserves a portion for people with disabilities. The County Council approved $12.2 million for four housing projects (including Cedar Flats) at its September 2, 2025 meeting. The total Cedar Flats cost is nearly $109 million.

Cedar Flats developer identity: There is a gap between Pierce County’s social media and The Urbanist. Pierce County’s social media names Southport as a partner. The Urbanist names Macdonald Ladd Development, LLC as the lead developer. The relationship between Southport and Macdonald Ladd on Cedar Flats is unverified. They may be co-developers. Or Southport may be the LIHTC partner while Macdonald Ladd leads development. This needs to be checked with Pierce County Human Services or the project’s LIHTC allocation documents.
PDC campaign finance: The graph records a donation edge to Kelly Chambers (weight 3). A direct PDC query is needed for itemized contributions from Southport Financial Services, J. David Page, Zac Baker, or other Southport principals to confirm amount, date, and election cycle.
J. David Page background: Identified as Southport’s leader or founder in industry publications. His background, ownership stake, and role in Tacoma office operations are unverified from primary sources. No public LinkedIn profile or detailed biography located.
Pierce County property portfolio: Beyond Cedar Flats, Southport’s specific property holdings and management contracts in Pierce County are unverified. The Tacoma office suggests ongoing operations. Viridian Grove project: A $42M, about 100-unit affordable housing project with Southport’s market study cited. The location, current status, and Southport’s exact role (developer vs. market study consultant) need clarification.
Tacoma office operations: The Tacoma office at 1911 65th Ave W is a physical presence. Staffing and how it operates (vs. Tampa HQ) are unverified. It is unclear if this office handles development, management, or finance.

1. Who they are

The bottom line. Southport Financial Services has special know-how in LIHTC affordable housing finance. That is a niche but real power domain. It helps decide which projects get built in Pierce County and elsewhere. Its Tacoma office gives it a local base. Its AHC board seat (through VP Zac Baker) gives it a direct line to local affordable housing policy. Its Cedar Flats partnership with Pierce County government ($7M public investment) ties it to public money. The company’s national scale (12,000 units, 18 states, 120+ LIHTC properties) gives it capacity that local developers may lack. But its power depends on government partnerships and tax credit allocations. It does not hold any independent regulatory authority.
Conflicts-of-interest flags: A defense attorney would flag the overlap. Southport’s business depends on government programs (LIHTC, public housing funds). It also gave money to Kelly Chambers. That mix could look like pay-to-play. Counter: affordable housing development is a public-private partnership. Developers’ political activity is normal civic engagement. The $7M county investment in Cedar Flats went through a competitive public process by the County Council, not a sole-source deal. Southport’s LIHTC allocations come from state housing finance agencies through competitive scoring, not political discretion.
Analysis of alternatives: The opposing reading: Southport is a mid-sized national developer (11-50 employees). Its Pierce County presence is just one office and one known project (Cedar Flats). Its local power is modest — it is one of several affordable housing developers competing for limited county and state funds. Its actual development pipeline in Pierce County may be small. Cedar Flats may even be led by Macdonald Ladd rather than Southport, which would shrink Southport’s direct local power. This reading would place Southport’s composite power lower than rank 45/163 suggests.

David Page’s background, and the full scope of Pierce County operations remain UNVERIFIED or ambiguous.

Graph description: South Sound Military & Communities Partnership — 50+ member intergovernmental coalition coordinating JBLM-community relations across Pierce and Thurston Counties; fiduciary agent is City of Lakewood; JBLM generates ~$9B statewide economic impact.
Known facts:.

Formed in 2011 by memorandum of agreement among communities and JBLM advocates (source 1, 2).
50+ members: cities, counties, tribes, nonprofits, corporations, organizations, and JBLM (source 1, 3).
Fiduciary agent: City of Lakewood. Executive Leadership includes City of Lacey (Chair), City of Lakewood, Pierce County, JBLM (ex officio), Nisqually Indian Tribe (source 2).
Two full-time paid staff with military service backgrounds (source 2).
JBLM economic impact: ~$9 billion statewide; 78,890 jobs; largest employer in Pierce County (source 5, 6).
Elected Officials Council (EOC) meets semiannually; co-chaired by Mayor of Lakewood, Pierce County Executive, and Chair of Thurston County Commissioners (source 2).
Status: ✅ researched — 2026-09-19 — tier2-chunk5.

0. Why this person or group is on the map

Why it is here: South Sound Military and Communities Partnership is a formal intergovernmental group. It works between Joint Base Lewis-McChord and 50+ nearby cities, counties, tribes, and groups. JBLM is the largest employer in Pierce County. The Elected Officials Council brings together top leaders from the county, the city of Lakewood, and JBLM command. It is a clear exercise of cross-jurisdictional power.
Who is left out: The Office of Local Defense Community Cooperation is a federal funder of SSMCP. It is not a local power node. JBLM has its own profile. Member cities like Lakewood, Lacey, and DuPont may get their own profiles too.

1. Who they are

Exact legal name: South Sound Military & Communities Partnership (SSMCP).
Entity type: Intergovernmental partnership — not a separate legal body. The memorandum of agreement (MOA) says SSMCP is a regional partnership. It can fund staff but does not directly employ anyone. The City of Lakewood acts as the fiduciary agent. It provides legal advice and administrative services.
Formed: 2011, by memorandum of agreement. The current MOA is dated 2018.
Governing law: The MOA among member jurisdictions. The Elected Officials Council (EOC) follows Washington’s Open Public Meetings Act (Revised Code of Washington (RCW) 42.30).
Staff: Two full-time paid staff with military backgrounds, funded by SSMCP. Program Manager: Maria Tobin (253-983-7804, mtobin@cityoflakewood.us). Past Program Director: Bill Adamson (retired Colonel).

3. Where their power comes from

What power does SSMCP hold? SSMCP works on land use, housing, transport, childcare, and economic development across Pierce and Thurston Counties. It has no legal authority. It shapes policy through the MOA, the Elected Officials Council, working groups, and studies. Its influence grows with JBLM’s huge economic footprint.
Budget it controls: SSMCP is funded by member dues and grants. Grants come from OLDCC. OLDCC is the federal Office of Local Defense Community Cooperation. That office used to be called the Office of Economic Adjustment. Exact budget numbers are not verified.
Appointment or veto powers: None. The EOC makes policy suggestions and coordinates legislative strategies.
Area covered: Pierce and Thurston Counties. This includes Lakewood, Lacey, Tacoma, DuPont, University Place, Yelm, Olympia, and nearby areas.

5. How they touch government

Pierce County: Executive Leadership member. The Pierce County Executive serves as an EOC co-chair. Ryan Mello is the current Pierce County Executive. He sits on the EOC.
City of Lakewood: Fiduciary agent and Executive Leadership member. It provides legal and administrative services. SSMCP staff are Lakewood city employees.
JBLM: Ex officio Executive Leadership member. JBLM commanders take part in EOC meetings. These commanders include Col. Phil Lamb, Col. Dave Fazenbaker, and Lt. Gen. Xavier Brunson.
Office of Local Defense Community Cooperation: Federal grant funder. Known as OLDCC.
Legislative advocacy: SSMCP runs a Legislative Agenda. It pushes for state and federal funding for JBLM-community projects. Key efforts include the Defense Community Compatibility Account. They also include the North Clear Zone. They include the I-5 Nisqually River Delta Project.
Requests for Proposals: SSMCP puts out RFPs for professional services. In 2025 it asked for bids on the JBLM Growth Implementation II plan. That plan covers three things: a Transportation Corridor Readiness Study, a Communications Interoperability Plan, and an Energy Grid Readiness Plan.

City of Lakewood: Fiduciary agent. SSMCP staff sit in Lakewood.
City of Lacey: SSMCP Chair.

Amazon: Sponsored an EOC event in May 2026.
Elected Officials Council participants: Bruce Dammeier is the former Pierce County Executive. Ryan Mello is the current Pierce County Executive. Don Anderson is the Lakewood Mayor. Marilyn Strickland is the U.S. Representative for WA-10.

1. Who they are

Verdict: SSMCP is the main coordinating body between JBLM and 50+ nearby civilian jurisdictions. JBLM is Pierce County’s largest employer. Its statewide impact is $9 billion. SSMCP’s power comes from its structure, not from law. The Elected Officials Council meets twice a year. It is the region’s formal forum for military-community policy coordination. It is co-chaired by the Pierce County Executive, the Lakewood Mayor, and the Thurston County Commission Chair. SSMCP shapes regional land-use strategy. It also shapes infrastructure planning, housing policy, and legislative advocacy. Lakewood is the fiduciary agent. That means SSMCP staff are effectively Lakewood employees. Amazon’s sponsorship of EOC events shows corporate interest in SSMCP’s work.
Conflicts-of-interest flags: SSMCP has a dual mission. It supports both JBLM military readiness and community interests. These can clash. Military land-use needs like the North Clear Zone and noise zones may conflict with civilian development. The EOC’s one-vote-per-government structure may favor larger places. Corporate sponsorship by Amazon of EOC events raises questions about influence. SSMCP-commissioned economic impact studies may inflate JBLM’s perceived importance.
Analysis of alternatives : The opposing reading is that SSMCP is a voluntary coordination body. It has no binding authority. It cannot force member jurisdictions to adopt any policy. Its suggestions are advisory. Members keep local control. The “$9 billion economic impact” figure comes from an economic model. That model, called input-output analysis, may overstate JBLM’s real marginal impact. SSMCP’s actual policy outputs beyond studies and forums may be modest.
Confidence: High — SSMCP’s structure, membership, economic impact data, and how they touch government are extensively documented in primary sources including its own MOA, official website, U.S. Army publications, and Pierce County government records. The organization’s coordinating role is well-established and verifiable.

1. Who they are

Verdict: Stanley J. Rumbaugh exercises tier-3 power to make decisions as a Pierce County Superior Court trial-court judge (Department 18, elected 2012; re-elected unopposed 2016) and amplifies that authority through cross-domain civic-board service spanning 25+ years on the Tacoma Housing Authority Board, 9 years on the Bates Technical College Board of Trustees, 5 years on the Planned Parenthood of Western Washington Board, plus statewide policy roles on the WA Sentencing Guideline Commission (since 2014). FACT: He has served as Criminal Presiding Judge (2016) and as Chair of the Pierce County Superior Court Pre-Trial Services Committee (2019-present), indicating internal court-leadership recognition. FACT: He was selected as WSAJ Judge of the Year 2026 by the Washington State Association for Justice — the trial-lawyer bar’s highest judicial honor. FACT: His pre-judicial career (1979-2013) was as founding partner of Rumbaugh, Rideout, Barnett & Adkins, where he tried hundreds of cases and authored several landmark state-law decisions (Cockle v. L&I; Fowler v. Ho; Little v. King; Morales Cruz v. Pacific Coast Containers). FACT: He lost the 2010 Washington Supreme Court race in the primary (37%) before winning the Pierce County Superior Court seat in 2012. INFERENCE: Rumbaugh is best characterized as a long-tenured, civically-engaged trial-court judge whose power extends from his judicial docket across Pierce County’s nonprofit and educational institutions. His tier-3 composite power (0.006) reflects his trial-court role rather than an appellate or statewide position; his reputational standing (WSAJ Judge of the Year, civic-board service) amplifies his influence beyond what the single-judge role alone would suggest.
Conflicts-of-interest flags (defense counter-argument): A defense would argue Rumbaugh’s election is nonpartisan; his decisions are subject to appellate review by Division II; he recuses per Washington Code of Judicial Conduct; his civic-board service is publicly disclosed; his criminal-defense background before becoming a judge is publicly known. The WSAJ Judge of the Year recognition indicates peer validation from the trial-lawyer bar (consistent with his prior plaintiff-side practice). Long-term civic-board service (e.g., 25 years on Tacoma Housing Authority) is consistent with judicial-community-engagement norms and not in itself a conflict.
Analysis of alternatives (investigative control document (ICD)-203): The opposing reading is that Rumbaugh’s individual trial-court power is constrained by (a) random case assignment; (b) appellate review; (c) collegial-decision dynamics for multi-judge panels; (d) the higher-volume nature of trial-court work (limited agenda-setting capacity); and (e) the WA Constitution’s prohibition on most extra-judicial commentary. His civic-board positions are diverse (housing authority, technical-college trustee, Planned Parenthood, Centro Latino, World Trade Council) — these could be characterized as institutional breadth rather than concentrated influence. The composite power of 0.006 is consistent with a tier-3 trial-court judge with statewide reputational standing and a long civic footprint.
Confidence: High — Office, docket, education, career history, civic-board positions, and 2026 WSAJ Judge of the Year selection are all primary-sourced (Pierce County official bio + Pierce County news release + WA Courts Directory + Ballotpedia + Kitsap Sun archive); biographical detail (DOB, residence, family) is UNVERIFIED but not material to the tier-3 power assessment.

0. Why this person or group is on the map

Why she’s on the map: Stephanie Pedersen is President and Editor of The News Tribune in Tacoma. That is the only daily newspaper in Pierce County. She is also Regional Editor for McClatchy’s Washington state papers. Those are the Bellingham Herald, the Tri-City Herald, The Olympian, and The News Tribune. She is the editorial decision-maker at the main print outlet covering Pierce County politics, business, and courts. The graph places her as a media node. She ties to News Tribune, and through it to McClatchy and Chatham Asset Management.
Neighbors NOT added to the map: Josh Dunn runs South Sound Biz / Premier Media. Suzanne Schotzko and other editors work at Tacoma Weekly or South Sound Talk. KIRO and MyNorthwest.com cover the area digitally. All are nearby media figures, but they are not the same node.

1. Who they are

Full legal name: Stephanie Pedersen.
Born / birthplace: Not located in public sources (UNVERIFIED).
Lives in: Tacoma, WA (RocketReach location field matches her employer).
Family / spouse: Not in public sources (UNVERIFIED).
Schooling: BA in Public Relations and Communications from Auburn University, 2003 to 2007 (per RocketReach).
Career path:
2007 to 2011: Copy Desk Chief, then Metro Editor, then Senior Editor for Digital at the Columbus Ledger-Enquirer in Georgia.
2012: Metro Editor at the Ledger-Enquirer.
2016 to 2020: Executive Editor at The Sun News in Myrtle Beach, SC.
April 2020: Promoted to President and Editor of The News Tribune. Also named Regional Editor for McClatchy’s Washington state papers. Announced April 7, 2020 via PR Newswire.
2025 to now: SVP of Local News at McClatchy. Editor of The News Tribune and The Olympian (per RocketReach).
Sanctions / criminal / civil: None located.

3. Where their power comes from

Domain is media. Her power comes from running the only daily newspaper in Pierce County. She also has regional say over three other McClatchy dailies in Washington state.
No law-based power. She has no statutory role. She has real influence on the public-information environment for about 880,000 Pierce County residents.
How she wields influence:
Editorial agenda-setting: She picks which Pierce County stories get investigative follow-up. She picks which council or county-executive actions get a board nod. She shapes how coverage frames police-accountability, business, and political races.
Board nod power: The News Tribune board (which she leads) issues primary and general-election nods that swing local races. Past nods include Tacoma mayoral, Pierce County Executive, and school-board races.
Hiring and budget: As President and Editor she controls local newsroom headcount, beat assignments, and contractor ties.
Cross-paper reach: As Regional Editor, she sets cross-state newsroom strategy for McClatchy in Washington. She covers the Bellingham Herald, Tri-City Herald, and The Olympian.
Key facts:
Reach: The News Tribune has the largest print circulation in Pierce County. It also has digital subscriptions. McClatchy’s WA cluster reaches about 1 million combined digital readers. Current paid-subscriber counts were not in primary sources (UNVERIFIED).
Ownership chain: News Tribune is owned by McClatchy LLC. McClatchy is owned by Chatham Asset Management. Chatham is a hedge fund that bought McClatchy out of bankruptcy in 2020 for $312 million. Pedersen does not own equity. Her power is operational and editorial.
Editorial stance: She has publicly backed local journalism and accountability reporting. Specific 2024 to 2026 Pierce County investigative projects were not enumerated in primary sources (UNVERIFIED).

1. Who they are

Verdict: Stephanie Pedersen makes the editorial calls at the only daily paper in Pierce County. She also has that role at three other McClatchy papers in Washington. As President and Editor she controls hiring, beat priorities, and who gets the newsroom’s nod in local races. Her power is operational and agenda-setting — not equity ownership. She exercises it inside a Chatham Asset Management–owned newsroom. That newsroom faces the cost pressure typical of post-bankruptcy McClatchy.
Conflicts of interest (defense-attorney counter-argument expected): Possible critique: newsroom picks in the main local daily distort democracy. They lift some candidates and silence others. Counter-defense: newsroom picks are a long-standing newspaper tradition. The board that makes them (which Pedersen chairs) operates apart from the newsroom’s reporting side, per standard SPJ and Cox principles.
The other reading: In a fragmented media market where many Pierce County voters get news from social media, The News Tribune’s sway is smaller than its historic reach. That reading lowers her weight. The reading that elevates Pedersen: News Tribune remains the cited source-of-record for official Pierce County business. That includes council minutes, court filings, and campaign-finance data. Her board’s picks are still covered as news by other outlets. tier3 placement at rank 158 fits — she has influence but not authority.

0. Why this person or group is on the map

Why it’s on the map: Sumner-Bonney Lake School District (SBLSD) is a Title 28A state law (RCW) public school district. It serves about 10,000 students in eastern Pierce County. That includes the cities of Sumner and Bonney Lake plus nearby unincorporated areas. It is included for two reasons. First, it makes decisions — it adopts its own budget, levies local property taxes through voter-approved EP&O and Capital levies, and signs contracts with its employees. Second, it is well-connected — it is one of about 15 Pierce County school districts that talks to the County Council about tax collection and to state legislators about funding formulas.
Neighbors NOT added to the map: Bethel, Puyallup, Dieringer, White River, Orting, and Carbonado school districts are peer districts mapped on their own. Pierce County Skills Center (a cooperative vocational facility) is excluded. SBL Education Foundation (a 501c3 fundraising arm) is excluded.

1. Who they are

Exact legal name: Sumner-Bonney Lake School District. District Number 454 (INFERENCE: district numbers for Pierce County public K-12 districts come from OSPI; the district is publicly known as Sumner-Bonney Lake and serves the area noted; the 454 designation is UNVERIFIED in this pass).
Entity type: Government. It is a public school district organized under Title 28A RCW (Washington state school-district statutes).
Governing law: Title 28A RCW. The state’s Superintendent of Public Instruction (OSPI) oversees it. The Washington State Board of Education sets learning standards.
Board structure: 5-member Board of Directors. Each is elected from one of 5 director districts. Each serves a 4-year term. Board duties per the district: check progress toward district goals, watch the budget, adopt instructional programs, approve hiring and union contracts, and link families, schools, and the community.
Executive leadership: Superintendent Dr. Laurie Dent, effective July 1, 2016. She earned a doctorate from Northwest Nazarene University in 2018. She got her superintendent certificate from WSU in 2016. She was named 2013 Pierce County Principal of the Year while principal of Liberty Ridge Elementary.
Operating posture: SBLSD publicly posts its budget presentations, monthly budget-status reports, Annual Financial Reports, and enrollment reporting on its website. That fits the OSPI-required reporting.

3. Where their power comes from

Power from the law (FACT): As a Washington public school district under Title 28A RCW, SBLSD is a junior taxing district. Pierce County collects property taxes for it. It can: (a) run a public K-12 system, (b) levy voter-approved local excess levies (EP&O and Capital Project levies) under RCW 84.52.053, (c) adopt annual budgets, (d) sign union contracts, and (e) issue bonds with voter approval.
Local-levy power (FACT): Per the district’s February 2024 levy Q&A: “The levy accounts for 16 percent of the district’s overall budget. The average levy increase in a four-year levy would be $11.31 a month ($136 annually).” This is the district’s main local fiscal lever above state funding.
Budget size (FACT): The district’s 2025–26 general-fund budget is $136.5 million per the district’s Budget page. Spending categories per the FY2022–23 summary: Regular Instruction $78.1M, Special Education $16.6M, CTE $4M, Compensatory Education $6.8M, Community Services $2.6M, and Support Services $28.1M.
Hiring power (FACT): The Board of Directors hires and supervises the Superintendent, approves all hiring decisions, and approves union contracts. The Board is the district’s ultimate employer of record.
Where the domains overlap:

inst ↔ econ: SBLSD is one of the largest employers in Sumner and Bonney Lake. The annual budget is about $136.5M and payroll is the biggest line.
inst ↔ community: Union bargaining shapes teacher and staff pay across all district schools.

1. Who they are

Verdict: Sumner-Bonney Lake School District is a Title 28A RCW public K-12 district with a $136.5M general-fund budget (2025–26). It serves about 9,900 to 10,000 students across Sumner, Bonney Lake, and unincorporated east Pierce County. Its discretionary fiscal power comes from voter-approved local excess levies (EP&O and Capital Project / Technology). The district says those levies fund 16% of its total budget. The rest comes from state funding. Its hiring power is significant locally: the 5-member Board hires and supervises the Superintendent, adopts the annual budget, and approves union contracts.
Conflicts of interest: Three flags. (1) The Board is elected from 5 director districts. But Board members represent the whole district, not just their sub-area. So one Board member from a small area can sway district-wide policy. (2) Local levy money is collected through Pierce County. That creates a fiscal dependency on county collection accuracy and timing. (3) The district’s reliance on local levies (about 16% of total) makes it vulnerable to state-funding-formula changes. When the state underfunds basic education, the district must turn to voters for relief. That is a structural pressure, not a discretionary one.
The other reading: A defense-attorney reading would say SBLSD is procedurally constrained. Board meetings follow the Open Public Meetings Act. Budgets and AFRs are posted publicly. Levy votes are public elections. The Board’s power is set by statute, not by choice. The Superintendent and staff operate under policies adopted by an elected board. The opposing reading: school-board elections in Pierce County usually draw very low turnout (often under 25% even in contested races). So the actual power of a Board member is closer to that of an appointed official than a competitive elected one. Incumbents rarely face a real challenge. Union-aligned candidates (SBL EA, Puget Sound Energy (PSE), and others) face a friendly field. The levy dependency on Pierce County Council collection is a passive but real board overlap.
Confidence: High. Structural facts (Board makeup, Superintendent, levy share, budget size, statutory framework) match the district’s own website with multiple pages. FY2022–23 spending matches the Budget Summary page. The February 2024 levy outcome (yes/no vote tally) is UNVERIFIED in this pass.

Known facts: 23 departments (judges); 10 commissioners; 2026-2027 budget $51.7M (county General Fund) + juvenile court $54.9M; presiding judge Susan Adams (elected May 2020)
