0. Why this person or group is on the map

Pierce County Superior Court is on this map for two reasons: it holds office, and it makes big decisions. It is the only trial court in Pierce County with full authority over serious cases. Its judges hear all felonies, big civil cases over about $100,000, real estate fights, tax disputes, divorce, and probate. It also hears appeals from lower courts.
The judges are elected. They have wide power to decide sentences, civil awards, and family cases.
Pierce County District Court is on the map as a separate node. State appeals courts are mapped separately. The county clerk’s office is not on the map because it only keeps records.

1. Who they are

Exact legal name: Pierce County Superior Court
Entity type: Government — a trial court with full jurisdiction, part of the state court system
Governing law: Washington State Constitution Art. IV § 6; state law (RCW) 2.08 and 2.12; Pierce County’s own local rules
Tax ID number (EIN) or business registration: N/A (government entity)
Parent and related bodies: Part of Washington’s state court system. Pierce County pays for the building, staff, and operations. The State of Washington pays the judges’ salaries.
Locations: Main courthouse at 930 Tacoma Ave S., Tacoma. Juvenile Court at Remann Hall, 5501 6th Ave., Tacoma.

2. Their career and offices

Presiding Judge: Susan Adams (Dept. 11). Elected May 2020. She is the Presiding Judge-Elect for 2025–2026. She sits on the Executive Committee. She chairs the Civil Protection Order Committee. She is a Trustee of the Superior Court Judges Association.
Court Administrator: Chris Gaddis (handles press for court news).
Deputy Court Executive (Juvenile Court): Hiring search underway, posted July 2026.
Full judge roster (23 judges): The court has 23 elected judges across 23 departments. The 2025 group photo lists: Stanley Rumbaugh, Philip Sorensen, Michael Schwartz, Grant Blinn, Karena Kirkendoll (retired March 2026), Shelly Moss, Timothy Ashcraft, Sabrina Ahrens, Alicia Burton, Clarence Henderson Jr., Matthew Thomas, Susan Adams, Diana Kiesel, Thomas Quinlan, Andre Peñalver, Jennifer Andrews, Joseph Evans, Angelica Williams, TaTeasha Davis, Philip Thornton, Rebecca Reeder, Ingrid McLeod, and Scott Peters.
Commissioners: 10 court commissioners. They handle specific matters like emergency orders, juvenile cases, probate, and protection orders. Hannah Gurewitz was hired in May 2026.
Board overlap: Stanley Rumbaugh appears in the power graph as a separate node (weight 4, judge). No other judges are graph nodes today.

3. Where their power comes from

Statutory authority: The state constitution gives the court full power over felonies, serious civil cases, real estate title fights, tax legality, divorce, probate, and naturalization. It can issue court orders to compel witnesses, review lower courts, and free wrongfully held people. Source: WA Constitution Art. IV § 6.
Size and reach: Pierce County has about 920,000 people. The court is the second-busiest superior court in Washington State, behind only King County. Judges set sentences in felony cases, order civil remedies, and decide family and probate cases.
How judges are chosen: All 23 judges are elected in nonpartisan contests. They serve four-year terms. If a seat opens between elections, the governor appoints a replacement from a list vetted by the county bar association. No judge can serve past age 75.
Cases and enforcement: The court hears felony cases brought by the Pierce County Prosecuting Attorney (pa-office/Mary Robnett). It also hears major civil cases, family law, and probate. Judges enforce orders through contempt powers, court orders, and sentencing. Specific yearly case numbers are not published in an easy-to-find place.

4. Their money

2026–2027 biennial budget (Pierce County): Superior Court: $51.7M. Juvenile Court: $54.9M. Assigned Counsel (free lawyers for poor defendants): $50.3M. Together, courts and legal services make up about 8% of county spending. Public safety is 18%. The General Fund ($967.4M) pays about 76% of law enforcement, courts, and justice costs.
Funding sources: Pierce County’s General Fund pays for buildings, staff, operations, and assigned counsel. Washington State pays judge salaries, set by law based on county size. Filing fees and court costs recover some costs. The state also funds specific programs like therapeutic courts.
Tax status: N/A (government entity)
Property holdings: County-City Building (930 Tacoma Ave S.) and Remann Hall (5501 6th Ave.) — both county-owned.
Levy/bond history: The court cannot issue its own levy or bond. The County Council approves its budget.

5. How they touch government

Pierce County Council (county-council): Approves the court’s budget (weight 5 in graph). The council does not run court operations, but it sets the funding level.
Governor of Washington (bob-ferguson): Fills judicial vacancies (weight 5). Gov. Ferguson, elected Nov 2024, appoints to vacancies in counties over 100,000 people.
Pierce County Prosecuting Attorney (pa-office / Mary Robnett mary-robnett): The PA prosecutes all felony cases in the court (weight 5/4). This is the most common government contact — the PA files most of the court’s criminal cases.
Keith Swank (keith-swank): Listed in the graph as “enforces” (weight 4). Likely a law enforcement officer who carries out court orders. UNVERIFIED in this pass.
Federal District Court (WDWA/Tacoma) (federal-district-court): Federal review of state convictions through habeas corpus petitions (weight 3).
Court of Appeals Division II (court-appeals): Hears appeals from Superior Court (weight 4).
Lobbying: None. Courts do not lobby.
Other oversight: The Washington Supreme Court oversees court administration. The State Court Administrator’s Office and the Commission on Judicial Conduct handle discipline.

6. Other seats they hold

Stanley Rumbaugh (stanley-rumbaugh): Judge, Dept. 18. Elected 2012, sworn in Jan 2013. WSAJ 2026 Judge of the Year. Former presiding judge. Graph node (weight 4).
Mary Robnett (mary-robnett): Pierce County Prosecuting Attorney. Prosecutes cases before the court. Graph node (weight 5).
Pierce County Council (county-council): Budget approver. Graph node (weight 5).
Bob Ferguson (bob-ferguson): WA Governor. Fills judicial vacancies. Graph node (weight 5).
Pierce County Bar Association: Local group of lawyers who practice in the court. Not a graph node.
Washington State Bar Association (WSBA): State licensing body for lawyers. Not a graph node.
Superior Court Judges’ Association (SCJA): Judges’ professional group. Presiding Judge Adams is a Trustee and serves on the Education Committee.

Keith Swank relationship: The graph lists Swank as “enforces” (weight 4). Need to verify Swank’s role — likely law enforcement executing court orders, but identity/title UNVERIFIED in this pass.
Judicial vacancy appointments: When judges retire mid-term (e.g., Kirkendoll March 2026), the governor appoints replacements. Need to trace whether Gov. Ferguson’s appointees to Pierce County Superior Court have any network ties to graph entities.
Caseload data: Annual filings, dispositions, and clearance rates not published in readily accessible primary sources. Need WA State Court Caseload Statistics reports.
Assigned Counsel ($50.3M): This budget line funds indigent defense (attorneys appointed to represent defendants who cannot afford counsel). This is a significant spending stream — who receives these contracts?
Therapeutic courts: Does Pierce County Superior Court operate drug court, mental health court, or other therapeutic courts? These are significant power nodes in the criminal justice system.

1. Who they are

Verdict: Pierce County Superior Court holds strong structural power as the only trial court with full jurisdiction in the county. Its 23 elected judges set sentences in all felony cases, decide big civil disputes (over about $100K), and control family and probate cases for about 920,000 people. The court’s budget — $51.7M plus $54.9M for juvenile and $50.3M for assigned counsel — is about 8% of county spending. Its power is shared across 23 independently elected judges, not held by one person. Presiding Judge Adams runs administration, but she does not decide cases in other departments.
Conflicts-of-interest flags (defense counter-argument anticipated): A defense attorney would say the court’s close work with the Prosecuting Attorney’s Office could push outcomes toward the prosecution side. The $50.3M assigned counsel budget creates a financial system where free-defense lawyers depend on court appointments, which may push them to avoid angering judges. The counter: judges are elected on their own, not picked by the PA, and elections hold them accountable.
Analysis of alternatives: The opposing view is that the court is a neutral body with limited political power. It just handles cases brought by others — the prosecutor and civil plaintiffs. Under this view, the real power sits with the Prosecuting Attorney (who decides what to charge) and the County Council (who sets the budget), not the court itself. The court’s rank of 17 out of 163 may overstate its independent political power.
Confidence: High — court structure, jurisdiction, judge roster, and budget are well-documented in primary government sources. The main unknowns are caseload data and Keith Swank’s exact role.

Why TAM is on the map: it is the largest art museum in Pierce County. The Tacoma Art Museum (TAM) holds $58.6 million in net assets. Its board president, Dona Ponepinto, also runs United Way of Pierce County. TAM’s board ties into the county’s civic network — United Way, MultiCare (a hospital system), Wellfound Behavioral Health (a mental health nonprofit), Workforce Development Council (a jobs agency), and Tacoma Community College. That overlap makes TAM a meeting place for Pierce County’s civic leaders, not just a museum.
Other museums nearby: the Museum of Glass, Washington State History Museum, LeMay Family Collection, and Seattle Art Museum. They are nearby but are not the same organization.

Cultural programming: TAM is the main fine-art museum in Pierce County. Its shows (notably the Haub Western American Art collection and Chihuly glass) draw tourists, school field trips, and shape the cultural story of the region.
Donor convening: The Board of Trustees includes leaders from MultiCare, United Way, Wellfound Behavioral Health, Coordinated Care (a health plan), Workforce Development Council, and Tacoma Community College. Board President Dona Ponepinto also serves as President & CEO of United Way of Pierce County — the county’s largest funder.
Government funding: TAM gets grants from the Washington State Arts Commission. It may also get hotel-lodging-tax money from the city or county for tourism-linked shows.
Real estate: Located at 1701 Pacific Avenue in Tacoma’s downtown cultural district. The Museum of Glass, Washington State History Museum, and University of Washington Tacoma are all nearby.

0. Why this person or group is on the map

The Tacoma City Council is on the map for two reasons: it holds office, and it makes big decisions. It governs Tacoma (about 220,000 residents), the biggest city in the county and the county’s economic core.
The council writes city laws, adopts a two-year budget of about $4.7 billion, and confirms the mayor’s top appointments. Tacoma uses a council-manager system. The council sets policy. The city manager runs the city.
The council sits on screens at places like the Pierce Transit Board, Sound Transit Board, and the Tacoma-Pierce County Board of Health. This makes it a key power node.
Not on the map: the city manager (executes policy, appointed by council). The city attorney (gives legal advice). Individual council members get their own pages where they matter (Anders Ibsen, Kristina Walker). Advisory boards and ethics boards do not make decisions.

1. Who they are

Exact legal name: Tacoma City Council (City of Tacoma)
Entity type: Government — city council (the law-making body of a first-class city)
Governing law: Tacoma City Charter (set up the council-manager system in 1952); state law (RCW) 35 (cities and towns); Tacoma Municipal Code

2. Their career and offices

1. Who they are

Term expiration dates: Only Diaz (Dec 31, 2027) and Ibsen (Dec 31, 2029) have verified term expirations. Other members’ terms need verification from the City Clerk or individual council member pages.
Council member PDC finances: Individual campaign finance data not aggregated at council level. Each member’s PDC filings should be reviewed for donor overlap with graph entities (Chamber, unions, developers).
City manager appointment: Ibsen stated he plans to confirm a new city manager in Q1 2026. Who was appointed? This is a critical power decision — the city manager executes all policy.
Police chief appointment: Ibsen also planned to confirm a new police chief in Q1 2026. Status?
Land-use decisions pending: Tideflats Subarea Plan implementation is ongoing. What specific development proposals are before the council?
Open Public Meetings Act compliance: The 1999 Miller v. City of Tacoma ruling and 2010 controversy suggest a pattern of executive session transparency issues. Are there recent complaints?
Tacoma Public Utilities (tacoma-public-utilities): The city council appoints the Public Utility Board. This is a significant power board overlap not reflected in the current graph edges.

1. Who they are

Verdict: The Tacoma City Council controls a $4.7B two-year budget and makes laws for the county’s biggest city. The council’s power works through the full body passing laws, adopting the budget, and confirming mayoral picks. In the council-manager system, the council sets direction while the manager runs it — so the council’s power is agenda-setting and oversight, not administration. Council members’ seats on regional boards (Pierce Transit, Sound Transit, Board of Health) extend the council’s reach beyond city limits. The $40M General Fund deficit limits new spending.
Conflicts-of-interest flags (defense counter-argument anticipated): A defense attorney would point to past Open Public Meetings Act problems (Miller v. City of Tacoma 1999, 2010 controversy) — a pattern of closed-door decisions that hurt public scrutiny. The council’s partnership with the Chamber of Commerce (weight 3) could create a pro-business policy tilt. Three council members on the Pierce Transit Board could create conflicts between city interests and county-wide transit priorities. The counter: the council-manager system was set up in 1952 to replace a corrupt commissioner system. Public meeting transparency has improved since the Miller ruling.
Analysis of alternatives: The opposing view is that the council’s power is split across 9 members with no one person in charge. That makes it slow and consensus-driven, with limited ability to act fast. The mayor’s veto (overridden by 6/9) is a weak tool. The $40M deficit caps new spending. Under this reading, rank 20/163 is fair, but the council’s power is institutional rather than personal — no single council member wields the kind of power a county executive or prosecuting attorney does.
Confidence: High — council structure, current roster, budget, committee system, and government type are well-documented in primary sources (City of Tacoma website). Main gaps are individual term expiration dates, city manager/police chief appointment status, and PDC financial data for individual members.

Tacoma Housing Authority — Deep Profile
Case: INV-2026-002 · Profile: profiles/tacoma-housing-auth.md
Entity ID: tacoma-housing-auth · Type: organization · Domain: government
Tier: tier2 · Rank: 71/163 · Composite power: 0.030
Graph description: Housing authority administering federal vouchers, public housing, and redevelopment in Tacoma.
Known facts: THA is a Moving to Work (MTW) demonstration PHA; governed by 5-person Board appointed by Tacoma Mayor; Executive Director April Black since 2021; FY2026 budget adopted Jan 2026.
Status: ✅ researched — 2026-09-19 — tier2-chunk10
Sources: 7/5 (minimum for tier2)

0. Why this person or group is on the map

THA is the main public housing agency for the City of Tacoma. It runs thousands of housing units. It also hands out federal housing vouchers. It is a key partner in big city projects like Salishan. Its choices shape land use, affordable housing, and community growth across Pierce County’s largest city.
THA is on the map because it has power from running a big organization. It controls federal housing money and a large redevelopment budget.
A few related groups sit outside this map. Pierce County runs its own housing programs in a different area. Lakewood and Bremerton have their own housing agencies. They do not work inside Pierce County’s main power structure, so they are left out.

1. Who they are

Exact legal name: Housing Authority of the City of Tacoma. It does business as Tacoma Housing Authority, also called THA.
Entity type: THA is a public housing agency. It is a part of government. It was set up under Washington state law. It is not a 501(c)(3) nonprofit. It is not an LLC. It is a quasi-governmental agency.
Governing law: A Washington state law says THA must have a five-person Board of Commissioners. The Mayor of Tacoma picks each member. They serve five-year terms. Since 1998, one of the five members must be a current THA housing aid recipient (Source 1).
tax ID number (EIN): UNVERIFIED — could not find the EIN in public records.
Parent/subsidiaries: THA has no parent group. It runs as an independent agency. It manages tax-credit partnerships, like Hillside Terrace and Bay Terrace, through its property arm.
MTW designation: THA takes part in the Moving to Work (MTW) program. This is run by the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD). Only a few agencies nationwide get this status. It lets THA design its own housing plans (Source 6).

3. Where their power comes from

Power held — statutory authority: THA has the legal power to run housing aid programs in Tacoma. It manages federal HUD money. It runs public housing units. It gives out Housing Choice Vouchers (HCVs). It controls about 3,552 Section 8 vouchers. It also gives out special vouchers: VASH, FUP, FYI, NHT, and EHV (Source 4).
Market share / scale: THA is the biggest housing authority in Pierce County. Its Board adopted the FY2026 budget on January 28, 2026. The FY2022 budget had about $55.3 million in revenue and $50.8 million in spending. It added 57 new Project-Based Voucher units (Source 5). The FY2026 budget covers departments: Asset Management & Real Estate Development ($4,081,892), Client Support & Empowerment ($2,954,327), Executive ($904,800), Finance ($2,733,284) (Source 2).
Redevelopment authority: THA ran the largest housing redevelopment in Tacoma’s history. It was the $200 million Salishan project. THA tore down 855 public housing units from the World War II era. It then rebuilt a mixed-income neighborhood on 188 acres. HUD gave THA a $35 million HOPE VI grant in 2001. THA picked Lorig Associates as its development partner (Source 7).
Budget controlled: THA controls an annual operating budget in the tens of millions. Most of the money comes from HUD. Monthly cash payments were $11,792,969 in November 2025 (Source 2).
Appointment/veto powers: The Board of Commissioners approves the yearly budget. It signs off on contracts and payments. It hires and fires the Executive Director. It sets policy. The Mayor of Tacoma picks the Board members. So the Mayor has indirect control over THA through these picks.

3. Where their power comes from

Ronelle Jones (Commissioner, pastor, appointed 2026); Nathe Lawver (Commissioner, Pierce County Central Labor Council AFL-CIO Secretary-Treasurer).1Who governsExecutive Director April Black (first woman to lead THA in its 81-year history, appointed 2021; previously Deputy Executive Director for 6 years). Board Chair Stanley Rumbaugh has served on the Board since 1998.1, 3Who winsTHA has successfully secured major federal grants (HOPE VI $35M) and MTW designation. Its development partners benefit from THA-controlled project-based voucher allocations and tax-credit partnerships. Labor is represented on the Board via Nathe Lawver (AFL-CIO).1, 7
5. How they touch government

Federal (HUD): HUD is THA’s main funder. THA gets HUD money for Section 8, HCV, public housing, VASH, FUP, FYI, NHT, and EHV vouchers. THA sends its MTW plan to HUD each year for approval. Congress’s FY2026 budget gave THA more voucher money (Source 6).
City of Tacoma: The Mayor picks THA Board members. THA works with the city on land use, redevelopment, and community growth.
Pierce County Council: THA works with Pierce County on regional housing, human services, and law and justice issues (connection weight 3).
Tacoma City Council: THA works with the Tacoma City Council on redevelopment projects (connection weight 3).
Contracts and grants: THA partners with private developers on housing redevelopment. Its partners include Lorig Associates, 1DROP, LMC Construction, and Brawner. THA has also gotten state money for supportive housing.
Lobbying: THA lobbies at the federal level through CLPHA, the Council of Large Public Housing Authorities. Executive Director April Black joined the CLPHA board in September 2023 (Source 3).

6. Other seats they hold

Board overlaps:
Stanley Rumbaugh (Chair) is a founding partner at the law firm Rumbaugh, Rideout, Adkins and Wallace. He is a former Pierce County Superior Court judge. He served 10 years on the Bates Technical College Board of Trustees. He is a World Trade Council director. He sits on the WA State Association for Justice Board of Governors.
Dr. Minh-Anh Hodge (Vice Chair) directs Second Language Acquisition, Elementary Education and Leadership at Tacoma Public Schools.
Nathe Lawver (Commissioner) is Secretary-Treasurer of the Pierce County Central Labor Council AFL-CIO. He is a member of LiUNA Laborers’ Local 252. He chairs United Way of Pierce County. He sits on the Pierce County Workforce Board, the Greater Tacoma Community Foundation Executive Board, and the Pierce County Economic Development Board.
Rev. Ronelle Jones (Commissioner) is Senior Pastor at True Vine Community Church COGIC. She is International VP of the COGIC Youth Department.
Executive Director board overlaps: April Black joined the CLPHA Board of Directors in September 2023. She had been THA Deputy Executive Director for six years under longtime Executive Director Michael Mirra.
Development partnerships: Lorig Associates worked on Salishan. 1DROP, LMC Construction, and Brawner worked on the Salishan-Hillside renovation in 2026.

1. Who they are

Verdict: THA controls a large set of affordable housing and federal funding in Tacoma. Its power comes from its legal role as Tacoma’s housing agency. It also comes from its MTW status, which gives it more freedom. And it comes from its ability to run big projects like Salishan. The volunteer Board has deep ties across Pierce County: Rumbaugh in law and the courts, Lawver in labor, Hodge in schools. This gives THA reach across many areas. Executive Director April Black runs day-to-day work. She also represents THA at the national level through CLPHA.
Conflicts-of-interest flags: The Mayor picks Board members who then decide on redevelopment deals. This could lead to conflicts. Board members may back the Mayor’s political goals. Developers who get THA vouchers may have reasons to shape who sits on the Board. Nathe Lawver serves on the THA Board and leads the AFL-CIO. This creates a possible tie between THA contracts and labor interests. Stanley Rumbaugh has served since 1998. That is 28 years. It shows deep, lasting influence rather than rotating civic service.
Analysis of alternatives: A different reading would say THA is just a federal-policy tool. Its budget comes mostly from HUD. The Mayor picks its Board. Under this view, THA’s “power” is borrowed from federal money and mayoral priorities. The Salishan project, while big, came from a federal grant. So it could be seen as a federal project, not an independent THA choice.
Confidence: Medium — THA’s who they are legally, governance structure, budget, and major projects are well-documented in primary sources. However, the full extent of its informal political influence (lobbying, developer relationships, Board appointment dynamics) is under-documented in available sources.

0. Why this person or group is on the map

Inclusion rule: well-connected + decision-making. Tacoma Police Union Local #6, I.U.P.A. is the certified union for Tacoma police officers, detectives, and sergeants. It bargains with the city. It also gives money to local campaigns. The graph links it directly to Kelly Chambers ($2,400). That puts Local 6 on the Pierce County political-power map.
Adjacent but excluded: Tacoma Police Management Association Local #26 (sergeants and lieutenants). Tacoma Firefighters Union Local 31 (“Active in Democracy” PAC). AFSCME and SEIU 1199NW (other unions). All are labor actors, but they are not the same node.

1. Who they are

Legal name: Tacoma Police Union Local #6, I.U.P.A. (International Union of Police Associations).
Entity type: Labor union. Local chapter of IUPA. Also linked with Washington Council of Police and Sheriffs (WACOPS).
tax ID number (EIN) / UBI: No public 501(c)(5) EIN verified in the federal tax agency (IRS) files (UNVERIFIED). Unions under 29 U.S.C. § 159 are usually 501(c)(5) tax-exempt.

Phone / email: 253-272-2119; tacomalocal6@gmail.com.
Bargaining unit: Sworn officers, detectives, and sergeants below lieutenant. Lieutenants and above are in Tacoma Police Management Association Local #26.
Governing law: state law (RCW) 41.76 (police collective bargaining in Washington). The 2024–2026 contract is the current deal.

3. Where their power comes from

Domain = political. State law gives Local 6 the sole right to bargain for its unit. The union also runs a Political Action Committee (PAC) that funds local campaigns.
Statutory authority: Under RCW 41.76, Local 6 is the sole certified representative for its unit. The city must meet and confer on wages, hours, and working conditions. The 2024–2026 collective bargaining agreement (CBA) runs Jan 1, 2024 – Dec 31, 2026 (filed by City of Tacoma HR/Labor Relations).
Market / political power:
Runs a registered Tacoma Police Union PAC. It gives direct contributions under the Washington $1,200-per-candidate local-election cap (per News Tribune 2021 PAC analysis).
Records show a $1,000 contribution to a Tacoma City Council candidate in 2018. The $2,400 to Kelly Chambers (Council District 1 / Pierce County Council) is the specific edge in our graph.
Endorsements and public statements from President Henry Betts appear on KING 5, the Jason Rantz show, and KNKX. He has criticized Police Chief Avery Moore. These moves shape the public-safety story in local news cycles.
Key facts answers:
Who is funded and endorsed: Kelly Chambers (graph edge), past council candidates (per News Tribune 2021). Full 2024 endorsement list is UNVERIFIED.
PAC spending: No standalone summary on the state campaign-finance agency (PDC) page (UNVERIFIED on totals, but individual contributions are verified through secondary reporting).
Party-machinery control: None. Police labor usually leans Republican, but Local 6 has backed both parties in primaries. Not a partisan-machine actor.
Candidate recruitment / training output: None documented.

1. Who they are

The bottom line. Local 6 holds political power in two ways: (a) it is the only certified union under RCW 41.76 for its unit, and (b) it runs a PAC that gives up to $1,200 per candidate under Washington law. Its $2,400 donation to Kelly Chambers ($1,200 primary + $1,200 general) shows it picked sides in a competitive local race. The power shows up in labor-contract results and modest donations — not in control of any party.
Conflicts of interest (defense-attorney counter-argument): One critique: the union’s public statements on active criminal cases (e.g., 2026 Burbank/Collins/Rankine matter) blur the line between officer-advocacy and outside commentary. Counter-defense: union presidents commonly speak on matters that affect officer morale and due process; the speech is protected labor advocacy.
Analysis of alternatives (ICD-203): Counter-reading: a $1,200-cap PAC has little sway in a city of 220,000. Reading that elevates Local 6: in low-turnout primaries, a $1,200 endorsement plus phone-bank plus member door-knock is decisive. The visible donations are the tip of a broader member turnout operation. The tier3 ranking at 156 fits: narrowly political, contained to Tacoma, with cross-county reach only through WACOPS and Kelly Chambers.
Confidence: High on who they are legally, affiliation, and PAC activity (three primary sources: union site, City CBA posting, official Facebook); Medium on cumulative donation totals and current membership size (no public IRS filing located).

Tacoma Public Utilities — Deep Profile
Case: INV-2026-002 · Profile: profiles/tacoma-public-utilities.md
Entity ID: tacoma-public-utilities · Type: organization · Domain: government
Tier: tier3 · Rank: 77/163 · Composite power: 0.028
Graph description: Customer-owned municipal utility; not-for-profit; operates Tacoma Power, Tacoma Water, Tacoma Rail; serves 166,000+ customers across Tacoma, Fircrest, University Place, Fife, JBLM, Lakewood, Steilacoom, parts of Pierce County; 130-year operating history; largest department in Tacoma city government
Known facts: Formed 1893 by voter purchase of privately owned Tacoma Light & Water; 2025-2026 biennial budget approved Nov 2024; 6.5% power / 6.3% water annual rate increase for 2025-2026; CEO/Director Jackie Flowers since 2018; governed by 5-member Public Utility Board appointed by Mayor/City Council
Status: ✅ researched — 2026-09-19 — tier3-chunk1
Sources: 5/3 (minimum for tier3)

0. Why this person or group is on the map

Tacoma Public Utilities (TPU) is the city’s electric, water, and rail company. It serves about 187,000 homes and businesses across central Pierce County, including Joint Base Lewis-McChord (JBLM), the big military base near Tacoma.
TPU is on this map for four reasons: it holds a public office (the city gave it the right to be the only electric and water provider in its area); it makes big decisions (its board sets rates and runs the city’s largest budget); it has a long record (130 years in operation); and it is well-connected (its CEO sits on national utility boards, and its rail arm moves freight for the Port of Tacoma).
Adjacent but EXCLUDED candidates: The 5-member Public Utility Board is not a separate node — it is covered below as the group that governs TPU. Tacoma City Council is a separate node. Puget Sound Energy (PSE) is the main private power company in the region and is mapped on its own. The state’s utility regulator (the Washington Utilities and Transportation Commission, or UTC) is excluded — TPU is not under it. The Tacoma-Pierce County Economic Development Board (EDB) is a separate node. Click! Network was TPU’s cable and internet arm — UNVERIFIED whether it still operates under TPU after the 2024 sale.

1. Who they are

Exact legal name: Tacoma Public Utilities. It is a department of the City of Tacoma. Its three divisions are Tacoma Power, Tacoma Water, and Tacoma Rail.
Entity type: A department of city government, not a private company. Voters created it in 1893 when they bought out a private firm called Tacoma Light & Water Company. It does not aim to make a profit for owners. It runs on money from the bills customers pay, not from taxes.
Tax ID (EIN)/registration: It uses the City of Tacoma’s EIN. There is no separate EIN because it is a city department, not its own company.
Parent/subsidiaries: The parent is the City of Tacoma. The three operating divisions are Tacoma Power (electricity), Tacoma Water (drinking water), and Tacoma Rail (a short freight railroad serving the Port of Tacoma, Lakeview, and the Frederickson industrial area).
Ownership chain: Public. The City of Tacoma owns it. There are no private shareholders. Money left over goes back into the system.
Governing law: The Tacoma City Charter and Washington State laws on city utilities. The state regulator (UTC) does not oversee TPU because it is a city utility.
Founded: 1893, when voters bought the old private company. The first big dam (Mayfield Dam) came online in 1929. The rail division was added later.
Headquarters: Public Utilities Building, 3628 South 35th Street, Tacoma, WA 98409.

3. Where their power comes from

Power held: TPU has the power of a city-owned monopoly. In its service area, it is the only legal electric, water, and rail provider. It is the largest department in Tacoma’s city government. Its power comes from: the city charter (the law that gives it the franchise); market share (about 187,000 customers over a 180 square-mile electric service area); self-rule (it answers to the City Council, not the state regulator); its wires and dams (2,286 miles of power lines plus a large hydro dam system); and freight rail (it runs the trains in and out of the Port of Tacoma, a key shipping hub).
Government domain overlap: TPU is a government body that also acts like a big business. It collects its own money (about $1.2 billion a year in the 2025–2026 budget). Its board and the City Council approve its budget. It spends money on pipes, wires, and rails across Pierce County.
Budget: About $1.2 billion a year for 2025–2026 (a two-year budget). Tacoma Power alone reported $516.5 million in operating revenue in 2024.
Jobs controlled: Between 1,001 and 5,000 workers (the LinkedIn range). Tacoma Power alone has about 805 workers. Citywide, the utility had about 1,777 workers in 2018.
Rate authority: The 5-member Public Utility Board recommends rates and the budget. The Tacoma City Council gives final approval. For 2025–2026, the Council approved a 6.5% electric rate hike and a 6.3% water rate hike.
Land/real-estate: TPU owns a set of old dams (Mayfield, Cushman, and others), 2,286 miles of power lines (1,524 above ground, 862 below), and rail track in and around the Port of Tacoma and Frederickson.

3. Where their power comes from

JBLM and large factories get steady, publicly owned power. The Port of Tacoma relies on Tacoma Rail to move freight.#1, #2, #3Who sitsTPU’s CEO is Jackie Flowers (since 2018). The 5-member Public Utility Board is nominated by the Mayor and approved by the City Council. Flowers also serves on the steering committee of the Large Public Power Council, co-chairs the American Public Power Association (APPA) Climate Change Task Force, chairs the Grid Forward Board, and sits on the Tacoma-Pierce County Chamber and EDB boards.#4, #5Who governsThe Public Utility Board sets rates and policy for Tacoma Power, Water, and Rail. The Tacoma City Council gives final budget approval (state law requires it). Through Tacoma Rail, TPU controls freight movement at the Port of Tacoma — a key bottleneck. TPU’s big project choices (dams, the Click! Network sale, new meters) shape Pierce County’s infrastructure for decades.#2, #3, #4Who winsTPU customers win from not-for-profit rates. Big commercial and industrial users win from steady power. The City of Tacoma wins because TPU is its biggest department and supports the local economy. The 2025–2026 rate hike passed the Council without big fights — TPU’s rate-setting power keeps winning there.#1, #3

Its link to the Pierce County Council (weight 4) reflects shared work on water service for unincorporated areas, power lines, and rail rights-of-way. The graph undercounts two big ties: the Port of Tacoma (Tacoma Rail is its freight arm — weight UNVERIFIED in the graph) and JBLM (TPU is JBLM’s electric provider — weight UNVERIFIED). TPU’s rank (77/163) understates its power: a $1.2 billion city utility is bigger than most other economic groups on this map.

1. Who they are

Verdict: Tacoma Public Utilities runs the city’s electric, water, and rail service for about 187,000 customers across central Pierce County. It has a $1.2 billion two-year budget and between 1,001 and 5,000 workers. Its power comes from being the only legal provider in its area (a city monopoly since 1893) and from owning 2,286 miles of power lines, a set of dams, and the freight railroad at the Port. It answers to its own Public Utility Board and the Tacoma City Council — not the state regulator — which gives it more freedom to set rates than private utilities like PSE have.
Conflicts-of-interest flags: TPU’s not-for-profit setup shields it from some abuses private utilities face, but it also answers to no outside rate regulator. CEO Jackie Flowers sits on several outside boards (Large Public Power Council, APPA, Grid Forward, the Chamber, the EDB). She runs TPU and also sits on regional boards that push for the same industrial customers TPU serves — a possible conflict. The defense: utility CEOs often hold such seats to represent their city in national policy. The Public Utility Board’s 5-year appointed terms (not elected) keep rate decisions away from voters. That is good for expertise, but limits public say. The 2025–2026 6.5% rate hike passed without a fight, showing the current setup usually goes TPU’s way.
Analysis of alternatives: The opposing view is that TPU is held in check by the City Council’s budget approval, by public-notice rules, and by customers’ option to move (limited — there is no other electric provider in the area). Under this reading, TPU is a well-run public utility with proper checks. But the 2024–2025 rate cycle shows a different picture: TPU’s board approved the rate hike on October 23, 2024, and the City Council approved the budget in November 2024. Both votes were largely pro-forma, with no real changes. The real story is that TPU has far more freedom to set rates than its private peer PSE has before the UTC.
Confidence: Medium-High. TPU’s legal form, governing setup, leadership, customer base, and rate process are confirmed by primary TPU and City of Tacoma sources (reliability 0.95), backed by Wikipedia (reliability 0.8). Tacoma Power’s 2024 operating revenue ($516.5M) comes from a primary financial report. Main unverified items: TPU’s specific Pierce County land holdings, the exact number of rail customers Tacoma Rail served in 2024, and Click! Network’s status after the 2024 sale (UNVERIFIED).

0. Why this person or group is on the map

Inclusion rule: Tacoma Public Schools (TPS) is on this map because it holds office and makes decisions. It is the largest school district in Pierce County. It has 28,272 students across 69 schools (2023-24). It runs a large budget (with a $30M shortfall for 2025-26) and hires hundreds of staff. Its elected board sets education policy for tens of thousands of families. The superintendent, Josh Garcia, is one of the highest-paid public officials in Tacoma at $342,038 (per OpenPayrolls). The district’s school-bond link with Pierce County Council (graph edge weight 4) and its partnership with MultiCare Health (weight 3) spread its reach into county finance and healthcare.
Adjacent but EXCLUDED candidates: Puyallup School District is the second-largest in the county and is a separate entity. Franklin Pierce Schools is a separate district (linked through Lance Goodpaster on the Greater Tacoma Community Foundation board). Bethel School District is separate. Clover Park School District is separate (linked through Alice Phillips). These districts are outside the boundary at the current tier.

1. Who they are

Exact legal name: Tacoma Public Schools (also Tacoma School District No. 10)
Entity type: Public school district (government entity)
Location: Central Administration Building, 601 South 8th Street, Tacoma, WA 98405 (sources #1, #5)
Governing law: state law (RCW) 28A (Common School Code); Washington State Board of Education rules; Tacoma School Board policies
EIN / registration: N/A — government entity, not a separately registered organization
Parent: None; independent school district run by an elected board
Board composition: 5 members, elected at-large to 6-year terms (sources #2, #3)

3. Where their power comes from

Statutory authority: As a public school district, TPS can levy taxes (with voter-approved bonds and levies), run schools, hire and fire staff, set curriculum, and manage facilities. The board approves budgets and sets policy.
Budget and fiscal power: TPS is facing a $30 million shortfall for the 2025-26 school year, which means “major position eliminations” (source #4). A $10 million shortfall is projected for 2026-27 (source #4). The district’s budget process has public hearings and board votes, giving the board real fiscal power.
Enrollment and scale: 28,272 students across 69 schools (2023-24). Minority enrollment 70%. About 43.1% of students are economically disadvantaged (source #6). That makes TPS the largest educational institution in Pierce County.
Superintendent power: Superintendent Josh Garcia runs day-to-day operations. His salary is about $342,038 (source #7). That makes him one of the highest-paid public officials in the region. His three-year contract started at $292,750 when he was first hired in 2012 (source #8).
Domain overlaps: Institutional (education), political (elected board, bond elections), economic (major employer, budget authority), health (MultiCare partnership).

Pierce County Council: School_bond link (graph edge weight 4). The Council’s budget decisions and bond approvals affect TPS facility funding.
State funding: TPS receives state basic-education funding under RCW 28A.150 (the McCleary framework, a 2012 state Supreme Court ruling on school funding). State funding is the majority of TPS revenue — exact share UNVERIFIED from current sources.
Federal funding: TPS gets federal Title I money for students from low-income families (43.1% of students qualify). Exact amounts UNVERIFIED from current sources.
Budget adoption process: The School Board adopts the annual budget after public hearings. For 2026-27, adoption is set for June 25, 2026, with a public hearing on June 4, 2026 (source #4).
Campaign finance: School board races are non-partisan in Washington. Board members file with the state’s campaign-finance agency (PDC). Exact 2024–2026 spending for current members is UNVERIFIED from current sources.

6. Other seats they hold

Korey Strozier — Board President, Position 3. Appointed 2020, elected 2021, re-elected 2023. Term ends 2029. He is a Central Washington University (CWU) alumnus (sources #2, #3, #9). He links TPS to community leadership and education advocacy.
Josh Garcia — Superintendent since 2012 (chosen by the board). Before that he was Deputy Superintendent. Salary about $342,038 (sources #7, #8). He links TPS to state education policy networks (he has spoken at the ASU GSV Summit, a national education-technology conference).
MultiCare Health — Partnership (graph edge weight 3). Likely school-based health services or wellness programs. Exact nature of the partnership is UNVERIFIED from primary sources.

1. Who they are

Verdict: Tacoma Public Schools is a major institutional power in Pierce County. It educates 28,272 students across 69 schools. It has a large budget and many employees. The elected 5-member board sets policy and approves budgets. Superintendent Josh Garcia (salary about $342K) runs operations. The $30M budget shortfall for 2025-26 creates real pressure: the board must decide which positions and programs to cut. Those choices affect thousands of staff and students. TPS’s power comes mostly from holding office (legal authority over education) and being a major employer and budget holder.
Conflicts-of-interest flags: The MultiCare Health partnership (graph edge weight 3) could create conflicts if health-program choices favor one provider. Board members’ other ties (UNVERIFIED for most) could create conflicts with budget choices. The shortfall context adds scrutiny to all financial decisions. Shawna Freeman Lane was appointed (not elected) to Position 2 in March 2026, which may raise questions about democratic input on budget-cut decisions before her election.
Analysis of alternatives: The other reading is that TPS’s power is limited by state funding formulas (McCleary), federal rules (Title I, IDEA — the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act), and union contracts. The $30M shortfall shows that the district’s freedom is limited by enrollment drops and state funding levels. The board mainly chooses which cuts to make, not whether to grow. Still, the district sets the agenda for how cuts are spread and which programs are kept.
Confidence: High — official TPS website, Ballotpedia, and U.S. News Education data give strong primary and secondary sourcing for enrollment, board makeup, and budget situation.

Tacoma Weekly — Deep Profile
Case: INV-2026-002 · Profile: profiles/tacoma-weekly.md
Entity ID: tacoma-weekly · Type: organization · Domain: media
Tier: tier3 · Rank: 114/163 · Composite power: 0.016
Graph description: Tacoma Weekly — free weekly community newspaper serving the Tacoma / Pierce County area; broadsheet format since 2001; ~10,000 weekly circulation; published by Matt Nagle; founded 1987 as Tacoma Monthly, renamed Tacoma Weekly in 1994; published under Pierce County Community Newspaper Group (PCCNG).
Known facts: Free weekly community newspaper; founded 1987 as Tacoma Monthly; renamed Tacoma Weekly 1994; broadsheet format since 2001; ~10,000 weekly circulation; distributed Wednesdays to “hundreds of businesses and public spaces”; current publisher Matt Nagle; published via Pierce County Community Newspaper Group (PCCNG). Prior publisher John Weymer accumulated over $170,000 in judgments against him and his business since 1995; $9,157.06 in wage-theft claims paid over a two-year period; $5,000 judgment in 2019 to Grand Cinema; September 2021 — fined $15,000 by Washington State PDC for offering political candidates news stories/endorsements in exchange for money.
Status: ✅ researched — 2026-09-19 — tier3-chunk8
Sources: 4/3 (minimum for tier3)

0. Why this person or group is on the map

Why it is on the map: Tacoma Weekly is one of a few print news outlets that cover Pierce County government and local politics. It is on the map for two reasons. First, it is named in Washington State Public Disclosure Commission (PDC) actions. That shows a paper-trail link to political coverage. Second, it serves as a low-cost place to publish legal notices. The City of Tacoma runs some legal ads in it. It is part of the legal-notice system in Pierce County.
Other papers NOT on this map: The News Tribune (Tacoma’s daily paper, owned by McClatchy). KING 5 / KOMO / KCPQ (Seattle-Tacoma TV stations). The Stranger and Seattle Weekly (Seattle papers that sometimes cover Pierce County). Tacoma Ledger and other newer digital outlets. Gig Harbor Now (a separate small paper on the Key Peninsula).

1. Who they are

Name: Tacoma Weekly (newspaper).
Type: A for-profit community newspaper.
Owner: Matt Nagle is the publisher and editor. The paper comes out under Pierce County Community Newspaper Group (PCCNG). PCCNG calls itself “a locally owned and operated newspaper organization.”
Address: P.O. Box 7185, Tacoma, WA 98417.
History: Started in 1987 as the Tacoma Monthly. Renamed Tacoma Weekly in 1994. Has used broadsheet format since 2001.
Old owner: John Weymer was the prior publisher. Weymer had over $170,000 in court judgments against him and his business since 1995. His business paid $9,157.06 in wage-theft claims to the Washington Department of Labor and Industries (L&I) over two years. In 2019 a judge ruled Weymer owed $5,000 to the Grand Cinema for failing to deliver a paid printing job.

3. Where their power comes from

Reach (FACT): About 10,000 copies each week. Distributed on Wednesdays to “hundreds of businesses and public spaces in the Tacoma area.”
Legal notices (FACT): Tacoma Weekly runs a “Submit Legals” portal. Governments and people can publish legal notices there. That is a quasi-official role under Washington newspaper-of-record laws.
Editorial problems (FACT): In September 2021, the Washington State Public Disclosure Commission (PDC) fined Tacoma Weekly $15,000. The PDC found the paper offered political candidates a news story or endorsement in exchange for money. The paper ran cover stories for two paying candidates under a staff member’s byline without saying they were paid ads. This kind of finding raises real questions about Tacoma Weekly’s reliability as a news source.
Editor and owner (FACT): Publisher Matt Nagle is also the editor. Editorial and ownership are in one person.
Domain overlap:
Media and government: Legal notices, political coverage, and the 2021 PDC fine put the paper at the meeting point of local government, elections, and campaign-finance rules.
Media and business: A small for-profit paper. Its payroll and contracts have been in court (wage-theft claims, the Grand Cinema judgment).
FACT vs INFERENCE: The paper’s reach, founding, and PDC fine are FACT. Whether Tacoma Weekly is really a “community newspaper” in the sense of doing solid accountability reporting is INFERENCE. It may be more of a place for legal notices and ads. The sources reviewed do not say directly.

3. Where their power comes from






























IndicatorFindingEvidence (source #)Who benefitsReaders (about 10,000 a week) and advertisers benefit. Legal-notice submitters benefit from a low-cost place to publish. 1. Who they are

Verdict: Tacoma Weekly is a free weekly community paper with about 10,000 readers a week. It has used broadsheet format since 2001. Matt Nagle is the publisher under the Pierce County Community Newspaper Group (PCCNG). Its real power is (a) a low-cost place for legal notices, and (b) a place where local advertisers and political candidates can buy favorable coverage. The second use was flagged in a 2021 Washington State Public Disclosure Commission action. The PDC fined the paper $15,000 for offering news-story placement to paying candidates without saying so. The paper is on the Pierce County power map not because of a big audience (10,000 is modest) but because legal notices and political access are places where the paper has real say.
Conflicts-of-interest flags: The 2021 PDC finding shows a pattern of selling news coverage to political candidates without disclosure. Editorial and revenue were mixed on purpose. This is the main trust concern for any use of Tacoma Weekly as a source of civic news. On top of that, old publisher John Weymer’s track record of judgments ($170K+ since 1995, including wage-theft claims and a failed printing job) is a red flag about business practices. Whether current publisher Matt Nagle has kept or fixed those practices is UNVERIFIED.
Analysis of alternatives: A defense reading would say the 2021 PDC fine was a single case settled without admitting broader wrongdoing. The paper kept publishing. Current publisher Matt Nagle is different from old publisher John Weymer. The opposing reading is that the PDC fine is a sign of a structural problem in community-newspaper business models. With no paywall and small ad budgets, the urge to monetize political coverage is built in, not a one-off. A paper whose 2021 conduct included undisclosed paid political coverage should be cross-checked with other outlets before being trusted for any contested civic fact in this investigation.
Confidence: Medium — circulation, founding, format, publisher, and PDC fine verified against Wikipedia and the paper’s own website; the Wikipedia article references PDC and court records that were not directly extracted in this pass, so the PDC-fine detail is at one degree of remove from the primary record; UNVERIFIED for the specific 2021 PDC case number and any subsequent PDC actions against the paper under current ownership.

0. Why this person or group is on the map

Why it is on the map — from holding office / institutional: Tacoma Community College is on the map as a public college in Pierce County. It has a large budget (about $84M a year). Its Board of Trustees is appointed by the Governor and makes policy. Board members connect the school to major Pierce County power players (MultiCare, United Way, Pierce County Executive’s office, Puyallup Tribe). Its inclusion is from holding office (it runs a public institution with a budget and land) and well-connected (board members link it to MultiCare, United Way, Pierce County government, and tribal government) — Laumann, Marsden & Prensky 1983.
Adjacent but EXCLUDED candidates: The TCC Foundation (a separate 501(c)(3) supporting organization) is treated as part of TCC, not profiled separately. The Washington State Board for Community and Technical Colleges (SBCTC) is the statewide coordinating body and is excluded as a state-level entity outside Pierce County.

1. Who they are

Exact legal name: Tacoma Community College (also called TCC).
Type of entity: A public community college district. One of 34 community and technical college districts in Washington State. It is a government entity, not a nonprofit or private company.
tax ID number (EIN)/registration: Not publicly available in sources checked. As a public entity, it is part of the Washington State public higher education system.
Parent/subsidiaries: TCC is a standalone college district. It is coordinated by (not a subsidiary of) the Washington State Board for Community and Technical Colleges (SBCTC), which sends state money to individual colleges. The TCC Foundation is a separate 501(c)(3) supporting organization.
Ownership: Public entity of the State of Washington. A 5-member Board of Trustees governs it. The Governor appoints trustees, and the State Senate confirms them.
Governing law: state law (RCW) 28B.50.100. The Board sets and reviews college policies, oversees management, sets direction, approves budgets, and protects the school’s finances.
Established: 1965.

3. Where their power comes from

Statutory authority: The Board of Trustees holds authority under RCW 28B.50.100. It sets college policy, approves budgets, sets direction, and oversees management. The Governor appoints trustees to 5-year terms. The State Senate confirms them. This is a Governor appointment — political patronage at the state level.
Budget size: FY2023 total expenses: $83,971,405 (per the TCC FY23 Financial Report). Major categories: instruction ($31,7M), student services ($12.5M), institutional support ($10.1M), operations/maintenance ($9.7M), scholarships/fellowships/aid ($9.3M), academic support ($6.0M), auxiliary enterprises ($4.5M). Net position at end of FY2023: $105.9M.
Students: About 9,912 students (per the FY2023 report). Other sources report different numbers depending on the date and method. TCC serves about 9,000 to 10,000 students a year.
Revenue sources: Per the FY2023 report: 42% state money (through SBCTC), 24% tuition and fees, 19% local funds and grants, 8% auxiliary, 6% other, 1% federal. The state is the largest single source. TCC’s budget depends on state legislative choices.
Tax status: Public entity. It does not pay income tax. It is funded through state appropriations (tax dollars), tuition, grants, and auxiliary revenue.
Board roster and overlaps: See Section 6 for board overlaps.
Government share of revenue: About 42% state (the largest source), plus about 1% federal grants and about 19% local/grant funding. Government funding is most of TCC’s revenue.

1. Who they are


The bottom line: Tacoma Community College is a public community college with moderate institutional power. It has an $84M annual budget, about 9,912 students, and a Governor-appointed Board of Trustees. Its power is mostly institutional. It runs a college, a budget, a campus, and a workforce pipeline. It influences policy through its Board. Board members hold overlapping seats with MultiCare (2 members), United Way (CEO as Board Chair), the Pierce County Executive’s office (Andrew Strobel), the Puyallup Tribe (Strobel’s former role), Tacoma Public Utilities (Wortham), and the WA State LGBTQ Commission (Santiago). The TCC Foundation Board adds more overlaps with KeyBank, BECU, TAPCO Credit Union, and Virginia Mason Franciscan Health. That makes TCC a key institutional link between health care, banking, government, tribal, and nonprofit sectors in Pierce County.


Conflicts-of-interest flags: Trustee Andrew Strobel’s dual role — Strategic Advisor to Pierce County Executive Ryan Mello AND former Puyallup Tribe Planning Director — could conflict when TCC matters touch county policy or tribal relations. Trustee Lois Bernstein’s dual service on the TCC Board of Trustees AND the TCC Foundation Board could blur the line between public governance and private fundraising. Two MultiCare executives on the Foundation Board (Michael McDonald, Dr. Scott Meehan) plus Bernstein (retired MultiCare) create a strong MultiCare-to-TCC overlap — relevant if TCC’s health training programs or campus health services touch MultiCare’s interests.


Analysis of alternatives: The opposing reading: TCC is a standard community college with standard board appointments. The overlaps reflect the natural makeup of Pierce County civic leadership, not deliberate power-building. Board members are Governor-appointed (not self-selected), and their multi-board service is typical of civic leaders in mid-sized cities. TCC’s $84M budget is modest compared to MultiCare ($7.2B) or Joint Base Lewis-McChord ($12.1B impact). TCC is a mid-tier institution, not a power center. Its 42% state funding dependency means its fiscal health is controlled by the Legislature, not by its board.


Confidence: Medium — primary sources (TCC website, WA Governor’s office, TCC financial report) confirm the board composition, trustee terms, budget, enrollment, and presidential leadership. The board overlap analysis is based on documented board memberships. The significance of these board overlaps for actual policy influence is inferential — no specific instance of board overlap-driven policy change has been documented. The financial data is from FY2023 and may not reflect current-year figures.

The MultiCare-to-TCC board overlap (3 members across Trustee + Foundation boards) and whether TCC’s nursing/allied health programs create a training pipeline that benefits MultiCare’s workforce needs.

0. Why this person or group is on the map

Why included: big member count plus well-connected. Teamsters Local 117 is the largest Teamsters local in Washington, with 19,500 members. Many work in Pierce County, especially as state corrections officers. Joint Council 28 covers 50,000+ members in Washington, Alaska, and Idaho. Both groups back Pierce County candidates. Both are part of the Pierce County Central Labor Council (PCCLC), the local AFL-CIO body. (Sources 1, 3, 5, 6)
Who was left out and why: UFCW 3000, SEIU 925, SEIU 1199NW, and the Washington Education Association (WEA) are other unions. They sit in WSLC/PCCLC but are not Teamsters. Other Teamsters locals (174, 313, 38, 252, 763) are also part of Joint Council 28 but are smaller and less focused on Pierce County.

1. Who they are

Full legal name: Teamsters Local Union No. 117. It is part of the International Brotherhood of Teamsters (IBT).
Type: Labor union. Tax status: 501(c)(5), a tax-exempt labor group under the U.S. tax code.
Parent: International Brotherhood of Teamsters (IBT), based in Washington, D.C.
Regional group: Teamsters Joint Council No. 28 (JC 28), in Tukwila, WA. It links Teamsters locals in Washington, Alaska, and the Idaho Panhandle. It has 50,000+ members. (Sources 6, 7)

3. Where their power comes from

Members give them weight. Local 117 speaks for 19,500 workers in Washington, both public and private jobs. That includes 6,000+ state corrections officers (DOC), plus nurses, maintenance, and office staff. (Sources 3, 4)
They bargain contracts. The local holds contracts covering Washington State DOC workers (2023–2025 contract on file), freight drivers, and public safety staff. In April 2025 they won the top regional pay for fuel truck drivers under the APP/World Kinect deal. (Sources 4, 6)
They play politics. They run a federal PAC (a political action committee that raises and spends money on elections) called DRIVE, funded by voluntary member donations. They also run a state PAC called Teamsters Local 117 Working Families PAC. They back candidates in Pierce County, King County, and across the state. A Political Advisory Committee screens candidates and picks who to back. (Sources 1, 5, 9)
They organize new workers. In August 2026, 500 public safety workers from PSEU Local 519 voted to join Local 117 — a major organizing win. (Source 3)
Domains they span: politics (endorsements, PAC), labor (contracts), government (DOC workforce), and corrections (6,000+ officers).

Its JC 28 link (50,000+ members) and PCCLC link boost its political reach. Its power comes from how many workers it speaks for in key sectors (corrections, public safety, freight) and from running endorsements as a group.
Conflicts-of-interest flags: They once ran a dues-funded political fund (Segregated Fund) until Freedom Foundation sued in 2020. DRIVE now uses voluntary donations only. But the line between dues-funded organizing and political activity is still debated. Backing politicians who regulate their own workplaces also raises conflict questions.
Counter-argument: Local 117’s 19,500 members are still only a small share of all Washington workers. Their endorsements often back Democrats who would win anyway. So direct impact is hard to measure. The PSEU win was modest (500 workers). Their PAC spends less than bigger statewide PACs.
Confidence: High — strong primary sources from union websites, IBT press releases, the state OFM contract file, PCCLC endorsement records, and JC 28 official data.

0. Why this person or group is on the map

Why he’s on the map: Tim Reynon sits in three places at once. He is on the Puyallup Tribal Council, sworn in June 11, 2026. He runs the Washington Governor’s Office of Indian Affairs (GOIA), since January 2025. He used to be the City of Seattle’s Tribal Relations Director (February 2022 to January 2025). Few people hold this much reach across tribal, state, and city government. It shapes treaty, gaming, environmental, and police policy across Western Washington.
Other people nearby: Bill Sterud (Puyallup Tribal Chairman — his own profile); David Z. Bean (former chairman); other Council members Sylvia Miller, Annette Bryan, Anna Bean, Amber Hayward, and Fred Dillon. They are noted as open questions for follow-up.

1. Who they are

DOB / birthplace: Not public in the sources we checked. UNVERIFIED.
Residence: Puyallup/Tacoma area (per the Puyallup Tribe council roster and LinkedIn).
Family: Married about 30 years to Maile Reynon. Three sons (per GOIA bio).

Bachelor of Social Work, BYU–Hawaii.
Admitted to the Washington State Bar in 1999.

3. Where their power comes from

What power does he hold?

Tribal elected office. On the Puyallup Tribal Council since June 11, 2026 (three-year term). He also served on the Council from 2014 to 2020. The Puyallup Tribe is the largest federally recognized tribe in Pierce County. It owns major land in Tacoma and runs the Emerald Queen Casino. It has strong say over Tacoma-Pierce County policy.
State executive-branch authority. Director of GOIA, appointed by Governor-elect Bob Ferguson, effective January 2025. GOIA is the state’s main link to Washington’s 29 federally recognized tribes. The Director runs the Centennial Accord process (a state-tribal meeting agreement).
Municipal and civil-rights leadership. Former Vice Chair of the Washington State Criminal Justice Training Commission. Former Vice Chair of the Washington Coalition for Police Accountability. Co-Chair of De-Escalate WA, which led the winning 2018 Initiative 940 campaign on police training. Served on the Governor’s Task Force on Independent Investigations of Police Use of Force (2019) and the 2016 Joint Legislative Task Force on Use of Deadly Force in Community Policing.
Legal and HR expertise. Over 22 years as a tribal attorney, Executive Director of HR / Training / Education, and People Operations Director / Compliance Officer at the Puyallup Tribal Health Authority.


Key facts:

Tax status: he serves in tribal, state, and (formerly) municipal roles. None carry private tax implications for him personally.
Board overlaps: Vice Chair of the CJTC (Criminal Justice Training Commission). Secretary of the Purpose Dignity Action (PDA) Board. Former Vice Chair of the Washington Coalition for Police Accountability.

1. Who they are

Verdict: Reynon is a key figure who links tribal, state, and city government. He sits on the Puyallup Tribal Council (elected, June 2026) and runs the Governor’s Office of Indian Affairs (appointed, January 2025). That gives him a rare “inside both rooms” view on tribal-state talks. Why he is on the map: Tom Pierson holds two power roles at once. He is the Interim CEO of the Tacoma-Pierce County Chamber (the county’s main business-advocacy group). He was also the Acting Director of Pierce County Economic Development — a county-government role. That makes him a classic “revolving door” figure. He went back and forth between private-sector advocacy and a county job.
He earned his place because he makes decisions. As Chamber CEO he led the lobbying coalition that won funding for the SR-167 Completion project (a key highway project). He also formed the Manufacturing Industrial Council for the South Sound. Both were real policy wins.

1. Who they are

Pierce County Economic Development appointment: PRIMARY SOURCE NEEDED. Pierson’s LinkedIn says “Acting Director” but no Pierce County government press release, appointment letter, or PDC F-1 financial affairs statement was found. Search Pierce County Executive’s office press releases and PDC F-1 database for “Tom Pierson” to confirm dates, scope, and salary.
PDC contributor search: Search WA PDC contributions database for “Tom Pierson” personally — does he donate to candidates? Which ones? This would reveal political preferences and potential quid pro quo patterns.
Pierce County Assessor records: Search for property holdings under “Tom Pierson” in Pierce County — any real-estate interests that could conflict with economic development decisions?
Chamber audit findings: The FY2022 and FY2024 “Material noncompliance” findings, plus FY2023 and FY2025 internal-control deficiencies (source #3) — was Pierson CEO during the audit periods? What specific federal grant programs were affected? Obtain the actual audit reports from ProPublica/Federal Audit Clearinghouse.
SR-167 Completion funding: Trace the specific legislative appropriations and coalition lobbying expenditures Pierson led. Who benefited? Were Chamber members among the contractors?
Bruce Kendall (EDB): The Economic Development Board operates in parallel to the Chamber — is there a formal relationship or rivalry? Map the EDB–Chamber–County Econ Dev triangle.

1. Who they are

Verdict: Tom Pierson controls the organized business voice in Pierce County through the Chamber CEO role. He also held a government economic-development decision-maker role (Acting Director). His power comes from the offices he holds and his network. He is not rich on his own — he is a salaried executive (top pay $195K, source #3). His rank of 11 out of 163 comes from his role as the main bridge between economic and government power. The two strong graph edges (CEO=5, acting_director=6) reflect that bridge.
Possible conflicts of interest (defense expected): The revolving-door pattern creates an apparent conflict. The same person lobbies for business, then runs a county economic-development office, then returns to lobbying. Defense: Economic development pros often move between public and private roles. That is the industry norm, not corruption. Pierson’s certifications (Economic Development Essentials, Accredited Chamber Executive) and his 14+ years of Chamber leadership show he is qualified. No ethics complaints or legal actions were found. The revolving door is a structural feature of the field, not a sign of personal misconduct.
Other ways to read this: The opposite reading is that Pierson is a mid-career professional. His network comes from his jobs, not personal power — if the Chamber hired a different CEO, that person would fill the same role. The acting_director role is, by definition, temporary. Under this reading, his 0.131 composite score overstates his personal power and understates the power of the office. But his specific wins (SR-167 funding, forming the Manufacturing Industrial Council) and his re-appointment as interim CEO show personal ties and institutional knowledge that are not easy to swap out.
Confidence: Medium. Primary sources confirm the Chamber CEO role and compensation (IRS 990, reliability 0.95) and the 2012 EDC board appointment (Pierce County Council minutes, reliability 0.9). The Acting Director of Economic Development role is only self-attested (LinkedIn, reliability 0.4) and requires government-source confirmation. The revolving-door inference is directionally correct but the specific government role is not yet primary-sourced.

Self-described “#1 Volume Toyota dealership in the Puget Sound.” Federally documented political donor to multiple WA Republican candidates, including a $1,000 contribution to Kelly Chambers (R) on 2020-07-12.
Known facts: 1400 River Rd, Puyallup WA 98371; founded 1970; owner = Kerry Sawyer Odeman (President & GM); second-generation family business; 26-time Toyota President’s Award winner.

0. Why this person or group is on the map

Toyota of Puyallup is on the map for two reasons. First, the graph already lists it as a donor to Kelly Chambers (weight 3). Second, it sits on Puyallup’s River Rd corridor. That corridor is inside the same land-use and downtown-redevelopment zone that Jim Kastama and the Puyallup City Council control. The dealership calls itself the “#1 Volume Toyota dealership in the Puget Sound.” That gives it name recognition in any commercial-corridor policy fight.
A few related names sit outside this map.
Glenn Sawyer, the founder, has passed away. He is Kerry’s father. He is listed as an open question.
Any sister stores in Tacoma or Federal Way are unverified. They are also open questions.

1. Who they are

Trade name: Toyota of Puyallup.
Entity form: It is a privately-held auto dealership in Washington state. The corporate parent is the Sawyer/Odeman family. The exact legal entity name, likely an LLC, is not listed on the dealer website. It is unverified at the state level.
Operating address: 1400 River Rd, Puyallup, WA 98371. This comes from the Toyota of Puyallup website and DealerRater.
Founded: 1970. The Facebook page says “Her father was awarded the Toyota franchise in 1970” (Source 2). A 2023 PRWeb release says “Toyota of Puyallup was founded by my father, Glenn Sawyer, in 1970” (Source 3).
Owner / leadership: Kerry Sawyer Odeman is the President & General Manager. She calls herself “a second generation auto dealer, serving the South Sound for more than 48 years” (Facebook post, 2017). She is the listed owner on the Our Story page.
Awards: A Facebook post says “The only dealership in the state of Washington to receive Toyota’s prestigious ‘President’s Award’ for twenty-six [years].” The same 26-time award claim appears on other dealer pages.
Governing law: Washington state law on Motor Vehicle Dealers (state law RCW 46.70) covers this dealership. It also has a franchise agreement with Toyota Motor Sales, U.S.A.

3. Where their power comes from

Market position: The dealership’s homepage says it is the “#1 Volume Toyota Dealership in the Puget Sound” (Source 1). The Sawyer family has run it since 1970. It is now second-generation. Winning the President’s Award for many years shows strong sales volume.
Political influence: Federal records show political donations. See Sources. The dealership gave $1,000 to Kelly Chambers (R) on July 12, 2020. It also gave to Hans Zeiger (R-WA) in 2015 and 2016, to Rob McKenna (R) in 2011, and to Reagan Dunn (R) in 2011 (Source 4).
Civic / community influence: The dealership’s Community Involvement page lists ongoing charity work. It has ties to the Washington Premier Football Club (Source 3, a 2023 Kerry Odeman quote).
Government contracts / grants: No public records show direct government contracts. This is normal for a retail car dealer.
Jobs / land: Employee count is unverified. The River Rd store is large and likely adds to local jobs and the tax base. But no primary source confirms exact numbers.

1. Who they are

Verdict: Toyota of Puyallup is a single-store, family-run Toyota franchise. It is a high-volume store and it is a known Republican donor in Pierce County politics. The graph edge to Kelly Chambers (weight 3) is confirmed by a verified $1,000 federal donation on July 12, 2020. The same store gave federal money to Hans Zeiger (R, 25th LD), Rob McKenna (R, former WA AG), and Reagan Dunn (R, King County). Its standalone political weight is low (composite 0.001). But the pattern is clear: this is one of the two main River Rd dealers backing the 25th LD and Pierce County Republican donor pool. The story: Glenn Sawyer got the franchise in 1970. His family ran the store for decades. His daughter Kerry Sawyer Odeman took over and grew it to “#1 volume” status. It has won the President’s Award 26 times. It has kept giving to federal candidates.
Conflicts-of-interest flags: No direct city-contract conflict shows up in public records. The store only gives to Republican candidates in the records reviewed. That is consistent, but not a legal problem.
Analysis of alternatives: The other reading is that Toyota of Puyallup is just a successful family business. Its political donations are routine civic work. A single $1,000 federal donation is well within normal small-business political activity. That reading is fair. The argument for including it is the pattern. The same store gave to the entire 25th LD Republican group: Zeiger, Chambers, and McKenna-era Pierce Republicans. That fits a dealer-class donor group, not isolated civic donations.
Confidence: High — corporate-identity facts and the political-contribution claim to Kelly Chambers are corroborated by primary-source FEC filings via OpenSecrets, with corporate self-disclosure as secondary corroboration; the cross-corroboration across 5 independent sources is sufficient for a tier3 deep profile.

Tacoma-Pierce County Health Dept — Deep Profile
Case: INV-2026-002 · Profile: profiles/tpchd.md
Entity ID: tpchd · Type: organization · Domain: government
Tier: tier2 · Rank: 42/163 · Composite power: 0.046
Graph description: Independent government health agency serving ~952K Pierce County residents; 2026-27 budget $102.9M; ~284 FTE; governed by appointed Board of Health
Known facts: Founded 1972; Director of Public Health: Chantell Harmon Reed; Health Officer: Dr. James S. Miller; 3629 S. D St., Tacoma, WA 98418; PHAB-accredited
Status: ✅ researched — 2026-09-19 — tier2-chunk4
Sources: 10/5 (minimum for tier2)

0. Why this person or group is on the map

Why TPCHD is on the map: TPCHD is the sole local public health agency for Pierce County (about 952,600 people as of 2024). State law (RCW 70.05) gives it power to protect health. It does this through disease prevention, food safety, septic permits, and family health services. Its $102.9M two-year budget and about 284 full-time staff (FTE) give it real muscle. The Board of Health — made up of Pierce County Council members, Tacoma City Council members, the County Executive, and others — sets policy for the whole county.
Why others near it are NOT on the map: The Washington State Department of Health is a separate state-level agency. Franciscan Health System / Virginia Mason Franciscan Health (a hospital system) is mapped separately. The Perinatal Collaborative of Pierce County (a TPCHD-affiliated 501c3) is a sub-entity. The Pierce County Medical Society (which appoints one Board of Health member) is mapped separately.

1. Who they are

Legal name: Tacoma-Pierce County Health Department (TPCHD)
Type: Independent government agency (local health jurisdiction)
Founded: 1972 (per Wikipedia). Created by an interlocal agreement between Pierce County and the City of Tacoma.
Governing law: Revised Code of Washington (RCW) 70.05 (local health departments); RCW 70.05.070 (powers and duties of local health officers); RCW 70.28.031; interlocal agreement between Pierce County and the City of Tacoma.
Tax ID (EIN): Government entity. Pierce County acts as the fiduciary agent.
Parent/subsidiaries: No parent. Run by the Tacoma-Pierce County Board of Health, an independent policy body. Pierce County is the fiduciary agent.
Accreditation: One of about 400 local health departments in the U.S. that meet Public Health Accreditation Board (PHAB) standards.
Headquarters: 3629 South D Street, Tacoma, WA 98418-6813. Also has a Key Peninsula office at 9013 Key Peninsula Hwy N, Lakewood, WA 98349 (open Thursdays 11am-2pm).

3. Where their power comes from

Statutory authority: RCW 70.05 gives TPCHD power over food safety (restaurant inspections, food worker cards), drinking water safety, septic system permits, disease control (TB, HIV/AIDS, whooping cough), environmental health, and vital records (birth and death certificates). The Health Officer (Dr. James S. Miller) has powers under RCW 70.05.070 and RCW 70.28.031.
Budget: 2026-2027 two-year budget: $102,899,820 (later amended to about $108.7M per the April 2026 Board agenda). That is 3.2% of the total Pierce County budget. Funding sources: Federal 9.1%, State 30.4%, Pierce County 12.8%, City of Tacoma 2.5%, Permits & fees 39%, Private/local/misc 6.2%. The budget fell 19% from the 2024-25 amended budget of $127.6M. The drop came from the end of federal COVID money.
Regulatory authority: TPCHD enforces food safety codes, septic rules (including a new do-it-yourself septic inspection program), environmental health codes, and disease control rules. It inspects restaurants, issues food worker cards, and regulates on-site sewage systems.
Area covered: All of Pierce County (about 952,600 people in 2024). This includes cities like Tacoma, Puyallup, Lakewood, Gig Harbor, and University Place, plus unincorporated areas.
Staffing: 284 FTE in 2026. Down from 349 in 2025 and 355 in 2024. The drop reflects post-COVID budget cuts. Four divisions: Disease Prevention & Management, Environmental Health, Strengthening Families, Administrative Services.
Domain overlap: Government (health rules, statutory authority), Social (public health services, family support, substance abuse prevention), Economic (food safety permits, septic permits that affect property values).

3. Where their power comes from
