5. How they touch government

Board of Health: TPCHD’s governing body. Three members appointed by Pierce County Council. One by Tacoma City Council. Plus the Pierce County Executive and Tacoma Mayor (or their picks). One from Pierce County Cities and Towns Association. One from Pierce County Medical Society. Two-year terms.
Budget: Pierce County Council appropriates the county share ($7,546,490 from the General Fund for 2026-27). The Board of Health recommended the 2026-27 budget via Resolution 2023-4795 (July 2, 2025).
Ryan Mello link: Pierce County Executive Ryan Mello sits on the Board of Health. He has appeared with Director Reed on public health events (like a youth violence prevention funding event with Tacoma Police Chief Patti Jackson and the Billy Ray Shirley III Foundation).
Federal money: 9.1% of the budget (about $9.4M) is federal. Reed told the Board that a $1M Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) grant (3-year, awarded 2023 for wildfire smoke health effects) was ended. That is an early sign of federal funding changes.
State money: 30.4% of the budget (about $31.3M) is state. This includes Foundational Public Health Services revenue ($8.7M per year, down $374K in SFY 2026).
Regulatory work: TPCHD regulates food businesses (permits, inspections), septic systems (permits, inspections, the new DIY program), drinking water, and enforces environmental health codes. It also runs the food worker card program.
Campaign donations: None. As a government entity, TPCHD does not donate. The department may push for public health money through the Board of Health and professional groups.

6. Other seats they hold

Ryan Mello (ryan-mello): Pierce County Executive; sits on the Board of Health. Weight 3 in the graph (board_of_health).
Pierce County Council (county-council): Appoints three Board of Health members (Hitchen, Herrera, Yambe). Appropriates county money. Weight 3 in the graph (board_of_health).
Tacoma City Council (tacoma-city-council): Appoints one Board of Health member (Bushnell or Sadalge). Mayor serves or sends a delegate. Weight 3 in the graph (board_of_health).
KNKX (knkx): South Sound public radio covers TPCHD, including the probe into Director Reed. Weight 2 in the graph (covered_by).
Pierce County Medical Society: Appoints one Board of Health member (Nicholas Rajacich, MD) and one alternate (Stephen Cook, MD).
Pierce County Cities and Towns Association: Appoints one Board of Health member (Dave Olson, Edgewood Mayor).
Perinatal Collaborative of Pierce County (PCPC): A 501(c)(3) nonprofit linked to TPCHD. The board includes TPCHD staff (Jax Hermer, Megan Monson) and reps from MultiCare, Mary Bridge, Sea Mar, Puyallup Tribal Health Authority, and other health groups.
ALF Tacoma Pierce County: Several TPCHD staff are ALF fellows or board members. They include Nancy Sutton (Immediate Past President, retired TPCHD Deputy Director), Jessica Gehle (Division Director, Environmental Health), Benjii Bittle (Business Development Director), and Leah Ford (Community Health Program Manager).

1. Who they are

Director Reed probe details: The Board of Health did not release the independent investigator’s full report. News Tribune reporter Becca Most asked for the documents. The full findings, the scope of complaints, and any ongoing fixes remain partly UNVERIFIED. This is a real accountability gap.
Budget amendment path: The 2026-27 budget started at $102.9M (a 19% cut). Then in August 2026 it was amended up to about $108.7M. What drove the $5.8M bump and whether more amendments are coming needs watching.
Federal money impacts: Reed told the Board that a $1M EPA grant was ended. The full scope of federal losses (beyond COVID-era cuts and the EPA grant) and what they mean for specific programs needs more digging.
Staff reduction context: FTE fell from 355 (2024) to 284 (2026) — a 20% drop. The link between this drop, the budget cuts, and the workplace culture probe is not clear. Whether services are still being delivered well needs checking.
PCPC governance: The Perinatal Collaborative of Pierce County (501c3) has TPCHD staff on its board alongside hospital reps. The financial and working ties between TPCHD and PCPC need more clarity.

1. Who they are

The bottom line. TPCHD controls public health rules for all of Pierce County (about 952K residents). It does this through state law (RCW 70.05), a $102.9M+ two-year budget, and about 284 staff. Its power runs through the Board of Health (which includes the County Executive, three County Council members, and Tacoma City Council members) and through the Director of Public Health. The department’s reach covers food safety, septic systems, drinking water, disease control, and environmental health. It touches daily life in ways most people do not notice. The 19% budget cut and 20% staff drop since 2024 come from the end of COVID money and have cut capacity.
Conflicts to watch (defense counter-argument expected): The Board of Health’s refusal to release the full probe report on Director Reed’s workplace conduct raises an accountability concern. A defense attorney could say the Board protected staff privacy and that coaching was a fair fix. The counter: the lack of detail hurts public trust, especially while staff cuts continue.
The other side: TPCHD is a low-power agency tied to its funders. Only 12.8% of its money comes from the county. Most comes from state and federal pass-throughs. Board members are part-time appointees with other day jobs. Its rule-making power is bounded by state law and its budget. Budget cuts may shrink TPCHD’s real power, even though the law still gives it authority.
Confidence: High — the department’s legal structure, budget, staffing, governance, and leadership are extensively documented in primary sources (TPCHD website, Board of Health packets, Pierce County budget documents). The workplace investigation is well-covered by secondary sources (KNKX, News Tribune) but the full report remains undisclosed.

Why we added Tucci & Sons: They are one of the biggest heavy-road builders in Pierce County. They hold many state and federal road contracts. They also donate to political campaigns and sit in local business groups. So they help shape how Pierce County builds its roads (source 1, 4, 9).

1. Who they are

Verdict: Tucci & Sons has real market power in Pierce County. They are one of the largest heavy-road builders and asphalt makers here. Their power comes from three generations of family ownership, two high-capacity asphalt plants, and a steady flow of state and federal contracts. Their two main federal awards alone total about $47.1 million. Their ties to county land-use decisions and the Chamber of Commerce give them influence in the local development coalition. Their donation to Kelly Chambers shows they engage in politics. The full scope of their political donations still needs PDC verification.
Conflicts of interest: They are both a major WSDOT contractor and a political donor. That puts them at the meeting point of road spending and political influence. The CBCA 4779 case shows they will sue over federal contract disputes. Their McChord plant is on or near Joint Base Lewis-McChord (JBLM), a military base. That raises questions about land use near a military site. No evidence of bid-rigging or corrupt deals was found.

The WSDOT bid check report shows they were the lowest bidder among several competitors. Active Construction, Inc. was the second-lowest bidder. 0. Why this person or group is on the map

She is the Chair of the Higher Education and Workforce Development Committee. She is Vice Chair of the Early Learning and K-12 Education Committee. Those roles give her real power over education policy and state funding for Pierce County schools and colleges.
She is also the only Black member of the Washington State Senate. That gives her a strong voice as a trailblazer and coalition-builder.

1. Who they are

Legal name: T’wina Nobles. Full legal name beyond public records is not confirmed.
Aliases: None on record. Campaign site: twinanobles.com. Facebook: SenatorTwinaNobles. LinkedIn: twinanobles.
Born: December 14, 1981, in Frankfurt, Germany. Both parents were in the U.S. military.
Lives in: Fircrest, Washington (28th LD). She has lived in the district for almost 20 years. She first moved there when her family was stationed at JBLM (then Fort Lewis) in 2000.
Family: Mother of four. Her husband’s name is not in public records. She entered a shelter in Alabama at 13 and went into foster care at 15 before reuniting with her father in California.
Education: Tacoma Community College (transferred). University of Puget Sound — BA in Politics and Government (2006). University of Puget Sound — Master of Arts in Teaching (2007).
Jobs: Taught at Stadium High School and Lincoln High School through Metropolitan Development Council’s College Bound program. President and CEO of Tacoma Urban League from 2017 to 2021. State Senator since 2021. Founder of Ladies First in 2012, an in-school and after-school program for young women. CEO of Black Future Co from 2022 (per BallotReady).

Budget power: As committee chair, she shapes state funding for higher education and K-12 programs that flow to Pierce County. Specific dollar amounts were not confirmed in this pass.

1. Who they are

Verdict: T’wina Nobles controls a major policy portfolio as Chair of the Higher Education and Workforce Development Committee. She shapes laws and state funding for higher education in Washington, with direct impact on Pierce County schools and colleges. Her power comes from winning two close elections in a swing district, her committee leadership, and her unique status as the only Black state senator. Her dual role on the University Place School Board creates a direct line between state education policy and local schools. Her life story (foster care, military family, educator) gives her real standing on education, equity, and military family issues that matter in her JBLM-containing district.
Conflicts-of-interest flags (defense-attorney counter-argument anticipated): A defense lawyer would flag her dual office-holding (State Senator plus School Board Member) as a structural conflict. She votes on state education funding that affects the district she governs. The counter: the roles are at different levels of government, Washington does not ban holding both at once, and her school board work gives her ground-level insight that helps her legislate. No formal ethics complaint has been filed.
Analysis of alternatives : The opposing view: Nobles is a junior senator with limited power in a chamber run by long-time leaders. Her committee chair role is real but limited by the majority caucus agenda and budget talks. Her 2020 win was very narrow (1,009 votes) against a weak incumbent, and her district is still competitive (though her 2024 margin was stronger). In this view, her power is mostly symbolic (as a trailblazer) rather than structural, and her composite power (rank 43 of 163) may be too high.

0. Why this person or group is on the map

Why he is here: Uli Chi is the board chair of Virginia Mason Franciscan Health (VMFH). VMFH was formed in January 2021 when Virginia Mason merged with CHI Franciscan. It is part of CommonSpirit Health. It runs the main Catholic hospital chain in Pierce County and Western Washington. As board chair, he is the top lay governance officer for a system that runs St. Joseph Medical Center (Tacoma), St. Anthony (Gig Harbor), St. Clare (Lakewood), St. Elizabeth (Enumclaw), and St. Francis (Federal Way). He decides on mission, ethics, capital projects, and regional strategy.
Who is left out: Ketul J. Patel runs CommonSpirit from Chicago — out of state. Julie Manas runs VMFH day-to-day as CommonSpirit Northwest Region President since 2024. She has her own profile or one coming under vmfh. Other VMFH board members are not on this map. Kevin McClatchy is not on VMFH; he runs Chatham AM.

1. Who they are

Full name: Uli Chi, PhD.
Roles and ties:

Chair, Virginia Mason Franciscan Health Board of Directors (since January 2021; before that, board chair of CHI Franciscan).
Vice chair and senior fellow, Max De Pree Center for Leadership, Fuller Theological Seminary (Pasadena, CA).
Faculty, Regent College (Vancouver, BC) — Master of Arts (MA) in Leadership, Theology and Society.
Fellow, Center for Faithful Business, Seattle Pacific University.
Board member, Benaroya Research Institute and Virginia Mason Institute (both in Seattle).
Former chair, Board of Governors, Regent College.


Education: Doctorate in Computer Science from the University of Washington.
Career: Award-winning tech entrepreneur. He founded Chi-LLC, a software company that made 3-D virtual reality space planning and visualization software for consumers and businesses. Founding date and current company status are not verified. He has shifted to governance and teaching.
Home: Greater Seattle and Tacoma area (LinkedIn lists Tacoma, WA).
Family: Not found in public sources.
Politics and ties: Publicly tied to Christian-theological-academic institutions (Fuller Seminary, Regent College, Seattle Pacific University). His governance role in a Catholic hospital system is professional, not religious.

3. Where their power comes from

What power he holds: Three power levers.

Hospital governance (VMFH Board Chair). VMFH is one of the largest private employers in Pierce County. It runs the region’s main Catholic hospital chain. The board chair sets the agenda. He hires and reviews the regional president. He approves big capital projects and major deals. He links CommonSpirit Health’s Catholic sponsorship system to local operations.
Ideas and thought leadership. He wrote The Wise Leader (Eerdmans, May 2024, ISBN 0802884040). He teaches at Regent College and is vice chair of the De Pree Center. This gives him standing in faith and leadership circles.
Network. He sits on the Benaroya Research Institute (Seattle immunology and autoimmune research) and the Virginia Mason Institute (lean-healthcare consulting). Both connect to Seattle biotech and academic-medical networks.


Power scoring:

Hospital-system governance = main source of decision-making power.
Christian-academic governance = reputational and cultural power.
Tech-entrepreneur background = economic base, now realized through governance pay and book royalties.


Key facts: VMFH and CHI Franciscan are public charities (501(c)(3) tax-exempt). Government funding comes mainly through Medicare and Medicaid. His board ties span Catholic healthcare, evangelical Fuller, mainline-evangelical Seattle Pacific, Anabaptist-evangelical Regent College Vancouver, and biotech (Benaroya).

Verdict: Uli Chi is a mid-tier but key governance actor. As VMFH board chair he sits at the top of a healthcare system that shapes Pierce County’s medical care, jobs, and real estate. His authority is governance authority, not ownership. But in a sector where the chair sets the agenda and approves deals, that is real power. His theological-academic network (Fuller, Regent, SPU) gives him extra cultural reach.
Conflicts-of-interest flags: (a) He is board chair of a Catholic hospital system while tied to evangelical Protestant institutions (Fuller, Regent). Theologically unusual but not improper. CommonSpirit allows it because lay board members do not need to be Catholic. A defense lawyer would call this the kind of cross-confessional ecumenism CommonSpirit encourages. (b) He sits on Benaroya Research Institute plus Virginia Mason Institute plus VMFH. That creates a tight intra-Virginia-Mason-ecosystem board overlap. (c) VMFH covers Pierce, King, Kitsap, and Mason counties. Chi’s reach is not limited to Pierce.

Graph description: County’s primary federated fundraising + grant-making 501(c)(3); convenes county social-service backbone; CEO Dona Ponepinto cross-chairs regional networks.
Known facts: United Way of Pierce County (UWPC); EIN 91-0650669; CEO Dona Ponepinto (joined Jan 2014); Board Chair Nathe Lawver (Pierce County Central Labor Council, AFL-CIO); FY23 CEO compensation $189,439 + $19,038 (per Form 990).
Status: ✅ researched — 2026-09-19 — tier3-chunk3
Sources: 5/3 (minimum for tier3)

0. Why this person or group is on the map

Why United Way is on the map. UWPC is the main private fundraiser and regranter in Pierce County. It runs the “From Poverty to Possibilities” summit. It is the local steward of the ALICE study — ALICE stands for Asset Limited, Income Constrained, Employed, a measure of working-poor households. That makes UWPC a hub. It ties together Pierce County government and labor (Lawver). It ties in banks such as Columbia Bank, Bank of America, and Banner. It ties in utilities (Tacoma Public Utilities — Jackie Flowers), transit (Mike Griffus, Pierce Transit), and health (Beth Johnson, Coordinated Care). UWPC touches nearly every tier-1 and tier-2 institution on this map. It also has a strong reputation as the “go-to” local philanthropy.
What is NOT on the map. The Greater Tacoma Community Foundation (gtcf) is a tier-1 partner with overlap but is a separate legal entity. The two groups coordinate but are distinct. United Way Worldwide (the national office) is not on the map. UWPC is an independent licensee, not a subsidiary.

1. Who they are

Legal name: United Way of Pierce County (operating brand: UWPC).
Type: 501(c)(3) nonprofit, Washington State. Federal tax ID number (EIN) 91-0650669 (per ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer).
Affiliate relationship: Independent licensee of United Way Worldwide. Part of United Way Pacific Northwest (Ponepinto chaired UWPNW per her UWPC bio).
Founding and governing law: Washington Nonprofit Corporation Act (state law (RCW) 24.03). IRS Form 990 filings (FY 2023 most recent reviewed).
Key personnel (FY24-26):
President & CEO: Dona Ponepinto (joined Jan 2014); FY23 pay $189,439 + $19,038 other; FY22 $196,908 + $20,271.
CDO: Emily Mendez-Bryant (~$109K–$115K across FY22-FY24).
CFO/SVP Finance: Peter J. Grignon (~$93K–$96K).
VP Community Impact: Jarrett Brunny (FY22 $105,508); current VP is Shawn Paton.
Board Chair: Nathe Lawver (Pierce County Central Labor Council, AFL-CIO).
Board Vice Chair: Jackie Flowers (Tacoma Public Utilities).
Board Secretary: Tanisha Jumper (Tacoma Public Schools).
Board Treasurer: AJ Gordon (Northwest Bank).
Directors include: Mike Griffus (Pierce Transit CEO). Beth Johnson (Coordinated Care CEO). Renee McClain (Washington State Fair CEO). Lua Pritchard (Asia Pacific Cultural Center). Sabrina Smith (Columbia Bank). Yelda Bryant (Bank of America). Pamela Devi Chandran (union attorney). Jeff Mincheff (J Squared Investments). Carlos Ortiz (Zeta-Maya Entertainment). Brandon Ervin (Ervin Consulting Group). Anthony R. Stancil (Ryder System).

3. Where their power comes from

Grant-making: UWPC raises money in the annual workplace campaign and regrants to about 30–40 partner agencies across human services. It also runs the Center for Strong Families and the From Poverty to Possibilities summit. Individual grants are small ($25K–$250K), but the annual pool and the convening power set the de-facto priorities for the local human-services network.
ALICE convening power: UWPC is the regional steward of the ALICE study. ALICE stands for Asset Limited, Income Constrained, Employed. Ponepinto helped develop it at her prior job. Pierce County government, United Way Worldwide, and state agencies cite ALICE when setting the official “self-sufficiency” income number.
Dense board overlap: The board reads like a who’s-who of the Pierce County institutional map. Pierce Transit has a seat. So do Tacoma Public Utilities, Tacoma Public Schools, Coordinated Care, and Washington State Fair. Banks include Columbia Bank, Bank of America, and Northwest Bank. Insurers include Regence BlueShield and State Farm. Labor includes AFSCME-aligned union attorneys. Other groups include Ryder System and Asia Pacific Cultural Center. Outside the Chamber and GTCF, this is the single best cross-institutional networking node in Pierce County.
Government contracting: UWPC partners with the City of Tacoma, Pierce County, and DSHS (the state Department of Social and Health Services). Together they run family-financial-stability programs through the Center for Strong Families. UWPC acts as a fiscal middleman for publicly funded services. That gives it quasi-governmental standing.
Cultural and regional voice: The annual campaign shapes the public conversation about poverty and self-sufficiency. Dona Ponepinto also served as President of the Association of Junior Leagues International, starting in 2022. That extends UWPC’s reach nationally.

1. Who they are

The bottom line. UWPC is the most important private cross-institutional board in the county after the Tacoma-Pierce Chamber and GTCF. It works like a standing executive networking chamber for the public, nonprofit, banking, and labor elite. Every director is a bridge to another tier-1 or tier-2 node. Grant dollars are modest (single-digit millions re-granted each year). The real power is the board seats and the convening role.
Conflicts-of-interest flags:
Board members from Tacoma Public Utilities (Flowers), Pierce Transit (Griffus), Coordinated Care (Johnson), and Tacoma Public Schools (Jumper) are quasi-public officials. UWPC’s agenda-setting affects their agencies’ funding.
The CEO’s concurrent AJLI presidency is allowed but extends UWPC’s reach into a national women’s-leadership group.
AFL-CIO board chair (Lawver) lines up labor policy with UWPC’s “self-sufficiency” framing. Some labor scholars say that framing moves the poverty talk away from wage and labor-law reform.
Alternative reading. UWPC is a normal community-foundation-style operation. The dense board reflects the small size of the Pierce County elite pool. Every executive knows every other executive. Coordinated power is not the only reading. Calling UWPC a “shadow council” is alarmist.
Confidence: High — board composition, CEO, EIN, and 990 pay figures are verified from primary sources (ProPublica + UWPC website + official news).

0. Why this person or group is on the map

Why it is on the map. University Place School District (UPSD) is in the map because of two reasons. First, State Sen. T’wina Nobles (D-28) sits on its 5-member Board of Directors. That gives the district a direct line to two state Senate committees: Higher Education & Workforce Development, and Early Learning & K-12. Second, UPSD puts levy and bond measures on the ballot. In February 2026, it placed a $320 million bond on the ballot. That makes it an active player in Pierce County Council levy decisions.
Who is left out. Tacoma Public Schools, Clover Park, Bethel, and Peninsula are separate districts. Each is on its own page or in open questions.

1. Who they are

Legal name: University Place School District No. 83 (Washington). It does business as University Place School District (UPSD).
Type: A Washington public school district. It is a junior taxing district (a local government body with limited tax power) under state law RCW 28A (common schools) and Title 84 RCW (property tax levies). It has no EIN (federal tax ID). It is a tax-exempt government body.
Governing law: RCW 28A.315 (school director elections); RCW 28A.500-525 (levies and bonds); RCW 84.52.053 (levy lids — the legal cap on how much a school district can raise through local property taxes).
Superintendent (current): Jeff Chamberlin (per UPSD83.org).
Current board (5 members): Marisa Peloquin (2017–2029); Ethelda Burke (2015–2029); Rick Maloney (2019–2027); T’wina Nobles (2015–2027); Mary Lu Dickinson (1995–2027). Source: Ballotpedia 2024 election page. Nobles was first sworn in in 2015.
Schools: 8 (2023–24).
Students: 5,606 (2023–24, OSPI — the Office of Superintendent of Public Instruction).
FY24 total spending: $98,082,000 ($17,474 per student).

3. Where their power comes from

Local decision-making: The 5-member Board sets policy for about 5,600 students and a $98 million budget. It approves bond and levy measures that go before Pierce County voters. The February 2026 special-election ballot includes two replacement levies and a $320 million bond. That gives the Board direct control of the building pipeline.
Bridge to the state Legislature: Sen. Nobles wears two hats. She is a UPSD board director and a state senator on the Higher Education & Workforce Development and Early Learning & K-12 committees. That gives UPSD a direct line into K-12 funding formulas (the rules that decide how much state money each district gets) and any McCleary-fix changes (court-ordered updates to K-12 funding). Most mid-sized districts do not have that kind of access.
Community power: UPSD is the main K-12 institution for the City of University Place and nearby unincorporated areas. It shapes school boundaries, land use, and where new schools get built across about 3 square miles of incorporated UP.
Why it scores this way: The score comes from the Nobles board overlap (graph weight 4) and the levy ties to Pierce County Council (graph weight 3).

1. Who they are

Verdict: UPSD is a tier-3 institutional node. Its influence does not come from size — only 5,606 students. It comes from Nobles wearing two hats: she is a school-board director and a state senator on the very committees that set K-12 funding. That makes UPSD a stronger policy pipeline than its mid-tier budget suggests.

Any votes where she recused herself should be reviewed. (b) The February 2026 ballot has a $320 million construction bond. The campaign-finance filings for that measure should be checked for contractor contributions.

UW Tacoma is included because it is the major public university campus in Pierce County. It has real institutional, economic, and community-development influence.
Power from holding an office: UW Tacoma is one of three campuses of the University of Washington, a major public research university. The Chancellor runs the campus with C-suite (executive officer) authority over a $100M-plus operation.
Reputational power: U.S. News 2026 ranked UW Tacoma #1 Top Performer for Social Mobility in the West (source #1). Washington Monthly 2025 ranked it #1 Best Bang for the Buck in Washington (source #1).
Power from connections: The graph shows edges to Chancellor Sheila Lange, John Wiborg, and the Pierce County Council for redevelopment partnerships. Chancellor Lange sits on the board of the Economic Development Board (EDB), the source for source #3.
The campus has been called “a catalyst for the revival of downtown Tacoma” (source #4).
Related but separate groups (not on the map as separate nodes): UW Seattle is the parent campus. It was founded in 1861 and is based in Seattle. UW Bothell is a sister campus. Tacoma Community College is a separate community college. It sends many transfer students to UW Tacoma. Pierce College is another top transfer feeder.

1. Who they are

Official name: University of Washington Tacoma (source #1). It is accredited by the Northwest Commission on Colleges and Universities as a unit of the University of Washington (source #1).
Type: Public university campus. One of three campuses of the University of Washington (source #1). It is not a separate 501(c)(3) nonprofit or LLC. It is a unit of the University of Washington, a state public institution. The UW Board of Regents governs it.
Tax ID (EIN): NOT CONFIRMED. As a unit of the UW, UW Tacoma does not have its own EIN. The University of Washington’s EIN applies. The UW Foundation, the fundraising arm, has its own 501(c)(3) status.
Parent and related units: Parent: University of Washington (founded 1861, source #1). UW Tacoma is one of three campuses. They are Seattle (Robert J. Jones, President), Tacoma (Sheila Edwards Lange, Chancellor), and Bothell (Kristin G. Esterberg, Chancellor) (source #1). UW Tacoma has no subsidiaries.
Ownership chain: State of Washington → University of Washington (public institution) → UW Tacoma (campus unit). The UW Board of Regents governs. The Chancellor reports to the UW President and Provost (source #4).
Governing law: Washington State higher education law, found in state law (RCW) 28B. The UW Board of Regents governs. Executive Order 20 of the UW Policy Directory sets the rules for chancellor searches (source #4).

3. Where their power comes from

Power held: UW Tacoma has institutional and cultural power. As a public university campus, it shapes who goes to college, who gets trained for jobs, and how the community sees itself in Pierce County. It does not have legal authority over county government. But as an anchor institution in downtown Tacoma, it has real power over land use, the economy, and community development. The campus has been called “a catalyst for the revival of downtown Tacoma” (source #4). Chancellor Lange also lobbies the state legislature in Olympia (source #5). UW Tacoma also has economic power as an employer and a buyer. The specific employee count and payroll were NOT CONFIRMED.
Power-domain overlap:
Tax status: Public university, a state entity. Not a 501(c)(3). It is tax-exempt as a state institution. Gifts to the UW Foundation (a 501(c)(3)) are tax-deductible.
Board roster and overlaps: Chancellor Sheila Edwards Lange sits on the EDB Board (source #3). She also sits on these outside boards: Pugh Capital Management, the Seattle Branch of the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco, Washington Campus Compact, AAA Washington, and the Seattle Art Museum (source #4). The UW Board of Regents governs the whole university. UW Tacoma has an Advisory Board (source #4).
Government funding share: Tuition is the “largest single source of revenue” (source #2). State “proviso” budget investments (special line items in the state budget) are large and growing (source #6: “UW Tacoma has seen significant growth in ‘proviso’ state budget investments, such as recent increases for engineering”). Specific state appropriation amounts are NOT CONFIRMED. Chancellor Lange pushes for permanent state funding for student services (source #5).
Key facts:
Enrollment: 5,059 total headcount in 2025-26 (source #1). 4,301 undergraduates plus 758 graduate students (source #1). Enrollment rose 3.97% in autumn 2024 (source #6). That put the campus within 7.4% of its peak enrollment in 2020-21 (source #6).
Student demographics: 52% are first-generation college students (source #1). 46% are Pell-eligible, meaning they qualify for federal grants for low-income students (source #1). 19% are military-affiliated (source #1). 60% of undergraduates are from underrepresented minorities (source #1). The breakdown is 32% Caucasian, 19% Asian American, 16% Hispanic/Latinx, and 11% African American (source #1). 51% are male, 49% female. 86% are full-time. The student-to-faculty ratio is 15 to 1 (source #1).
Academic programs: Over 50 undergraduate degree programs and options. There are 15 graduate programs (source #1). The largest schools are the School of Engineering & Technology (1,148 students), the School of Interdisciplinary Arts & Sciences (925), the Milgard School of Business (795), and the School of Social Work & Criminal Justice (392) (source #1). The most popular majors are Computer Science, Biomedical Sciences, Information Technology, Psychology, Accounting, and Finance (source #1).
Money: UW Tacoma gave out $60 million in financial aid in 2023-24 (source #1). Undergraduate tuition is $13,577 per year for 2025-26 (source #1). Graduate tuition is $22,668 per year (source #1). 68% of students get financial aid, including loans. 57% get scholarships or grants (source #1).

State funding: UW Tacoma gets state appropriations through the UW system. Chancellor Lange goes to Olympia to push for permanent state funding for student services (source #5: “visited Olympia last week to advocate for permanent state funding for student success services”). She pointed out that “nearly half of students are Pell eligible, more than half are first generation, and one-fifth are military-affiliated” to argue that “deep budget cuts would uniquely impact UW Tacoma” (source #5).
State proviso investments: UW Tacoma has received growing state “proviso” budget investments. These include $854K in fiscal year 2024 and $2M ongoing starting fiscal year 2025 to grow engineering enrollments (source #7). A one-time state appropriation paid for student support positions (re-enrollment, financial aid, mental health, career readiness) that launched the HuskiesCare online hub (source #5). A House capital budget proposal also included $7.7M for land acquisition at UW Tacoma (source #5 context).
Federal funding: NOT CONFIRMED. No specific federal grants to UW Tacoma were found in this research pass. As a unit of a major research university, federal research grants likely flow through the UW system.
Lobbying: Chancellor Lange does direct lobbying in Olympia (source #5). The UW has a State Relations office (source #5 domain). Specific L-2 lobbyist registrations for UW Tacoma were NOT CONFIRMED.
Contracts and grants: NOT CONFIRMED. No specific government contracts were identified.
Land-use actions: The 46-acre campus sits in downtown Tacoma (source #1). The campus has driven downtown redevelopment since 1990 (source #4). State capital budget proposals include $7.7M for land acquisition at UW Tacoma (source #5 context), showing that the campus is still growing. The Campus Master Plan is updated (source #4).
Campaign donations: None. As a public institution, UW Tacoma cannot make political contributions.
Puyallup Tribe relationship: The Puyallup Tribe of Indians is the “Tribal Sponsor of UW Tacoma” (source #4 and source #1). The campus sits on “traditional lands of the Puyallup Tribe of Indians” (source #1). This is a formal institutional tie to the region’s major tribal sovereign.

1. Who they are

Verdict: UW Tacoma runs a 46-acre campus in downtown Tacoma. It serves 5,059 students. It gives out $60 million a year in financial aid. State “proviso” investments are growing, including $2M-plus ongoing for engineering (source #7). Its power is institutional and anchor-institution power. It does not have legal authority over county government. But its role as downtown Tacoma’s revival catalyst (source #4), its workforce output (35,424 degrees since 1990, source #1), and Chancellor Lange’s many board seats (EDB, Federal Reserve, Pugh Capital, source #4) give it real power from connections. The campus’s social mobility mission (#1 in the West per U.S. News 2026, source #1) and its student demographics (52% first-gen, 46% Pell, 19% military-affiliated) give it moral authority and political leverage when it asks for state money (source #5). The Puyallup Tribe Tribal Sponsor tie (source #1) adds a tribal-sovereignty layer.
Conflicts-of-interest flags (the defense would make these points): (1) Chancellor Lange’s board seats on the EDB (economic development), the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco (finance), and Pugh Capital Management (asset management) span multiple domains. That could clash with UW Tacoma’s public-mission role. (2) The campus’s downtown redevelopment role (graph edge: redevelopment, weight 4) puts UW Tacoma’s interests in line with real estate developers. That could clash with community interests in affordable housing. (3) Lobbying for state money (source #5) while sitting on economic development boards mixes government lobbying with business advocacy. Defense reply: (1) Sitting on boards of financial and cultural groups is normal for university chancellors. It brings outside views. No direct conflict with UW Tacoma’s educational mission was found. (2) UW Tacoma’s revival role has been mostly good for downtown Tacoma. The campus’s social mobility mission helps underserved communities. (3) Lobbying for state funding is a core job for public university leaders. It is not a conflict.
Analysis of alternatives: The other reading is that UW Tacoma is a small regional campus (5,059 students, source #1). It has limited research output. It has no independent governing authority. It reports to the UW Seattle president and the Board of Regents. Under this view, the weight-5 chancellor edge overstates the campus’s power. The Chancellor is a subordinate executive, not an independent power holder. But the Chancellor’s CEO authority over a $100M-plus campus operation (implied from $60M in financial aid alone, source #1), her direct lobbying in Olympia (source #5), and her many board seats (source #4) give her and the campus more influence than their formal status suggests. The campus’s #1 social mobility ranking (source #1) also gives it outsized reputational power.
Confidence: Medium-High. UW Tacoma’s enrollment, demographics, campus footprint, academic programs, financial aid, tuition, and Chancellor biography are confirmed by primary sources (UW Tacoma official website, reliability 0.95; UW News, reliability 0.9; WA Legislature report, reliability 0.95). The main gaps are: specific campus operating budget (total revenue/expenditures not publicly broken out from the UW system), employee count/payroll, and specific federal research grants. The power assessment is well-grounded in documented institutional characteristics and board overlaps.

VMFH/CHI — Deep Profile
Case: INV-2026-002 · Profile: profiles/vmfh.md
Entity ID: vmfh · Type: organization · Domain: institutional
Tier: tier1 · Rank: 10/163 · Composite power: 0.142
Graph description: Virginia Mason Franciscan Health; formed 2021 merger of CHI Franciscan and Virginia Mason; affiliated with CommonSpirit Health; 10 hospitals including St. Joseph in Tacoma
Known facts: Formed Jan 2021; 501(c)(3); 18,000+ employees; ~5,000 physicians; 10 hospitals; ~1,500 beds; CEO Ketul Patel (departing for Wellstar late Oct 2025); CommonSpirit Health parent; $304M community benefits
Status: ✅ researched — 2026-09-19 — tier1-chunk2
Sources: 13/10 (minimum for tier1)

0. Why this person or group is on the map

Inclusion rule: Virginia Mason Franciscan Health (VMFH) is on the map for both office-holding and economic reasons. It is one of the two major health systems in Pierce County (along with MultiCare). It runs St. Joseph Medical Center in Tacoma — the largest hospital on the Tacoma skyline. VMFH has 18,000+ employees, about 5,000 doctors, 10 hospitals, and about 1,500 beds across western Washington. It is a major employer and care provider. Its board overlaps with Weyerhaeuser, Wellfound (a joint venture with MultiCare), the Washington State Hospital Association (WSHA), and the Catholic Archdiocese. Its parent, CommonSpirit Health, is one of the largest nonprofit health systems in the U.S.
Adjacent but EXCLUDED candidates: CommonSpirit Health (commonspirit) is a separate node in the graph. CHI Franciscan and Franciscan Health System are predecessor entities (excluded as historical). Virginia Mason Health System is also a predecessor. The Benaroya Research Institute is a VMFH subsidiary (excluded as the research arm). Bailey-Boushay House is a VMFH facility (excluded as a care site, not a governance node).

1. Who they are

Exact legal name: Virginia Mason Franciscan Health (VMFH) [Source #1, #2]
Entity type: Nonprofit 501(c)(3) organization [Source #1]
tax ID number (EIN): 86-1332353 (GuideStar profile) [Source #3]. Note: Virginia Mason Medical Center, a subsidiary, has EIN 91-0565539 [Source #4]. Virginia Mason Health System (the parent pre-merger entity) has EIN 91-1351110 [Source #5].
Formation: January 2021 — CHI Franciscan and Virginia Mason finalized their merger to form VMFH [Source #2, #6]
Parent company: CommonSpirit Health. VMFH is part of CommonSpirit, one of the largest nonprofit health systems in the U.S. VMHS and CommonSpirit are the only corporate members of VMFH. [Source #1, #5]
Corporate structure: Virginia Mason Health System (VMHS) and CommonSpirit Health are the sole corporate members of VMFH. VMFH is the sole voting member of Virginia Mason Medical Center (VMMC). [Source #5]
Governing law: Washington State nonprofit corporation law; IRS 501(c)(3) tax-exempt status; Ethical and Religious Directives for Catholic Health Care Services [Source #1, #5]
Religious sponsor: Catholic Archdiocese (graph node catholic-archdiocese, religious_sponsor, weight 3). The Sisters of St. Francis of Philadelphia founded CHI Franciscan in 1891. VMFH follows the Ethical and Religious Directives for Catholic Health Care Services. [Source #2, #1]
Headquarters: Tacoma, WA (St. Joseph Medical Center is the Tacoma flagship). The broader system HQ is in Seattle at Virginia Mason Medical Center. [Source #1, #2]
Hospitals (10): [Source #1]


St. Anne Hospital, Burien
St. Anthony Hospital, Gig Harbor
St. Clare Hospital, Lakewood
St. Elizabeth Hospital, Enumclaw
St. Francis Hospital, Federal Way
St. Joseph Medical Center, Tacoma (flagship, founded 1891)
St. Michael Medical Center, Silverdale
Virginia Mason Medical Center, Seattle
Rehabilitation Hospital, Tacoma
Wellfound Behavioral Health Hospital, Tacoma (JV with MultiCare)

2. Their career and offices

CEO: Ketul J. Patel — CEO of VMFH and President of the Pacific Northwest Region of CommonSpirit Health. He led the January 2021 merger of CHI Franciscan and Virginia Mason. Pay: $2,613,387 (FY2024, per VMMC 990). Total pay including CommonSpirit/Franciscan Health: $3,097,504 (per WA DOH report). Leaving: He was picked as the next president and CEO of Wellstar Health System (Marietta, GA). He is expected to start late October 2025. [Source #4, #7, #8]
Board governance: Per FY2022 Form 990 (Virginia Mason Health System): “VMHS is governed by a 3-person, independent Board of Directors.” All board members and officers must fill out conflict-of-interest forms. Officers follow CommonSpirit Health’s COI policy. [Source #5]
Board Chair: Uli Chi (uli-chi in graph, board_chair, weight 6) [graph]
Board member: Diann Puls (diann-puls in graph, board, weight 4) [graph]
Weyerhaeuser tie: Weyerhaeuser (weyerhaeuser in graph, board_tie, weight 3) [graph]
Julie Manas: President (julie-manas in graph, president, weight 5) [graph]
Board roster detail: UNVERIFIED beyond the graph nodes. The 3-person board (per 990) is small for an 18,000-employee system. That suggests governance sits mostly at the CommonSpirit parent level. The full VMFH board roster was not found in public sources.

3. Where their power comes from

Market power: VMFH is one of the two dominant health systems in Pierce County (alongside MultiCare). It runs 10 hospitals with about 1,500 beds, 18,000+ staff, about 5,000 doctors, and nearly 300 care sites across western Washington. In Pierce County it runs St. Joseph Medical Center (Tacoma), St. Clare Hospital (Lakewood), St. Anthony Hospital (Gig Harbor), and Wellfound Behavioral Health Hospital (Tacoma, JV). [Source #1] FACT.
Competitive position: VMFH is MultiCare’s main competitor in Pierce County. The two systems jointly run Wellfound Behavioral Health Hospital — a zone of cooperation in a competitive market. [Source #1, graph]
Religious and moral authority: As a Catholic-affiliated system, VMFH follows the Ethical and Religious Directives for Catholic Health Care Services. That gives it power over moral and ethical health policy — including rules on reproductive health and end-of-life care. This is a power that secular MultiCare does not have. [Source #1]
Corporate scale: Parent CommonSpirit Health is one of the largest nonprofit health systems in the U.S. (formed from the merger of Catholic Health Initiatives and Dignity Health). VMFH can tap national resources, buying power, and political advocacy through CommonSpirit. [Source #5, #6]
key facts:
Tax status: 501(c)(3) nonprofit [Source #1]
Board roster and overlaps: 3-person independent board at the VMHS level. Board overlaps with Weyerhaeuser, Wellfound, WSHA, the Catholic Archdiocese, and CommonSpirit [Source #5, graph]
Government funding share: UNVERIFIED exact percentage, but as a hospital system, a large share of revenue comes from Medicare and Medicaid. VMMC alone reported $1.4B in FY2024 revenue [Source #4].

3. Where their power comes from

Score each indicator with evidence:
| Indicator | Finding | Evidence (source #) |
|-----------|---------|---------------------|
| Who benefits | Patients at 10 hospitals and 300 care sites; 18,000+ employees; about 5,000 doctors; the Catholic institutional network (Archdiocese); CommonSpirit Health members. Community benefits: $304M in free, subsidized, and reduced-cost care. | #1 |
| Who sits | 3-person independent board (VMHS level) with Uli Chi as chair. CEO Patel also serves as President of the PNW Region of CommonSpirit — a dual role that gives him a direct line to the national parent. The Weyerhaeuser board tie shows corporate board overlap. | #5, graph |
| Who governs | VMFH is governed by its board, but final authority flows through its corporate members: VMHS and CommonSpirit Health. VMFH is the sole voting member of VMMC. This is a multi-layered structure with power concentrated at the CommonSpirit level. | #5 |
| Who wins | VMFH was formed through the 2021 merger, creating a regional powerhouse with national backing. The merger reduced competition in the western WA hospital market. Catholic ethical directives restrict reproductive health care, a policy outcome favored by religious conservatives. | #1, #6 |

4. Their money

VMFH system-level revenue: UNVERIFIED at the consolidated level. VMFH does not appear to file a single consolidated 990. Financials are spread across subsidiaries (VMMC, Franciscan Health System, etc.).
Virginia Mason Medical Center (subsidiary) financials: [Source #4]
FY2024 revenue: $1.4B; expenses: $1.4B; net assets: $426.0M
FY2024 total assets: $1.42B (per Instrumentl data: $1.03B in 2025 — likely a different reporting period)
FY2022 revenue: $1.275B; expenses: $1.231B; net income: $43.9M
FY2021 revenue: $1.008B; expenses: $977M; net income: $30.4M
FY2020 revenue: $990.4M; expenses: $984.3M; net income: $6.1M
Pre-merger revenue (2019, per Healthcare Dive): CHI Franciscan had $2.45B. Virginia Mason had $1.15B. Combined: about $3.6B. [Source #6]
Community benefits: $304 million in free, subsidized, and reduced-cost care and programs [Source #1]
Funding sources: Patient service revenue (Medicare, Medicaid, private insurance); grants and contributions; investment income. Government health programs are a major revenue source, as with all hospital systems. FACT.
Tax status: 501(c)(3) nonprofit — property tax exempt, sales tax exempt, donations tax-deductible [Source #1]
Property holdings: 10 hospital campuses plus about 300 care sites across western WA. St. Joseph Medical Center sits in an iconic tower on the Tacoma skyline (designed by Bertrand Goldberg, 1974). [Source #2] Parcel-level data UNVERIFIED.
Levy/bond history: UNVERIFIED. There is no public record of VMFH running under a public levy. VMFH is a private nonprofit, not a public hospital district.

5. How they touch government

WSHA membership: VMFH is a member of the Washington State Hospital Association [Source #1]. This gives VMFH a voice in state hospital policy, alongside MultiCare (whose CEO was WSHA board chair).
Lobbying: The graph shows a lobbying link with the Pierce County Council (weight 4). Specific lobbying spending was NOT verified — that requires WA Public Disclosure Commission (PDC) L2 lobbyist reports.
Tax exemption: 501(c)(3) status gives VMFH property and sales tax exemption — a large fiscal subsidy from Pierce County and Washington State taxpayers. [Source #1]
Medicare/Medicaid dependency: As a hospital system, much of VMFH’s revenue comes from government health programs. VMMC alone brings in $1.4B/yr, much of it from government payments. FACT.
Catholic ethical directives: VMFH follows the Ethical and Religious Directives for Catholic Health Care Services. That gives it a power tied to regulation — it imposes its own rules on reproductive health (contraception, sterilization, abortion, assisted dying). Washington State law protects reproductive rights, so there is tension between VMFH’s religious rules and state policy. [Source #1]

1. Who they are

What is VMFH’s consolidated system-level revenue? The current data only covers VMMC ($1.4B) and pre-merger entities (about $3.6B combined). A consolidated VMFH 990 or a CommonSpirit regional financial report is needed.
Who are the 3 members of the VMHS board beyond Uli Chi? The 990 shows a 3-person board, but only Uli Chi is named in the graph.
What is the nature of the Weyerhaeuser board_tie (weight 3)? Is a Weyerhaeuser executive on the VMFH or VMHS board?
What is Julie Manas’s exact role? Is she president of VMFH or of a subsidiary (like St. Joseph Medical Center)?
What are VMFH’s specific lobbying expenses at the state and county level? This requires WA PDC L2 filings.
How does the Catholic ethical directives framework interact with WA State’s reproductive rights protections? Has there been any legal challenge or policy conflict?
What is the governance structure of the Wellfound JV — what is VMFH vs MultiCare’s financial commitment and decision-making authority?
Who will replace Ketul Patel as CEO? What is the succession plan at VMFH after he leaves for Wellstar?
What is VMFH’s total property tax exemption value in Pierce County (St. Joseph, St. Clare, Wellfound)?

1. Who they are

Verdict: Virginia Mason Franciscan Health runs the second-largest hospital network in Pierce County. It operates St. Joseph Medical Center (Tacoma’s flagship), St. Clare (Lakewood), St. Anthony (Gig Harbor), and the Wellfound behavioral health JV. Its power comes from four sources: (1) market position — 10 hospitals, about 1,500 beds, 18,000+ employees, about 5,000 doctors, and about 300 care sites across western WA; (2) corporate parentage — CommonSpirit Health, one of the largest U.S. nonprofit health systems, gives VMFH national resources and buying power; (3) religious power — Catholic ethical directives give VMFH moral authority over health policy that secular MultiCare lacks, especially on reproductive health restrictions; (4) board overlaps with Weyerhaeuser (corporate), Catholic Archdiocese (religious), WSHA (industry), and through the Wellfound JV, MultiCare (competitor). VMFH reached its current size through the January 2021 merger of CHI Franciscan ($2.45B pre-merger revenue) and Virginia Mason ($1.15B), creating an about-$3.6B regional powerhouse under CommonSpirit. CEO Ketul Patel’s departure for Wellstar Health System (Oct 2025) creates a leadership transition worth watching.
Conflicts-of-interest flags (defense counter-argument): A defense would say: (1) VMFH is a nonprofit providing essential health care, including $304M in community benefits, so its tax exemption is justified; (2) the CommonSpirit tie gives resources that help patients, not corporate extraction; (3) the Catholic ethical directives are constitutionally protected religious exercise, not policy imposition; (4) the Wellfound JV with MultiCare is a cooperative arrangement that expands behavioral health access, not anti-competitive collusion; (5) the 3-person board is standard for a subsidiary of a larger system, with CommonSpirit providing oversight.
Analysis of alternatives: The opposing reading is that VMFH is a form of unaccountable consolidated health care power — a $3.6B+ regional system run by a 3-person board, ultimately controlled by a national parent (CommonSpirit) with no direct public accountability, despite receiving hundreds of millions in tax exemptions. The 2021 merger reduced competition in the western WA hospital market. It may have raised prices and reduced patient choice. The Catholic ethical directives restrict access to legal reproductive health services in a state (WA) that protects those rights. That creates a gap between state policy and patient access at VMFH facilities. The Weyerhaeuser board tie connects VMFH to the corporate timber power structure. The Wellfound JV with MultiCare is a cooperative bridge between the two main competitors. It could enable coordination rather than competition. The CEO’s departure for Wellstar raises questions about leadership stability and whether CommonSpirit’s commitment to the PNW region is strategic or short-term.
Confidence: Medium — VMFH’s structure, hospital list, and Catholic affiliation are well-sourced from the official VMFH website (primary, 0.9). Financial data comes from subsidiary 990s (VMMC) and pre-merger reports, but consolidated VMFH financials are UNVERIFIED. Board composition beyond the graph nodes is UNVERIFIED (the 3-person board is confirmed by 990 but other members were not identified). CEO pay is sourced from WA DOH and IRS 990 (primary, 0.9-0.95).

0. Why this person or group is on the map

Why it is on the map. The Washington Realtors Political Action Committee holds power from the PAC role and from the decisions it makes. It is one of the top 10 PACs by spending in Washington State (the state’s campaign-finance agency (PDC) data, source #1). It picks which candidates to fund and endorse. The graph also shows ties to the Chamber of Commerce and Pierce County Council. The PAC acts as a pipeline between the real estate industry and elected officials.
Who is left out: The National Association of Realtors PAC (RPAC) is the federal-level parent PAC. It works at the congressional level, so it is not in this Pierce County-focused graph. Local REALTOR® associations (like Seattle-King County and Tacoma-Pierce County) run their own local PACs, but they are not listed here. The Washington REALTORS® trade association itself (the 501(c)(6) parent) is a related but separate group from the PAC.

1. Who they are

Legal name: Washington Realtors Political Action Committee.
Type: A Political Action Committee (PAC) registered with the Washington State Public Disclosure Commission (PDC). A PAC is a group that raises and spends money to influence elections.
Parent organization: Washington REALTORS® (a statewide not-for-profit trade group with about 20,000+ members, source #3).
National affiliation: National Association of Realtors (NAR) / REALTORS® Political Action Committee (RPAC). The state PAC is part of the national RPAC network.
Registration address: 504 14th Ave SE, Olympia, WA 98501 (sources #1, #2, #3).
Phone: (360) 943-3100 (parent org); (360) 628-8129 (PDC filing contact).
Governing law: State law RCW 29B (Campaign Disclosure and Contribution Act, formerly RCW 42.17A). Run by the Washington State Public Disclosure Commission.
CEO of parent org: Lori Adler (source #3).
Tax ID (EIN)/UBI: UNVERIFIED — not directly available from PDC filings.

3. Where their power comes from

Power held: The PAC holds power to make decisions by choosing which candidates to endorse and fund. It is one of the top 10 PACs by spending in Washington State, with about $1,005,504.24 in spending in the current PDC reporting cycle (source #1). Its parent group, Washington REALTORS®, has 20,000+ members statewide (source #3), giving the PAC money and name recognition.
Political domain overlap: The PAC only works in politics. It endorses and funds candidates for state, local, and legislative offices. Its “REALTOR Party” idea is nonpartisan. The PAC backs candidates who defend REALTOR® policy goals, no matter the party (source #4).
Funded and endorsed: Candidates for statewide, legislative, judicial, and local offices across Washington. Nationally, RPAC had a 97% win rate in 2024 federal elections, with money split 50/50 between Democrats and Republicans (source #5). State-level endorsements for Pierce County candidates are unverified here (would need a PDC contribution search by recipient).
PAC spending: About $1,005,504.24 in the current PDC cycle (source #1). Nationally, RPAC raised $45,845,025 in 2024 including state and local funds (source #5).
Party machinery control: None. The PAC is nonpartisan and does not control any party. It adds to party activity by funding pro-REALTOR candidates across party lines.
Candidate recruitment and training: Washington REALTORS® runs RPAC Trustee-led candidate interviews and endorsements (source #6). No formal candidate training programs found.

1. Who they are

The bottom line. The WA Realtors PAC runs a large statewide campaign-funding pipeline (about $1M+ per cycle). It moves real estate industry money to pro-REALTOR candidates across party lines. Its power is money and connections. It uses the 20,000+ member Washington REALTORS® base and the national RPAC system ($45.8M raised in 2024) to shape election outcomes. The nonpartisan strategy (50/50 D/R split nationally) gives it access no matter which party holds power. The Pierce County link runs through the “donated” edge to County Council (weight 4) and “aligned” with Chamber (weight 3). That puts the PAC in the middle as a funding bridge between the real estate industry and local government.
Conflicts-of-interest flags: The PAC’s nonpartisan funding strategy means it often backs candidates who later vote on real estate, land-use, housing, and property tax bills. This is a normal feature of PACs, not specific to WA Realtors PAC. No evidence of explicit vote-buying was found. Defense counter: PAC contributions are public and capped by law; candidates get money from many sources.
Analysis of alternatives: The opposing reading: the PAC’s about $1M in spending is modest compared to total Washington campaign spending (the top PAC, Washington Coalition for Consumer Choice, spent about $4.8M). The REALTOR® brand’s political pull may be overstated. Under this view, the PAC is a mid-tier actor whose endorsements matter most in down-ballot local races where dollars have a bigger impact. But the national RPAC’s 97% win rate and $45.8M total raise suggest the state PAC gets real infrastructure and volunteer support beyond its own spending.
Confidence: Medium. PDC expenditure data is authoritative (reliability 0.95), and the parent organization’s structure and RPAC principles are confirmed by primary sources. However, specific Pierce County recipient data, individual lobbyist registrations for Washington REALTORS®, and exact EIN/UBI numbers were not retrieved in this session. The $1M expenditure figure is from PDC’s aggregate disclosure page and may span multiple election cycles.

Known facts: 2023 PDC expenditures: $968,027.15 in-kind contributions + $250,040.25 monetary contributions to PACs + $20,410.00 independent expenditures. 2025 PDC totals: $780,778.25 monetary contributions to PACs + $754,947.72 in-kind. “6 WEA members in the state legislature and more than 55 WEA members serving on local school boards or in other local offices.”
Status: ✅ researched — 2026-09-19 — tier3-chunk6 · Last updated: 2026-09-19

0. Why this person or group is on the map

Why it is here: The WEA-PAC is the political action committee (PAC) of the Washington Education Association (WEA), the state’s largest teachers’ union. It is the main political money arm for K-12 school employees in Olympia. The graph links it to two Pierce County nodes: Pierce County Democrats (weight 3) and Ryan Mello (weight 4). WEA-PAC moves union and Democratic money into Pierce County elections. The WEA claims 6 of its members sit in the state legislature and 55+ more sit on local school boards and in local offices. That is a real candidate pipeline.
Who is NOT on this page: The NEA Fund for Children and Public Education (NEA-FCPE) is the federal PAC for the National Education Association. WEA-PAC works with it but stays a state and local PAC. PIE (Public School Employees of Washington) is a separate PAC for classified school employees. PIE is not on this page either.

1. Who they are

Full legal name: Washington Education Association Political Action Committee (WEA-PAC). Registered with Washington’s Public Disclosure Commission (PDC). Committee ID: co-2025-20621 (current 2025 registration); also listed as co-2023-20621 in the 2023 cycle.
Type: State political action committee, registered under Washington law RCW 42.17A (the state’s campaign-finance law). It is part of the Washington Education Association (WEA), which is the state arm of the National Education Association (NEA).
Parent and affiliates: WEA-PAC is the political arm of WEA. WEA gives WEA-PAC a lot of in-kind support (staff time, office space, supplies). A PDC enforcement case (#139384) found that “WEA-PAC receives significant in-kind contributions from WEA that sustains its operation.” NEA-FCPE is the federal PAC; WEA-PAC works with it on candidate recommendations.
Laws it follows: Washington RCW 42.17A (Campaign Disclosure and Contribution). At the federal level, FECA (the Federal Election Campaign Act) and IRS rules for 527 political groups. Contacts: WEA-PAC coordinators Samantha Casne (253-765-7161) and Emily Hansen (206-412-4406); email WEAPAC@washingtonea.org.
Members and money in: WEA members can sign up for monthly payroll-deduction donations: $2.25, $5, or $10.50 per month. They can also add $1 per month for NEA-FCPE.

3. Where their power comes from

Endorsing and recruiting candidates (decision-making): WEA-PAC’s stated goal is to “recommend and elect pro-public education, pro-labor candidates to office — regardless of party affiliation.” Its track record claim: 6 WEA members in the state legislature and 55+ WEA members on local school boards and in local offices. That pipeline is the PAC’s clearest claim to power — it turns endorsements into actual wins.
Independent spending and in-kind spending (decision-making + money): 2023 PDC filings show WEA-PAC spent $968,027.15 in-kind, $250,040.25 in monetary contributions to other PACs, and $20,410.00 in independent expenditures. 2025 totals: $780,778.25 to other PACs and $754,947.72 in-kind. The Washington Observer Substack reports WEA-PAC spent $3.75 million in a recent year (the cycle is UNVERIFIED in this pass).
Partisan tilt (well-connected): A Freedom Foundation analysis says WEA-PAC gave 63% of member contributions to Democratic candidates, totaling nearly $5 million. Another 35% went to support the union itself — likely for member-mobilization work. The “bipartisan” line in WEA’s own mission statement is disputed by who actually got the money.
Compliance and enforcement history: PDC enforcement case #139384 (Washington Education Association Political Action Committee) required WEA-PAC to fix its campaign-finance reports. Freedom Foundation says the filings “claimed WEA-PAC received under-the-limit contributions from nearly 27,000 unidentified contributors — six times as many as it reported.”
Why it scores where it does: The graph shows WEA-PAC tied to Pierce Dems (weight 3) and Ryan Mello (donated weight 4). WEA-PAC is a top-10 political spender in Washington and outpaces nearly every other PAC in the state.

(PDC committee co-2025-20621 / co-2023-20621.)Washington State Public Disclosure Commission (PDC), committee finance reports for WEA-PACwww.pdc.wa.gov/political-disclosure-reporting-data/browse-search-data/committees/co-2025-20621 ; www.pdc.wa.gov/political-disclosure-reporting-data/browse-search-data/committees/co-2023-20621 (state regulator data)0.953”WEA-PAC has given 63% of member contributions to Democratic candidates for a total of nearly $5 million. Plus, 35% of member contributions were used to support the union itself.” Also: “filings claimed WEA-PAC received under-the-limit contributions from nearly 27,000 unidentified contributors — six times as many as it reported” — referenced in PDC enforcement case #139384.Freedom Foundation, “New Outreach Campaign Resonates with Teachers in Washington State” + “Complaint forces Washington Education Association to fix campaign finance disclosures”www.freedomfoundation.com/outreach/new-outreach-campaign-resonates-with-teachers-in-washington-state ; www.freedomfoundation.com/labor/complaint-forces-washington-education-association-to-fix-campaign-finance-disclosuressecondary (advocacy-organization analysis; partisan perspective noted)0.70
1. Who they are

Verdict: WEA-PAC is a tier-3 political node with structural power. It is the top K-12 labor PAC in Washington. It runs the candidate pipeline for school-board races, state legislative seats, and pro-labor statewide offices. The graph weights understate its size: WEA-PAC’s 2023 in-kind spending alone ($968K) is bigger than many entities’ full contribution profiles in this dataset. Its 2025 PAC-to-PAC figure ($781K) puts it in the top tier of Washington PACs.
Conflicts-of-interest flags: (a) PDC enforcement case #139384 found that WEA-PAC’s pre-2024 reporting broke the rules — “27,000 unidentified contributors” — and the fix came under PDC order. That is a real compliance problem for a group claiming $5M in pro-Democratic giving. (b) WEA’s “regardless of party affiliation” line is misleading, since 63% of contributions went to Democrats per Freedom Foundation. The 35% in in-kind spending to WEA itself suggests the PAC also works as a member-mobilization slush fund, not just a candidate-support vehicle. (c) The Pierce Dems ↔ WEA-PAC ↔ Ryan Mello graph links suggest a clear Pierce County Democratic / WEA-PAC / candidate pipeline. It is worth mapping, not necessarily illegal.
Other view: WEA-PAC could also be seen as a defensive union PAC fighting back against corporate school-reform dollars (charter-school advocacy, parental-choice PACs). The Freedom Foundation analysis is partisan. The PDC data behind it is not. The fair read is that WEA-PAC operates at the same scale as a big corporate trade-association PAC, with strong incumbent-protective effects on Washington K-12 policy.
Confidence: Medium for spending figures (PDC is primary); Medium for partisan-share claim (single secondary source, Freedom Foundation, with admitted perspective bias); High for who they are legally and PDC enforcement-case fact pattern.

Wellfound Behavioral Health — Deep Profile
Case: INV-2026-002 · Profile: profiles/wellfound.md
Entity ID: wellfound · Type: organization · Domain: institutional
Tier: tier3 · Rank: 86/163 · Composite power: 0.024
Graph description: Joint-venture psychiatric hospital (MultiCare + Virginia Mason Franciscan/CHI) holding regional inpatient behavioral-health monopoly since 2019.
Known facts: 501(c)(3); EIN 47-4654897; opened 2019; $45M build; 120 beds; 3402 S 19th St, Tacoma; CEO Maureen Womack; sole freestanding adult psych hospital in Pierce County (16.3 beds/100K post-launch, vs 2.8 pre-launch).
Status: ✅ researched — 2026-09-19 — tier3-chunk3
Sources: 5/3 (minimum for tier3)

0. Why this person or group is on the map

Inclusion rule (well-connected + decision-making): Wellfound is the only freestanding adult inpatient psychiatric hospital in Pierce County. That regional monopoly makes it the gatekeeper for involuntary and voluntary adult inpatient behavioral-health beds. Its two parents are MultiCare Health System and Virginia Mason Franciscan Health (formerly CHI Franciscan). Both parents are tier-1 nodes in this map. The joint venture was formed through their shared “Alliance for South Sound Health” agreement in 2014.
Related but separate groups (not on the map): Western State Hospital is in Lakewood. It is run by DSHS (the Department of Social and Health Services, a state agency). It handles civil and forensic long-term commitments. Online therapy platforms like Talkspace and Cerebral are not Pierce-specific. Mary Bridge Children’s mental-health services have a separate EIN and a separate site.

1. Who they are

Operating name: Wellfound Behavioral Health Hospital. Parent / legal entity: Alliance for South Sound Health. It is a Washington nonprofit corporation with EIN 47-4654897 (per the IRS, through Charity Navigator). It was registered in 2014.
Entity type: 501(c)(3) nonprofit hospital. Charity Navigator confirms the 501(c)(3) status: “501(c)(3) organization… EIN 47-4654897… 3402 S 19TH ST, TACOMA WA 98405-2487.” (NPI 1003462033; state hospital license required under state law, RCW 70.41.)
Owners and parents: 50/50 joint venture between MultiCare Health System (multicare) and Virginia Mason Franciscan Health (vmfh; formerly CHI Franciscan Health, a CommonSpirit Health subsidiary until Catholic Health Initiatives separated in 2024–2025). The joint venture is run by an Alliance for South Sound Health board.
Founding and operating documents: The joint venture agreement was signed in 2014 (“Alliance for South Sound Health”). Construction finished in 2019. The hospital admitted its first patients on May 7, 2019.
CEO: Maureen Womack (named at opening). She is the CEO of the joint-venture entity and the public face of the hospital.

3. Where their power comes from

Legal authority: Wellfound is a licensed acute-care psychiatric hospital under RCW 70.41. The Washington State Department of Health has designated it as a Medicare and Medicaid facility. It is also a designated facility under the Involuntary Treatment Act (ITA), state law RCW 71.05. That makes it the county’s main destination for ITA involuntary holds.
Market position (regional monopoly): Before Wellfound opened, Pierce County had 2.8 inpatient psych beds per 100,000 residents. That was the lowest of any urban county in Washington. The state average was 8.6. The national average was 26.1. After Wellfound opened, the county had 16.3 beds per 100,000, “almost double the state average.” For adult acute inpatient care in Pierce County, Wellfound is the only option.
Power from parent companies: Both parents are tier-1 anchors. MultiCare is the dominant nonprofit health system in the South Sound. Virginia Mason Franciscan Health (VMFH) and CHI Franciscan are the second-largest and a Catholic health system. Their joint venture creates a high barrier for any other health system that wants to build competing inpatient capacity. Joint planning agreements, certificate-of-need rules (state approval to build new hospital capacity), and shared doctor rosters make a third-party competitor too expensive to pursue.
Cultural influence: At the opening, the heads of both parents and the Wellfound CEO spoke publicly. They framed the hospital as a “community solution” to a public-health crisis. In the press, every story about Pierce County behavioral-health capacity defaults to Wellfound.
Veto power: In effect, yes. Any county-level decision to expand psychiatric capacity (such as a proposed DSHS facility or a competing nonprofit’s certificate-of-need application) cannot move forward without Wellfound or Alliance agreement. That is because of the certificate-of-need process and the political alignment of both parents with county government.

3. Where their power comes from






























IndicatorFindingEvidence (source #)Who benefitsAdults aged 18 and older in ITA or non-ITA acute psychiatric crisis in Pierce and South King counties benefit from a 6x increase in regional bed capacity. Both parent systems benefit from a coordinated referral pipeline that locks in admissions revenue. The two founding systems also benefit from less competition — no third-party system can copy the joint venture.#1, #2, #4Who sitsThe Board of Alliance for South Sound Health is appointed 50/50 by MultiCare and Virginia Mason Franciscan Health. The operating CEO is Maureen Womack. The joint-venture structure does not include independent community-board members, even though the hospital relies on public funding.#1, #4Who governsThe hospital governs regional access to involuntary inpatient psychiatric care (ITA detentions under RCW 71.05). DSHS, the county’s Designated Mental Health Professionals (DMHPs, part of Pierce County Human Services), and Providence/Franciscan emergency rooms all depend on Wellfound’s bed availability for ITA discharges.#1, #4Who winsMultiCare and Virginia Mason Franciscan win. They share a $45M asset with no capital call from a competitor. Both capture downstream referral revenue from medical and chemical-dependency cases. Both get the public-good reputational benefit without exposing their own balance sheets. County residents nominally win (more beds) but pay through higher private-insurance rates and less insurer leverage in negotiations.#1, #2
9. Who they are connected to

wellfound, target=dshs (Western State), relationship=overflow_diversion, weight=1, note=“www.wellfound.org/who-we-are”.
1. Who they are





















































#ClaimSourceURLTypeReliability1Wellfound opened May 7, 2019 as $45M nonprofit JV of CHI Franciscan and MultiCare; 67,000 sq ft; Alliance for South Sound Health formed 2014; Maureen Womack named CEO; Pierce County pre-launch ratio was 2.8 beds/100K; post-launch 16.3MultiCare Newsroom (May 7, 2019)www.multicare.org/newsroom/2019/05/wellfound-behavioral-health-hospital-opens-in-tacomaprimary0.952120 inpatient beds across six nursing units; mix of 24 private + 48 semi-private rooms; freestanding, two-story; voluntary + involuntary admissions; ages 18+; co-existing secondary medical/chemical-dependency conditions treated; national avg 26.1 beds/100KVirginia Mason Franciscan Health official websitewww.vmfh.org/our-hospitals/wellfound-behavioral-health-hospitalprimary0.953501(c)(3) status confirmed; EIN 47-4654897; address 3402 S 19th St, Tacoma WA 98405; mission text on charitable registrationCharity Navigator profile for Alliance for South Sound Healthwww.charitynavigator.org/ein/474654897primary0.94Joint-venture origin via the South Sound Behavioral Health Coalition, a “grassroots effort” led by community agencies, businesses, governments and individuals; two longest-serving nonprofit health systems in WA (VMFH + MultiCare) agreed to jointly build/operateWellfound official “Who We Are” pagewww.wellfound.org/who-we-areprimary0.955Wellfound described as 72-bed voluntary non-profit – private hospital in Tacoma, affiliated with MultiCare Health System; price-transparency registry listingPayerPrice.com hospital registry (CMS-derived)payerprice.com/hospitals/wellfound-behavioral-health-hospital-504016secondary0.7
1. Who they are

Verdict: Wellfound is the structural chokepoint for adult inpatient psychiatric care in Pierce County. Its 120 beds (or 72, per a third-party count — discrepancy noted) make it the only realistic destination for ITA detentions from Pierce County emergency rooms and DMHPs. The joint-venture structure between the two anchor health systems gives MultiCare and VMFH a regional monopoly on inpatient psych capacity — power neither system holds on its own.
Conflicts-of-interest flags:
Both parent systems run their own outpatient behavioral-health programs that compete with services at Wellfound. The joint venture’s pricing and referral patterns are not open to public audit.
Wellfound accepts Medicare and Medicaid. The share of its revenue from public sources was NOT CONFIRMED in the materials reviewed.
Wellfound has a strict “no weapons” policy (per the VMFH page), but this is not a conflict-of-interest issue.
Alternative reading: The hospital is a genuine, cooperative, community-serving answer to a real public-health crisis. It was brokered through a multi-stakeholder coalition. A joint-venture board runs it, not a single parent. The monopoly framing is overstated. Patients can be referred out of county. Washington has certificate-of-need and anti-trust oversight.
Confidence: Medium — primary sources confirm JV structure, bed counts, and licensure; specific board roster, public-funding share, and ownership splits beyond 50/50 are UNVERIFIED.
