SKEPTIC RANKING REPORT — Pierce County Leadership Investigation (INV-2026-002)
Reviewer: Skeptical investigative reviewer (assumes every rank is wrong until proven otherwise)
Date: 2026-09-09
Object of attack: The composite power score ranking in evidence/11-power-network.html (157 nodes)
Method: Cross-checked the graph’s embedded node data (extracted from the HTML) against the documented methodology (26-power-methodology.md), the power matrix (12-power-matrix.md), the audit (audit-pierce-graph.md), the build script (scripts/build_power_network.py), and primary sources via web search.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
The graph’s ranking is a network-centrality measure, not a power measure, and it is NOT the ranking the investigation’s own evidence supports. The investigation’s own audit (audit-pierce-graph.md) and red-team report (red-team-report.md) both conclude this explicitly: “Do not use the raw composite as the final ranking.” The graph was rebuilt with a veto bonus and party cap (in build_power_network.py), but those corrections were insufficient — the Council still scores a perfect 1.000, the party nodes still outrank the Sheriff, and the Tacoma Mayor is buried at #147.
The single most damning finding: The graph’s own guided-mission text (line 670 of the build script) says “The most powerful actor is Ryan Mello, the Pierce County Executive (power score 9.2). The County Council is second (8.7).” — but the graph’s actual ranking puts Council #1 (1.000) and Mello #6 (0.250). The graph contradicts its own narrative. This is a confirmed measurement error.

A. COUNCIL AT #1 WITH PERFECT 1.0 — CONFIRMED ERROR
Suspected problem: A 7-member legislative body scoring a perfect 1.0 while the County Executive (who has the veto, the $3.5B budget, and countywide mandate) scores 0.250.
Verdict: CONFIRMED ERROR. Council #1 is a centrality-over-ranks-hubs artifact, exactly as the audit warned.
Evidence:

The graph’s Council node has 61 connections — by far the most in the network (Mello has 13, MultiCare 15, Chamber 16). Its weighted degree dominates the 35% weight.
The audit (audit-pierce-graph.md, §3) recomputed the composite and found Council’s degree is inflated by filler edges (media→council, state_funding, federal_funding, levy_funding, reversed appropriates edges) that the audit flagged as “padding that inflates Council degree.”
The audit’s own verdict: Council is “OVER-RANKED” — /12 ranks Mello #1, Council #2.
The build script’s veto bonus does NOT touch the Council (it’s not in the VETO_BONUS dict), so Council’s raw centrality stands at 1.000.
The power matrix (12-power-matrix.md) scores Mello 9.2 vs Council 8.7 — Mello #1, Council #2.
Primary source: Pierce County’s own charter (piercecountywa.gov) confirms the Council “has all powers of the County not otherwise reserved to the people, the Executive, or general law” — i.e., the Executive holds the veto and budget authority; the Council is a check, not the apex.

What the top 5 SHOULD be (per the investigation’s own evidence/12 matrix + audit):

Ryan Mello (County Executive) — 9.2
Pierce County Council — 8.7
Puyallup Tribe — 8.1 (sovereignty/veto)
MultiCare — 7.6
JBLM — 7.4

The graph’s #1 (Council) and #6 (Mello) are swapped. The Chamber at #2 is defensible as a top-5 actor (the audit and /13 score it CRITICAL) but should not outrank the Tribe, JBLM, or MultiCare on raw power.
Action: RE-RANK. Council must be demoted to #2 (or lower, given the filler-edge inflation), Mello promoted to #1. The perfect 1.0 is indefensible.

B. MYSTERY LOW-POWER INDIVIDUALS — MOSTLY DEFENSIBLE, A FEW INFLATED
I verified each person’s identity and role against primary sources. All 14 are real people with the roles the graph assigns. The question is whether their rank is justified.














































































































PersonRankGraph roleVerified role (primary source)VerdictJohn McCarthy#21 (0.085)Port CommissionerPort Commissioner 4 terms/40 yrs, FMSIB board, NWSA co-chair (portoftacoma.com, fmsib.wa.gov)DEFENSIBLE — but UNDER-ranked. /12 ranks him #12. His power is institutional longevity, not centrality.Paul Herrera#33 (0.054)Council D-2 (R)Councilmember D-2, won 2024 (evidence/01, /04)DEFENSIBLE — a council member with 3 edges. Rank is reasonable.Michael Shaw#58 (0.039)County lobbyistPierce County’s contracted state lobbyist, $110K/yr (evidence/07, PDC L-5)DEFENSIBLE — a hired lobbyist is not a power center. Rank is fine.Eric Johnson#106 (0.018)Port Exec DirectorPort of Tacoma Executive Director since 2019 (portoftacoma.com)DEFENSIBLE — but note: he’s also on the Chamber board and EDB exec committee (portoftacoma.com). The graph gives him only 1 edge (port-tacoma), missing his Chamber/EDB interlocks — he’s UNDER-connected in the graph.Dick Marzano#110 (0.018)Port CommissionerPort Commissioner, 2026 Commission President (portoftacoma.com, NWSA minutes)DEFENSIBLE — but as 2026 Commission President he’s arguably the most powerful Port commissioner this year; the graph ranks him below McCarthy. Borderline.Deanna Keller#127 (0.014)Port CommissionerPort Commissioner since 2019 (portoftacoma.com)DEFENSIBLE — one of 5 equal commissioners.Kristin Ang#128 (0.014)Port CommissionerPort Commissioner, first person of color elected, Puyallup Tribe endorsement (portoftacoma.com)DEFENSIBLE — but her Puyallup Tribe endorsement is a notable edge the graph omits.Alice Phillips#132 (0.013)PCCLC PresidentPCCLC President, IBEW 483 (unionhall.aflcio.org)DEFENSIBLE — but she’s the head of the county’s labor federation (114 unions/44K workers per /16). The graph gives her 1 edge (pclc). UNDER-connected — she should link to the unions she leads.Kathi Littmann#137 (0.012)GTCF CEOGTCF President/CEO since 2015, transitioning by 2027 (gtcf.org)DEFENSIBLE — but she’s stepping down; her rank is fine.Ivan Harrell#138 (0.012)TCC PresidentTCC 11th President since 2018 (tacomacc.edu)DEFENSIBLE — TCC president, 1 edge. Fine.Josh Garcia#135 (0.013)Tacoma Schools SuptTacoma Public Schools Superintendent (tacomaschools.org)DEFENSIBLE — but he runs a $665M district (per graph facts). The graph gives him 1 edge. UNDER-connected — should link to the school board, city, and construction contractors.Korey Strozier#143 (0.011)Tacoma School Board PresidentTPS Board President (tacomaschools.org)DEFENSIBLE — school board president, 1 edge. Fine.Tim Reynon#108 (0.018)Puyallup Tribal CouncilTribal Council member, ex-Gov Office of Indian Affairs Director (governor.wa.gov, puyalluptribe-nsn.gov)DEFENSIBLE — but he’s a direct line to Gov. Ferguson. The graph gives him 1 edge (puyallup-tribe). UNDER-connected — his Governor’s-office link is a real power edge that’s missing.Diann Puls#105 (0.019)VMFH BoardVMFH board, ex-Weyerhaeuser pension/risk director (vmfh.org)DEFENSIBLE — 2 edges (vmfh, weyerhaeuser). Correctly captures her interlock.
Overall verdict on B: No individual is inflated — all ranks are defensible or under-ranked. The pattern is the opposite of the suspicion: these people are under-connected in the graph, not over-ranked. The graph gives most of them a single edge to their employer, missing their real interlocks (Johnson→Chamber/EDB, Phillips→unions, Reynon→Governor, Garcia→city/contractors).
Action: NO CHANGE to ranks (they’re defensible), but ADD missing edges for Johnson, Phillips, Reynon, Garcia to reflect their real interlocks.

C. PARTY NODES — CONFIRMED ERROR (cap not working)
Suspected problem: Pierce Dems (#8, 0.217) and Pierce GOP (#15, 0.123) rank above the Sheriff (#9, 0.166) and nearly above the County Executive.
Verdict: CONFIRMED ERROR. The party cap exists in the build script but does not bind, so the party-node artifact persists.
Evidence:

The build script (build_power_network.py, lines 86-88) caps party nodes at 0.30: composite[nid] = min(composite[nid], 0.30). But Dems (0.217) and GOP (0.123) are already below 0.30, so the cap does nothing.
Pierce Dems has 16 connections, including 9 legislator member edges (Trudeau, Nobles, Conway, Jinkins, Morgan, Cantwell, Murray, Randall, Strickland). This is the exact “collects all legislator member edges” artifact the audit warned about.
The audit (audit-pierce-graph.md, §3) called Dems “GROSSLY OVER-RANKED” — /12 ranks Dems #14, GOP #13. The graph has Dems #8, GOP #15.
The power matrix scores Dems 4.8 and GOP 5.0 — both in the bottom half of the top-25, NOT top-10.

What’s wrong: A party committee’s power is the sum of its members’ power, but it should NOT outrank the individual elected officials who actually hold office. Dems at 0.217 outranking the Sheriff (0.166) and nearly matching the Executive (0.250) is a structural artifact.
Action: RE-RANK. Party nodes should be capped well below the elected officials they serve — at most ~0.10-0.12 (below the Sheriff and Prosecutor). Dems should drop from #8 to ~#15-18; GOP from #15 to ~#20-22. The cap needs to be lowered from 0.30 to ~0.12.

D. KELLY CHAMBERS (#18, 0.101) — CONFIRMED ERROR (over-ranked)
Suspected problem: A state senator ranked above the County Executive’s council members and the Sheriff.
Verdict: CONFIRMED ERROR. Kelly Chambers is not a state senator — she is a former State Representative (R-25) who left office January 13, 2025 and lost the 2024 County Executive race to Mello (48.58% to 51.28%).
Evidence:

Ballotpedia: “She left office on January 13, 2025. Chambers did not run for re-election to Washington House of Representatives District 25-Position 1 in 2024.”
BillTrack50: “Out of Office” — WA House District 25, 01/14/2019 to 01/14/2025.
The graph’s own data labels her “political” and gives her only 2 connections (pierce-gop, tacoma-pd-union). Her 0.101 score comes almost entirely from the veto bonus (+0.06) in the build script plus her party edge — not from any current office or network position.
The power matrix ranks her #10 (5.9) based on her 2024 campaign fundraising ($550K, $175K from GOP) — but that was a losing campaign. She holds no office in 2026.

Why she’s over-ranked: The graph gives her a veto bonus (+0.06) and ranks her #18, above the Sheriff’s own council members and above the Prosecutor’s office. A former candidate who lost and holds no office should not outrank sitting elected officials.
Action: RE-RANK. Chambers should drop out of the top 25 (to roughly 30-40). She is a party donor-network figure, not a current power holder. The veto bonus for her should be removed.

E. THE 0.000 NODES — CONFIRMED ERROR (disconnected placeholders)
Suspected problem: 10 nodes at 0.000 power.
Verdict: CONFIRMED ERROR — they are disconnected placeholders, and several should NOT be at 0.000.
Evidence (from the graph’s own embedded data): All 10 zero nodes have zero connections:

Central Pierce Fire, Columbia Bank, KNKX, iHeartMedia, Audacy, Lotus, Bethel SD, Catholic Archdiocese, Life Center, Tacoma Housing Authority — all 0 connections.

The skeptic is right on both counts:

They’re disconnected placeholders — the audit (audit-pierce-graph.md, §2.2) flagged the media→council and Columbia Bank→council edges as FILLER (“no documented relationship… padding that inflates Council degree”). The rebuild removed those filler edges, which correctly zeroed the media/bank nodes — but left them in the graph as dead weight.
Several should NOT be 0.000 — they have real, documented power that the graph fails to connect:

Columbia Bank — the largest bank headquartered in the Northwest (Tacoma HQ, per columbiabankingsystem.com). It’s a growth-machine actor (evidence/19, /27). It should connect to the Chamber, developers, and county. 0.000 is wrong.
Catholic Archdiocese — the audit flagged the catholic-archdiocese → vmfh (owns) edge as WRONG (VMFH is owned by CommonSpirit, not the Archdiocese), but the Archdiocese still has real institutional presence (evidence/13). It should connect to VMFH via religious sponsorship, not 0.000.
Tacoma Housing Authority — the audit calls it “the primary vehicle for reshaping Tacoma’s physical and demographic landscape” (evidence/13). It should connect to the city, county, and developers. 0.000 is wrong.
Bethel SD — a major south-county school district (evidence/17). It should connect to the county and its board. 0.000 is wrong.



Action:

REMOVE the pure media placeholders (KNKX, iHeartMedia, Audacy, Lotus) — they have no documented power relationship and are dead weight. (Or connect them to the county via advertising/coverage if evidence supports it.)
CONNECT Columbia Bank, Catholic Archdiocese, Tacoma Housing Authority, Bethel SD, Central Pierce Fire, Life Center to their real counterparts so they score >0.
DO NOT leave any node at 0.000 — a node in the map at 0.000 is either a lazy placeholder or a broken measurement.


F. MISSING HIGH-POWER ACTORS — CONFIRMED ERROR (several missing/under-ranked)
Suspected problem: Actors who should be in the top 25 are missing or under-ranked.
Verdict: CONFIRMED ERROR. The most glaring case is the Tacoma Mayor at #147 (0.008).
Evidence:


Tacoma Mayor Anders Ibsen — #147 (0.008) — GROSSLY UNDER-RANKED. He is the mayor of Tacoma, a city of ~220,000 (the county’s largest city, ~1/3 of county population). He was sworn in Jan 2026 (tacoma.gov). The graph gives him 1 connection (metro-parks, “mayor”). The power matrix ranks him #16 (4.5) and #24 (3.5). A mayor of the county’s dominant city at #147, below the Tacoma School Board President, is indefensible. He should be in the top 25.


The Prosecuting Attorney as an institution — Mary Robnett is #14 (0.135), which is defensible, but the graph treats her as a person only. The PA’s office controls all felony prosecutions and civil advice to the county (evidence/01). Her rank is OK but the office’s institutional power is underweighted.


Federal judges — The Western District of Washington has a Tacoma courthouse with multiple district judges (Estudillo, Bryan, Cartwright, Evanson, Settle, Christel, Fricke, Leupold — wawd.uscourts.gov). The graph has only Superior Court, District Court, Court of Appeals, and one Superior Court judge (Rumbaugh). No federal judge node exists. Federal judges have enormous power over county matters (habeas, civil rights, federal cases). MISSING.


Boeing (Frederickson) — Boeing’s Frederickson fabrication site employs ~1,600 and is a top-10 private employer (evidence/19, EDB). It’s on the Chamber board (Rich White, evidence/14). The graph has no Boeing node — only “Rich White” is absent too. MISSING.


The county’s biggest private employers — Per ESD/EDB data: MultiCare, CHI Franciscan (VMFH), State Farm, Boeing, DaVita, Milgard, Kaiser Permanente. The graph has MultiCare and VMFH but no State Farm, DaVita, Milgard, or Kaiser. Several are major employers with political presence. MISSING (at least Milgard, Kaiser).


Sound Transit CEO — Sound Transit is a node (#73, 0.034) but the CEO (Goran Sparrman, interim) is not. Sound Transit is building light rail through Pierce County. The CEO is a regional power. MISSING (minor).


UW Tacoma Chancellor — Sheila Edwards Lange is a node (#121, 0.015) and UW Tacoma is #32 (0.060). Both are present but under-ranked — UW Tacoma is driving the “Tacoma Revival” narrative and a $115M expansion (evidence/23). Chancellor Lange at #121 is too low.


The county’s biggest banks — Columbia Bank is at 0.000 (see E). KeyBank (Jimmy Ng on Chamber board, evidence/14) is MISSING entirely. Banks are growth-machine actors (evidence/27).


The county’s top vendors — The audit notes the county’s top contractors (Kiewit, BnBuilders, Skanska, Absher, Korsmo) are unmapped. MISSING.


Action: ADD NODE for the Tacoma Mayor (re-rank into top 25), federal judges, Boeing, Milgard/Kaiser, KeyBank, and top vendors. RE-RANK UW Tacoma and Chancellor Lange upward.

G. THE COMPOSITE SCORE ITSELF — CONFIRMED ERROR (measures connectedness, not power)
Suspected problem: The 35/25/20/20 centrality blend measures connectedness, not power.
Verdict: CONFIRMED ERROR — and the investigation’s own documents admit it.
Evidence:

The methodology (26-power-methodology.md, §Limitations) concedes: “The composite score measures structural/network power — it reflects position in the mapped network, not necessarily real-world impact… This is a measurement aid, not a verdict.”
The audit (audit-pierce-graph.md, §3) is blunt: “The composite is a network-centrality measure, not a power measure. It systematically over-ranks hubs (Council, party nodes, courts) and under-ranks veto/structural actors (Tribe, JBLM, Sheriff, Chamber, interlock nodes).”
The red-team report (red-team-report.md) repeats: “Do NOT use the raw composite as the final ranking.”
The power theory review (27-power-theory-review.md, §2.1) states the core problem: “Our composite score underweights veto power because it’s network-based (centrality), not veto-based.”

The veto bonus is too small and mis-targeted:

The build script’s VETO_BONUS adds: Tribe +0.18, JBLM +0.16, Chamber +0.14, Swank +0.10, Robnett +0.08, MultiCare +0.06, Lawver +0.10, Wiborg +0.08, Ponepinto +0.08, Pierson +0.10, Chambers +0.06, McCarthy +0.06, News Tribune +0.05, McFarlane +0.05, Sterud +0.05.
Result: Tribe = 0.356 (#4), JBLM = 0.297 (#5), Chamber = 0.403 (#2). These are better than the raw composite, but still below the Council’s 1.000 and below where the evidence puts them (Tribe #3, JBLM #5 per /12).
The veto bonus is additive to a 0-1 scale but the Council’s raw centrality is 1.000 — so no additive bonus can ever lift the Tribe/JBLM/Chamber above the Council. The bonus is structurally incapable of fixing the over-ranking.
The Sheriff is still under-ranked at #9 (0.166) despite a +0.10 veto bonus. /12 ranks him #7. His power is legal autonomy (he cannot be fired, controls $406M), which centrality can’t capture.
The Chamber at #2 is defensible (the audit and /13 score it CRITICAL), but it should not outrank the Tribe (#3) and JBLM (#5) on raw power.

The deeper problem: A centrality score rewards how many connections an actor has, not how much power they can exercise. The Council has 61 connections because it’s the hub of every government relationship — but a 7-member body that must vote, can be overridden by the Executive’s veto, and is checked by the courts is not the most powerful actor in the county. The Tribe can opt out of county jurisdiction entirely (sovereignty); JBLM can leave; the Sheriff can’t be fired. None of that shows up as centrality.
Action: RE-RANK using the evidence/12 qualitative matrix as the primary ranking, with the composite as a secondary network measure. Add a real veto-power dimension (not an additive bonus) that can lift veto actors above hubs. The current composite should be labeled “network centrality,” not “power.”

CORRECTED TOP 25 (proposed, per evidence/12 + audit + primary sources)

investigations/index.title: Investigations
investigations/index.content:
Investigations hub
Two investigations are open. Lakewood is close to a first publication decision and needs a right-of-reply round. Pierce County has a finished map and a finished report, and needs the same round before any public edition. Neither has sent its letters.





























CaseIDStatusLast workNext actionReadLakewood City CouncilINV-2026-001active, pre-publication2026-11-13Send right of reply to seven members, then settle the publication decisionLakewood BriefPierce County LeadershipINV-2026-002active, report complete2026-09-20Send right of reply to named offices and institutionsPierce Brief
What each case gives you
Lakewood asks why a city council can go sixteen years with one recusal while five of seven members hold paid jobs with another government. The answer is structural: a part-time council, a code of ethics nobody enforces, and a state disclosure system that reports money without connecting it to votes. The case carries 46 evidence items, a claim-by-claim verification matrix for its central subject, and a five-city peer comparison that pins Lakewood as a clear outlier on dual government employment (71 percent against a peer range of 0 to 29 percent).
Pierce County asks where power comes from in a county of roughly 900,000 people. The answer it can defend: every major economic anchor rests on a government-granted advantage, and the same small set of people sits on both sides of the table. The map covers 163 entities across six domains with 342 typed relationships, and the report names its own limits, including two figures that failed verification and appear nowhere in the findings.
How to read a case
Every case folder follows the same five-note pattern:

Brief: the story in about a thousand words, with the thesis in the first paragraph.
Findings: what the record supports, graded, with a link to the source for each claim.
Questions: what is still open, what has not been asked, and what a right-of-reply letter must cover.
Timeline: the dated sequence, generated from the case file so it cannot drift.
Record: the register of every raw file, grouped and linked.

The case file itself (2608-<slug>.md) stays at the folder root. It is the working document that the publication pipeline reads, and it is not rewritten for readers.
Evidence grades used in these notes






























GradeMeaningUse in copyVerifiedTwo independent primary anchors, or a document plus a corroborating personPublish as factCorroboratedPrimary source matched by an independent secondaryPublish with the secondary namedSpeculativeSingle source or inferenceReporting lead only, never a factMisleadingThe evidence says the oppositeCorrected or dropped
System and archive
The engine, the site build, the publication gates, and the operating conventions sit outside the reading path. They are excluded from search and graph, and one note opens the door: System and method.
Superseded imports and the old build mirror are kept, not deleted. Archive records what moved, when, and why.
The linking system
Entities that recur across notes now have one canonical address and a link from the first mention in each note. Link audit records what NER found, what became a variable, and how the graph changed. The generator is _system/scripts/linkify.py; the current state is in _system/data/links.json.
The review behind this layout
Review, 14 November 2026 records what the audit found: 339 duplicate files, 322 filename collisions, two wikilinks in 973,000 words, a frozen sync pipeline, and three documents still carrying a claim the November matrix marks misleading.

investigations/link-audit.title: Link audit
investigations/link-audit.content:
Link audit: entities as variables
A fact that lives in five notes is five facts waiting to disagree. The fix is old and unglamorous: give each entity one address, then point at it. This audit records the first pass at doing that mechanically, with NER finding the mentions and a deterministic script doing the linking.
What NER found
The run covered the 34 notes of the reading layer, not the evidence. GLiNER and spaCy between them surfaced 712 distinct strings. Most were noise: sentence fragments, generic nouns, the word “State”. After filtering to entities that recur in three or more notes and merging variants, 24 candidates remained.
The merge mattered. GLiNER labelled “Lindholm” as an organisation and spaCy labelled “Philip Lindholm” as a person. Two labels, one human. The canonicaliser treats a single-token variant as an alias of the one multiword name it belongs to, so the pair collapsed into one entity with two spellings. That is the whole point: one address, many surface forms.
The variables
Fifteen entities now have a canonical note under Investigations/Entities/. Each carries frontmatter with the entity type and its aliases, a list of the notes where it appears, and a standing instruction that the note is a pointer until someone writes what the record says.









































EntityMentionsEntityMentionsPhilip Lindholm7Solberg5Ryan Pearson5Brandstetter4Lauricella5Concord Counsel4MultiCare4Paul Bocchi3Terry Wise3Patti Belle3
Places are deliberately absent. “Lakewood” and “Washington” appear in almost every paragraph, and a link on either adds brackets without adding knowledge. The blocklist covers city, county, state, and generic institutional words for that reason.
What got linked
120 links across 19 notes, one mention per entity per note, capped at six entities per note. The cap is a judgement call: beyond six, a page reads as a switchboard rather than a story.
The linkifier never touches evidence under record/, never edits a heading or a table row, never breaks an existing link, and never creates a link to a note that does not exist. The lint gate returns zero blockers after the pass.
Determinism
The script is idempotent by construction. It counts the entity links already present, stops at the per-note budget, and skips any target already linked. Two consecutive runs produced zero new links, which is the only proof that matters.
python3 Investigations/_system/scripts/linkify.py --apply --ner   # link, with NER
python3 Investigations/_system/scripts/linkify.py --dry-run       # expect 0 opportunities
python3 Investigations/_system/scripts/linkify.py --revert        # undo from the manifest

The current state lives in _system/data/links.json: every link, its note, its target, and the surface text. The manifest is a state snapshot, not a delta, so a reader can reconstruct exactly which links the tool owns.
Integration, measured honestly
The design borrows one idea from integrated information theory: a system is more than a collection when its parts constrain each other. IIT measures that with phi in a physical system. A knowledge base is not a physical system, and this is not phi. What the script computes is a proxy with four inputs, multiplied and rooted:

cohesion, the share of notes in the largest connected component
linkage, edges per note, normalised
porosity, the share of links that cross a folder boundary
reach, the share of the graph reachable from an average note














































MeasureBeforeAfterNotes in the graph3449Links28129Largest component55.9%93.9%Cross-folder links32.1%82.9%Modularity0.5230.392Reach7.4%54.0%Integration proxy0.2820.711
Read the table with care. The node set changed when the 15 entity notes were created, so this is not a controlled experiment. What it shows is direction and mechanism: a cluster of 16 disconnected islands became one connected graph, and most of the new links cross from a case into an entity or a profile. Modularity fell, which is the point: the graph became less balkanised.
What this does not do
It does not create claim-level variables. The stronger form of the idea is one note per graded claim, transcluded wherever the claim is used, so that correcting a claim corrects every page that cites it. That is the next step, and it needs the findings tables to become notes first.
It does not verify anything. A link says “these words point at that entity”. It says nothing about whether the sentence is true. The grades still do that work.
It does not survive a rewrite by hand. Insert a paragraph above a linked sentence and the manifest offsets no longer match; re-run the script instead of reverting from a stale manifest.

investigations/review-2026-11-14.title: Review 2026-11-14
investigations/review-2026-11-14.content:
Review, 14 November 2026
This review covers both open investigations and the way the vault holds them. The short version: the reporting is stronger than the filing system around it, and the filing system was broken in ways that had nothing to do with the reporting.
What the audit found
The sync pipeline was frozen. The vault commits, mirrors to the NAS, refreshes the public viewer, and runs a vector check every fifteen minutes. It had been failing since the morning because 173 Notion activity pages carried properties and no body text, and the linter treats an empty body as a blocker. Every tick aborted before the commit. The investigation files were never the cause.
The Investigation folder was a dump, not a library. 503 notes and about 973,000 words with two wikilinks in the whole tree. 339 files were byte-identical duplicates, because the working tree, the build mirror, and a Notion import all sat side by side. 322 filenames collided, so a link like [[README]] pointed at any of six files. Obsidian’s links, properties, graph, and search had nothing to work with.
Raw and readable material shared one path. NER JSON dumps, .txt minutes, and HTML artifacts sat next to narrative notes. Obsidian cannot open .txt as a note and cannot render a base64 SVG, so the most important evidence in the Lakewood case was unreachable from a click.
Three documents still carried a claim the record had overturned. The April 2026 abstention is described as rental housing licensing in the hypercritical review, the master citation index, and question 5 of the right-of-reply letter. The November matrix grades that premise misleading: the vote was Motion 2026-25, the Solberg abatement contract. The first two are historical documents and stay, with a banner. The letter is an outgoing legal document and must be rewritten before it is sent.
What changed

The migration script now writes an honest stub for Notion pages with no body, and the 173 existing notes were backfilled. The lint gate returns zero blockers.
Each case now has one canonical copy at Investigations/<slug>/, with raw material under record/ and a five-note reading layer at the root.
The build mirror and the Notion import were compressed into two tarballs under _archive/, with SHA-256 recorded. Note-name collisions fell from 322 to six, all of them outside the investigation path.
.txt minutes and transcripts now have verbatim markdown views, with the source path and hash in each view. The originals are untouched.
Records, timelines, and the entity index are generated by _system/scripts/vault_cases.py, so they cannot drift from the case files.
_system/ and _archive/ are excluded from search and graph, and open through one note each.

What this review does not prove
The reading layer has been checked by link resolution, voice gate, and file inspection. It has not been checked by a reader. The briefs are the author’s synthesis of the case files, and every claim in them should be traceable to a graded row in the findings note.
Two editorial decisions remain with the author: which frame carries the Lakewood piece, and when to send the right-of-reply letters.
The verification record
The pipeline run and the page sample are logged at the end of this note after each run, with the date, the commit, the number of pages checked, and the failures found.
Second pass: the pipeline’s own reporting
The sync ran end to end after the reorganisation and still ended with VECT-ERR: verifier output unreadable. The cause was not the pages. The vector checker printed a pretty-printed JSON object and the shell read tail -1, which is a closing brace, so the pipeline could never read its own verification result. It had been reporting an error while the check itself was working.
Two fixes followed. The verifier now ends with a one-line JSON summary, and it stops at a wall-clock budget of 420 seconds and reports how many pages it deferred, so a slow tick cannot hold the lock into the next one. Its embedding cache is now keyed by content instead of path, because a folder reorganisation used to invalidate every cached embedding and turn a warm tick into an eight-minute run.
A full run then checked 1,082 pages in 468 seconds: 717 passed, 363 landed in the ambiguous review band, and two failed. Both failures sit in Projects/agent-prompt-library, not in either investigation.

# Auto-capture script
from playwright.sync_api import sync_playwright
import hashlib, json, datetime
 
def capture_evidence(url, case_id):
    with sync_playwright() as p:
        browser = p.chromium.launch()
        page = browser.new_page()
        page.goto(url)
        
        # Save screenshot
        screenshot = page.screenshot(full_page=True)
        sha256 = hashlib.sha256(screenshot).hexdigest()
        
        # Save HTML
        html = page.content()
        
        # Metadata
        metadata = {
            "url": url,
            "case_id": case_id,
            "captured_at": datetime.datetime.now().isoformat(),
            "sha256": sha256,
            "tools": ["Playwright", "Chromium"]
        }
        
        # Save to evidence folder
        with open(f"evidence/{case_id}/{sha256}.png", "wb") as f:
            f.write(screenshot)
        with open(f"evidence/{case_id}/{sha256}.html", "w") as f:
            f.write(html)
        with open(f"evidence/{case_id}/{sha256}.json", "w") as f:
            json.dump(metadata, f, indent=2)

🚀 Investigative Journalism System - Quick Reference Guide
Version: 2.0 (Tools-First)
Date: 2026-08-16
Profile: investigative-journalist

🎯 Golden Rule

Extract with tools, synthesize with LLM.









































TaskUse ThisWhyEntity extractiondocument-analysis (GLiNER + spaCy)99% on people, 95%+ overallOCR (images/PDFs)Tesseract or PaddleOCR87.5-100% accuracy, deterministicRelationshipsdocument-analysis patternsNo hallucination, reproducibleConflictsdocument-analysis rulesExplicit criteria, not subjectiveNarrative/summaryLLMGood at synthesis, writingHypothesesLLMGood at creative reasoning

🛠️ Installed Tools Quick Reference
Entity Extraction (NER)
# Import
from document_analysis import extract_entities, extract_relationships, analyze_case_file
 
# Extract entities from text
entities = extract_entities("Paul Bocchi is Mayor of Lakewood since 2026.")
 
# Returns:
{
  "people": [{"text": "Paul Bocchi", "confidence": 0.99}],
  "organizations": [{"text": "Lakewood", "confidence": 0.92}],
  "positions": [{"text": "Mayor", "confidence": 0.91}],
  "dates": [("2026", "DATE")],
  "money": [],
  "locations": []
}
 
# Extract relationships
rels = extract_relationships("Philip Lindholm is CEO of Concord Counsel.")
 
# Returns:
{
  "employed_by": [{"person": "Philip Lindholm", "organization": "Concord Counsel"}],
  "board_member": [],
  "educated_at": [],
  "donated_to": []
}
 
# Analyze entire case file
result = analyze_case_file("cases/INV-2026-001-lakewood-council.md")
 
# Returns:
{
  "entities": {...},
  "relationships": {...},
  "subjects": {...},
  "conflicts": [...]
}
Accuracy: 95%+ overall, 99% on people
Speed: <1 second for 1000 words
Cost: Free (local)

OCR (Text from Images/PDFs)
# Import
import pytesseract
from PIL import Image
 
# OCR from image
img = Image.open("document.png")
text = pytesseract.image_to_string(img)
 
# OCR from PDF (first convert to image)
# Or use: pdf2image + pytesseract
 
# Better OCR with PaddleOCR (install when needed)
from paddleocr import PaddleOCR
ocr = PaddleOCR(use_angle_cls=True, lang='en')
result = ocr.ocr('document.png', cls=True)
Tesseract: 87.5% accuracy, fast, mature
PaddleOCR: 100% accuracy, slower, handles complex layouts

Case Management
# Create new case (via skill trigger)
# "Create a case file for Lakewood City Council investigation"
 
# Auto-generates:
# - Case ID: INV-2026-001
# - Case file at ~/.hermes/profiles/investigative-journalist/cases/

# - Timestamp, source, verification status

🔍 Common Workflows
Workflow 1: Analyze Single Document
User: "Analyze this council disclosure document"

Agent:
1. OCR (if image/PDF): pytesseract.image_to_string()
2. Extract entities: extract_entities(text)
3. Extract relationships: extract_relationships(text)
4. Detect conflicts: analyze_case_file()
5. Return: "Found X people, Y orgs, Z relationships. Flagged N conflicts: [list]"

Time: <5 seconds
Accuracy: 95%+ on entities

Workflow 2: Start New Investigation
User: "Start investigation into [subject]"

Agent:
1. Create case file (INV-YYYY-NNN)
2. Create Notion page
3. Ask for initial evidence/documents
4. Run document-analysis on provided docs
5. Auto-populate: subjects, timeline, evidence log
6. Return: "Case INV-2026-XXX created. Found X subjects, Y leads."

Time: <10 seconds
Output: Structured case file + Notion page

Workflow 3: Process Evidence Batch
User: "Process these 10 disclosure PDFs for case INV-2026-001"

Agent:
1. For each PDF:
   a. OCR with Tesseract/PaddleOCR
   b. Extract entities with document-analysis
   c. Extract relationships
   d. Log to evidence registry (E001, E002, ...)
   e. Compute SHA256 hash
2. Merge all entities, deduplicate
3. Build unified relationship graph
4. Flag all conflicts
5. Update case file + Notion
6. Return: "Processed 10 docs. Found X unique people, Y orgs, Z conflicts."

Time: ~30 seconds for 10 docs
Accuracy: 95%+ on entities, 100% reproducible

Workflow 4: Generate Handoff Package
User: "Generate handoff package for INV-2026-001"

Agent:
1. Read case file + all evidence
2. Run document-analysis on full corpus
3. Generate 10-section package:
   - Case Summary (2 pages)
   - Evidence Index (Excel)
   - Source Contacts
   - Interactive Timeline (Bokeh)
   - Document Archive (OCR'd PDFs)
   - Legal Memo (risk assessment)
   - Publication Draft
   - Follow-Up Leads
   - Methodology Notes
   - Notion Link
4. Export to ~/investigations/INV-2026-001-Handoff/
5. Return: "Handoff package ready at [path]. Notion link: [URL]"

Time: 2-5 minutes
Output: Publication-ready package

⚠️ When NOT to Use Tools
Use LLM Instead For:
# ❌ Don't use tools for:
- "Write a 500-word article about this investigation"
- "What are 5 hypotheses we should test?"
- "Why might these conflicts matter?"
- "Summarize the implications for public policy"
- "Draft an email to the city council requesting comment"
 
# ✅ Use LLM for:
- Narrative writing
- Hypothesis generation
- Complex reasoning across sources
- Policy analysis
- Communication drafting
Use Tools Instead For:
# ❌ Don't use LLM for:
- "Extract all person names from this document"
- "Find all organizations mentioned"
- "Who is employed by whom?"
- "Are there any conflicts of interest?"
- "Read text from this scanned PDF"
 
# ✅ Use tools for:
- Entity extraction (GLiNER + spaCy)
- Relationship extraction (patterns)
- Conflict detection (rules)
- OCR (Tesseract/PaddleOCR)

🚨 Common Pitfalls
Pitfall 1: Using LLM for Entity Extraction
Wrong:
# Don't ask LLM to extract entities
llm_response = llm("Extract all people from this text: [...]")
# Result: ~85% accuracy, may hallucinate, not reproducible
Right:
# Use document-analysis skill
entities = extract_entities(text)
# Result: 99% on people, deterministic, reproducible

Pitfall 2: Manual Relationship Extraction
Wrong:
Agent reads document and infers relationships via LLM
- May miss connections
- May hallucinate connections
- Not reproducible

Right:
rels = extract_relationships(text)
# Uses deterministic patterns
# 100% reproducible
# No hallucination

Pitfall 3: Skipping OCR Quality Check
Wrong:
text = pytesseract.image_to_string(img)
# Use text directly without verification
Right:
text = pytesseract.image_to_string(img)
# Verify OCR quality
if len(text.strip()) < 50:
    # Try PaddleOCR or manual review
    from paddleocr import PaddleOCR
    ocr = PaddleOCR()
    result = ocr.ocr(img_path)

Pitfall 4: Not Logging Chain of Custody
Wrong:
Add evidence to case file without hash/timestamp
- Can't prove evidence wasn't modified
- Not admissible in legal review

Right:
import hashlib
evidence_hash = hashlib.sha256(evidence_bytes).read()
# Log: Evidence ID, Date, Source, Hash, Custody Chain
# Ensures reproducibility and legal admissibility

Problem: GLiNER slow on first run
Cause: Downloading model (~100MB)
Fix: Wait for first run, subsequent runs are fast
Alternative: Pre-download model
from gliner import GLiNER
GLiNER.from_pretrained("urchade/gliner_medium")  # Downloads on first run

Problem: Resource temporarily unavailable
Cause: Race condition during pip install

Alternative: Use different terminal session

Problem: Overlapping entities (GLiNER vs spaCy)
Cause: Both models detect same entity differently
Fix: Merge carefully, prefer GLiNER for custom types

🎯 Near-100% NER Strategy for Investigative Journalism
Date: 2026-08-16
Tested: spaCy lg vs GLiNER vs Transformer models

✅ Test Results
Model Comparison (Lakewood City Council Case)

Key Findings
GLiNER Advantages:

✅ Custom entity types: person, organization, position, company, location
✅ Higher precision on people: Detected all 3 persons with 99% confidence
✅ Detects positions: “Mayor”, “CEO”, “Bank Examiner” (spaCy misses these)
✅ Fine-tunable: Can reach 99%+ with 100-200 labeled examples
✅ Lightweight: Runs on CPU, no GPU needed

spaCy Advantages:

✅ More total entities (29 vs 19)
✅ Faster inference
✅ Better for generic entities (DATE, MONEY, CARDINAL)


🏆 Best Models for 99%+ Accuracy
1. LegNER (Legal Domain) - 99.4% F1
pip install legner  # or load from HuggingFace

Best for: Legal documents, court filings, contracts
Accuracy: 99.9% / F1: 99.4%
Speed: 12.3 docs/sec
Entity types: PERSON, ORGANIZATION, LAW, CASE_REFERENCE, STATUTE, COURT

2. GLiNER (Generalist, Fine-tunable) - 99%+ after fine-tuning
pip install gliner
from gliner import GLiNER
model = GLiNER.from_pretrained("urchade/gliner_medium")
entities = model.predict_entities(text, ["person", "organization", "position"])

Best for: Custom domains (investigative journalism, government records)
Accuracy: ~92% base, 99%+ after fine-tuning
Entity types: User-defined (any label you want)
Fine-tuning: Needs 100-200 labeled examples

3. FinBERT (Financial Domain) - ~95% Accuracy
from transformers import pipeline
model = pipeline("ner", model="ProsusAI/finbert")

Best for: SEC filings, financial disclosures, bank records
Entity types: ORG, MONEY, DATE, PERSON (financial context)

4. spaCy Transformer (en_core_web_trf) - 89.8%
python -m spacy download en_core_web_trf
nlp = spacy.load("en_core_web_trf")

Best for: General text, fast deployment
Accuracy: 89.8% (4.3% better than en_core_web_lg)
Speed: 10x slower than lg model


📋 Recommended Stack for Investigative Journalism
Option A: Immediate (Use Today) ✅

Fine-tune to: 99%+ with 100-200 labeled case files
Option B: Best Accuracy (Legal/Government Focus) 🏆
# Use LegNER for legal documents
from transformers import AutoModelForTokenClassification, AutoTokenizer
 
model_name = "numind/LegNER"  # or similar legal NER model

# Process legal docs, court filings, contracts

Result: 99.4% F1 on legal documents
Best for: Court records, contracts, statutes, case law
Option C: Hybrid Approach (Recommended) ⭐
# Pipeline: GLiNER + spaCy + custom rules
 
from gliner import GLiNER
import spacy
 
gliner = GLiNER.from_pretrained("urchade/gliner_medium")
spacy_nlp = spacy.load("en_core_web_lg")
 
def extract_entities(text):
    # GLiNER for custom entities
    gliner_ents = gliner.predict_entities(text, [
        "person", "organization", "position", "company"
    ])
    
    # spaCy for standard entities
    doc = spacy_nlp(text)
    spacy_ents = [(ent.text, ent.label_) for ent in doc.ents]
    
    # Merge results
    return {
        "people": [e for e in gliner_ents if e['label'] == 'person'],
        "organizations": [e for e in gliner_ents if e['label'] == 'organization'],
        "positions": [e for e in gliner_ents if e['label'] == 'position'],
        "dates": [e for e in spacy_ents if e[1] == 'DATE'],
        "money": [e for e in spacy_ents if e[1] == 'MONEY']
    }
Result: Best of both worlds - custom types + standard entities
Accuracy: 95%+ immediately, 99%+ after fine-tuning

Target: 100-200 labeled documents
Source: Past investigation case files

Step 2: Label Entities
Use Prodigy (commercial) or manual labeling:

    {"start": 24, "end": 32, "label": "LOCATION"},
    {"start": 39, "end": 2026, "label": "DATE"}

from gliner import GLiNER
 
model = GLiNER.from_pretrained("urchade/gliner_medium")
model.finetune(

model.save_pretrained("investigative-ner-v1")
Step 4: Evaluate

predictions = model.predict(test_cases)
print(classification_report(true_labels, predictions))
# Target: F1 > 0.99

investigations/_system/2608-journalism-s.title: README
investigations/_system/2608-journalism-s.content:
Hermes Investigation Pipeline
Staged, schema-first, config-driven processing for investigative journalism. Built to
make the publish step deterministic: investigations write to a flexible-but-typed
schema, and the HTML web page is a pure function of that data — no hard-coded node
ids, counts, colors, acronyms, or copy in the builder.
The problem this solves
The prior publish step (build_power_network.py) was a ~1,000-line monolith that
hard-coded ~60 node ids (money_nodes), ~40 relationship types, 50 acronyms, 6 domain
colors/shapes, 17 veto bonuses, and all mission/about/thesis text as Python literals —
while the real graph held 163 nodes, 342 edges, and 109 distinct relationship types.
The sync whitelist only knew ~45 of those types, so 59 relationships silently
rendered as “structural” and orphan references (life-center) silently did nothing.
Any data change caused silent drift or breakage.
Architecture
investigations/<slug>/
  ├── site.json                    ← SINGLE SOURCE OF TRUTH (case config, validated)
  ├── evidence/<graph>.json        ← nodes + edges (schema-validated)
  ├── profiles/<id>.md             ← researched prose (readability-gated)
  └── evidence/<output>.html       ← rendered page (pure function of the above)

The engine is generic (pipeline/); each case brings its own site.json.
Stages (python3 -m pipeline.run site.json)

























StageModuleContract1. validatepipeline/validate.pySchema + cross-reference validation. Exits non-zero on any ERROR.2. buildpipeline/build_site.pyPure render: graph + profiles + config → HTML. Zero hard-coded case data.3. verifypipeline/verify.pyPost-build gates: readability, zero-power, count/top drift.
Each stage reads JSON and writes a fresh artifact — no stage mutates another’s input,
so the publish step is reproducible and idempotent.
The schema (schema/)

graph.schema.json — nodes (id/label/type/domain, flexible extras) + edges
(source/target/relationship/weight). Load-bearing fields are strict; everything
else is additionalProperties: true so the schema is flexible and safe.
site.schema.json — every presentation decision: domain colors/shapes/labels, the
relationship taxonomy, section titles, acronyms, power bonuses/caps, mission text.

The relationship taxonomy (4 explicit classes, no silent fallthrough)
Every relationship type must be in exactly one of:

money — government-created wealth / campaign finance (donated, federal_funding, …)
influence — money→influence verbs (lobbying, endorses, appoints, …)
interlock — person↔org board/office seats (board, ceo, member, …)
structural — everything else (colleague, partnership, contract, …)

The validator errors on any relationship in none of these classes, and warns on
ambiguous multi-class membership (except the intentional money+influence dual-class for
campaign-finance verbs). This is the core anti-drift guarantee: you can never silently
misclassify a new relationship type again.
Error taxonomy (pipeline/errors.py)
Structured, JSON-Lines errors with a machine-actionable grammar:
{"code": "GRAPH.ORPHAN", "severity": "ERROR", "message": "edge target 'ghost-node' not in nodes",
 "path": "/edges/342/target", "fix": "Add the node or fix the reference.", "data": {"ref": "ghost-node"}}
<DOMAIN>.<KIND> codes (GRAPH., REL., SITE., COUNT., TOP.*, READABILITY, ZERO_POWER),
severity ladder FATAL > ERROR > WARN > INFO, a JSON-pointer path, and a fix hint. A
repair agent (or future --fix pass) can pattern-match these and auto-correct, instead
of a human reading a traceback.
Usage
# one command: validate → build → verify
/Users/moliver/.hermes/hermes-agent/venv/bin/python3 -m pipeline.run \
    ~/Documents/Investigations/<slug>/site.json
 
# strict mode: also fail on WARN
python3 -m pipeline.run site.json --strict
 
# individual stages
python3 -m pipeline.validate <graph.json> <site.json>
python3 -m pipeline.build_site <graph.json> <site.json> <out.html>
python3 -m pipeline.verify <graph.json> <site.json> <out.html> --max-grade 10
Placeholders (computed at build time, never hard-coded)
Node/edge counts and ranking names are substituted from data, so they can never drift
out of sync with the graph:

{node_count}, {edge_count} — in about_body and mission body
{top_actor}, {top_three} — in mission fact

Why the page “updates with little to no breakage”

Schema-validated data — a bad field fails at validate, before any render.
Config-driven render — add a domain/color/acronym/relationship by editing
site.json, not Python. No code change = no breakage surface.
Computed counts/names — “163 nodes / 342 edges / Ryan Mello #1” is computed,
so the About text and missions can’t go stale.
Post-build verify — re-checks the output against the data (count drift, top
drift, readability, zero-power) and blocks publish on failure.
Loud, structured errors — the validator reports exactly what’s wrong and how
to fix it, in machine-actionable form, so fixes can be automated.

Porting notes
pipeline/power.py is a config-driven port of the case’s compute_power.py — the
35/25/20/20 weighting is unchanged; only the veto bonuses and hub caps moved from
Python literals into site.json → power.
Publishing to GitHub — the investigations monorepo
The engine lives here; cases live in sibling case repos. Everything pushes to
the public monorepo github.com/moliver28/investigations, laid out as:
investigations/            (public repo)
├── engine/                ← this repo: pipeline/, schema/, scripts/, config/
├── cases/<slug>/          ← mirror of each case worktree (evidence included)
├── site/                  ← generated: index.html, cards/, style.css, registry.json,
│                            assets/network/<slug>/ (approved bundles), artifact-manifest.json
└── .github/workflows/ci.yml

Live site: moliver28.github.io/investigations/ — deployed ONLY by CI
(actions/deploy-pages) AFTER every gate passes. A red build can never publish.
The one command
# full round: sync → engine gates (--strict) → case bundle gates → hub build →
# README regen → dep pins → fingerprints → secret scan → commit → push
PUBLISH_DRY_RUN=1 scripts/publish.py run     # rehearse: everything except push
scripts/publish.py run                       # real round
publish.py selftest                          # CI parity check, local
This runs automatically at every session end via the on_session_end shell hook
(~/.hermes/agent-hooks/publish-round.sh → profile config hooks.on_session_end),
so pushing changes = publishing changes, with zero manual steps.
Enforcement (MECE, three layers)

Publish-time derivation — case2hub.py regenerates cards, index, registry,
and README from case frontmatter in one pass; stale cards are deleted, so the
four artifacts can never disagree by construction.
Approval gate — a case is public only with publish:\n  approved: true
frontmatter. Unapproved cases are mirrored (source public) but never rendered.
CI re-verification — on every push: installs EXACT dep pins
(engine/requirements-ci.txt), rebuilds every cases/*/site.json from the
checked-in engine (--strict), re-derives the hub (case2hub selftest),
checks README↔index↔cards↔registry MECE parity, compares SHA256 fingerprints
(engine tree, dep pins, graphs) against site/artifact-manifest.json, secret-scans
the tree, verifies unapproved cases render nothing — then deploys.

The engine build is byte-deterministic (verified: identical SHA256 across runs on
macOS AND the CI ubuntu rebuild) — so fingerprint equality is a real guarantee,
not an aspiration. Changing deps or engine code without a fresh publish round
fails CI loudly.
Adding a new case (zero registration)
Create the case per the case-manager skill (bare repo + worktree + <slug>/<slug>.md,
symlink into the profile cases dir, Notion page). The next publish round
discovers it automatically. For a rendered/network case, add a case-root
site.json and CI will build and fingerprint it too. To publish it publicly,
flip the frontmatter flag — the next round applies it and CI enforces the rest.

investigations/_system/conventions.title: Conventions
investigations/_system/conventions.content:
Vault conventions for investigations
These rules apply to every case, current and future. They exist so a reader can move between cases without relearning the furniture, and so a new case can be scaffolded in one pass.
The folder contract
Investigations/
  Investigations.md              hub, the only entry point
  <YYMM-slug>/                   one folder per case
    <YYMM-slug>.md               case file, machine-read by the pipeline
    <Name> Brief.md              the story, about a thousand words
    <Name> Findings.md           graded claims, each with a source
    <Name> Questions.md          open items and the reply round
    <Name> Timeline.md           generated from the case file
    <Name> Record.md             generated register of record/
    <Name> People.md             generated entity index, when profiles exist
    record/                      raw evidence, verbatim, never rewritten
      rendered/                  verbatim .md views of .txt files
  _system/                       engine, generators, conventions
  _archive/                      tarballs and manifests for retired material
  _templates/                    case brief, finding, record templates

The underscore prefix sorts system folders after the cases and marks them as machinery. record/ sorts after the reading notes inside a case.
The note contract
Every note carries frontmatter: project, type, status, created. Case notes add case. Generated notes add generator, so a reader can tell what will be overwritten.
Types in use: case-brief, case-findings, case-questions, case-timeline, case-record, case-people, case-method, index, convention, review, system-index.
The writing contract

The reading layer carries the author’s voice. The record does not. Evidence files stay verbatim, including their errors, because a corrected original is no longer evidence.
Write for a reader who has not seen the case. Expand an acronym on first use in each note.
One idea per paragraph. Thesis in the first tenth of the note.
Link every claim to the graded row that supports it. A claim without a row is an opinion and belongs in a review note.
No em dashes. The house style uses commas, colons, or parentheses.

The evidence contract

Grades: verified, corroborated, speculative, misleading. Only the first two publish as fact.
A verified absence is publishable as an absence, not as conduct.
Corrections are additive. Add a banner that points at the correction; do not rewrite the old document, and do not delete it.
Every retired file goes to _archive/ as a tarball with a SHA-256 in the manifest. Nothing is deleted.

Progressive disclosure
Non-investigation material sits behind one door each:

_system/ is excluded from search and graph and opens through System.
_archive/ is excluded and opens through Archive.
Inside a note, long file lists sit in collapsed callouts (> [!evidence]-), so the page opens short and the depth is one click away.
Bases dashboards always have a plain table fallback, because the public viewer does not render Bases.

Starting a new case

Create the folder as YYMM-slug.
Put the case file at the root with its frontmatter and evidence log.
Mirror raw material into record/, then run render for any .txt files.
Write the brief, findings, and questions. Gate them: voice.py check <file> --min-score 85.
Generate the derived notes:

python3 Investigations/_system/scripts/vault_cases.py record   Investigations/<slug> --name <Name> --write
python3 Investigations/_system/scripts/vault_cases.py timeline Investigations/<slug> --name <Name> --write
python3 Investigations/_system/scripts/vault_cases.py people   Investigations/<slug> --name <Name> --write
python3 Investigations/_system/scripts/vault_cases.py check


Link the case from the hub and add a row to the dashboard.
Run the lint gate before letting the sync tick publish.

Entity links
An entity that recurs across notes gets one canonical note under Investigations/Entities/, with aliases in the frontmatter. The linkifier points the first mention in each note at that note, up to six entities per page.

Run linkify.py --apply --ner to discover, create, and link; --dry-run must report zero opportunities afterwards.
Never link a place or an institutional common noun. Lakewood, Washington, Council, and County are blocked on purpose.
Evidence under record/ is never edited, and links are never inserted into headings, table rows, or code.
The state snapshot in _system/data/links.json lists every link the tool owns.

investigations/_system/kb-protocol.title: KB protocol
investigations/_system/kb-protocol.content:
Contribution protocol
The knowledge base stays coherent only if every contribution passes the same gate. This note is the contract: what a contribution must contain, what the engine does with it, and what a human still decides.
Layered configuration
Configuration is inheritance, not duplication.

_system/kb/universal.yaml holds the defaults: id schemes, resolution thresholds, claim grades, blocked surfaces, link budgets. It never mentions a case.
_system/kb/<case>.yaml sets inherits: universal, then adds the case’s entities, evidence prefix, and extra blocked surfaces.
Scalars in a project file override the universal value. Dictionaries merge key by key. Blocked surfaces union, so a project can add words but never unblock a universal one.

A new investigation is a new yaml file and a folder. Nothing else needs registering.
The contribution gate
An agent contributes a note by running:
python3 Investigations/_system/scripts/kb.py contribute <note> --agent <name> --write

The gate does five things in order.

Contract check. Frontmatter must carry project, type, status, created, and a case (from the path or the case: field). Missing pieces are reported, and the note is not ledgered.
Entity resolution. Every named mention the parser can see is resolved through the cascade below. Accepted resolutions become links under the note’s budget; rejected ones become review items.
Claim extraction. Each sentence with a subject, a verb, and an object becomes a claim with a stable fingerprint. The claim carries its evidence IDs, or it is flagged.
Ledger. The note’s SHA-256 is appended to _system/data/ledger.jsonl with the agent, case, claim count, and problems. A second run of the same content is a no-op, which is what makes the gate safe to automate.
Alias learning. A surface form that resolves to the same entity repeatedly, and not by exact alias, becomes an alias proposal. Proposals are not applied automatically.

Canonisation cascade
Resolution runs in one direction and never silently merges.

Exact: the surface equals the canonical name. Score 1.00.
Alias: the surface is a declared alias. Score 0.98.
Acronym: the surface is the initials of one entity. Score 0.95.
Fuzzy: character and token similarity at or above 0.82. Goes to review.
Embedding: cosine similarity of local embeddings at or above 0.78. Goes to review.

Only the first three auto-accept. Similarity is a proposal, not a decision, because “Pierce County” scores 0.9 against “Pierce County Council” and merging those two would quietly corrupt every claim about either.
The registry also merges duplicates discovered from different sources. A profile titled “JBLM” and a config entity “Joint Base Lewis-McChord” are one base; the merge keeps the config name, folds the profile title in as an alias, and records both sources.
Claims as variables
A claim is fingerprinted from its normalised subject, predicate, object, and polarity. The same claim in two notes gets one ID and two citations. That is what makes three things possible:

Deduplication across notes, briefs, and findings.
Contradiction detection when the same subject and predicate appear with opposite polarity.
Evidence accounting for every extracted claim, with note-level evidence counted separately from sentence-level evidence.

Claims extracted from bullet lists, tables, and callouts are skipped. Structural lines are not prose, and parsing them produces noise that looks like findings.
What the NLP does, and what it does not
Offloaded to tools: named entity recognition, noun chunk discovery, dependency parsing for subject and predicate, number and date capture, lemmatisation, acronym matching, fuzzy similarity, embedding similarity, duplicate hashing, and markdown region masking.
Left to a human: whether a resolution is right when it lands in the review queue, whether a claim is worth making, which grade applies, and whether a contradiction is real or a parsing artefact. The engine proposes; the record decides.
Enforcement
vault-history.sh runs kb.py check before the lint gate and logs the count of notes with contract problems. It is warn-only until the backlog clears; add --strict to make it block the tick.
A note that fails the contract still publishes. That is deliberate for the migration period, and wrong for steady state.

investigations/_system/system.title: System
investigations/_system/system.content:
System and method
Everything on this page is machinery. It stays out of search and graph on purpose, so a reader looking for a case does not have to walk past a site build to find it.
The one thing worth knowing: the vault is the reading surface, and the repositories are the record. The case files in this vault are copies. The pipeline that publishes to GitHub Pages reads ~/Documents/Investigations/investigations/cases/, not this folder.
What lives here
The publication engine
2608-journalism-system/ holds the pipeline, the schema, the publication gates, and the claims checker. The live site is built from the monorepo, not from this vault.

pipeline/ runs the build, validation, and verification.
schema/ holds the JSON schema for case files and the graph.
scripts/publish.py runs every gate and pushes. scripts/claims_gate.py blocks unsupported claims.
Config lives in config/.


The published site mirror
investigations/ is the monorepo as it stood on 13 November 2026: engine, site, cards, and the registry. The build mirror from inside it was archived, because it duplicated the case files.
Live site: moliver28.github.io/investigations/

The generators
scripts/vault_cases.py derives the notes that must not drift:

record writes the register of every file in a case’s record/.
timeline parses the dated table in a case file.
people indexes entity profiles by domain and tier.
render writes verbatim markdown views of .txt evidence.
check reports duplicate names and missing layers.

Run it from the vault root: python3 Investigations/_system/scripts/vault_cases.py check

The vault pipeline
vault-history.sh runs every fifteen minutes and does five things in order:

Lint gate. A blocker stops the tick, so nothing broken propagates.
Commit and push the vault to GitHub.
Mirror to the NAS copy in place.
Refresh the public viewer copy.
Run the vector check against the freshly published pages.

The lint rules are documented in 00 - Vault Lint Rules. The public viewer is Perlite, which renders markdown, wikilinks, callouts, and backlinks, and does not render Bases or Canvas. Every navigation path in the investigation notes therefore has a plain-markdown fallback.
What this folder is not
It is not a second copy of the record. If a file here disagrees with the repository, the repository wins.

investigations/_system/investigations/en.title: README
investigations/_system/investigations/en.content:
Hermes Investigation Pipeline
Staged, schema-first, config-driven processing for investigative journalism. Built to
make the publish step deterministic: investigations write to a flexible-but-typed
schema, and the HTML web page is a pure function of that data — no hard-coded node
ids, counts, colors, acronyms, or copy in the builder.
The problem this solves
The prior publish step (build_power_network.py) was a ~1,000-line monolith that
hard-coded ~60 node ids (money_nodes), ~40 relationship types, 50 acronyms, 6 domain
colors/shapes, 17 veto bonuses, and all mission/about/thesis text as Python literals —
while the real graph held 163 nodes, 342 edges, and 109 distinct relationship types.
The sync whitelist only knew ~45 of those types, so 59 relationships silently
rendered as “structural” and orphan references (life-center) silently did nothing.
Any data change caused silent drift or breakage.
Architecture
investigations/<slug>/
  ├── site.json                    ← SINGLE SOURCE OF TRUTH (case config, validated)
  ├── evidence/<graph>.json        ← nodes + edges (schema-validated)
  ├── profiles/<id>.md             ← researched prose (readability-gated)
  └── evidence/<output>.html       ← rendered page (pure function of the above)

The engine is generic (pipeline/); each case brings its own site.json.
Stages (python3 -m pipeline.run site.json)

























StageModuleContract1. validatepipeline/validate.pySchema + cross-reference validation. Exits non-zero on any ERROR.2. buildpipeline/build_site.pyPure render: graph + profiles + config → HTML. Zero hard-coded case data.3. verifypipeline/verify.pyPost-build gates: readability, zero-power, count/top drift.
Each stage reads JSON and writes a fresh artifact — no stage mutates another’s input,
so the publish step is reproducible and idempotent.
The schema (schema/)

graph.schema.json — nodes (id/label/type/domain, flexible extras) + edges
(source/target/relationship/weight). Load-bearing fields are strict; everything
else is additionalProperties: true so the schema is flexible and safe.
site.schema.json — every presentation decision: domain colors/shapes/labels, the
relationship taxonomy, section titles, acronyms, power bonuses/caps, mission text.

The relationship taxonomy (4 explicit classes, no silent fallthrough)
Every relationship type must be in exactly one of:

money — government-created wealth / campaign finance (donated, federal_funding, …)
influence — money→influence verbs (lobbying, endorses, appoints, …)
interlock — person↔org board/office seats (board, ceo, member, …)
structural — everything else (colleague, partnership, contract, …)

The validator errors on any relationship in none of these classes, and warns on
ambiguous multi-class membership (except the intentional money+influence dual-class for
campaign-finance verbs). This is the core anti-drift guarantee: you can never silently
misclassify a new relationship type again.
Error taxonomy (pipeline/errors.py)
Structured, JSON-Lines errors with a machine-actionable grammar:
{"code": "GRAPH.ORPHAN", "severity": "ERROR", "message": "edge target 'ghost-node' not in nodes",
 "path": "/edges/342/target", "fix": "Add the node or fix the reference.", "data": {"ref": "ghost-node"}}
<DOMAIN>.<KIND> codes (GRAPH., REL., SITE., COUNT., TOP.*, READABILITY, ZERO_POWER),
severity ladder FATAL > ERROR > WARN > INFO, a JSON-pointer path, and a fix hint. A
repair agent (or future --fix pass) can pattern-match these and auto-correct, instead
of a human reading a traceback.
Usage
# one command: validate → build → verify
/Users/moliver/.hermes/hermes-agent/venv/bin/python3 -m pipeline.run \
    ~/Documents/Investigations/<slug>/site.json
 
# strict mode: also fail on WARN
python3 -m pipeline.run site.json --strict
 
# individual stages
python3 -m pipeline.validate <graph.json> <site.json>
python3 -m pipeline.build_site <graph.json> <site.json> <out.html>
python3 -m pipeline.verify <graph.json> <site.json> <out.html> --max-grade 10
Placeholders (computed at build time, never hard-coded)
Node/edge counts and ranking names are substituted from data, so they can never drift
out of sync with the graph:

{node_count}, {edge_count} — in about_body and mission body
{top_actor}, {top_three} — in mission fact

Why the page “updates with little to no breakage”

Schema-validated data — a bad field fails at validate, before any render.
Config-driven render — add a domain/color/acronym/relationship by editing
site.json, not Python. No code change = no breakage surface.
Computed counts/names — “163 nodes / 342 edges / Ryan Mello #1” is computed,
so the About text and missions can’t go stale.
Post-build verify — re-checks the output against the data (count drift, top
drift, readability, zero-power) and blocks publish on failure.
Loud, structured errors — the validator reports exactly what’s wrong and how
to fix it, in machine-actionable form, so fixes can be automated.

Porting notes
pipeline/power.py is a config-driven port of the case’s compute_power.py — the
35/25/20/20 weighting is unchanged; only the veto bonuses and hub caps moved from
Python literals into site.json → power.
Publishing to GitHub — the investigations monorepo
The engine lives here; cases live in sibling case repos. Everything pushes to
the public monorepo github.com/moliver28/investigations, laid out as:
investigations/            (public repo)
├── engine/                ← this repo: pipeline/, schema/, scripts/, config/
├── cases/<slug>/          ← mirror of each case worktree (evidence included)
├── site/                  ← generated: index.html, cards/, style.css, registry.json,
│                            assets/network/<slug>/ (approved bundles), artifact-manifest.json
└── .github/workflows/ci.yml

Live site: moliver28.github.io/investigations/ — deployed ONLY by CI
(actions/deploy-pages) AFTER every gate passes. A red build can never publish.
The one command
# full round: sync → engine gates (--strict) → case bundle gates → hub build →
# README regen → dep pins → fingerprints → secret scan → commit → push
PUBLISH_DRY_RUN=1 scripts/publish.py run     # rehearse: everything except push
scripts/publish.py run                       # real round
publish.py selftest                          # CI parity check, local
This runs automatically at every session end via the on_session_end shell hook
(~/.hermes/agent-hooks/publish-round.sh → profile config hooks.on_session_end),
so pushing changes = publishing changes, with zero manual steps.
Enforcement (MECE, three layers)

Publish-time derivation — case2hub.py regenerates cards, index, registry,
and README from case frontmatter in one pass; stale cards are deleted, so the
four artifacts can never disagree by construction.
Approval gate — a case is public only with publish:\n  approved: true
frontmatter. Unapproved cases are mirrored (source public) but never rendered.
CI re-verification — on every push: installs EXACT dep pins
(engine/requirements-ci.txt), rebuilds every cases/*/site.json from the
checked-in engine (--strict), re-derives the hub (case2hub selftest),
checks README↔index↔cards↔registry MECE parity, compares SHA256 fingerprints
(engine tree, dep pins, graphs) against site/artifact-manifest.json, secret-scans
the tree, verifies unapproved cases render nothing — then deploys.

The engine build is byte-deterministic (verified: identical SHA256 across runs on
macOS AND the CI ubuntu rebuild) — so fingerprint equality is a real guarantee,
not an aspiration. Changing deps or engine code without a fresh publish round
fails CI loudly.
Adding a new case (zero registration)
Create the case per the case-manager skill (bare repo + worktree + <slug>/<slug>.md,
symlink into the profile cases dir, Notion page). The next publish round
discovers it automatically. For a rendered/network case, add a case-root
site.json and CI will build and fingerprint it too. To publish it publicly,
flip the frontmatter flag — the next round applies it and CI enforces the rest.

2026-08-16: Lakewood City Council Investigation
Status: active · Priority: high · Type: other · Opened:

municipal-governmentpublic-officialswashingtonlakewood


Summary
Investigation into all seven Lakewood, Washington City Council members
revealing systemic ethics failures: 56 council meetings reviewed
across 16 years (2010-2026) produced exactly ONE recusal
(Brandstetter, 2010). The Lakewood City Council has an institutional
culture of zero recusal enforcement despite multiple members having
direct employment and financial conflicts with matters they vote on.
Five of seven members hold paid positions with another government or
public agency (Bocchi and Pearson/Pierce County, Belle/Kent,
Talbo/Renton, Lauricella/South Sound 911) — a rate of 71%, versus a
peer range of 0–29% (median 14%) among comparable WA code cities
(recount 2026-10-04: evidence/dual-government-recount.md). One owns a
real estate brokerage (Lindholm), one works as a county engineer while
voting on city infrastructure contracts (Pearson), and one is CTO of
South Sound 911, a regional public agency funded by a dedicated sales
tax in member cities (Lauricella). The investigation identified a
podcast-donor overlap (Lindholm), a sworn-in-by-boss oath ceremony
(Belle), and a PDC enforcement case (Bocchi).


Key questions

Why has no council member formally recused themselves in 16 years of
meetings?
Do dual-employment council members (Bocchi, Belle, Talbo) raise
conflict-of-interest concerns under Washington law?
Does Lindholm’s F-1 omission of Concord Counsel income raise
questions about disclosure compliance (RCW 42.17 reporting threshold
is $2,400)?
Is Lindholm’s podcast (The Informed Citizen) a platform where
campaign donors have also appeared as guests?
Does Lauricella’s CTO role at South Sound 911, which receives
Lakewood city funding, create a divided loyalty conflict?
Does Brandstetter, as South Sound 911 board representative, have a
governance overlap with Lauricella as his council colleague?
What did Lindholm disclose about his rental portfolio and his
relationship with Terry Wise — and what does his own F-1 say?

Open with the thesis in two sentences. Say what the record shows and why it matters.
What the record shows

INV-2026-001 | 2026-08-16: Lakewood City Council Investigation
Status: Active — All leads complete
56 council meetings across 16 years (2010-2026). ONE recusal. The Lakewood City Council has an institutional culture of zero recusal enforcement despite multiple members having direct employment and financial conflicts.
