projects/uxr-blog/blog-db/context-window.title: The Future of Prompting Is Frameworks
projects/uxr-blog/blog-db/context-window.content:
The conventional wisdom says prompt engineering is dying. That AI systems are getting smart enough to understand vague instructions, and the craft of writing good prompts will soon be irrelevant.
The conventional wisdom is wrong. Prompting isn’t dying. It’s growing up. And the practitioners who recognize what it’s becoming will have a significant edge over those still debating whether it matters.
Context Windows Are Smaller Than You Think
Every large language model operates within a context window: the total amount of information it can hold in working memory for any given interaction. Providers advertise massive numbers. The reality is more constrained.
Recent research on what scholars call the Maximum Effective Context Window (MECW) reveals a striking gap between advertised capacity and usable capacity [1]. The effective window, the point beyond which additional input stops helping and starts hurting, is drastically smaller than the technical maximum. More surprising: sheer input length alone degrades performance, even when every token is relevant and retrieval is perfect [2].
This matters because every token you send to an AI model is a resource allocation decision. Noise competes with signal. Redundancy crowds out reasoning space. The practitioners who learn to pack maximum meaning into minimum tokens will consistently outperform those who treat the context window as infinite.
Frameworks Are Compression Engines
This is where frameworks enter the picture.
A framework is a structured way to articulate domain knowledge so that it can be reliably consumed and executed. Think of it as a compression algorithm for expertise. Years of professional knowledge, distilled into a repeatable protocol that tells an AI exactly what to attend to, in what order, and with what constraints.
The academic literature supports this intuition. A comprehensive ACM Computing Surveys review catalogued the rapidly growing taxonomy of prompting frameworks, documenting how structured approaches consistently outperform unstructured ones [3]. Separately, researchers demonstrated that the Task-Method-Knowledge (TMK) framework, borrowed from cognitive and educational science, measurably improves LLM performance on planning tasks beyond what Chain-of-Thought prompting achieves alone [4]. The pattern is clear: when you give a model structured knowledge instead of raw instructions, it reasons better.
The Prompt Report, a systematic survey cataloguing 58 distinct prompting techniques across the field, reinforces the same conclusion from a different angle. The discipline has already moved well beyond “write a clear sentence” into structured, composable methodologies [5].
From Clever Phrasing to Knowledge Architecture
The shift happening right now is subtle but consequential. Prompting is moving from a communication skill to a design discipline.
The early era of prompt engineering was about finding the right words. Chain-of-thought. Few-shot examples. Role assignments. These techniques matter, but they operate at the surface level of interaction. The next era is about something deeper: designing structured knowledge artifacts that an AI can reliably interpret and execute.
This mirrors a pattern familiar to anyone in UX or information architecture. When a new medium emerges, the first instinct is to optimize the old workflow for the new tool. (Remember when websites were just digitized brochures?) The real transformation happens when practitioners start designing for the medium’s native strengths and constraints.
For AI, the native constraint is the context window. The native strength is pattern execution. Frameworks serve both.
I explored this idea from a different angle in Four Mental Models That Transform How You Use AI, where the core argument was that your mental model of how AI works determines how effectively you use it. Frameworks are the natural next step: once you understand how the system thinks, you can architect knowledge in the shape it thinks best.
What This Means for You
If you use AI tools regularly, here is the practical takeaway: start building frameworks for your most repeated tasks.
Not prompt templates. Not copy-paste snippets. Frameworks: structured protocols that encode your domain expertise, your quality criteria, and your decision logic into a format an AI can execute consistently.
The value of professional knowledge is shifting. Information that can be codified into structured frameworks becomes disproportionately powerful in an AI-augmented world. Tacit expertise that resists structuring remains a uniquely human edge. But the bridge between tacit and explicit knowledge, the ability to architect what you know into formats that scale, is where the real leverage lives.
The future of prompting is not cleverer words. It’s structured knowledge. The people who build that bridge first will define how the rest of us work with AI.
Start with one framework. Pick the task you do most often with AI. Write down the role, the context, the constraints, and the output format you need. Run it. Refine it. Watch what happens when you stop improvising and start architecting.

References
[1] “Context Is What You Need: The Maximum Effective Context Window for Real World Limits of LLMs.” arXiv, 2025.
[2] “Context Length Alone Hurts LLM Performance Despite Perfect Retrieval.” arXiv, 2025.
[3] “Prompting Frameworks for Large Language Models: A Survey.” ACM Computing Surveys, 2026.
[4] “Knowledge Model Prompting Increases LLM Performance on Planning Tasks.” arXiv, 2025.
[5] Schulhoff, S. et al. “The Prompt Report: A Systematic Survey of Prompting Techniques.” arXiv, 2024.

projects/uxr-blog/blog-db/designing-surv.title: Survey Design That Delivers: Writing Quantitative UX Surveys That Drive Decisions
projects/uxr-blog/blog-db/designing-surv.content:
Designing Surveys That Get You The Data You Actually Need
Most organizations collect survey data they never use. The problem isn’t insufficient data—it’s poorly designed surveys that don’t align with analysis needs. By working backwards from your analytical goals, you can create surveys that deliver actionable insights.
Introduction
Despite careful planning, many researchers find themselves unable to answer key stakeholder questions from their survey data. This common problem stems from designing surveys without a clear analysis strategy. Starting with your end goals ensures every question serves a purpose.
1. Know What Story You Need to Tell
Begin your survey design by mapping out exactly how you’ll use the data:
Identify the specific decisions your research needs to influence. Each type of decision—whether it’s feature prioritization, design evaluation, or user segmentation—requires different data points. Transform these decisions into concrete research questions, then map each to specific metrics.
Create your analysis template before building the survey:

Define your key metrics and calculations
Plan your data visualizations
List the stakeholder questions you’ll answer

2. Design for Clean Data
Getting actionable data requires careful question design.
Closed-ended questions provide the cleanest data for analysis. Choose your rating scales strategically:

Likert scales for measuring attitudes
Semantic differential scales for comparing opposing concepts
Numeric scales for measuring frequency or quantity
The choice between odd and even scales affects your results. Odd scales allow neutral responses, while even scales force a direction. Choose based on whether neutral responses provide value for your analysis.

3. Keep It Simple, Keep It Clean
Complex surveys lead to poor data quality. A straightforward survey flow improves completion rates and response reliability.
Avoid excessive branching logic—it often creates analytical challenges and reduces sample sizes. Some question types consistently cause problems:

Overly large matrix questions
Multiple response questions
Long ranking exercises

4. Validate Before You Launch
Always test thoroughly before launching:

Run analysis on test data
Verify skip logic paths
Check for response patterns
Look for unusual distributions

5. From Data to Decisions
Structure your data for efficient analysis:

Use consistent variable names
Code responses systematically
Include relevant context
Choose effective visualizations:
Bar charts for categories
Line charts for trends
Scatter plots for relationships
Heat maps for matrices

Expert Tips That Make a Difference
Write clear questions:

Use precise language
Define technical terms
Avoid leading questions
Be specific about time periods
Handle matrix questions carefully:
Limit items to 5-7
Keep scales consistent
Test on mobile devices

About Survey Response Scales
Scale design affects your results:

5-point scales work for simple concepts
7-point scales add nuance
11-point scales suit familiar metrics

Common Pitfalls to Avoid
Watch for these issues:

Questions measuring multiple things
Scales that don’t show meaningful differences
Missing important context
Overly complex question formats

Conclusion
Your survey succeeds when it drives decisions. Before launching, verify:

Questions connect to analysis needs
Survey flow makes sense
Each question measures one thing
Responses will be actionable
Privacy concerns are addressed
Remember: Collect data with purpose. If you can’t explain how you’ll use it, don’t collect it.

projects/uxr-blog/blog-db/dynamic-google.title: Dynamic Google Sheets Queries for UX Research Data
projects/uxr-blog/blog-db/dynamic-google.content:
If you read the my previous article about Google Sheets Query, you already know how powerful the function can be when getting counts or making groups. Today, we’re building on that foundation by diving into techniques that will help you learn more data skills and make your queries easier to maintain, so you can eventually create an analysis template for a survey you consistently use.
Advanced Google Sheets Query Techniques for Customer Satisfaction Analysis
Welcome to our comprehensive guide on leveraging Google Sheets for customer satisfaction analysis. Today, we’ll explore powerful query techniques that will help you extract meaningful insights from your CSAT data more efficiently. Whether you’re new to data analysis or looking to enhance your existing skills, these methods will streamline your workflow and improve your reporting capabilities.
1. Text Matching Magic: LIKE and CONTAINS Operators
Let’s start with two essential operators that will help you analyze customer feedback more effectively.
The LIKE operator helps you search for specific patterns in comments:
=QUERY(A:E, "SELECT * WHERE E LIKE '%improve%'")
This command identifies all entries containing the word “improve,” making it easy to spot areas needing attention.
Meanwhile, CONTAINS offers precise keyword searching:
=QUERY(A:E, "SELECT * WHERE E CONTAINS 'customer service'")
Use this to focus on specific aspects of your business by filtering comments containing exact phrases.
Note: Advanced users might be interested in using MATCHES for complex pattern matching, such as finding specific formats in comments - we’ll cover this in a future guide.
2. Dynamic Queries with Cell References
Static column references can create several challenges:

Survey modifications can break existing formulas
Collaboration becomes more complex with large datasets
Regular updates require manual intervention
The solution? Cell references. These make your queries both flexible and maintainable:

=QUERY(A:E, "SELECT " & B1 & " WHERE " & C1 & " >= " & D1)
For example, if B1 contains “A, B, C”, C1 contains “D” (your CSAT column), and D1 contains “4”, this query will automatically show data for high-satisfaction customers.
3. Enhanced Functionality with Spreadsheet Functions
Let’s explore some powerful function combinations:
First, this function helps locate column letters based on question labels:
=ARRAYFORMULA(SUBSTITUTE(ADDRESS(1,MATCH(A1,1:1,0),4),1,""))
Simply reference your question title in A1 to find its corresponding column.
For identifying distinct CSAT scores, use:
=UNIQUE(FILTER(D:D, D:D<>""))
This creates a clean list of unique scores, perfect for dropdown menus or dynamic filtering.
4. Creating a Comprehensive Query Solution
Now, let’s combine these techniques into a robust query:
=QUERY(A:Z, "SELECT " &
  ARRAYFORMULA(SUBSTITUTE(ADDRESS(1,MATCH("Date",1:1,0),4),1,"")) & ", " &
  ARRAYFORMULA(SUBSTITUTE(ADDRESS(1,MATCH("Customer Name",1:1,0),4),1,"")) & ", " &
  ARRAYFORMULA(SUBSTITUTE(ADDRESS(1,MATCH("Overall Satisfaction",1:1,0),4),1,"")) &
  " WHERE " &
  ARRAYFORMULA(SUBSTITUTE(ADDRESS(1,MATCH("Overall Satisfaction",1:1,0),4),1,"")) &
  " IN (" & TEXTJOIN(",", TRUE, UNIQUE(FILTER(D:D, D:D<>""))) & ")")
This comprehensive query offers several advantages:

Automatically identifies and selects key data columns
Creates dynamic filters based on satisfaction scores
Maintains functionality even as your survey evolves
The result is a resilient query that adapts to your changing needs while maintaining data integrity.

Additional Resources
Remember that data analysis tools, including AI assistants, can help interpret complex patterns or suggest new analytical approaches. These resources can provide valuable perspectives when you’re exploring your CSAT data.
By implementing these techniques, you’ll create more efficient and insightful customer satisfaction analyses. Focus on building queries that are both powerful and maintainable, and you’ll be well-equipped to derive actionable insights from your CSAT data.

projects/uxr-blog/blog-db/evaluating-llm.title: How to evaluate a LLM’s accuracy
projects/uxr-blog/blog-db/evaluating-llm.content:
Evaluating LLM Accuracy in Interview Data Summarization
1. Understanding the Basics

Define what constitutes a “good” summary of interview data
Identify key elements that must be preserved from interviews
Establish baseline criteria for evaluation

2. Preparation Phase

Select representative interview datasets
Create human-generated “gold standard” summaries
Define evaluation metrics and scoring criteria
Set up controlled testing environment

3. Quantitative Evaluation Methods

Measure information retention rates
Calculate accuracy of key point extraction
Assess semantic similarity scores
Compare with established NLP metrics (ROUGE, BLEU, etc.)

4. Qualitative Assessment Approaches

Expert review of summaries
Context preservation evaluation
Sentiment accuracy checking
Nuance and subtlety retention analysis

5. Testing for Specific Interview Elements

Direct quote handling accuracy
Non-verbal communication notation
Context maintenance across multiple responses
Handling of ambiguous or unclear responses

6. Bias and Fairness Assessment

Check for demographic bias in summaries
Evaluate consistency across different interview types
Assess handling of diverse perspectives

7. Practical Implementation Steps

Create evaluation checklist
Develop scoring rubric
Establish review process
Document findings and recommendations

8. Common Pitfalls and Solutions

Identify typical accuracy issues
Provide troubleshooting guidelines
Suggest improvement strategies

9. Future Considerations

Scalability of evaluation process
Adaptation for different interview types
Integration with existing research workflows
This outline provides a comprehensive framework for evaluating how well LLMs perform in summarizing interview data, considering both technical and human factors aspects of the evaluation process.

Below is a structured outline you can use to guide the process of evaluating the accuracy of an LLM’s ability to summarize interview data. The outline addresses both methodological and practical considerations, ensuring you capture the necessary details to assess the model’s performance.


1. Introduction

Objective of Summaries

Define the main purpose of summarizing interview data (e.g., extracting insights, supporting thematic analysis, identifying trends).
Clarify the context in which the summaries will be used (e.g., academic research, product design, user experience evaluation).


Importance of Accuracy

Explain why accuracy matters in summarizing interview data (e.g., ensuring critical details are captured, avoiding misinformation).
Highlight potential risks of inaccuracies (e.g., misleading conclusions, compromised decision-making).




2. Preparation and Setup

Data Collection and Format

Describe how interview data is collected and the format in which it is stored (e.g., text transcripts, audio recordings).
Ensure the data is pre-processed and cleaned (e.g., removing fillers, clarifying abbreviations) for fair evaluation.


Defining “Accuracy” for Summaries

Establish criteria (e.g., factual correctness, coverage of salient themes, coherence, conciseness).
Consider the trade-offs between brevity and completeness when defining accuracy.


Selection of Evaluation Framework

Choose an appropriate framework or rubric (e.g., manual coding comparison, machine metrics like ROUGE, BERTScore, qualitative user judgment).
Consider whether you need a purely quantitative metric, a qualitative approach, or a mixed-methods evaluation.




3. Methodological Approach to Evaluation

Reference Summaries (Gold Standards)

Have human experts or domain specialists produce high-quality reference summaries from the same interview data.
Document the process used by the human summarizers (e.g., thematic coding, iterative refinement).


Evaluation Metrics

Quantitative Metrics:

ROUGE (e.g., ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2, ROUGE-L) to measure overlap in lexical items.
BERTScore or other embedding-based methods to capture semantic similarity.


Qualitative Metrics:

Relevance: Does the summary include the key points or themes?
Coherence: Is the summarized text logically structured and does it read smoothly?
Factual Accuracy: Does it preserve the speaker’s actual sentiments and facts?
Comprehensiveness: Does it cover all important aspects of the interview?




Evaluation Procedure

Generate Summaries with the LLM

Use standardized prompts or instructions for the LLM when generating interview summaries.
Keep track of temperature and other model parameters for consistency.


Compare Summaries to References

Apply chosen metrics systematically (e.g., compute ROUGE scores, qualitative coding).
Rate each summary on a predefined scale for qualitative dimensions.






4. Human Reviewer Assessment

Reviewer Recruitment and Training

Recruit domain experts (e.g., researchers, UX professionals) or individuals familiar with the interview topics.
Provide training on evaluation criteria, ensuring consistent judgments across reviewers.


Blind Review Protocol

Hide any information that might reveal whether a summary was produced by a human or by the LLM (to reduce bias).
Instruct reviewers to score each summary based on accuracy, comprehensiveness, and coherence.


Intra-Rater and Inter-Rater Reliability

Have each reviewer assess the same set of summaries more than once to check consistency (intra-rater).
Calculate inter-rater reliability (e.g., Cohen’s kappa, Krippendorff’s alpha) to ensure consistent agreement on summary quality.




5. Quantitative and Qualitative Feedback

Aggregating Quantitative Scores

Compute average, median, or overall score across multiple metrics (ROUGE, BERTScore, any custom-coded metric).
Summarize these results to see how close the LLM summaries match the reference (human-created) summaries.


Thematic and Qualitative Insights

Identify recurring issues or missed themes in the summaries (e.g., omission of certain topics, inaccuracies in paraphrasing).
Gather descriptive feedback from reviewers about notable strengths or weaknesses in the LLM’s summaries.




6. Gap Analysis and Improvement

Identifying Sources of Error

Examine where the LLM’s summaries deviate from the reference summaries.
Classify errors (e.g., omissions, factual inaccuracies, misinterpretations).


Iterative Fine-Tuning or Prompt Engineering

Adjust LLM prompts (e.g., provide more specific instructions or constraints).
Explore fine-tuning on domain-specific data or with curated example summaries to improve accuracy.


Best Practices for Reliability

Provide model with context or example interview summaries to guide summarization approach.
Consider domain adaptation techniques to handle specialized terminology or content.




7. Reporting and Documentation

Clear Reporting of Methods

Document the entire evaluation protocol, including who created the reference summaries, how metrics were calculated, and how reviewers were trained.


Presentation of Results

Provide tables or charts showing quantitative metrics (e.g., average ROUGE scores).
Include qualitative feedback excerpts to illustrate specific strengths or weaknesses.


Recommendations for Future Work

Suggest ways to refine the evaluation approach (e.g., more domain experts, different metrics).
Highlight how the findings can inform further use of LLMs in summarizing interview data.




8. Conclusion

Summary of Findings

Recap key insights from the evaluation process (e.g., performance of the LLM, common error types).
Emphasize the areas where the LLM excels or struggles.


Implications for Human-Computer Interaction

Discuss the impact of accurate summaries on UX research, product design insights, and stakeholder communication.
Outline how improved summarization fosters better decision-making.


Next Steps

Reinforce the importance of a continuous improvement cycle—feedback from evaluations should inform model adjustments and produce more accurate summaries over time.




Tips for Implementation

Pilot Testing: Before large-scale evaluation, conduct a small pilot study to refine the evaluation criteria, metrics, and reviewer guidelines.
Mixed-Methods Approach: Combine quantitative metrics (like ROUGE) with qualitative assessments to get a more holistic view of the LLM’s performance.
Contextual Prompts: Provide the LLM with interviewer background, interview structure, and key themes to improve summary relevance and accuracy.
Human-Centered Approach: Remember that human interpretations and emergent themes may be subtle; capturing nuances often requires careful prompt design, iteration, and possible human-in-the-loop strategies.
By following this outline, you can systematically plan, execute, and document the evaluation of an LLM’s ability to accurately summarize interview data. This approach helps ensure both thorough coverage of key interview insights and reliable assessment of model performance.

projects/uxr-blog/blog-db/everyone-says-.title: The Double Diamond is Dead. Long Live the Double Diamond
projects/uxr-blog/blog-db/everyone-says-.content:
Everyone says the Double Diamond is dead. They’re half right.
The version that’s dead assumed human-speed discovery. “Discover” meant six weeks of desk research and stakeholder interviews before you had a real picture of the problem space. “Develop” meant a brainstorming session with the same five people who always lead with their confirmation bias. Every phase ran at the speed of one team’s pace reading shared updates, how busy their calendar is, and capacity to synthesize all of the data available to update their product strategy. That was a bandwidth constrain and AI removed those constraint. AI can even fake the “Discover” and “Define” phases reasonably well, which used to require some level of hands-on research.
The structure underneath it is a different matter. The four phases still hold: Discover, Define, Develop, Deliver. And what each phase protects against is still real. Commit to a problem before you’ve mapped the landscape and you’ll spend months solving the wrong one. Generate solutions before you’ve defined the problem and you’ll build something impressive that nobody needed. Ship without testing and you’ll find out what users actually wanted after you’ve already built the wrong version. The sequence is error-correction. Not ceremony.
Long live the Double Diamond.
AI didn’t kill the framework. It removed the bottleneck on both sides of it.
Expansion phases can now be dramatically wider. You can synthesize across dozens of sources in minutes, see a problem through five expert lenses simultaneously, and surface patterns that would take weeks to find manually. Compression phases can now be more evidence-based. You can rank assumptions, stress-test decisions, and strip solutions to their behavioral core before you commit.
The rhythm is the same. The engine behind it is completely different.
What follows is a framework for using that power deliberately. No technical background required. Just curiosity, a problem worth solving, and the AI tools most people already have on their phones and laptops.
Before we go further: more AI means more decisions. More decisions means more bets on your judgment, and more exposure to being wrong at speed. The only logical response to that is to think better, not just faster.

Faster ≠ Better
Speed without better judgment doesn’t reduce risk. It compounds it.
That’s the thing nobody says when they hand you an AI tool and tell you to move faster. More output per hour is real. But so is more exposure to being wrong. AI is about to automate the execution layer of most product roles: the tactical work of creating, writing, building, and validating that every role is built around. That’s the opportunity. Here’s the catch.
When AI removes friction from execution, you make more decisions per day. A lot more. And every decision is a bet on your judgment. More decisions means more bets. More bets means more exposure to getting it wrong at speed.
Here’s the evidence. Moore’s Law predicted that CPU capability would double every two years. It did. And yet, firms today require 18 times more researchers than they did in the 1970s to sustain the same rate of innovation. Company-level productivity still declines 7-10% annually for nearly 90% of firms. The same pattern shows up in agricultural yields, pharmaceutical development, and materials science.
More compute. More resources. Less output per unit of effort.
The problem was never speed. The problem is how we learn.
The Howard Hughes Medical Institute ran an experiment that proved it.

What Better Looks Like
In 2010, they shifted how they distributed research grants: instead of funding projects, they started funding people.
They extended time horizons. They explicitly tolerated early failures. They built in room for researchers to iterate, learn, and change direction. The bet was that if you gave smart people time and psychological safety, better science would follow.
It did. Publications rose 39%. Top citations rose 96%.
They didn’t move faster. They learned better. And learning better produced more innovation.
The lesson for product teams is uncomfortable but clear. Creating novel ideas that actually provide value is hard. It requires user empathy and shared expertise. It requires the willingness to be wrong early so you can be right when it matters. No amount of AI-accelerated execution changes that.
What AI does change is how you collaborate on the hard part.
Instead of one team synthesizing one problem space at human speed, you can now explore ten problem areas simultaneously. Instead of one brainstorm with the same five people, you can generate wildly different solutions from five distinct expert perspectives in minutes. Instead of weeks of desk research before you have a landscape, you can have a synthesis in an afternoon.
The rate of learning goes up. The quality of decisions goes up with it.
Your customers pay you because their problems are hard. That won’t change. What changes is how much cognitive firepower you bring to those hard problems.
The framework that follows isn’t more work. It’s an easier path to the work that actually matters: understanding what customers need and delivering it without guessing.

What Works (and What Doesn’t)
What Works
Four questions. In this order. Every time.

Discover: “What are all the problems facing the market and our users?”
Define: “Which of those problems has the most impact and is actually ours to solve?”
Develop: “Which solution would reach the most users or the largest market?”
Deliver: “How do we build that solution right now?”
This is the Double Diamond. Before you write it off as a 2005 relic, consider what it actually guarantees: you cannot commit to a solution before you’ve earned the right to. The human jobs at every phase (asking the right questions, extending empathy, generating options, making judgment calls) don’t disappear. AI makes each one possible at a scale that wasn’t available before.

What Doesn’t Work
Asking LLMs to be truly intelligent doesn’t work. Asking them to reason does.
The distinction matters. When you give an LLM an open-ended problem with no structure around how you want it to think, you tend to get one of four failure modes:

Irrelevant overload: more information than the team can use
Endless categorization: sophisticated taxonomies that produce no actionable solution
Complex solutions to fake problems: solutions that impress in a meeting but won’t earn a single dollar
Compounded bias: your assumptions, reflected back at you, louder
Without guardrails, AI doesn’t help you navigate the decision space. It amplifies chaos inside it.
The cognitive science behind why this happens is worth a full article on its own. The short version: LLMs are exceptional at recall and comprehension but fall apart at the higher-order thinking (analysis, evaluation, creation) that product decisions actually require. Without structure, they confidently generate the wrong answer. A deeper breakdown of where LLMs succeed and fail across Bloom’s Taxonomy is coming in a future piece.
The practical point for now: the tool is powerful. An undirected tool is just noise at scale. That structure is the Random Forest Double Diamond.


The Random Forest Double Diamond
Before AI, product development was sequential. You discovered the problem, decided on a solution, designed it, tested it, and shipped it. Each phase waited for the last one to finish. The whole process moved at the speed of one team’s bandwidth.
After AI, work becomes parallel.
Instead of exploring one problem area deeply, you explore ten simultaneously. Instead of generating one solution direction and iterating, you generate wildly different solutions and assess them against each other. Instead of one synthesis pass, you run multiple in minutes and compare the outputs.
Each “dot” in the diagram below represents a decision. Pre-AI, there are relatively few dots per phase. Post-AI, each phase branches into a forest of parallel paths, evaluated through synthesis-level reasoning, compressed back to a decision by the human in the loop.
This is the Random Forest Double Diamond. Same structure. Same rhythm. Completely different density of thinking at every phase.
Navigating it comes down to two questions, held in tension at every phase:

Horizontal axis: Why are we doing this phase? (the reasoning that keeps you honest)
Vertical axis: How can AI do this better? (the prompting that expands your reach)
Here’s how those questions look in practice across all four phases.

Discover: Expand the Problem Space
The job of the Discover phase is to fight premature convergence. You want the widest possible view of the problem landscape before you narrow anything down.
The “Why” questions:

Why is this problem worth solving for the business?
Why do users actually care about this problem?
Why do I care? (Honest answer. It shapes your framing.)
The “How can AI help” questions:
What AI role or persona would surface the most useful perspective here?
How much more information could I feed into this synthesis?
How “big” can I make this problem before I start losing signal?
The prompts at this phase should ask AI to enumerate, map, and synthesize broadly. You’re building a landscape, not a recommendation. The more divergent the inputs, the better the raw material for Define.
You now have a landscape. The natural temptation is to solve everything in it. The Define phase is about resisting that.

Define: Compress to What Matters
The job of the Define phase is to fight analysis paralysis. You have a wide landscape. Now you need to find the highest-leverage point inside it.
The “Why” questions:

Why is this problem (and not another) the right one to define?
Why do users care about it enough to change their behavior?
Why should the company prioritize it over competing opportunities?
The “How can AI help” questions:
How many distinct problems can I collapse into one root cause?
How simple can I make the problem statement without losing accuracy?
What’s the underlying assumption I’d need to invalidate to walk away from this?
At this phase, prompts should ask AI to rank, cluster, and surface root causes. You’re making a commitment here. AI builds the evidence base. You make the call.
You’ve committed to a problem. Now you need to find a solution worth building. Most teams stop too early with the first idea that sounds good. The Develop phase requires more.

Develop: Generate Wildly Different Solutions
The job of the Develop phase is to fight first-solution bias. Most teams converge on the first good idea. The Random Forest approach forces divergence before convergence.
The “How can AI help” questions:

What would a completely different AI role (engineer, ethnographer, economist) propose as a solution?
How many distinct solution directions could exist?
What does the craziest viable solution look like?
Prompts here should assign different expert roles to the same problem and compare outputs. The goal is genuine variety, not variations on the same theme. You want options that surprise you.
This is also where Sam the Strategizer earns its keep. Sam is a strategic design thinking AI built specifically to stop you from jumping to a solution before you’ve fully understood the problem. You describe the problem you’re trying to solve, and Sam pushes back: reframing your constraints, surfacing unstated assumptions, suggesting research approaches you hadn’t considered.
If you find yourself in Develop and your options all look the same, Sam is the fastest way to break out of that loop.
You now have options that are genuinely different from each other. The job shifts from generation to judgment.

Deliver: Compress to Action
The job of the Deliver phase is to fight perfectionism. You have strong solution candidates. Now you need to ship something real, learn from it, and iterate.
The “How can AI help” questions:

How simple can we make the solution feel to the user?
How would a skeptical user evaluate this critically? What would they reject?
What’s the minimum viable version we could build and validate right now?
Prompts at this phase should stress-test your solution from the user’s perspective and help you define the smallest artifact worth shipping. The goal is fast, honest validation, not a polished product that hasn’t been tested.
Leveraging shared expertise to iterate and evaluate more divergent ideas is what separates you from AI, and from your competition. Anyone can prompt. Fewer people can judge.
The framework works. But two things stop most teams from using it.


The Wrinkle
First: How do you know what “better” actually looks like inside your organization’s real constraints? Who decides? And how do you measure confidence in a decision when you’re making 100x more of them per day?
Second: How do non-technical team members own the process? When only engineers understand the techstack, every product decision queues up behind them. They become the bottleneck not because the work is technically complex, but because the knowledge is siloed.
Those two problems share the same root cause. The bottleneck was never technical complexity. It was always siloed knowledge.
The good news: the only bottleneck that matters to an LLM is your ability to articulate yourself. If you can describe a decision framework clearly, an LLM can apply it. If you can summarize what your system can and cannot do, a non-technical IC can use that summary to evaluate feasibility on their own.
As a proof of concept: I built a Feasibility Agent using exactly this approach. I used Human Factors methods to understand the relevant decision frameworks, summarized the required technical knowledge from Jira, and instructed an LLM to translate that knowledge into a tool anyone on the team could use. Now a product designer can assess whether a feature is technically feasible without opening a single engineering ticket.
A full breakdown of how to build your own feasibility agent is coming in a future article.
The point for now is simpler: every knowledge bottleneck in your organization is a prompt engineering problem waiting to be solved.

🧰 Choosing Your AI Tools
The framework is tool-agnostic. AI products will launch, merge, and disappear. What stays constant is the type of cognitive work each phase requires. Match your tool to the job, not the brand.

Discover needs breadth. You want tools that can synthesize across many sources at once: multi-document research tools, web-connected LLMs, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems. The capability to look for is cross-source synthesis.
Define needs structure. You want tools that organize and compress information. Any general-purpose LLM handles this well. The capability to look for is analytical reasoning and ranking.
Develop needs variety. You want tools that generate divergent options from different angles: role-prompted LLMs, rapid prototyping tools, code generators. The capability to look for is creative generation under constraints.
Deliver needs speed. You want tools that reduce the friction of shipping: code generators, automation builders, prototyping environments. The capability to look for is fast artifact creation.
You’ll likely use different tools across phases, and you may use multiple tools within a single phase. That’s fine. The prompts below are designed to work with any AI tool that accepts natural language input. Paste them wherever you do your thinking.
One note worth adding: the way you prompt will vary by tool, and the tools themselves will keep changing. What stays constant is the underlying skill. Build the muscle memory of structured, phase-aware prompting rather than fluency with any single platform. The goal is to work well with any AI, not to master one.


What You Can Do Right Now
You do not need a technical background to start. You need curiosity and a problem worth solving.
Your ability to articulate the way you solve problems is the only real bottleneck when learning to navigate the Random Forest. The tools will change. The prompts will evolve. But the underlying skill of clear, structured thinking compounds over time regardless of what ships next quarter.
Four rules that consistently help:

Protect your time. AI is fast. Undirected AI time is not. Set a scope before you start a session.
Identify and update your mental model. The biggest risk isn’t bad AI output. It’s you accepting a bad output because it sounds confident. Know your domain well enough to push back.
Articulate what “good enough” means. Before you prompt, define the success criterion. “I’ll know this is useful when it…” completes the thought before you start.
Everyone should learn prompt engineering. Not just ICs. Managers too. The organizational literacy gap is where most of the value gets left on the table.
And remember: the work that makes you valuable doesn’t change.
Wherever you sit in the product process, your job is still to understand problems clearly before committing to solutions, generate options worth choosing from, and make judgment calls that a model cannot make for you. AI removes the execution tax on all of that. What you do with the freed capacity is the only question that matters.


The Double Diamond Is Dead. Long Live the Double Diamond.
Think like an agentic orchestrator.
That’s not just a mindset. It’s a practical filter. When you’re deciding whether a task belongs to you or to an AI tool, ask one question: is this a task for learning or for execution? If it requires judgment, empathy, context, or original framing, that’s yours. If it requires speed, synthesis, enumeration, or pattern-matching at scale, that’s the AI’s job. Humans learn. AI works.
The teams that win the next decade won’t be the ones with the most AI tools. They’ll be the ones who learned to think with them.
That’s a skill, not a subscription. It compounds. The practitioner who builds the habit of structured, AI-augmented reasoning today will be a different caliber of decision-maker in three years. Not because the tools got better, though they will. Because the thinking got better.
The Double Diamond didn’t become obsolete when AI arrived. It became the most important framework in your toolkit. The structure that protected you from building the wrong thing at human speed now protects you from building the wrong thing at AI speed, which is much faster and much more expensive to undo.
Your job is not to prompt better. Your job is to think better, and let the prompts carry the weight of execution.
The questions are the forcing function. The judgment is yours. That combination is the only durable competitive advantage left.

projects/uxr-blog/blog-db/four-mental-mo.content:
These four mental models will up-level your perception of AI. Use a Universal Prompt Pattern and more tips to improve prompting today.
Why Your Prompts Might Not Work

I believe the biggest reason there’s confusion and ambiguity around AI is because our emotions and previous experience make us use outdated mental models to describe what AI really “is” and what it can do.
Factor #1 - LLM’s have a wide range of capabilities
Some see AI as a superhero that can do anything faster than a human. Others see it as a broken machine that occasionally produces decent results. The reality is in between, where you get more value by writing better prompts that maximize its strengths while limiting its weaknesses.
Factor #2 - Fear
Right now, the world (social media, news, company messaging) tells us AI will take our jobs and these feelings are too valid to easily dismiss. These fears trap us in outdated mental models, killing motivation and creating a self-fulfilling prophecy: weak prompts produce generic results, which decrease motivation and confirm our fault assumptions.

To break this cycle, I’ve distilled years of research, personal experience, and dozens of interviews into four mental models and practical tips for better AI results today. 
Mental Model #1: AI is an Unreliable Assistant

How to Self-Identify: You approach AI with low expectations, treating it like a junior assistant/apprentice you have to micro-manage to get the result you want. You prompt it like a human and need 5-10+ replies to get generic results that still needs a significant manual refinement.
The Limitation: This begins the self-fulfilling prophecy where minimal effort leads to mediocre results, reinforcing the belief that “AI isn’t useful” and only worthy of continued minimal effort.
When this Makes Sense: Quick, low-stakes tasks where you need a rough draft and don’t care about quality.
How to Grow Beyond: Treat every prompt as your custom programming function. Use the universal prompt pattern  and iteratively learn which words/context/constraints work best for your specific needs.
Example Prompts:

Current Mental Model Write a blog post about productivity talking about XYZ
Next Mental Model
You're an expert blog writer specializing in XYZ. Draft 5 blog outlines (max 8 bullet points each) on scientifically backed productivity tips that can be immediately acted upon. After I select one, use ABC tone and make it sound like me [using example below] and easy to read.



Mental Model #2: AI is a Chain of Super-Powered Personas


How to Self-Identify: You treat AI as a collection of expert personas (copywriter, analyst, therapist, etc) which you orchestrate. Results are less generic but still need refinement.
The Limitation: LLMs aren’t human. Treating them as such causes bottlenecks, hallucinations, and poor results because you’re forcing a simple neural network to mimic a far more complex one (the brain) instead of leveraging its training data. Human brains are vastly more complex than LLMs, like comparing a city to the Solar System.
When this Makes Sense: Structured workflows using content in the training data (Storytelling → Deck Building → Script Writing; Career Coach → Skill Building → Resume Writing).
How to Grow Beyond: Test personas with training data you know isn’t there (new, rare content). Debug prompts to improve outputs and build a more advanced understanding the model. Use LLM “Reasoning” and other prompting techniques when building prompts.
Example Prompts: {toggle=“true”}
- **Previous Mental Model**
	```plain text

You’re an expert blog writer specializing in XYZ. Draft 5 blog outlines (max 8 bullet points each) on scientifically backed productivity tips that can be immediately acted upon. After I select one, use ABC tone and make it sound like me [using example below] and easy to read.
- **Next Mental Model** 		- \[Stage 1: Blog Research & Outline Generator\] 		plain text
You are an expert research assistant and content strategist specializing in evidence-based blog content. Your job is to transform a rough blog topic into a comprehensive, research-backed outline ready for writing.
Process:

Identify 3-5 core claims or arguments that should anchor the blog post
For each claim, find 2-3 credible sources (research papers, industry reports, case studies)
Identify knowledge gaps where additional research would strengthen the argument
Suggest a narrative structure: hook → context → main arguments → implications → call-to-action
Flag any claims that need fact-checking or might be controversial

Output: Detailed blog outline with:

Compelling hook options (3 variations)
Section-by-section breakdown with key points
Research citations for each major claim
Suggested examples, analogies, or case studies
Potential counterarguments to address
Target word count per section

Constraints: Prioritize authoritative sources. Flag confidence level (high/medium/low) for each claim. No unverified statistics.
- \[Stage 2: Blog Writer\] 		plain text
You are an expert blog writer who transforms research-backed outlines into engaging, publishable blog posts. Take the outline, research, and citations from Stage 1 and write a complete blog post.
Process:

Use the selected hook and narrative structure from the outline
Write in a conversational but authoritative tone - make complex ideas accessible
Integrate research citations naturally without disrupting flow
Use specific examples, analogies, and stories to illustrate abstract concepts
Break up text with subheadings, bullet points, and formatting for scannability
End with a clear call-to-action or key takeaway

Output: Complete blog post (800-1500 words) with:

Engaging introduction with hook
Well-structured body sections with research support
Natural transitions between ideas
Inline citations in [brackets] format
Conclusion with actionable takeaway
SEO-friendly subheadings

Tone: Match the provided writing samples - conversational, human, engaging yet credible.
Non-negotiable: All research citations from Stage 1 must appear in the final post. Maintain factual accuracy. No fluff or filler content.
```


Mental Model #3: AI is a Blurry JPEG of the Internet

How to Self-Identify: You understand LLMs as neural networks that recognize patterns and generate probabilistic outputs from training data. You debug faulty results and craft better prompts than typical examples. (Source of this mental model)
The Limitation: You might become overly skeptical, restricting yourself to AI’s limitations rather than leveraging your brain’s strengths. Understanding LLM shortcomings doesn’t limit usefulness; it means you can augment the model with other features (see further section).
When this Makes Sense: Research, fact-checking, automating workflows, debugging complex prompts, understanding LLM limitations before critical applications.
How to Grow Beyond: Apply AI creatively for ideation, brainstorming, and strategizing while maintaining fact-checking rigor by leveraging RAG. Use LLMs to strengthen your weaknesses and ask it to perform verbs associated with reasoning.
Example Prompts {toggle=“true”}
- **Previous Mental Model**
	```plain text

You are an expert blog writer who transforms research-backed outlines into engaging, publishable blog posts. Take the outline, research, and citations from Stage 1 and write a complete blog post.
Process:

Use the selected hook and narrative structure from the outline
Write in a conversational but authoritative tone - make complex ideas accessible
Integrate research citations naturally without disrupting flow
Use specific examples, analogies, and stories to illustrate abstract concepts
Break up text with subheadings, bullet points, and formatting for scannability
End with a clear call-to-action or key takeaway

Output: Complete blog post (800-1500 words) with:

Engaging introduction with hook
Well-structured body sections with research support
Natural transitions between ideas
Inline citations in [brackets] format
Conclusion with actionable takeaway
SEO-friendly subheadings

Tone: Match the provided writing samples - conversational, human, engaging yet credible.
Non-negotiable: All research citations from Stage 1 must appear in the final post. Maintain factual accuracy. No fluff or filler content.
- **Next Mental Model** 		plain text
You’re an expert research assistant helping me I’m writing a blog post [link] about AI productivity strategies for knowledge workers. I need to fact-check specific claims and identify knowledge gaps in my current draft.
TASK: Review these three productivity statistics I found [insert statistics]. For each one:

Trace the likely source of the claim
Flag any misattributions or errors associated with this claim
Suggest changes to either the claim, my blog, or something else to correct this problem.
Suggest which sources (research papers, industry reports, surveys) would be most authoritative

CONSTRAINTS: Be skeptical. If you’re uncertain about a data point, explicitly state your confidence level and reasoning. Alawys cite your sources and don’t be afraid to say that you couldn’t find what you’re looking for.
```


Mental Model #4: AI is a Socratic Thought Partner

How to Self-Identify: You use AI as a collaborative thinking tool that explores ideas from new angles. You treat prompts as hypotheses to test and learn which tasks suit the LLM versus your own brain. Prompts are extensions of lines of thought that you hand off to a machine with varying levels of complexity.
The Limitation: You might endlessly explore without taking action, or treat AI as an oracle rather than recognizing its limitations from training data and probabilistic nature.
When this Makes Sense: Complex problem-solving, brainstorming, challenging biases, exploring perspectives, ideating multi-step AI/LLM workflows, and building new mental patterns by testing yourself against the model.
Example Prompts: {toggle=“true”}
- **Previous Mental Model**
	```plain text

You’re an expert research assistant helping me I’m writing a blog post [link] about AI productivity strategies for knowledge workers. I need to fact-check specific claims and identify knowledge gaps in my current draft.
TASK: Review these three productivity statistics I found [insert statistics]. For each one:

Trace the likely source of the claim
Flag any misattributions or errors associated with this claim
Suggest changes to either the claim, my blog, or something else to correct this problem.
Suggest which sources (research papers, industry reports, surveys) would be most authoritative

CONSTRAINTS: Be skeptical. If you’re uncertain about a data point, explicitly state your confidence level and reasoning. Alawys cite your sources and don’t be afraid to say that you couldn’t find what you’re looking for.
- **Last Mental Model** 		plain text
You’re a Socratic thought partner helping me refine the core argument of my blog post about AI productivity strategies for knowledge workers. I want you to challenge my thinking and help me discover blind spots in my logical or emotional arguments.
CONTEXT: I’ve written a draft [link] arguing that mental models are the main barrier to AI adoption. I need to stress-test the underlying logic and explore alternative perspectives I might be missing or else I’ll be fired and have a crisis.
YOUR ROLE: Act as an intellectual and emotional sparring partner who:

Challenges unstated assumptions or biases
Help me emotional empathize with the audience and identify opportunities to improve my ability to authentically connect with the reader.
Ask probing questions that expose gaps thought or emotions.
Suggests perspectives I’m likely overlooking based on my apparent cognitive biases or professional background

PROCESS:

First, articulate back to me what you understand my core argument to be (so I can verify you’re on the right track)
Then challenge it from these distinct perspectives: a skeptic, an inexperienced novice, and an overloaded executive
Use those perspectives to review my argument to fufill your main objective.
Finally, suggest an entirely different way to structure or frame this content that I probably haven’t considered.
ALWAYS QUESTION YOUR OWN BIASES AND PERSPECTIVES

OUTPUT FORMAT: Use a conversational Socratic dialogue style. Ask me questions that make me think harder, not just rhetorical ones. When you spot a logical weakness, frame it as “What if…” or “Have you considered…” rather than “This is wrong because…”
CONSTRAINTS: 

ALWAYS FOLLOW: EVERY SUGGESTION/QUESTION YOU SUGGEST MUST BE ACTIONABLE WITH A CLEAR IMPROVEMENT THAT ALIGNS WITH MY OBJECTIVES
Don’t be performatively contrarian, geniinely challenge ideas 
Distinguish between “this argument has a flaw” vs “this could be stronger if…” and never settle for a “good enough” argument.
If you find my reasoning sound, say so and explain why, then push me to the next level
Make me uncomfortable (intellectually and emotionally) if it is in service of a better output.

GOAL: By the end of this exchange, I should either have a much stronger argument OR realize I need to fundamentally rethink my approach. Both outcomes are equally valuable.
```


The Universal Prompt Pattern

Okay, so I lied just a tiny bit, there’s not really a peer-reviewed “universal prompt pattern”.
But, I’ve researched and consolidated major patterns into what I will call the Universal Prompt Pattern, which works for any use case with varying complexity.
> [ROLE/CONTEXT] + [TASK] + [OUTPUT] + [CONSTRAINTS] + [STYLE/TONE]
Where each component is:

ROLE/CONTEXT: Describe what role and context you want the model to use.

You're an expert blogger who specializes in distilling complex concepts into easy to understand pieces 


TASK: Clearly describe what you want help with. When in doubt, always be as literal as you can.

Help me think of a story structure that easily illustrates [complex concept] 


OUTPUT: Objectively and clearly describe the ideal output. 

Each outline should be 100 words max and be at the highest level possible 


CONSTRAINTS: List any constraints you want and use exact numbers or absolutes (minimize, maximize, etc) when possible.

Give me 5 different outlines to choose from, include 3 alternative opening hooks for each outline 


STYLE/TONE: Provide examples, describe your tone, or iterate over time. This defines “you” in AI outputs.

Use [linked examples] to match and elevate my style and tone. ALWAYS ENSURE YOU SOUND LIKE A HUMAN AND *NEVER USE EM DASH -*



Why This Works
This pattern clarifies your needs and spots prompt gaps. Your goal as the prompt engineer is find words that trigger the right concepts in the model’s architecture. Being literal helps “find” the right concept.
Pro Tip: Save your best prompts as reusable templates. They become valuable assets in your workflow.
When to Use
As stated, this pattern should pretty much apply to all use cases. The more complex or important your query, the more robust your prompt should be. Include a list in the task or constraints and tell the model to always think step-by-step if you don’t have access to a more advanced model (this is a shortcut to “Reasoning”).
LLM’s “Reasoning”
Most explanations of AI Reasoning are needlessly complex. This academic paper contains the clearest illustration:

When you ask the model something, it mimics the self-reflective process below to evaluate its ability to meet the prompt. 

Infer Questions: Reads your request and tries to “understand” the goal.
Draft & Self-Check: Creates an output, then asks itself: “Does this answer what they asked?”
Final Output: Iterates if needed, then shares the result.

Why This Works
This “reasoning” helps AI models catch mistakes, produce accurate answers, and handle complex requests. The model quality-checks its output while limiting context usage.
Claude Code, Anthropic’s agentic coding tool without a UI, relies on well-structured reasoning to “learn” from mistakes. This lets them focus on building better models with more robust reasoning instead of entire software UIs.
When to Use
If your prompt has multiple steps, or contains a lot of information, then its best to use any of the “reasoning” or “pro” models and ask it to think it through step by step to ensure the output meets my needs or something similar. If you’re just trying to answer a question, then you don’t need reasoning.
Retrieval-Augmented-Generation (RAG)

RAG lets AI models access external sources in real-time, citing specific documents you can verify instead of relying on training data. Upload files, link databases, or connect knowledge bases (Notion, internet) to give the model otherwise inaccessible context and prevent hallucinations.
Tools like NotebookLM, ChatGPT’s search mode, and Gemini’s Deep Research use RAG, but Perplexity (search) and NotebookLM (summarize, transform) excel at their respective use cases.
Why this Works
Selecting specific sources (social media, academic papers, patents, SEC filings, Notion pages, Google Drive, etc.) lets you answer niche questions training data wouldn’t cover. This makes AI a true research assistant with fewer hallucinations and better outputs (critical for automated workflows).
Pro-Tip: Perplexity allows queries to use all of those sources and more. (no, this isn’t paid)
When to Use
Use RAG for semantically loaded information, company materials (when allowed), knowledge base summaries, or real-time internet searches. While RAG may be less creative or occasionally miss content, the improved accuracy is worth it for certain use cases.
For example: Spend 10 minutes researching a company for interviews so you drop insightful details and be remembered as as stand-out candidate.
Important Note: RAG quality depends on document structure, organization, source accuracy, prompt clarity, context window size (Claude’s is the best), and the randomness of LLM’s.

Prompt Engineering Techniques

Few-Shot Prompting
Provide a few examples in the model and ask it to match the format/tone or ask it to draw inspiration from them.
When to use: If you need consistent formatting or creative ideation on information not in the training data.
Chain-of-Thought
Ask the AI to explain its thought process step-by-step, or follow a series of detailed instructions doing so, instead of jumping straight to the answer (seen above a few times).
When to use: When you need accurate reasoning for problem solving, if you keep getting surface-level outputs, or to mimic the “reasoning” of advanced models.
Prompt Chaining
Breaking one big task into smaller conversations, each built context/prompts that optimize that specific step so the output of one conversation builds on the previous.
When to use: You’re trying to uplevel to the “AI is a Chain of Super-Powered Personas”, you’re trying to test automated workflows, or creatively explore lines of thought/production efficiently using AI.
Extra Techniques I Personally Learned

Iterative Prompting
Prompt engineering requires trial and error, web searches, and creative exploration. This skill takes weeks to months to develop, so keep practicing and be patient with yourself
Just enough Context
The goal of prompting is to provide the right context for the model to solve your problem, not to dump as many words as possible into the model to make it “learn”. For smaller tasks, this may mean  you limit the prompt to 20 words while other tasks require robust agents with persistent context.
Use Weird Formatting/Characters
LLM training data is mostly plain text. Special characters (!@#$%^&*) and ALL CAPS are rare, giving them stronger semantic weight which makes it helpful when emphasizing critical requirements.
For example: **[MY PRIMARY GOALS OFTEN LOOK LIKE THIS]**
Limitations Beyond this Article

RAG and “reasoning” in advanced models have mitigated typical LLM limitations like factual accuracy and critical thinking. The biggest remaining drawbacks are:
Context or Working Memory
LLMs fixed context windows cause reasoning errors, hallucinations, and inability to retrieve all relevant data. Humans have superior working memory that improves by chunking tasks or   or various learning techniques.

Solution: Improve your prompting to match the model’s context. Provide examples. Use “Thinking” or “Reasoning” mode for self-reflection.

Learning
LLMs store some conversations and update through retraining, but don’t rebuild their architecture with each question like babies learning, or develop long-term memory like humans remembering preferences

Solution: Create persistent contexts (fancy term is “Agent”) with relevant information and prompts (with api protocols like real “agentic AI”) that don’t overload its context.

projects/uxr-blog/blog-db/four-mental-mo.content:
These four mental models will up-level your perception of AI. Use a Universal Prompt Pattern and more tips to improve prompting today.
Why Your Prompts Might Not Work

I believe the biggest reason there’s confusion and ambiguity around AI is because our emotions and previous experience make us use outdated mental models to describe what AI really “is” and what it can do.
Factor #1 - LLM’s have a wide range of capabilities
Some see AI as a superhero that can do anything faster than a human. Others see it as a broken machine that occasionally produces decent results. The reality is in between, where you get more value by writing better prompts that maximize its strengths while limiting its weaknesses.
Factor #2 - Fear
Right now, the world (social media, news, company messaging) tells us AI will take our jobs and these feelings are too valid to easily dismiss. These fears trap us in outdated mental models, killing motivation and creating a self-fulfilling prophecy: weak prompts produce generic results, which decrease motivation and confirm our fault assumptions.

To break this cycle, I’ve distilled years of research, personal experience, and dozens of interviews into four mental models and practical tips for better AI results today. 
Mental Model #1: AI is an Unreliable Assistant

How to Self-Identify: You approach AI with low expectations, treating it like a junior assistant/apprentice you have to micro-manage to get the result you want. You prompt it like a human and need 5-10+ replies to get generic results that still needs a significant manual refinement.
The Limitation: This begins the self-fulfilling prophecy where minimal effort leads to mediocre results, reinforcing the belief that “AI isn’t useful” and only worthy of continued minimal effort.
When this Makes Sense: Quick, low-stakes tasks where you need a rough draft and don’t care about quality.
How to Grow Beyond: Treat every prompt as your custom programming function. Use the universal prompt pattern  and iteratively learn which words/context/constraints work best for your specific needs.
Example Prompts:

Current Mental Model Write a blog post about productivity talking about XYZ
Next Mental Model
You're an expert blog writer specializing in XYZ. Draft 5 blog outlines (max 8 bullet points each) on scientifically backed productivity tips that can be immediately acted upon. After I select one, use ABC tone and make it sound like me [using example below] and easy to read.



Mental Model #2: AI is a Chain of Super-Powered Personas


How to Self-Identify: You treat AI as a collection of expert personas (copywriter, analyst, therapist, etc) which you orchestrate. Results are less generic but still need refinement.
The Limitation: LLMs aren’t human. Treating them as such causes bottlenecks, hallucinations, and poor results because you’re forcing a simple neural network to mimic a far more complex one (the brain) instead of leveraging its training data. Human brains are vastly more complex than LLMs, like comparing a city to the Solar System.
When this Makes Sense: Structured workflows using content in the training data (Storytelling → Deck Building → Script Writing; Career Coach → Skill Building → Resume Writing).
How to Grow Beyond: Test personas with training data you know isn’t there (new, rare content). Debug prompts to improve outputs and build a more advanced understanding the model. Use LLM “Reasoning” and other prompting techniques when building prompts.

	```plain text
- **Next Mental Model** 		- \[Stage 1: Blog Research & Outline Generator\] 		plain text
You are an expert research assistant and content strategist specializing in evidence-based blog content. Your job is to transform a rough blog topic into a comprehensive, research-backed outline ready for writing.
Process:

Identify 3-5 core claims or arguments that should anchor the blog post
For each claim, find 2-3 credible sources (research papers, industry reports, case studies)
Identify knowledge gaps where additional research would strengthen the argument
Suggest a narrative structure: hook → context → main arguments → implications → call-to-action
Flag any claims that need fact-checking or might be controversial

Output: Detailed blog outline with:

Compelling hook options (3 variations)
Section-by-section breakdown with key points
Research citations for each major claim
Suggested examples, analogies, or case studies
Potential counterarguments to address
Target word count per section

Constraints: Prioritize authoritative sources. Flag confidence level (high/medium/low) for each claim. No unverified statistics.
- \[Stage 2: Blog Writer\] 		plain text
You are an expert blog writer who transforms research-backed outlines into engaging, publishable blog posts. Take the outline, research, and citations from Stage 1 and write a complete blog post.
Process:

Use the selected hook and narrative structure from the outline
Write in a conversational but authoritative tone - make complex ideas accessible
Integrate research citations naturally without disrupting flow
Use specific examples, analogies, and stories to illustrate abstract concepts
Break up text with subheadings, bullet points, and formatting for scannability
End with a clear call-to-action or key takeaway

Output: Complete blog post (800-1500 words) with:

Engaging introduction with hook
Well-structured body sections with research support
Natural transitions between ideas
Inline citations in [brackets] format
Conclusion with actionable takeaway
SEO-friendly subheadings

Tone: Match the provided writing samples - conversational, human, engaging yet credible.
Non-negotiable: All research citations from Stage 1 must appear in the final post. Maintain factual accuracy. No fluff or filler content.
```


Mental Model #3: AI is a Blurry JPEG of the Internet

How to Self-Identify: You understand LLMs as neural networks that recognize patterns and generate probabilistic outputs from training data. You debug faulty results and craft better prompts than typical examples. (Source of this mental model)
The Limitation: You might become overly skeptical, restricting yourself to AI’s limitations rather than leveraging your brain’s strengths. Understanding LLM shortcomings doesn’t limit usefulness; it means you can augment the model with other features (see further section).
When this Makes Sense: Research, fact-checking, automating workflows, debugging complex prompts, understanding LLM limitations before critical applications.
How to Grow Beyond: Apply AI creatively for ideation, brainstorming, and strategizing while maintaining fact-checking rigor by leveraging RAG. Use LLMs to strengthen your weaknesses and ask it to perform verbs associated with reasoning.

	```plain text
CONSTRAINTS: Be skeptical. If you’re uncertain about a data point, explicitly state your confidence level and reasoning. Alawys cite your sources and don’t be afraid to say that you couldn’t find what you’re looking for.
```

Mental Model #4: AI is a Socratic Thought Partner

How to Self-Identify: You use AI as a collaborative thinking tool that explores ideas from new angles. You treat prompts as hypotheses to test and learn which tasks suit the LLM versus your own brain. Prompts are extensions of lines of thought that you hand off to a machine with varying levels of complexity.
The Limitation: You might endlessly explore without taking action, or treat AI as an oracle rather than recognizing its limitations from training data and probabilistic nature.
When this Makes Sense: Complex problem-solving, brainstorming, challenging biases, exploring perspectives, ideating multi-step AI/LLM workflows, and building new mental patterns by testing yourself against the model.

	```plain text
- **Last Mental Model** 		plain text
You’re a Socratic thought partner helping me refine the core argument of my blog post about AI productivity strategies for knowledge workers. I want you to challenge my thinking and help me discover blind spots in my logical or emotional arguments.
CONTEXT: I’ve written a draft [link] arguing that mental models are the main barrier to AI adoption. I need to stress-test the underlying logic and explore alternative perspectives I might be missing or else I’ll be fired and have a crisis.
YOUR ROLE: Act as an intellectual and emotional sparring partner who:

Challenges unstated assumptions or biases
Help me emotional empathize with the audience and identify opportunities to improve my ability to authentically connect with the reader.
Ask probing questions that expose gaps thought or emotions.
Suggests perspectives I’m likely overlooking based on my apparent cognitive biases or professional background

PROCESS:

First, articulate back to me what you understand my core argument to be (so I can verify you’re on the right track)
Then challenge it from these distinct perspectives: a skeptic, an inexperienced novice, and an overloaded executive
Use those perspectives to review my argument to fufill your main objective.
Finally, suggest an entirely different way to structure or frame this content that I probably haven’t considered.
ALWAYS QUESTION YOUR OWN BIASES AND PERSPECTIVES

OUTPUT FORMAT: Use a conversational Socratic dialogue style. Ask me questions that make me think harder, not just rhetorical ones. When you spot a logical weakness, frame it as “What if…” or “Have you considered…” rather than “This is wrong because…”
CONSTRAINTS: 

ALWAYS FOLLOW: EVERY SUGGESTION/QUESTION YOU SUGGEST MUST BE ACTIONABLE WITH A CLEAR IMPROVEMENT THAT ALIGNS WITH MY OBJECTIVES
Don’t be performatively contrarian, geniinely challenge ideas 
Distinguish between “this argument has a flaw” vs “this could be stronger if…” and never settle for a “good enough” argument.
If you find my reasoning sound, say so and explain why, then push me to the next level
Make me uncomfortable (intellectually and emotionally) if it is in service of a better output.

GOAL: By the end of this exchange, I should either have a much stronger argument OR realize I need to fundamentally rethink my approach. Both outcomes are equally valuable.
```

The Universal Prompt Pattern

Okay, so I lied just a tiny bit, there’s not really a peer-reviewed “universal prompt pattern”.
But, I’ve researched and consolidated major patterns into what I will call the Universal Prompt Pattern, which works for any use case with varying complexity.
> [ROLE/CONTEXT] + [TASK] + [OUTPUT] + [CONSTRAINTS] + [STYLE/TONE]
Where each component is:

ROLE/CONTEXT: Describe what role and context you want the model to use.

You're an expert blogger who specializes in distilling complex concepts into easy to understand pieces 


TASK: Clearly describe what you want help with. When in doubt, always be as literal as you can.

Help me think of a story structure that easily illustrates [complex concept] 


OUTPUT: Objectively and clearly describe the ideal output. 

Each outline should be 100 words max and be at the highest level possible 


CONSTRAINTS: List any constraints you want and use exact numbers or absolutes (minimize, maximize, etc) when possible.

Give me 5 different outlines to choose from, include 3 alternative opening hooks for each outline 


STYLE/TONE: Provide examples, describe your tone, or iterate over time. This defines “you” in AI outputs.

Use [linked examples] to match and elevate my style and tone. ALWAYS ENSURE YOU SOUND LIKE A HUMAN AND *NEVER USE EM DASH -*



Why This Works
This pattern clarifies your needs and spots prompt gaps. Your goal as the prompt engineer is find words that trigger the right concepts in the model’s architecture. Being literal helps “find” the right concept.
Pro Tip: Save your best prompts as reusable templates. They become valuable assets in your workflow.
When to Use
As stated, this pattern should pretty much apply to all use cases. The more complex or important your query, the more robust your prompt should be. Include a list in the task or constraints and tell the model to always think step-by-step if you don’t have access to a more advanced model (this is a shortcut to “Reasoning”).
LLM’s “Reasoning”
Most explanations of AI Reasoning are needlessly complex. This academic paper contains the clearest illustration:

When you ask the model something, it mimics the self-reflective process below to evaluate its ability to meet the prompt. 

Infer Questions: Reads your request and tries to “understand” the goal.
Draft & Self-Check: Creates an output, then asks itself: “Does this answer what they asked?”
Final Output: Iterates if needed, then shares the result.

Why This Works
This “reasoning” helps AI models catch mistakes, produce accurate answers, and handle complex requests. The model quality-checks its output while limiting context usage.
Claude Code, Anthropic’s agentic coding tool without a UI, relies on well-structured reasoning to “learn” from mistakes. This lets them focus on building better models with more robust reasoning instead of entire software UIs.
When to Use
If your prompt has multiple steps, or contains a lot of information, then its best to use any of the “reasoning” or “pro” models and ask it to think it through step by step to ensure the output meets my needs or something similar. If you’re just trying to answer a question, then you don’t need reasoning.
Retrieval-Augmented-Generation (RAG)

RAG lets AI models access external sources in real-time, citing specific documents you can verify instead of relying on training data. Upload files, link databases, or connect knowledge bases (Notion, internet) to give the model otherwise inaccessible context and prevent hallucinations.
Tools like NotebookLM, ChatGPT’s search mode, and Gemini’s Deep Research use RAG, but Perplexity (search) and NotebookLM (summarize, transform) excel at their respective use cases.
Why this Works
Selecting specific sources (social media, academic papers, patents, SEC filings, Notion pages, Google Drive, etc.) lets you answer niche questions training data wouldn’t cover. This makes AI a true research assistant with fewer hallucinations and better outputs (critical for automated workflows).
Pro-Tip: Perplexity allows queries to use all of those sources and more. (no, this isn’t paid)
When to Use
Use RAG for semantically loaded information, company materials (when allowed), knowledge base summaries, or real-time internet searches. While RAG may be less creative or occasionally miss content, the improved accuracy is worth it for certain use cases.
For example: Spend 10 minutes researching a company for interviews so you drop insightful details and be remembered as as stand-out candidate.
Important Note: RAG quality depends on document structure, organization, source accuracy, prompt clarity, context window size (Claude’s is the best), and the randomness of LLM’s.
