How UX Researchers Can Build Strong Relationships with Stakeholders
Why Building Stakeholder Relationships Matters
Imagine spending weeks on meticulous research that could transform your product. Your findings are solid, your recommendations are actionable, and your presentation is flawless. Yet somehow, when you share with stakeholders, your insights get overlooked or deprioritized. Or, better yet, you’re stakeholders express excitement when you share the insights, but weeks go by and no one makes progress on the changes, and then quarters go by and you realize that no the insights have been collecting dust.
The lesson is simple - insights create value only when implemented. Stakeholders are the key to turning your research into reality, and their trust ensures your work drives change, even when they can’t scrutinize every detail. By positioning yourself as a strategic partner rather than just a researcher, you become essential to their success, as your research directly influences their decisions and career trajectories.
While trust forms the foundation, it’s just the beginning. True innovation flourishes through effective collaboration, and organizations thrive when teams work in harmony. As a UX researcher, your role extends beyond data collection - you’re a strategic advisor helping to shape decisions. This leadership position demands trust, which grows through genuine, collaborative partnerships.
Remember: building these relationships isn’t about being popular - it’s about fostering an environment where your insights can catalyze meaningful change.
How to Start Building Stakeholder Relationships
Trust forms the cornerstone of every successful relationship. Instead of diving straight into work, invest time in understanding the people you’ll be collaborating with.
Begin by connecting with your stakeholders on a human level. Explore their motivations, professional interests, and problem-solving approaches. Practice genuine curiosity - this isn’t networking for networking’s sake, but rather a sincere effort to understand their perspectives and values.
Then, delve into their aspirations. Whether it’s launching an exceptional product, advancing their career, or achieving team milestones, understanding their definition of success allows you to align your research to support their goals.
Start small by identifying opportunities to provide immediate value. When they face challenges, demonstrate how research can illuminate solutions. Quick user tests or relevant insights sharing can show your commitment to their success.
Always seek alignment between goals. Consider how your research objectives complement their priorities and organizational aims. When you demonstrate how your work contributes to collective success, you create a stronger collaborative foundation.
The Power of Touchpoints
While establishing relationships is crucial, maintaining them ensures lasting impact. Regular check-ins serve as vital touchpoints that sustain strong connections efficiently.
Consider implementing bi-weekly coffee chats. Keep them informal - let conversations flow naturally. Share updates on current projects, gather feedback, and learn about upcoming initiatives. Understanding their decision points and challenges helps you identify opportunities where your research can add value.
These conversations provide valuable insights into improving your research impact. By discussing what works and what doesn’t, you demonstrate your commitment to continuous improvement.
Maintain authenticity throughout. Show interest in their lives beyond work. Celebrate their team’s achievements and personal milestones. These genuine interactions transform professional relationships into meaningful partnerships.
When meeting new stakeholders, first impressions are critical. Learn from their previous experiences with UX research, both positive and negative. Understand their preferred collaboration style - some want deep involvement, others prefer high-level updates. This knowledge helps you tailor your approach effectively.
Early on, identify their research priorities - whether it’s speed, quality, scope, or innovation. Their preferences will guide how you optimize your work to deliver maximum value.
Final Thoughts

projects/uxr-blog/blog-db/how-to-automat.content:
You can test a codebase for bugs in milliseconds. You can lint for accessibility violations before a pull request merges. But what about usability? What about the question every UX researcher actually cares about: will this interface make sense to a human being?
For decades, that question required scheduling time with experts, recruiting participants, and waiting days (or weeks) for results. Meanwhile, the code shipped anyway.
That gap is closing. Recent research shows that large language models can perform structured heuristic evaluations on source code and UI screenshots with moderate-to-substantial reliability. Not as replacements for human researchers. As automated quality gates embedded directly in your DevOps pipeline, triggered on command, owned by your team.
This is not about devaluing UX research. It is about amplifying it. When companies can research, publish, iterate, and own their design evaluations inside the same CI/CD workflows they already trust, UX stops being a bottleneck and starts being a competitive advantage.
Here is how to make that real.
The Problem: UX Research Cannot Keep Pace with DevOps
Modern development teams ship fast. Continuous integration, continuous deployment, automated test suites, canary releases. The engineering side of quality assurance has never been more sophisticated.
But the design side? Still largely manual.
Traditional heuristic evaluation, the method Jakob Nielsen and Rolf Molich introduced in 1990, requires trained evaluators to inspect an interface against a set of usability principles. It is effective. It is also resource-intensive and difficult to scale (Nielsen & Molich, 1990). Small teams rarely have access to dedicated UX evaluators. Even large organizations struggle to run evaluations at the speed their release cycles demand.
The result: visual and interaction quality becomes the one dimension of software that doesn’t get tested in the pipeline. Design decisions ship without structured review. Small usability regressions accumulate. And the teams that care most about quality are stuck playing catch-up.
The ISO 25010:2023 standard recognizes usability as one of nine key software product quality characteristics alongside reliability, security, and maintainability. DevOps practices have matured automated testing for most of these. Usability remains the exception.
The Breakthrough: LLMs Can Perform Heuristic Evaluations
In late 2025, researchers at Virginia Tech published one of the first rigorous studies on using GPT-4o to perform automated heuristic evaluations on website source code (Platt, Luchs, & Nizamani, 2025). Their approach was elegantly simple:

Translate each of Nielsen’s 10 usability heuristics into a structured prompt
Feed the website’s source code (HTML, CSS, JavaScript) to the model
Collect evaluations in a standardized JSON format with severity ratings, issue descriptions, code references, and recommendations
They tested this across 30 open-source websites, running three independent evaluations per site (over 850 total evaluations). The results:


82-85% agreement on whether a usability issue existed (Cohen’s Kappa ≈ 0.50)
Weighted Kappa of ~0.63 for severity ratings, indicating moderate-to-substantial consistency
The model excelled at detecting issues related to error prevention and match between system and real world
To put that in context: human expert evaluators also show significant variability in heuristic evaluation. Different experts routinely identify different issues and disagree on severity (Rubin & Chisnell, 2008). An LLM achieving 82-85% self-consistency is not perfect, but it is useful, particularly as a first-pass screen.
A parallel study from Graz University of Technology (Lubos et al., 2025) took a multimodal approach, feeding screenshots and persona descriptions to LLMs and framing usability evaluation as a recommendation task where issues are ranked by severity. Their finding: LLMs aligned best with expert assessments when using structured evaluation criteria with explicit pass/fail ratings, exactly the kind of evaluation you can encode in a prompt.
At CHI 2025, the UXAgent framework demonstrated that LLM agents can simulate thousands of users interacting with a live website, generating both qualitative interview data and quantitative behavioral logs for UX researchers to analyze (UXAgent, 2025). The researchers were not trying to eliminate human evaluation. They were trying to help UX teams pre-test and iterate their study designs before running expensive human studies.
The convergence is clear: LLMs are becoming reliable enough to serve as preliminary usability evaluators, especially when guided by well-structured heuristic prompts.

Why This Amplifies UX Research (Instead of Replacing It)
Let’s address the elephant in the room. If a machine can run a heuristic evaluation, why hire a UX researcher?
Because the machine cannot do what matters most.
LLM-based heuristic evaluation handles the structured, repeatable, criterion-referenced portion of usability assessment. It answers: “Does this interface violate known usability principles?” That is valuable. It is also the floor, not the ceiling.
What LLMs cannot do:

Discover unmet user needs through contextual inquiry or diary studies
Interpret emotional and social dynamics in user behavior
Generate novel design directions from ambiguous research signals
Navigate organizational politics to get research acted upon
Validate with real users in real contexts with real stakes
What automated heuristic evaluation actually does for UX researchers is remove the low-value, repetitive screening work so they can focus on the high-value, irreplaceable work. Your researchers stop spending time catching “missing error messages” and “inconsistent button labels” and start spending time on the strategic questions that move products forward.
Think of it like automated accessibility testing. Tools like axe-core and Lighthouse did not make accessibility experts obsolete. They made accessibility more pervasive by catching the obvious violations automatically, freeing experts to focus on the nuanced, context-dependent judgments that require human understanding.
The same pattern applies here. Automate the heuristic floor. Elevate the human ceiling.

Writing Your First Heuristic Evaluation Prompt
The key insight from the Virginia Tech study: prompt design matters enormously. Their initial attempts with generic prompts produced “flawed and, in some cases, completely inaccurate results.” Structured, specific prompts with clear output formats transformed the quality.
Here is a practical template you can adapt. This prompt evaluates a single heuristic against a provided codebase or screenshot:
You are a usability evaluation expert. Evaluate the provided [source code / screenshot] against the following Nielsen usability heuristic:
 
**Heuristic: [Heuristic Name]**
**Definition:** [One-sentence definition of the heuristic]
**Evaluation Questions:**
1. [Specific question about how this heuristic applies]
2. [Specific question about how this heuristic applies]
3. [Specific question about how this heuristic applies]
 
For your evaluation, provide:
- IssueFound: true/false
- SeverityRating: 0 (no issue) to 4 (usability catastrophe)
- IssueDescription: What specific problem exists
- Location: Where in the code/interface the issue occurs
- Recommendation: A clear, actionable fix
 
Output your evaluation as valid JSON.
Here is a concrete example for the “Error Prevention” heuristic (which showed the highest agreement rates in the Virginia Tech study):
You are a usability evaluation expert. Evaluate the provided source code against the following Nielsen usability heuristic:
 
**Heuristic: Error Prevention**
**Definition:** The design should prevent problems from occurring in the first place by eliminating error-prone conditions or presenting users with a confirmation option before they commit to an action.
 
**Evaluation Questions:**
1. Are there form inputs without validation that could accept incorrect data?
2. Are there destructive actions (delete, submit, purchase) without confirmation dialogs?
3. Are there input fields missing constraints, placeholder text, or format hints that would prevent user errors?
 
For your evaluation, provide:
- IssueFound: true/false
- SeverityRating: 0 (no issue) to 4 (usability catastrophe)
- IssueDescription: What specific problem exists
- Location: File name and relevant code section
- Recommendation: A clear, actionable fix
 
Output as valid JSON only. No commentary outside the JSON.

	**Pro Tip:** Write one prompt per heuristic. The Graz University study found that LLMs produce more precise assessments when evaluating a single criterion per prompt rather than bundling multiple heuristics together (Lubos et al., 2025). Yes, it means 10 prompts for a full Nielsen evaluation. The tradeoff in accuracy is worth it.

### The 10 Prompts You Need
For a complete automated heuristic evaluation, write one prompt for each of Nielsen's 10 heuristics:
1. **Visibility of System Status** (Does the interface keep users informed?)
2. **Match Between System and Real World** (Does it speak the user's language?)
3. **User Control and Freedom** (Can users undo and escape?)
4. **Consistency and Standards** (Does it follow conventions?)
5. **Error Prevention** (Does the design prevent mistakes?)
6. **Recognition Rather Than Recall** (Is information visible, not memorized?)
7. **Flexibility and Efficiency of Use** (Are there shortcuts for experts?)
8. **Aesthetic and Minimalist Design** (Is every element earning its place?)
9. **Help Users Recognize, Diagnose, and Recover from Errors** (Are error messages helpful?)
10. **Help and Documentation** (Is guidance available when needed?)
Each prompt follows the same structure: heuristic name, definition, 2-3 specific evaluation questions, and a standardized JSON output format. Consistency in your output format is what makes these results *parseable by your pipeline*.
## Integrating Into Your DevOps Pipeline
Once you have your 10 heuristic prompts tested and tuned, integration into a CI/CD pipeline follows a pattern any DevOps engineer will recognize. Here is a simplified architecture:
### Pipeline Stage: UX Heuristic Gate
```javascript
trigger: on pull request (or on-demand)
steps:
  1. Extract UI-relevant files (HTML, CSS, JS, screenshots)
  2. For each of 10 heuristic prompts:
     - Send code/screenshots + prompt to LLM API
     - Parse JSON response
     - Log results to evaluation database
  3. Aggregate severity scores
  4. Gate logic:
     - Severity 4 (catastrophe): Block merge, notify team
     - Severity 3 (major): Flag for UX review before merge
     - Severity 1-2 (minor/cosmetic): Log, continue
     - Severity 0: Pass
  5. Generate evaluation report (diff against previous run)
```
### What This Looks Like in Practice
**Scenario:** A developer submits a pull request that changes the checkout flow. The pipeline runs the 10 heuristic evaluation prompts against the modified code.
The "Error Prevention" prompt flags a severity 3 issue: the new payment form accepts submission without validating the credit card number format. The "Visibility of System Status" prompt flags a severity 2 issue: no loading indicator appears after the user clicks "Pay Now."
The pipeline blocks the merge on the severity 3 finding and posts both findings as comments on the pull request with specific code references and recommendations. The developer fixes the validation issue, the UX lead reviews the loading indicator finding, and the PR merges 45 minutes later.
No meeting was scheduled. No evaluator was recruited. No sprint was delayed. The usability check happened at the same speed as the linting check.

	**Important caveat:** LLM evaluations show moderate reliability, not perfect reliability. The Virginia Tech study found exact severity agreement at only 56%. **Never use automated heuristic evaluation as your sole quality gate for critical user-facing changes.** Use it as a first-pass screen that escalates to human review when severity thresholds are crossed. The goal is triage, not replacement.

## The Business Case for Small Organizations
This approach hits hardest for organizations that need quality but cannot afford a full-time UX team. Consider the math:
- **Traditional heuristic evaluation:** 3-5 expert evaluators × 2-4 hours each × \$100-200/hr = **\$600-4,000 per evaluation cycle**
- **LLM-based automated evaluation:** API calls for 10 prompts × pennies per call = **under \$1 per evaluation cycle**
The cost difference is not 10x. It is **1,000x or more.** And automated evaluations can run on every pull request, not once per quarter.
For a 10-person startup shipping weekly, this means:
- **De-risking important changes** by catching usability regressions before users see them
- **Faster development** because the feedback loop shrinks from days to minutes
- **Reduced overhead** because you do not need to pause development for evaluation cycles
- **Owned evaluations** because your heuristic prompts become a codified, version-controlled expression of your team's design standards
That last point deserves emphasis. When you write heuristic evaluation prompts, you are not just creating a testing tool. You are **documenting your organization's usability standards in executable form**. Those prompts become institutional knowledge. They can be reviewed, debated, improved, and versioned just like any other code artifact.
## Getting Started: A Practical Checklist
Ready to build your first automated heuristic evaluation pipeline? Here is the sequence:
- [ ] **Select your heuristic framework.** Nielsen's 10 heuristics are the standard starting point. You can extend or customize for your domain (e.g., adding mobile-specific or accessibility-specific heuristics).
- [ ] **Write and test your 10 prompts.** Use the template above. Test each prompt against 3-5 representative pages from your product. Compare the LLM output against your own expert judgment. Tune the evaluation questions until the output is useful.
- [ ] **Standardize your JSON output format.** Every prompt should produce identically structured output. This is what makes parsing and aggregation possible.
- [ ] **Set severity thresholds.** Decide what severity levels block a merge, require review, or simply log. Start conservative (block on severity 3+) and adjust based on signal quality.
- [ ] **Integrate with your CI/CD tool.** GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Jenkins, whatever you use. The integration is an API call wrapped in a script.
- [ ] **Build your evaluation dashboard.** Track findings over time. Look for patterns. Which heuristics flag most often? Which components generate the most issues? This is the data your UX researcher (or your future UX researcher) will use to prioritize strategic work.
- [ ] **Iterate on your prompts quarterly.** As your product evolves and your understanding deepens, refine the evaluation questions. Treat prompts like living documentation.
## The Bigger Picture
We are in the early days of a shift that will reshape how organizations think about design quality. The same pattern played out with automated testing for code correctness, then for security, then for accessibility. Each time, the fear was that automation would eliminate the human role. Each time, the opposite happened: automation raised the floor, expanded coverage, and freed experts to work on harder problems.
Usability evaluation is next.
The research is clear that LLMs are not yet expert-level evaluators. Severity judgments vary. Some heuristics (like "Help and Documentation") show low inter-rater reliability. Dynamic interaction issues that require clicking through a live interface remain difficult to assess from static code or screenshots alone.
But the research is equally clear that these tools are *useful right now*, especially for teams that currently have **zero automated usability evaluation**. Going from nothing to an 82% consistent first-pass screen is a massive quality improvement.
The organizations that move first will build institutional muscle in prompt engineering for design quality. They will accumulate evaluation data that informs strategic UX decisions. They will ship faster and with more confidence. And their UX researchers, freed from the mechanical work of catching obvious violations, will do the creative, strategic, deeply human work that actually differentiates products.
Start with one heuristic. Test it on one component. See what comes back.
Then automate it.
---
### References
- Nielsen, J. & Molich, R. (1990). Heuristic evaluation of user interfaces. *Proceedings of the SIGCHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems*, 249-256.
- Platt, N., Luchs, E., & Nizamani, S. (2025). Catching UX Flaws in Code: Leveraging LLMs to Identify Usability Flaws at the Development Stage. *arXiv:2512.04262*.
- Lubos, S., Felfernig, A., Leitner, G., & Schwazer, J. (2025). Towards Recommending Usability Improvements with Multimodal Large Language Models. *arXiv:2508.16165*.
- UXAgent (2025). UXAgent: An LLM Agent-Based Usability Testing Framework for Web Design. *CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems*.
- Rubin, J. & Chisnell, D. (2008). *Handbook of Usability Testing: How to Plan, Design, and Conduct Effective Tests*, 2nd ed. Wiley.
- ISO/IEC 25010:2023. Systems and software engineering: Systems and software Quality Requirements and Evaluation (SQuaRE).

The Art of UX Data Visualization: A Beginner’s Guide to Understanding Research Results
As UX researchers, we often collect valuable data about how users interact with our products. But raw numbers alone don’t tell the complete story. The way we visualize this data can dramatically impact how we—and our stakeholders—interpret and act upon our findings. This guide will help you understand how different visualization methods can shape our understanding of UX research results.
Why Visualization Matters in UX Research
Imagine you’ve just completed a usability study with 20 participants. You have task completion rates, time-on-task measurements, and satisfaction scores. How you present this data can either illuminate crucial insights or inadvertently obscure them. The right visualization can help you:

Quickly identify patterns and trends
Communicate findings effectively to stakeholders
Make data-driven decisions with confidence
Spot potential issues that might be hidden in raw numbers

Common UX Metrics and Their Ideal Visualizations
1. Task Success Rates
Task success rates are binary measurements: users either complete a task or they don’t. While you could present this as a simple percentage (e.g., “75% success rate”), different visualizations can provide richer context:
Bar Charts:

Best for: Comparing success rates across different tasks
Impact: Makes it easy to spot which features or workflows need the most attention
Warning: Can be misleading if sample sizes vary between tasks
Stacked Bar Charts:
Best for: Showing success, partial success, and failure rates together
Impact: Provides more nuanced understanding of user performance
Warning: Can become cluttered with too many categories

2. Time-on-Task Measurements
Time-based metrics often have more complexity than simple success/failure rates. The way you visualize these can dramatically affect interpretation:
Box Plots:

Best for: Showing distribution of completion times
Impact: Reveals outliers and helps identify if problems affect all users or just some
Warning: Can be intimidating for stakeholders unfamiliar with statistics
Line Charts:
Best for: Tracking changes in task completion time over multiple iterations
Impact: Makes it easy to see if design changes are improving efficiency
Warning: Can mask individual user experiences

3. Satisfaction Scores (e.g., SUS, NPS)
User satisfaction data often comes from surveys and questionnaires. The visualization choice here can significantly impact stakeholder reactions:
Radar/Spider Charts:

Best for: Comparing multiple satisfaction metrics simultaneously
Impact: Provides a holistic view of user satisfaction across dimensions
Warning: Can become difficult to read with too many variables
Horizontal Bar Charts:
Best for: Showing Likert scale responses
Impact: Makes it easy to compare positive versus negative sentiment
Warning: Averaging Likert data can be misleading

Common Pitfalls in UX Data Visualization
1. The Scale Trap
One of the most common ways visualizations can mislead is through manipulated scales. For example:

A bar chart starting at 50% instead of 0% can make small differences appear dramatic
Logarithmic scales can mask significant variations in user behavior
Inconsistent scales between comparable charts can lead to misinterpretation

2. The Aggregation Problem
Averaging data can hide important patterns:

Mean completion times might mask a bimodal distribution where two distinct user groups exist
Overall satisfaction scores might hide significant problems with specific features
Combined success rates might obscure important demographic differences

3. Color Confusion
Color choices can significantly impact interpretation:

Red/green color schemes can be inaccessible to colorblind users
Cultural associations with colors can bias interpretation
Too many colors can make visualizations harder to understand

Best Practices for Clear Communication
1. Choose the Right Chart Type
Match your visualization to your data type and message:

Use bar charts for comparisons
Use line charts for trends over time
Use scatter plots for correlations
Use pie charts sparingly (they’re often harder to interpret than alternatives)

2. Keep It Simple

Remove unnecessary decorative elements
Use clear, consistent labeling
Provide context through titles and annotations
Include sample sizes and confidence intervals where appropriate

3. Consider Your Audience

Technical stakeholders might appreciate more detailed visualizations
Executive stakeholders often prefer high-level summary views
Design teams might need detailed breakdowns by feature or workflow

Practical Examples
Example 1: Task Success Visualization
Instead of saying “Task A had 80% success rate, Task B had 60% success rate,” consider a visualization that shows:

Success rates as bars
Sample size as annotations
Confidence intervals to show uncertainty
Clear labels and context

Example 2: User Journey Analysis
Rather than presenting raw time-on-task data, consider:

A timeline visualization showing where users spend most time
Highlight points where users commonly encounter issues
Include qualitative data points (user quotes) at key moments

Conclusion
The way we visualize UX research data has a profound impact on how it’s interpreted and acted upon. By understanding these principles, you can create visualizations that:

Tell accurate stories about your users
Drive better design decisions
Communicate insights effectively to stakeholders
Remember: The goal isn’t to make the data look good, but to make it clear and actionable. When in doubt, opt for simpler visualizations that tell a clear story over complex ones that might confuse or mislead.

Additional Resources
For deeper learning about data visualization in UX:

Stephen Few’s “Information Dashboard Design”
Edward Tufte’s “The Visual Display of Quantitative Information”
Nielsen Norman Group’s articles on UX metrics and visualization
Remember that your role as a UX researcher is to illuminate insights that drive better design decisions. The right visualization can make the difference between data that sits unused and insights that drive meaningful change.

Evaluating LLM Accuracy in Interview Data Summarization
1. Understanding the Basics

Define what constitutes a “good” summary of interview data
Identify key elements that must be preserved from interviews
Establish baseline criteria for evaluation

2. Preparation Phase

Select representative interview datasets
Create human-generated “gold standard” summaries
Define evaluation metrics and scoring criteria
Set up controlled testing environment

3. Quantitative Evaluation Methods

Measure information retention rates
Calculate accuracy of key point extraction
Assess semantic similarity scores
Compare with established NLP metrics (ROUGE, BLEU, etc.)

4. Qualitative Assessment Approaches

Expert review of summaries
Context preservation evaluation
Sentiment accuracy checking
Nuance and subtlety retention analysis

5. Testing for Specific Interview Elements

Direct quote handling accuracy
Non-verbal communication notation
Context maintenance across multiple responses
Handling of ambiguous or unclear responses

6. Bias and Fairness Assessment

Check for demographic bias in summaries
Evaluate consistency across different interview types
Assess handling of diverse perspectives

7. Practical Implementation Steps

Create evaluation checklist
Develop scoring rubric
Establish review process
Document findings and recommendations

8. Common Pitfalls and Solutions

Identify typical accuracy issues
Provide troubleshooting guidelines
Suggest improvement strategies

9. Future Considerations

Scalability of evaluation process
Adaptation for different interview types
Integration with existing research workflows
This outline provides a comprehensive framework for evaluating how well LLMs perform in summarizing interview data, considering both technical and human factors aspects of the evaluation process.

Below is a structured outline you can use to guide the process of evaluating the accuracy of an LLM’s ability to summarize interview data. The outline addresses both methodological and practical considerations, ensuring you capture the necessary details to assess the model’s performance.


1. Introduction

Objective of Summaries

Define the main purpose of summarizing interview data (e.g., extracting insights, supporting thematic analysis, identifying trends).
Clarify the context in which the summaries will be used (e.g., academic research, product design, user experience evaluation).


Importance of Accuracy

Explain why accuracy matters in summarizing interview data (e.g., ensuring critical details are captured, avoiding misinformation).
Highlight potential risks of inaccuracies (e.g., misleading conclusions, compromised decision-making).




2. Preparation and Setup

Data Collection and Format

Describe how interview data is collected and the format in which it is stored (e.g., text transcripts, audio recordings).
Ensure the data is pre-processed and cleaned (e.g., removing fillers, clarifying abbreviations) for fair evaluation.


Defining “Accuracy” for Summaries

Establish criteria (e.g., factual correctness, coverage of salient themes, coherence, conciseness).
Consider the trade-offs between brevity and completeness when defining accuracy.


Selection of Evaluation Framework

Choose an appropriate framework or rubric (e.g., manual coding comparison, machine metrics like ROUGE, BERTScore, qualitative user judgment).
Consider whether you need a purely quantitative metric, a qualitative approach, or a mixed-methods evaluation.




3. Methodological Approach to Evaluation

Reference Summaries (Gold Standards)

Have human experts or domain specialists produce high-quality reference summaries from the same interview data.
Document the process used by the human summarizers (e.g., thematic coding, iterative refinement).


Evaluation Metrics

Quantitative Metrics:

ROUGE (e.g., ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2, ROUGE-L) to measure overlap in lexical items.
BERTScore or other embedding-based methods to capture semantic similarity.


Qualitative Metrics:

Relevance: Does the summary include the key points or themes?
Coherence: Is the summarized text logically structured and does it read smoothly?
Factual Accuracy: Does it preserve the speaker’s actual sentiments and facts?
Comprehensiveness: Does it cover all important aspects of the interview?




Evaluation Procedure

Generate Summaries with the LLM

Use standardized prompts or instructions for the LLM when generating interview summaries.
Keep track of temperature and other model parameters for consistency.


Compare Summaries to References

Apply chosen metrics systematically (e.g., compute ROUGE scores, qualitative coding).
Rate each summary on a predefined scale for qualitative dimensions.






4. Human Reviewer Assessment

Reviewer Recruitment and Training

Recruit domain experts (e.g., researchers, UX professionals) or individuals familiar with the interview topics.
Provide training on evaluation criteria, ensuring consistent judgments across reviewers.


Blind Review Protocol

Hide any information that might reveal whether a summary was produced by a human or by the LLM (to reduce bias).
Instruct reviewers to score each summary based on accuracy, comprehensiveness, and coherence.


Intra-Rater and Inter-Rater Reliability

Have each reviewer assess the same set of summaries more than once to check consistency (intra-rater).
Calculate inter-rater reliability (e.g., Cohen’s kappa, Krippendorff’s alpha) to ensure consistent agreement on summary quality.




5. Quantitative and Qualitative Feedback

Aggregating Quantitative Scores

Compute average, median, or overall score across multiple metrics (ROUGE, BERTScore, any custom-coded metric).
Summarize these results to see how close the LLM summaries match the reference (human-created) summaries.


Thematic and Qualitative Insights

Identify recurring issues or missed themes in the summaries (e.g., omission of certain topics, inaccuracies in paraphrasing).
Gather descriptive feedback from reviewers about notable strengths or weaknesses in the LLM’s summaries.




6. Gap Analysis and Improvement

Identifying Sources of Error

Examine where the LLM’s summaries deviate from the reference summaries.
Classify errors (e.g., omissions, factual inaccuracies, misinterpretations).


Iterative Fine-Tuning or Prompt Engineering

Adjust LLM prompts (e.g., provide more specific instructions or constraints).
Explore fine-tuning on domain-specific data or with curated example summaries to improve accuracy.


Best Practices for Reliability

Provide model with context or example interview summaries to guide summarization approach.
Consider domain adaptation techniques to handle specialized terminology or content.




7. Reporting and Documentation

Clear Reporting of Methods

Document the entire evaluation protocol, including who created the reference summaries, how metrics were calculated, and how reviewers were trained.


Presentation of Results

Provide tables or charts showing quantitative metrics (e.g., average ROUGE scores).
Include qualitative feedback excerpts to illustrate specific strengths or weaknesses.


Recommendations for Future Work

Suggest ways to refine the evaluation approach (e.g., more domain experts, different metrics).
Highlight how the findings can inform further use of LLMs in summarizing interview data.




8. Conclusion

Summary of Findings

Recap key insights from the evaluation process (e.g., performance of the LLM, common error types).
Emphasize the areas where the LLM excels or struggles.


Implications for Human-Computer Interaction

Discuss the impact of accurate summaries on UX research, product design insights, and stakeholder communication.
Outline how improved summarization fosters better decision-making.


Next Steps

Reinforce the importance of a continuous improvement cycle—feedback from evaluations should inform model adjustments and produce more accurate summaries over time.




Tips for Implementation

Pilot Testing: Before large-scale evaluation, conduct a small pilot study to refine the evaluation criteria, metrics, and reviewer guidelines.
Mixed-Methods Approach: Combine quantitative metrics (like ROUGE) with qualitative assessments to get a more holistic view of the LLM’s performance.
Contextual Prompts: Provide the LLM with interviewer background, interview structure, and key themes to improve summary relevance and accuracy.
Human-Centered Approach: Remember that human interpretations and emergent themes may be subtle; capturing nuances often requires careful prompt design, iteration, and possible human-in-the-loop strategies.
By following this outline, you can systematically plan, execute, and document the evaluation of an LLM’s ability to accurately summarize interview data. This approach helps ensure both thorough coverage of key interview insights and reliable assessment of model performance.

projects/uxr-blog/blog-db/human-judgment.title: Human Judgment Is the Edge. Stop Guarding It, Start Architecting It.
projects/uxr-blog/blog-db/human-judgment.content:
Human judgment is the last line of defense.

The field has reached consensus on this point with unusual speed. Rosala put the point bluntly: outsource your analysis to AI and you risk your credibility [1]. Sixty-nine percent of UX researchers now use AI in at least some of their projects, a 19% jump from last year [2], and the reassurance is consistent: the tools change, but human judgment remains the edge.
The instinct is sound. If you have spent years developing the ability to read between the lines of a participant interview, to sense when someone’s words diverge from their behavior, to know which finding will move a stakeholder and which will collect dust, the suggestion that a machine might replicate these capabilities feels like a category error. The capabilities are real. They are hard-won. They matter.
But the consensus misses how fast the landscape changes when you build agentic systems.
foreground
background
narrative 

I’ve been building AI-augmented research workflows for the past year, designing systems where AI agents handle parts of the research process that used to be entirely manual. Literature review. Market analysis. Argument construction. Report synthesis. And in that work, I keep watching something happen that the “human judgment” consensus doesn’t account for: the AI makes judgment calls: not perfectly, not always well, but it makes them.
An AI agent scans hundreds of academic papers and decides which sources are most relevant to a research question. Another ranks topic opportunities by strategic fit against a scoring framework. A third synthesizes interview data into a structured report, deciding which findings deserve emphasis. Each one is a judgment call.
Whether you call these outputs “judgments” or “classifications” depends on a distinction worth unpacking. For now, notice that each one shapes a downstream decision a human used to make. The industry treats judgment as a wall between human and machine. This side is ours, that side is theirs. But the boundary keeps moving. The conversation feels stuck because we’re defending the wrong thing.
Judgment is the shared terrain of human-AI interaction, not a wall separating them. And shared terrain needs an architect.
Judgment Is Designable, Not Sacred
Here’s the uncomfortable shift. In an agentic AI workflow, someone decides which judgments stay human and which get automated. That someone is the architect: the person designing the system where human and AI judgment interact.
This is not hypothetical. It is the operational condition of any architect who has deployed an AI workflow in the past two years. Configure a pipeline that filters data before you see it, and you have made an allocation decision. Let an AI tool cluster themes from interview transcripts, and you have delegated a call that once lived in your head. These allocations are set by design. They can be changed tomorrow.

Here is why the wall metaphor breaks down. Most expert judgment is not the careful, deliberate reasoning we imagine. It is fast pattern recognition, shaped by accumulated exposure to similar situations. Cognitive science has known this for decades, and the implications for AI are more uncomfortable than the consensus admits.
Gary Klein’s Recognition-Primed Decision model found that firefighters, military commanders, and emergency physicians do not weigh options analytically. They recognize patterns from prior experience, run a rapid mental simulation, and act [3]. There is no comparison shopping. No decision matrix. Pure pattern matching, refined through thousands of hours of domain exposure.
Large language models produce outputs that look like expert intuition: pattern completion shaped by prior exposure, without the real-world experience that grounds the human version. The mechanism is different. But both shape downstream decisions. Both can be right or wrong.
The strongest version of this objection is that AI outputs lack intentionality: the machine does not “understand” what it decides, and human expertise is grounded in physical context, emotional resonance, and embodied signals that no statistical model replicates [4]. Grant the point entirely. It does not change the architectural question: who allocates which decisions, on what basis, within which system?
Kahneman’s dual-process framework sharpens the stakes. System 1 thinking (fast, automatic, intuitive) drives most expert judgment through accumulated experience. System 2 (slow, deliberate, analytical) activates when System 1 encounters something unexpected [5]. The consensus treats all human judgment as System 2 work: reflective, effortful, irreplaceable by automation. Most expert judgment is System 1. Fast, automatic, experience-based. Precisely the territory where LLMs already operate at scale.
That is a design question. And design questions have answers.
The Architect’s Audit: What to Automate
The first task is auditing this territory.
Every workflow generates hundreds of judgment calls. Which participants to recruit. Which questions to prioritize in a study. How to interpret a pause in an interview. Whether a finding is strong enough to change a roadmap. Most architects never inventory these judgments explicitly. They flow through the work like water through familiar channels, invisible until something breaks.
Building an agentic AI system forces the inventory. You cannot delegate a judgment you have not identified. And identification is where most of the value lives.

The combination you do not usually see is Kahneman’s dual-process model mapped onto Endsley’s situation awareness levels from human factors research [6]. Together they produce something neither offers alone: a practical audit lens for deciding which judgments to delegate. Kahneman tells you how each judgment fires (fast intuition vs. deliberate analysis). Endsley tells you what each judgment operates on. Her three levels of environmental understanding map directly onto what you are looking for when you inventory a workflow’s judgments:
Level 1: Perception. Noticing data points, flagging patterns, categorizing inputs. Scanning forty transcripts for a specific pain point. Clustering survey responses by semantic similarity. These are real judgments that shape downstream decisions, and they operate at a scale and speed no human matches. This is where AI earns its keep.
Level 2: Comprehension. Integrating patterns into a coherent picture. Understanding why three independent usability findings share a single root cause. Recognizing that a drop-off pattern in onboarding reflects not confusion but distrust. This layer requires reading across the full landscape, not just the individual stream.
Level 3: Anticipation. Anticipating what happens next. Sensing that a stakeholder’s resistance is political rather than methodological. Recognizing when applied findings diverge from published assumptions, opening a question the field has not yet thought to ask.
The perceptual layer is the strongest candidate for automation. The comprehension and anticipation layers are where you earn your value. Not because AI cannot attempt them (it can, and increasingly does) but because these layers require the kind of contextual awareness that no training set captures in real time: organizational politics, strategic history, the subtle dynamics of a team that has been burned before.
The audit is the first act of architecture. Before you build anything, map every judgment in the workflow, classify it by cognitive level, and make a deliberate allocation decision. That decision is not binary. Sheridan and Verplank’s foundational taxonomy identified ten levels between fully manual and fully automated [25], and Parasuraman, Sheridan, and Wickens later mapped those levels across four information-processing stages [26]. Most useful allocations live in the intermediate range, where human and machine share control in different configurations. The allocations will be wrong in places. That is expected. They exist to be revised. But they must exist before you touch a single prompt.
Designing the Human-AI Judgment Architecture
Knowing what to automate is necessary. It is not sufficient. The design of the system determines whether automated judgments produce reliable outputs or confident errors.
Most architects who build AI workflows start by delegating tasks: “summarize this transcript,” “extract the key themes,” “draft an affinity map.” The outputs feel useful. The efficiency gains are real. But there is a gap between delegating a task and delegating a judgment that most workflows obscure.
A task has defined inputs and outputs. A judgment has context. When you ask an AI agent to cluster interview themes, the output depends entirely on what context you provide: the research questions, the participant demographics, the product domain, the strategic priorities the study was designed to inform. Strip the context and the clustering is technically competent but strategically useless. The same data, framed by different context, produces different and legitimate clusterings.
Edwin Hutchins observed something essential while studying navigation teams on naval vessels [7]. His central finding reframes the entire picture: cognition does not live in any single person’s head. It is distributed across people, instruments, charts, and procedures. The system thinks. The quality of the system’s thinking depends on how those elements are connected, what information flows between them, and what each element can see.
An agentic AI workflow is exactly this kind of distributed cognitive system. The AI agents, the data they process, the prompts that shape them, the human who reviews their outputs: all nodes in a shared cognitive architecture. The quality of judgment depends not on the capability of any single node but on how the whole thing fits together.

This is why architecture matters more than capability. “Can the AI cluster themes?” Of course it can. The real issue is whether you have designed the joint system so the AI’s calls are grounded in the right context, constrained by the right boundaries, and connected to the right downstream decisions?
Most AI workflows never ask that question. Donella Meadows mapped where interventions in complex systems actually produce change [8]. Her hierarchy shows where small changes produce big effects: the most common interventions (tweaking parameters, adjusting prompts, swapping models) rank at the bottom. The highest-leverage interventions change a system’s information flows, its rules, and its goals. Each of the three principles below operates at a higher leverage point than task delegation alone.
Context architecture
Every AI agent in the system needs a defined context window: what information it can see, what it cannot, and why. Think of it as need-to-know access. An agent tasked with identifying usability issues in a transcript needs the task flows being tested and the participant’s experience level. It does not need the product roadmap. An agent synthesizing across multiple studies needs the strategic questions driving the research program. The agent sees exactly what it needs to make its judgment, nothing more.
In practice, my literature review agent receives the research question, the target domains, and the inclusion criteria. It does not receive my content calendar, my audience analytics, or my competitive positioning. Each boundary is a deliberate judgment allocation decision. Designing context architecture changes the structure of what the system can know, a fundamentally higher-leverage intervention than adjusting any individual prompt.
Escalation paths
Not every judgment stays where you put it. A well-designed architecture includes clear triggers for surfacing an AI-allocated judgment to human review. Confidence thresholds. Contradiction detection. Novel patterns that fall outside what the model has seen before. The escalation path is the override mechanism that activates when the fast system encounters something it was not built for.
Leveson’s STAMP framework makes the principle concrete: system failures trace to breakdowns in control, not chains of broken components [9]. An agentic AI workflow without escalation paths is a control system without a safety structure. The AI will encounter something outside its scope. The only question is whether the human-in-the-loop architecture routes it to a human before the error compounds. The design challenge is clear boundaries between judgment zones, with triggers simple and rare enough to be taken seriously when they fire.
I trigger escalation when an agent’s output contradicts its own prior classification on similar data, or when it encounters a source that matches none of its existing categorization criteria. These triggers are deliberately rare: two to three escalations per literature review cycle, not twenty.
Feedback loops
I structure this as a decision log the agent generates alongside every output: what it decided, which context it weighted most heavily, and its confidence level. Reviewing ten decision logs takes five minutes. Reviewing ten raw outputs takes an hour. The log is the feedback loop, the simplest form of AI transparency in practice.
The principle behind it is straightforward. The sensemaking research is clear [10]: making sense of ambiguous situations requires information that is interpretable and reviewable, not buried in logs. Meadows identified the strength of feedback loops as one of the most powerful leverage points in any system [8]. A feedback loop that is too slow, too noisy, or disconnected from the decisions it should inform is functionally the same as no feedback at all. Can the human architect see what the system decided, on what basis, and what happened as a result? If yes, the feedback loop is working. If not, the system is flying blind.

The systems I have built that work share a common trait: they were designed around judgment, not around tasks.
The pipeline that scores and ranks blog topics against live market conversations works because the scoring criteria are explicitly defined, the context window includes the content strategy and academic literature base, the escalation path surfaces anything ambiguous, and the feedback loop lets me see what was weighted and why.
The pipeline that failed was the one I built around a task (“summarize these sources”) without designing the judgment architecture around it.
The difference between a useful AI workflow and a dangerous one is rarely capability. It is the presence or absence of deliberate architecture around context, escalation, and feedback.
The Architect’s Paradox: Review and Control
The architecture ships. The system runs. And here the hardest work begins: maintaining human oversight of a system designed to operate without you.
The AI trust research is unambiguous on one point: calibration is everything. A single automation failure can produce distrust that sticks, even after the system returns to high reliability [16]. Lee and See’s foundational framework showed how this works: when people trust a system more than it deserves, or less than it deserves, they stop using it well [11]. One bad call in a high-stakes moment erases the credibility built by a hundred good calls in routine ones. Your review process must catch miscalibrations before they reach high-stakes decisions, not after.
I have watched this fail firsthand. An agent I configured to score market opportunities performed well for months. Then my content direction shifted. The agent kept scoring by the old criteria. The outputs looked clean. They were not. The terrain shifted and the architecture did not notice.
This creates a risk that runs in two directions. The risk to you: when the AI makes a judgment calibrated to old conditions, you act on outdated ground truth. An AI agent flags a compliance workflow as routine because it matched historical patterns, but new regulations have made it high-stakes. The risk to the system: that failure does not erode confidence in one judgment. It erodes trust in the architecture’s capacity to judge at all [11].

The complacency literature deepens the problem for architects specifically. Operators who rely on automated systems show measurable declines in monitoring and detection performance [12]. In cognitive automation specifically, expert workers experience gradual, invisible skill erosion in the very tasks they delegated [13]. When the system handles the work reliably, you stop practicing the skill. When it eventually fails, you lack the capacity to catch it. Stop reviewing the territory and you lose the ability to see when conditions shift.
And here the deepest tension in agentic work surfaces. Chris Argyris and Donald Schön drew the distinction between single-loop learning (“Did we do the thing right?”) and double-loop learning (“Are we doing the right thing?”) [14]. Most review processes are single-loop: check the AI’s output for accuracy, fix errors, move on. An architect who reviews AI-clustered themes for accuracy is doing single-loop work. One who reads the same clusters for structure, asking “What does the clustering pattern reveal about how participants organize their experience?”, is doing double-loop work. Same output. Different question. Your review process must be double-loop.
But the orchestration paradox makes this difficult. If you spend your cognitive energy managing the system (checking outputs, troubleshooting failures, adjusting prompts), you are not spending it learning from the system’s outputs. The tasks the system demands of its human are frequently the opposite of the tasks that make the human valuable.
Willpower will not solve it. Architecture will.
The agentic ecosystem has already demonstrated why. Through deployment failures and operational surprises, the industry has arrived at the same structural requirements that cognitive systems engineering identified decades ago through theory. In 2002, Christoffersen and Woods studied coordination breakdowns across aviation, process control, and military command [17]. Every failure traced to two missing properties: observability (the human could not see what the automation decided or why) and directability (the human could not redirect it when circumstances changed). In March 2026, the agentic AI industry arrived at the identical insight independently. Kyndryl named “agentic drift” as the hidden risk of deploying AI at scale [18]. CIO Magazine reported that agentic systems “don’t fail suddenly; they drift over time” [19]. IBM launched “agentic observability” as a new infrastructure category [20]. McKinsey reframed the foundational question: “Agency isn’t a feature. It’s a transfer of decision rights” [21].
The engineering teams are building monitoring tools. The management consultancies are naming organizational risks. Neither conversation has the design framework that connects them. Three commitments provide that framework. Each is grounded in principles that predate AI. Each is validated by the deployment patterns emerging now.
Design for visibility of judgements
Woods developed the theory of graceful extensibility to explain why some systems absorb surprises while others shatter [22]. The core insight: resilient systems do not just detect failure. They maintain reserve capacity for maneuver: slack between normal operation and the boundary where things break. The question is not whether a judgment allocation will encounter surprise, but whether the system has room to absorb it. For each judgment allocation in the architecture, define three conditions: the operating condition (where it works), the boundary condition (where it breaks), and the reserve condition (what slack exists between current operation and the boundary). Three questions per node: Under what conditions does this allocation work? Under what conditions does it fail? How close are we to the failure condition, and what buffer exists?
Then build the controls. Every agent in the architecture must satisfy two structural requirements. Observability: the architect can see what the agent decided, what context it had access to, what it weighted, and what was invisible to it. Directability: the architect can redirect any agent’s priorities, constraints, or context window without rebuilding the pipeline. The decision log I described earlier is observability. What most agentic workflows lack is directability: the ability to intervene mid-pipeline, not just review after the fact. If you can only audit an agent’s output but cannot change its operating parameters in response, you are monitoring, not commanding. The observability tools now shipping from major platforms build this infrastructure. Your job is to ensure these properties are designed into the judgment allocation itself, not bolted on afterward.
Design detection signals at multiple levels: data distribution changes (perceptual), pattern shifts in agent behavior (comprehension), and strategic misalignment between outputs and goals (projection). I design my detection signals around categories of shift (changes in data distribution, changes in agent behavior patterns, changes in strategic alignment) rather than specific signals. Categories hold as capabilities expand. Specific signals age out with the next model update.
Build oversight that sharpens the overseer
Skill maintenance cannot be a personal discipline. It must be a structural property of the workflow. The difference: “exercise regularly” versus “design your commute so that walking is the only option.”
Instead of reviewing AI-clustered themes for accuracy (single-loop, skill-atrophying), structure the workflow to require independent analysis of a sample before viewing the AI’s output, then compare (double-loop, skill-maintaining). You cannot complete the second version without exercising the judgment it preserves. You do not need willpower. The workflow demands it.
Prioritize by cognitive level. Projection skills (anticipating consequences, sensing organizational dynamics, recognizing strategic misalignment) degrade fastest and matter most. They depend on accumulated contextual awareness that no refresher quickly restores. Comprehension skills (integrating patterns into a coherent picture) degrade more slowly. Perception skills (noticing data, flagging patterns) are the easiest to offload and quickest to recover. Weight your maintenance investment toward projection. That is where your irreplaceable value lives.
Audit for drift, not just defects
Rasmussen studied how complex systems (nuclear plants, hospitals, transportation networks) behave under real operating pressure [23]. He found that every system drifts toward the boundary of acceptable performance when efficiency pressure mounts. In agentic architectures, this takes a specific form: you delegate a judgment. It works. Confidence grows. Adjacent judgments get informally delegated (an expanded prompt here, a loosened constraint there) without updating the architecture. I have seen this firsthand: a scoring agent that started with three judgment types quietly absorbed five because each expansion worked and nobody logged the change. Over time, the documented allocation diverges from the actual allocation. The system looks the same on paper. It is not the same system. Kyndryl’s analysis found that “AI agents can appear reliable while working toward unwanted outcomes” [18]. CIO Magazine documented the pattern: degradation is quiet, and “by the time the failure is visible, the risk has often been accumulating for months” [19].
The practical mechanism: maintain a live allocation map that records which judgments are human, which are automated, and which are shared. Schedule reviews with the same rigor as sprint retrospectives, but also trigger them based on three event types: repeated escalation patterns (the system surfaces the same ambiguity type more than twice in a cycle), capability step-changes (a model update, a new agent, a context window expansion), and drift signals (the live allocation map has diverged from the designed allocation).

For the audit itself, five questions adapted from cognitive work analysis (a method for analyzing how work actually gets done in complex environments, developed by Vicente [24]) provide the structure:

Constraints: What has changed in the environment, the tools, or the stakeholder expectations?
Allocations: Are the judgment allocations still appropriate given current constraints?
Strategies: Are there new approaches the system should support that the current architecture does not?
Undocumented shifts: Has the human-AI division drifted from the designed allocation without deliberate redesign?
Competence: Has the architect’s practiced judgment kept pace with the system’s expanded scope?
Prioritize the highest-leverage allocations first: where downstream consequences of error are greatest, where the AI’s context is most constrained, or where the terrain has shifted most since the last review. Without a method, audits become ceremonial. Without prioritization, they become infeasible as the system scales.
Design for these three properties and you stay in command. Neglect them and you become a custodian of a system you no longer fully understand.

The Expanding Question
Three studies landed on my desk in the same week last month. Different researchers, different products, different lifecycle stages. One found usability friction in an AI feature. Another documented adoption hesitation among power users. The third tracked a drop-off pattern in onboarding. Solid work, each of them. Clear recommendations. Nothing that would move a roadmap on its own.
I happened to be reading all three at once. A pattern surfaced that none of them reported. Users were not resisting our AI features because of usability problems. They were resisting because they could not figure out whether the AI was worth the risk of trusting. The question behind every finding was identical: not “Can I use this?” but “Should I bet on this?”
No single study asked that question. No AI agent, working from one data stream, would have connected those three signals. I saw it because I was sitting at the intersection of all three, doing the projection-level work the architecture had preserved my capacity to do.
That insight changed everything downstream. Instead of three follow-up studies, I launched six systematic literature reviews across trust in automation, psychometric best practices, and economic value modeling. I built a new taxonomy connecting AI readiness, adoption barriers, and risk tolerance to our existing jobs-to-be-done framework. From a single insight, two deliverables: an executive report grounding the strategic case in economics and a product-engineering-design report translating the findings into tactical priorities. Three isolated studies became the foundation for our enterprise AI adoption research strategy.
That kind of synthesis only happens when the architect still walks the terrain.
The better question is architectural. It applies to every architect who designs systems where humans and AI share judgment. Which decisions need what level of human involvement, in which circumstances, within which systems? The question never settles. But it has a design practice. Build visibility and command so you can see and steer the system. Structure oversight that sharpens your judgment rather than letting it atrophy. Audit for drift, catching the slow divergence between what you designed and what you are actually running.
These three commitments reinforce each other. Visibility reveals where oversight needs strengthening. Active oversight maintains the judgment that makes audits meaningful. Audits surface the drift signals that update the visibility architecture. Each cycle sharpens the next.
The tech industry has spent two years drawing boundaries. What can humans do that AI cannot? What is ours to protect? Boundaries are lines on a map. The terrain does not hold still for cartographers.
Where to draw the line was never the right question. The right question is who designs the system. Who builds the architecture where every agent, human and AI, makes better decisions because of how the whole thing fits together?
That is the question worth protecting.

Human judgment is the last line of defense.

The field has reached consensus on this point with unusual speed. Rosala put the point bluntly: outsource your analysis to AI and you risk your credibility [1]. Sixty-nine percent of UX researchers now use AI in at least some of their projects, a 19% jump from last year [2], and the reassurance is consistent: the tools change, but human judgment remains the edge.
The instinct is sound. If you have spent years developing the ability to read between the lines of a participant interview, to sense when someone’s words diverge from their behavior, to know which finding will move a stakeholder and which will collect dust, the suggestion that a machine might replicate these capabilities feels like a category error. The capabilities are real. They are hard-won. They matter.
But the consensus misses how fast the landscape changes when you build agentic systems.

An AI agent scans hundreds of academic papers and decides which sources are most relevant to a research question. Another ranks topic opportunities by strategic fit against a scoring framework. The industry treats judgment as a wall between human and machine. This side is ours, that side is theirs. But the boundary keeps moving. The conversation feels stuck because we’re defending the wrong thing.
