- **Tag quotes by type** (emotional, story, pain, decision, natural language) during analysis
- **Create a highlight reel** of your 5 to 10 strongest quotes for stakeholder presentations
- **Pair each quote with a design implication** so the insight leads directly to action
- **Use exact user language** in your personas, journey maps, and requirement documents
The techniques in this article come from decades of research methodology, from Flanagan's Critical Incident Technique (1954) to modern JTBD switch interviews and the NNGroup's funnel technique. They work because they're grounded in how people actually recall and describe their experiences.
The best part? These aren't skills you need special training for. They're questions. **You can start using them in your very next interview.**
Here's your challenge: before your next interview, pick **one question from each of three categories** above and add them to your script. After the interview, review your transcript and highlight every quote that could stand on its own in a stakeholder presentation. Compare that count to your last interview.
I'll bet the number doubles.

projects/uxr-blog/blog-db/judgment-is-de.title: Human Judgment Is the Edge. Stop Guarding It, Start Architecting It.
projects/uxr-blog/blog-db/judgment-is-de.content:
Human judgment is the last line of defense.

The field has reached consensus on this point with unusual speed. Rosala put the point bluntly: outsource your analysis to AI and you risk your credibility [1]. Sixty-nine percent of UX researchers now use AI in at least some of their projects, a 19% jump from last year [2], and the reassurance is consistent: the tools change, but human judgment remains the edge.
The instinct is sound. If you have spent years developing the ability to read between the lines of a participant interview, to sense when someone’s words diverge from their behavior, to know which finding will move a stakeholder and which will collect dust, the suggestion that a machine might replicate these capabilities feels like a category error. The capabilities are real. They are hard-won. They matter.
But the consensus misses how fast the landscape changes when you build agentic systems.
foreground
background
narrative 

I’ve been building AI-augmented research workflows for the past year, designing systems where AI agents handle parts of the research process that used to be entirely manual. Literature review. Market analysis. Argument construction. Report synthesis. And in that work, I keep watching something happen that the “human judgment” consensus doesn’t account for: the AI makes judgment calls: not perfectly, not always well, but it makes them.
An AI agent scans hundreds of academic papers and decides which sources are most relevant to a research question. Another ranks topic opportunities by strategic fit against a scoring framework. A third synthesizes interview data into a structured report, deciding which findings deserve emphasis. Each one is a judgment call.
Whether you call these outputs “judgments” or “classifications” depends on a distinction worth unpacking. For now, notice that each one shapes a downstream decision a human used to make. The industry treats judgment as a wall between human and machine. This side is ours, that side is theirs. But the boundary keeps moving. The conversation feels stuck because we’re defending the wrong thing.
Judgment is the shared terrain of human-AI interaction, not a wall separating them. And shared terrain needs an architect.
Judgment Is Designable, Not Sacred
Here’s the uncomfortable shift. In an agentic AI workflow, someone decides which judgments stay human and which get automated. That someone is the architect: the person designing the system where human and AI judgment interact.
This is not hypothetical. It is the operational condition of any architect who has deployed an AI workflow in the past two years. Configure a pipeline that filters data before you see it, and you have made an allocation decision. Let an AI tool cluster themes from interview transcripts, and you have delegated a call that once lived in your head. These allocations are set by design. They can be changed tomorrow.

Here is why the wall metaphor breaks down. Most expert judgment is not the careful, deliberate reasoning we imagine. It is fast pattern recognition, shaped by accumulated exposure to similar situations. Cognitive science has known this for decades, and the implications for AI are more uncomfortable than the consensus admits.
Gary Klein’s Recognition-Primed Decision model found that firefighters, military commanders, and emergency physicians do not weigh options analytically. They recognize patterns from prior experience, run a rapid mental simulation, and act [3]. There is no comparison shopping. No decision matrix. Pure pattern matching, refined through thousands of hours of domain exposure.
Large language models produce outputs that look like expert intuition: pattern completion shaped by prior exposure, without the real-world experience that grounds the human version. The mechanism is different. But both shape downstream decisions. Both can be right or wrong.
The strongest version of this objection is that AI outputs lack intentionality: the machine does not “understand” what it decides, and human expertise is grounded in physical context, emotional resonance, and embodied signals that no statistical model replicates [4]. Grant the point entirely. It does not change the architectural question: who allocates which decisions, on what basis, within which system?
Kahneman’s dual-process framework sharpens the stakes. System 1 thinking (fast, automatic, intuitive) drives most expert judgment through accumulated experience. System 2 (slow, deliberate, analytical) activates when System 1 encounters something unexpected [5]. The consensus treats all human judgment as System 2 work: reflective, effortful, irreplaceable by automation. Most expert judgment is System 1. Fast, automatic, experience-based. Precisely the territory where LLMs already operate at scale.
That is a design question. And design questions have answers.
The Architect’s Audit: What to Automate
The first task is auditing this territory.
Every workflow generates hundreds of judgment calls. Which participants to recruit. Which questions to prioritize in a study. How to interpret a pause in an interview. Whether a finding is strong enough to change a roadmap. Most architects never inventory these judgments explicitly. They flow through the work like water through familiar channels, invisible until something breaks.
Building an agentic AI system forces the inventory. You cannot delegate a judgment you have not identified. And identification is where most of the value lives.

The combination you do not usually see is Kahneman’s dual-process model mapped onto Endsley’s situation awareness levels from human factors research [6]. Together they produce something neither offers alone: a practical audit lens for deciding which judgments to delegate. Kahneman tells you how each judgment fires (fast intuition vs. deliberate analysis). Endsley tells you what each judgment operates on. Her three levels of environmental understanding map directly onto what you are looking for when you inventory a workflow’s judgments:
Level 1: Perception. Noticing data points, flagging patterns, categorizing inputs. Scanning forty transcripts for a specific pain point. Clustering survey responses by semantic similarity. These are real judgments that shape downstream decisions, and they operate at a scale and speed no human matches. This is where AI earns its keep.
Level 2: Comprehension. Integrating patterns into a coherent picture. Understanding why three independent usability findings share a single root cause. Recognizing that a drop-off pattern in onboarding reflects not confusion but distrust. This layer requires reading across the full landscape, not just the individual stream.
Level 3: Anticipation. Anticipating what happens next. Sensing that a stakeholder’s resistance is political rather than methodological. Recognizing when applied findings diverge from published assumptions, opening a question the field has not yet thought to ask.
The perceptual layer is the strongest candidate for automation. The comprehension and anticipation layers are where you earn your value. Not because AI cannot attempt them (it can, and increasingly does) but because these layers require the kind of contextual awareness that no training set captures in real time: organizational politics, strategic history, the subtle dynamics of a team that has been burned before.
The audit is the first act of architecture. Before you build anything, map every judgment in the workflow, classify it by cognitive level, and make a deliberate allocation decision. That decision is not binary. Sheridan and Verplank’s foundational taxonomy identified ten levels between fully manual and fully automated [25], and Parasuraman, Sheridan, and Wickens later mapped those levels across four information-processing stages [26]. Most useful allocations live in the intermediate range, where human and machine share control in different configurations. The allocations will be wrong in places. That is expected. They exist to be revised. But they must exist before you touch a single prompt.
Designing the Human-AI Judgment Architecture
Knowing what to automate is necessary. It is not sufficient. The design of the system determines whether automated judgments produce reliable outputs or confident errors.
Most architects who build AI workflows start by delegating tasks: “summarize this transcript,” “extract the key themes,” “draft an affinity map.” The outputs feel useful. The efficiency gains are real. But there is a gap between delegating a task and delegating a judgment that most workflows obscure.
A task has defined inputs and outputs. A judgment has context. When you ask an AI agent to cluster interview themes, the output depends entirely on what context you provide: the research questions, the participant demographics, the product domain, the strategic priorities the study was designed to inform. Strip the context and the clustering is technically competent but strategically useless. The same data, framed by different context, produces different and legitimate clusterings.
Edwin Hutchins observed something essential while studying navigation teams on naval vessels [7]. His central finding reframes the entire picture: cognition does not live in any single person’s head. It is distributed across people, instruments, charts, and procedures. The system thinks. The quality of the system’s thinking depends on how those elements are connected, what information flows between them, and what each element can see.
An agentic AI workflow is exactly this kind of distributed cognitive system. The AI agents, the data they process, the prompts that shape them, the human who reviews their outputs: all nodes in a shared cognitive architecture. The quality of judgment depends not on the capability of any single node but on how the whole thing fits together.

This is why architecture matters more than capability. “Can the AI cluster themes?” Of course it can. The real issue is whether you have designed the joint system so the AI’s calls are grounded in the right context, constrained by the right boundaries, and connected to the right downstream decisions?
Most AI workflows never ask that question. Donella Meadows mapped where interventions in complex systems actually produce change [8]. Her hierarchy shows where small changes produce big effects: the most common interventions (tweaking parameters, adjusting prompts, swapping models) rank at the bottom. The highest-leverage interventions change a system’s information flows, its rules, and its goals. Each of the three principles below operates at a higher leverage point than task delegation alone.
Context architecture
Every AI agent in the system needs a defined context window: what information it can see, what it cannot, and why. Think of it as need-to-know access. An agent tasked with identifying usability issues in a transcript needs the task flows being tested and the participant’s experience level. It does not need the product roadmap. An agent synthesizing across multiple studies needs the strategic questions driving the research program. The agent sees exactly what it needs to make its judgment, nothing more.
In practice, my literature review agent receives the research question, the target domains, and the inclusion criteria. It does not receive my content calendar, my audience analytics, or my competitive positioning. Each boundary is a deliberate judgment allocation decision. Designing context architecture changes the structure of what the system can know, a fundamentally higher-leverage intervention than adjusting any individual prompt.
Escalation paths
Not every judgment stays where you put it. A well-designed architecture includes clear triggers for surfacing an AI-allocated judgment to human review. Confidence thresholds. Contradiction detection. Novel patterns that fall outside what the model has seen before. The escalation path is the override mechanism that activates when the fast system encounters something it was not built for.
Leveson’s STAMP framework makes the principle concrete: system failures trace to breakdowns in control, not chains of broken components [9]. An agentic AI workflow without escalation paths is a control system without a safety structure. The AI will encounter something outside its scope. The only question is whether the human-in-the-loop architecture routes it to a human before the error compounds. The design challenge is clear boundaries between judgment zones, with triggers simple and rare enough to be taken seriously when they fire.
I trigger escalation when an agent’s output contradicts its own prior classification on similar data, or when it encounters a source that matches none of its existing categorization criteria. These triggers are deliberately rare: two to three escalations per literature review cycle, not twenty.
Feedback loops
I structure this as a decision log the agent generates alongside every output: what it decided, which context it weighted most heavily, and its confidence level. Reviewing ten decision logs takes five minutes. Reviewing ten raw outputs takes an hour. The log is the feedback loop, the simplest form of AI transparency in practice.
The principle behind it is straightforward. The sensemaking research is clear [10]: making sense of ambiguous situations requires information that is interpretable and reviewable, not buried in logs. Meadows identified the strength of feedback loops as one of the most powerful leverage points in any system [8]. A feedback loop that is too slow, too noisy, or disconnected from the decisions it should inform is functionally the same as no feedback at all. Can the human architect see what the system decided, on what basis, and what happened as a result? If yes, the feedback loop is working. If not, the system is flying blind.

The systems I have built that work share a common trait: they were designed around judgment, not around tasks.
The pipeline that scores and ranks blog topics against live market conversations works because the scoring criteria are explicitly defined, the context window includes the content strategy and academic literature base, the escalation path surfaces anything ambiguous, and the feedback loop lets me see what was weighted and why.
The pipeline that failed was the one I built around a task (“summarize these sources”) without designing the judgment architecture around it.
The difference between a useful AI workflow and a dangerous one is rarely capability. It is the presence or absence of deliberate architecture around context, escalation, and feedback.
The Architect’s Paradox: Review and Control
The architecture ships. The system runs. And here the hardest work begins: maintaining human oversight of a system designed to operate without you.
The AI trust research is unambiguous on one point: calibration is everything. A single automation failure can produce distrust that sticks, even after the system returns to high reliability [16]. Lee and See’s foundational framework showed how this works: when people trust a system more than it deserves, or less than it deserves, they stop using it well [11]. One bad call in a high-stakes moment erases the credibility built by a hundred good calls in routine ones. Your review process must catch miscalibrations before they reach high-stakes decisions, not after.
I have watched this fail firsthand. An agent I configured to score market opportunities performed well for months. Then my content direction shifted. The agent kept scoring by the old criteria. The outputs looked clean. They were not. The terrain shifted and the architecture did not notice.
This creates a risk that runs in two directions. The risk to you: when the AI makes a judgment calibrated to old conditions, you act on outdated ground truth. An AI agent flags a compliance workflow as routine because it matched historical patterns, but new regulations have made it high-stakes. The risk to the system: that failure does not erode confidence in one judgment. It erodes trust in the architecture’s capacity to judge at all [11].

The complacency literature deepens the problem for architects specifically. Operators who rely on automated systems show measurable declines in monitoring and detection performance [12]. In cognitive automation specifically, expert workers experience gradual, invisible skill erosion in the very tasks they delegated [13]. When the system handles the work reliably, you stop practicing the skill. When it eventually fails, you lack the capacity to catch it. Stop reviewing the territory and you lose the ability to see when conditions shift.
And here the deepest tension in agentic work surfaces. Chris Argyris and Donald Schön drew the distinction between single-loop learning (“Did we do the thing right?”) and double-loop learning (“Are we doing the right thing?”) [14]. Most review processes are single-loop: check the AI’s output for accuracy, fix errors, move on. An architect who reviews AI-clustered themes for accuracy is doing single-loop work. One who reads the same clusters for structure, asking “What does the clustering pattern reveal about how participants organize their experience?”, is doing double-loop work. Same output. Different question. Your review process must be double-loop.
But the orchestration paradox makes this difficult. If you spend your cognitive energy managing the system (checking outputs, troubleshooting failures, adjusting prompts), you are not spending it learning from the system’s outputs. The tasks the system demands of its human are frequently the opposite of the tasks that make the human valuable.
Willpower will not solve it. Architecture will.
The agentic ecosystem has already demonstrated why. Through deployment failures and operational surprises, the industry has arrived at the same structural requirements that cognitive systems engineering identified decades ago through theory. In 2002, Christoffersen and Woods studied coordination breakdowns across aviation, process control, and military command [17]. Every failure traced to two missing properties: observability (the human could not see what the automation decided or why) and directability (the human could not redirect it when circumstances changed). In March 2026, the agentic AI industry arrived at the identical insight independently. Kyndryl named “agentic drift” as the hidden risk of deploying AI at scale [18]. CIO Magazine reported that agentic systems “don’t fail suddenly; they drift over time” [19]. IBM launched “agentic observability” as a new infrastructure category [20]. McKinsey reframed the foundational question: “Agency isn’t a feature. It’s a transfer of decision rights” [21].
The engineering teams are building monitoring tools. The management consultancies are naming organizational risks. Neither conversation has the design framework that connects them. Three commitments provide that framework. Each is grounded in principles that predate AI. Each is validated by the deployment patterns emerging now.
Design for visibility of judgements
Woods developed the theory of graceful extensibility to explain why some systems absorb surprises while others shatter [22]. The core insight: resilient systems do not just detect failure. They maintain reserve capacity for maneuver: slack between normal operation and the boundary where things break. The question is not whether a judgment allocation will encounter surprise, but whether the system has room to absorb it. For each judgment allocation in the architecture, define three conditions: the operating condition (where it works), the boundary condition (where it breaks), and the reserve condition (what slack exists between current operation and the boundary). Three questions per node: Under what conditions does this allocation work? Under what conditions does it fail? How close are we to the failure condition, and what buffer exists?
Then build the controls. Every agent in the architecture must satisfy two structural requirements. Observability: the architect can see what the agent decided, what context it had access to, what it weighted, and what was invisible to it. Directability: the architect can redirect any agent’s priorities, constraints, or context window without rebuilding the pipeline. The decision log I described earlier is observability. What most agentic workflows lack is directability: the ability to intervene mid-pipeline, not just review after the fact. If you can only audit an agent’s output but cannot change its operating parameters in response, you are monitoring, not commanding. The observability tools now shipping from major platforms build this infrastructure. Your job is to ensure these properties are designed into the judgment allocation itself, not bolted on afterward.
Design detection signals at multiple levels: data distribution changes (perceptual), pattern shifts in agent behavior (comprehension), and strategic misalignment between outputs and goals (projection). I design my detection signals around categories of shift (changes in data distribution, changes in agent behavior patterns, changes in strategic alignment) rather than specific signals. Categories hold as capabilities expand. Specific signals age out with the next model update.
Build oversight that sharpens the overseer
Skill maintenance cannot be a personal discipline. It must be a structural property of the workflow. The difference: “exercise regularly” versus “design your commute so that walking is the only option.”
Instead of reviewing AI-clustered themes for accuracy (single-loop, skill-atrophying), structure the workflow to require independent analysis of a sample before viewing the AI’s output, then compare (double-loop, skill-maintaining). You cannot complete the second version without exercising the judgment it preserves. You do not need willpower. The workflow demands it.
Prioritize by cognitive level. Projection skills (anticipating consequences, sensing organizational dynamics, recognizing strategic misalignment) degrade fastest and matter most. They depend on accumulated contextual awareness that no refresher quickly restores. Comprehension skills (integrating patterns into a coherent picture) degrade more slowly. Perception skills (noticing data, flagging patterns) are the easiest to offload and quickest to recover. Weight your maintenance investment toward projection. That is where your irreplaceable value lives.
Audit for drift, not just defects
Rasmussen studied how complex systems (nuclear plants, hospitals, transportation networks) behave under real operating pressure [23]. He found that every system drifts toward the boundary of acceptable performance when efficiency pressure mounts. In agentic architectures, this takes a specific form: you delegate a judgment. It works. Confidence grows. Adjacent judgments get informally delegated (an expanded prompt here, a loosened constraint there) without updating the architecture. I have seen this firsthand: a scoring agent that started with three judgment types quietly absorbed five because each expansion worked and nobody logged the change. Over time, the documented allocation diverges from the actual allocation. The system looks the same on paper. It is not the same system. Kyndryl’s analysis found that “AI agents can appear reliable while working toward unwanted outcomes” [18]. CIO Magazine documented the pattern: degradation is quiet, and “by the time the failure is visible, the risk has often been accumulating for months” [19].
The practical mechanism: maintain a live allocation map that records which judgments are human, which are automated, and which are shared. Schedule reviews with the same rigor as sprint retrospectives, but also trigger them based on three event types: repeated escalation patterns (the system surfaces the same ambiguity type more than twice in a cycle), capability step-changes (a model update, a new agent, a context window expansion), and drift signals (the live allocation map has diverged from the designed allocation).

For the audit itself, five questions adapted from cognitive work analysis (a method for analyzing how work actually gets done in complex environments, developed by Vicente [24]) provide the structure:

Constraints: What has changed in the environment, the tools, or the stakeholder expectations?
Allocations: Are the judgment allocations still appropriate given current constraints?
Strategies: Are there new approaches the system should support that the current architecture does not?
Undocumented shifts: Has the human-AI division drifted from the designed allocation without deliberate redesign?
Competence: Has the architect’s practiced judgment kept pace with the system’s expanded scope?
Prioritize the highest-leverage allocations first: where downstream consequences of error are greatest, where the AI’s context is most constrained, or where the terrain has shifted most since the last review. Without a method, audits become ceremonial. Without prioritization, they become infeasible as the system scales.
Design for these three properties and you stay in command. Neglect them and you become a custodian of a system you no longer fully understand.

The Expanding Question
Three studies landed on my desk in the same week last month. Different researchers, different products, different lifecycle stages. One found usability friction in an AI feature. Another documented adoption hesitation among power users. The third tracked a drop-off pattern in onboarding. Solid work, each of them. Clear recommendations. Nothing that would move a roadmap on its own.
I happened to be reading all three at once. A pattern surfaced that none of them reported. Users were not resisting our AI features because of usability problems. They were resisting because they could not figure out whether the AI was worth the risk of trusting. The question behind every finding was identical: not “Can I use this?” but “Should I bet on this?”
No single study asked that question. No AI agent, working from one data stream, would have connected those three signals. I saw it because I was sitting at the intersection of all three, doing the projection-level work the architecture had preserved my capacity to do.
That insight changed everything downstream. Instead of three follow-up studies, I launched six systematic literature reviews across trust in automation, psychometric best practices, and economic value modeling. I built a new taxonomy connecting AI readiness, adoption barriers, and risk tolerance to our existing jobs-to-be-done framework. From a single insight, two deliverables: an executive report grounding the strategic case in economics and a product-engineering-design report translating the findings into tactical priorities. Three isolated studies became the foundation for our enterprise AI adoption research strategy.
That kind of synthesis only happens when the architect still walks the terrain.
The better question is architectural. It applies to every architect who designs systems where humans and AI share judgment. Which decisions need what level of human involvement, in which circumstances, within which systems? The question never settles. But it has a design practice. Build visibility and command so you can see and steer the system. Structure oversight that sharpens your judgment rather than letting it atrophy. Audit for drift, catching the slow divergence between what you designed and what you are actually running.
These three commitments reinforce each other. Visibility reveals where oversight needs strengthening. Active oversight maintains the judgment that makes audits meaningful. Audits surface the drift signals that update the visibility architecture. Each cycle sharpens the next.
The tech industry has spent two years drawing boundaries. What can humans do that AI cannot? What is ours to protect? Boundaries are lines on a map. The terrain does not hold still for cartographers.
Where to draw the line was never the right question. The right question is who designs the system. Who builds the architecture where every agent, human and AI, makes better decisions because of how the whole thing fits together?
That is the question worth protecting.

projects/uxr-blog/blog-db/naturalistic-d.content:
Thesis
Gary Klein’s Naturalistic Decision Making, developed studying firefighters and military commanders, is the perfect framework for understanding how product teams make decisions under uncertainty with AI. Recognition-Primed Decision Making applies directly to how designers, PMs, and researchers evaluate AI outputs — and it predicts why rational-choice frameworks keep failing in practice.
Why Only You
Deep NDM grounding + Terrain of Judgment already established the bridge. You can operationalize RPD for product teams in a way that’s immediately usable — not another academic summary, but a practitioner translation.
Enters Conversation

UX generalist return (NN/g) — generalists need decision frameworks, not just design skills
Agentic AI demanding human judgment at escalation points
Research ascending to boardroom but lacking decision-theoretic framing

Builds On
The Terrain of Judgment, Decision Advisor, Human×AI Augmented Decision Making
Suggested Depth
deep

projects/uxr-blog/blog-db/outline.title: What Strategic Research Actually Looks Like in B2B Enterprise (A Practitioner's Field Guide)
projects/uxr-blog/blog-db/outline.content:
**Through-line:** Strategic research isn't research that *informs* strategy. It's research that *becomes* strategy by operating at the level of market switching behavior, not feature validation.
	**Hook:** You're an individual contributor. No MBA. No P&L experience. And you're about to tell the CEO their strategy is wrong. (Or you're about to make your biggest competitor change theirs.) Both are what "strategic research" actually means. And neither has anything to do with the consumer-product playbooks the industry keeps publishing.
	**Meta description:** Strategic research in B2B enterprise means shifting market switching behavior or overturning C-suite strategy with evidence. Here's the operational model. *(156 chars)*

---

	### Keyword Brief
	- **Primary keyword:** `strategic UX research B2B`
	- **Secondary keywords:** `switch interviews UX research`, `B2B enterprise research strategy`, `UX research C-suite influence`, `research-driven product strategy`
	- **Search intent:** Informational (practitioners searching for *how* to make their research strategic)
	- **Target audience query:** "how to do strategic research in B2B enterprise"
	- **Competing content gap:** Every published "strategic research" playbook uses consumer examples. Nobody connects Moesta's switching framework to research strategy. Nobody addresses the IC-vs-C-suite evidence problem.

---
## Outline
### 1. The Label Everyone Uses, Nobody Defines *(\~200 words)*
- "Strategic research" is the aspiration of the moment. Maze reports it ascending to the boardroom. NN/g says research should "design deeper to differentiate."
- Strip the aspirational language and you find a vacuum: no operational definition, no mechanism, no B2B playbook.
- Every published example is consumer. In B2B enterprise (compliance, multi-stakeholder buying, multi-year contracts), the model is fundamentally different.
- **This post defines the mechanism.**
- *\[Sources: Maze Future of UXR, NN/g State of UX 2026, Jyothi Venkat "Why UX Research Fails to Influence the C-Suite"\]*
### 2. The Mechanism: Switching at the Market Population Level *(\~300 words)*
- Bob Moesta's demand-side framework: the four forces of switching (push of current situation, pull of new solution, anxiety of change, habit of the present).
- In consumer contexts, the unit of switching is a person. In B2B, the unit is an *organization*, and the forces play out across a buying committee where **user personas must convince buyer personas**.
- The gap between user experience and buyer decision-making is *where strategic research lives* in B2B. The user who feels the pain is not the buyer who signs the check. Consumer playbooks don't transfer because the unit of analysis is fundamentally different.
- Strategic research maps these switching forces across enough accounts to reveal *market-level patterns*, not just individual pain points.
- The shift: from "what do users need?" to "what makes organizations move?"
- *\[Sources: Moesta, Demand-Side Sales 101; Moesta & Spiek, "Uncovering the Jobs to Be Done"\]*
### 3. The External Move: Forcing Competitor Strategy Shifts *(\~250 words)*
- When you understand at population level what makes organizations switch contracts, you can shape product, positioning, and go-to-market to *accelerate switching toward you*.
- Do this across enough of the market's switching behavior, and competitors must respond. Your research becomes their strategic problem.
- This is research as the *intelligence function* behind competitive moves, not a validation service.
- Desired outcome measures at the market population level are the leading indicators. Feature requests are the lagging ones.
- **Composite example:** A B2B platform's churn dashboard showed steady attrition but no pattern. Switch interviews across 12 recently churned accounts revealed the primary force wasn't dissatisfaction with the product. It was *anxiety reduction*: a competitor offered compliance certification that eliminated audit risk. The switching force was invisible in NPS, CSAT, and feature requests. Research redesigned the go-to-market around compliance confidence, not feature parity. Win rate on competitive deals increased within two quarters. The competitor responded by accelerating their own certification messaging.
- *\[Sources: Moesta framework applied; composite drawn from B2B enterprise patterns\]*
### 4. The Internal Move: Complementary Access to Behavioral Evidence *(\~300 words)*
- The harder and more common scenario. Your company's strategy is wrong, and the switching data shows it. You have no MBA, no P&L authority, no seat at the table by default.
- The standard advice ("learn to speak business") is necessary but insufficient. The real mechanism is **evidence density from a position the C-suite cannot occupy**.
- The C-suite has strategic context: market positioning, financial models, board priorities, competitive intelligence. The researcher has behavioral evidence: the actual forces acting on actual accounts as they decide to stay, switch, or stall. These are *complementary*, not competing. Strategic research is what happens when both are in the same room.
- Accumulate enough switching evidence that the alternative strategy becomes undeniable. Frame it in their terms: revenue risk, competitive exposure, contract churn rate. Make the data do the arguing.
- *\[Sources: Jyothi Venkat on framing findings as decisions; Spool on organization-changing UX strategy\]*
### 5. The Operating Model: Evidence, Argument, and Coalition *(\~400 words)*

	**Pacing note:** This section introduces the three-legged stool framework with enough to be actionable, but deliberately holds back deep tactical detail. The reader should finish this section understanding *what* the operating model requires and *why* each leg matters, while wanting the full playbook. This is the hook for a future follow-up post (e.g., "The Strategic Research Playbook: Running Quant + Qual Switching Programs in B2B").

**5a. The Evidence Base: What Researchers Measure That Nobody Else Can** *(\~150 words)*
- Your sales team runs win/loss calls. Your analytics team tracks churn. What does the researcher add? **Prediction, not postmortem.**
- Researchers can design and field instruments (switching propensity scales, force-mapping surveys, anxiety inventories) that measure forces acting on accounts *that haven't churned yet*. CRM data captures outcomes. Research captures the forces *before* the outcome.
- Switch interviews (qual) reveal the *why*: the forces, the timeline, the tipping point. Researcher-designed quant instruments reveal *how many accounts are experiencing those same forces right now*.
- Practical rhythm: run switch interviews continuously (churned, won, stalled accounts). Layer researcher-designed quant on a quarterly cadence to measure force strength across the portfolio.
**5b. The Argument: Convincing and Easy to Consume** *(\~130 words)*
- Evidence alone doesn't move executives. The presentation must be **simultaneously convincing and effortless to consume**.
- One-page strategic briefs, not 40-slide research readouts. Lead with the business implication, support with the switching pattern, anchor with the quant.
- Executives don't lack information. They lack *clarity*. Your job is to eliminate the cognitive work between "here's data" and "here's the decision."
- Repeat the argument across formats: the one-pager, the 5-minute standup, the Slack summary, the quarterly review. Same story, compressed to fit each container.
**5c. The Coalition: Switching the Organization's Beliefs** *(\~120 words)*
- The C-suite has its own switching forces around their current strategy: the push of declining metrics, the pull of a new direction, the anxiety of admitting the old bet was wrong, the habit of sunk-cost commitment. The researcher who understands that the *organization itself* is a switching problem is operating at a fundamentally different level.
- Build the coalition *before* you need it. Directors, VPs, senior PMs who saw early findings, who were consulted along the way, who feel partial ownership of the insight. When you present to the C-suite, the research shouldn't be a surprise to anyone with influence. The surprise should only be the *conclusion*, not the existence of the work.
- Evidence density is necessary (Section 4). Evidence density + a pre-built coalition is the actual mechanism that changes strategy.
- *\[Connects back to Section 4: complementary access requires organizational trust built over time, not a single readout.\]*
### 6. Close: Research That Moves the Needle vs. Research That Reports It *(\~150 words)*
- The distinction isn't about the method, the stakeholder, or the deliverable. It's about whether the research changes what the organization does.
- If you're measuring the needle, you're doing analytics. If you're moving the needle, you're doing strategic research.
- **CTA:** Ask your researcher to run one switch interview with a recently churned account and present back the four forces. See if it tells you something your churn dashboard doesn't.
---

	### Outline Metadata
	- **Estimated word count:** \~1,800 (fits `standard` depth target of 1,500-2,000)
	- **Structure:** Mechanism-first (define switching → show two applications → operating model → close)
	- **Suggested depth:** `standard`
	- **Suggested tags:** UX Research, Career/Leadership, Research Operations
	- **Source page:** Blog Market Analysis: 2026-03-15
	- **Follow-up post hook:** The Operating Model Playbook (deep tactical guide to running quant + qual switching programs in B2B)

projects/uxr-blog/blog-db/research-as-re.content:
Thesis
The ROI conversation in UXR is stuck on “cost avoidance” — we prevented a bad redesign, we saved engineering hours. But generative research creates new market categories and can be quantified as revenue contribution, not just savings. The field abandoned its most powerful function and is now surprised it’s seen as a cost center.
Why Only You
Your “Research for Innovation” thesis is unique in the practitioner space. B2B enterprise context where you’ve seen research directly drive product strategy and revenue decisions. Content Direction goal #1: research as a revenue driver.
Enters Conversation

Maze: 2.7x better outcomes when research embedded in strategy, but 42% can’t connect findings to business outcomes
MockFlow: “Connecting UX research to business outcomes” as top 2026 trend
Lyssna: Research proving ROI remains the #1 challenge

Builds On
What Strategic Research Actually Looks Like in B2B Enterprise, Visible by Design strategy

standard

projects/uxr-blog/blog-db/research-in-th.title: Research in the Age of AI: Using Decision Science to Build LLM Personas That Actually Think
projects/uxr-blog/blog-db/research-in-th.content:
Most conversations about AI and decision-making start in the wrong place. They start with the technology: what can LLMs do, how many parameters, which benchmarks. But decisions are fundamentally human. They’re shaped by experience, context, cognitive limits, and the messy reality of working with other people. The interesting question isn’t whether AI can make decisions for us. It’s whether we can design AI that helps people make better decisions themselves.
That distinction matters more than it sounds. The difference between AI that automates human judgment and AI that supports it is the difference between a tool that replaces your thinking and one that sharpens it. One makes you dependent. The other makes you more capable over time.
I’ve spent the last several months pulling apart the academic literature on human decision-making, cognitive offloading, and AI-assisted reasoning. What I found reframed how I think about building AI tools. Not because the research shows LLMs can be made “smart” in some philosophical sense, but because it reveals something more practical: decades of cognitive psychology research already tell us how people actually think under pressure, and that science translates directly into better AI design.
The frameworks exist. The evidence is there. The gap is that most AI development ignores it.
This post is about closing that gap. Here’s what the science says, and what it looks like when you apply it.
The Science of How We Actually Decide (and Why LLMs Should Care)
Before we can build AI that supports decisions, we need to understand a counterintuitive truth about human expertise. The best decision-makers in the world don’t reason the way you’d expect.
Dual Process Theory: Two Systems, One Decision
You’re a product leader. It’s Wednesday morning. You open Slack to 47 unread messages, a Jira board full of overdue tickets, and a stakeholder asking whether you should delay a launch.
Your brain doesn’t pull up a spreadsheet. It reacts. You feel a flash of recognition (“this is like the Q3 situation”), a tightening in your gut (“we’re not ready”), and a quick mental simulation (“if we push two weeks, we clear the blockers”). In about three seconds, you’ve made a preliminary decision. Only then, maybe, do you slow down and pressure-test it with data.
That’s dual process theory in action. Daniel Kahneman’s framework partitions cognition into Type 1 (fast, automatic, intuitive) and Type 2 (slow, deliberate, analytical). Most decisions, even important ones, start in System 1. System 2 is the auditor, not the driver (Kahneman, 2011).
Now here’s what makes this directly relevant for AI design. De Neys (2024) proposed that dual-process theory can serve as a literal architectural blueprint for AI systems: one subsystem for statistical pattern matching (what LLMs already do), another for structured symbolic reasoning.[1]
What this looks like in practice: Imagine you ask an LLM to help you decide whether to delay that launch. A vanilla LLM gives you a 500-word pro/con list. A dual-process LLM first pattern-matches against similar past launches in your company’s data (System 1), then flags the two assumptions most likely to be wrong and walks you through stress-testing them (System 2). Same question. Completely different cognitive experience.
Naturalistic Decision Making: Experts Are Pattern Matchers (Just Like LLMs)
Here’s the uncomfortable truth that should make every AI skeptic pause.
Gary Klein spent decades studying how firefighters, military commanders, and ER nurses make life-or-death decisions. His Recognition-Primed Decision (RPD) model found that these experts don’t weigh all the options. They recognize patterns from prior experience, mentally simulate a single course of action, and act. No comparison shopping. No decision matrix (Klein, 1993).[2]
Sound familiar? That’s essentially what an LLM does: pattern completion shaped by prior exposure. The difference isn’t mechanism. It’s structure. Human experts have organized their patterns around validated frameworks, contextual cues, and hard-won failure modes. LLMs have organized theirs around… whatever was on the internet.
Klein’s work also highlights that real-world decisions happen under time pressure, ambiguous information, ill-defined goals, and changing conditions.[3] If your AI decision tool only works when the problem is clean and well-structured, you’ve solved the easy version and shipped it as the solution.
What this looks like in practice: A senior UX researcher doesn’t need to see every data point to know a design is going to fail in usability testing. They’ve seen that pattern before. An LLM persona built on RPD principles wouldn’t give you “here are 10 things to consider.” It would say: “This looks like [recognized pattern]. Here’s the one thing most likely to go wrong based on similar situations. Want to simulate what happens if that risk materializes?”
Fast-and-Frugal Heuristics: When Less Information Beats More
Gerd Gigerenzer’s adaptive toolbox framework makes a claim that sounds heretical in the age of big data: simple heuristics that deliberately ignore available information can outperform complex models in uncertain environments (Gigerenzer & Todd, 1999). “By exploiting features of the environment and capabilities of the decision makers, heuristics can be simple without trading off accuracy.”[4]
This directly challenges the prevailing assumption in AI: that more data, more parameters, and more computation always produce better outputs.
What this looks like in practice: You’re hiring for a UX research role. A “comprehensive” AI tool scores 47 candidate attributes against weighted criteria and produces a ranked list. A fast-and-frugal AI asks three questions in sequence: (1) Do they have direct experience with the method your team needs most? If no, stop. (2) Can they articulate a research finding that changed a product decision? If no, stop. (3) Does the team want to work with them?
Three cues. No weighting. And if Gigerenzer’s research holds, it probably outperforms the 47-attribute model in real hiring conditions, because the environment is too uncertain for complex models to add value.
Cognitive Offloading: Two Versions of the Same Conversation
Cognitive offloading is using external tools to reduce mental effort (Risko & Gilbert, 2016). Your calendar, your to-do list, your calculator. LLMs are the newest and most powerful addition to this toolkit.
But there’s a critical design choice hiding inside every AI interaction. Let me show you.
Version A: Naive Offloading

You: Should we build Feature X or Feature Y first?
AI: Based on market analysis, Feature X has higher potential ROI due to competitive positioning, while Feature Y addresses a critical usability gap. I recommend Feature X with a 65% confidence score.
You: Okay, Feature X it is.
What just happened? You offloaded the decision entirely. You didn’t engage with the trade-offs. You didn’t surface your own assumptions. You didn’t learn anything you could apply next time. A 2025 arXiv paper calls this belief offloading: people don’t just offload tasks to AI, they begin offloading the very process of forming and upholding beliefs. The downstream consequences include changes in behavior and the structure of entire belief systems.[6]

Version B: Scaffolded Offloading

You: Should we build Feature X or Feature Y first?
AI: Before I weigh in, let me surface the decision. You’re prioritizing between competitive positioning (Feature X) and usability debt (Feature Y). Two questions first: Which of these carries more risk if you get it wrong? And what would need to be true for the less obvious choice to be the right one?
You: Hmm. If we ship Feature X with the current usability issues, adoption might tank anyway…
AI: That’s a dependency worth testing. Here’s a quick way to validate that assumption before committing.
Same question. Completely different cognitive outcome. In Version B, the AI used a framework (pre-mortem + assumption testing) to scaffold your reasoning instead of replacing it. You still own the decision. You just got help thinking it through.
A 2025 paper in Frontiers in Psychology captures this tension precisely: AI can enable cognitive offloading that supports adaptive coping, or it can create cognitive overload through “erosion of introspection, over-reliance on algorithmic feedback, and anxiety induced by hyper-monitoring.”[5] The difference between these outcomes is design, not technology.

LLMs Have Cognitive Biases (and That’s Actually the Unlock)
Here’s something that should reframe the whole conversation: LLMs exhibit decision heuristics that mirror human cognitive biases. Hagendorff et al. (2023) tested GPT-3.5 against the same bias prompts used in human psychology studies. The result? LLMs show anchoring effects, framing effects, and other context-sensitive decision patterns, just like humans.[7]
The skeptic sees this as proof that LLMs are “just mirrors.” But flip it: if LLMs are susceptible to the same cognitive biases humans are, then the same debiasing interventions cognitive psychology has developed for humans should work on LLMs too.
And they do. Two recent frameworks prove it:

BiasBuster (2024) uncovers, evaluates, and mitigates cognitive bias in LLMs across 16,800 prompts. It targets prompt-induced, sequential, and inherent biases.[8]
Self-debiasing (2025) uses an iterative three-step process (bias determination, bias analysis, cognitive debiasing) and outperformed existing approaches across finance, healthcare, and legal decision-making tasks.[9]
This is the argument that should change the skeptic’s mind. Cognitive psychology doesn’t just describe what goes wrong with reasoning. It provides causal models of why reasoning goes wrong and where to intervene. Those causal models transfer directly to LLMs. That’s not a metaphor. It’s an empirical finding.

From Token Prediction to Cognitive Architecture
Several research groups are now building what I think is the most promising direction in AI: LLMs that don’t just generate text, but operate within cognitive architectures modeled on how humans actually process decisions.
Cognitive LLMs: Giving AI a Decision-Making Operating System
Wu et al. (2025) introduced Cognitive LLMs, where cognitive architectures (specifically ACT-R, one of the most validated models of human cognition) instruct large language models for decision-making. Rather than relying solely on statistical patterns, these systems transfer structured knowledge that represents how humans process information, form strategies, and make choices.[10]
The human parallel: An experienced product manager doesn’t just “know things.” They have internalized decision patterns, priority frameworks, and failure modes that shape how they process new information. Cognitive LLMs attempt to give AI that same structural layer.
Persona Alchemy: Psychologically Grounded Stakeholder Agents
Zhu et al. (2025) developed a Social Cognitive Theory (SCT) agent design framework using four personal factors (cognitive, motivational, biological, and affective) to create AI personas that respond to scenarios in psychologically consistent ways.[11]
The human parallel: Before a big decision, you might informally poll three colleagues you trust because they think differently from you. Persona Alchemy formalizes that. You test your decision against psychologically grounded stakeholder agents and get diversity of perspective without the politics, the scheduling conflicts, or the groupthink.
Personality-Driven Decision Agents
The SANDMAN architecture uses the Big Five (OCEAN) personality model to create agents whose decision patterns shift predictably based on induced personality traits. Different personality profiles produce “distinct task-selection patterns aligned with induced OCEAN attributes.”[12]
The human parallel: You already know that your team’s most conscientious member spots risks others miss, while your most open member generates options nobody else considers. SANDMAN suggests we can build AI tools that replicate those cognitive diversity patterns on demand.
The Group Decision Problem: A Story in Two Acts
Act 1: The Meeting Without AI
It’s the third meeting about the roadmap. The VP speaks first and anchors the group on Option A. Two junior PMs have concerns but don’t speak up because the VP seems decided. The data scientist mentions a risk in the numbers, but it gets lost in the crosstalk. The group “aligns” on Option A. Three months later, the risk the data scientist mentioned materializes. Everyone remembers the meeting differently.
This is the textbook cocktail: anchoring bias from the first speaker, authority bias suppressing dissent, information loss from unstructured discussion, and groupthink papering over the cracks.
Act 2: The Same Meeting With a Framework-Aware AI Facilitator
The AI opens by surfacing the decision structure: “You’re choosing between three roadmap options. Before discussing preferences, I’d like each person to independently flag their top concern. I’ll synthesize these anonymously.”
After collecting inputs, the AI identifies a convergence: three of five people flagged the same adoption risk for Option A, but none of them had said it out loud yet. The AI surfaces it: “There’s a shared concern about adoption risk that hasn’t been discussed. Want to explore that before evaluating options?”
The VP, now seeing the pattern, adjusts. The group discusses the risk openly. They modify Option A to address it, or pivot to Option B. Either way, the decision is better because the AI facilitated the cognitive process, not just the information flow.
This isn’t science fiction. Research by Chiang et al. (2022) found that involving users in AI’s reasoning process increased both compliance and perceived collaboration.[13] And work on LLM-based group systems envisions AI that actively monitors groups, identifies members who haven’t been heard, and even de-escalates conflicts (Ricci et al., 2025).[15]
But here’s the design nuance that cognitive load theory warns us about: more explanation isn’t always better. Detailed AI explanations can actually increase perceived task complexity and impair decision quality (Sweller, 1994).[14] The right AI facilitator knows when to surface information and when to stay quiet. That calibration is a UX Research problem, not an engineering problem.
The Questions We Haven’t Answered Yet
If this synthesis is right, and I think the evidence is strong, then there are six open questions that should shape the next wave of research. These aren’t abstract. Each one has direct implications for what you build next.
1. Can LLMs Learn to Recognize Decision Contexts Automatically?
Right now, LLMs only apply frameworks when you explicitly prompt them. What would it take to build systems that detect the type of decision being made and apply the appropriate cognitive strategy without being told? That’s Klein’s RPD model, but for AI.
2. How Do You Calibrate Cognitive Offloading in Real Time?
Too much support and you get belief offloading. Too little and you get cognitive overload. Is there a measurable signal (response time, question patterns, confidence indicators) that could help an AI system dynamically adjust how much scaffolding to provide?
3. What Does “Cognitive Load” Mean for a Group Using AI?
We have solid models of individual cognitive load. We have almost nothing for group cognitive load in AI-mediated contexts. When five people use an AI facilitator in a meeting, how does cognitive burden distribute? Who gets overloaded? Who gets underserved?
4. What Happens to Belief Formation After a Year of AI-Assisted Decisions?
The belief offloading research is brand new. We need longitudinal studies. If you use an AI decision tool daily for 12 months, do you get better at decisions or worse? Does the answer depend on how the tool is designed?
5. Which Decisions Need Heuristics and Which Need Full Analysis?
Gigerenzer’s ecological rationality says the heuristic needs to match the environment. But we don’t have empirically validated guidelines for which AI decision contexts benefit from simple heuristic responses and which ones require deep analytical treatment. Building those guidelines is a UXR problem.
6. Do These Frameworks Work Across Cultures?
Naturalistic decision-making research comes primarily from Western military and emergency contexts. Recognition-primed processes, heuristic preferences, and group dynamics all vary across cultures. What does that mean for globally deployed AI decision tools? We don’t know yet.
The Bottom Line
The skeptic is right that LLMs don’t “understand” decisions. But the skeptic is solving the wrong problem.
Decades of cognitive psychology research converge on a single insight: intelligence has always been about the fit between a cognitive strategy and the environment it operates in. Not some magical internal property of the reasoner. A firefighter isn’t smart because of raw brainpower. A firefighter is smart because years of experience have organized pattern recognition around the right cues in the right contexts.
UX Research is the field purpose-built to study that fit. Applied cognitive psychology provides the theoretical architecture. Together, they offer something that scaling parameters alone never will: a principled way to match AI capabilities to human cognitive needs, context by context, decision by decision.
The opportunity isn’t to make AI “smart.” It’s to make AI useful in the ways that matter. Design the interaction well, embed the right frameworks, and the system produces intelligent outcomes. Design it poorly, and you get a very expensive autocomplete that makes people worse at thinking.
That’s not an engineering problem. It’s a cognitive design problem. And we already have the science to solve it.

References

Chiang, C. W., et al. (2022). Mitigating knowledge imbalance in AI-advised decision-making through collaborative user involvement. International Journal of Human-Computer Studies.
De Neys, W. (2024). Dual-process theories of thought as potential architectures for developing neuro-symbolic AI models. Frontiers in Cognition.
Gigerenzer, G., & Todd, P. M. (1999). Simple heuristics that make us smart. Oxford University Press.
Grinschgl, S., & Neubauer, A. C. (2022). Cognitive offloading: Systematic integration and a revised framework. Perspectives on Psychological Science.
Hagendorff, T., Fabi, S., & Kosinski, M. (2023). Do large language models show decision heuristics similar to humans? Journal of Experimental Psychology: General.
Kahneman, D. (2011). Thinking, fast and slow. Farrar, Straus and Giroux.
Klein, G. A. (1993). A recognition-primed decision (RPD) model of rapid decision making. In G. A. Klein et al. (Eds.), Decision making in action (pp. 138–147). Ablex Publishing.
Klein, G. (2008). Naturalistic decision making. Human Factors, 50(3), 456–460.
Ricci, F., et al. (2025). Rethinking group recommender systems in the era of LLMs. arXiv preprint.
Risko, E. F., & Gilbert, S. J. (2016). Cognitive offloading. Trends in Cognitive Sciences, 20(9), 676–688.
Simon, H. A. (1955). A behavioral model of rational choice. The Quarterly Journal of Economics, 69(1), 99–118.
Sweller, J. (1994). Cognitive load theory, learning difficulty, and instructional design. Learning and Instruction, 4(4), 295–312.
Wu, S., et al. (2025). Cognitive LLMs: Toward human-like artificial intelligence by integrating cognitive architectures and large language models for manufacturing decision-making. SAGE Journals.
Zhu, J. N. Y., et al. (2025). Persona alchemy: Designing, evaluating, and implementing psychologically-grounded LLM agents for diverse stakeholder representation. arXiv preprint arXiv:2505.18351.

The human parallel: You already know that your team’s most conscientious member spots risks others miss, while your most open member generates options nobody else considers. SANDMAN suggests we can build AI tools that replicate those cognitive diversity patterns on demand.
The Group Decision Problem: A Story in Two Acts
Act 1: The Meeting Without AI
It’s the third meeting about the roadmap. The VP speaks first and anchors the group on Option A. Two junior PMs have concerns but don’t speak up because the VP seems decided. The data scientist mentions a risk in the numbers, but it gets lost in the crosstalk. The group “aligns” on Option A. Three months later, the risk the data scientist mentioned materializes. Everyone remembers the meeting differently.
This is the textbook cocktail: anchoring bias from the first speaker, authority bias suppressing dissent, information loss from unstructured discussion, and groupthink papering over the cracks.
Act 2: The Same Meeting With a Framework-Aware AI Facilitator
The AI opens by surfacing the decision structure: “You’re choosing between three roadmap options. Before discussing preferences, I’d like each person to independently flag their top concern. I’ll synthesize these anonymously.”
After collecting inputs, the AI identifies a convergence: three of five people flagged the same adoption risk for Option A, but none of them had said it out loud yet. The AI surfaces it: “There’s a shared concern about adoption risk that hasn’t been discussed. Want to explore that before evaluating options?”
The VP, now seeing the pattern, adjusts. The group discusses the risk openly. They modify Option A to address it, or pivot to Option B. Either way, the decision is better because the AI facilitated the cognitive process, not just the information flow.
This isn’t science fiction. Research by Chiang et al. (2022) found that involving users in AI’s reasoning process increased both compliance and perceived collaboration.[13] And work on LLM-based group systems envisions AI that actively monitors groups, identifies members who haven’t been heard, and even de-escalates conflicts (Ricci et al., 2025).[15]
But here’s the design nuance that cognitive load theory warns us about: more explanation isn’t always better. Detailed AI explanations can actually increase perceived task complexity and impair decision quality (Sweller, 1994).[14] The right AI facilitator knows when to surface information and when to stay quiet. That calibration is a UX Research problem, not an engineering problem.
The Questions We Haven’t Answered Yet
If this synthesis is right, and I think the evidence is strong, then there are six open questions that should shape the next wave of research. These aren’t abstract. Each one has direct implications for what you build next.
1. Can LLMs Learn to Recognize Decision Contexts Automatically?
Right now, LLMs only apply frameworks when you explicitly prompt them. What would it take to build systems that detect the type of decision being made and apply the appropriate cognitive strategy without being told? That’s Klein’s RPD model, but for AI.
2. How Do You Calibrate Cognitive Offloading in Real Time?
Too much support and you get belief offloading. Too little and you get cognitive overload. Is there a measurable signal (response time, question patterns, confidence indicators) that could help an AI system dynamically adjust how much scaffolding to provide?
3. What Does “Cognitive Load” Mean for a Group Using AI?
We have solid models of individual cognitive load. We have almost nothing for group cognitive load in AI-mediated contexts. When five people use an AI facilitator in a meeting, how does cognitive burden distribute? Who gets overloaded? Who gets underserved?
4. What Happens to Belief Formation After a Year of AI-Assisted Decisions?
The belief offloading research is brand new. We need longitudinal studies. If you use an AI decision tool daily for 12 months, do you get better at decisions or worse? Does the answer depend on how the tool is designed?
5. Which Decisions Need Heuristics and Which Need Full Analysis?
Gigerenzer’s ecological rationality says the heuristic needs to match the environment. But we don’t have empirically validated guidelines for which AI decision contexts benefit from simple heuristic responses and which ones require deep analytical treatment. Building those guidelines is a UXR problem.
6. Do These Frameworks Work Across Cultures?
Naturalistic decision-making research comes primarily from Western military and emergency contexts. Recognition-primed processes, heuristic preferences, and group dynamics all vary across cultures. What does that mean for globally deployed AI decision tools? We don’t know yet.
The Bottom Line
The skeptic is right that LLMs don’t “understand” decisions. But the skeptic is solving the wrong problem.
Decades of cognitive psychology research converge on a single insight: intelligence has always been about the fit between a cognitive strategy and the environment it operates in. Not some magical internal property of the reasoner. A firefighter isn’t smart because of raw brainpower. A firefighter is smart because years of experience have organized pattern recognition around the right cues in the right contexts.
UX Research is the field purpose-built to study that fit. Applied cognitive psychology provides the theoretical architecture. Together, they offer something that scaling parameters alone never will: a principled way to match AI capabilities to human cognitive needs, context by context, decision by decision.
The opportunity isn’t to make AI “smart.” It’s to make AI useful in the ways that matter. Design the interaction well, embed the right frameworks, and the system produces intelligent outcomes. Design it poorly, and you get a very expensive autocomplete that makes people worse at thinking.
That’s not an engineering problem. It’s a cognitive design problem. And we already have the science to solve it.

Researcher, Agentic Experiences
Greater Seattle Area | oliver.researching@gmail.com | linkedin.com/in/michaeleoliver
Summary
Seven-plus years of UX research in high-growth B2B SaaS across developer tools, security, and GRC. The through-line of recent work: how people build or lose trust in AI-driven experiences where the output is nondeterministic, why reviewers adopt, override, or ignore AI-flagged guidance, and which signals (provenance, verification, control) gate adoption over time. I pair qualitative and quantitative methods, read SQL, and build my own evaluation tooling (NLP pipelines, LLM baselines, provenance checks), partnering with data as a peer rather than outsourcing the numbers. I own problem spaces end to end and raise the craft bar around me through mentorship and reusable standards.
Experience
AuditBoard (SaaS, GRC)
Staff UX Researcher (first embedded UX researcher; grew the practice solo into a four-person team)

Built the research practice from 0 to 1: generative discovery, rapid evaluative sprints, competitive benchmarking, behavioral analytics.
Studied trust in AI-driven guidance directly: why reviewers adopt, override, or ignore AI-flagged risk, using decision-focused methods (Critical Decision Method) rather than opinion interviews; findings became design principles for how AI-assisted outputs earn calibrated reliance.
Ran 30+ interviews with enterprise customers, non-customers, and director-level stakeholders; synthesized nine jobs to be done and three vision stories that became the product organization’s top three priorities and anchored a board-level plan to 3x revenue in five years.
Built a continuous insights loop: a standardized benchmarking program cut study cycles from eight weeks to four and set the 80/100 usability score directors now mandate for every new product launch.
Shipped the first research repository and intake workflow, the department’s single source of truth, with sample plans and method standards that let non-researchers run templated studies.
Mentored AI-forward research practice across Product, Engineering, and Design: when to trust LLM-assisted synthesis and when provenance and human judgment stay in the loop; those evaluation habits are now standard on the team’s AI-assisted workflows.
Designed scenario-based hiring protocols that screened for reasoning over polish; both hires succeeded immediately. Interim manager of the four-person team for six months; one report entered the promotion track.

GitLab (developer tools, enterprise)
Senior UX Researcher, Security

Defined strategic roadmaps for three feature groups; an Outcome-Driven Innovation survey surfaced 25+ application security opportunities, prioritized across eight market segments.
Built six security personas from 20+ interviews, each tied to benchmarkable tasks and design principles; the template was published to the research repository for repeat use.
Designed and ran the first research on GitLab Docs: two annual surveys with 1,200+ responses, paired with qualitative follow-up on the anomalies the numbers surfaced.

Higher Logic (community SaaS)
Senior UX Researcher / UX Researcher

Built the Engagement Benchmarking Score (EBS), an analytical instrument grounded in expert interviews and statistical modeling, mapping engagement segments to success metrics; later integrated into the product dashboard.
Market segmentation research on firmographics and subscription add-ons shaped the 2021 Engagement Benchmarking Report, contributing to over $1 million ARR in its first year.
Revamped search UX from SQL usage-data analysis and rapid iterative testing; produced a 15-point SUS increase within a fixed research budget.
Ran NLP analysis (topic modeling, sentiment) over 1,200+ open-response entries, converting free text into trackable themes.

Public artifacts on AI trust

“Why UX Researchers Undertrust AI Synthesis” (published, Oct 2026): the adoption-trust gap in AI synthesis, calibration over skepticism, and the provenance demands that gate AI adoption in research practice.
Hands-on evaluation: built and benchmarked classifiers against LLM baselines for feedback labeling, with multi-annotator agreement analysis.

Methods

Research on AI-powered products: Critical Decision Method, trust-calibration studies, evaluations where there is no single correct output.
Participatory design, early concept testing, and formative and summative usability testing across a portfolio of products.
Interviews, jobs to be done, and hierarchical task analysis for motivation and behavior; survey design with sample plans set by precision needs; A/B testing; usability benchmarking.
Product telemetry: SQL, R, Python; NLP on open text; model behavior evaluated against human baselines.
Research operations: repository, intake and prioritization, reusable templates, coaching and mentoring junior researchers.

projects/uxr-blog/blog-db/stakeholder-ma.title: Stakeholder Management Chapter 1: Foundations for building a relationship
projects/uxr-blog/blog-db/stakeholder-ma.content:
How UX Researchers Can Build Strong Relationships with Stakeholders
Why Building Stakeholder Relationships Matters
Imagine spending weeks on meticulous research that could transform your product. Your findings are solid, your recommendations are actionable, and your presentation is flawless. Yet somehow, when you share with stakeholders, your insights get overlooked or deprioritized. Or, better yet, you’re stakeholders express excitement when you share the insights, but weeks go by and no one makes progress on the changes, and then quarters go by and you realize that no the insights have been collecting dust.
The lesson is simple - insights create value only when implemented. Stakeholders are the key to turning your research into reality, and their trust ensures your work drives change, even when they can’t scrutinize every detail. By positioning yourself as a strategic partner rather than just a researcher, you become essential to their success, as your research directly influences their decisions and career trajectories.
While trust forms the foundation, it’s just the beginning. True innovation flourishes through effective collaboration, and organizations thrive when teams work in harmony. As a UX researcher, your role extends beyond data collection - you’re a strategic advisor helping to shape decisions. This leadership position demands trust, which grows through genuine, collaborative partnerships.
Remember: building these relationships isn’t about being popular - it’s about fostering an environment where your insights can catalyze meaningful change.
How to Start Building Stakeholder Relationships
Trust forms the cornerstone of every successful relationship. Instead of diving straight into work, invest time in understanding the people you’ll be collaborating with.
Begin by connecting with your stakeholders on a human level. Explore their motivations, professional interests, and problem-solving approaches. Practice genuine curiosity - this isn’t networking for networking’s sake, but rather a sincere effort to understand their perspectives and values.
Then, delve into their aspirations. Whether it’s launching an exceptional product, advancing their career, or achieving team milestones, understanding their definition of success allows you to align your research to support their goals.
Start small by identifying opportunities to provide immediate value. When they face challenges, demonstrate how research can illuminate solutions. Quick user tests or relevant insights sharing can show your commitment to their success.
Always seek alignment between goals. Consider how your research objectives complement their priorities and organizational aims. When you demonstrate how your work contributes to collective success, you create a stronger collaborative foundation.
The Power of Touchpoints
While establishing relationships is crucial, maintaining them ensures lasting impact. Regular check-ins serve as vital touchpoints that sustain strong connections efficiently.
Consider implementing bi-weekly coffee chats. Keep them informal - let conversations flow naturally. Share updates on current projects, gather feedback, and learn about upcoming initiatives. Understanding their decision points and challenges helps you identify opportunities where your research can add value.
These conversations provide valuable insights into improving your research impact. By discussing what works and what doesn’t, you demonstrate your commitment to continuous improvement.
Maintain authenticity throughout. Show interest in their lives beyond work. Celebrate their team’s achievements and personal milestones. These genuine interactions transform professional relationships into meaningful partnerships.
When meeting new stakeholders, first impressions are critical. Learn from their previous experiences with UX research, both positive and negative. Understand their preferred collaboration style - some want deep involvement, others prefer high-level updates. This knowledge helps you tailor your approach effectively.
Early on, identify their research priorities - whether it’s speed, quality, scope, or innovation. Their preferences will guide how you optimize your work to deliver maximum value.
Final Thoughts
Let’s be clear: exceptional UX research requires strong stakeholder relationships to drive impact. Even groundbreaking insights need stakeholder support to create change.
By cultivating authentic connections and trust with stakeholders, you evolve beyond the role of researcher to become a trusted strategic advisor they turn to for complex challenges.
While relationship building requires investment, the returns are invaluable. Consistent engagement and alignment position you and your research as essential drivers of success.
Remember that UX research fundamentally centers on understanding people - both our users and the colleagues who help transform insights into impact. Stay curious, maintain authenticity, and focus on collective success. That’s the path to creating lasting change.

Alternative Names for Stakeholder Management:

Relationship Design & Strategy
Collaborative UX
Product-Design-Research Alliance Building
Research Impact Optimization
Research Alliance Development
The Art of Stakeholder Relations
Building Trust with Stakeholders
UXR Blog Workflow
