projects/uxr-blog/blog-db/stats-101-chap.title: Stats 101 Chapter 1: Measures of dispersion central tendency, generalization and approximation mean
projects/uxr-blog/blog-db/stats-101-chap.content:
Understanding Data’s Story: Central Tendency & Dispersion in Statistics
In the world of social science, statistics serves as our lens to understand what we cannot directly observe. From human behavior to economic trends, researchers use sampling to reveal patterns in populations through two key concepts: central tendency and dispersion.
Central Tendency: Finding the Center
Think of central tendency as the “typical” value in your data. Let’s explore three main ways to find it:
1. The Mean (Average)
The mean is your classic mathematical average - sum everything up and divide by the count. For instance, if five people earn between $30k and $70k, the mean income is $50k. But watch out - extreme values can pull this number in misleading directions.
2. The Median (Middle Value)
The median sits right in the middle when you line up all your numbers. Take these household incomes: 45k, 48k, 50k, 52k, 55k. The median is $50k - perfect for data with outliers like housing prices.
3. The Mode (Most Common)
The mode is simply what shows up most often. In election data, it tells you which party got the most votes.
Dispersion: Understanding the Spread
But knowing the center isn’t enough - we need to understand how data spreads out around it.
1. Basic Range
The range is your quickest measure - just subtract the smallest value from the largest. If test scores run from 65 to 95, your range is 30 points.
2. Interquartile Range (IQR)
The IQR focuses on the middle 50% of your data. Take these ages: 22, 25, 28, 30, 35. The IQR is 5 years (30 minus 25), showing where most values cluster while ignoring outliers.
3. Standard Deviation & Variance
These give us precision. Variance measures average squared differences from the mean, while standard deviation (SD) brings it back to our original scale. In a normal distribution, about 68% of data falls within one SD of the mean, and 95% within two.
From Sample to Population: Making the Connection
Your population is everyone you’re studying - like all US voters. Since measuring everyone is usually impossible, we take samples to estimate population parameters. For example, finding a sample mean income of $55k with an SD of $15k suggests most population incomes fall between $40k and $70k.
The Bottom Line
Statistics isn’t about finding exact answers - it’s about understanding uncertainty. When you see statistics in headlines, ask about the spread and methodology. Was the sample representative? Could there be bias?
In our next article, we’ll explore how these concepts help us understand relationships between variables, like education levels and crime rates.

Food for Thought: Consider a city where the median rent is $2k with an SD of $1k. What might this tell us about housing inequality?

projects/uxr-blog/blog-db/summary.title: Resume - Staff Mixed Methods User Researcher at EvenUp
projects/uxr-blog/blog-db/summary.content:
Staff Mixed Methods User Researcher
Greater Seattle Area | oliver.researching@gmail.com | linkedin.com/in/michaeleoliver
Summary
Mixed methods UX researcher across enterprise SaaS and developer tools. I run the quantitative side myself: SQL over usage data, survey design, benchmarking instruments, NLP on open text. I pair the quantitative what with the qualitative why, then connect the result to adoption and revenue. I have stood up research functions from scratch: built a solo practice into a four-person team, shipped the first research repository and intake workflow, and published templates that made insights self-serve for partners who were not researchers.
Experience
AuditBoard (SaaS, GRC)
Staff UX Researcher (first embedded UX researcher; grew the practice solo into a four-person team)

Built research operations from zero: intake and prioritization workflow, first research repository as the department’s single source of truth, and a standardized benchmarking program that cut study cycles from eight weeks to four.
Ran 30+ interviews with customers, non-customers, and director-level stakeholders; nine jobs-to-be-done and three vision stories became the product organization’s top three priorities and anchored a board-level plan to 3x revenue in five years.
Set the quality bar directors enforced on every new product launch: an 80/100 usability threshold.
Designed scenario-based hiring protocols that screened for reasoning over polish; both hires succeeded immediately. Interim manager of the four-person team for six months.

GitLab (developer tools, B2B SaaS)
Senior UX Researcher, Security

Built six security personas from 20+ interviews, each mapped to opportunity areas, design principles, and benchmarkable tasks; template published to the research repository for repeat use across squads.
Outcome-Driven Innovation survey uncovered 25+ application security opportunities, prioritized across eight market segments.
Two annual documentation surveys, 1,200+ responses analyzed, paired with qualitative follow-up; shipped templates so squads answered recurring questions without waiting on a researcher.

Higher Logic (community SaaS)
Senior UX Researcher / UX Researcher

Built the Engagement Benchmarking Score, an analytical instrument from expert interviews and statistical modeling mapping behavioral engagement segments to success metrics; later integrated into the product’s dashboard.
Led market segmentation and benchmarking research; findings shaped the 2021 Engagement Benchmarking Report and contributed to over $1 million ARR in the first year.
Applied NLP (topic modeling, sentiment) to 1,200+ open-response survey entries, turning free text into trackable themes.
Revamped search UX from SQL usage-data analysis and rapid iterative testing: 15-point SUS increase within a fixed research budget.

Methods
Mixed methods is how I work, not a bullet point: interviews and jobs-to-be-done for the felt experience; surveys, A/B testing, and benchmarking for the behavioral claim. SQL, R, Python. NLP on open text: topic modeling, TF-IDF, sentiment analysis. Reads data-science output and chooses the method by the decision at stake.

projects/uxr-blog/blog-db/survey-design-.title: Survey Design That Delivers: Writing Quantitative UX Surveys That Drive Decisions
projects/uxr-blog/blog-db/survey-design-.content:
Designing Surveys That Get You The Data You Actually Need
Most organizations collect survey data they never use. The problem isn’t insufficient data—it’s poorly designed surveys that don’t align with analysis needs. By working backwards from your analytical goals, you can create surveys that deliver actionable insights.
Introduction
Despite careful planning, many researchers find themselves unable to answer key stakeholder questions from their survey data. This common problem stems from designing surveys without a clear analysis strategy. Starting with your end goals ensures every question serves a purpose.
1. Know What Story You Need to Tell
Begin your survey design by mapping out exactly how you’ll use the data:
Identify the specific decisions your research needs to influence. Each type of decision—whether it’s feature prioritization, design evaluation, or user segmentation—requires different data points. Transform these decisions into concrete research questions, then map each to specific metrics.
Create your analysis template before building the survey:

Define your key metrics and calculations
Plan your data visualizations
List the stakeholder questions you’ll answer

2. Design for Clean Data
Getting actionable data requires careful question design.
Closed-ended questions provide the cleanest data for analysis. Choose your rating scales strategically:

Likert scales for measuring attitudes
Semantic differential scales for comparing opposing concepts
Numeric scales for measuring frequency or quantity
The choice between odd and even scales affects your results. Odd scales allow neutral responses, while even scales force a direction. Choose based on whether neutral responses provide value for your analysis.

3. Keep It Simple, Keep It Clean
Complex surveys lead to poor data quality. A straightforward survey flow improves completion rates and response reliability.
Avoid excessive branching logic—it often creates analytical challenges and reduces sample sizes. Some question types consistently cause problems:

Overly large matrix questions
Multiple response questions
Long ranking exercises

4. Validate Before You Launch
Always test thoroughly before launching:

Run analysis on test data
Verify skip logic paths
Check for response patterns
Look for unusual distributions

5. From Data to Decisions
Structure your data for efficient analysis:

Use consistent variable names
Code responses systematically
Include relevant context
Choose effective visualizations:
Bar charts for categories
Line charts for trends
Scatter plots for relationships
Heat maps for matrices

Expert Tips That Make a Difference
Write clear questions:

Use precise language
Define technical terms
Avoid leading questions
Be specific about time periods
Handle matrix questions carefully:
Limit items to 5-7
Keep scales consistent
Test on mobile devices

About Survey Response Scales
Scale design affects your results:

5-point scales work for simple concepts
7-point scales add nuance
11-point scales suit familiar metrics

Common Pitfalls to Avoid
Watch for these issues:

Questions measuring multiple things
Scales that don’t show meaningful differences
Missing important context
Overly complex question formats

Conclusion
Your survey succeeds when it drives decisions. Before launching, verify:

Questions connect to analysis needs
Survey flow makes sense
Each question measures one thing
Responses will be actionable
Privacy concerns are addressed
Remember: Collect data with purpose. If you can’t explain how you’ll use it, don’t collect it.

projects/uxr-blog/blog-db/the-agentic-wo.title: What Is an Agentic Workflow? The Definition Cognitive Science Already Had
projects/uxr-blog/blog-db/the-agentic-wo.content:
The AI industry spent two years defining “agentic workflow.” Cognitive scientists defined the same thing four decades ago. The gap between these two definitions is where most agentic systems fail.
The Agentic Workflow Definition Everyone Agrees On
An agentic workflow is a multi-step process where an AI agent breaks down a complex goal, reasons about how to achieve it, takes actions, and refines its approach through iteration.
That much should be familiar. Andrew Ng outlined four design patterns that anchor most implementations [1]: reflection (the agent critiques and improves its own output), tool use (the agent interacts with external systems and data), planning (the agent decomposes a complex task into manageable steps), and multi-agent collaboration (specialized agents coordinate to solve problems no single agent could handle alone).
The industry consensus is clear. IBM defines agentic workflows as “AI-driven processes where autonomous agents make decisions, take actions, and coordinate tasks with minimal human intervention” [2]. AWS, NVIDIA, and Atlassian offer variations on the same theme [3][4][5]. Every major tech company has published its version.
What these definitions share is a focus on what agentic workflows do: they reason, they plan, they act, they adapt. What they miss is why these particular patterns work. And understanding the “why” is how you build systems that don’t break in unpredictable ways.
The answer has been sitting in HCI textbooks since 1983.
What Cognitive Science Already Knew
The four patterns that define modern agentic workflows map directly to cognitive process models that researchers have studied, validated, and refined for decades. This isn’t a loose analogy. The structural parallels are precise enough to be useful.
GOMS: The Original Task Decomposition
In 1983, Stuart Card, Thomas Moran, and Allen Newell published The Psychology of Human-Computer Interaction, introducing the GOMS model: Goals, Operators, Methods, and Selection Rules [6]. GOMS describes how humans decompose complex tasks into hierarchical goal structures, select methods to achieve sub-goals, and execute operators (the atomic actions that actually change the world).
Read that list again: goals, operators, methods, selection rules. Now consider how you design an agentic workflow. You define a goal for the agent. You give it operators (tool calls, API actions, code execution). You specify methods (chains, strategies, prompts that achieve sub-goals). And you build selection rules (routing logic that chooses between methods based on context).
GOMS is the cognitive blueprint that agentic workflow architects have been unknowingly replicating. The model predicted, 40 years in advance, that any system performing complex tasks would need exactly these four components. Not because they are elegant engineering choices, but because they reflect the irreducible structure of goal-directed cognition.
ACT-R: The Production System Blueprint
John Robert Anderson’s ACT-R (Adaptive Control of Thought, Rational) is a cognitive architecture developed at Carnegie Mellon that models human cognition as a production system [7]. It has three core components: declarative memory (stored facts and knowledge), procedural memory (if-then production rules that govern behavior), and a pattern matcher that selects which production to fire based on the current state and expected utility.
This maps cleanly to agentic AI reasoning loops. An agent’s context window and retrieved knowledge function as declarative memory. Its instructions, system prompts, and behavioral rules function as procedural memory. And its action selection process (choosing which tool to call, which sub-agent to invoke, which strategy to pursue) is utility-based pattern matching.
ACT-R’s central finding is that every task a human performs consists of a series of discrete, irreducible cognitive operations [7]. Each operation retrieves relevant knowledge, matches it against the current situation, and fires the highest-utility production. This is precisely what happens in an agentic reasoning loop: perceive context, match patterns, select action, execute. The iterative, multi-step nature of agentic workflows isn’t an engineering preference. It’s a cognitive necessity.
Recognition-Primed Decision Making: Why Reflection Works
Gary Klein’s Recognition-Primed Decision (RPD) model, developed through studying how fireground commanders make decisions under extreme pressure, reveals something counterintuitive about expert decision-making [8]. Experts don’t compare options analytically. They recognize situational patterns from experience, mentally simulate a course of action, and if the simulation succeeds, they execute. If it fails, they modify and simulate again.
This is the reflection pattern in agentic AI. When an agent generates output, evaluates it against criteria, identifies problems, and iterates, it follows the exact cognitive sequence Klein documented in human experts. The RPD model explains why reflection produces such surprising performance gains. Ng noted that even simple self-critique implementations dramatically improve output quality [1]. Reflection works because it mirrors the cognitive process that distinguishes expert performance from novice performance: the ability to simulate outcomes before committing to action.
The RPD model also predicts when reflection will fail. Mental simulation depends on having accurate mental models of the domain. When an agent lacks sufficient context, or its training data doesn’t cover the problem space, reflection loops degenerate into confident-sounding confabulation. Klein’s framework gives architects a diagnostic: if your agent’s reflection cycles aren’t improving output, the problem isn’t the loop. It’s the model’s domain knowledge.
Distributed Cognition: The Multi-Agent Blueprint
Edwin Hutchins’ distributed cognition theory, developed through studying navigation teams aboard Navy ships, argues that cognition doesn’t happen exclusively inside individual heads [9]. It extends across people, tools, artifacts, and environments. The unit of analysis isn’t the individual thinker. It’s the entire cognitive system.
This directly explains why multi-agent collaboration works. When you distribute a complex task across specialized agents (a researcher, a writer, an editor, a fact-checker), you distribute cognitive load across a system in exactly the way Hutchins described. Each agent handles a cognitive sub-function that would overwhelm a single agent’s context and reasoning capacity. David Kirsh’s work on coordination and environment design [10] extends this: the structure of the workflow itself (how agents pass information, what artifacts they create, how they signal state) is part of the cognitive architecture.
Multi-agent collaboration isn’t just an engineering convenience for managing complexity. It’s a fundamental principle of how complex cognition operates. Hutchins’ theory also predicts the failure mode that plagues poorly designed multi-agent systems: when coordination mechanisms between agents break down, the distributed cognitive system fails, even if each individual agent performs well in isolation.
If you’re interested in how these cognitive principles play out in practical human-AI collaboration scenarios, Human*AI Augmented Decision Making: What It Actually Looks Like explores the applied side of this research.
What This Means for Anyone Building Agents
The convergence between cognitive science and agentic AI isn’t academic trivia. It’s a design resource.
Every one of Ng’s four agentic design patterns has a cognitive science precedent that predicts not just when it will work, but when and why it will fail. GOMS tells you that task decomposition must be hierarchical and goal-structured, not flat lists of steps. ACT-R tells you that action selection depends on the quality of the agent’s “declarative memory” (its context and retrieved knowledge). Klein’s RPD model tells you that reflection only improves output when the agent has sufficient domain models to simulate accurately. Hutchins tells you that multi-agent coordination artifacts matter as much as the agents themselves.
The architects building the most robust agentic systems aren’t necessarily the ones with the fanciest models. They’re the ones who, whether they realize it or not, apply the same structural principles cognitive science established decades ago. The question is whether you want to rediscover those principles through trial and error, or start with the blueprint.
For more on how cognitive load shapes the success and failure of AI-augmented workflows, see The Cognitive Load of AI: Why More Features Means Worse Decisions.
A Practical Definition Architects Can Use
Here is an agentic workflow defined through its cognitive foundations:

An agentic workflow is a goal-directed system that decomposes complex tasks into cognitive operations (perception, reasoning, action, evaluation), distributes those operations across specialized agents or modules, and iterates through reflection cycles that mirror human expert decision-making.

This definition gives you three design tests for any agentic system you build:

Cognitive clarity. Does each agent or module have a clear cognitive role? Can you name what it perceives, what it reasons about, what actions it takes, and what it evaluates?
Reflection integrity. Are reflection cycles built into the workflow architecture, not bolted on as an afterthought? Does the reflecting agent have sufficient domain knowledge to simulate outcomes accurately?
Distributed coherence. Is cognitive load distributed appropriately across agents? Are the coordination mechanisms (handoff artifacts, state signals, shared context) as well-designed as the agents themselves?
If you can answer yes to all three, you’re building on the same structural foundations that support expert human cognition. If you can’t, now you know where to look.
For a deeper exploration of how mental models shape effective AI use, see Four Mental Models That Transform How You Use AI.


References
[1] Ng, A. (2024). Agentic design patterns. DeepLearning.AI / The Batch. www.deeplearning.ai/the-batch/how-agents-can-improve-llm-performance/
[2] IBM. (2025). What are agentic workflows? IBM Think. www.ibm.com/think/topics/agentic-workflows
[3] AWS. (2025). What is agentic AI? aws.amazon.com/what-is/agentic-ai/
[4] NVIDIA. (2025). What is agentic AI? NVIDIA Blog. blogs.nvidia.com/blog/what-is-agentic-ai/
[5] Atlassian. (2025). Understanding AI agentic workflows. www.atlassian.com/blog/artificial-intelligence/ai-agentic-workflows
[6] Card, S. K., Moran, T. P., & Newell, A. (1983). The psychology of human-computer interaction. Lawrence Erlbaum Associates.
[7] Anderson, J. R. (2007). How can the human mind occur in the physical universe? Oxford University Press. See also: Budiu, R. & Anderson, J. R. (2019). ACT-R: A cognitive architecture for modeling cognition. Wiley Interdisciplinary Reviews: Cognitive Science, 10(3), e1488.
[8] Klein, G. A. (1993). A recognition-primed decision (RPD) model of rapid decision making. In G. A. Klein, J. Orasanu, R. Calderwood, & C. E. Zsambok (Eds.), Decision making in action: Models and methods (pp. 138-147). Ablex.
[9] Hutchins, E. (1995). Cognition in the wild. MIT Press.
[10] Kirsh, D. (2001). Distributed cognition, coordination and environment design. Proceedings of the European Cognitive Science Society.

projects/uxr-blog/blog-db/the-art-of-ux-.content:
The Art of UX Data Visualization: A Beginner’s Guide to Understanding Research Results
As UX researchers, we often collect valuable data about how users interact with our products. But raw numbers alone don’t tell the complete story. The way we visualize this data can dramatically impact how we—and our stakeholders—interpret and act upon our findings. This guide will help you understand how different visualization methods can shape our understanding of UX research results.
Why Visualization Matters in UX Research
Imagine you’ve just completed a usability study with 20 participants. You have task completion rates, time-on-task measurements, and satisfaction scores. How you present this data can either illuminate crucial insights or inadvertently obscure them. The right visualization can help you:

Quickly identify patterns and trends
Communicate findings effectively to stakeholders
Make data-driven decisions with confidence
Spot potential issues that might be hidden in raw numbers

Common UX Metrics and Their Ideal Visualizations
1. Task Success Rates
Task success rates are binary measurements: users either complete a task or they don’t. While you could present this as a simple percentage (e.g., “75% success rate”), different visualizations can provide richer context:
Bar Charts:

Best for: Comparing success rates across different tasks
Impact: Makes it easy to spot which features or workflows need the most attention
Warning: Can be misleading if sample sizes vary between tasks
Stacked Bar Charts:
Best for: Showing success, partial success, and failure rates together
Impact: Provides more nuanced understanding of user performance
Warning: Can become cluttered with too many categories

2. Time-on-Task Measurements
Time-based metrics often have more complexity than simple success/failure rates. The way you visualize these can dramatically affect interpretation:
Box Plots:

Best for: Showing distribution of completion times
Impact: Reveals outliers and helps identify if problems affect all users or just some
Warning: Can be intimidating for stakeholders unfamiliar with statistics
Line Charts:
Best for: Tracking changes in task completion time over multiple iterations
Impact: Makes it easy to see if design changes are improving efficiency
Warning: Can mask individual user experiences

3. Satisfaction Scores (e.g., SUS, NPS)
User satisfaction data often comes from surveys and questionnaires. The visualization choice here can significantly impact stakeholder reactions:
Radar/Spider Charts:

Best for: Comparing multiple satisfaction metrics simultaneously
Impact: Provides a holistic view of user satisfaction across dimensions
Warning: Can become difficult to read with too many variables
Horizontal Bar Charts:
Best for: Showing Likert scale responses
Impact: Makes it easy to compare positive versus negative sentiment
Warning: Averaging Likert data can be misleading

Common Pitfalls in UX Data Visualization
1. The Scale Trap
One of the most common ways visualizations can mislead is through manipulated scales. For example:

A bar chart starting at 50% instead of 0% can make small differences appear dramatic
Logarithmic scales can mask significant variations in user behavior
Inconsistent scales between comparable charts can lead to misinterpretation

2. The Aggregation Problem
Averaging data can hide important patterns:

Mean completion times might mask a bimodal distribution where two distinct user groups exist
Overall satisfaction scores might hide significant problems with specific features
Combined success rates might obscure important demographic differences

3. Color Confusion
Color choices can significantly impact interpretation:

Red/green color schemes can be inaccessible to colorblind users
Cultural associations with colors can bias interpretation
Too many colors can make visualizations harder to understand

Best Practices for Clear Communication
1. Choose the Right Chart Type
Match your visualization to your data type and message:

Use bar charts for comparisons
Use line charts for trends over time
Use scatter plots for correlations
Use pie charts sparingly (they’re often harder to interpret than alternatives)

2. Keep It Simple

Remove unnecessary decorative elements
Use clear, consistent labeling
Provide context through titles and annotations
Include sample sizes and confidence intervals where appropriate

3. Consider Your Audience

Technical stakeholders might appreciate more detailed visualizations
Executive stakeholders often prefer high-level summary views
Design teams might need detailed breakdowns by feature or workflow

Practical Examples
Example 1: Task Success Visualization
Instead of saying “Task A had 80% success rate, Task B had 60% success rate,” consider a visualization that shows:

Success rates as bars
Sample size as annotations
Confidence intervals to show uncertainty
Clear labels and context

Example 2: User Journey Analysis
Rather than presenting raw time-on-task data, consider:

A timeline visualization showing where users spend most time
Highlight points where users commonly encounter issues
Include qualitative data points (user quotes) at key moments

Conclusion
The way we visualize UX research data has a profound impact on how it’s interpreted and acted upon. By understanding these principles, you can create visualizations that:

Tell accurate stories about your users
Drive better design decisions
Communicate insights effectively to stakeholders
Remember: The goal isn’t to make the data look good, but to make it clear and actionable. When in doubt, opt for simpler visualizations that tell a clear story over complex ones that might confuse or mislead.

Additional Resources
For deeper learning about data visualization in UX:

Stephen Few’s “Information Dashboard Design”
Edward Tufte’s “The Visual Display of Quantitative Information”
Nielsen Norman Group’s articles on UX metrics and visualization
Remember that your role as a UX researcher is to illuminate insights that drive better design decisions. The right visualization can make the difference between data that sits unused and insights that drive meaningful change.

projects/uxr-blog/blog-db/the-automation.title: The Automation Bias Audit: A Practitioner's Guide to Testing AI Overreliance
projects/uxr-blog/blog-db/the-automation.content:
Thesis
Automation bias is the most documented and least designed-against cognitive bias in AI products. Parasuraman & Riley (1997) showed that humans systematically over-rely on automated systems even when evidence of failure is visible. Here’s a practical audit framework any product team can deploy to test for — and design against — AI overreliance in their own products.
Why Only You
Decision Advisor framework + AI Measurement Library + the ability to translate Parasuraman’s complacency/bias taxonomy into a step-by-step audit. This is Open Expertise in action: a published, usable framework for ICs and small teams.
Enters Conversation

Agentic AI demanding guardrails but no practitioner-level overreliance testing exists
Forbes: Trust pivot from “can we use AI” to “can we trust it”
Greenbook: Human touch essential for AI quality — but how do you test for it?

Builds On
Human×AI Augmented Decision Making, AI Measurement Library, Decision Advisor
Suggested Depth
standard (strong open-framework candidate)

projects/uxr-blog/blog-db/the-cognitive-.title: The Cognitive Load of AI: Why More Features Means Worse Decisions
projects/uxr-blog/blog-db/the-cognitive-.content:
Thesis
AI feature proliferation isn’t just bad UX — it’s a cognitive science problem with precise, predictable mechanisms. Choice overload + satisficing behavior (Simon, 1956) + attention bottleneck theory means users systematically underuse the best AI features and overuse the worst. The solution isn’t better onboarding; it’s cognitive load architecture.
Why Only You
Cognitive psychology foundation lets you go beyond “too many features bad” to the actual mechanisms: Sweller’s cognitive load theory, Hick’s Law applied to AI feature discovery, and Miller’s chunking applied to AI capability sets.
Enters Conversation

Akraya: UX research 2026 trends noting AI tool overwhelm

projects/uxr-blog/blog-db/the-core-insig.title: The Most Accurate Mental Model of an LLM
projects/uxr-blog/blog-db/the-core-insig.content:
Think of an LLM as a brain without a body, consciousness, or goals. It has structures that look like cognition, but they work fundamentally differently. Understanding these differences unlocks better prompting and realistic expectations.
This mental model synthesizes foundational research on Transformers, attention mechanisms, chain-of-thought prompting, and retrieval-augmented generation into one brain-inspired framework.

The Core Insight
An LLM predicts the next word. That’s it.
To do this well, it needs to:

Understand what each word means
Remember what came before
Figure out which previous words matter most
Use patterns learned from reading billions of sentences
Every capability you’ve seen—writing code, analyzing data, creative writing—emerges from this single mechanism: sophisticated next-word prediction.




How It Actually Works (Technical, But Accessible)
Step 1: Tokenization
Text gets chopped into small pieces called “tokens.” Think Lego blocks—not individual letters or whole words, but common chunks:

“unhappiness” → [“un”, “happi”, “ness”]
“The cat sat” → [“The”, ” cat”, ” sat”]
A typical LLM knows about 50,000 different tokens.

Step 2: Embeddings
Each token becomes a list of numbers called a “vector”—a point in space with hundreds of dimensions. Similar words end up near each other. “King” and “queen” are close together. “King” and “pizza” are far apart.
Step 3: Attention
For each word, the model asks three questions:

Query: “What information do I need?”
Key: “What does each other word offer?”
Value: “What’s the actual content?”
It calculates scores showing how much each word should “attend to” each other word, then creates a new representation mixing the most relevant information together.

Step 4: Prediction
After many layers of attention and processing, the model outputs a probability for every possible next token:

“mat” → 35% likely
“floor” → 25% likely
“couch” → 15% likely
(and 49,997 other options with smaller percentages)
Then it samples from this distribution to pick the actual next word.

Step 5: Repeat
Add that word to the sequence, predict the next one. Keep going until you hit a stopping point.
What This Explains About LLM Behavior
Why Chain-of-Thought Prompting Works
Asking the model to “think step by step” forces it to use its context window more effectively, building up intermediate results.
Instead of:

Q: What is 15% of 80?
A: 12
You get:
Q: What is 15% of 80?
A: Let me work through this step-by-step:

Convert 15% to decimal: 0.15
Multiply: 0.15 × 80 = 12
Therefore, the answer is 12.
Showing reasoning steps improves accuracy on complex problems by 10-30%.


Why Hallucinations Happen
The model doesn’t “know” things—it predicts what words should come next based on patterns. If a plausible-sounding but false statement fits the pattern, it gets generated with confidence.
Why Temperature Matters
Low temperature (0.2): Nearly deterministic. “The capital of France is Paris” (99% confident). Best for factual tasks.
High temperature (1.5): Very random. “The capital of France is… Paris, Lyon, Marseille, or perhaps the Eiffel Tower’s shadow.” Best for creative writing.

Fundamental Strengths

Parallel processing: Processes entire sequences simultaneously via attention
Long-range dependencies: Can connect information 1000+ tokens apart
Transfer learning: Knowledge from general training helps specialized tasks
Flexibility: Same architecture works for text, code, images (with tokenization)
Contextual understanding: Captures nuanced semantic relationships


Fundamental Weaknesses

No true reasoning: Only pattern matching. Struggles with novel logical problems.
Hallucination: Confidently generates plausible but false information.
Fixed knowledge: Cannot learn from conversation. Each response is independent.
Context limits: Cannot process books or long documents in one pass.
Bias: Inherits biases from training data.
No world model: Doesn’t understand physics, causation, or object permanence.


The Mental Model Visualization
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│             USER (Executive Control)                │
│   • Sets goals via prompts                          │
│   • Chooses temperature (creativity dial)           │
│   • Provides context                                │
└─────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────┘
                      │
                      ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│         CONTEXT WINDOW (Working Memory)             │
│   • Limited capacity: ~4,000-128,000 tokens         │
│   • Holds recent conversation                       │
│   • Everything outside is forgotten                 │
└─────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────┘
                      │
                      ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│        ATTENTION MECHANISM (Selective Focus)        │
│   • Multi-head: 8-16 different focus patterns       │
│   • Parallel: Processes all positions at once       │
│   • Query-Key-Value: Matches what's needed          │
└─────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────┘
                      │
                      ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│          PARAMETERS (Long-term Memory)              │
│   • Billions of weights: 175B in GPT-3              │
│   • Stores statistical patterns                     │
│   • Fixed after training                            │
└─────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────┘
                      │
                      ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              OUTPUT (Prediction)                    │
│   • Probability distribution over vocabulary        │
│   • Temperature sampling for randomness             │
│   • Autoregressive: One token at a time             │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Key Takeaways

LLMs are pattern-matching engines, not thinking machines. They excel at statistical completion but lack genuine understanding.
You are the executive controller. You’re not conversing with an intelligent being—you’re programming a sophisticated autocomplete system through natural language.
Attention is the breakthrough. It lets models focus on relevant context dynamically.
Knowledge is frozen at training time. Stored in billions of weights, not in a searchable database.
Generation is probabilistic. Same input can give different outputs. Temperature controls randomness.
Limitations are fundamental. These aren’t bugs to be fixed but inherent to the architecture. No amount of scaling fixes lack of reasoning.


Best mental model: Think of it as an incredibly sophisticated “autocomplete” that learned patterns from reading the entire internet, with you as the programmer using English instead of code.
This explains both what LLMs can do amazingly well (pattern completion, style mimicry, contextual generation) and what they fundamentally cannot do (genuine reasoning, learning from experience, maintaining coherent beliefs across conversations).

projects/uxr-blog/blog-db/the-double-dia.filePath: Projects/uxr-blog/Blog DB/The Double Diamond is Dead. Long Live the Double Diamond (5a7180).md
projects/uxr-blog/blog-db/the-double-dia.title: The Double Diamond is Dead. Long Live the Double Diamond
projects/uxr-blog/blog-db/the-double-dia.content:
Everyone says the Double Diamond is dead. They’re half right.
The version that’s dead assumed human-speed discovery. “Discover” meant six weeks of desk research and stakeholder interviews before you had a real picture of the problem space. “Develop” meant a brainstorming session with the same five people who always lead with their confirmation bias. Every phase ran at the speed of one team’s pace reading shared updates, how busy their calendar is, and capacity to synthesize all of the data available to update their product strategy. That was a bandwidth constrain and AI removed those constraint. AI can even fake the “Discover” and “Define” phases reasonably well, which used to require some level of hands-on research.
The structure underneath it is a different matter. The four phases still hold: Discover, Define, Develop, Deliver. And what each phase protects against is still real. Commit to a problem before you’ve mapped the landscape and you’ll spend months solving the wrong one. Generate solutions before you’ve defined the problem and you’ll build something impressive that nobody needed. Ship without testing and you’ll find out what users actually wanted after you’ve already built the wrong version. The sequence is error-correction. Not ceremony.
Long live the Double Diamond.
AI didn’t kill the framework. It removed the bottleneck on both sides of it.
Expansion phases can now be dramatically wider. You can synthesize across dozens of sources in minutes, see a problem through five expert lenses simultaneously, and surface patterns that would take weeks to find manually. Compression phases can now be more evidence-based. You can rank assumptions, stress-test decisions, and strip solutions to their behavioral core before you commit.
The rhythm is the same. The engine behind it is completely different.
What follows is a framework for using that power deliberately. No technical background required. Just curiosity, a problem worth solving, and the AI tools most people already have on their phones and laptops.
Before we go further: more AI means more decisions. More decisions means more bets on your judgment, and more exposure to being wrong at speed. The only logical response to that is to think better, not just faster.

Faster ≠ Better
Speed without better judgment doesn’t reduce risk. It compounds it.
That’s the thing nobody says when they hand you an AI tool and tell you to move faster. More output per hour is real. But so is more exposure to being wrong. AI is about to automate the execution layer of most product roles: the tactical work of creating, writing, building, and validating that every role is built around. That’s the opportunity. Here’s the catch.
When AI removes friction from execution, you make more decisions per day. A lot more. And every decision is a bet on your judgment. More decisions means more bets. More bets means more exposure to getting it wrong at speed.
Here’s the evidence. Moore’s Law predicted that CPU capability would double every two years. It did. And yet, firms today require 18 times more researchers than they did in the 1970s to sustain the same rate of innovation. Company-level productivity still declines 7-10% annually for nearly 90% of firms. The same pattern shows up in agricultural yields, pharmaceutical development, and materials science.
More compute. More resources. Less output per unit of effort.
The problem was never speed. The problem is how we learn.
The Howard Hughes Medical Institute ran an experiment that proved it.

What Better Looks Like
In 2010, they shifted how they distributed research grants: instead of funding projects, they started funding people.
They extended time horizons. They explicitly tolerated early failures. They built in room for researchers to iterate, learn, and change direction. The bet was that if you gave smart people time and psychological safety, better science would follow.
It did. Publications rose 39%. Top citations rose 96%.
They didn’t move faster. They learned better. And learning better produced more innovation.
The lesson for product teams is uncomfortable but clear. Creating novel ideas that actually provide value is hard. It requires user empathy and shared expertise. It requires the willingness to be wrong early so you can be right when it matters. No amount of AI-accelerated execution changes that.
What AI does change is how you collaborate on the hard part.
Instead of one team synthesizing one problem space at human speed, you can now explore ten problem areas simultaneously. Instead of one brainstorm with the same five people, you can generate wildly different solutions from five distinct expert perspectives in minutes. Instead of weeks of desk research before you have a landscape, you can have a synthesis in an afternoon.
The rate of learning goes up. The quality of decisions goes up with it.
Your customers pay you because their problems are hard. That won’t change. What changes is how much cognitive firepower you bring to those hard problems.
The framework that follows isn’t more work. It’s an easier path to the work that actually matters: understanding what customers need and delivering it without guessing.

What Works (and What Doesn’t)
What Works
Four questions. In this order. Every time.

Discover: “What are all the problems facing the market and our users?”
Define: “Which of those problems has the most impact and is actually ours to solve?”
Develop: “Which solution would reach the most users or the largest market?”
Deliver: “How do we build that solution right now?”
This is the Double Diamond. Before you write it off as a 2005 relic, consider what it actually guarantees: you cannot commit to a solution before you’ve earned the right to. The human jobs at every phase (asking the right questions, extending empathy, generating options, making judgment calls) don’t disappear. AI makes each one possible at a scale that wasn’t available before.

What Doesn’t Work
Asking LLMs to be truly intelligent doesn’t work. Asking them to reason does.
The distinction matters. When you give an LLM an open-ended problem with no structure around how you want it to think, you tend to get one of four failure modes:

Irrelevant overload: more information than the team can use
Endless categorization: sophisticated taxonomies that produce no actionable solution
Complex solutions to fake problems: solutions that impress in a meeting but won’t earn a single dollar
Compounded bias: your assumptions, reflected back at you, louder
Without guardrails, AI doesn’t help you navigate the decision space. It amplifies chaos inside it.
The cognitive science behind why this happens is worth a full article on its own. The short version: LLMs are exceptional at recall and comprehension but fall apart at the higher-order thinking (analysis, evaluation, creation) that product decisions actually require. Without structure, they confidently generate the wrong answer. A deeper breakdown of where LLMs succeed and fail across Bloom’s Taxonomy is coming in a future piece.
The practical point for now: the tool is powerful. An undirected tool is just noise at scale. That structure is the Random Forest Double Diamond.


The Random Forest Double Diamond
Before AI, product development was sequential. You discovered the problem, decided on a solution, designed it, tested it, and shipped it. Each phase waited for the last one to finish. The whole process moved at the speed of one team’s bandwidth.
After AI, work becomes parallel.
Instead of exploring one problem area deeply, you explore ten simultaneously. Instead of generating one solution direction and iterating, you generate wildly different solutions and assess them against each other. Instead of one synthesis pass, you run multiple in minutes and compare the outputs.
Each “dot” in the diagram below represents a decision. Pre-AI, there are relatively few dots per phase. Post-AI, each phase branches into a forest of parallel paths, evaluated through synthesis-level reasoning, compressed back to a decision by the human in the loop.
This is the Random Forest Double Diamond. Same structure. Same rhythm. Completely different density of thinking at every phase.
Navigating it comes down to two questions, held in tension at every phase:

Horizontal axis: Why are we doing this phase? (the reasoning that keeps you honest)
Vertical axis: How can AI do this better? (the prompting that expands your reach)

Discover: Expand the Problem Space

Why is this problem worth solving for the business?
Why do users actually care about this problem?
Why do I care? (Honest answer. It shapes your framing.)
The “How can AI help” questions:

How much more information could I feed into this synthesis?
How “big” can I make this problem before I start losing signal?
The prompts at this phase should ask AI to enumerate, map, and synthesize broadly. You’re building a landscape, not a recommendation. The more divergent the inputs, the better the raw material for Define.
You now have a landscape. The natural temptation is to solve everything in it. The Define phase is about resisting that.

Define: Compress to What Matters
The job of the Define phase is to fight analysis paralysis. You have a wide landscape. Now you need to find the highest-leverage point inside it.
The “Why” questions:

Why is this problem (and not another) the right one to define?
Why do users care about it enough to change their behavior?
Why should the company prioritize it over competing opportunities?
The “How can AI help” questions:
How many distinct problems can I collapse into one root cause?
How simple can I make the problem statement without losing accuracy?
What’s the underlying assumption I’d need to invalidate to walk away from this?
At this phase, prompts should ask AI to rank, cluster, and surface root causes. You’re making a commitment here. AI builds the evidence base. You make the call.
You’ve committed to a problem. Now you need to find a solution worth building. Most teams stop too early with the first idea that sounds good. The Develop phase requires more.

The job of the Develop phase is to fight first-solution bias. Most teams converge on the first good idea. The Random Forest approach forces divergence before convergence.

What would a completely different AI role (engineer, ethnographer, economist) propose as a solution?
How many distinct solution directions could exist?
What does the craziest viable solution look like?

This is also where Sam the Strategizer earns its keep. Sam is a strategic design thinking AI built specifically to stop you from jumping to a solution before you’ve fully understood the problem. You describe the problem you’re trying to solve, and Sam pushes back: reframing your constraints, surfacing unstated assumptions, suggesting research approaches you hadn’t considered.

You now have options that are genuinely different from each other. The job shifts from generation to judgment.

Deliver: Compress to Action

How simple can we make the solution feel to the user?
How would a skeptical user evaluate this critically? What would they reject?
What’s the minimum viable version we could build and validate right now?

The framework works. But two things stop most teams from using it.


The Wrinkle
First: How do you know what “better” actually looks like inside your organization’s real constraints? Who decides? And how do you measure confidence in a decision when you’re making 100x more of them per day?
Second: How do non-technical team members own the process? When only engineers understand the techstack, every product decision queues up behind them. They become the bottleneck not because the work is technically complex, but because the knowledge is siloed.
Those two problems share the same root cause. The bottleneck was never technical complexity. It was always siloed knowledge.
The good news: the only bottleneck that matters to an LLM is your ability to articulate yourself. If you can describe a decision framework clearly, an LLM can apply it. If you can summarize what your system can and cannot do, a non-technical IC can use that summary to evaluate feasibility on their own.

The point for now is simpler: every knowledge bottleneck in your organization is a prompt engineering problem waiting to be solved.

🧰 Choosing Your AI Tools
The framework is tool-agnostic. AI products will launch, merge, and disappear. What stays constant is the type of cognitive work each phase requires. Match your tool to the job, not the brand.

Define needs structure. You want tools that organize and compress information. Any general-purpose LLM handles this well. The capability to look for is analytical reasoning and ranking.
Develop needs variety. You want tools that generate divergent options from different angles: role-prompted LLMs, rapid prototyping tools, code generators. The capability to look for is creative generation under constraints.
Deliver needs speed. You want tools that reduce the friction of shipping: code generators, automation builders, prototyping environments. The capability to look for is fast artifact creation.

You do not need a technical background to start. You need curiosity and a problem worth solving.
Your ability to articulate the way you solve problems is the only real bottleneck when learning to navigate the Random Forest. The tools will change. The prompts will evolve. But the underlying skill of clear, structured thinking compounds over time regardless of what ships next quarter.
Four rules that consistently help:

Wherever you sit in the product process, your job is still to understand problems clearly before committing to solutions, generate options worth choosing from, and make judgment calls that a model cannot make for you. Think like an agentic orchestrator.
That’s not just a mindset. It’s a practical filter. When you’re deciding whether a task belongs to you or to an AI tool, ask one question: is this a task for learning or for execution? If it requires judgment, empathy, context, or original framing, that’s yours. If it requires speed, synthesis, enumeration, or pattern-matching at scale, that’s the AI’s job. Humans learn. AI works.
The teams that win the next decade won’t be the ones with the most AI tools. They’ll be the ones who learned to think with them.
That’s a skill, not a subscription. It compounds. The practitioner who builds the habit of structured, AI-augmented reasoning today will be a different caliber of decision-maker in three years. Not because the tools got better, though they will. Because the thinking got better.
The Double Diamond didn’t become obsolete when AI arrived. It became the most important framework in your toolkit. The structure that protected you from building the wrong thing at human speed now protects you from building the wrong thing at AI speed, which is much faster and much more expensive to undo.
Your job is not to prompt better. Your job is to think better, and let the prompts carry the weight of execution.
The questions are the forcing function. The judgment is yours. That combination is the only durable competitive advantage left.

Long live the Double Diamond.
AI didn’t kill the framework. It removed the bottleneck on both sides of it.
Expansion phases can now be dramatically wider. More compute. More resources. Less output per unit of effort.
The problem was never speed. The problem is how we learn.
The Howard Hughes Medical Institute ran an experiment that proved it.

It did. Publications rose 39%. Top citations rose 96%.
They didn’t move faster. They learned better. And learning better produced more innovation.

The rate of learning goes up. The quality of decisions goes up with it.

projects/uxr-blog/blog-db/the-future-of-.title: The Future of Prompting Is Frameworks
projects/uxr-blog/blog-db/the-future-of-.content:
The conventional wisdom says prompt engineering is dying. That AI systems are getting smart enough to understand vague instructions, and the craft of writing good prompts will soon be irrelevant.
The conventional wisdom is wrong. Prompting isn’t dying. It’s growing up. And the practitioners who recognize what it’s becoming will have a significant edge over those still debating whether it matters.
Context Windows Are Smaller Than You Think
Every large language model operates within a context window: the total amount of information it can hold in working memory for any given interaction. Providers advertise massive numbers. The reality is more constrained.
Recent research on what scholars call the Maximum Effective Context Window (MECW) reveals a striking gap between advertised capacity and usable capacity [1]. The effective window, the point beyond which additional input stops helping and starts hurting, is drastically smaller than the technical maximum. More surprising: sheer input length alone degrades performance, even when every token is relevant and retrieval is perfect [2].
This matters because every token you send to an AI model is a resource allocation decision. Noise competes with signal. Redundancy crowds out reasoning space. The practitioners who learn to pack maximum meaning into minimum tokens will consistently outperform those who treat the context window as infinite.
Frameworks Are Compression Engines
This is where frameworks enter the picture.
A framework is a structured way to articulate domain knowledge so that it can be reliably consumed and executed. Think of it as a compression algorithm for expertise. Years of professional knowledge, distilled into a repeatable protocol that tells an AI exactly what to attend to, in what order, and with what constraints.
The academic literature supports this intuition. A comprehensive ACM Computing Surveys review catalogued the rapidly growing taxonomy of prompting frameworks, documenting how structured approaches consistently outperform unstructured ones [3]. Separately, researchers demonstrated that the Task-Method-Knowledge (TMK) framework, borrowed from cognitive and educational science, measurably improves LLM performance on planning tasks beyond what Chain-of-Thought prompting achieves alone [4]. The pattern is clear: when you give a model structured knowledge instead of raw instructions, it reasons better.
The Prompt Report, a systematic survey cataloguing 58 distinct prompting techniques across the field, reinforces the same conclusion from a different angle. The discipline has already moved well beyond “write a clear sentence” into structured, composable methodologies [5].
From Clever Phrasing to Knowledge Architecture
The shift happening right now is subtle but consequential. Prompting is moving from a communication skill to a design discipline.
The early era of prompt engineering was about finding the right words. Chain-of-thought. Few-shot examples. Role assignments. These techniques matter, but they operate at the surface level of interaction. The next era is about something deeper: designing structured knowledge artifacts that an AI can reliably interpret and execute.
This mirrors a pattern familiar to anyone in UX or information architecture. When a new medium emerges, the first instinct is to optimize the old workflow for the new tool. (Remember when websites were just digitized brochures?) The real transformation happens when practitioners start designing for the medium’s native strengths and constraints.
For AI, the native constraint is the context window. The native strength is pattern execution. Frameworks serve both.
I explored this idea from a different angle in Four Mental Models That Transform How You Use AI, where the core argument was that your mental model of how AI works determines how effectively you use it. Frameworks are the natural next step: once you understand how the system thinks, you can architect knowledge in the shape it thinks best.
What This Means for You
If you use AI tools regularly, here is the practical takeaway: start building frameworks for your most repeated tasks.
Not prompt templates. Not copy-paste snippets. Frameworks: structured protocols that encode your domain expertise, your quality criteria, and your decision logic into a format an AI can execute consistently.
The value of professional knowledge is shifting. Information that can be codified into structured frameworks becomes disproportionately powerful in an AI-augmented world. projects/uxr-blog/blog-db/the-future-of-.content:
The conventional wisdom says prompt engineering is dying. That AI systems are getting smart enough to understand vague instructions, and the craft of writing good prompts will soon be irrelevant.
The conventional wisdom is wrong. Prompting isn’t dying. It’s growing up. And the practitioners who recognize what it’s becoming will have a significant edge over those still debating whether it matters.
Context Windows Are Smaller Than You Think
Every large language model operates within a context window: the total amount of information it can hold in working memory for any given interaction. Providers advertise massive numbers. The reality is more constrained.
Recent research on what scholars call the Maximum Effective Context Window (MECW) reveals a striking gap between advertised capacity and usable capacity [1]. The effective window, the point beyond which additional input stops helping and starts hurting, is drastically smaller than the technical maximum. More surprising: sheer input length alone degrades performance, even when every token is relevant and retrieval is perfect [2].
This matters because every token you send to an AI model is a resource allocation decision. Noise competes with signal. Redundancy crowds out reasoning space. The practitioners who learn to pack maximum meaning into minimum tokens will consistently outperform those who treat the context window as infinite.
Frameworks Are Compression Engines
This is where frameworks enter the picture.
A framework is a structured way to articulate domain knowledge so that it can be reliably consumed and executed. Think of it as a compression algorithm for expertise. Years of professional knowledge, distilled into a repeatable protocol that tells an AI exactly what to attend to, in what order, and with what constraints.
The academic literature supports this intuition. A comprehensive ACM Computing Surveys review catalogued the rapidly growing taxonomy of prompting frameworks, documenting how structured approaches consistently outperform unstructured ones [3]. Separately, researchers demonstrated that the Task-Method-Knowledge (TMK) framework, borrowed from cognitive and educational science, measurably improves LLM performance on planning tasks beyond what Chain-of-Thought prompting achieves alone [4]. The pattern is clear: when you give a model structured knowledge instead of raw instructions, it reasons better.
The Prompt Report, a systematic survey cataloguing 58 distinct prompting techniques across the field, reinforces the same conclusion from a different angle. The discipline has already moved well beyond “write a clear sentence” into structured, composable methodologies [5].
From Clever Phrasing to Knowledge Architecture
The shift happening right now is subtle but consequential. Prompting is moving from a communication skill to a design discipline.
The early era of prompt engineering was about finding the right words. Chain-of-thought. Few-shot examples. Role assignments. These techniques matter, but they operate at the surface level of interaction. The next era is about something deeper: designing structured knowledge artifacts that an AI can reliably interpret and execute.
This mirrors a pattern familiar to anyone in UX or information architecture. When a new medium emerges, the first instinct is to optimize the old workflow for the new tool. (Remember when websites were just digitized brochures?) The real transformation happens when practitioners start designing for the medium’s native strengths and constraints.
For AI, the native constraint is the context window. The native strength is pattern execution. Frameworks serve both.
I explored this idea from a different angle in Four Mental Models That Transform How You Use AI, where the core argument was that your mental model of how AI works determines how effectively you use it. Frameworks are the natural next step: once you understand how the system thinks, you can architect knowledge in the shape it thinks best.

If you use AI tools regularly, here is the practical takeaway: start building frameworks for your most repeated tasks.
Not prompt templates. Not copy-paste snippets. Frameworks: structured protocols that encode your domain expertise, your quality criteria, and your decision logic into a format an AI can execute consistently.

Tacit expertise that resists structuring remains a uniquely human edge. projects/uxr-blog/blog-db/the-last-usabi.title: The Last Usability Benchmarking Template you’ll need
projects/uxr-blog/blog-db/the-last-usabi.content:
A useful Benchmarking Template
After five years of running UX research programs at tech startups, I’ve watched countless teams chase the wrong metrics, celebrate false victories, and spend too much time and energy only to miss critical insights hiding in plain sight. So, I took everything I liked and left our what I didn’t when making this Usability Benchmarking Template. It has automatic data analysis, includes standardized error tags and UX measurements, and can easily be customized and expanded, and it’s free.
Why you should use this template
After using various templates in the past, I believe this template is best to help you:

Save time: With previous templates, it took me between 4 and 8 hours per participant to collect, synthesize, and summarize data. With this template, the results are automatic, so a 1-hour session with each participant is all you need after you set it up.
Make moderating easy: This template is designed to help moderate a session while also collecting data, so you don’t need a note-taker. It also includes a practice sheet to ensure you’re comfortable with the material.
Improve internal consistency: If an entire team uses the same template and UX measurements, then it can become a standardized usability benchmarking system rather than a one-off test.
Make Results Accessible: An easy-to-read results tab and matching report template ensures researchers and stakeholders have the quantitative and qualitative information they need to evaluate the experience.
Customize: You can customize the moderation script, introduction questions (free-text), jobs you test, job scenarios, job steps, success criteria, error tags, post-job questions (5pt Agree Likert Scale), and exit questions (5pt Agree Likert Scale). (It’s currently set up for UMUX-like’s Usefulness and Ease of Use questions and grading scale, but you can change them or add more.)

Preparation
I use the JTBD Framework to help set up the benchmarking test. If you’re not familiar with the framework, I suggest this article for a 5 minute read or the first three chapters of Jim Kalbach’s JTBD Playbook for a deeper understanding. You don’t need to be an expert, but the gist of it is that you have a [Job Performer] who is in a specific [Circumstance], and they’re doing the [Job] that we’re going to evaluate.
Set it all up (30–60 min)
First, copy the template to your Google Drive and re-label it. It contains multiple interconnected sheets, so avoid deleting any tabs — even if they seem unnecessary at first. The template includes some scripts that will be flagged when copying, but don’t be intimated!
Then, go to the Setup tab and follow the steps under the “Directions” column. (Please read the directions!) I created an example benchmarking sheet for the content in this blog.
A screenshot of the usability benchmarking template showing the list of jobs, scenarios, and steps.

Steps 1–4: Product and Environment Info (5 min)
Steps 1–3 involve adding your product’s name, the test environment login information (or however else your participants will interact with your product, service, or prototype), and the introduction questions. The script is reusable so there shouldn’t be much to change besides the test environment or prototype information. I recommend using an environment as close to the real thing as possible to get accurate results.
Step 4 is the test scenario that covers all of the jobs you’ll be testing. This ‘big job statement’ should be at a higher level than the other tested jobs. For example, Maintain a code repository is a higher-level job compared to manage user access and controls.
Steps 5–8: Jobs, Job Scenarios, and Success Criteria (20–50 min)
I recommend doing the steps below while you have the test environment open so you can see what the real user experience looks like.
You can enter up to 10 jobs during Steps 5–8, though I strongly suggest limiting this to 7 for the sake of session length. Each job requires four components in the template:
Job statement (Step 5): The syntax should follow Verb + Object + Clarifier and describe what actions the participant will be doing, in the language they are used to.
Test Scenarios (Step 6): Write this carefully; it should provide ALL of the context a participant needs to complete their tasks.
Job Steps (Step 7): The template includes conditional formatting that allows up to 10 steps for each job. Enter steps sequentially, adding {Optional} when needed.
Success Criteria (Step 8): An ideal, objective, end-state in the product that is measurable and accomplishable based on the information in the Test Scenario. The participants’ ability to achieve all the success criteria will determine their completion status for each job, and therefore the overall usability grade for the test. Because of this, your success criteria should be supported by previous research.
For example; A completed intake form with name and zip code.
Review each step, but especially the test scenario (step 6) since you’ll be sharing that exact phrasing with the participant for each job. You may fine-tune the language during your practice sessions.
Step 9–11: Configuring Measurements (5 min)

A screenshot of the usability benchmarking template showing area to enter new error tags, post-job questions, and exit questions.
Add any additional Error Tags (Step 9) you may want to use. There are over a dozen tags already included, and the sheet has a custom script that adds additional error tags from the Setup tab to the Tags Master tab. You can also add tags in the middle of a session, so don’t worry too much about it now.
Post-Job and Exit Questions (Steps 10 & 11) are questions at the end of each job and the end of the overall test, respectively. The template currently uses:
A modified version of the UMUX-Lite, sometimes called the UX-Lite, which includes Usefulness and Ease of Use measures, both on a 5 point agree-disagree scale. This is asked after each job, and after the overall test.
I also like to add a reverse coded version of the CES and an extra trust measure at the end of the test, but feel free to remove or modify these.
The template enables you to add up to three post-job questions and up to five exit questions, although all questions must be on a 5pt Agree-Disagree scale (without significantly changing the sheet).
Lastly, if you want to make moderating sessions as easy as possible, I recommend you go into each Participant - ## and hide any of the rows where the job areas are not filled with content from the Setup tab. (This was the one bit of automation I couldn’t fit in)
Moderating Sessions
A screenshot of the usability benchmarking template showing the area to moderate a session, with the list of steps in the job, area for error tags and count, success status, workaround status, post-job questions, and observational notes.

There’s a Practice Session tab that mirros the Participant - ## tabs. I recommend conducting a practice session with a colleague who is less familiar with the product area, and then make any final adjustments to the language in the scenario or order of steps.
The script is everything in blue text
You say anything in blue outloud to the participant. You should also send the Job Scenarios to the participant over your video conference chat (e.g., Zoom chat) so they can read the scenarios at their own speed.
Collecting data
The sheet moves from left to right and top to bottom during moderation to help with data collection.
Step Completion. Use the checkbox under each step to mark whether the participant accomplished that step. Personally, I will allow the participant to ask a small question to clarify the goal and still ‘pass’ them, but anything more, and I fail them. If they do miss a step, I will tell the participant how to accomplish the task, leave that step unchecked, and continue to collect data on the rest of the experience.
Error Tags. If the participant deviates from the expected path, you can record their behavior using an error tag on the left side with the drop-down items. Most pre-loaded tags describe common UX problems and/or heuristics. You can type in a new tag and use it for future sessions if you’d like. Press the checkbox under the ‘Count + 1’ to add a count to each error tag. The list of tags is also on the far right of the first job test area so you can refresh your memory during moderation.
Job Completion Rate. Each job can end as either Pass, Recovery, or Fail. ‘Pass’ and ‘fail’ are self explanatory, and ‘recovery’ is when the moderator needs to provide a gentle prompt or the participant uses trial and error to complete the task successfully. You can change these definitions based on your organization’s preferred criteria though
Workaround. A workaround (True/False) is when the participant completes the job in an usual way. This data doesn’t go into the usability grade, but it can be helpful when painting the picture of what the user experienced.
Post-Job Questions. Currently set up for the two UMUX questions on a 5 point agreeability scale.
Observation Notes. A textbox for other notes on the participant’s experience.
Summarizing Data
A screenshot of the results, showing completion rate for each step of each job.

Thankfully, you don’t have to do anything to summarize the data. Just go to the Results tab to see the summarized data. There’s conditional formatting throughout the results tab to highlight anything under 75% with yellow text and anything under 60% with red text.
The bulk of the results tab will be the completion rate for each step of the jobs tested (see the image below).
Further to the right is the average error count per participant, overall job completion rate, UMUX score, and a numeric usability grade. You can see the Ease of Use and Usefulness question (and any other post-job question you added) in the hidden column next to the UMUX score. The numeric usability grade uses almost all of the data you previously collected in the following way;

Usability Grade = Average of (Completion Rate for Steps #1–10 + Overall Completion Rate + UMUX-Score ) — Average Error Count*1.25

A screenshot of the results, showing average error count, completion rate, UMUX, and usability grade for each job.
Below the results for each step are the results from the post-test questions you asked the participant. If you add or edit any of the question in the setup tab, those changes will be reflected here.

A screenshot of the results, showing the overall UMUX question results.
Finally, the last data presented is the error tag breakdown across each job. This will help paint the story of the participants’ struggles during the test. You can also use this information to guide you in what types of quotes you may want to highlight in reporting, so stakeholders have both quantitative and qualitative information about the experience.

A screenshot of the results, showing the overall error tags across each job.

Sharing the data to stakeholders
The easiest way to explain the data is by following the users’ experience for each job you tested. I like to have the test environment open so I can go through the steps in each job and show what the most common types of errors participants had, what the completion rate for each step and the overall job was, and what the UMUX scores were. If the UMUX was low, then I will report if either the Ease of Use or Usefulness question was the primary cause.
You can use this report template that aligns with the template and includes some helpful color coding.

Thankfully, you don’t have to do anything to summarize the data. Just go to the Results tab to see the summarized data. There’s conditional formatting throughout the results tab to highlight anything under 75% with yellow text and anything under 60% with red text.
The bulk of the results tab will be the completion rate for each step of the jobs tested (see the image below).
Further to the right is the average error count per participant, overall job completion rate, UMUX score, and a numeric usability grade. You can see the Ease of Use and Usefulness question (and any other post-job question you added) in the hidden column next to the UMUX score. The numeric usability grade uses almost all of the data you previously collected in the following way;

Usability Grade = Average of (Completion Rate for Steps #1–10 + Overall Completion Rate + UMUX-Score ) — Average Error Count*1.25

A screenshot of the results, showing average error count, completion rate, UMUX, and usability grade for each job.
Below the results for each step are the results from the post-test questions you asked the participant. If you add or edit any of the question in the setup tab, those changes will be reflected here.

A screenshot of the results, showing the overall UMUX question results.
Finally, the last data presented is the error tag breakdown across each job. This will help paint the story of the participants’ struggles during the test. You can also use this information to guide you in what types of quotes you may want to highlight in reporting, so stakeholders have both quantitative and qualitative information about the experience.

A screenshot of the results, showing the overall error tags across each job.

Sharing the data to stakeholders
The easiest way to explain the data is by following the users’ experience for each job you tested. I like to have the test environment open so I can go through the steps in each job and show what the most common types of errors participants had, what the completion rate for each step and the overall job was, and what the UMUX scores were. If the UMUX was low, then I will report if either the Ease of Use or Usefulness question was the primary cause.
You can use this report template that aligns with the template and includes some helpful color coding.

projects/uxr-blog/blog-db/the-measuremen.title: The Measurement Crisis: Why Your UX Metrics Don't Work for AI Products
projects/uxr-blog/blog-db/the-measuremen.content:
Thesis
Standard UX metrics (SUS, task success rate, time-on-task) assume deterministic interfaces with predictable outputs. AI products are probabilistic — the same input yields different outputs. We need a new measurement ontology grounded in signal detection theory: hits, misses, false alarms, and correct rejections.
Why Only You
AI Measurement Library + psychometric grounding + SLR capability. You can show practitioners exactly where standard metrics break and what to replace them with, backed by signal detection theory that’s in every Human Factors textbook but absent from UX practice.
Enters Conversation

Dynamic/Generative UI breaking traditional measurement (Forbes, Nielsen)
Maze: 42% of research teams struggle to connect research to business outcomes
Lyssna: AI-assisted synthesis adopted by 88% but judgment operationalization missing

Builds On
