projects/uxr-blog/blog-db/the-most-accur.title: The Most Accurate Mental Model of an LLM
projects/uxr-blog/blog-db/the-most-accur.content:
Think of an LLM as a brain without a body, consciousness, or goals. It has structures that look like cognition, but they work fundamentally differently. Understanding these differences unlocks better prompting and realistic expectations.
This mental model synthesizes foundational research on Transformers, attention mechanisms, chain-of-thought prompting, and retrieval-augmented generation into one brain-inspired framework.

The Core Insight
An LLM predicts the next word. That’s it.
To do this well, it needs to:

Understand what each word means
Remember what came before
Figure out which previous words matter most
Use patterns learned from reading billions of sentences
Every capability you’ve seen—writing code, analyzing data, creative writing—emerges from this single mechanism: sophisticated next-word prediction.




How It Actually Works (Technical, But Accessible)
Step 1: Tokenization
Text gets chopped into small pieces called “tokens.” Think Lego blocks—not individual letters or whole words, but common chunks:

“unhappiness” → [“un”, “happi”, “ness”]
“The cat sat” → [“The”, ” cat”, ” sat”]
A typical LLM knows about 50,000 different tokens.

Step 2: Embeddings
Each token becomes a list of numbers called a “vector”—a point in space with hundreds of dimensions. Similar words end up near each other. “King” and “queen” are close together. “King” and “pizza” are far apart.
Step 3: Attention
For each word, the model asks three questions:

Query: “What information do I need?”
Key: “What does each other word offer?”
Value: “What’s the actual content?”
It calculates scores showing how much each word should “attend to” each other word, then creates a new representation mixing the most relevant information together.

Step 4: Prediction
After many layers of attention and processing, the model outputs a probability for every possible next token:

“mat” → 35% likely
“floor” → 25% likely
“couch” → 15% likely
(and 49,997 other options with smaller percentages)
Then it samples from this distribution to pick the actual next word.

Step 5: Repeat
Add that word to the sequence, predict the next one. Keep going until you hit a stopping point.
What This Explains About LLM Behavior
Why Chain-of-Thought Prompting Works
Asking the model to “think step by step” forces it to use its context window more effectively, building up intermediate results.
Instead of:

Q: What is 15% of 80?
A: 12
You get:
Q: What is 15% of 80?
A: Let me work through this step-by-step:

Convert 15% to decimal: 0.15
Multiply: 0.15 × 80 = 12
Therefore, the answer is 12.
Showing reasoning steps improves accuracy on complex problems by 10-30%.


Why Hallucinations Happen
The model doesn’t “know” things—it predicts what words should come next based on patterns. If a plausible-sounding but false statement fits the pattern, it gets generated with confidence.
Why Temperature Matters
Low temperature (0.2): Nearly deterministic. “The capital of France is Paris” (99% confident). Best for factual tasks.
High temperature (1.5): Very random. “The capital of France is… Paris, Lyon, Marseille, or perhaps the Eiffel Tower’s shadow.” Best for creative writing.

Fundamental Strengths

Parallel processing: Processes entire sequences simultaneously via attention
Long-range dependencies: Can connect information 1000+ tokens apart
Transfer learning: Knowledge from general training helps specialized tasks
Flexibility: Same architecture works for text, code, images (with tokenization)
Contextual understanding: Captures nuanced semantic relationships


Fundamental Weaknesses

No true reasoning: Only pattern matching. Struggles with novel logical problems.
Hallucination: Confidently generates plausible but false information.
Fixed knowledge: Cannot learn from conversation. Each response is independent.
Context limits: Cannot process books or long documents in one pass.
Bias: Inherits biases from training data.
No world model: Doesn’t understand physics, causation, or object permanence.


The Mental Model Visualization
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│             USER (Executive Control)                │
│   • Sets goals via prompts                          │
│   • Chooses temperature (creativity dial)           │
│   • Provides context                                │
└─────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────┘
                      │
                      ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│         CONTEXT WINDOW (Working Memory)             │
│   • Limited capacity: ~4,000-128,000 tokens         │
│   • Holds recent conversation                       │
│   • Everything outside is forgotten                 │
└─────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────┘
                      │
                      ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│        ATTENTION MECHANISM (Selective Focus)        │
│   • Multi-head: 8-16 different focus patterns       │
│   • Parallel: Processes all positions at once       │
│   • Query-Key-Value: Matches what's needed          │
└─────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────┘
                      │
                      ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│          PARAMETERS (Long-term Memory)              │
│   • Billions of weights: 175B in GPT-3              │
│   • Stores statistical patterns                     │
│   • Fixed after training                            │
└─────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────┘
                      │
                      ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              OUTPUT (Prediction)                    │
│   • Probability distribution over vocabulary        │
│   • Temperature sampling for randomness             │
│   • Autoregressive: One token at a time             │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Key Takeaways

LLMs are pattern-matching engines, not thinking machines. They excel at statistical completion but lack genuine understanding.
You are the executive controller. You’re not conversing with an intelligent being—you’re programming a sophisticated autocomplete system through natural language.
Attention is the breakthrough. It lets models focus on relevant context dynamically.
Knowledge is frozen at training time. Stored in billions of weights, not in a searchable database.
Generation is probabilistic. Same input can give different outputs. Temperature controls randomness.
Limitations are fundamental. These aren’t bugs to be fixed but inherent to the architecture. No amount of scaling fixes lack of reasoning.


Best mental model: Think of it as an incredibly sophisticated “autocomplete” that learned patterns from reading the entire internet, with you as the programmer using English instead of code.
This explains both what LLMs can do amazingly well (pattern completion, style mimicry, contextual generation) and what they fundamentally cannot do (genuine reasoning, learning from experience, maintaining coherent beliefs across conversations).

projects/uxr-blog/blog-db/the-problem--u.title: How to Automate UX Heuristic Evaluations with LLM Prompts in Your DevOps Pipeline
projects/uxr-blog/blog-db/the-problem--u.content:
You can test a codebase for bugs in milliseconds. You can lint for accessibility violations before a pull request merges. But what about usability? What about the question every UX researcher actually cares about: will this interface make sense to a human being?
For decades, that question required scheduling time with experts, recruiting participants, and waiting days (or weeks) for results. Meanwhile, the code shipped anyway.
That gap is closing. Recent research shows that large language models can perform structured heuristic evaluations on source code and UI screenshots with moderate-to-substantial reliability. Not as replacements for human researchers. As automated quality gates embedded directly in your DevOps pipeline, triggered on command, owned by your team.
This is not about devaluing UX research. It is about amplifying it. When companies can research, publish, iterate, and own their design evaluations inside the same CI/CD workflows they already trust, UX stops being a bottleneck and starts being a competitive advantage.
Here is how to make that real.
The Problem: UX Research Cannot Keep Pace with DevOps
Modern development teams ship fast. Continuous integration, continuous deployment, automated test suites, canary releases. The engineering side of quality assurance has never been more sophisticated.
But the design side? Still largely manual.
Traditional heuristic evaluation, the method Jakob Nielsen and Rolf Molich introduced in 1990, requires trained evaluators to inspect an interface against a set of usability principles. It is effective. It is also resource-intensive and difficult to scale (Nielsen & Molich, 1990). Small teams rarely have access to dedicated UX evaluators. Even large organizations struggle to run evaluations at the speed their release cycles demand.
The result: visual and interaction quality becomes the one dimension of software that doesn’t get tested in the pipeline. Design decisions ship without structured review. Small usability regressions accumulate. And the teams that care most about quality are stuck playing catch-up.
The ISO 25010:2023 standard recognizes usability as one of nine key software product quality characteristics alongside reliability, security, and maintainability. DevOps practices have matured automated testing for most of these. Usability remains the exception.
The Breakthrough: LLMs Can Perform Heuristic Evaluations
In late 2025, researchers at Virginia Tech published one of the first rigorous studies on using GPT-4o to perform automated heuristic evaluations on website source code (Platt, Luchs, & Nizamani, 2025). Their approach was elegantly simple:

Translate each of Nielsen’s 10 usability heuristics into a structured prompt
Feed the website’s source code (HTML, CSS, JavaScript) to the model
Collect evaluations in a standardized JSON format with severity ratings, issue descriptions, code references, and recommendations
They tested this across 30 open-source websites, running three independent evaluations per site (over 850 total evaluations). The results:


82-85% agreement on whether a usability issue existed (Cohen’s Kappa ≈ 0.50)
Weighted Kappa of ~0.63 for severity ratings, indicating moderate-to-substantial consistency
The model excelled at detecting issues related to error prevention and match between system and real world
To put that in context: human expert evaluators also show significant variability in heuristic evaluation. Different experts routinely identify different issues and disagree on severity (Rubin & Chisnell, 2008). An LLM achieving 82-85% self-consistency is not perfect, but it is useful, particularly as a first-pass screen.
A parallel study from Graz University of Technology (Lubos et al., 2025) took a multimodal approach, feeding screenshots and persona descriptions to LLMs and framing usability evaluation as a recommendation task where issues are ranked by severity. Their finding: LLMs aligned best with expert assessments when using structured evaluation criteria with explicit pass/fail ratings, exactly the kind of evaluation you can encode in a prompt.
At CHI 2025, the UXAgent framework demonstrated that LLM agents can simulate thousands of users interacting with a live website, generating both qualitative interview data and quantitative behavioral logs for UX researchers to analyze (UXAgent, 2025). The researchers were not trying to eliminate human evaluation. They were trying to help UX teams pre-test and iterate their study designs before running expensive human studies.
The convergence is clear: LLMs are becoming reliable enough to serve as preliminary usability evaluators, especially when guided by well-structured heuristic prompts.

Why This Amplifies UX Research (Instead of Replacing It)
Let’s address the elephant in the room. If a machine can run a heuristic evaluation, why hire a UX researcher?
Because the machine cannot do what matters most.
LLM-based heuristic evaluation handles the structured, repeatable, criterion-referenced portion of usability assessment. It answers: “Does this interface violate known usability principles?” That is valuable. It is also the floor, not the ceiling.
What LLMs cannot do:

Discover unmet user needs through contextual inquiry or diary studies
Interpret emotional and social dynamics in user behavior
Generate novel design directions from ambiguous research signals
Navigate organizational politics to get research acted upon
Validate with real users in real contexts with real stakes
What automated heuristic evaluation actually does for UX researchers is remove the low-value, repetitive screening work so they can focus on the high-value, irreplaceable work. Your researchers stop spending time catching “missing error messages” and “inconsistent button labels” and start spending time on the strategic questions that move products forward.
Think of it like automated accessibility testing. Tools like axe-core and Lighthouse did not make accessibility experts obsolete. They made accessibility more pervasive by catching the obvious violations automatically, freeing experts to focus on the nuanced, context-dependent judgments that require human understanding.
The same pattern applies here. Automate the heuristic floor. Elevate the human ceiling.

Writing Your First Heuristic Evaluation Prompt
The key insight from the Virginia Tech study: prompt design matters enormously. Their initial attempts with generic prompts produced “flawed and, in some cases, completely inaccurate results.” Structured, specific prompts with clear output formats transformed the quality.
Here is a practical template you can adapt. This prompt evaluates a single heuristic against a provided codebase or screenshot:
You are a usability evaluation expert. Evaluate the provided [source code / screenshot] against the following Nielsen usability heuristic:
 
**Heuristic: [Heuristic Name]**
**Definition:** [One-sentence definition of the heuristic]
**Evaluation Questions:**
1. [Specific question about how this heuristic applies]
2. [Specific question about how this heuristic applies]
3. [Specific question about how this heuristic applies]
 
For your evaluation, provide:
- IssueFound: true/false
- SeverityRating: 0 (no issue) to 4 (usability catastrophe)
- IssueDescription: What specific problem exists
- Location: Where in the code/interface the issue occurs
- Recommendation: A clear, actionable fix
 
Output your evaluation as valid JSON.
Here is a concrete example for the “Error Prevention” heuristic (which showed the highest agreement rates in the Virginia Tech study):
You are a usability evaluation expert. Evaluate the provided source code against the following Nielsen usability heuristic:
 
**Heuristic: Error Prevention**
**Definition:** The design should prevent problems from occurring in the first place by eliminating error-prone conditions or presenting users with a confirmation option before they commit to an action.
 
**Evaluation Questions:**
1. Are there form inputs without validation that could accept incorrect data?
2. Are there destructive actions (delete, submit, purchase) without confirmation dialogs?
3. Are there input fields missing constraints, placeholder text, or format hints that would prevent user errors?
 
For your evaluation, provide:
- IssueFound: true/false
- SeverityRating: 0 (no issue) to 4 (usability catastrophe)
- IssueDescription: What specific problem exists
- Location: File name and relevant code section
- Recommendation: A clear, actionable fix
 
Output as valid JSON only. No commentary outside the JSON.

	**Pro Tip:** Write one prompt per heuristic. The Graz University study found that LLMs produce more precise assessments when evaluating a single criterion per prompt rather than bundling multiple heuristics together (Lubos et al., 2025). Yes, it means 10 prompts for a full Nielsen evaluation. The tradeoff in accuracy is worth it.

### The 10 Prompts You Need
For a complete automated heuristic evaluation, write one prompt for each of Nielsen's 10 heuristics:
1. **Visibility of System Status** (Does the interface keep users informed?)
2. **Match Between System and Real World** (Does it speak the user's language?)
3. **User Control and Freedom** (Can users undo and escape?)
4. **Consistency and Standards** (Does it follow conventions?)
5. **Error Prevention** (Does the design prevent mistakes?)
6. **Recognition Rather Than Recall** (Is information visible, not memorized?)
7. **Flexibility and Efficiency of Use** (Are there shortcuts for experts?)
8. **Aesthetic and Minimalist Design** (Is every element earning its place?)
9. **Help Users Recognize, Diagnose, and Recover from Errors** (Are error messages helpful?)
10. **Help and Documentation** (Is guidance available when needed?)
Each prompt follows the same structure: heuristic name, definition, 2-3 specific evaluation questions, and a standardized JSON output format. Consistency in your output format is what makes these results *parseable by your pipeline*.
## Integrating Into Your DevOps Pipeline
Once you have your 10 heuristic prompts tested and tuned, integration into a CI/CD pipeline follows a pattern any DevOps engineer will recognize. Here is a simplified architecture:
### Pipeline Stage: UX Heuristic Gate
```javascript
trigger: on pull request (or on-demand)
steps:
  1. Extract UI-relevant files (HTML, CSS, JS, screenshots)
  2. For each of 10 heuristic prompts:
     - Send code/screenshots + prompt to LLM API
     - Parse JSON response
     - Log results to evaluation database
  3. Aggregate severity scores
  4. Gate logic:
     - Severity 4 (catastrophe): Block merge, notify team
     - Severity 3 (major): Flag for UX review before merge
     - Severity 1-2 (minor/cosmetic): Log, continue
     - Severity 0: Pass
  5. Generate evaluation report (diff against previous run)
```
### What This Looks Like in Practice
**Scenario:** A developer submits a pull request that changes the checkout flow. The pipeline runs the 10 heuristic evaluation prompts against the modified code.
The "Error Prevention" prompt flags a severity 3 issue: the new payment form accepts submission without validating the credit card number format. The "Visibility of System Status" prompt flags a severity 2 issue: no loading indicator appears after the user clicks "Pay Now."
The pipeline blocks the merge on the severity 3 finding and posts both findings as comments on the pull request with specific code references and recommendations. The developer fixes the validation issue, the UX lead reviews the loading indicator finding, and the PR merges 45 minutes later.
No meeting was scheduled. No evaluator was recruited. No sprint was delayed. The usability check happened at the same speed as the linting check.

	**Important caveat:** LLM evaluations show moderate reliability, not perfect reliability. The Virginia Tech study found exact severity agreement at only 56%. **Never use automated heuristic evaluation as your sole quality gate for critical user-facing changes.** Use it as a first-pass screen that escalates to human review when severity thresholds are crossed. The goal is triage, not replacement.

## The Business Case for Small Organizations
This approach hits hardest for organizations that need quality but cannot afford a full-time UX team. Consider the math:
- **Traditional heuristic evaluation:** 3-5 expert evaluators × 2-4 hours each × \$100-200/hr = **\$600-4,000 per evaluation cycle**
- **LLM-based automated evaluation:** API calls for 10 prompts × pennies per call = **under \$1 per evaluation cycle**
The cost difference is not 10x. It is **1,000x or more.** And automated evaluations can run on every pull request, not once per quarter.
For a 10-person startup shipping weekly, this means:
- **De-risking important changes** by catching usability regressions before users see them
- **Faster development** because the feedback loop shrinks from days to minutes
- **Reduced overhead** because you do not need to pause development for evaluation cycles
- **Owned evaluations** because your heuristic prompts become a codified, version-controlled expression of your team's design standards
That last point deserves emphasis. When you write heuristic evaluation prompts, you are not just creating a testing tool. You are **documenting your organization's usability standards in executable form**. Those prompts become institutional knowledge. They can be reviewed, debated, improved, and versioned just like any other code artifact.
## Getting Started: A Practical Checklist
Ready to build your first automated heuristic evaluation pipeline? Here is the sequence:
- [ ] **Select your heuristic framework.** Nielsen's 10 heuristics are the standard starting point. You can extend or customize for your domain (e.g., adding mobile-specific or accessibility-specific heuristics).
- [ ] **Write and test your 10 prompts.** Use the template above. Test each prompt against 3-5 representative pages from your product. Compare the LLM output against your own expert judgment. Tune the evaluation questions until the output is useful.
- [ ] **Standardize your JSON output format.** Every prompt should produce identically structured output. This is what makes parsing and aggregation possible.
- [ ] **Set severity thresholds.** Decide what severity levels block a merge, require review, or simply log. Start conservative (block on severity 3+) and adjust based on signal quality.
- [ ] **Integrate with your CI/CD tool.** GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Jenkins, whatever you use. The integration is an API call wrapped in a script.
- [ ] **Build your evaluation dashboard.** Track findings over time. Look for patterns. Which heuristics flag most often? Which components generate the most issues? This is the data your UX researcher (or your future UX researcher) will use to prioritize strategic work.
- [ ] **Iterate on your prompts quarterly.** As your product evolves and your understanding deepens, refine the evaluation questions. Treat prompts like living documentation.
## The Bigger Picture
We are in the early days of a shift that will reshape how organizations think about design quality. The same pattern played out with automated testing for code correctness, then for security, then for accessibility. Each time, the fear was that automation would eliminate the human role. Each time, the opposite happened: automation raised the floor, expanded coverage, and freed experts to work on harder problems.
Usability evaluation is next.
The research is clear that LLMs are not yet expert-level evaluators. Severity judgments vary. Some heuristics (like "Help and Documentation") show low inter-rater reliability. Dynamic interaction issues that require clicking through a live interface remain difficult to assess from static code or screenshots alone.
But the research is equally clear that these tools are *useful right now*, especially for teams that currently have **zero automated usability evaluation**. Going from nothing to an 82% consistent first-pass screen is a massive quality improvement.
The organizations that move first will build institutional muscle in prompt engineering for design quality. They will accumulate evaluation data that informs strategic UX decisions. They will ship faster and with more confidence. And their UX researchers, freed from the mechanical work of catching obvious violations, will do the creative, strategic, deeply human work that actually differentiates products.
Start with one heuristic. Test it on one component. See what comes back.
Then automate it.
---

- Platt, N., Luchs, E., & Nizamani, S. (2025). Catching UX Flaws in Code: Leveraging LLMs to Identify Usability Flaws at the Development Stage. *arXiv:2512.04262*.
- Lubos, S., Felfernig, A., Leitner, G., & Schwazer, J. (2025). Towards Recommending Usability Improvements with Multimodal Large Language Models. *arXiv:2508.16165*.
- UXAgent (2025). UXAgent: An LLM Agent-Based Usability Testing Framework for Web Design. *CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems*.
- Rubin, J. & Chisnell, D. (2008). *Handbook of Usability Testing: How to Plan, Design, and Conduct Effective Tests*, 2nd ed. Wiley.

projects/uxr-blog/blog-db/the-science-of.title: Research in the Age of AI: Using Decision Science to Build LLM Personas That Actually Think
projects/uxr-blog/blog-db/the-science-of.content:
Most conversations about AI and decision-making start in the wrong place. They start with the technology: what can LLMs do, how many parameters, which benchmarks. But decisions are fundamentally human. They’re shaped by experience, context, cognitive limits, and the messy reality of working with other people. The interesting question isn’t whether AI can make decisions for us. It’s whether we can design AI that helps people make better decisions themselves.
That distinction matters more than it sounds. The difference between AI that automates human judgment and AI that supports it is the difference between a tool that replaces your thinking and one that sharpens it. One makes you dependent. The other makes you more capable over time.
I’ve spent the last several months pulling apart the academic literature on human decision-making, cognitive offloading, and AI-assisted reasoning. What I found reframed how I think about building AI tools. Not because the research shows LLMs can be made “smart” in some philosophical sense, but because it reveals something more practical: decades of cognitive psychology research already tell us how people actually think under pressure, and that science translates directly into better AI design.
The frameworks exist. The evidence is there. The gap is that most AI development ignores it.
This post is about closing that gap. Here’s what the science says, and what it looks like when you apply it.
The Science of How We Actually Decide (and Why LLMs Should Care)
Before we can build AI that supports decisions, we need to understand a counterintuitive truth about human expertise. The best decision-makers in the world don’t reason the way you’d expect.
Dual Process Theory: Two Systems, One Decision
You’re a product leader. It’s Wednesday morning. You open Slack to 47 unread messages, a Jira board full of overdue tickets, and a stakeholder asking whether you should delay a launch.
Your brain doesn’t pull up a spreadsheet. It reacts. You feel a flash of recognition (“this is like the Q3 situation”), a tightening in your gut (“we’re not ready”), and a quick mental simulation (“if we push two weeks, we clear the blockers”). In about three seconds, you’ve made a preliminary decision. Only then, maybe, do you slow down and pressure-test it with data.
That’s dual process theory in action. Daniel Kahneman’s framework partitions cognition into Type 1 (fast, automatic, intuitive) and Type 2 (slow, deliberate, analytical). Most decisions, even important ones, start in System 1. System 2 is the auditor, not the driver (Kahneman, 2011).
Now here’s what makes this directly relevant for AI design. De Neys (2024) proposed that dual-process theory can serve as a literal architectural blueprint for AI systems: one subsystem for statistical pattern matching (what LLMs already do), another for structured symbolic reasoning.[1]
What this looks like in practice: Imagine you ask an LLM to help you decide whether to delay that launch. A vanilla LLM gives you a 500-word pro/con list. A dual-process LLM first pattern-matches against similar past launches in your company’s data (System 1), then flags the two assumptions most likely to be wrong and walks you through stress-testing them (System 2). Same question. Completely different cognitive experience.
Naturalistic Decision Making: Experts Are Pattern Matchers (Just Like LLMs)
Here’s the uncomfortable truth that should make every AI skeptic pause.
Gary Klein spent decades studying how firefighters, military commanders, and ER nurses make life-or-death decisions. His Recognition-Primed Decision (RPD) model found that these experts don’t weigh all the options. They recognize patterns from prior experience, mentally simulate a single course of action, and act. No comparison shopping. No decision matrix (Klein, 1993).[2]
Sound familiar? That’s essentially what an LLM does: pattern completion shaped by prior exposure. The difference isn’t mechanism. It’s structure. Human experts have organized their patterns around validated frameworks, contextual cues, and hard-won failure modes. LLMs have organized theirs around… whatever was on the internet.
Klein’s work also highlights that real-world decisions happen under time pressure, ambiguous information, ill-defined goals, and changing conditions.[3] If your AI decision tool only works when the problem is clean and well-structured, you’ve solved the easy version and shipped it as the solution.
What this looks like in practice: A senior UX researcher doesn’t need to see every data point to know a design is going to fail in usability testing. They’ve seen that pattern before. An LLM persona built on RPD principles wouldn’t give you “here are 10 things to consider.” It would say: “This looks like [recognized pattern]. Here’s the one thing most likely to go wrong based on similar situations. Want to simulate what happens if that risk materializes?”
Fast-and-Frugal Heuristics: When Less Information Beats More
Gerd Gigerenzer’s adaptive toolbox framework makes a claim that sounds heretical in the age of big data: simple heuristics that deliberately ignore available information can outperform complex models in uncertain environments (Gigerenzer & Todd, 1999). “By exploiting features of the environment and capabilities of the decision makers, heuristics can be simple without trading off accuracy.”[4]
This directly challenges the prevailing assumption in AI: that more data, more parameters, and more computation always produce better outputs.
What this looks like in practice: You’re hiring for a UX research role. A “comprehensive” AI tool scores 47 candidate attributes against weighted criteria and produces a ranked list. A fast-and-frugal AI asks three questions in sequence: (1) Do they have direct experience with the method your team needs most? If no, stop. (2) Can they articulate a research finding that changed a product decision? If no, stop. (3) Does the team want to work with them?
Three cues. No weighting. And if Gigerenzer’s research holds, it probably outperforms the 47-attribute model in real hiring conditions, because the environment is too uncertain for complex models to add value.
Cognitive Offloading: Two Versions of the Same Conversation
Cognitive offloading is using external tools to reduce mental effort (Risko & Gilbert, 2016). Your calendar, your to-do list, your calculator. LLMs are the newest and most powerful addition to this toolkit.
But there’s a critical design choice hiding inside every AI interaction. Let me show you.
Version A: Naive Offloading

You: Should we build Feature X or Feature Y first?
AI: Based on market analysis, Feature X has higher potential ROI due to competitive positioning, while Feature Y addresses a critical usability gap. I recommend Feature X with a 65% confidence score.
You: Okay, Feature X it is.
What just happened? You offloaded the decision entirely. You didn’t engage with the trade-offs. You didn’t surface your own assumptions. You didn’t learn anything you could apply next time. A 2025 arXiv paper calls this belief offloading: people don’t just offload tasks to AI, they begin offloading the very process of forming and upholding beliefs. The downstream consequences include changes in behavior and the structure of entire belief systems.[6]

Version B: Scaffolded Offloading

You: Should we build Feature X or Feature Y first?
AI: Before I weigh in, let me surface the decision. You’re prioritizing between competitive positioning (Feature X) and usability debt (Feature Y). Two questions first: Which of these carries more risk if you get it wrong? And what would need to be true for the less obvious choice to be the right one?
You: Hmm. If we ship Feature X with the current usability issues, adoption might tank anyway…
AI: That’s a dependency worth testing. Here’s a quick way to validate that assumption before committing.
Same question. Completely different cognitive outcome. In Version B, the AI used a framework (pre-mortem + assumption testing) to scaffold your reasoning instead of replacing it. You still own the decision. You just got help thinking it through.
A 2025 paper in Frontiers in Psychology captures this tension precisely: AI can enable cognitive offloading that supports adaptive coping, or it can create cognitive overload through “erosion of introspection, over-reliance on algorithmic feedback, and anxiety induced by hyper-monitoring.”[5] The difference between these outcomes is design, not technology.

LLMs Have Cognitive Biases (and That’s Actually the Unlock)
Here’s something that should reframe the whole conversation: LLMs exhibit decision heuristics that mirror human cognitive biases. Hagendorff et al. (2023) tested GPT-3.5 against the same bias prompts used in human psychology studies. The result? LLMs show anchoring effects, framing effects, and other context-sensitive decision patterns, just like humans.[7]
The skeptic sees this as proof that LLMs are “just mirrors.” But flip it: if LLMs are susceptible to the same cognitive biases humans are, then the same debiasing interventions cognitive psychology has developed for humans should work on LLMs too.
And they do. Two recent frameworks prove it:

BiasBuster (2024) uncovers, evaluates, and mitigates cognitive bias in LLMs across 16,800 prompts. It targets prompt-induced, sequential, and inherent biases.[8]
Self-debiasing (2025) uses an iterative three-step process (bias determination, bias analysis, cognitive debiasing) and outperformed existing approaches across finance, healthcare, and legal decision-making tasks.[9]
This is the argument that should change the skeptic’s mind. Cognitive psychology doesn’t just describe what goes wrong with reasoning. It provides causal models of why reasoning goes wrong and where to intervene. Those causal models transfer directly to LLMs. That’s not a metaphor. It’s an empirical finding.

From Token Prediction to Cognitive Architecture
Several research groups are now building what I think is the most promising direction in AI: LLMs that don’t just generate text, but operate within cognitive architectures modeled on how humans actually process decisions.
Cognitive LLMs: Giving AI a Decision-Making Operating System
Wu et al. (2025) introduced Cognitive LLMs, where cognitive architectures (specifically ACT-R, one of the most validated models of human cognition) instruct large language models for decision-making. Rather than relying solely on statistical patterns, these systems transfer structured knowledge that represents how humans process information, form strategies, and make choices.[10]
The human parallel: An experienced product manager doesn’t just “know things.” They have internalized decision patterns, priority frameworks, and failure modes that shape how they process new information. Cognitive LLMs attempt to give AI that same structural layer.
Persona Alchemy: Psychologically Grounded Stakeholder Agents
Zhu et al. (2025) developed a Social Cognitive Theory (SCT) agent design framework using four personal factors (cognitive, motivational, biological, and affective) to create AI personas that respond to scenarios in psychologically consistent ways.[11]
The human parallel: Before a big decision, you might informally poll three colleagues you trust because they think differently from you. Persona Alchemy formalizes that. You test your decision against psychologically grounded stakeholder agents and get diversity of perspective without the politics, the scheduling conflicts, or the groupthink.
Personality-Driven Decision Agents
The SANDMAN architecture uses the Big Five (OCEAN) personality model to create agents whose decision patterns shift predictably based on induced personality traits. Different personality profiles produce “distinct task-selection patterns aligned with induced OCEAN attributes.”[12]
The human parallel: You already know that your team’s most conscientious member spots risks others miss, while your most open member generates options nobody else considers. SANDMAN suggests we can build AI tools that replicate those cognitive diversity patterns on demand.
The Group Decision Problem: A Story in Two Acts
Act 1: The Meeting Without AI
It’s the third meeting about the roadmap. The VP speaks first and anchors the group on Option A. Two junior PMs have concerns but don’t speak up because the VP seems decided. The data scientist mentions a risk in the numbers, but it gets lost in the crosstalk. The group “aligns” on Option A. Three months later, the risk the data scientist mentioned materializes. Everyone remembers the meeting differently.
This is the textbook cocktail: anchoring bias from the first speaker, authority bias suppressing dissent, information loss from unstructured discussion, and groupthink papering over the cracks.
Act 2: The Same Meeting With a Framework-Aware AI Facilitator
The AI opens by surfacing the decision structure: “You’re choosing between three roadmap options. Before discussing preferences, I’d like each person to independently flag their top concern. I’ll synthesize these anonymously.”
After collecting inputs, the AI identifies a convergence: three of five people flagged the same adoption risk for Option A, but none of them had said it out loud yet. The AI surfaces it: “There’s a shared concern about adoption risk that hasn’t been discussed. Want to explore that before evaluating options?”
The VP, now seeing the pattern, adjusts. The group discusses the risk openly. They modify Option A to address it, or pivot to Option B. Either way, the decision is better because the AI facilitated the cognitive process, not just the information flow.
This isn’t science fiction. Research by Chiang et al. (2022) found that involving users in AI’s reasoning process increased both compliance and perceived collaboration.[13] And work on LLM-based group systems envisions AI that actively monitors groups, identifies members who haven’t been heard, and even de-escalates conflicts (Ricci et al., 2025).[15]
But here’s the design nuance that cognitive load theory warns us about: more explanation isn’t always better. Detailed AI explanations can actually increase perceived task complexity and impair decision quality (Sweller, 1994).[14] The right AI facilitator knows when to surface information and when to stay quiet. That calibration is a UX Research problem, not an engineering problem.
The Questions We Haven’t Answered Yet
If this synthesis is right, and I think the evidence is strong, then there are six open questions that should shape the next wave of research. These aren’t abstract. Each one has direct implications for what you build next.
1. Can LLMs Learn to Recognize Decision Contexts Automatically?
Right now, LLMs only apply frameworks when you explicitly prompt them. What would it take to build systems that detect the type of decision being made and apply the appropriate cognitive strategy without being told? That’s Klein’s RPD model, but for AI.
2. How Do You Calibrate Cognitive Offloading in Real Time?
Too much support and you get belief offloading. Too little and you get cognitive overload. Is there a measurable signal (response time, question patterns, confidence indicators) that could help an AI system dynamically adjust how much scaffolding to provide?
3. What Does “Cognitive Load” Mean for a Group Using AI?
We have solid models of individual cognitive load. We have almost nothing for group cognitive load in AI-mediated contexts. When five people use an AI facilitator in a meeting, how does cognitive burden distribute? Who gets overloaded? Who gets underserved?
4. What Happens to Belief Formation After a Year of AI-Assisted Decisions?
The belief offloading research is brand new. We need longitudinal studies. If you use an AI decision tool daily for 12 months, do you get better at decisions or worse? Does the answer depend on how the tool is designed?
5. Which Decisions Need Heuristics and Which Need Full Analysis?
Gigerenzer’s ecological rationality says the heuristic needs to match the environment. But we don’t have empirically validated guidelines for which AI decision contexts benefit from simple heuristic responses and which ones require deep analytical treatment. Building those guidelines is a UXR problem.
6. Do These Frameworks Work Across Cultures?
Naturalistic decision-making research comes primarily from Western military and emergency contexts. Recognition-primed processes, heuristic preferences, and group dynamics all vary across cultures. What does that mean for globally deployed AI decision tools? We don’t know yet.
The Bottom Line
The skeptic is right that LLMs don’t “understand” decisions. But the skeptic is solving the wrong problem.
Decades of cognitive psychology research converge on a single insight: intelligence has always been about the fit between a cognitive strategy and the environment it operates in. Not some magical internal property of the reasoner. A firefighter isn’t smart because of raw brainpower. A firefighter is smart because years of experience have organized pattern recognition around the right cues in the right contexts.
UX Research is the field purpose-built to study that fit. Applied cognitive psychology provides the theoretical architecture. Together, they offer something that scaling parameters alone never will: a principled way to match AI capabilities to human cognitive needs, context by context, decision by decision.
The opportunity isn’t to make AI “smart.” It’s to make AI useful in the ways that matter. Design the interaction well, embed the right frameworks, and the system produces intelligent outcomes. Design it poorly, and you get a very expensive autocomplete that makes people worse at thinking.
That’s not an engineering problem. It’s a cognitive design problem. And we already have the science to solve it.

References

De Neys, W. (2024). Dual-process theories of thought as potential architectures for developing neuro-symbolic AI models. Frontiers in Cognition.
Gigerenzer, G., & Todd, P. M. (1999). Simple heuristics that make us smart. Oxford University Press.

projects/uxr-blog/blog-db/the-ux-measure.content:
An article about the different ways to calculate data from UX measurements such as sus, umux, CSAT, and other similar scores.
Instead of looking at each equation, measurement by measurement, we will look at the type of functions used in the equations and what effect those functions have on the result
For example, SUS doesn’t use median, mean, or anything like that. It breaks the respondents into three groups and looks at the percent difference between the top and bottom groups. Because it doesn’t use the literal scores in a mean-like function, we’re less suspectable to outliers. And because we’re looking at groups that have a positive and negative experience, and create each group asymmetrically, our outcome will be more effected by negative experience than most other metrics.

# Understanding the Math Behind UX Metrics: A Guide for Non-Statisticians
When we measure user experience, the way we calculate our metrics can dramatically affect how we interpret our results. In this article, we’ll explore how different mathematical approaches in UX metrics shape our understanding of user feedback, written specifically for UX researchers who don’t have a background in statistics.
## Why Mathematical Methods Matter in UX
Before diving into specific calculations, let’s understand why the mathematical approach matters. Imagine you’re trying to understand how tall people are in a room. You could:
- Take the average (mean) height
- Find the middle person’s height (median)
- Look at the shortest and tallest people (range)
- Group people into “tall” and “short” categories
Each approach tells you something different about height in the room. The same is true for UX metrics – the math we use shapes what we learn about our users’ experiences.
## Common Mathematical Approaches in UX Metrics
### 1. Grouping and Contrast (Used in SUS)
The System Usability Scale (SUS) uses a fascinating approach that many researchers don’t fully appreciate. Instead of treating all scores equally, it:
- Creates three groups: satisfied users, neutral users, and dissatisfied users
- Focuses on the gap between satisfied and dissatisfied groups
- Weights negative experiences more heavily than positive ones
Why This Matters:
- More resistant to outliers than averages
- Better at catching significant usability issues
- Helps identify polarizing features (ones users either love or hate)
- Particularly useful for spotting critical problems that might be masked by general satisfaction
### 2. Simple Averages (Used in CSAT)
Customer Satisfaction Score (CSAT) typically uses straightforward averages, which:
- Takes all responses and calculates their mean
- Treats all scores with equal weight
- Can be significantly affected by extreme responses
Why This Matters:
- Easy to understand and communicate to stakeholders
- Good for tracking general trends over time
- More susceptible to being skewed by outliers
- Most useful when you have a large sample size
### 3. Top-Box Scoring (Used in NPS)
Net Promoter Score (NPS) uses a distinct approach:
- Focuses only on the extreme ends of the scale
- Subtracts detractors from promoters
- Ignores neutral responses
- Results in a score that can range from -100 to +100
Why This Matters:
- Emphasizes strong opinions over mild ones
- Good at predicting word-of-mouth behavior
- Can miss nuanced feedback
- Useful for competitive benchmarking
### 4. Weighted Averages (Used in UMUX-LITE)
The Usability Metric for User Experience (UMUX-LITE) uses weighted scoring where:
- Different questions carry different weights
- Scores are normalized to a 0-100 scale
- Results are adjusted based on the importance of each factor
Why This Matters:
- More nuanced than simple averages
- Can better reflect the real impact of different aspects of the experience
- More complex to explain to stakeholders
- Good for detailed diagnosis of specific issues
## Practical Implications for UX Researchers
### When to Use Which Approach
1. Use Grouping and Contrast (SUS-style) when:
- You need to identify critical usability issues
- You want to minimize the impact of outliers
- You’re working with smaller sample sizes
- You need to prioritize fixing negative experiences
2. Use Simple Averages (CSAT-style) when:
- You need to track trends over time
- You have a large sample size
- You need to communicate results simply
- You’re measuring straightforward satisfaction
3. Use Top-Box Scoring (NPS-style) when:
- You’re interested in extreme opinions
- You need competitive benchmarking
- You’re measuring loyalty or advocacy
- You want to predict word-of-mouth behavior
4. Use Weighted Averages (UMUX-style) when:
- You need detailed diagnostic information
- Different aspects of the experience have different importance
- You have complex user goals to measure
- You need to balance multiple factors
## Common Pitfalls to Avoid
1. Don’t Mix Methods Without Understanding Why
- Each method tells a different story
- Mixing methods can lead to confused interpretation
- Be consistent in your approach over time
2. Don’t Ignore Sample Size
- Different methods need different minimum sample sizes
- Smaller samples work better with grouping approaches
- Larger samples are needed for reliable averages
3. Don’t Forget Context
- The best method depends on your research goals
- Consider your audience when choosing a method
- Think about how you’ll need to communicate results
## Making the Right Choice
When choosing a calculation method, ask yourself:
- What am I trying to learn about the user experience?
- Who needs to understand these results?
- How will this information be used?
- What kind of sample size do I have?
- Do I need to track this over time?
## Conclusion
The mathematical approach you choose for your UX metrics isn’t just about numbers – it’s about understanding your users in the most meaningful way possible. By understanding how different calculations affect your results, you can choose the right method for your specific needs and communicate your findings more effectively.
Remember: The goal isn’t to find the “best” method, but rather to choose the method that best helps you understand and improve your users’ experience. Sometimes this means using multiple approaches to get a complete picture, as long as you understand what each one is telling you.

When we measure user experience, the way we calculate our metrics can dramatically affect how we interpret our results. In this article, we’ll explore how different mathematical approaches in UX metrics shape our understanding of user feedback, written specifically for UX researchers who don’t have a background in statistics.
## Why Mathematical Methods Matter in UX
Before diving into specific calculations, let’s understand why the mathematical approach matters. Imagine you’re trying to understand how tall people are in a room. You could:
- Take the average (mean) height
- Find the middle person’s height (median)
- Look at the shortest and tallest people (range)
- Group people into “tall” and “short” categories
Each approach tells you something different about height in the room. The same is true for UX metrics – the math we use shapes what we learn about our users’ experiences.
## Common Mathematical Approaches in UX Metrics
### 1. Grouping and Contrast (Used in SUS)
The System Usability Scale (SUS) uses a fascinating approach that many researchers don’t fully appreciate. Instead of treating all scores equally, it:
- Creates three groups: satisfied users, neutral users, and dissatisfied users
- Focuses on the gap between satisfied and dissatisfied groups
- Weights negative experiences more heavily than positive ones
Why This Matters:
- More resistant to outliers than averages
- Better at catching significant usability issues
- Helps identify polarizing features (ones users either love or hate)
- Particularly useful for spotting critical problems that might be masked by general satisfaction
### 2. Simple Averages (Used in CSAT)
Customer Satisfaction Score (CSAT) typically uses straightforward averages, which:
- Takes all responses and calculates their mean
- Treats all scores with equal weight
- Can be significantly affected by extreme responses
Why This Matters:
- Easy to understand and communicate to stakeholders
- Good for tracking general trends over time
- More susceptible to being skewed by outliers
- Most useful when you have a large sample size
### 3. Top-Box Scoring (Used in NPS)
Net Promoter Score (NPS) uses a distinct approach:
- Focuses only on the extreme ends of the scale
- Subtracts detractors from promoters
- Ignores neutral responses
- Results in a score that can range from -100 to +100
Why This Matters:
- Emphasizes strong opinions over mild ones
- Good at predicting word-of-mouth behavior
- Can miss nuanced feedback
- Useful for competitive benchmarking
### 4. Weighted Averages (Used in UMUX-LITE)
The Usability Metric for User Experience (UMUX-LITE) uses weighted scoring where:
- Different questions carry different weights
- Scores are normalized to a 0-100 scale
- Results are adjusted based on the importance of each factor
Why This Matters:
- More nuanced than simple averages
- Can better reflect the real impact of different aspects of the experience
- More complex to explain to stakeholders
- Good for detailed diagnosis of specific issues
## Practical Implications for UX Researchers
### When to Use Which Approach
1. Use Grouping and Contrast (SUS-style) when:
- You need to identify critical usability issues
- You want to minimize the impact of outliers
- You’re working with smaller sample sizes
- You need to prioritize fixing negative experiences
2. Use Simple Averages (CSAT-style) when:
- You need to track trends over time
- You have a large sample size
- You need to communicate results simply
- You’re measuring straightforward satisfaction
3. Use Top-Box Scoring (NPS-style) when:
- You’re interested in extreme opinions
- You need competitive benchmarking
- You’re measuring loyalty or advocacy
- You want to predict word-of-mouth behavior
4. Use Weighted Averages (UMUX-style) when:
- You need detailed diagnostic information
- Different aspects of the experience have different importance
- You have complex user goals to measure
- You need to balance multiple factors
## Common Pitfalls to Avoid
1. Don’t Mix Methods Without Understanding Why
- Each method tells a different story
- Mixing methods can lead to confused interpretation
- Be consistent in your approach over time
2. Don’t Ignore Sample Size
- Different methods need different minimum sample sizes
- Smaller samples work better with grouping approaches
- Larger samples are needed for reliable averages
3. Don’t Forget Context
- The best method depends on your research goals
- Consider your audience when choosing a method
- Think about how you’ll need to communicate results
## Making the Right Choice
When choosing a calculation method, ask yourself:
- What am I trying to learn about the user experience?
- Who needs to understand these results?
- How will this information be used?
- What kind of sample size do I have?
- Do I need to track this over time?
## Conclusion
The mathematical approach you choose for your UX metrics isn’t just about numbers – it’s about understanding your users in the most meaningful way possible. By understanding how different calculations affect your results, you can choose the right method for your specific needs and communicate your findings more effectively.
Remember: The goal isn’t to find the “best” method, but rather to choose the method that best helps you understand and improve your users’ experience. Sometimes this means using multiple approaches to get a complete picture, as long as you understand what each one is telling you.

projects/uxr-blog/blog-db/the-ux-researc.title: The UX Research Portfolio That Gets You Hired: A Strategic Guide
projects/uxr-blog/blog-db/the-ux-researc.content:
Your portfolio isn’t a research report—it’s a sales pitch for your thinking. And most UX researchers are terrible salespeople.
We spend our careers helping others understand users, yet we struggle to help hiring managers understand us. This guide will change that.

1. The Portfolio Paradox
Here’s the uncomfortable truth: UX researchers document everything except their own value.
We meticulously capture user quotes, synthesize findings, and present insights with precision. But when it comes to our portfolios? We dump process screenshots and hope someone connects the dots.
The problem: We treat portfolios like research reports when they should be treated like marketing collateral.
A research report aims for objectivity. A portfolio aims for persuasion. These require fundamentally different approaches:


Research Report
Portfolio


Comprehensive
Selective


Objective
Persuasive


Process-focused
Impact-focused


Internal audience
External audience


The sooner you embrace this shift, the sooner your portfolio starts working for you.
---
## 2. What Hiring Managers Actually Evaluate
After reviewing hundreds of portfolios and sitting on both sides of the hiring table, I've learned that hiring managers aren't evaluating what you think they're evaluating.
**They're looking for evidence of four things:**
### Decision Quality
Did your research lead to better decisions? Not "did you conduct research" but "did it matter?"
### Scope Handling
Can you operate at different altitudes? Tactical usability fixes *and* strategic discovery work? Show range.
### Stakeholder Influence
Research that sits in a repository is worthless. Show me you can move people.
### Methodological Judgment
Not "do you know 15 methods" but "do you know when to use which one and why?"
> **Pro tip:** For each case study, ask yourself: "Does this demonstrate at least two of these four qualities?" If not, rework it or cut it.
---
## 3. Anatomy of a Winning Case Study
The best case studies follow an **impact-first structure**:
### The Formula
1. **Lead with the outcome** (1-2 sentences)
	- "This research prevented a \$2M feature investment and redirected the roadmap."
2. **Set the context** (2-3 sentences)
	- Business situation, stakeholders, constraints
3. **Frame the challenge** (1 paragraph)
	- What decision needed to be made? What were the stakes?
4. **Show your thinking** (2-3 paragraphs)
	- Why this method? What trade-offs did you make? How did you adapt?
5. **Deliver the insight** (1-2 paragraphs)
	- What did you learn? Make it concrete and memorable.
6. **Close with impact** (1 paragraph)
	- What changed because of this work? Quantify if possible.
### The "So What?" Test
After every section, ask: "So what?" If you can't answer it, neither can the reader.
- ❌ "I conducted 12 user interviews"
- ✅ "12 interviews revealed that 80% of users abandoned the workflow at the same step—a pattern the team had attributed to 'user error' for two years"
---
## 4. Common Mistakes (and How to Fix Them)
### Mistake 1: The Process Dump
**Symptom:** Your case study reads like a methodology textbook.
**Fix:** Cut 50% of your process description. Replace with insight and impact.
### Mistake 2: Missing Outcomes
**Symptom:** The story ends at "I presented my findings."
**Fix:** Follow up. What shipped? What changed? If you don't know, find out.
### Mistake 3: Over-Confidentiality
**Symptom:** "I can't show anything due to NDA."
**Fix:** You can almost always show *something*. Anonymize. Generalize. Focus on your thinking, not the specifics.
### Mistake 4: No Narrative Arc
**Symptom:** It reads like a bulleted list of activities.
**Fix:** Every case study needs tension. What was uncertain? What surprised you? What was the turning point?
---
## 5. Templates & Resources
Ready to rebuild your portfolio? Here are resources to accelerate your work:
### Templates
- **Figma UX Case Study Template** — Clean, component-based structure
- **dscout Case Study Outline** — Narrative-focused framework
- **UXfolio 2026 Structure Guide** — Platform-specific optimization
### Portfolio Examples Worth Studying
- **Rachel Hanna Green** — Leads with business impact on every case study
- **Sahar Naderi** — Shows methodological range across research types
- **Lina Žigelytė** — Balances depth with scanability
### Quick Self-Assessment
Before submitting your portfolio, check:
- [ ] Does each case study lead with impact, not process?
- [ ] Can a hiring manager understand the value in 30 seconds of scanning?
- [ ] Do I show range (strategic + tactical, qual + quant)?
- [ ] Is there a clear narrative arc with tension and resolution?
- [ ] Have I removed everything that doesn't serve persuasion?
---
## Final Thought
Your portfolio is not a comprehensive record of your work. It's a carefully curated argument for why you're the right person for the job.
Every sentence should earn its place. Every case study should make someone want to work with you.
Now go make that argument.

projects/uxr-blog/blog-db/the-wrong-ques.title: The Wrong Question About AI and Your UX Skills
projects/uxr-blog/blog-db/the-wrong-ques.content:
**Status:** First Draft  
	**Estimated read time:** \~12 minutes  
	**Working thesis:** The right question is not how to keep your skills sharp under AI. It is which skills will pay rent in 2030, and which ones you are still rehearsing out of habit.

## A Confession Before the Argument
Last month I caught myself opening a blank document and typing out a discussion guide from scratch. I had an LLM open in another tab. I knew, in the analytical part of my brain, that the LLM would have produced a serviceable first draft in fifteen seconds, and that I would then have spent my real cognitive effort on what mattered: whether the questions actually mapped to the decision the team had committed to making, whether the order created demand effects, whether the constructs were operationalized the same way they would be coded.
I did not do that. I wrote the draft myself. Slowly. By hand.
Why? Because writing a discussion guide is something I am good at. It is one of the things that makes me feel like a researcher. There is a particular pleasure in choosing the right opening question, and I did not want to give that pleasure up.
I am telling you this because I think a lot of us are doing some version of this, and I do not want the rest of this essay to read like a scolding. The instinct to keep your hands on your craft is not naive. It is not Luddism. It is, in many ways, the most professionally serious instinct we have. But I have come to believe it is pointed at the wrong target, and the cost of leaving it pointed there is bigger than we have admitted.
This is not an essay about how to use AI better. It is an essay about which question to ask in the first place.
## What Most of the Conversation Gets Wrong
The dominant question in our field right now is some variation of: *how do I make sure I do not lose any skills?* Practice your synthesis muscles. Hand-code a transcript every so often. Write the draft yourself first. Treat the AI as a junior partner, not a co-author. The advice is everywhere, and most of it is well-intentioned.
It is also, I think, a question that cannot be answered.
The skill list of a working UX researcher is enormous. You have screening logic, sampling math, study design, instrument writing, moderation craft, transcription, coding, synthesis, theming, visualization, narrative construction, executive translation, stakeholder negotiation, and the social engineering of getting any of it acted on. Nobody has the practice budget to keep all of it sharp without AI help. Trying to is a recipe for either burnout or quiet decline. The researchers I know who are most committed to *not losing their skills* are also the most exhausted, and not coincidentally.
There is a second problem. The probability that an LLM will be available to help write your next interview script, screener, or readout is one hundred percent. Not eighty. Not *depends on policy*. One hundred. Any skill you are practicing on the assumption that the AI will not be there is a skill you are practicing for a world that no longer exists. That is not a moral failing. It is just a fact about the timeline we live on.
So we are defending a position that cannot be held, with a budget we do not have, against a tool that is not going away. This is what makes the question feel impossible. It *is* impossible. We are asking it wrong.
## What the Worry Gets Right
Before I propose a different question, I want to take the existing one seriously, because there is real wisdom inside it.
The cognitive science backs up the worry. A 2025 Microsoft and Carnegie Mellon survey of 319 knowledge workers using GenAI tools at least once a week found that the more confident people were in the AI, the less critical thinking they did with its output. Higher self-confidence led to more scrutiny; higher AI-confidence led to less. The authors describe a shift in what critical thinking even *means* in AI-assisted work, away from production and toward information verification, response integration, and task stewardship \[1\]. A randomized lab study published in the *British Journal of Educational Technology* found that ChatGPT made student essays better while making the students worse, a phenomenon the authors call *metacognitive laziness* \[2\]. Ganuthula's theoretical model formalizes this as the Paradox of Augmentation: the capacities AI augments are precisely the ones that atrophy under that augmentation \[3\].
Aviation has known this for thirty years. NASA work on cockpit automation found that pilots who lean heavily on autopilot lose specific cognitive skills, particularly the ability to keep track of the aircraft's situation without instrument support \[4\]. Medical imaging research warns that AI assistance can both accelerate skill decay in experts and hinder skill development in novices, while making both groups *less* aware of the deficit \[5\].
So the worry is not paranoid. The risk is documented. The instinct to keep your own hands on the work, to maintain manual skill so you can catch the system when it is quietly wrong, is the same instinct that keeps pilots alive and patients diagnosed. It is the most professionally responsible instinct in the field.
I do not want to argue against that instinct. I want to argue that we are pointing it at the wrong layer of the work.
## The Layer Confusion
Here is the move. For about thirty years, in our craft, you could not produce the artifact without the cognition. You could not write a good discussion guide unless you understood demand effects, construct operationalization, and decision-relevance. You could not synthesize a transcript unless you could hold competing interpretations in your head and adjudicate between them. The artifact was downstream evidence of the thinking. We treated production as the skill because, for our entire careers, production *required* the skill. The two were welded together.
LLMs decoupled them.
You can now produce a plausible-looking discussion guide in fifteen seconds with no real understanding of what makes it good. A junior researcher cannot easily tell the difference. Sometimes a senior researcher cannot either, especially when the AI has gotten the surface right and the substance wrong in a subtle way. This is exactly the medical imaging case from the literature: the output looks competent enough that the user's metacognitive alarm does not fire, and they accept work that they would have caught had they done it themselves \[5\].
Notice what this means. The skill we were protecting, *writing a guide from scratch*, is not actually the skill that kept the research honest. The skill that kept the research honest was the *evaluation* happening in the senior researcher's head when they reviewed the junior's draft: does the opening establish behavioral, not attitudinal, framing? Do the warmups validate recruitment, or burn time? Does the question order create demand effects? Are constructs operationalized the same way they will be coded? Does each question map to a decision someone has actually committed to making?
Nothing on that list is something an LLM does well unsupervised. All of it is what experienced researchers were *already* doing implicitly, every time they reviewed a draft. The skill was always there. We just got to keep it hidden inside the production work, where we did not have to name it.
The AI did not eliminate the skill. It promoted it. It moved evaluation from background quality control to foreground job description.
## The Reframe
So the question changes, and the change is a kindness.
*How do I keep all my skills sharp?* is unwinnable. *Which skills will pay rent in 2030, and which can I let go of with a clear conscience?* is a question I can actually answer. It gives me permission to stop defending positions that are not worth defending, and to put my scarce cognitive effort where it compounds.
I want to be honest about what this asks. Letting go of skills you spent years building is a kind of grief. The pleasure I take in writing a good discussion guide is not negligible, and I am not going to pretend it is. The migration from production to evaluation is harder, less visible, and harder to take pride in. There is no equivalent of the satisfaction you get from a beautifully constructed instrument. The new work is mostly judgment exercised privately, and it leaves fewer artifacts to point at.
That is a real cost. I do not think the field has reckoned with it. Most of the AI-and-UX content out there talks about productivity gains and tool stacks. Almost none of it talks about what it feels like to lose the visible craft and have to rebuild your professional identity around something quieter. We should talk about it. We should let people grieve.
But the reframe is still the right one. Because the alternative, defending the production layer, is what gets us treated as a cost center. It is what makes researchers replaceable in the eyes of an organization that has noticed the AI can produce comparable artifacts at zero marginal cost. The path through this is not louder defense of the artifact. It is honest migration to the layer where our judgment actually lives.
## What Is Worth Releasing, What Is Worth Honoring
A simple way to think about this is two columns. Skills you can release with a clear conscience because they have stopped distinguishing you, and skills worth honoring and deepening because they are now the entire job.


**Skills to Release with Grace**
**Skills to Honor and Deepen**


Producing the discussion guide from scratch
Evaluating the guide for construct validity and decision-relevance


Writing the screener
Specifying the population frame and quota math the screener has to satisfy


First-pass coding and theme production
Auditing AI-generated codes for construct drift, salience bias, and missing voices


Drafting the readout deck
Framing what decision the readout has to unblock and what to leave out


Recall of every method's procedure
Match-making between business question, evidence standard, and method stack


Producing personas and journey maps
Governing what gets canonized as a persona and what stays a working hypothesis


Note-taking during sessions
Live sense-making, including reading what was *not* said


Knowing the literature
Translating the literature into operational decisions stakeholders can act on


The pattern is consistent. Production gets cheaper. Judgment gets scarcer. The skill we cared about all along was always in the right column. We just got to leave it implicit, because the left column required it as a prerequisite. That is no longer true. The cognition has to stand on its own now, and that is harder, but it is also more honest.
The left column is not where the craft lived. It is where the craft *showed*. The right column is where the craft actually was, all along.
## A Closer Look at the Discussion Guide
Let me drill into one row, because the abstract framing only does so much work.
When a senior researcher reviewed a junior's discussion guide draft, what were they actually doing? Not admiring the prose. They were running a private checklist that almost never got written down:
- Does the opening establish *behavioral* framing? "Tell me about the last time you..." rather than "How do you usually feel about..."?
- Are the warmup questions doing recruitment validation, confirming the person is in the population we sampled for, or are they wasted minutes?
- Does the question order create demand effects on later answers? Does asking about brand affinity early bias responses to feature questions later?
- Are constructs operationalized in the instrument the same way they will be operationalized in the analysis? If we are measuring *trust*, is the question worded the same way the codebook will define it?
- Does each question map to a decision the team has committed to making, or are some of them there because they are interesting but unactionable?
- Are we leaving room for the participant to surprise us, or has the question structure already pre-determined the answer space?
That list is the actual skill. It always was. The LLM did not take it. It just stopped letting us hide it inside the writing work.
Senior researchers who are good at this can run that checklist on an AI-drafted guide in two minutes and produce a better guide than they could have written from scratch in an hour. That is not a loss of craft. That is craft finally being able to operate at the speed of the questions it cares about.
Junior researchers cannot run that checklist yet. That is the real concern under all of this, and it is one I take seriously. The implicit apprenticeship of writing your own drafts and getting them critiqued was how most of us learned to evaluate. If the AI writes the drafts, where does that learning happen? I do not have a complete answer. What I have is a guess: the apprenticeship has to become explicit. Senior researchers will need to teach the evaluation checklist directly, rather than letting juniors absorb it through years of red ink. That is harder to do, and the field is behind on it. But it is the actual problem, and it is not solved by junior researchers writing more drafts by hand.
## The Strategic Stakes
Step back from the individual practitioner for a moment. The field-level argument is this: UX research has been stuck between two equally weak positions on AI. *Panic* (the AI will replace us) and *denial* (the AI cannot do real research). Both positions leave UXR positioned as a *production function*, the team that makes the artifacts. That position is exactly the one labor markets punish hardest under automation.
Stanford HAI's work on automation finds that occupations that lose inexpert tasks while gaining expert tasks see employment fall and wages rise. Occupations that gain inexpert tasks while losing expert ones see the opposite \[6\]. The IMF's 2026 analysis finds that AI-related skills carry a wage premium, but that AI-vulnerable occupations are seeing entry-level employment drop where AI adoption is high \[7\]. HBS research by Bojinov and McFowland finds that GenAI lets novices reach further into adjacent tasks, but cannot turn novices into experts; the expert layer is where the durable human value lives \[8\].
The pattern is clear. Production is becoming a commodity. Expert evaluation is where the wage premium and the strategic influence both sit. Researchers who migrate up the stack get treated as strategic infrastructure. Researchers who keep defending the production layer get treated as overhead the AI is gradually making redundant.
This is not a tooling argument. It is a positioning argument, and it is the argument the field needs to be having instead of the one it is currently having.
## What This Looks Like in Practice
If the reframe is right, here is what changes about how a researcher spends their week.
**Less time on first drafts. More time specifying.** Specifying the decision a study has to unblock, before any instrument is written. Specifying the construct definitions that the instrument and the analysis both have to share. Specifying the evidence standard that will count as *we know enough.*
**Less time producing artifacts. More time auditing them.** Treating an AI-drafted guide, screener, codebook, or readout as a defendant, not a deliverable. What is missing? What construct has drifted? Whose voice is absent? What question is the artifact answering that nobody actually asked?
**Less time on methods recall. More time on methods match-making.** The skill is no longer remembering what a critical incident technique looks like in procedure. The LLM has that. The skill is knowing when CIT is the right tool for the question on the table, and when a diary study, a switch interview, or a think-aloud would buy more decision-relevant evidence.
**Less time finishing decks. More time framing what the deck has to do.** What decision is on the table? What is the executive afraid of? What finding, if true, would change the roadmap, and what finding would not? What are we choosing *not* to include, and why?
**Less individual production. More apprenticeship.** The evaluation skills that used to transfer implicitly have to transfer explicitly now. That is a leadership task, and it is on the senior tier of the profession to figure it out.
None of this is glamorous. None of it produces the satisfying artifact-shaped output that used to be the felt reward of the work. But all of it is the work that actually moves a research practice from cost center to revenue driver, and it is all work the AI cannot do unsupervised.
## A Closing Invitation

	If you are tired of trying to defend everything, you have permission to stop.

Pick the three skills that govern your judgment. Mine, this year, are construct operationalization, decision-framing for stakeholders, and live sense-making in unmoderated sessions. They are not the skills I am best at. They are the skills I most want to compound. I am going to put my practice budget there. I am going to let the AI take a much larger share of the production work, and I am going to spend the time I save on getting better at evaluation. I expect this to be uncomfortable for a while. I expect to grieve the visible craft, the way you grieve any identity you outgrow.
If you do this, you are not abandoning the craft. You are finally being asked to do it without the artifact as cover. That is harder. It is also more honest. The craft was always in the judgment, and the judgment is what is left.
The right question was never *how do I keep my skills.* It was always *which skills are worth keeping.* The answer to that question, today, is shorter than it used to be, and that is not a loss. That is the work finally showing itself.
---
