projects/uxr-blog/blog-db/the-wrong-ques.content:
**Status:** First Draft  
	**Estimated read time:** \~12 minutes  
	**Working thesis:** The right question is not how to keep your skills sharp under AI. It is which skills will pay rent in 2030, and which ones you are still rehearsing out of habit.

## A Confession Before the Argument
Last month I caught myself opening a blank document and typing out a discussion guide from scratch. I had an LLM open in another tab. I knew, in the analytical part of my brain, that the LLM would have produced a serviceable first draft in fifteen seconds, and that I would then have spent my real cognitive effort on what mattered: whether the questions actually mapped to the decision the team had committed to making, whether the order created demand effects, whether the constructs were operationalized the same way they would be coded.
I did not do that. I wrote the draft myself. Slowly. By hand.
Why? Because writing a discussion guide is something I am good at. It is one of the things that makes me feel like a researcher. There is a particular pleasure in choosing the right opening question, and I did not want to give that pleasure up.
I am telling you this because I think a lot of us are doing some version of this, and I do not want the rest of this essay to read like a scolding. The instinct to keep your hands on your craft is not naive. It is not Luddism. It is, in many ways, the most professionally serious instinct we have. But I have come to believe it is pointed at the wrong target, and the cost of leaving it pointed there is bigger than we have admitted.
This is not an essay about how to use AI better. It is an essay about which question to ask in the first place.
## What Most of the Conversation Gets Wrong
The dominant question in our field right now is some variation of: *how do I make sure I do not lose any skills?* Practice your synthesis muscles. Hand-code a transcript every so often. Write the draft yourself first. Treat the AI as a junior partner, not a co-author. The advice is everywhere, and most of it is well-intentioned.
It is also, I think, a question that cannot be answered.
The skill list of a working UX researcher is enormous. You have screening logic, sampling math, study design, instrument writing, moderation craft, transcription, coding, synthesis, theming, visualization, narrative construction, executive translation, stakeholder negotiation, and the social engineering of getting any of it acted on. Nobody has the practice budget to keep all of it sharp without AI help. Trying to is a recipe for either burnout or quiet decline. The researchers I know who are most committed to *not losing their skills* are also the most exhausted, and not coincidentally.
There is a second problem. The probability that an LLM will be available to help write your next interview script, screener, or readout is one hundred percent. Not eighty. Not *depends on policy*. One hundred. Any skill you are practicing on the assumption that the AI will not be there is a skill you are practicing for a world that no longer exists. That is not a moral failing. It is just a fact about the timeline we live on.
So we are defending a position that cannot be held, with a budget we do not have, against a tool that is not going away. This is what makes the question feel impossible. It *is* impossible. We are asking it wrong.
## What the Worry Gets Right
Before I propose a different question, I want to take the existing one seriously, because there is real wisdom inside it.
The cognitive science backs up the worry. A 2025 Microsoft and Carnegie Mellon survey of 319 knowledge workers using GenAI tools at least once a week found that the more confident people were in the AI, the less critical thinking they did with its output. Higher self-confidence led to more scrutiny; higher AI-confidence led to less. The authors describe a shift in what critical thinking even *means* in AI-assisted work, away from production and toward information verification, response integration, and task stewardship \[1\]. A randomized lab study published in the *British Journal of Educational Technology* found that ChatGPT made student essays better while making the students worse, a phenomenon the authors call *metacognitive laziness* \[2\]. Ganuthula's theoretical model formalizes this as the Paradox of Augmentation: the capacities AI augments are precisely the ones that atrophy under that augmentation \[3\].
Aviation has known this for thirty years. NASA work on cockpit automation found that pilots who lean heavily on autopilot lose specific cognitive skills, particularly the ability to keep track of the aircraft's situation without instrument support \[4\]. Medical imaging research warns that AI assistance can both accelerate skill decay in experts and hinder skill development in novices, while making both groups *less* aware of the deficit \[5\].
So the worry is not paranoid. The risk is documented. The instinct to keep your own hands on the work, to maintain manual skill so you can catch the system when it is quietly wrong, is the same instinct that keeps pilots alive and patients diagnosed. It is the most professionally responsible instinct in the field.
I do not want to argue against that instinct. I want to argue that we are pointing it at the wrong layer of the work.
## The Layer Confusion
Here is the move. For about thirty years, in our craft, you could not produce the artifact without the cognition. You could not write a good discussion guide unless you understood demand effects, construct operationalization, and decision-relevance. You could not synthesize a transcript unless you could hold competing interpretations in your head and adjudicate between them. The artifact was downstream evidence of the thinking. We treated production as the skill because, for our entire careers, production *required* the skill. The two were welded together.
LLMs decoupled them.
You can now produce a plausible-looking discussion guide in fifteen seconds with no real understanding of what makes it good. A junior researcher cannot easily tell the difference. Sometimes a senior researcher cannot either, especially when the AI has gotten the surface right and the substance wrong in a subtle way. This is exactly the medical imaging case from the literature: the output looks competent enough that the user's metacognitive alarm does not fire, and they accept work that they would have caught had they done it themselves \[5\].
Notice what this means. The skill we were protecting, *writing a guide from scratch*, is not actually the skill that kept the research honest. The skill that kept the research honest was the *evaluation* happening in the senior researcher's head when they reviewed the junior's draft: does the opening establish behavioral, not attitudinal, framing? Do the warmups validate recruitment, or burn time? Does the question order create demand effects? Are constructs operationalized the same way they will be coded? Does each question map to a decision someone has actually committed to making?
Nothing on that list is something an LLM does well unsupervised. All of it is what experienced researchers were *already* doing implicitly, every time they reviewed a draft. The skill was always there. We just got to keep it hidden inside the production work, where we did not have to name it.
The AI did not eliminate the skill. It promoted it. It moved evaluation from background quality control to foreground job description.
## The Reframe
So the question changes, and the change is a kindness.
*How do I keep all my skills sharp?* is unwinnable. *Which skills will pay rent in 2030, and which can I let go of with a clear conscience?* is a question I can actually answer. It gives me permission to stop defending positions that are not worth defending, and to put my scarce cognitive effort where it compounds.
I want to be honest about what this asks. Letting go of skills you spent years building is a kind of grief. The pleasure I take in writing a good discussion guide is not negligible, and I am not going to pretend it is. The migration from production to evaluation is harder, less visible, and harder to take pride in. There is no equivalent of the satisfaction you get from a beautifully constructed instrument. The new work is mostly judgment exercised privately, and it leaves fewer artifacts to point at.
That is a real cost. I do not think the field has reckoned with it. Most of the AI-and-UX content out there talks about productivity gains and tool stacks. Almost none of it talks about what it feels like to lose the visible craft and have to rebuild your professional identity around something quieter. We should talk about it. We should let people grieve.
But the reframe is still the right one. Because the alternative, defending the production layer, is what gets us treated as a cost center. It is what makes researchers replaceable in the eyes of an organization that has noticed the AI can produce comparable artifacts at zero marginal cost. The path through this is not louder defense of the artifact. It is honest migration to the layer where our judgment actually lives.
## What Is Worth Releasing, What Is Worth Honoring
A simple way to think about this is two columns. Skills you can release with a clear conscience because they have stopped distinguishing you, and skills worth honoring and deepening because they are now the entire job.


**Skills to Release with Grace**
**Skills to Honor and Deepen**


Producing the discussion guide from scratch
Evaluating the guide for construct validity and decision-relevance


Writing the screener
Specifying the population frame and quota math the screener has to satisfy


First-pass coding and theme production
Auditing AI-generated codes for construct drift, salience bias, and missing voices


Drafting the readout deck
Framing what decision the readout has to unblock and what to leave out


Recall of every method's procedure
Match-making between business question, evidence standard, and method stack


Producing personas and journey maps
Governing what gets canonized as a persona and what stays a working hypothesis


Note-taking during sessions
Live sense-making, including reading what was *not* said


Knowing the literature
Translating the literature into operational decisions stakeholders can act on


The pattern is consistent. Production gets cheaper. Judgment gets scarcer. The skill we cared about all along was always in the right column. We just got to leave it implicit, because the left column required it as a prerequisite. That is no longer true. The cognition has to stand on its own now, and that is harder, but it is also more honest.
The left column is not where the craft lived. It is where the craft *showed*. The right column is where the craft actually was, all along.
## A Closer Look at the Discussion Guide
Let me drill into one row, because the abstract framing only does so much work.
When a senior researcher reviewed a junior's discussion guide draft, what were they actually doing? Not admiring the prose. They were running a private checklist that almost never got written down:
- Does the opening establish *behavioral* framing? "Tell me about the last time you..." rather than "How do you usually feel about..."?
- Are the warmup questions doing recruitment validation, confirming the person is in the population we sampled for, or are they wasted minutes?
- Does the question order create demand effects on later answers? Does asking about brand affinity early bias responses to feature questions later?
- Are constructs operationalized in the instrument the same way they will be operationalized in the analysis? If we are measuring *trust*, is the question worded the same way the codebook will define it?
- Does each question map to a decision the team has committed to making, or are some of them there because they are interesting but unactionable?
- Are we leaving room for the participant to surprise us, or has the question structure already pre-determined the answer space?
That list is the actual skill. It always was. The LLM did not take it. It just stopped letting us hide it inside the writing work.
Senior researchers who are good at this can run that checklist on an AI-drafted guide in two minutes and produce a better guide than they could have written from scratch in an hour. That is not a loss of craft. That is craft finally being able to operate at the speed of the questions it cares about.
Junior researchers cannot run that checklist yet. That is the real concern under all of this, and it is one I take seriously. The implicit apprenticeship of writing your own drafts and getting them critiqued was how most of us learned to evaluate. If the AI writes the drafts, where does that learning happen? I do not have a complete answer. What I have is a guess: the apprenticeship has to become explicit. Senior researchers will need to teach the evaluation checklist directly, rather than letting juniors absorb it through years of red ink. That is harder to do, and the field is behind on it. But it is the actual problem, and it is not solved by junior researchers writing more drafts by hand.
## The Strategic Stakes
Step back from the individual practitioner for a moment. The field-level argument is this: UX research has been stuck between two equally weak positions on AI. *Panic* (the AI will replace us) and *denial* (the AI cannot do real research). Both positions leave UXR positioned as a *production function*, the team that makes the artifacts. That position is exactly the one labor markets punish hardest under automation.
Stanford HAI's work on automation finds that occupations that lose inexpert tasks while gaining expert tasks see employment fall and wages rise. Occupations that gain inexpert tasks while losing expert ones see the opposite \[6\]. The IMF's 2026 analysis finds that AI-related skills carry a wage premium, but that AI-vulnerable occupations are seeing entry-level employment drop where AI adoption is high \[7\]. HBS research by Bojinov and McFowland finds that GenAI lets novices reach further into adjacent tasks, but cannot turn novices into experts; the expert layer is where the durable human value lives \[8\].
The pattern is clear. Production is becoming a commodity. Expert evaluation is where the wage premium and the strategic influence both sit. Researchers who migrate up the stack get treated as strategic infrastructure. Researchers who keep defending the production layer get treated as overhead the AI is gradually making redundant.
This is not a tooling argument. It is a positioning argument, and it is the argument the field needs to be having instead of the one it is currently having.
## What This Looks Like in Practice
If the reframe is right, here is what changes about how a researcher spends their week.
**Less time on first drafts. More time specifying.** Specifying the decision a study has to unblock, before any instrument is written. Specifying the construct definitions that the instrument and the analysis both have to share. Specifying the evidence standard that will count as *we know enough.*
**Less time producing artifacts. More time auditing them.** Treating an AI-drafted guide, screener, codebook, or readout as a defendant, not a deliverable. What is missing? What construct has drifted? Whose voice is absent? What question is the artifact answering that nobody actually asked?
**Less time on methods recall. More time on methods match-making.** The skill is no longer remembering what a critical incident technique looks like in procedure. The LLM has that. The skill is knowing when CIT is the right tool for the question on the table, and when a diary study, a switch interview, or a think-aloud would buy more decision-relevant evidence.
**Less time finishing decks. More time framing what the deck has to do.** What decision is on the table? What is the executive afraid of? What finding, if true, would change the roadmap, and what finding would not? What are we choosing *not* to include, and why?
**Less individual production. More apprenticeship.** The evaluation skills that used to transfer implicitly have to transfer explicitly now. That is a leadership task, and it is on the senior tier of the profession to figure it out.
None of this is glamorous. None of it produces the satisfying artifact-shaped output that used to be the felt reward of the work. But all of it is the work that actually moves a research practice from cost center to revenue driver, and it is all work the AI cannot do unsupervised.
## A Closing Invitation

	If you are tired of trying to defend everything, you have permission to stop.

Pick the three skills that govern your judgment. Mine, this year, are construct operationalization, decision-framing for stakeholders, and live sense-making in unmoderated sessions. They are not the skills I am best at. They are the skills I most want to compound. I am going to put my practice budget there. I am going to let the AI take a much larger share of the production work, and I am going to spend the time I save on getting better at evaluation. I expect this to be uncomfortable for a while. I expect to grieve the visible craft, the way you grieve any identity you outgrow.
If you do this, you are not abandoning the craft. You are finally being asked to do it without the artifact as cover. That is harder. It is also more honest. The craft was always in the judgment, and the judgment is what is left.
The right question was never *how do I keep my skills.* It was always *which skills are worth keeping.* The answer to that question, today, is shorter than it used to be, and that is not a loss. That is the work finally showing itself.
---

projects/uxr-blog/blog-db/the-first-step.title: Upgrade your resume by learning Google Sheets Query in 5 minutes
projects/uxr-blog/blog-db/the-first-step.content:
The first step to improving your quantitative skillset
If you ever wanted to up-level your quantitative analysis skills or become a quantitative UX Researcher but didn’t know where to start, Google Sheets Query is your answer.
It combines SQL’s power with Google Sheet’s ease of use and accessibility, letting you unlock insights from your data in minutes. By learning GS Query, your analysis workflow will be streamlined and stress-free, you’ll boost your career prospects by adding an attractive skill, and you’ll open the door to learning other programming or querying languages.
A bit of backstory first… SQL (pronounced as either “S-Q-L” or “Sequel”, but I prefer the latter) is a language used to retrieve or modify data in relational databases. GS Query is like SQL’s friendly cousin. It has many of the same functions and uses similar syntax and structure. Once you master GS Query, SQL becomes a breeze – and your resume moves up a tier.
Getting Started
For this tutorial, I’m using a modified version of the Qualtrics CSAT survey template, which includes an additional question about which product modules respondents use.
You can take the original survey here to see the layout and questions.
To get started, create a new Google Sheet with three tabs: 

Raw Results - where you’ll paste the survey data
Cleaned Results- where we’ll organize the data
Summary - for our final analysis
Copy the data in the Raw Results tab in this Google Sheet and paste them in your Raw Results. 

Select the Columns
The most consistent way to build a query is to first select the data range to see all of the data. Then, select the columns you need and any filters on the data you want. Finally, use any summarization or aggregation functions (avg, min, max, group by, etc.) you need to get your final result.
The first query you’ll use will be in the Cleaned Results tab, and it will looks like this =QUERY('Raw Results'!A:U,,3) . The first part, (’Raw Results’!A:U), is the data range, the second is the query (which we will leave blank at first), and the last is the number of rows included in your header (three in our case).
Here’s what our first output looks like:

Next, we’ll edit that query to select the columns that we’ll need to analyze; 
=QUERY('Raw Results'!A:U,"select I, R, S, T, U where I is not null",3)
So, the output should look like this:

Not so scary, right? We’re selecting the columns for response_id, satisfaction scores (CSAT), NPS, which product modules the user pays for, and the open-text response at the end of the survey. The last part, where I is not null, a condition statement that filters out any rows without a response_id.
Calculating CSAT
Per Qualtrics, the formula for CSAT is;
(Number of satisfied customers (4 and 5) / Number of survey responses) x 100

Our final queries will be in the `Summary` tab, pulling data from our `Cleaned Results` tab. This compartmentalized approach simplifies each query which makes any troubleshooting much easier and allows for seamless integration of typical Google Sheet formulas with query results down the road. Use this same approach to create your own queries in the future.

First, select the columns we need, in our case the CSAT scores in column B of the `Cleaned Results` tab. Then, show only the responses of 4 or 5. We do this using the `where` function again, followed by some logic;
```sql
=QUERY('Cleaned Results'!A:D,"select B where B>=4",1)
```

If your data is text instead of numbers, your query could look like this;
```sql
=QUERY('Cleaned Results'!A:D,"select B where B='Satisfied' or B='Extremely Satisfied' ",1)
```

Next, we add a `count` to that query to find the number of responses who were satisfied with their experience;
```sql
=QUERY('Cleaned Results'!A:D,"select count(B) where B>=4",1)
```

Next, we need the total number of responses. The easiest way will be to add another query in the cell next to your previous one. This will be the same query but with a different condition statement;
```sql
=QUERY('Cleaned Results'!A:D,"select count(B) where B is not null",1)
```

Now we can calculate the CSAT in the next empty cell by finding the percent of responses who select 4 or 5 out of the total responses. This will look something like;
```notion formula
=A2/B2
```

The final result will look like this:

You now have your CSAT Score! CSAT scores are great for delivering results to stakeholders. But what if you want to actually impress them?
## One Step Farther..
A common goal for stakeholders is to understand how the experience differs across various groups of users or, in our case, different product modules. In Qualtrics’ results feature, this is typically when I run into problems that cause delays. So instead, I use use a query with a `group by` function.

To do this, use a new cell in the summary tab and copy the previous query that looks at respondents who selected 4 or 5 for satisfaction. Don't hesitate to reuse existing queries—whether they're from your previous work, found online, or generated by AI. Now add the product modules column to our `select` and `group by` functions. The query should look like this;
```sql
=QUERY('Cleaned Results'!A:D,"select D, count(B) where B>=4 group by D",1)
```

Since we want to calculate the percentage for each product module, we need to copy the query that counts total responses and add the same `select` and `group by` statements. The query should look like this:
```sql
=QUERY('Cleaned Results'!A:D,"select D, count(B) where B is not null group by D",1)
```

Now, you can add a formula to find the percent of satisfied responses out of the total responses for each product module and drag it down each row.
```notion formula
=B6/D6
```

The grouped output will look something like this;
![Screenshot of ‘Summary’ tab showing final CSAT, grouped by Product Modules.](prod-files-secure.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/b79521c0-6f03-4409-8172-5ecba799b7c2/d17bae23-aa69-48ed-b407-1d6f90cba42d/image.png%2F20261114%2Fus-west-2%2Fs3%2Faws4_request&X-Amz-Date=20261114T000840Z&X-Amz-Expires=3600&X-Amz-Security-Token=IQoJb3JpZ2luX2VjEMP%2F%2F%2F%2F%2F%2F%2F%2F%2F%2FwEaCXVzLXdlc3QtMiJGMEQCIDs0PWREPo8QxpZFu7CXp8bTEgIjdpfbFaHjK0NyNQk9AiBxp7RRC0gMnOqfAWOqqt1fYTgcIgT0pTa3dAvDi6XVoSqIBAiM%2F%2F%2F%2F%2F%2F%2F%2F%2F%2F8BEAAaDDYzNzQyMzE4MzgwNSIMzvVFkjynHUHp1SJNKtwDPQK7D%2Faghz2FCc%2FUnQoRD%2BL5m2DmYdzs3ANI2Q8DtUkZZULjrAKIxAX%2F3SLM9%2Fwz4%2BoxZHs69fBTsUlsjkRS%2Fe1TFvPwM3x63FZy2a5tv6EqIkb%2FqsjekMztcQub86u63ac%2FS43kNdvTFMv0npOw4ZKXdUwdEzuj01EA7EPFGH0Zis6Hb3FgtieFEtiDG%2Bc9tdN5Hjf9S0QuXK3LMNW%2F1sTW3c94WSz%2FqC%2BZYg02UapYXNNH96gcN9p%2Bb33jWT9BfB1nJ7CakmiI5d3OYgdIb6hQcpkDOozZuXiClOfTdbg6ma4Z6RW8pI%2FZyuVdjVpYC%2FwEEUjaOjSnXjleNIUA%2FVTfDCLoSjWlb68Nw8WEVXH77MSKuaRZ0I0kDt6KDRykKlQAYTVfuGnixlvnrcFBU31ebZz4F1cEg%2BDkNb9cy%2BPSbBgBwppTMI%2FWUj6WvtGD%2Bk3eJzTziDlAZJnm3VL8MZm9i38PGoAtv6fwCJiMsPW%2FXYpSM9nR8DT4nbKg%2BeDPd9Wm1ZfK6Yr8n12VGi%2BFINs1m3TxkhQe97FIezgA%2B88AjHjTCIP87FGSi09ANXv1zI4rHkjG4BM06Ryoo1axaOQRPYUC4jZ4cDoudLJ%2FwPeDYlWjjTTzHT67hYQwjbfd1wY6pgHnY0wye5hWCnr2OOXMA3AAiY2lrERj8292yW5Bu5csO98E5Sv7RVRCGXZUQg6uJdmBM%2FC3AY7iQMZiRwG5hBmxufzryrad0kBRC09Yw%2FqyI%2BMUKW7DZPUUzAOpnAGdkSNxhSMXqfJv7r5XBVvGBsrFe%2Bekzqz7xumrXAqsUIVfOZuig10AJIdAu4C8ZibGfReCeBIlRT%2FJtSv8JWxXQVx1q%2BMpCu68&X-Amz-Signature=437d397564dd59fc64f696a6c01857dc57c0a4fdd7304b5b7836acb74d864859&X-Amz-SignedHeaders=host&x-amz-checksum-mode=ENABLED&x-id=GetObject#notion_record=block.187ef56c-b23c-808a-9ef4-fe6974978dd4.b79521c0-6f03-4409-8172-5ecba799b7c2)

Ta-da! The data clearly shows that respondents using Product Modules 2 and 4 have a worse experience compared to other modules. You can hide distracting columns, create charts, or add conditional formatting to guide the reader's attention and focus on the actionable insights so the data speaks for itself—all of which I will cover soon.
## Labeling Columns
If you’re wondering how I made the column names easier to read in the previous queries, you can look towards the `label` function. You can add `label D 'Product Modules', count(B) 'Number of Satisfied Respondents'` to the end of the query like this;
```sql
=QUERY('Cleaned Results'!A:D,"select D, count(B) where B=4 OR B=5 group by D label D 'Product Modules', count(B) 'Number of Satisfied Respondents'",1)
```
## Pro Tip
One of the benefits of this method is that you can do this using computer-generated data from Qualtrics ***before* **you actually begin collection.  Go to Tools \> Generate test responses, and enter the number of responses you want (I recommend \~20-50).

## Extending these skills
The `count` and `group by` functions are the two most powerful tools for beginning data analysts, as they can answer 70% of common stakeholder questions. You can expand your queries to include additional groups or create multiple queries in a single sheet to build live data dashboards.
After mastering the `count` and `group by` functions, you can explore functions such as `avg`, `min`, `max`, and `sum` to extract deeper insights from your data—quickly enough to earn yourself a bonus nap. By following a structured approach that includes selecting columns, applying conditions, adding functions, and using standard workbook features, you will be able to build complex queries with minimal headaches.

Additional Resources
If you’re interested in learning more right now, I found [this is helpful resource](spreadsheetpoint.com/formulas/google-sheets-query-function/) with many practical examples.

This quick guide shows how to use Google Sheets Query to analyze CSAT scores across product modules in just 5 minutes. Google Sheets Query is a user-friendly language that can launch you toward mastering more advanced skills like SQL.

projects/uxr-blog/blog-db/the-quiet-cost.title: Why You Keep Replaying That Meeting
projects/uxr-blog/blog-db/the-quiet-cost.content:
**Meta description:** Second-guessing isn't weakness. It's your instincts catching up to what you saw. Here's how to turn the loop into a lesson and close the tab.
	**Primary keyword:** how to stop second-guessing yourself at work

The meeting ended two hours ago. Your laptop is closed. Slack is quiet. But you are still in the room.
You are still in the moment where you started to say something and pulled it back. You are still in the quiet after your idea landed and nobody picked it up. You are still running the conversation, rewriting your lines, trying on a version of yourself who would have held the room.
You did not stay late tonight. The meeting did.
## The quiet cost of circling
Here is the part that matters, and then we can stop talking about it.
Not all self-examination is the same. Psychologists Paul Trapnell and Jennifer Campbell drew a clean line between two kinds of inward attention that look identical from the outside. **Reflection** is curiosity turned on yourself. **Rumination** is self-punishment wearing a reasonable coat. Both produce thought. Only one produces change \[1\].
Follow-up research found the loop can actually cancel the upside. Hiroaki Takano and Yoshihiko Tanno showed that when rumination rides alongside reflection, it quietly wipes out reflection's adaptive effect \[2\]. The self-knowledge accumulates; the life does not.
This is the cost of circling. You come away more expert on what happened and no closer to what you want to do about it. You pay rent on a room you already left.
That is the logical case. The rest of this piece is about something else.
## Your gut saw more than you did
Here is what second-guessing actually is, before anyone told you to be ashamed of it.
Somewhere in that meeting, your body noticed a gap. A pattern your words could not yet carry. The feature was not quite right. The stakeholder was not really asking the question she was asking. The confidence in the room was thinner than the certainty. You knew it before you could say it.
Then the moment passed. Someone moved to the next slide. You nodded. And now, hours later, the gap is still there, still humming, still asking you to look at it.
That hum is not weakness. It is signal. Your nervous system is a pattern-matching engine that sees more than it can caption. The replay you hate is the engine trying to caption what it saw. Sometimes the caption is: *I saw more than I said.* Sometimes it is: *I saw less than I thought.* Sometimes it is: *A piece was missing, and I am only now noticing the shape of what was missing.*
None of these are failures. They are all the same thing. Your intuition is catching up with the room.
## The mismatch is the message
If the loop is a signal, then the question changes.
You have been asking *was I wrong?* That is the wrong question because it has only two answers and neither of them helps. Try a different one: *What did my body notice that my words could not carry?*
This is not a softer question. It is a more precise one. You are no longer trying to litigate the past. You are trying to surface what your intuition was pointing at when it did not have time to explain itself.
Psychologists Neal Roese and Kai Epstude spent years on what the brain actually does when it runs these "what if" loops. They call them counterfactuals, and the functional theory they built says counterfactuals are not malfunctions. They are goal-directed cognition \[3\]. Aimed at something you can change next time, they become rehearsal. Aimed at something you cannot change, they become a cage.
The replay wants a job. Give it one. Ask it what it saw. Then ask what a version of you with that information would do tomorrow.
## Compassion is not a softer standard. It's a sharper one.
Here is the counterintuitive part, and it is the heart of the piece.
You cannot see clearly while you are also punishing yourself for not seeing sooner.
The self-criticism feels productive. It feels like you are taking the mistake seriously, holding yourself accountable, refusing to let yourself off the hook. It is none of those things. It is a flinch. It is your nervous system turning away from the exact data you need to look at, dressed up as discipline.
The research is blunt about this. Kristin Neff and colleagues have shown across two decades that self-criticism is a transdiagnostic risk factor, a predictor of almost every flavor of distress, while self-compassion is one of the most durable resilience factors in the literature \[4\]. Not because compassion feels nicer. Because it creates the conditions under which you can actually look at what happened without flinching.
Think about the last time someone you love made a serious mistake. You did not soften your honesty. You softened your delivery. The honesty was the point; the warmth was what made the honesty land. You are capable of holding a high standard and holding a person at the same time. You do it for other people every week.
The standard you hold for yourself does not get sharper when you make yourself smaller. It gets sharper when you make yourself safe enough to look.
## From loop to lesson
So what do you actually do when you are at your desk, and the meeting will not end?
Not nothing. The loop is asking to be used. The only justification for staying with the thought is to extract something you can carry. Self-growth. A shift in how you see the system. A change in intent. A new goal. If the thought cannot produce one of those, it is not working and you can let it go. If it can, sit with it long enough to name it.
Four questions do most of the work:
1. **What did I see that I did not name?** The pattern your body caught and your words missed.
2. **What did the room see that I did not?** The perspective you only have access to now.
3. **What would a more honest version of me have done, specifically?** Not a better self. A more honest one.
4. **What does this tell me about who I want to be the next time I am in a room like that?** The goal under the goal.
Write one sentence that answers whichever question has the most pull. One sentence. That is the lesson.
This move has a clinical name. Psychologists call it cognitive reappraisal, and in workplace studies it correlates with lower negative affect and higher job performance over time \[5\]. In plain language, it is the difference between suffering and growth.
## Close the tab
The meeting is still over.
You are at your desk, the tab is still open, and you get to choose between two futures. In one, you replay the conversation a fifth time, a sixth, until you are tired enough to sleep and no wiser than you were at six. In the other, you write one sentence about what you learned, and you close the tab.
The sentence does not have to be profound. It just has to be true, and it has to be yours.
Then close the tab. Your best work is waiting for the energy you are spending here.
---
## References
1. Trapnell, P. D., & Campbell, J. D. (1999). Private self-consciousness and the five-factor model of personality: Distinguishing rumination from reflection. *Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 76*(2), 284–304. [doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.76.2.284](doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.76.2.284)
2. Takano, K., & Tanno, Y. (2009). Self-rumination, self-reflection, and depression: Self-rumination counteracts the adaptive effect of self-reflection. *Behaviour Research and Therapy, 47*(3), 260–264. [doi.org/10.1016/j.brat.2008.12.008](doi.org/10.1016/j.brat.2008.12.008)
3. Roese, N. J., & Epstude, K. (2017). The functional theory of counterfactual thinking: New evidence, new challenges, new insights. In J. M. Olson (Ed.), *Advances in Experimental Social Psychology* (Vol. 56, pp. 1–79). Elsevier Academic Press. [doi.org/10.1016/bs.aesp.2017.02.001](doi.org/10.1016/bs.aesp.2017.02.001)
4. Warren, R., Smeets, E., & Neff, K. D. (2016). Self-criticism and self-compassion: Risk and resilience for psychopathology. *Current Psychiatry, 15*(12), 18–32.
5. Zhu, Y., Tang, Y., & Frese, M. (2025). Cognitive reappraisal emotion regulation interventions in the workplace and their impact on job performance: An ecological momentary intervention approach. *Journal of Occupational and Organizational Psychology.* [doi.org/10.1111/joop.70020](doi.org/10.1111/joop.70020)
---

🎨 Visual Concept
	```markdown
# Scene Narrative
A mid-career designer sits alone at her desk in the blue-grey light after sundown. The laptop is closed but one browser tab still glows faintly through the translucent lid. Her head is turned slightly toward a half-open door behind her, as if she is still listening to the meeting that ended hours ago. Her desire: to know whether she was right. Her obstacle: the room is already empty. Before: a meeting full of faces and voices. Now: the aftermath, full of silence and her own thinking. After: the moment she decides whether to replay the conversation again or to write one sentence and close the tab.
Foreground + Background
Foreground: her hands resting still on the closed laptop, the faint glow of the open tab leaking around its edges. A small notebook open beside her, blank, with a pen resting across a single unwritten line. Background: through the half-open door, an empty conference room in low light, chairs pulled back unevenly, a whiteboard with half-erased diagrams. Scale favors the desk and her stillness; the meeting room recedes, smaller, behind her.
Emotion + Symbolism
Dominant emotion: quiet wrestling. Not anguish, not resolve. The moment before choosing. Cues: shoulders slightly forward, jaw relaxed but eyes unfocused, breath held a beat too long. Symbols: the closed laptop with a glowing tab (the thought that will not close), the blank notebook with waiting pen (the lesson not yet written), the empty meeting room behind her (the past she is physically past but not yet mentally past), the half-open door (the threshold between loop and learning).
Focal Priority & Viewer Stance
First the viewer notices her hands on the closed laptop and the glowing edge of the open tab. Second, her profile turned toward the door. Third, the empty meeting room fading behind her. Viewer position: detached, observing from slightly behind her shoulder, close enough to feel the stillness but outside her eyeline.
```

Ideas meet friction in the room: scope pushback, data objections, quiet overrides from leadership. Scales to anyone in tech who ships judgment calls for a living.
	
	Pain Points: Meetings end but don't end. She replays conversations on the walk home, at dinner, at 1 a.m. Oscillates between "I should have fought harder" and "maybe I was wrong." The loop eats creative energy before the next thing starts.

projects/uxr-blog/blog-db/thesis.title: The Measurement Crisis: Why Your UX Metrics Don't Work for AI Products
projects/uxr-blog/blog-db/thesis.content:
Thesis
Standard UX metrics (SUS, task success rate, time-on-task) assume deterministic interfaces with predictable outputs. AI products are probabilistic — the same input yields different outputs. We need a new measurement ontology grounded in signal detection theory: hits, misses, false alarms, and correct rejections.
Why Only You
AI Measurement Library + psychometric grounding + SLR capability. You can show practitioners exactly where standard metrics break and what to replace them with, backed by signal detection theory that’s in every Human Factors textbook but absent from UX practice.
Enters Conversation

Dynamic/Generative UI breaking traditional measurement (Forbes, Nielsen)
Maze: 42% of research teams struggle to connect research to business outcomes
Lyssna: AI-assisted synthesis adopted by 88% but judgment operationalization missing

Builds On
AI Measurement Library, How to Automate UX Heuristic Evaluations
Suggested Depth
deep (strong SLR candidate)

projects/uxr-blog/blog-db/ux-researcher,.content:
UX Researcher, Quantitative
Greater Seattle Area | oliver.researching@gmail.com | linkedin.com/in/michaeleoliver
Summary
Seven-plus years running research end to end for enterprise SaaS, developer tools, and security: survey science, validated trust measurement, and human evaluation of AI systems. I design studies that decide things: sample plans set by precision needs, decision rules committed before fielding, and findings presented as recommendations with effect sizes and confidence, not adjectives. I read the SQL, R, and Python myself, I build AI tooling into my own workflow (LLM baselines, provenance checks), and I validate every machine-assisted output against human judgment. Recent through-line: how enterprises come to trust, or refuse, AI-driven guidance, published and practiced.
Experience
AuditBoard (SaaS, GRC)
Staff UX Researcher (first embedded UX researcher; grew the practice solo into a four-person team)

Built the research practice 0 to 1: generative discovery, rapid evaluative sprints, competitive benchmarking, behavioral analytics.
Ran 30+ interviews with customers, non-customers, and director-level stakeholders, synthesized into nine jobs to be done and three vision stories. Those became the product organization’s top three priorities and anchored a board-level plan to 3x revenue in five years.
Studied trust in AI-flagged risk decisions with the Critical Decision Method: why reviewers adopt, override, or ignore AI guidance. Findings became design principles for calibrated reliance, the question of whether user trust matches how reliable the system actually is.
Built a continuous benchmarking program that cut study cycles from eight weeks to four; directors then mandated the 80/100 usability score for every new product launch.
Shipped the first research repository and intake workflow, then set the standards that let non-researchers run sound templated studies themselves.
Designed scenario-based hiring protocols that screened for reasoning over polish; interim manager of the four-person team for six months.

GitLab (developer tools, enterprise)
Senior UX Researcher, Security

Designed and ran an Outcome-Driven Innovation survey that surfaced 25+ application security opportunities, prioritized across eight market segments; the prioritization changed the strategic roadmaps for three feature groups.
Built six security personas from 20+ interviews, each tied to benchmarkable tasks and design principles; template published for repeat use.
Ran the first research on GitLab Docs: two annual surveys with 1,200+ responses, followed by qualitative probes on exactly the anomalies the numbers surfaced.

Higher Logic (community SaaS)
Senior UX Researcher / UX Researcher

Built and validated the Engagement Benchmarking Score (EBS): an instrument grounded in expert interviews and statistical modeling, integrated into the product dashboard. Segmentation research on firmographics and add-ons fed the 2021 Engagement Benchmarking Report, which generated over $1 million ARR in its first year.
Rebuilt search UX from SQL usage-data analysis and rapid iterative testing: a 15-point SUS increase inside a fixed budget.
Ran NLP (topic modeling, sentiment) over 1,200+ open-response entries, converting free text into trackable themes.

Methods

Survey design with sample plans set by precision needs; instrument design and bias control; segmentation and experimental design basics, A/B testing, usability benchmarking.
Conjoint trade-off study designs for features, benefits, and messaging questions.
Interviews, Critical Decision Method, and jobs to be done for decision research; hierarchical task analysis for behavior.
Data science: SQL, R, Python; NLP on open text; model behavior evaluated against human baselines.
Research operations: repository, intake and prioritization, reusable templates, coaching non-researchers and junior researchers.

Human evaluation of AI systems

Benchmarked classifiers against LLM baselines for feedback labeling, with multi-annotator agreement analysis.
Published, October 2026: “Why UX Researchers Undertrust AI Synthesis” on the adoption-trust gap, calibrated reliance, and the provenance demands that gate AI adoption.

Education
M.A. Human Factors, George Mason University (2017, 2019)
B.A. Psychology, CSU Long Beach

projects/uxr-blog/blog-db/understanding-.title: Stats 101 Chapter 1: Measures of dispersion central tendency, generalization and approximation mean
projects/uxr-blog/blog-db/understanding-.content:
Understanding Data’s Story: Central Tendency & Dispersion in Statistics
In the world of social science, statistics serves as our lens to understand what we cannot directly observe. From human behavior to economic trends, researchers use sampling to reveal patterns in populations through two key concepts: central tendency and dispersion.
Central Tendency: Finding the Center
Think of central tendency as the “typical” value in your data. Let’s explore three main ways to find it:
1. The Mean (Average)
The mean is your classic mathematical average - sum everything up and divide by the count. For instance, if five people earn between $30k and $70k, the mean income is $50k. But watch out - extreme values can pull this number in misleading directions.
2. The Median (Middle Value)
The median sits right in the middle when you line up all your numbers. Take these household incomes: 45k, 48k, 50k, 52k, 55k. The median is $50k - perfect for data with outliers like housing prices.
3. The Mode (Most Common)
The mode is simply what shows up most often. In election data, it tells you which party got the most votes.
Dispersion: Understanding the Spread
But knowing the center isn’t enough - we need to understand how data spreads out around it.
1. Basic Range
The range is your quickest measure - just subtract the smallest value from the largest. If test scores run from 65 to 95, your range is 30 points.
2. Interquartile Range (IQR)
The IQR focuses on the middle 50% of your data. Take these ages: 22, 25, 28, 30, 35. The IQR is 5 years (30 minus 25), showing where most values cluster while ignoring outliers.
3. Standard Deviation & Variance
These give us precision. Variance measures average squared differences from the mean, while standard deviation (SD) brings it back to our original scale. In a normal distribution, about 68% of data falls within one SD of the mean, and 95% within two.
From Sample to Population: Making the Connection
Your population is everyone you’re studying - like all US voters. Since measuring everyone is usually impossible, we take samples to estimate population parameters. For example, finding a sample mean income of $55k with an SD of $15k suggests most population incomes fall between $40k and $70k.
The Bottom Line
Statistics isn’t about finding exact answers - it’s about understanding uncertainty. When you see statistics in headlines, ask about the spread and methodology. Was the sample representative? Could there be bias?
In our next article, we’ll explore how these concepts help us understand relationships between variables, like education levels and crime rates.

Food for Thought: Consider a city where the median rent is $2k with an SD of $1k. What might this tell us about housing inequality?

projects/uxr-blog/blog-db/upgrade-your-r.title: Upgrade your resume by learning Google Sheets Query in 5 minutes
projects/uxr-blog/blog-db/upgrade-your-r.content:
The first step to improving your quantitative skillset
If you ever wanted to up-level your quantitative analysis skills or become a quantitative UX Researcher but didn’t know where to start, Google Sheets Query is your answer.
It combines SQL’s power with Google Sheet’s ease of use and accessibility, letting you unlock insights from your data in minutes. By learning GS Query, your analysis workflow will be streamlined and stress-free, you’ll boost your career prospects by adding an attractive skill, and you’ll open the door to learning other programming or querying languages.
A bit of backstory first… SQL (pronounced as either “S-Q-L” or “Sequel”, but I prefer the latter) is a language used to retrieve or modify data in relational databases. GS Query is like SQL’s friendly cousin. It has many of the same functions and uses similar syntax and structure. Once you master GS Query, SQL becomes a breeze – and your resume moves up a tier.
Getting Started
For this tutorial, I’m using a modified version of the Qualtrics CSAT survey template, which includes an additional question about which product modules respondents use.
You can take the original survey here to see the layout and questions.
To get started, create a new Google Sheet with three tabs: 

Raw Results - where you’ll paste the survey data
Cleaned Results- where we’ll organize the data
Summary - for our final analysis
Copy the data in the Raw Results tab in this Google Sheet and paste them in your Raw Results. 

Select the Columns
The most consistent way to build a query is to first select the data range to see all of the data. Then, select the columns you need and any filters on the data you want. Finally, use any summarization or aggregation functions (avg, min, max, group by, etc.) you need to get your final result.
The first query you’ll use will be in the Cleaned Results tab, and it will looks like this =QUERY('Raw Results'!A:U,,3) . The first part, (’Raw Results’!A:U), is the data range, the second is the query (which we will leave blank at first), and the last is the number of rows included in your header (three in our case).
Here’s what our first output looks like:

Next, we’ll edit that query to select the columns that we’ll need to analyze; 
=QUERY('Raw Results'!A:U,"select I, R, S, T, U where I is not null",3)
So, the output should look like this:

Not so scary, right? We’re selecting the columns for response_id, satisfaction scores (CSAT), NPS, which product modules the user pays for, and the open-text response at the end of the survey. The last part, where I is not null, a condition statement that filters out any rows without a response_id.
Calculating CSAT
Per Qualtrics, the formula for CSAT is;
(Number of satisfied customers (4 and 5) / Number of survey responses) x 100

Our final queries will be in the `Summary` tab, pulling data from our `Cleaned Results` tab. This compartmentalized approach simplifies each query which makes any troubleshooting much easier and allows for seamless integration of typical Google Sheet formulas with query results down the road. Use this same approach to create your own queries in the future.

First, select the columns we need, in our case the CSAT scores in column B of the `Cleaned Results` tab. Then, show only the responses of 4 or 5. We do this using the `where` function again, followed by some logic;
```sql
=QUERY('Cleaned Results'!A:D,"select B where B>=4",1)
```

If your data is text instead of numbers, your query could look like this;
```sql
=QUERY('Cleaned Results'!A:D,"select B where B='Satisfied' or B='Extremely Satisfied' ",1)
```

Next, we add a `count` to that query to find the number of responses who were satisfied with their experience;
```sql
=QUERY('Cleaned Results'!A:D,"select count(B) where B>=4",1)
```

Next, we need the total number of responses. The easiest way will be to add another query in the cell next to your previous one. This will be the same query but with a different condition statement;
```sql
=QUERY('Cleaned Results'!A:D,"select count(B) where B is not null",1)
```

Now we can calculate the CSAT in the next empty cell by finding the percent of responses who select 4 or 5 out of the total responses. This will look something like;
```notion formula
=A2/B2
```

The final result will look like this:
![Screenshot of ‘Summary’ tab showing final ](prod-files-secure.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/b79521c0-6f03-4409-8172-5ecba799b7c2/ad852d11-98d9-4707-a480-6aee37faaa2d/image.png%2F20261115%2Fus-west-2%2Fs3%2Faws4_request&X-Amz-Date=20261115T171225Z&X-Amz-Expires=3600&X-Amz-Security-Token=IQoJb3JpZ2luX2VjEPH%2F%2F%2F%2F%2F%2F%2F%2F%2F%2FwEaCXVzLXdlc3QtMiJGMEQCIDOiouudGAnzlUqnuLdogg6m4M1HUeePK8wD4JhCVbSaAiAieM3rOWj9pshpzzeAs%2FG9f5JPfVCh8jdJpRGAGP9QeyqIBAi5%2F%2F%2F%2F%2F%2F%2F%2F%2F%2F8BEAAaDDYzNzQyMzE4MzgwNSIMrwiMZhLKoG2qM6lPKtwDbKu%2FVgt%2FyiFQVeimTGc4eB44F4rzGRSiHrpfwIfnX6vuuw73SGzYoNJsyw7uWCxbfC9LcW18PmtjzSw%2BPNa%2Fe%2BKcj8yCMhMsO%2FFBRKbeQwyFlKdeKc3imPJtzIh9oefKZb0U%2FhCLupDkPeV8xKzoLcDsK3%2FwqyeODgAYKzJO5GH2TAPkQCeUpEfnEVp4ph%2FFACKppIGH9tf1WJc5C3wdPq93dH7iy6xKg%2F%2B24cbNDDqRI1bFHQY7%2BE8dEswESUSSj6VWeSOCpVzV2BRy7o834DJmBsXCU9obHSdkxsRWZmYqt8owHEie1gHXLgH5y%2B52UQ3ny5MCH1b%2BEXRrppDyqHdjpCQ5lp17bGZ33Ejlwv03dSxUv8bbD5nKge1rn7WHXRpTUgpK%2Fc18X91aGmeoXkquQsBihg4ywkaIU1a3SHzBTd8X8L5xGMh%2BPil9ohtvrMjlmXQ6CbVY7KPq5xHccsT6AtFIorWiT37mkFJDAeiL6fREg2ExdDvYLvXEmOKNniwQm7EkoxKl7ReSRsTKAHJFv0WMjVIGPp36abCRQ8Zh8k%2BiDFyEoThZ%2F7Dp9wcImsgkxG5UGjGPMDogBWOQyqbco%2FTkTGty2mWiTOXWcCdmRMz9b8JPzpS7%2Bq0wl8jn1wY6pgGBXAi0x2vWR4Lg2WzQC2XDzdOMeU81HrqM%2FipPoMTNq0h4XhWK6Af0omB1aMJiTqg6YGUhctS3xnu9zGrx7O0iHlSiTP7y0ctckezU7znPg2uHt9K%2FPI6HTiqOeqI4%2BRnMrc%2FD496cZwgNRHQ1hDJS42o2J8F%2Bg7YA5fsEFtr5YLnhFHhGbr9Ru5ts2KIg85hpgB8P%2FYqqtfxfdlNuHZZA0GbInN3U&X-Amz-Signature=69c542c1c9489c4ed877daeb9ebc5bf3ef3246630e5448c061d99efc9f9693e0&X-Amz-SignedHeaders=host&x-amz-checksum-mode=ENABLED&x-id=GetObject#notion_record=block.187ef56c-b23c-8020-9da2-f2e2feab02db.b79521c0-6f03-4409-8172-5ecba799b7c2)
You now have your CSAT Score! CSAT scores are great for delivering results to stakeholders. But what if you want to actually impress them?
## One Step Farther..
A common goal for stakeholders is to understand how the experience differs across various groups of users or, in our case, different product modules. In Qualtrics’ results feature, this is typically when I run into problems that cause delays. So instead, I use use a query with a `group by` function.

To do this, use a new cell in the summary tab and copy the previous query that looks at respondents who selected 4 or 5 for satisfaction. Don't hesitate to reuse existing queries—whether they're from your previous work, found online, or generated by AI. Now add the product modules column to our `select` and `group by` functions. The query should look like this;
```sql
=QUERY('Cleaned Results'!A:D,"select D, count(B) where B>=4 group by D",1)
```

Since we want to calculate the percentage for each product module, we need to copy the query that counts total responses and add the same `select` and `group by` statements. The query should look like this:
```sql
=QUERY('Cleaned Results'!A:D,"select D, count(B) where B is not null group by D",1)
```

Now, you can add a formula to find the percent of satisfied responses out of the total responses for each product module and drag it down each row.
```notion formula
=B6/D6
```

The grouped output will look something like this;
![Screenshot of ‘Summary’ tab showing final CSAT, grouped by Product Modules.](prod-files-secure.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/b79521c0-6f03-4409-8172-5ecba799b7c2/d17bae23-aa69-48ed-b407-1d6f90cba42d/image.png%2F20261115%2Fus-west-2%2Fs3%2Faws4_request&X-Amz-Date=20261115T171225Z&X-Amz-Expires=3600&X-Amz-Security-Token=IQoJb3JpZ2luX2VjEPH%2F%2F%2F%2F%2F%2F%2F%2F%2F%2FwEaCXVzLXdlc3QtMiJGMEQCIDOiouudGAnzlUqnuLdogg6m4M1HUeePK8wD4JhCVbSaAiAieM3rOWj9pshpzzeAs%2FG9f5JPfVCh8jdJpRGAGP9QeyqIBAi5%2F%2F%2F%2F%2F%2F%2F%2F%2F%2F8BEAAaDDYzNzQyMzE4MzgwNSIMrwiMZhLKoG2qM6lPKtwDbKu%2FVgt%2FyiFQVeimTGc4eB44F4rzGRSiHrpfwIfnX6vuuw73SGzYoNJsyw7uWCxbfC9LcW18PmtjzSw%2BPNa%2Fe%2BKcj8yCMhMsO%2FFBRKbeQwyFlKdeKc3imPJtzIh9oefKZb0U%2FhCLupDkPeV8xKzoLcDsK3%2FwqyeODgAYKzJO5GH2TAPkQCeUpEfnEVp4ph%2FFACKppIGH9tf1WJc5C3wdPq93dH7iy6xKg%2F%2B24cbNDDqRI1bFHQY7%2BE8dEswESUSSj6VWeSOCpVzV2BRy7o834DJmBsXCU9obHSdkxsRWZmYqt8owHEie1gHXLgH5y%2B52UQ3ny5MCH1b%2BEXRrppDyqHdjpCQ5lp17bGZ33Ejlwv03dSxUv8bbD5nKge1rn7WHXRpTUgpK%2Fc18X91aGmeoXkquQsBihg4ywkaIU1a3SHzBTd8X8L5xGMh%2BPil9ohtvrMjlmXQ6CbVY7KPq5xHccsT6AtFIorWiT37mkFJDAeiL6fREg2ExdDvYLvXEmOKNniwQm7EkoxKl7ReSRsTKAHJFv0WMjVIGPp36abCRQ8Zh8k%2BiDFyEoThZ%2F7Dp9wcImsgkxG5UGjGPMDogBWOQyqbco%2FTkTGty2mWiTOXWcCdmRMz9b8JPzpS7%2Bq0wl8jn1wY6pgGBXAi0x2vWR4Lg2WzQC2XDzdOMeU81HrqM%2FipPoMTNq0h4XhWK6Af0omB1aMJiTqg6YGUhctS3xnu9zGrx7O0iHlSiTP7y0ctckezU7znPg2uHt9K%2FPI6HTiqOeqI4%2BRnMrc%2FD496cZwgNRHQ1hDJS42o2J8F%2Bg7YA5fsEFtr5YLnhFHhGbr9Ru5ts2KIg85hpgB8P%2FYqqtfxfdlNuHZZA0GbInN3U&X-Amz-Signature=f166e83c4134b8a993d6d22e8c0a564f2237a71348f9c1aa8e7cdfeaf8456b92&X-Amz-SignedHeaders=host&x-amz-checksum-mode=ENABLED&x-id=GetObject#notion_record=block.187ef56c-b23c-808a-9ef4-fe6974978dd4.b79521c0-6f03-4409-8172-5ecba799b7c2)

Ta-da! The data clearly shows that respondents using Product Modules 2 and 4 have a worse experience compared to other modules. You can hide distracting columns, create charts, or add conditional formatting to guide the reader's attention and focus on the actionable insights so the data speaks for itself—all of which I will cover soon.
## Labeling Columns
If you’re wondering how I made the column names easier to read in the previous queries, you can look towards the `label` function. You can add `label D 'Product Modules', count(B) 'Number of Satisfied Respondents'` to the end of the query like this;
```sql
=QUERY('Cleaned Results'!A:D,"select D, count(B) where B=4 OR B=5 group by D label D 'Product Modules', count(B) 'Number of Satisfied Respondents'",1)
```
## Pro Tip
One of the benefits of this method is that you can do this using computer-generated data from Qualtrics ***before* **you actually begin collection.  Go to Tools \> Generate test responses, and enter the number of responses you want (I recommend \~20-50).

projects/uxr-blog/blog-db/upgrade-your-r.title: Upgrade your resume by learning Google Sheets Query in 5 minutes
projects/uxr-blog/blog-db/upgrade-your-r.content:
The first step to improving your quantitative skillset
If you ever wanted to up-level your quantitative analysis skills or become a quantitative UX Researcher but didn’t know where to start, Google Sheets Query is your answer.
It combines SQL’s power with Google Sheet’s ease of use and accessibility, letting you unlock insights from your data in minutes. By learning GS Query, your analysis workflow will be streamlined and stress-free, you’ll boost your career prospects by adding an attractive skill, and you’ll open the door to learning other programming or querying languages.
A bit of backstory first… SQL (pronounced as either “S-Q-L” or “Sequel”, but I prefer the latter) is a language used to retrieve or modify data in relational databases. GS Query is like SQL’s friendly cousin. It has many of the same functions and uses similar syntax and structure. Once you master GS Query, SQL becomes a breeze – and your resume moves up a tier.
Getting Started
For this tutorial, I’m using a modified version of the Qualtrics CSAT survey template, which includes an additional question about which product modules respondents use.
You can take the original survey here to see the layout and questions.
To get started, create a new Google Sheet with three tabs: 

Raw Results - where you’ll paste the survey data
Cleaned Results- where we’ll organize the data
Summary - for our final analysis
Copy the data in the Raw Results tab in this Google Sheet and paste them in your Raw Results. 

Select the Columns
The most consistent way to build a query is to first select the data range to see all of the data. Then, select the columns you need and any filters on the data you want. Finally, use any summarization or aggregation functions (avg, min, max, group by, etc.) you need to get your final result.
The first query you’ll use will be in the Cleaned Results tab, and it will looks like this =QUERY('Raw Results'!A:U,,3) . The first part, (’Raw Results’!A:U), is the data range, the second is the query (which we will leave blank at first), and the last is the number of rows included in your header (three in our case).
Here’s what our first output looks like:

Next, we’ll edit that query to select the columns that we’ll need to analyze; 
=QUERY('Raw Results'!A:U,"select I, R, S, T, U where I is not null",3)
So, the output should look like this:

Not so scary, right? We’re selecting the columns for response_id, satisfaction scores (CSAT), NPS, which product modules the user pays for, and the open-text response at the end of the survey. The last part, where I is not null, a condition statement that filters out any rows without a response_id.
Calculating CSAT
Per Qualtrics, the formula for CSAT is;
(Number of satisfied customers (4 and 5) / Number of survey responses) x 100

Our final queries will be in the `Summary` tab, pulling data from our `Cleaned Results` tab. This compartmentalized approach simplifies each query which makes any troubleshooting much easier and allows for seamless integration of typical Google Sheet formulas with query results down the road. Use this same approach to create your own queries in the future.

First, select the columns we need, in our case the CSAT scores in column B of the `Cleaned Results` tab. Then, show only the responses of 4 or 5. We do this using the `where` function again, followed by some logic;
```sql
=QUERY('Cleaned Results'!A:D,"select B where B>=4",1)
```

If your data is text instead of numbers, your query could look like this;
```sql
=QUERY('Cleaned Results'!A:D,"select B where B='Satisfied' or B='Extremely Satisfied' ",1)
```

Next, we add a `count` to that query to find the number of responses who were satisfied with their experience;
```sql
=QUERY('Cleaned Results'!A:D,"select count(B) where B>=4",1)
```

Next, we need the total number of responses. The easiest way will be to add another query in the cell next to your previous one. This will be the same query but with a different condition statement;
```sql
=QUERY('Cleaned Results'!A:D,"select count(B) where B is not null",1)
```

Now we can calculate the CSAT in the next empty cell by finding the percent of responses who select 4 or 5 out of the total responses. This will look something like;
```notion formula
=A2/B2
```

The final result will look like this:
![Screenshot of ‘Summary’ tab showing final ](prod-files-secure.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/b79521c0-6f03-4409-8172-5ecba799b7c2/ad852d11-98d9-4707-a480-6aee37faaa2d/image.png%2F20261114%2Fus-west-2%2Fs3%2Faws4_request&X-Amz-Date=20261114T000744Z&X-Amz-Expires=3600&X-Amz-Security-Token=IQoJb3JpZ2luX2VjEMP%2F%2F%2F%2F%2F%2F%2F%2F%2F%2FwEaCXVzLXdlc3QtMiJGMEQCIEAVP%2B3xSpNTkE4I3dtwQRUiKftkgecNO7T6dTpzl43oAiBza7rP%2BEZHtETXKXAg5tjc0dMIGSqaBUNmInDoRva%2FryqIBAiL%2F%2F%2F%2F%2F%2F%2F%2F%2F%2F8BEAAaDDYzNzQyMzE4MzgwNSIMq6WXMpmSsvQvaFJhKtwDvzHi0VNR5t0ZsMDxny2K4xYFng0EQR%2FcPyyfPBbQMc%2BJBhm4Vr34kphGgi639btxAeCUAsjjPxz0h6lvOelZRPG4JjolkdryftRkw1cqM8PhWIS%2B49aulU8MndsWikyhMkYNhQqxAyF5rqk0Vf7c7SzNPIGzlM2ix7%2Fkp%2FR%2BfSFuWLG%2BSUvb%2F9lEGIQOIX4cPfhNxpGy%2FN4pUi9TKGvze91qCqjqdXyOLae7%2Bmm0iS3WgJvHJ5OIqKkAiu2jiWe%2B0lxiUCXGnPC8%2BQOhJ0Q3ydiVXuwK48BccVdO89cum8stkU4iOPmTkTsXc%2Fi4TcYXa9yJN05d9Vd1rnZzL8fFHFK7GAnCd1Z7aUr%2FrhUH6%2BAX9gjQNpSoxykpAdPfbsVOxVtGN4%2FwvnFMPx9WiPMC9NsafWTHR7iZow%2FQInH6SEfMv5EeDU%2B0E8mB%2FsI3UplcWkCjr9zpabiTwjI%2Frnrciv5XFJyzwquLDZie1M1d4A15JkunpirjjkyPqy1Co0N8d%2FaSFOzcGziaRSAKL3xxC0vIz%2FMXU5L2N8bR4arH1cyxrRnIoWLloln4f%2FxIGMvzaTA0G3WMHKHGaCUkxOz2MEjc4B2IWJy3TsLkb135OFjE8k0jhn%2FcvZa0CacwkLfd1wY6pgFlL0vLGt52fpE5FNG%2B5Zels0JdCxR8sdhgp%2BMWJkL3eYcwnmld%2FPRmo1lOgwkvWtSiZ9%2FHU4a8OJYgTfbiToQLORaZ9IEBRURYn5zegYEHhQF2uUZh1Pw4vj7QAZUk9rezsLr0URQs%2BIqgwH2dJdLWyGQR%2BaW%2F2iAwXbAKL1JWCLjorw9iiEktMSRwmY2OoVm4zqBQjMLczitVdIN8ezJoaxgLKYEl&X-Amz-Signature=92e51a30478705ee06d28636d66dd051e441477f2d0af10ee61c4c99117828e0&X-Amz-SignedHeaders=host&x-amz-checksum-mode=ENABLED&x-id=GetObject#notion_record=block.187ef56c-b23c-8020-9da2-f2e2feab02db.b79521c0-6f03-4409-8172-5ecba799b7c2)
You now have your CSAT Score! CSAT scores are great for delivering results to stakeholders. But what if you want to actually impress them?
## One Step Farther..
A common goal for stakeholders is to understand how the experience differs across various groups of users or, in our case, different product modules. In Qualtrics’ results feature, this is typically when I run into problems that cause delays. So instead, I use use a query with a `group by` function.

To do this, use a new cell in the summary tab and copy the previous query that looks at respondents who selected 4 or 5 for satisfaction. Don't hesitate to reuse existing queries—whether they're from your previous work, found online, or generated by AI. Now add the product modules column to our `select` and `group by` functions. The query should look like this;
```sql
=QUERY('Cleaned Results'!A:D,"select D, count(B) where B>=4 group by D",1)
```

Since we want to calculate the percentage for each product module, we need to copy the query that counts total responses and add the same `select` and `group by` statements. The query should look like this:
```sql
=QUERY('Cleaned Results'!A:D,"select D, count(B) where B is not null group by D",1)
```

Now, you can add a formula to find the percent of satisfied responses out of the total responses for each product module and drag it down each row.
```notion formula
=B6/D6
```

The grouped output will look something like this;
![Screenshot of ‘Summary’ tab showing final CSAT, grouped by Product Modules.](prod-files-secure.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/b79521c0-6f03-4409-8172-5ecba799b7c2/d17bae23-aa69-48ed-b407-1d6f90cba42d/image.png%2F20261114%2Fus-west-2%2Fs3%2Faws4_request&X-Amz-Date=20261114T000744Z&X-Amz-Expires=3600&X-Amz-Security-Token=IQoJb3JpZ2luX2VjEMP%2F%2F%2F%2F%2F%2F%2F%2F%2F%2FwEaCXVzLXdlc3QtMiJGMEQCIEAVP%2B3xSpNTkE4I3dtwQRUiKftkgecNO7T6dTpzl43oAiBza7rP%2BEZHtETXKXAg5tjc0dMIGSqaBUNmInDoRva%2FryqIBAiL%2F%2F%2F%2F%2F%2F%2F%2F%2F%2F8BEAAaDDYzNzQyMzE4MzgwNSIMq6WXMpmSsvQvaFJhKtwDvzHi0VNR5t0ZsMDxny2K4xYFng0EQR%2FcPyyfPBbQMc%2BJBhm4Vr34kphGgi639btxAeCUAsjjPxz0h6lvOelZRPG4JjolkdryftRkw1cqM8PhWIS%2B49aulU8MndsWikyhMkYNhQqxAyF5rqk0Vf7c7SzNPIGzlM2ix7%2Fkp%2FR%2BfSFuWLG%2BSUvb%2F9lEGIQOIX4cPfhNxpGy%2FN4pUi9TKGvze91qCqjqdXyOLae7%2Bmm0iS3WgJvHJ5OIqKkAiu2jiWe%2B0lxiUCXGnPC8%2BQOhJ0Q3ydiVXuwK48BccVdO89cum8stkU4iOPmTkTsXc%2Fi4TcYXa9yJN05d9Vd1rnZzL8fFHFK7GAnCd1Z7aUr%2FrhUH6%2BAX9gjQNpSoxykpAdPfbsVOxVtGN4%2FwvnFMPx9WiPMC9NsafWTHR7iZow%2FQInH6SEfMv5EeDU%2B0E8mB%2FsI3UplcWkCjr9zpabiTwjI%2Frnrciv5XFJyzwquLDZie1M1d4A15JkunpirjjkyPqy1Co0N8d%2FaSFOzcGziaRSAKL3xxC0vIz%2FMXU5L2N8bR4arH1cyxrRnIoWLloln4f%2FxIGMvzaTA0G3WMHKHGaCUkxOz2MEjc4B2IWJy3TsLkb135OFjE8k0jhn%2FcvZa0CacwkLfd1wY6pgFlL0vLGt52fpE5FNG%2B5Zels0JdCxR8sdhgp%2BMWJkL3eYcwnmld%2FPRmo1lOgwkvWtSiZ9%2FHU4a8OJYgTfbiToQLORaZ9IEBRURYn5zegYEHhQF2uUZh1Pw4vj7QAZUk9rezsLr0URQs%2BIqgwH2dJdLWyGQR%2BaW%2F2iAwXbAKL1JWCLjorw9iiEktMSRwmY2OoVm4zqBQjMLczitVdIN8ezJoaxgLKYEl&X-Amz-Signature=fe110a19c2f9565a1189311b7de5f8544e31dd1c9b4c56661edcbdb402d4b305&X-Amz-SignedHeaders=host&x-amz-checksum-mode=ENABLED&x-id=GetObject#notion_record=block.187ef56c-b23c-808a-9ef4-fe6974978dd4.b79521c0-6f03-4409-8172-5ecba799b7c2)

Ta-da! The data clearly shows that respondents using Product Modules 2 and 4 have a worse experience compared to other modules. You can hide distracting columns, create charts, or add conditional formatting to guide the reader's attention and focus on the actionable insights so the data speaks for itself—all of which I will cover soon.
## Labeling Columns
If you’re wondering how I made the column names easier to read in the previous queries, you can look towards the `label` function. You can add `label D 'Product Modules', count(B) 'Number of Satisfied Respondents'` to the end of the query like this;
```sql
=QUERY('Cleaned Results'!A:D,"select D, count(B) where B=4 OR B=5 group by D label D 'Product Modules', count(B) 'Number of Satisfied Respondents'",1)
```

projects/uxr-blog/blog-db/what-is-an-age.title: What Is an Agentic Workflow? The Definition Cognitive Science Already Had
projects/uxr-blog/blog-db/what-is-an-age.content:
The AI industry spent two years defining “agentic workflow.” Cognitive scientists defined the same thing four decades ago. The gap between these two definitions is where most agentic systems fail.
The Agentic Workflow Definition Everyone Agrees On
An agentic workflow is a multi-step process where an AI agent breaks down a complex goal, reasons about how to achieve it, takes actions, and refines its approach through iteration.
That much should be familiar. Andrew Ng outlined four design patterns that anchor most implementations [1]: reflection (the agent critiques and improves its own output), tool use (the agent interacts with external systems and data), planning (the agent decomposes a complex task into manageable steps), and multi-agent collaboration (specialized agents coordinate to solve problems no single agent could handle alone).
The industry consensus is clear. IBM defines agentic workflows as “AI-driven processes where autonomous agents make decisions, take actions, and coordinate tasks with minimal human intervention” [2]. AWS, NVIDIA, and Atlassian offer variations on the same theme [3][4][5]. Every major tech company has published its version.
What these definitions share is a focus on what agentic workflows do: they reason, they plan, they act, they adapt. What they miss is why these particular patterns work. And understanding the “why” is how you build systems that don’t break in unpredictable ways.
The answer has been sitting in HCI textbooks since 1983.
What Cognitive Science Already Knew
The four patterns that define modern agentic workflows map directly to cognitive process models that researchers have studied, validated, and refined for decades. This isn’t a loose analogy. The structural parallels are precise enough to be useful.
GOMS: The Original Task Decomposition
In 1983, Stuart Card, Thomas Moran, and Allen Newell published The Psychology of Human-Computer Interaction, introducing the GOMS model: Goals, Operators, Methods, and Selection Rules [6]. GOMS describes how humans decompose complex tasks into hierarchical goal structures, select methods to achieve sub-goals, and execute operators (the atomic actions that actually change the world).
Read that list again: goals, operators, methods, selection rules. Now consider how you design an agentic workflow. You define a goal for the agent. You give it operators (tool calls, API actions, code execution). You specify methods (chains, strategies, prompts that achieve sub-goals). And you build selection rules (routing logic that chooses between methods based on context).
GOMS is the cognitive blueprint that agentic workflow architects have been unknowingly replicating. The model predicted, 40 years in advance, that any system performing complex tasks would need exactly these four components. Not because they are elegant engineering choices, but because they reflect the irreducible structure of goal-directed cognition.
ACT-R: The Production System Blueprint
John Robert Anderson’s ACT-R (Adaptive Control of Thought, Rational) is a cognitive architecture developed at Carnegie Mellon that models human cognition as a production system [7]. It has three core components: declarative memory (stored facts and knowledge), procedural memory (if-then production rules that govern behavior), and a pattern matcher that selects which production to fire based on the current state and expected utility.
This maps cleanly to agentic AI reasoning loops. An agent’s context window and retrieved knowledge function as declarative memory. Its instructions, system prompts, and behavioral rules function as procedural memory. And its action selection process (choosing which tool to call, which sub-agent to invoke, which strategy to pursue) is utility-based pattern matching.
ACT-R’s central finding is that every task a human performs consists of a series of discrete, irreducible cognitive operations [7]. Each operation retrieves relevant knowledge, matches it against the current situation, and fires the highest-utility production. This is precisely what happens in an agentic reasoning loop: perceive context, match patterns, select action, execute. The iterative, multi-step nature of agentic workflows isn’t an engineering preference. It’s a cognitive necessity.
Recognition-Primed Decision Making: Why Reflection Works
Gary Klein’s Recognition-Primed Decision (RPD) model, developed through studying how fireground commanders make decisions under extreme pressure, reveals something counterintuitive about expert decision-making [8]. Experts don’t compare options analytically. They recognize situational patterns from experience, mentally simulate a course of action, and if the simulation succeeds, they execute. If it fails, they modify and simulate again.
This is the reflection pattern in agentic AI. When an agent generates output, evaluates it against criteria, identifies problems, and iterates, it follows the exact cognitive sequence Klein documented in human experts. The RPD model explains why reflection produces such surprising performance gains. Ng noted that even simple self-critique implementations dramatically improve output quality [1]. Reflection works because it mirrors the cognitive process that distinguishes expert performance from novice performance: the ability to simulate outcomes before committing to action.
The RPD model also predicts when reflection will fail. Mental simulation depends on having accurate mental models of the domain. When an agent lacks sufficient context, or its training data doesn’t cover the problem space, reflection loops degenerate into confident-sounding confabulation. Klein’s framework gives architects a diagnostic: if your agent’s reflection cycles aren’t improving output, the problem isn’t the loop. It’s the model’s domain knowledge.
Distributed Cognition: The Multi-Agent Blueprint
Edwin Hutchins’ distributed cognition theory, developed through studying navigation teams aboard Navy ships, argues that cognition doesn’t happen exclusively inside individual heads [9]. It extends across people, tools, artifacts, and environments. The unit of analysis isn’t the individual thinker. It’s the entire cognitive system.
This directly explains why multi-agent collaboration works. When you distribute a complex task across specialized agents (a researcher, a writer, an editor, a fact-checker), you distribute cognitive load across a system in exactly the way Hutchins described. Each agent handles a cognitive sub-function that would overwhelm a single agent’s context and reasoning capacity. David Kirsh’s work on coordination and environment design [10] extends this: the structure of the workflow itself (how agents pass information, what artifacts they create, how they signal state) is part of the cognitive architecture.
Multi-agent collaboration isn’t just an engineering convenience for managing complexity. It’s a fundamental principle of how complex cognition operates. Hutchins’ theory also predicts the failure mode that plagues poorly designed multi-agent systems: when coordination mechanisms between agents break down, the distributed cognitive system fails, even if each individual agent performs well in isolation.
If you’re interested in how these cognitive principles play out in practical human-AI collaboration scenarios, Human*AI Augmented Decision Making: What It Actually Looks Like explores the applied side of this research.
What This Means for Anyone Building Agents
The convergence between cognitive science and agentic AI isn’t academic trivia. It’s a design resource.
Every one of Ng’s four agentic design patterns has a cognitive science precedent that predicts not just when it will work, but when and why it will fail. GOMS tells you that task decomposition must be hierarchical and goal-structured, not flat lists of steps. ACT-R tells you that action selection depends on the quality of the agent’s “declarative memory” (its context and retrieved knowledge). Klein’s RPD model tells you that reflection only improves output when the agent has sufficient domain models to simulate accurately. Hutchins tells you that multi-agent coordination artifacts matter as much as the agents themselves.
The architects building the most robust agentic systems aren’t necessarily the ones with the fanciest models. They’re the ones who, whether they realize it or not, apply the same structural principles cognitive science established decades ago. The question is whether you want to rediscover those principles through trial and error, or start with the blueprint.
For more on how cognitive load shapes the success and failure of AI-augmented workflows, see The Cognitive Load of AI: Why More Features Means Worse Decisions.
A Practical Definition Architects Can Use
Here is an agentic workflow defined through its cognitive foundations:

An agentic workflow is a goal-directed system that decomposes complex tasks into cognitive operations (perception, reasoning, action, evaluation), distributes those operations across specialized agents or modules, and iterates through reflection cycles that mirror human expert decision-making.

This definition gives you three design tests for any agentic system you build:

Cognitive clarity. Does each agent or module have a clear cognitive role? Can you name what it perceives, what it reasons about, what actions it takes, and what it evaluates?
Reflection integrity. Are reflection cycles built into the workflow architecture, not bolted on as an afterthought? Does the reflecting agent have sufficient domain knowledge to simulate outcomes accurately?
Distributed coherence. Is cognitive load distributed appropriately across agents? Are the coordination mechanisms (handoff artifacts, state signals, shared context) as well-designed as the agents themselves?
If you can answer yes to all three, you’re building on the same structural foundations that support expert human cognition. If you can’t, now you know where to look.
