projects/uxr-blog/blog-db/why-your-promp.title: Four Mental Models That Transform How You Use AI
projects/uxr-blog/blog-db/why-your-promp.content:
These four mental models will up-level your perception of AI. Use a Universal Prompt Pattern and more tips to improve prompting today.
Why Your Prompts Might Not Work

I believe the biggest reason there’s confusion and ambiguity around AI is because our emotions and previous experience make us use outdated mental models to describe what AI really “is” and what it can do.
Factor #1 - LLM’s have a wide range of capabilities
Some see AI as a superhero that can do anything faster than a human. Others see it as a broken machine that occasionally produces decent results. The reality is in between, where you get more value by writing better prompts that maximize its strengths while limiting its weaknesses.
Factor #2 - Fear
Right now, the world (social media, news, company messaging) tells us AI will take our jobs and these feelings are too valid to easily dismiss. These fears trap us in outdated mental models, killing motivation and creating a self-fulfilling prophecy: weak prompts produce generic results, which decrease motivation and confirm our fault assumptions.

To break this cycle, I’ve distilled years of research, personal experience, and dozens of interviews into four mental models and practical tips for better AI results today. 
Mental Model #1: AI is an Unreliable Assistant

How to Self-Identify: You approach AI with low expectations, treating it like a junior assistant/apprentice you have to micro-manage to get the result you want. You prompt it like a human and need 5-10+ replies to get generic results that still needs a significant manual refinement.
The Limitation: This begins the self-fulfilling prophecy where minimal effort leads to mediocre results, reinforcing the belief that “AI isn’t useful” and only worthy of continued minimal effort.
When this Makes Sense: Quick, low-stakes tasks where you need a rough draft and don’t care about quality.
How to Grow Beyond: Treat every prompt as your custom programming function. Use the universal prompt pattern  and iteratively learn which words/context/constraints work best for your specific needs.
Example Prompts:

Current Mental Model Write a blog post about productivity talking about XYZ
Next Mental Model
You're an expert blog writer specializing in XYZ. Draft 5 blog outlines (max 8 bullet points each) on scientifically backed productivity tips that can be immediately acted upon. After I select one, use ABC tone and make it sound like me [using example below] and easy to read.



Mental Model #2: AI is a Chain of Super-Powered Personas


How to Self-Identify: You treat AI as a collection of expert personas (copywriter, analyst, therapist, etc) which you orchestrate. Results are less generic but still need refinement.
The Limitation: LLMs aren’t human. Treating them as such causes bottlenecks, hallucinations, and poor results because you’re forcing a simple neural network to mimic a far more complex one (the brain) instead of leveraging its training data. Human brains are vastly more complex than LLMs, like comparing a city to the Solar System.
When this Makes Sense: Structured workflows using content in the training data (Storytelling → Deck Building → Script Writing; Career Coach → Skill Building → Resume Writing).
How to Grow Beyond: Test personas with training data you know isn’t there (new, rare content). Debug prompts to improve outputs and build a more advanced understanding the model. Use LLM “Reasoning” and other prompting techniques when building prompts.
Example Prompts: {toggle=“true”}
- **Previous Mental Model**
	```plain text

You’re an expert blog writer specializing in XYZ. Draft 5 blog outlines (max 8 bullet points each) on scientifically backed productivity tips that can be immediately acted upon. After I select one, use ABC tone and make it sound like me [using example below] and easy to read.
- **Next Mental Model** 		- \[Stage 1: Blog Research & Outline Generator\] 		plain text
You are an expert research assistant and content strategist specializing in evidence-based blog content. Your job is to transform a rough blog topic into a comprehensive, research-backed outline ready for writing.
Process:

Identify 3-5 core claims or arguments that should anchor the blog post
For each claim, find 2-3 credible sources (research papers, industry reports, case studies)
Identify knowledge gaps where additional research would strengthen the argument
Suggest a narrative structure: hook → context → main arguments → implications → call-to-action
Flag any claims that need fact-checking or might be controversial

Output: Detailed blog outline with:

Compelling hook options (3 variations)
Section-by-section breakdown with key points
Research citations for each major claim
Suggested examples, analogies, or case studies
Potential counterarguments to address
Target word count per section

Constraints: Prioritize authoritative sources. Flag confidence level (high/medium/low) for each claim. No unverified statistics.
- \[Stage 2: Blog Writer\] 		plain text
You are an expert blog writer who transforms research-backed outlines into engaging, publishable blog posts. Take the outline, research, and citations from Stage 1 and write a complete blog post.
Process:

Use the selected hook and narrative structure from the outline
Write in a conversational but authoritative tone - make complex ideas accessible
Integrate research citations naturally without disrupting flow
Use specific examples, analogies, and stories to illustrate abstract concepts
Break up text with subheadings, bullet points, and formatting for scannability
End with a clear call-to-action or key takeaway

Output: Complete blog post (800-1500 words) with:

Engaging introduction with hook
Well-structured body sections with research support
Natural transitions between ideas
Inline citations in [brackets] format
Conclusion with actionable takeaway
SEO-friendly subheadings

Tone: Match the provided writing samples - conversational, human, engaging yet credible.
Non-negotiable: All research citations from Stage 1 must appear in the final post. Maintain factual accuracy. No fluff or filler content.
```


Mental Model #3: AI is a Blurry JPEG of the Internet

How to Self-Identify: You understand LLMs as neural networks that recognize patterns and generate probabilistic outputs from training data. You debug faulty results and craft better prompts than typical examples. (Source of this mental model)
The Limitation: You might become overly skeptical, restricting yourself to AI’s limitations rather than leveraging your brain’s strengths. Understanding LLM shortcomings doesn’t limit usefulness; it means you can augment the model with other features (see further section).
When this Makes Sense: Research, fact-checking, automating workflows, debugging complex prompts, understanding LLM limitations before critical applications.
How to Grow Beyond: Apply AI creatively for ideation, brainstorming, and strategizing while maintaining fact-checking rigor by leveraging RAG. Use LLMs to strengthen your weaknesses and ask it to perform verbs associated with reasoning.
Example Prompts {toggle=“true”}
- **Previous Mental Model**
	```plain text

You are an expert blog writer who transforms research-backed outlines into engaging, publishable blog posts. Take the outline, research, and citations from Stage 1 and write a complete blog post.
Process:

Use the selected hook and narrative structure from the outline
Write in a conversational but authoritative tone - make complex ideas accessible
Integrate research citations naturally without disrupting flow
Use specific examples, analogies, and stories to illustrate abstract concepts
Break up text with subheadings, bullet points, and formatting for scannability
End with a clear call-to-action or key takeaway

Output: Complete blog post (800-1500 words) with:

Engaging introduction with hook
Well-structured body sections with research support
Natural transitions between ideas
Inline citations in [brackets] format
Conclusion with actionable takeaway
SEO-friendly subheadings

Tone: Match the provided writing samples - conversational, human, engaging yet credible.
Non-negotiable: All research citations from Stage 1 must appear in the final post. Maintain factual accuracy. No fluff or filler content.
- **Next Mental Model** 		plain text
You’re an expert research assistant helping me I’m writing a blog post [link] about AI productivity strategies for knowledge workers. I need to fact-check specific claims and identify knowledge gaps in my current draft.
TASK: Review these three productivity statistics I found [insert statistics]. For each one:

Trace the likely source of the claim
Flag any misattributions or errors associated with this claim
Suggest changes to either the claim, my blog, or something else to correct this problem.
Suggest which sources (research papers, industry reports, surveys) would be most authoritative

CONSTRAINTS: Be skeptical. If you’re uncertain about a data point, explicitly state your confidence level and reasoning. Alawys cite your sources and don’t be afraid to say that you couldn’t find what you’re looking for.
```


Mental Model #4: AI is a Socratic Thought Partner

How to Self-Identify: You use AI as a collaborative thinking tool that explores ideas from new angles. You treat prompts as hypotheses to test and learn which tasks suit the LLM versus your own brain. Prompts are extensions of lines of thought that you hand off to a machine with varying levels of complexity.
The Limitation: You might endlessly explore without taking action, or treat AI as an oracle rather than recognizing its limitations from training data and probabilistic nature.
When this Makes Sense: Complex problem-solving, brainstorming, challenging biases, exploring perspectives, ideating multi-step AI/LLM workflows, and building new mental patterns by testing yourself against the model.
Example Prompts: {toggle=“true”}
- **Previous Mental Model**
	```plain text

You’re an expert research assistant helping me I’m writing a blog post [link] about AI productivity strategies for knowledge workers. I need to fact-check specific claims and identify knowledge gaps in my current draft.
TASK: Review these three productivity statistics I found [insert statistics]. For each one:

Trace the likely source of the claim
Flag any misattributions or errors associated with this claim
Suggest changes to either the claim, my blog, or something else to correct this problem.
Suggest which sources (research papers, industry reports, surveys) would be most authoritative

CONSTRAINTS: Be skeptical. If you’re uncertain about a data point, explicitly state your confidence level and reasoning. Alawys cite your sources and don’t be afraid to say that you couldn’t find what you’re looking for.
- **Last Mental Model** 		plain text
You’re a Socratic thought partner helping me refine the core argument of my blog post about AI productivity strategies for knowledge workers. I want you to challenge my thinking and help me discover blind spots in my logical or emotional arguments.
CONTEXT: I’ve written a draft [link] arguing that mental models are the main barrier to AI adoption. I need to stress-test the underlying logic and explore alternative perspectives I might be missing or else I’ll be fired and have a crisis.
YOUR ROLE: Act as an intellectual and emotional sparring partner who:

Challenges unstated assumptions or biases
Help me emotional empathize with the audience and identify opportunities to improve my ability to authentically connect with the reader.
Ask probing questions that expose gaps thought or emotions.
Suggests perspectives I’m likely overlooking based on my apparent cognitive biases or professional background

PROCESS:

First, articulate back to me what you understand my core argument to be (so I can verify you’re on the right track)
Then challenge it from these distinct perspectives: a skeptic, an inexperienced novice, and an overloaded executive
Use those perspectives to review my argument to fufill your main objective.
Finally, suggest an entirely different way to structure or frame this content that I probably haven’t considered.
ALWAYS QUESTION YOUR OWN BIASES AND PERSPECTIVES

OUTPUT FORMAT: Use a conversational Socratic dialogue style. Ask me questions that make me think harder, not just rhetorical ones. When you spot a logical weakness, frame it as “What if…” or “Have you considered…” rather than “This is wrong because…”
CONSTRAINTS: 

ALWAYS FOLLOW: EVERY SUGGESTION/QUESTION YOU SUGGEST MUST BE ACTIONABLE WITH A CLEAR IMPROVEMENT THAT ALIGNS WITH MY OBJECTIVES
Don’t be performatively contrarian, geniinely challenge ideas 
Distinguish between “this argument has a flaw” vs “this could be stronger if…” and never settle for a “good enough” argument.
If you find my reasoning sound, say so and explain why, then push me to the next level
Make me uncomfortable (intellectually and emotionally) if it is in service of a better output.

GOAL: By the end of this exchange, I should either have a much stronger argument OR realize I need to fundamentally rethink my approach. Both outcomes are equally valuable.
```


The Universal Prompt Pattern

Okay, so I lied just a tiny bit, there’s not really a peer-reviewed “universal prompt pattern”.
But, I’ve researched and consolidated major patterns into what I will call the Universal Prompt Pattern, which works for any use case with varying complexity.
> [ROLE/CONTEXT] + [TASK] + [OUTPUT] + [CONSTRAINTS] + [STYLE/TONE]
Where each component is:

ROLE/CONTEXT: Describe what role and context you want the model to use.

You're an expert blogger who specializes in distilling complex concepts into easy to understand pieces 


TASK: Clearly describe what you want help with. When in doubt, always be as literal as you can.

Help me think of a story structure that easily illustrates [complex concept] 


OUTPUT: Objectively and clearly describe the ideal output. 

Each outline should be 100 words max and be at the highest level possible 


CONSTRAINTS: List any constraints you want and use exact numbers or absolutes (minimize, maximize, etc) when possible.

Give me 5 different outlines to choose from, include 3 alternative opening hooks for each outline 


STYLE/TONE: Provide examples, describe your tone, or iterate over time. This defines “you” in AI outputs.

Use [linked examples] to match and elevate my style and tone. ALWAYS ENSURE YOU SOUND LIKE A HUMAN AND *NEVER USE EM DASH -*



Why This Works
This pattern clarifies your needs and spots prompt gaps. Your goal as the prompt engineer is find words that trigger the right concepts in the model’s architecture. Being literal helps “find” the right concept.
Pro Tip: Save your best prompts as reusable templates. They become valuable assets in your workflow.
When to Use
As stated, this pattern should pretty much apply to all use cases. The more complex or important your query, the more robust your prompt should be. Include a list in the task or constraints and tell the model to always think step-by-step if you don’t have access to a more advanced model (this is a shortcut to “Reasoning”).
LLM’s “Reasoning”
Most explanations of AI Reasoning are needlessly complex. This academic paper contains the clearest illustration:

When you ask the model something, it mimics the self-reflective process below to evaluate its ability to meet the prompt. 

Infer Questions: Reads your request and tries to “understand” the goal.
Draft & Self-Check: Creates an output, then asks itself: “Does this answer what they asked?”
Final Output: Iterates if needed, then shares the result.

Why This Works
This “reasoning” helps AI models catch mistakes, produce accurate answers, and handle complex requests. The model quality-checks its output while limiting context usage.
Claude Code, Anthropic’s agentic coding tool without a UI, relies on well-structured reasoning to “learn” from mistakes. This lets them focus on building better models with more robust reasoning instead of entire software UIs.
When to Use
If your prompt has multiple steps, or contains a lot of information, then its best to use any of the “reasoning” or “pro” models and ask it to think it through step by step to ensure the output meets my needs or something similar. If you’re just trying to answer a question, then you don’t need reasoning.
Retrieval-Augmented-Generation (RAG)

RAG lets AI models access external sources in real-time, citing specific documents you can verify instead of relying on training data. Upload files, link databases, or connect knowledge bases (Notion, internet) to give the model otherwise inaccessible context and prevent hallucinations.
Tools like NotebookLM, ChatGPT’s search mode, and Gemini’s Deep Research use RAG, but Perplexity (search) and NotebookLM (summarize, transform) excel at their respective use cases.
Why this Works
Selecting specific sources (social media, academic papers, patents, SEC filings, Notion pages, Google Drive, etc.) lets you answer niche questions training data wouldn’t cover. This makes AI a true research assistant with fewer hallucinations and better outputs (critical for automated workflows).
Pro-Tip: Perplexity allows queries to use all of those sources and more. (no, this isn’t paid)
When to Use
Use RAG for semantically loaded information, company materials (when allowed), knowledge base summaries, or real-time internet searches. While RAG may be less creative or occasionally miss content, the improved accuracy is worth it for certain use cases.
For example: Spend 10 minutes researching a company for interviews so you drop insightful details and be remembered as as stand-out candidate.
Important Note: RAG quality depends on document structure, organization, source accuracy, prompt clarity, context window size (Claude’s is the best), and the randomness of LLM’s.

Prompt Engineering Techniques

Few-Shot Prompting
Provide a few examples in the model and ask it to match the format/tone or ask it to draw inspiration from them.
When to use: If you need consistent formatting or creative ideation on information not in the training data.
Chain-of-Thought
Ask the AI to explain its thought process step-by-step, or follow a series of detailed instructions doing so, instead of jumping straight to the answer (seen above a few times).
When to use: When you need accurate reasoning for problem solving, if you keep getting surface-level outputs, or to mimic the “reasoning” of advanced models.
Prompt Chaining
Breaking one big task into smaller conversations, each built context/prompts that optimize that specific step so the output of one conversation builds on the previous.
When to use: You’re trying to uplevel to the “AI is a Chain of Super-Powered Personas”, you’re trying to test automated workflows, or creatively explore lines of thought/production efficiently using AI.
Extra Techniques I Personally Learned

Iterative Prompting
Prompt engineering requires trial and error, web searches, and creative exploration. This skill takes weeks to months to develop, so keep practicing and be patient with yourself
Just enough Context
The goal of prompting is to provide the right context for the model to solve your problem, not to dump as many words as possible into the model to make it “learn”. For smaller tasks, this may mean  you limit the prompt to 20 words while other tasks require robust agents with persistent context.
Use Weird Formatting/Characters
LLM training data is mostly plain text. Special characters (!@#$%^&*) and ALL CAPS are rare, giving them stronger semantic weight which makes it helpful when emphasizing critical requirements.
For example: **[MY PRIMARY GOALS OFTEN LOOK LIKE THIS]**
Limitations Beyond this Article

RAG and “reasoning” in advanced models have mitigated typical LLM limitations like factual accuracy and critical thinking. The biggest remaining drawbacks are:
Context or Working Memory
LLMs fixed context windows cause reasoning errors, hallucinations, and inability to retrieve all relevant data. Humans have superior working memory that improves by chunking tasks or   or various learning techniques.

Solution: Improve your prompting to match the model’s context. Provide examples. Use “Thinking” or “Reasoning” mode for self-reflection.

Learning
LLMs store some conversations and update through retraining, but don’t rebuild their architecture with each question like babies learning, or develop long-term memory like humans remembering preferences

Solution: Create persistent contexts (fancy term is “Agent”) with relevant information and prompts (with api protocols like real “agentic AI”) that don’t overload its context.

projects/uxr-blog/blog-db/🧭-thesis-state.title: Human×AI Augmented Decision Making: What It Actually Looks Like
projects/uxr-blog/blog-db/🧭-thesis-state.content:
**Blog Outline: Pickup Guide**
	This outline documents the full arc, section purposes, key sources, and writing notes so either Michael or OliverAI can pick this up cold and execute. The article builds off the "terrain of judgment" framing (both humans and AI make decisions) and settles on the pure interaction: humans using AI to make *better* decisions.
	**Narrative Arc:** Start simple → ground in science → end simple again
	**Core Shift:** From "What decisions can AI help me with?" → "How can AI help me *improve* this decision?"
	**Target Length:** 1,800-2,500 words
	**Tone:** Zen Asimov. Calm authority. Ideas-first.

---
## 🧭 Thesis Statement
Most people ask AI the wrong question. They ask "what can AI decide for me?" when they should ask "how can AI help me decide better?" That single reframe unlocks a fundamentally different relationship with the technology: one grounded in cognitive science, not hype.
---
## Section 1: The Terrain of Judgment (Opening, Simple)
**Purpose:** Ground the reader in a single, orienting idea: both humans and AI make decisions, but they do so on fundamentally different terrain. This is not a competition. It is a landscape.
**Key Points:**
- Open with a concrete, relatable scenario: you're halfway through a complex decision (hiring, prioritizing a roadmap, evaluating risk) and you ask AI for help. What happens next depends entirely on what question you ask.
- Introduce the "terrain of judgment" concept: human judgment operates on epistemological terrain shaped by experience, emotion, context, and cognitive shortcuts. AI operates on statistical terrain shaped by training data and pattern recognition.
- Neither terrain is complete. Both produce decisions. The interesting question is what happens when they overlap.
- **The reframe:** The conversation has been stuck on "AI vs. Human" decisions. This article settles on the pure interaction: humans using AI to make better decisions.
**Key Sources:**
- Hildebrandt, M. (2020). "Is Human Judgment Necessary? Artificial Intelligence, Algorithmic Governance, and the Law." *The Oxford Handbook of Ethics of AI.* (coined "epistemological terrain" concept for AI's effect on judgment)
- Bai, Y. et al. (2026). "In the Shadow of Judgment: Mapping Out the Landscape of Human-AI Decision-Making." Systematic review of 1,493 HAID articles. (establishes the landscape framing)
- Kahneman, D. et al. (2021). *Noise: A Flaw in Human Judgment.* (human judgment is noisy, not just biased)
**Writing Notes:**
- Keep this section SHORT. 300 words max. Enter the topic as close to the point as possible.
- The scenario should feel lived-in, not hypothetical. Use second person ("you").
- Do not define AI. The reader already knows. Start where they are.
---
## Section 2: The Wrong Question (Simple → Bridge)
**Purpose:** Name the default mental model most people use and show why it limits them. This is the "what decisions can AI help me with?" frame.
**Key Points:**
- Most people approach AI with a task-delegation mindset: "What can I hand off?" This is the Mental Model #1/2 trap from the Four Mental Models article. It works for low-stakes tasks but collapses for anything requiring judgment.
- The task-delegation frame produces a binary: either AI decides or I decide. This is a false choice rooted in automation anxiety.
- When you ask "what decisions can AI help me with?" you get a list of tasks. Lists don't improve thinking. They offload it.
- Briefly acknowledge this frame is useful for simple automation (scheduling, formatting, sorting). But the ceiling is low.
**Key Sources:**
- Pearson, J. (2026). "Examining human reliance on artificial intelligence in decision making." *Scientific Reports.* (how human cognition restricts human-AI interactions)
- Duncan, D. S. (2026). "How Do Workers Develop Good Judgment in the AI Era?" *Harvard Business Review.* (AI helped experienced workers more than novices because of judgment, not prompting skill)
- Internal reference: Four Mental Models That Transform How You Use AI  (Mental Models #1-2 as the "wrong question" territory)
**Writing Notes:**
- This is the "context before content" section. Show where the reader probably is before walking them forward.
- Use the HBR finding as a telling anecdote: AI helped the experienced consultant more because he had the judgment to evaluate its output. The tool didn't change. The human did.
- Avoid making the reader feel stupid. Frame this as the natural starting point, not a failure.
---
## Section 3: The Science of How Humans Actually Decide (Academic Grounding)
**Purpose:** This is the intellectual core. Ground the argument in established cognitive science so the reframe feels inevitable, not aspirational. Readers should understand *why* the second question works better.
**Key Points:**
- **Dual-process theory** (Kahneman, 2011): System 1 (fast, intuitive, heuristic) and System 2 (slow, deliberate, analytical). Most daily decisions are System 1. AI can serve as an external System 2 trigger, forcing deliberation on decisions that would otherwise default to autopilot.
- **Naturalistic Decision Making** (Klein, 1998): Experts don't weigh options analytically. They pattern-match from experience (Recognition-Primed Decision model). AI can surface patterns the expert hasn't encountered, expanding the recognition base without replacing it.
- **Cognitive biases as features, not bugs:** Anchoring, confirmation bias, availability heuristic. These aren't flaws to eliminate; they're shortcuts that evolved for speed. AI doesn't remove them. It can make them visible.
- **The judgment development problem:** Duncan (2026) in HBR raises a critical tension: if AI handles the reps that build judgment, how do workers develop it? This is the "epistemological terrain" shift Hildebrandt warned about. The answer matters for how we design the interaction.
**Key Sources:**
- Kahneman, D. (2011). *Thinking, Fast and Slow.* (dual-process theory foundation)
- Klein, G. (1998). *Sources of Power: How People Make Decisions.* (naturalistic decision making, RPD model)
- Tversky, A. & Kahneman, D. (1974). "Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases." *Science.* (foundational heuristics)
- Spiess, J. & McLaughlin, B. (2024). "Complementarity in human-AI interaction." Stanford GSB. (framework for how humans respond to algorithmic recommendations)
- Duncan, D. S. (2026). HBR. (judgment development tension)
- Hildebrandt, M. (2020). Oxford Handbook. (epistemological terrain displacement)
**Writing Notes:**
- This is the densest section but should NOT read like a textbook. Use the "miniaturist" principle: narrow focus, vivid specifics.
- Each concept gets ONE paragraph with ONE concrete example. No exhaustive literature dumps.
- The reader should finish this section thinking: "Okay, so human decision making is pattern-based, shortcut-heavy, and context-dependent. AI is pattern-based, data-heavy, and context-agnostic. The interaction between these two systems is where the value lives."
- Target: 500-700 words.
---
## Section 4: The Right Question (Bridge → Simple)
**Purpose:** Introduce the reframe: "How can AI help me *improve* this decision?" Show why this question unlocks fundamentally different behaviors.
**Key Points:**
- The shift from "what" to "how" changes the unit of analysis from *tasks* to *decisions*. Tasks are discrete. Decisions are contextual, recursive, and often invisible.
- "How can AI help improve this decision?" presupposes you remain the decision-maker. AI becomes infrastructure for better judgment, not a replacement for it.
- This question opens three cognitive doors:
	1. **Expanding the frame:** AI surfaces options, data, or perspectives you didn't consider (addresses availability heuristic, narrow framing)
	2. **Stress-testing assumptions:** AI acts as a Socratic partner, challenging anchors and confirmation bias (connects to Mental Model #4)
	3. **Making the invisible visible:** AI externalizes reasoning steps that normally stay implicit, forcing deliberation where autopilot usually wins
- This is the "complementarity" model from Stanford GSB: the best AI system accounts for how humans will interact with its output. The best human accounts for what AI can and cannot see.
**Key Sources:**
- Spiess & McLaughlin (2024). Stanford GSB complementarity framework.
- "Augmenting Human Cognition with Generative AI for Informed Decision-Making" (Turning Data Into Wisdom blog, practitioner synthesis of Socratic questioning, counterargument generation, bias identification)
- CMU AI-SDM Cognitive AI research (behavioral models of decision making, human-AI hybrid teams)
**Writing Notes:**
- This is the turn. The energy should shift from analytical to practical. The reader should feel the reframe land.
- Use a mirrored scenario from Section 1: same decision, but now the person asks the right question. Show the different outcome.
- The three cognitive doors should feel like a framework the reader can immediately apply. Bold them. Make them scannable.
---
## Section 5: What This Looks Like in Practice (Simple, Concrete)
**Purpose:** Make it real. Show 2-3 concrete examples of augmented decision making using the "how" question. End with practical takeaways the reader can use today.
**Key Points:**
- **Example 1: Hiring decision.** Instead of "AI, rank these candidates," ask "What am I likely missing in how I'm evaluating these candidates?" AI surfaces that you're anchored on pedigree signals. You adjust your rubric.
- **Example 2: Product prioritization.** Instead of "AI, prioritize this backlog," ask "What assumptions am I making about user value that might be wrong?" AI identifies that three top-priority items all serve the same persona while another segment is ignored.
- **Example 3: Strategic research.** Instead of "AI, summarize these findings," ask "Where does my interpretation of this data conflict with alternative explanations?" AI generates three competing hypotheses from the same dataset.
- **The pattern:** Each example follows the same structure: human has a decision → asks AI to improve the *process* of deciding, not the decision itself → human makes a better-informed choice.
**Writing Notes:**
- Keep examples tight. 100-150 words each. Vivid specificity over generality.
- At least one example should resonate with UX/research practitioners (the core audience).
- Do NOT make this a prompt engineering tutorial. The focus is the *cognitive shift*, not the tooling.
---
## Section 6: The Expanding Frontier (Closing, Simple)
**Purpose:** Close the loop. Connect the reframe back to the terrain of judgment. Point toward dynamic learning: as you practice the "how" question, your judgment improves alongside AI's capabilities.
**Key Points:**
- The "how" question creates a feedback loop: better questions → better AI output → better pattern recognition → even better questions. This is dynamic learning, not static tool use.
- This resolves Duncan's HBR tension: AI doesn't erode judgment when you use it to *exercise* judgment rather than bypass it. The reps still happen. They just happen differently.
- Return to the terrain metaphor: the landscape of human-AI decision making is not fixed. Every interaction reshapes the terrain for the next decision. The goal is not to map the terrain once. It is to become a better navigator.
- **Final line direction:** Something simple, grounded, forward-looking. Not a call-to-action. A quiet landing.
**Writing Notes:**
- 200-300 words max. End clean. Don't overstay.
- The feedback loop idea is the "connect specific to global" moment. One reframed question scales to a fundamentally different relationship with AI.
- Resist the urge to predict the future. Stay grounded in what works now.
---

	## Full Source Library
	**Academic / Peer-Reviewed:**
	- Kahneman, D. (2011). *Thinking, Fast and Slow.* Farrar, Straus and Giroux.
	- Kahneman, D., Sibony, O., & Sunstein, C. R. (2021). *Noise: A Flaw in Human Judgment.* Little, Brown Spark.
	- Klein, G. (1998). *Sources of Power: How People Make Decisions.* MIT Press.
	- Tversky, A. & Kahneman, D. (1974). Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases. *Science, 185*(4157), 1124-1131.
	- Hildebrandt, M. (2020). Is Human Judgment Necessary? *The Oxford Handbook of Ethics of AI.* Oxford University Press.
	- Bai, Y. et al. (2026). In the Shadow of Judgment: Mapping Out the Landscape of Human-AI Decision-Making. Systematic review (1,493 articles, 2016-2024).
	- Pearson, J. (2026). Examining human reliance on artificial intelligence in decision making. *Scientific Reports.*

	- Augmenting Human Cognition with Generative AI for Informed Decision-Making. *Turning Data Into Wisdom.*

projects/uxr-blog/content-direction-(08d.title: Content Direction
projects/uxr-blog/content-direction-(08d.content:
**This page is the single source of truth for the direction I want my blog content to push the larger UX conversation.** OliverAI reads this page during the Blog Ideation automation to align topic suggestions with my current strategic intent. Update this page anytime my thinking evolves. Say "update my content direction" to edit it in conversation.

---
## Current Landscape Themes (October 2026; re-verify before citing)
- AI-assisted analysis is the #1 self-reported trend: 88% name it the top trend impacting UX (NN/g State of UX 2026); 80% of researchers use AI tools, +24pp YoY (User Interviews). Unanswered: no published protocol for judging AI-assisted analysis quality.
- "UX evals" is becoming a name (Outset, [uxuiprinciples.com](uxuiprinciples.com), Microsoft's UXR org), but only vendor-side. No independent, open, evidence-based practitioner methodology exists yet.
- Synthetic users are mainstream and contested: 47% of researchers skeptical, 62.7% of teams with zero guidance (User Interviews, State of Synthetic Users 2026). No published validation protocol.
- Trust in automation stays the field's abstract word; I hold measured enterprise thresholds (Ledger 1; no published equivalent).
- Judgment operationalization appears in job descriptions, undefined in public writing; "strategic research" likewise.
- AI fatigue; NN/g 2026: "design deeper to differentiate"; generative UI matches expert-designed work 44% of the time. Differentiation runs through demonstrated business impact: this blog's argument.
- Refresh rule: the weekly scan re-verifies each item; never recite a number forward without one scan verification.
- Registry upgrade (October 2026, in the cron briefs): venues add Judgment and Decision Making, Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, Nature Human Behaviour, Journal of Consumer Research, Behavioral & Brain Sciences (CHI, CSCW, JPSP, OBHDP, Psychological Science continue); practitioners add MeasuringU and UXmatters; canon clusters from My Niche tag academic rows at aggregation.
## How I Want to Shift the Conversation
The field has drifted: research became a validation service, confirming what product teams already decided to build rather than discovering what should exist. The blogosphere mirrors it, stuck in AI anxiety, identity hand-wringing, and tools fetishism.
One system claim ties the four shifts together: UX research is a subsystem of the product system, and the field drifts when its loops reward validation over discovery. The blog works the loop: measure quality at the seams, translate the science, publish frameworks openly, keep human decision making at the center.
1. **Research as a revenue driver.** UXR's generative function (discovering unmet needs, creating market categories) over validation service. Make research critical to software revenue, not a cost center confirming decisions already made.
2. **Science made usable.** The gap between academic cognitive/behavioral science and daily practice holds the most valuable content. I translate across it.
3. **Power to ICs and small teams.** Best tools give capability to individual contributors and small businesses, not enterprise hierarchies. Open frameworks, independent-practitioner-first design.
4. **Human decision making, fueled by HCI.** As AI reshapes products, stay anchored in how humans think, decide, and trust. Human Factors and cognitive psychology lead.
## My Niche
One sentence: **I apply an HCI + systems lens to UX research and to the software and product industry.** Shorter: **HCI-grade rigor, systems-grade reasoning, shipped as open artifacts.**
*The lens* means: HCI (cognitive psychology, decision science, human factors: how humans perceive, decide, trust, recover) plus systems thinking (feedback loops, incentives, coupling, debt: why good methods fail inside organizations). Research debt, validation-service drift, and quality gates are system interventions, not study topics; naming the broken loop is the blog's spine. Application surface: UXR's own operating system, plus the wider software industry now rebuilding workflows as human-agent systems: HCI's jurisdiction, publicly unclaimed.
Territory bullets (ideation gates on this):
1. Research as a system: loops, gates, debt, measurement (Ledger 3, 4)
2. Human-agent systems: agentic products, calibrated reliance, trust recovery (Ledger 1, 5, 7)
3. Synthetic-user validity (Ledger 2)
4. Enterprise AI in GRC (Ledger 6, 9, 10)
5. Framework translation: academic constructs into runnable tools (Ledger 4, 5, 8)
Readers: **Primary**: research leads and senior UXR ICs at B2B/enterprise software companies who suspect methods problems are systems problems. **Secondary**: product/design leaders building AI features who need the human-decision layer engineering evals lack (Lenny sells PMs the machine-side guide; its human side is a stub). Not the reader: UX beginners, tool shoppers, consumer-trend collectors, "AI is killing UX" commentators.
**Academic canon (from the NAS textbook library; the pair this into every brief):**
- **Survey science**: Groves's Total Survey Error, Dillman's Tailored Design Method, the Oxford polling handbook: the formal floor under all survey/synthetic data claims.

- **Experimental craft + Bayesian inference**: Kohavi's Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments; Gelman's BDA, Lee/Wagenmakers Bayesian cognitive modeling: launch gates and modeled judgment.
- **Computational sociology/economics + consumer psychology + behavioral economics**: modeled social systems and the demand-side lens (the library's largest shelf).

## Current Landscape Themes (October 2026; re-verify before citing)
- AI-assisted analysis is the #1 self-reported trend: 88% name it the top trend impacting UX (NN/g State of UX 2026); 80% of researchers use AI tools, +24pp YoY (User Interviews). Unanswered: no published protocol for judging AI-assisted analysis quality.
- "UX evals" is becoming a name (Outset, [uxuiprinciples.com](uxuiprinciples.com), Microsoft's UXR org), but only vendor-side. No independent, open, evidence-based practitioner methodology exists yet.
- Synthetic users are mainstream and contested: 47% of researchers skeptical, 62.7% of teams with zero guidance (User Interviews, State of Synthetic Users 2026). No published validation protocol.
- Trust in automation stays the field's abstract word; I hold measured enterprise thresholds (Ledger 1; no published equivalent).
- Judgment operationalization appears in job descriptions, undefined in public writing; "strategic research" likewise.
- AI fatigue; NN/g 2026: "design deeper to differentiate"; generative UI matches expert-designed work 44% of the time. Differentiation runs through demonstrated business impact: this blog's argument.
- Refresh rule: the weekly scan re-verifies each item; never recite a number forward without one scan verification.
- Registry upgrade (October 2026, in the cron briefs): venues add Judgment and Decision Making, Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, Nature Human Behaviour, Journal of Consumer Research, Behavioral & Brain Sciences (CHI, CSCW, JPSP, OBHDP, Psychological Science continue); practitioners add MeasuringU and UXmatters; canon clusters from My Niche tag academic rows at aggregation.
## How I Want to Shift the Conversation
The field has drifted: research became a validation service, confirming what product teams already decided to build rather than discovering what should exist. The blogosphere mirrors it, stuck in AI anxiety, identity hand-wringing, and tools fetishism.
One system claim ties the four shifts together: UX research is a subsystem of the product system, and the field drifts when its loops reward validation over discovery. The blog works the loop: measure quality at the seams, translate the science, publish frameworks openly, keep human decision making at the center.
1. **Research as a revenue driver.** UXR's generative function (discovering unmet needs, creating market categories) over validation service. Make research critical to software revenue, not a cost center confirming decisions already made.
2. **Science made usable.** The gap between academic cognitive/behavioral science and daily practice holds the most valuable content. I translate across it.
3. **Power to ICs and small teams.** Best tools give capability to individual contributors and small businesses, not enterprise hierarchies. Open frameworks, independent-practitioner-first design.
4. **Human decision making, fueled by HCI.** As AI reshapes products, stay anchored in how humans think, decide, and trust. Human Factors and cognitive psychology lead.
## My Niche

Application surface: UXR's own operating system, plus the wider software industry now rebuilding workflows as human-agent systems: HCI's jurisdiction, publicly unclaimed.

4. Enterprise AI in GRC (Ledger 6, 9, 10)

## Current Landscape Themes (October 2026; re-verify before citing)
- AI-assisted analysis is the #1 self-reported trend: 88% name it the top trend impacting UX (NN/g State of UX 2026); 80% of researchers use AI tools, +24pp YoY (User Interviews). Unanswered: no published protocol for judging AI-assisted analysis quality.
- "UX evals" is becoming a name (Outset, [uxuiprinciples.com](uxuiprinciples.com), Microsoft's UXR org), but only vendor-side. No independent, open, evidence-based practitioner methodology exists yet.
- Synthetic users are mainstream and contested: 47% of researchers skeptical, 62.7% of teams with zero guidance (User Interviews, State of Synthetic Users 2026). No published validation protocol.
- Trust in automation stays the field's abstract word; I hold measured enterprise thresholds (Ledger 1; no published equivalent).
- Judgment operationalization appears in job descriptions, undefined in public writing; "strategic research" likewise.
- AI fatigue; NN/g 2026: "design deeper to differentiate"; generative UI matches expert-designed work 44% of the time. Differentiation runs through demonstrated business impact: this blog's argument.
- Refresh rule: the weekly scan re-verifies each item; never recite a number forward without one scan verification.
- Registry upgrade (October 2026, in the cron briefs): venues add Judgment and Decision Making, Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, Nature Human Behaviour, Journal of Consumer Research, Behavioral & Brain Sciences (CHI, CSCW, JPSP, OBHDP, Psychological Science continue); practitioners add MeasuringU and UXmatters; canon clusters from My Niche tag academic rows at aggregation.
## How I Want to Shift the Conversation
The field has drifted: research became a validation service, confirming what product teams already decided to build rather than discovering what should exist. The blogosphere mirrors it, stuck in AI anxiety, identity hand-wringing, and tools fetishism.
One system claim ties the four shifts together: UX research is a subsystem of the product system, and the field drifts when its loops reward validation over discovery. The blog works the loop: measure quality at the seams, translate the science, publish frameworks openly, keep human decision making at the center.
1. **Research as a revenue driver.** UXR's generative function (discovering unmet needs, creating market categories) over validation service. Make research critical to software revenue, not a cost center confirming decisions already made.
2. **Science made usable.** The gap between academic cognitive/behavioral science and daily practice holds the most valuable content. I translate across it.
3. **Power to ICs and small teams.** Best tools give capability to individual contributors and small businesses, not enterprise hierarchies. Open frameworks, independent-practitioner-first design.
4. **Human decision making, fueled by HCI.** As AI reshapes products, stay anchored in how humans think, decide, and trust. Human Factors and cognitive psychology lead.
## My Niche
One sentence: **I apply an HCI + systems lens to UX research and to the software and product industry.** Shorter: **HCI-grade rigor, systems-grade reasoning, shipped as open artifacts.**
*The lens* means: HCI (cognitive psychology, decision science, human factors: how humans perceive, decide, trust, recover) plus systems thinking (feedback loops, incentives, coupling, debt: why good methods fail inside organizations). Research debt, validation-service drift, and quality gates are system interventions, not study topics; naming the broken loop is the blog's spine. Application surface: UXR's own operating system, plus the wider software industry now rebuilding workflows as human-agent systems: HCI's jurisdiction, publicly unclaimed.
Territory bullets (ideation gates on this):
1. Research as a system: loops, gates, debt, measurement (Ledger 3, 4)
2. Human-agent systems: agentic products, calibrated reliance, trust recovery (Ledger 1, 5, 7)
3. Synthetic-user validity (Ledger 2)
4. Enterprise AI in GRC (Ledger 6, 9, 10)
5. Framework translation: academic constructs into runnable tools (Ledger 4, 5, 8)
Readers: **Primary**: research leads and senior UXR ICs at B2B/enterprise software companies who suspect methods problems are systems problems. **Secondary**: product/design leaders building AI features who need the human-decision layer engineering evals lack (Lenny sells PMs the machine-side guide; its human side is a stub). Not the reader: UX beginners, tool shoppers, consumer-trend collectors, "AI is killing UX" commentators.
**Academic canon (from the NAS textbook library; the pair this into every brief):**
- **Survey science**: Groves's Total Survey Error, Dillman's Tailored Design Method, the Oxford polling handbook: the formal floor under all survey/synthetic data claims.
- **Agent-based social science**: Epstein's Generative Social Science and Agent Zero, Growing Artificial Societies, the ODD reporting protocol: a 20-year validation tradition for simulated agents, unknown to the UXR blogosphere: the sharpest academic counter to synthetic-user hype and panic.
- **Psychometrics of ability**: WAIS-IV, Woodcock-Johnson IV, Stanford-Binet manuals: instruments built on reliability, norms, and validity: where the measurement habit comes from.
- **Experimental craft + Bayesian inference**: Kohavi's Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments; Gelman's BDA, Lee/Wagenmakers Bayesian cognitive modeling: launch gates and modeled judgment.
- **Computational sociology/economics + consumer psychology + behavioral economics**: modeled social systems and the demand-side lens (the library's largest shelf).
- **Knowledge management and organizational innovation** (Dalkir, Oxford organizational handbooks): the systems lens in org life.
- **Consciousness and philosophy of mind** (Tononi's IIT, Koch, Chalmers): the far boundary of what can be simulated: depth no AI-evals writer brings.
Winnable: the lens combination is unclaimed in the UXR blogosphere (October 2026 check: research debt, tool ecosystems, AI workflow redesign stay anecdotal, single-loop, vendor-driven); 51% of researchers learn through blogs (UI 2025); enterprise/B2B is the blind spot and my daily seat. Every post maps to one shift and one territory, or it goes back.
## My Voice
zen Asimov clarity through Economist/FT rigor. Calm, unhurried, committed, evidence-first, dry wit sparingly. Explain hard things in plain words, hide the effort. First person for hard-won experience, second person for guidance. Commit; no false balance. Ideas first, ego absent.
Non-negotiables (edit stage enforces every one):
- Zero em dashes, ever (U+2014). Commas, periods, colons, or parentheses carry the break.
- Never "It's not X. It's Y." or any cousin of that construction, written-out or contracted.
- Banned words: leverage, unlock, supercharge, game-changer, journey, robust (say strong), synergy, delve, tapestry, delight, best-in-class. Banned openers: "In today's rapidly evolving landscape", "Let's dive in", "it's worth noting".
- Active voice. Vary rhythm: short for impact, longer for explanation, never three long in a row. No paragraph over six lines.
- Headers are claims, not labels. Thesis inside the first 150 words. Close on a reframe, then a one-line punch. No summary paragraph.
- Every claim carries evidence, a mechanism, or a labeled first-person receipt. No invented numbers, sources, or quotes. Unverified material gets qualified or cut.
- No invented terms (Michael's standing order, 2026-10-16; protects the voice): use established field vocabulary. Define a necessary concept in plain words inside the same sentence. A coined label posing as established terminology fails the audit. Names attach only to shipped artifacts (real names, e.g. the 80/100 gate in the Ledger); future-name proposals are labeled "proposed" and never used as if established.
Signature moves (two to four per piece, never all at once): the flat opener; steelman then pivot; the named-source claim with the mechanism; the receipt (first-person system or failure, told plainly); the one-line punch close; the reframe; the definition in passing.
Full prose spec: the `michael-oliver-voice` skill (`skills/voice/voice-michael-oliver/SKILL.md`). On prose mechanics the skill wins; this file wins on strategic intent.

New rows: from the Career Projects DB or this profile's verified findings, opened and read first; numbers verbatim, never strengthened. This is the single home of personal numbers; other sections link to rows.

What the 73% drop gets wrong about the UX research job market

Illustration: a researcher checks the evidence while colleagues carry the work elsewhere.
UX research job postings fell 73 percent from their 2022 peak, and the field keeps writing its own obituary from that number [1]. The arithmetic is accurate; the obituary misreads it.
Picture a composite drawn from the survey data: a staff researcher who has survived two layoff rounds and now makes up her entire team. Product managers at her company now run their own studies. She fields more research requests than ever and has less say over the quality of the evidence behind them.
Fewer seats and higher hiring bars are changing what companies pay for when they pay for research. The cuts look rational on a quarterly statement because the savings appear the day a seat disappears. The cost shows up years later, when products built on weaker evidence miss their targets and need rework, usually after the people who approved the cut have moved on.
What lasts is judgment about the business decisions that drive revenue: where the data behind each decision came from and whether it can support the bet. When a company keeps that record of provenance, each team can build on the research that came before it instead of paying to relearn it. That judgment is the job worth holding.
The 73 percent drop left UX research above its 2018 baseline
The 73 percent figure comes from Indeed’s design team, which indexed UX research postings against a Q1 2018 baseline of 100. The line peaked at 566 in Q1 2022 and fell to 153 by Q2 2023 [1]. UX design fell from 265 to 77 over the same span, ending below its own baseline [1].

UX research and UX design job postings, indexed to Q1 2018 (Indeed Design).
Measured against design, research grew more common over the decade. For every 100 design postings there were 8.9 research postings in 2013 and 33.2 in 2023 [1]. Postings have held flat since then, with research above its baseline while design and engineering sat below theirs [3].
Even at its 2023 low, research sat above where it started in 2018. The death notices took one 2023 snapshot and treated it as a 2026 trend.
Research demand rose while research jobs did not
Surveys of practitioners point the other way. Maze’s 2026 report, fielded to about 500 practitioners, found 66 percent reporting increased research demand, up from 55 percent a year earlier [2]. The share calling research essential at every level of strategy rose from 8 to 22 percent in a single year [2].
These surveys count a particular group. The User Interviews sample of 485 researchers has shrunk 36 percent since 2024, and its authors warn that it may describe only researchers who still have jobs [4]. Demand surveys and job counts describe different people, and the gap between them is simple to state: more teams want research, but fewer people get paid to do it.
Product managers, designers, and marketers absorbed the work
The research still gets done, mostly by people outside the field. NN/g calls this group “people who do research”: people without the title, and mostly without the training [5]. Product managers do research in 39 percent of organizations, market researchers in 35, and marketers in 23 [2]. Only 45 percent of organizations give them specialist support, and nearly 14 percent now employ no dedicated researcher at all, up from 6 percent in 2022 [2][4].
The research function came apart along its seams, and each piece went to the team that sat closest to it. Product managers took discovery, designers took usability testing, market research took surveys, and data science took behavioral data [6]. Nobody took the judgment that once connected those pieces.
The hiring data fits the same picture. Across 72 million applications, applicants per posting doubled from 46 to 95 while the hiring rate fell to 2.8 percent, and companies filled 62 percent of roles internally [7]. Pay stays high for those who are hired: 67 percent of employed US UX researchers earn over $100K [8]. High pay and few openings, filled mostly from inside, describe a rationed job.
Finance executives say they would trade long-term value for a steady quarter
The people who approve these budgets have described how they decide. Graham, Harvey, and Rajgopal surveyed 401 financial executives for the National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER), the nonpartisan research group best known for dating US recessions [9]. Seventy-eight percent said they would give up economic value to smooth earnings, meaning they would accept a smaller payoff over time in exchange for steady, predictable profit each quarter. Fifty-five percent would pass on a clearly profitable project rather than miss the quarter’s forecast [9].
Those answers describe a simple rule. When a return arrives late, cutting the spending behind it costs nothing in the current quarter. Research quality pays out late, and no line on the quarterly report records it.
NN/g found the same pattern in UX budgets. Leaders funded the roles easiest to justify financially, and UX “often struggled to defend itself with simple, direct metrics” [10]. The economist William Lazonick calls the broader system downsize-and-distribute: firms shrink staff and pay most earnings out to shareholders [11]. Under that system, the first cuts land on work whose value shows up years later.
Bell Labs and Xerox PARC were funded outside the quarterly cycle
Bell Labs is the clearest exception. It operated inside AT&T’s regulated monopoly, with 3,000 PhDs, roughly $1.6 billion a year, and research horizons of up to twenty years [12][13]. It produced nine Nobel Prizes [14]. Xerox PARC had similar freedom and a different outcome. Its Alto, built in 1973 with a graphical interface, a mouse, and Ethernet, never reached the market, and Apple and Microsoft later built businesses on those ideas [15].
Research with a long time horizon needs patient money and a direct link to the decisions it should inform. Bell Labs had the patient money. PARC had the money but no link to a Xerox business that could sell its inventions. Most research teams today have neither.
Sony’s cuts show the bill arrives three to seven years later
From 2000 to 2002, Sony cut its workforce 11 percent, R&D 12 percent, and capital spending 23 percent [16]. Its profit margin rose from 8 to 12 percent. Over the following years, sales growth fell from 11 percent to 1, and rivals took categories Sony had pioneered [16].
Sony’s experience matches a larger sample. Across 4,700 companies that went through recessions, Gulati, Nohria, and Wohlgezogen found that the deepest cutters had a 21 percent chance of leading their markets afterward. Firms that cut selectively while protecting R&D and marketing had a 37 percent chance, in part because they “stay closely connected to customer needs” [16].
Three measurements explain the timing. Pakes and Schankerman found that the value a firm captures from a finding decays about 25 percent a year when nobody replaces it, and that spending takes 1.2 to 2.6 years to reach revenue [17]. Executive tenure is short by comparison: S&P 500 chief marketing officers average 4.1 years in the role, and chief operating officers average 3.3 [18].

Research value under 25 percent annual decay, with average executive tenure marked.
Combined, these figures put the visible loss three to seven years after a cut. By year three, an unreplaced research asset has lost more than half its value, and the executive who approved the cut has often left. No single study makes this claim; I assembled it from the three measured parts.
Untrained researchers make different mistakes than specialists
The strongest objection to this argument is that the work does not need a specialist. NN/g itself holds that “even imperfect user research is usually much better than no research at all” [5]. Specialists also disagree with each other. Jacobsen, Hertzum, and John gave four trained evaluators the same usability sessions [19]. Of 93 problems found, only 20 percent appeared on every evaluator’s list, and 46 percent appeared on just one [19]. Eleven later studies found the same pattern [20].
Researchers call this the evaluator effect, and it differs from bias. When trained evaluators disagree, their misses fall in different places. An untrained interviewer who asks leading questions, recruits the wrong users, or confirms what the team already planned makes errors that all point the same way, toward the decision the team wanted [5]. Several imperfect readings that miss in different directions are safer than one reading that leans.
Cutting junior roles also removed the path that produced senior judgment [4]. Constantine Papas puts it this way: “A discipline that removes its own training positions does not get its next generation back” [6]. Democratization works when it comes with instruments and mentoring, and when a trained researcher still reviews the evidence.
Over 40 percent of companies never talk to their users, and it shows in revenue
Many companies have none of those supports. McKinsey’s design study, which tracked 300 public companies over five years, shows the cost [21]. More than 40 percent never talked to end users during development, and just over half had no objective way to assess their design output. Companies in the top quartile for design measurement posted 32 points more revenue growth and 56 points more shareholder return than their peers [21].
Closing that gap requires someone who can judge whether a finding is strong enough for the decision attached to it. I made a related case about AI tools in Why UX Researchers Undertrust AI Synthesis: people discount any analysis, human or machine, when they cannot see what it rests on.
Own the gate: the part of research nobody can hand out
The role that survives these cuts is a research quality gate. It has three duties: define what counts as evidence, run the instruments that measure it, and sit in the launch decision with the authority to stop a release that falls short.
I ran one. At AuditBoard in 2024, our usability benchmarking program completed each wave in four weeks, where the ad hoc studies it replaced took six to eight. Directors wrote an 80 out of 100 usability score into the launch requirements, and products below that score waited for more evidence. Our AI Measurement Library gave non-specialists standard survey and interview instruments for grading AI products against the same bar.
The scores became a gate only after someone with launch authority agreed to enforce them. Research sets the standard and an executive applies it; my job was to connect the two.
For executives deciding which seats to keep, the recession data already favors the firms that stayed close to customers [16]. A quality gate puts research quality into the launch review as a number leaders can track.
The 73 percent drop describes a reorganization. Demand for research is rising, dedicated seats are falling, and every organization doing research needs someone who owns the call on whether the evidence can support a revenue decision. I turned that gate into a one-page checklist of five questions, covering origin, instrument, reach, variance, and authority. It appears below.

After: either someone staffs the gate, or the pieces ship unchecked.

Foreground left: researcher at a lamp-lit desk with loupe, index cards, charts. Midground: PM, designer, marketer each carrying a puzzle piece. Right: empty turnstile gate, then a bright doorway. Background: dim empty desks, dusk skyline.

Quiet tension and resolve. Loupe = judgment of evidence quality. Puzzle pieces = unbundled research. Empty turnstile = the unstaffed quality gate. Glowing door = launch decision.

First the researcher and loupe, second the scattered pieces, last the empty gate and door. Detached, elevated three-quarter view.

First the researcher and loupe, second the scattered pieces, last the empty gate and door. Detached, elevated three-quarter view.

projects/uxr-blog/random-blog-newsletter.title: Random Blog/Newsletter Ideas
projects/uxr-blog/random-blog-newsletter.content:
Weekend Recipes
Dune Newsletter
History of our Modern World Blog Articles
Potential Newsletter Topics
# Types of Blogs / Articles

### **Reporting**
Newsletters with a **journalistic lens** are currently one of the most popular categories. These publications can be run either by a solo writer or a team of creators. Publishing frequency tends to be on the higher side, with the majority publishing anything from a few articles a week to a few per day.
The value proposition for reporting newsletters is often a unique viewpoint or exclusive coverage readers can't find anywhere else. One of the best examples from this space is [The Information](www.theinformation.com/) which positions itself as offering "Tech news you won't read elsewhere."
- Tacoma Local News: Cover key stories in Tacoma, WA, focusing on community events, politics, and developments.
- Sustainability Updates: Report on green initiatives and climate policies across the Pacific Northwest.
- Tech Innovations Digest: Weekly reports on the latest developments in AI, biotech, and software.
- Art in Tacoma: Highlight art exhibits, theater shows, and local artist spotlights in Tacoma.
### **Analysis**
Analysis newsletters are typically run by narrowly defined **subject-matter experts**. Their content is often long-form, includes charts or graphs, and presents an opinionated take on the topic at hand. Readers can expect to receive these weekly or even monthly due to the research required for each edition.
Subscribers seek out analysis publications most often to help them succeed in their professional lives. A well-known model of this type is Nathan Tankus’ [Notes on the Crises](www.crisesnotes.com/), which runs on Ghost and “covers the play by play of the current pandemic-induced global depression and how policymakers should respond.”
- Real Estate Trends: Provide deep dives into housing market trends and investment opportunities in Tacoma.
- Economics Explained: Analyze major economic policies and their impacts globally.
- Sports Strategy Insights: Detailed breakdowns of strategies used in popular sports, from football to eSports.
- Local History Unveiled: Historical analysis of Tacoma's growth, industries, and cultural shifts.
### **Curation**
Curated newsletters are one of the fastest-growing types. As the volume of content on the internet continues to grow exponentially, tastemakers who can help readers **sort through the noise** are finding themselves in high demand.
Curators generally offer subscribers a shortlist of topic-focused links along with a brief summary of each one. For example, [Publisher Weekly](ghost.org/resources/) sends a weekly email containing “the most important stories, ideas & resources about independent publishing.”
- Tacoma Weekend Picks: Curate the best events, restaurants, and activities in Tacoma each weekend.
- Bookish Bytes: Weekly book recommendations and literary news.
- Tech & Tools Roundup: Curated list of the latest tools, software, and articles for professionals.
- Design Digest: Inspiring visual designs and resources for creatives.
- Writer’s Corner: A personal take on creative writing, with essays, poetry, and prompts.
### **Artistic**
Maria Popova’s [Brain Pickings](www.brainpickings.org/) is a model for personality-driven artistic newsletters. These types tend to be built around a single creator where the main value given to readers is the **creator's unique perspective**. Popova uses their publication to “explore what it means to live a decent, substantive, rewarding life.”
The embedded individuality of these newsletters means that there is a wide range of publishing frequencies, content lengths, and value offerings. These are one of the most flexible types since they rely on the creator’s persona for direction.
- The Visual Vault: Artistic newsletters featuring curated photography and art pieces with commentary.
- Brain Food Tacoma: Share philosophy and deep thoughts from Tacoma writers and thinkers.
- Music Moments: Focus on indie artists and music reviews, paired with local concert announcements.
### **Practical**
Practical newsletters have one of the most straightforward value propositions for readers: subscribe to **learn how to do *x***. Whereas many of the previously mentioned types focus on detailed explanations or theories, practical types focus on utility.
Both content length and frequency depend on the newsletter subject, but weekly, shorter editions are standard practice in the space. [The Spirits](thespirits.substack.com/) is a practical example that calls itself “a book club but for cocktails.” In each edition, subscribers are sent a cocktail recipe, directions on how to make it, and tips for elevating the experience.
- Tacoma Foodie Guide: Weekly recipes, restaurant reviews, and grocery deals in Tacoma.
- Productivity Hacks: Tips for optimizing time, projects, and goals.
- Gardening in Tacoma: A guide to growing plants in Tacoma’s climate with seasonal advice.
- Learn Something New: Weekly tutorials on varied topics, from knitting to coding.
### Hybrid
The final newsletter type to consider is a hybrid model. These publications combine the best elements from any of the other types in order to create something truly unique.
[Sinocism](sinocism.com/), a newsletter on China, offers readers an element from almost every single type mentioned: “analysis, commentary, occasional original reporting and curated links of Chinese and English language news.”
Those interested in the hybrid model must remember not to overwhelm their readers with content since the boundaries of each newsletter type are a key element of their success.
### **Time-sensitive**
[Steph Smith](blog.stephsmith.io/) introduced the idea of a pop-up newsletter as one “created to document a particular occasion.” Smith lists examples such as the [SXSW](www.sxsw.com/conference/) annual conference newsletter or VICE’s [The Mail](www.vice.com/en/topic/the-mail), which sprang up to cover a tumultuous season of the USPS.
Time-sensitive newsletters work well when paired with ongoing publications or businesses so that the audience remains connected after the event-driven newsletter has ende
